Title: Your agent's prompt is one layer, not the whole system
Description: Emerson Braun of Plan A Technologies at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026 splits agent reliability into six layers so a fix lands in the right one.
Body:
When an agent misbehaves, the first reflex is to open the prompt and add another sentence. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, Emerson Braun, Staff Engineer and Regional Director at Plan A Technologies, argued that the prompt is only one part of the design, and that a reliable agent needs context, contracts, outputs, retries and evals that live outside it.

His case study is small and relatable: a content pipeline he built for his own posts on X and LinkedIn. Threads published, the blog post went out, the newsletter got scheduled. Then one post was saved as an empty draft. He fixed the prompt, as everyone would, and then realised the prompt wasn't where the bug lived.

## Your agent is perfectly designed to get the result it gets

Emerson borrows the old systems-thinking line that every system is perfectly designed to get the result it gets, and points it at agents. If brand rules, approval policy, "don't post twice", output format and the draft-validate-publish steps all sit in one prompt, then a failure gives you no idea which of those layers broke. Everything is an instruction, and every instruction is a polite guess.

So he splits the work into six layers: context, contract, output, retries, the prompt itself, and evals. Each one gets its own diagnostic question.

## Context is an input, so version it

The first failure he describes is stale context. The agent was told to follow the brand guide and it did, faithfully, using version three, while marketing had shipped version four the week before. The prompt was fine. The input was wrong.

His fix is to treat context like any other input: record which version was loaded, when, and a hash, so you can reconstruct exactly what the agent saw. The question to ask is whether the agent had the right information and whether it was current.

## If the tool allows it, the prompt doesn't forbid it

"Never publish without approval" is a sentence. A publish tool that accepts any call is a capability. When the two disagree, the capability wins. Emerson tiers actions by risk: low-risk reads, searches and classification run alone; reversible actions run within policy limits and with enough record to reconstruct them; high-impact actions such as deletes go to a human. And the human needs the impact and the context of the decision in front of them, not a random ID and an approve button.

## The empty draft was a correct refusal

The empty post turned out to be the model doing the right thing. The draft was requested for another brand's account, the model refused, and the pipeline saved the refusal as an empty draft. The real bug was that nothing checked the output against a contract. Emerson's rule: parse and validate model output the way you'd validate a third-party API, and when it doesn't match, record why.

## Failure is a state, and retries need a key

Retries get the same treatment. A timeout on "publish" followed by a blind retry is how you publish twice. He uses idempotency keys, a state machine that knows what to do after a failure, bounded retries that hand off to a dead letter queue or a person, and recovery that regenerates only the missing part instead of starting from scratch. Automate the recovery decisions, not the retries.

## Shrink the prompt, then judge the purpose

Once the rules move out into code, the prompt shrinks to its core: stable policy, task context, retrieved knowledge and user intent, kept separate. A good test for whether something belongs there: does the failure change when you change the words? If it does, it's a prompt problem. If not, look elsewhere.

His first eval run is the warning shot. Seven drafts, all checks green, and the drafts were still empty or written with the wrong context. The checks measured format, not purpose. He ends with six questions to ask before touching the prompt, one per layer, and a closing challenge: which of your rules lives only in a prompt?

## Who should watch

Anyone running an agent with real side effects (posting, merging, sending, deleting) who keeps patching the system prompt after every incident. It's a short, practical talk built around one honest failure, and the six questions are easy to steal for a postmortem template. If you want the observability half, Emerson points to his earlier Conf42 talk on tracing agents.

Title: Verify AI-written code inside the agent's loop, not at the gate
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, TestSprite co-founder Yunhao Jiao argues coding agents need runtime checks while they work, using the CoderCup experiment.
Body:
Security and quality gates were built for code arriving at human typing speed. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Yunhao Jiao, CEO and co-founder of TestSprite and a former AWS software engineer, argued that coding agents broke that assumption, and that the useful question is no longer whether to verify AI-written code but when. His answer: inside the agent's own loop, while it works, not at the pull request.

Honest scope first. TestSprite builds a testing agent, and the evidence in the talk comes from CoderCup, an experiment his company ran and open-sourced. Read it as a vendor's argument backed by its own data, which is still more data than most opinions on this topic arrive with.

## The gate cannot read what arrives

Jiao's starting point is volume. An agent can run for hours and produce thousands of lines at a time. He shows one PR from his own company with roughly 40,000 lines added and more than 50,000 removed, and asks the room whether anyone really reviews that by hand. Agents are also not reliably correct, and they lose track of requirements as long tasks overflow the context window, so constraints quietly drop out mid-build.

The industry response is to let machines check machines, and he walks through the weaknesses of each option. AI code review reads the code but usually does not run the app, so it misses runtime issues. Agent-written unit tests tend to reflect the code rather than the spec, so a wrong assumption gets tested as correct. Integration tests catch more, but only if something keeps running them.

## What CoderCup measured

In the experiment, several frontier coding agents built the same ten-phase application from the same requirements: a web app predicting World Cup results, timed to the tournament. A separate testing agent acted as referee, checking after each phase which features actually worked and feeding failures back.

Three findings carry the talk. First, the loop lifts every agent: according to the abstract, agents got tasks right on the first attempt about 80% of the time and reached 94% once the verification loop caught failures and drove fixes. Second, the loop matters more than the model: the agent with the best final score started near the bottom on first tries, and in their run it was also the cheapest. Third, every agent breaks its own working features. The abstract puts it at between 31 and 57 times per build, and those regressions stayed invisible until something actually ran the application.

That third number is the one to show your team. A gate at the end sees the final state; it does not see the forty-odd times a feature worked, broke, and maybe got fixed by accident.

## Build the loop, keep the tests

His practical advice is to design the loop deliberately: how the agent reads requirements, writes code, and verifies its own work against a running app. And keep every test the loop generates in the workspace. Each iteration's UI and backend integration tests become assets for the next one, so the suite grows with the code base and old edge cases keep getting checked as the agent adds features.

He also pushes back on the cost objection. In the enterprises his team works with, he says a cloud run of hundreds of test cases usually takes around ten minutes, and the loop can be wired in through a CLI, MCP or GitHub Actions on every PR without a human in it. Ten minutes per iteration is cheap next to a regression found by a customer.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads whose PRs have quietly tripled in size since agents arrived, and platform teams deciding where verification sits in an agent-driven pipeline. It is short and argument-led rather than a deep technical demo, and it is clearly a pitch for agentic testing as a category. Bring your own scepticism about the benchmark, then go look at the open-source CoderCup data.

Title: Feature flags manage exposure, quality gates decide if AI earns it
Description: Adobe's Rajesh Lingam at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on three evaluation gates that decide when a GenAI feature behind a flag gets more traffic.
Body:
A GenAI feature can be operationally green, with low errors, fine latency and a perfectly behaved flag, while its answers quietly get worse. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Rajesh Lingam, who works in GenAI evaluation and engineering at Adobe, made the case for pairing flags with automated quality gates, so a rollout step only happens once the AI behaviour has the evidence to justify it. He notes up front that the views are his own, not Adobe's.

His one-line thesis: feature flags manage exposure, quality gates manage confidence.

## The prompt change that passed everything

The story that frames the talk is painfully ordinary. A team edits a prompt to make answers shorter and friendlier. Functional tests pass, the API returns green, latency even improves. But on a small set of retrieval-heavy questions, the model now summarises too aggressively and adds statements the source doesn't support. Rajesh mentions seeing models make up arithmetic, even page numbers, simply because numbers were around.

Normal monitoring misses all of it. The flag will help you roll back once someone notices; a gate is what notices before the exposure grows. The shorter, friendlier, wrong answer is a very polite kind of outage.

## One score hides the failure you care about

In deterministic software, a regression suite passing at a high percentage is a reasonable ship signal. With GenAI, Rajesh argues, a single average can mask exactly the failure that matters. He scores releases on separate dimensions: answer quality (useful and correct for the task), grounding (supported by the provided context), safety, regression against the last stable baseline, and latency and cost, since an accurate system that is too slow or expensive isn't release-ready either. The gate should say which dimension failed and what to fix.

He treats prompts, model versions, retrieval configuration and tools as releasable artifacts. If a change can alter user-facing behaviour, it deserves release evidence, even when no code changed.

## Three gates, three price points

Rather than one giant evaluation run, he describes three:

- **Change-level gate**: cheap and fast, before merge or early in CI. Focused scenarios, deterministic checks and quick judge metrics ask whether the change obviously broke something.
- **Release-level gate**: before broader rollout. Representative scenarios, comparisons against baselines and thresholds, plus human review.
- **Runtime gate**: after exposure starts. Telemetry, sampled evals on live traffic, user feedback, and the rollback decision.

How much evaluation is enough? Depth rises with uncertainty and consequence: how many users or workflows are affected, how bad a failure would be, how big the change is. A one-sentence prompt tweak doesn't need the full suite. He is explicit that this is a decision framework, not a certification formula.

## Exposure grows only as evidence grows

The gates map onto the familiar rollout ladder. At 0% you lean on offline evidence: golden scenarios, regression tests, internal review. At a 1% canary you add runtime evidence from real traffic. At 10% you look for failure categories the offline suite never showed, at 50% for long-tail behaviour, and at 100% you keep monitoring, because models, prompts, retrieval content and user behaviour all drift.

Back to the prompt story: with a gate, targeted evals catch the grounding drop on retrieval-heavy questions, exposure stays where it is, and the team fixes the prompt before widening. The failure still happened. Users just didn't meet it at scale. His last rule is the sharpest: a gate must produce an action (proceed, hold, roll back or review). If it only produces a dashboard, it isn't a gate.

## Who should watch

Teams shipping LLM features behind flags who currently decide rollout steps by gut feel or a demo. It's a concise, framework-level talk without tool specifics, so pair it with something hands-on if you want pipelines and code.

Title: GitHub security from A to Z, well past the three GHAS features
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Microsoft's Peter De Tender walks the alphabet of GitHub security, with CodeQL, Dependabot and push protection demos.
Body:
GitHub Advanced Security is three features, and the alphabet has twenty-six letters. That is the premise of Peter De Tender's talk at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026: the Senior Content Developer at Microsoft in Redmond takes the GHAS bundle as a starting point and walks A to Z through the rest of the GitHub settings that make up a DevSecOps posture, with live demos of the big three along the way. It is a Microsoft speaker showing GitHub, so expect the product front and centre.

## The three pieces you may already pay for

De Tender starts by unpacking the bundle. Secret scanning matches tokens from around 70 partner providers, and push protection can block the commit before it leaves your laptop. Code scanning uses CodeQL, which treats source code as data you can query. Dependabot flags vulnerable packages from the CVE database and can now hand fixes to GitHub Copilot to rewrite package files. His useful aside for small teams: a lot of this works on public repos with a personal account, and much of the foundation also exists in Azure DevOps.

## CodeQL from portal to VS Code

The first demo, on a public sample repo, enables code scanning and opens an alert where HTML built from library input could allow cross-site scripting, complete with the CWE link and a suggested fix. He then walks the generated CodeQL Actions workflow: push, pull request and cron triggers, a language matrix for JavaScript and C#, extraction, a .NET build, analysis and a SARIF file.

The part worth watching is the local loop. With the CodeQL CLI you create a database from the repo, and with the VS Code extension you write and run your own queries. His example query flags page models that are handed a logger they never use, and the results land inline on the offending methods.

## Dependabot and dependency review

The Dependabot demo shows alerts with affected versions, fix versions, CVSS details and an EPSS score, plus the cross-check to cve.org where other vendors list the same issue. He then adds a dependency review step to a pull request, deliberately adding a nokogiri version with known vulnerabilities, and the review flags it before merge, along with a license issue. Dependabot finds the problem; dependency review stops it at the PR.

## Push protection in action

The secret scanning demo plants a GitHub personal access token in an app settings file. Turning scanning on surfaces it from history within seconds. With push protection enabled, the next commit attempt is refused, and the developer has to state a reason, false positive, test, or "fix later", to bypass it. That last option, he notes, is not exactly best practice.

## The rest of the alphabet

The A to Z format turns into a checklist you can steal. A few of the letters:

- **B and Q:** branch protection, rulesets and quality gates, so a failing check is a barrier rather than a red badge.
- **E:** environment protection rules with approvals and branch restrictions before production.
- **F:** workflows from forks never automatically get repository secrets.
- **H:** hardening runners, GitHub-hosted or your own.
- **I:** infrastructure-as-code scanning for Terraform, Bicep, ARM and Kubernetes YAML.
- **K and O:** keyless auth via OpenID Connect, swapping short-lived tokens for cloud access instead of stored keys.
- **S:** SBOMs and SAST.
- **V:** vulnerability management, where dismissing an alert should be a documented risk decision, not a way to clean up the dashboard.
- **Z:** Zero Trust, never trust automatically, always verify, assume breach.

It is long, around 45 minutes, and deliberately broad rather than deep; with twenty-six letters some get a sentence each. The payoff is breadth: most teams have at least three of these settings off.

## Who should watch

GitHub org admins and DevSecOps engineers who switched on GHAS and stopped there, and Azure DevOps users wondering what transfers. If you want the mechanics of a single feature, the CodeQL section is the most hands-on.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Peter De Tender's earlier lap around Dependabot, CodeQL and built-in security](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql), the companion piece.
- [Dewan Ahmed on preventing accidental secret commits with Gitleaks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Dewan_Ahmed_securing_gitleaks_repos_secret).
- [Gresshma Atluri on proactive supply chain defence](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Gresshma_Atluri_supply_chain_threats).

Title: Deploy credit models dark, then let a governed flag activate them
Description: Pavan Rupanguntla at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on separating deployment from activation for ML credit models, with shadow challengers and governed kill switches.
Body:
A credit model that passed validation is ready to deploy, but that doesn't mean it should start deciding anyone's credit line. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Pavan Rupanguntla, a credit risk and model risk management practitioner listed with Bank of America, argued that feature flags give lenders the missing control point: deploy the model inactive, check it in production, then let an approved configuration change turn it on, cohort by cohort. He notes the views are his own, not his employers'.

He brings more than seventeen years in consumer credit, card underwriting and model validation, including roles at Bank of America and Barclays, and it shows in the questions he asks. Not only does the model work, but can we control it, explain it, observe it and stop it?

## Validation passed, production is a different population

Pavan's starting point is the difference between deterministic code and learned behaviour. A model can do well in validation and still surprise you live because of population shift, attributes that go missing or arrive late, or customer behaviour that moved with the economy. That is a known risk in any ML system; in credit, the surprise lands on real exposure and real customers.

So he splits one event into two. Deployment means the model is in production, infrastructure checked, logging confirmed, inference pipeline and monitoring connected. Activation is an approved configuration change that lets it influence decisions, with no new software release needed to widen or shrink exposure. That boundary also separates authority: technology verifies the system works, model risk verifies the model and its controls, and business and risk stakeholders decide when customers feel it. Between the two, you can check whether features actually arrive on time and whether decision distributions look as expected.

## Shadow challengers and governed canaries

Rollout runs as approved stages rather than an engineer nudging a percentage. Start with a small, documented population (his simple example is existing clients before non-clients), with traceability for every decision: which model version, which cohort, and why this customer got this outcome.

Champion and challenger fit naturally. The challenger runs in shadow first, getting the same inputs while its output is recorded and compared, never applied. Where do the two disagree, which segments diverge most, and does risk segmentation shift the way you expected? The advantage is learning in the real production environment without touching customer outcomes.

The canary needs a wider definition of healthy than a web service. Latency, error rate and CPU still matter, but a credit canary also watches decision distributions, credit exposure and fairness indicators, and customer and portfolio outcomes. Expansion criteria, investigation triggers and rollback conditions are agreed before anyone flips anything. Turning it on for a few customers to see what happens isn't a canary, it's a gamble with a dashboard.

## A kill switch needs a fallback that still works

The kill switch is where separating deployment from activation pays off: an authorised team can deactivate the new model and restore an approved fallback without a release. Pavan's governance rider is that someone has to define who holds that authority, what conditions justify it, how it's documented and what investigation follows. The critical dependency is fallback readiness. The previous model, or a rule-based business-as-usual policy, must stay production-ready during the rollout. A rollback strategy isn't real if the fallback path has been removed.

## Flags as governed assets

Every flag decision should log the model version, policy path, timestamp and rollout cohort, so you can trace a decision back through features, policy logic and governance records, explain adverse action reasons, and tell a one-off from a systemic issue. Approvals may span technical validation, model risk review, business and compliance. And every flag needs an owner, documentation, a periodic review and an end date, or the organisation collects permanent flags nobody can explain.

His platform warnings are practical: flag proliferation, flags that outlive their team, flags that depend on other flags, and poor naming. An identifier that makes sense to an engineer can be opaque to a risk analyst, so naming standards are part of governance. The cultural point lands last: under pressure for lift and growth, pausing, observing longer or rolling back is a legitimate control action, not a failure.

## Who should watch

ML engineers and platform teams in lending or other regulated decisioning, and model risk folks who want to see how flags fit their controls. It's process-heavy rather than code-heavy, from someone who has sat in audit exams.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [The Fairness Paradox: Why Your Compliant ML Model May Be Causing the Most Harm](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Neelima_Verma_fairness_compliant_harm) by Neelima Verma (FairLens) at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
- [Maximizing Credit Card Profitability with Machine Learning–Driven CLV](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Avaneendra_Kanaparti_experimentation_abtesting_optimization) by Avaneendra Kanaparti of American Express at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026.
- [Compliance as a Pipeline Stage: Automating AI Governance in MLOps](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Arpita_Sheth_compliance_governance_pipeline) by Arpita Sheth at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Title: When CSP and COOP break working JavaScript, and how to catch it first
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, SAP's Elena Darevskaya shows how browser security headers break popups, eval and blob workers, plus ESLint and Playwright fixes.
Body:
Your login popup works for years, then one morning it hangs with nothing in the console. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Elena Darevskaya, Senior Platform Engineer at SAP who builds a web SDK customers embed in their own pages, showed how browser security policies quietly break correct JavaScript, and how to catch that in design, lint, build, test and production rather than in a customer's bug report.

## A header you did not set broke your code

Darevskaya's angle is unusual for a security talk. Most CSP talks ask how to make the policy as strict as possible. She asks how to keep your code compatible with policies you do not control, because her SDK runs inside other people's sites with other people's headers.

Even if you own the environment, she gives three reasons to care: catching it early is cheaper than a redesign, CSP blocks things at execution time rather than load time (so an untested flow can hide an eval for months), and AI-generated code makes guardrails that stop risky patterns before commit more valuable.

Her demo is a sign-in popup with a third-party provider. Click sign in, click continue, nothing happens. Hours of debugging later: the provider added Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, which severs the popup from its parent, so `window.opener` is null and the `postMessage` that used to report login goes nowhere. The design assumed the popup would always see its opener, and tightening browser security broke that assumption.

## Ask what the API assumes before you use it

At design time she suggests asking whether an API depends on window relationships or specific origins, whether a header can block it, whether it needs a secure context, and whether a permissions policy can restrict it. The answers might change the design: a redirect flow instead of a popup, or a broadcast channel that does not depend on the opener. She also mentions an experimental MDN MCP server as a way to give AI coding agents real API documentation instead of hallucinated behaviour.

## ESLint is a policy engine you already have

Most JavaScript projects run ESLint for style, and she argues it is underused. Out of the box it bans eval and its cousins: `new Function` and `setTimeout` with a string. With `no-restricted-syntax` you can forbid `innerHTML` and `outerHTML` unless wrapped in a sanitiser, which her live demo shows failing on exactly one unsafe file. With Trusted Types now available in modern browsers, CSP can block that sink outright.

The architectural trick is more interesting. Blob workers are blocked by typical CSP unless explicitly allowed, and the blob URL may be created in a different file from the worker. So make one worker factory module the only place allowed to call `new Worker` and own URL creation, and let everything else call its function. The same approach can restrict `window.open` to calls with noopener and noreferrer, or `fetch` to approved URLs.

## Your bundler can add the eval back

Her favourite gotcha: she removed every eval from the source, lint was clean, and the page still threw a CSP eval error. The culprit was a webpack devtool source map setting starting with "eval", which injects eval into the build. Vite has its own surprises. Her fixes: lint the bundler config itself to forbid eval-based devtool values, and add a thin scanner over build artifacts for eval, blob and data resources, inline styles and dynamic scripts. Source code is not the thing that runs.

## Test under the policy you mean

Staging and production headers often differ, so she runs the same Playwright tests as separate projects, one with a permissive CSP that allows blob workers and one strict, injecting the header in a fixture and attaching CSP violation reports as test annotations. A worker test passes under permissive and fails with a clear violation under strict. She also writes tests that are expected to fail: under `frame-ancestors 'none'`, embedding the page in an iframe should break, and the report shows that as a pass.

## Watch production with report-only

Finally, report-only headers and reporting endpoints let you trial a stricter policy or keep watching violations after rollout. Two warnings: the endpoint is public, so validate and rate-limit what it accepts, and reported URLs can contain tokens you should not store. If you ship a third-party script and cannot set headers, the SecurityPolicyViolation event and ReportingObserver can capture violations from inside the page, with different coverage and browser support.

## Who should watch

Front-end and platform engineers shipping embeddable SDKs or widgets, and security teams rolling out CSP who want developers on side. Lots of live demos, and the example code is on GitHub.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Srinivasa Rao Gunda on a framework for front-end and Node.js vulnerability management](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Srinivasa_Rao_Gunda_securing_framework_frontend).
- [Gil Zilberfeld's Playwright in an hour](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Gil_Zilberfeld_26_playwright_automation_testing), if the test half is new to you.
- [Safeer C M on open-source SAST with Semgrep](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep), for static checks beyond ESLint.

Title: Conf42 AI Agents 2026: less LLM, more harness
Description: Conf42 AI Agents 2026 roundup - planning without model calls, AI coding harnesses, LLM-as-judge testing, runaway token bills and agent security, in 22 talks.
Body:
Conf42 AI Agents 2026 ran online on September 24, 2026, with 22 talks, and the loudest message was a sceptical one: the model is rarely the problem. Speaker after speaker argued that what makes an agent shippable is the system around it, meaning deterministic planning, typed tools, review harnesses, evals, budgets, and identity boundaries. There were plenty of demos, but the best talks were about what happens after the demo.

The full lineup is on the [Conf42 AI Agents 2026 event page](https://www.conf42.com/agents2026), and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCZ8u5VHJAm9eOB9KJTCZT8).

## Stop asking the model what to do next

[Maureese Williams](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Maureese_Williams_planning_search_graph), an AI Engineer at Disney, started from a mundane observation: at every step, an agent asks the language model what to do next, so a twenty-step task costs twenty model calls and gives a different plan each run. The GATS approach (Graph-Augmented Tree Search) runs UCB1 tree search over a state-transition graph the agent builds as it works. The LLM never picks an action; it is the last rung of an escalation ladder, after symbolic rules and learned statistics, and its answers are cached.

[Michael Haim](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Michael_Haim_orchestration_patterns_determinism), founder and CEO of Zindell Technologies, tackled the same non-determinism from the language side: you cannot orchestrate agents with a plain if or switch when their output is fuzzy, so use pattern matching to turn it into structured, auditable control flow. And [Elizabeth Fuentes Leone](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost) of AWS showed semantic tool selection: every call serialises every tool description into the context, so filter tools with vector search before they reach the LLM, cutting both wrong picks and token cost.

## The harness decides what ships

AI coding got its own track, and almost none of it was about prompts.

- [Ruben Marcus Luz Paschoarelli](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ruben_Marcus_Luz_Paschoarelli_coding_harness_evidence) of MultiVM Labs argued that AI coding fails because the system around the model trusts the wrong evidence, and showed his harness: short specs, isolated git worktrees, model routing by role, browser verification, screenshot gates, and cost controls.
- [Guido Scheffler](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Guido_Scheffler_code_review_harness) of CGI told the story of scaling AI code reviews across more than 70 projects, moving from brittle prompts to a deterministic review harness with an agent runner, an MCP server, managed checklists, and enforced completeness.
- [Suneet Malhotra](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Suneet_Malhotra_mcp_pipeline_accuracy), Senior Manager of Test Engineering at Motorola Solutions, presented a Claude Code and MCP pipeline whose three MCP servers turn product requirements into Jira stories, test cases, and Appium code at about 80% accuracy; the talk is about the other 20%, and why the human PR gate is mandatory.
- [Kemet Dugue](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Kemet_Dugue_workflows_productivity_onboarding) walked through how Uber's driver onboarding team turned script-heavy manual processes into agentic workflows, and [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Peter_De_Tender_azure_deployment_automation) of Microsoft showed how his open-source library of Azure demo scenarios became an agentic deployment system. [Kabir Ibraheem](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Kabir_Ibraheem_fullstack_tooling_productivity) of Meltwater offered a practical tour of AI tools for full-stack engineers.

## Who judges the agent

Testing non-deterministic systems came up again and again. [Liran Yushinsky](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen), who leads automation at JFrog, asked how you test an AI that never gives you the same answer twice when it generates executable code through a chain of tool calls, and answered with LLM-as-judge alongside conventional checks.

Diamond sponsor Harness made the enterprise case: [Shubham Jindal](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Shubham_Jindal_ai_demo_enterprise), Director of AI at Harness, laid out four pillars (context engineering, evals, memory, and governance) and argued that an eval suite should never pass at 100%, because then it cannot measure progress. [Shubham Sharma](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Shubham_Sharma_readiness_platform_enterprise) of Microsoft proposed a unified readiness framework, so models, retrieval, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop workflows are assessed together rather than team by team.

## The bill comes at 2 AM

[Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Yamini_Rathamsetty_Karthik_Akula_cost_loops_tokens) of AWS opened with the scene every agent operator dreads: 2 AM, no customers, no deploys, every dashboard green, and the bill climbing by multiples because their own agents were working hard all night on nothing. The talk dissects retry storms, runaway tool calls, context bloat, and multi-agent overhead.

[Vladimir Beskorovainyi](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Vladimir_Beskorovainyi_sql_orchestration_scale) of Besk Tech brought the most production-scarred talk of the day: an on-prem text-to-SQL platform with open-weight models across 500+ data marts and 30M+ users. The opener says it all: "Very few people have to answer for the number it gives at 9:00 in the morning."

## Don't give the agent a shell

The trust track was about boundaries. [Ahmed Tariq](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_identity_permissions_cloud) of Simplify9 argued for a small set of typed tools, a deliberately limited identity, and enforcement outside the model, instead of a shell and a broad credential. [Blaize Stewart](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Blaize_Stewart_rag_security_injection) of GBLI broke a RAG application live with prompt injection, poisoned documents, and broken document-level authorisation. [Morgan Willis](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Morgan_Willis_production_guardrails_trust) of AWS summed it up: don't trust the agent, trust the system you build around it, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Strands Agents SDK as the toolkit.

## Agents meet enterprise data

Agents are only as good as the data they act on. [Rohit Deshpande and Scott Young](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Rohit_Deshpande_Scott_Young_mcp_dashboards_live) of SAP showed a ReAct agent that turns a request like AR aging by customer into a deployed dashboard over live data via MCP. [Vishwak Thatikonda](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Vishwak_Thatikonda_mdm_data_retail) of Starbucks explained why master data management built for reporting breaks when agents make decisions on it. [Pon Murugesh Devendren](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Pon_Murugesh_Devendren_sap_incidents_events) of Deloitte built event-driven agents for proactive SAP incident management, [Nick Rezaee](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Nick_Rezaee_health_wearables_intervene) of Harvard showed agents that turn wearable data into timely interventions, and [Dmytro Hlotenko](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Dmytro_Hlotenko_serverless_photos_aws) of Sage confessed that his Step Functions DAG for judging 8,000 photos was a lie, and went agentic.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to diamond sponsors [Harness](https://www.harness.io/) and [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), gold sponsor the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/), the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and all the media partners on the event page.

The series returns with [Conf42 AI Agents 2027](https://www.conf42.com/agents2027) on September 23, 2027. Until then, the playlist holds enough harness engineering to keep your agents honest.

Title: A recovery can hit its RTO and still bring revoked access back to life
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, researcher Sanjay Iyer proposes a Semantic Recovery Envelope that bounds replay, staleness and irreversible effects.
Body:
RTO and RPO tell you when a system is back, not whether it came back correct. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, independent researcher Sanjay Iyer, who has spent about fourteen years on distributed systems and real-time data pipelines, proposed the Semantic Recovery Envelope: a decision layer that scores each recovery plan on five kinds of logical damage before it runs, and is allowed to reject the fastest one.

## An incident with a green dashboard

Iyer's example is a stream processor that comes back in ninety seconds while emitting duplicates, applying older state over newer, closing a window on incomplete input, or repeating an external action that cannot be reversed. Every one of those reads as a successful recovery. His security framing is memorable: a fast recovery that restores an authorization decision the system had already revoked "is an incident with a green dashboard."

Recovery is when a system rewrites its own state at scale, under time pressure, with fewer checks than normal. That is exactly when the attack surface shifts. Worse, conventional metrics reward the path that skips verification, because skipping verification is usually what makes it fast.

## Five dimensions, not two numbers

He models damage as a vector: missing events, duplicate effects, ordering inversions, state staleness and non-compensable divergence, each bounded over an explicit key scope and time horizon. Through a security lens, staleness is where revoked permissions return, duplication is where replay sneaks past fraud controls, and non-compensable divergence is where the audit boundary breaks, because you cannot unsend a message or unsettle a payment. For irreversible actions that last bound is zero, a prohibition rather than a weight.

The envelope does not replace checkpointing, exactly-once processing or replay. It sits above them in three moves: bound the damage for each candidate plan from evidence you actually hold, filter out any plan that could cross a hard constraint, then choose among survivors by Pareto dominance, then policy weights, and journal why.

## Evidence is collected, never inferred

Everything depends on proof: source offsets for which input a candidate covers, watermarks for whether a window or join closed on complete input, state digests for which version you really restored, sink receipts for committed output, and an external effect ledger for actions outside the transaction boundary. The fail-closed rule: missing evidence widens the bound. A lost sink receipt does not mean the write never happened; it means you do not know, and not knowing is priced as risk.

He maps responses to dimensions. Replay fixes missing events and ordering but raises duplicate risk outside the deduplication horizon. Rollback clears suspect epochs but raises staleness and is unsafe if newer state already reached the sink. Compensation is the only fix for duplicates past the effect boundary and is impossible for irreversible effects. Partial service and traffic isolation trade availability for integrity while evidence catches up.

## Three scenarios that hold up

Regional failover: fence the old epoch first so the old region's writers are rejected, bound the replica's state at one decision frontier, then promote per key range and isolate the rest. Never a blind global switch, which is how a session store that predates a revocation gets promoted.

Lost sink receipt: the offset says processed, the receipt is missing. Treating the offset as proof is how a replay charges a customer twice. The envelope widens the duplicate bound, rejects replay for irreversible effect classes, compensates what can be compensated, and replays only inside the deduplication horizon.

Split state: some consumers ahead, some behind. Instead of the reflex to replay everything, each key range resumes, trades off, gets quarantined, or stays read-only until evidence arrives.

## What auditors get for free

Plans carry monotonically increasing epochs, writes from older epochs are rejected, and all evidence is read at one stable frontier. Given the journal, policy version and planner version, an auditor gets the same feasible set and the same selected plan. Break-glass exists, but only as a separately audited policy that names its accepted damage bound; in his words, emergency access that cannot state its blast radius is bypass.

RTO and RPO stay. The envelope adds five per-workload objectives written down before the incident, so the availability-versus-correctness trade-off is a policy choice made calmly rather than an improvisation at 3am.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform security leads running Kafka- or Flink-style stateful pipelines, and anyone whose failover runbook ends at "time to green". It is a conceptual framework talk, research-flavoured and dense, building on Flink snapshots, watermark semantics and Kafka's ordering guarantees rather than shipping a tool.

Title: Release a regulated CRM migration like a feature, not a weekend
Description: United Therapeutics' Jaymin Sutarwala at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on cohorts, shadow runs and capability rollback for a patient CRM migration.
Body:
The riskiest feature most companies ever release is a whole platform, switched on for every user and every record over one weekend. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Jaymin Sutarwala, Associate Director of CRM Strategy and Operations at United Therapeutics, argued that the progressive delivery toolkit (flags, canaries, cohort rollouts) scales up to a regulated CRM migration, and walked through the control plane and state model that make it work.

The talk's abstract sets the context: retiring a legacy patient CRM in favour of a Salesforce ecosystem spanning Marketing Cloud, Data Cloud and Health Cloud, without disrupting live patient engagement or exposing health data. The recording itself stays at the pattern level rather than walking through that project screen by screen.

## The CRM is a hub, and its dependencies are undocumented

Jaymin's first point is that a CRM isn't really an application. Identity rules, web forms, support programmes, contact centres, warehouses, partner feeds, emails, texts and consent all hang off it. Most of those dependencies live in field names, nightly jobs and a workflow someone built years ago that nobody remembers until it stops.

A big-bang cutover moves data, integrations, users and communications across the line at the same moment, which maximises the size of the change and minimises your ability to isolate a problem. Rollback is the real trap. By Wednesday you'd have to unmigrate changed data, work out which emails already went out and repoint integrations that have written records, so rollback quietly turns into fix forward whatever it takes.

## Deploy the platform, then activate it

The way out is the separation this audience already lives by: deployment is not release. He credits Pete Hodgson's feature toggles article on Martin Fowler's site and James Governor's naming of progressive delivery. The new CRM can be fully deployed, integrated and loaded with data while still not being the system anyone depends on.

In between sits a migration control plane that answers one question everywhere: for this request, record or workflow, which path right now? The answer depends on cohort, capability, channel, region, integration and data domain. He's explicit that it needn't be a commercial flag product; gateway routing rules or a config table can do the job, with OpenFeature for the code-level piece. Each cohort or capability moves through explicit states: legacy only, shadow, dual run, pilot, new primary (legacy still fed so rollback stays cheap), legacy disabled. If you can't say what state a cohort is in, since when and who approved it, he says, you don't have a migration plan. You have hope.

## Three patterns that carry the risk

- **Deliberate cohorts.** Random percentages spread odd records evenly so nobody sees a pattern. Pick cohorts by team, segment, data complexity (clean recent records before ones with 15 years of merges), workflow, region or channel, and make assignments sticky by hashing a stable identifier.
- **Integration routing.** Integrations write whether you're watching or not, so a routing decision sits in front of them. That makes it a distributed system, with the usual non-negotiables: correlation IDs, idempotent writes, duplicate detection on business keys, bounded retries into a dead-letter queue someone watches, and a reconciliation store.
- **Shadow and dual run.** Legacy's result is what the person experiences; the new platform processes the same event and sends its output to a comparator. He cites GitHub's Scientist library and Sam Newman's parallel run. Shadow mode must suppress side effects, and not every difference is a bug: sometimes legacy has been quietly wrong for years.

## Flag, telemetry, threshold, rollback

A migration flag without telemetry tagged by flag state, a threshold and a named rollback action is a switch, not a control. Signals go beyond errors and latency to reconciliation mismatches, duplicates, stalled workflows, delivery failures and support tickets. OpenTelemetry's feature flag semantic conventions turn the question of whether things got worse after a flip into a query instead of a meeting.

Regulation makes this more valuable, not less. Audit every flag change, carry consent with the record whichever path is active, keep access control equivalent on both sides, and keep sensitive data out of flag evaluation context and telemetry. He also retells Knight Capital as the cautionary tale for repurposed flags, and closes with capability-level rollback: if one reminder workflow creates duplicates, flip that one route back to the warm legacy path and leave everything else alone.

## Who should watch

Anyone planning an enterprise platform migration, especially with personal or health data involved. The eight-step loop near the end (map, flag, shadow, compare, pilot, observe, expand, retire) is the slide to keep.

Title: Enterprise AI in four pillars: context, evals, memory, governance
Description: Shubham Jindal of Harness at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 on why AI demos stall before production, and the four pillars that get agents there.
Body:
An AI demo takes days to build and wows the room; the production version can take months and still embarrass you in front of a customer. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Shubham Jindal, Director of AI at Harness, laid out the blueprint his team uses to close that gap: four pillars called context, evals, memory, and governance, each with concrete habits you can copy.

This is a sponsor keynote, and Shubham says up front that Harness has built all four pillars into its own AI for the software delivery pipeline. But the talk is a framework, not a product tour. Almost everything in it applies to any team shipping agents to paying users.

## Demos run on prompts, production runs on context

Shubham's opening claim is that the mindset has to shift from prompt engineering to context engineering. In a demo you are not throwing large data at the model, so a clever prompt carries the day. In production the model meets your siloed systems, your company jargon, and your sensitive data, and that is where it starts to make things up with great confidence.

His line for it: "Context is the new code." His team's case is personal. Harness has separate CI, CD, and code products, and an LLM trained on the whole internet does not know that CI means something specific inside Harness.

He gave four practical tricks for keeping the context window healthy:

- **Compaction.** Summarise the conversation as it nears the limit and keep only the decisions. He compares it to a garbage collector.
- **Large outputs go to files.** A Jira or GitHub MCP call can return a giant JSON blob. Write it to a file and let the agent read the slice it needs, instead of flooding the window.
- **Context editing.** Proactively drop dead ends, like the five wrong Gradle commands the agent tried before finding the right one.
- **Semantic augmentation.** Load skills and reference material when they become relevant, not all at once in the system prompt.

## A knowledge graph is the compiler for your context

The most useful example in the talk is a question that sounds simple: which of my PRs caused an incident last week? The answer crosses the PR, the CI run, the CD deployment, the version that shipped, and the on-call page. Ask an agent to stitch that from three raw data sources and it will guess at relationships it does not understand.

Shubham's fix is to extract the entities you care about (services, users, incidents, releases), enrich them with metadata such as owners, link them into a graph, and expose that graph through an API the agent can query and walk. If context is the new code, he says, the knowledge graph is its compiler.

## Evals should fail on purpose

The second most important pillar, in his ranking, is evals. Unit tests assume deterministic code; agents are probabilistic, so many teams skip testing entirely because they cannot define what good looks like. His example is model switching: an agent tuned on Opus burns too many tokens, so you want to try Sonnet. Without evals you are changing a model name and hoping.

The framework he described:

- LLM-as-a-judge checks, ideally with a different model than the one being judged.
- Regression evals as a quality gate in CI/CD before any prompt, temperature, or model change ships.
- Evals on production traces. Harness runs a simple user temperament check that asks whether the user seems frustrated, types in caps, or repeats the same question.
- Every production failure becomes a new eval case.

The idea worth stealing is that an eval suite should not pass at 100%. Treat it like a benchmark: if 80 of 100 cases pass today, a change that moves you to 85 is progress and one that drops you to 75 is a regression. A suite that always passes can only tell you about the cases you already solved.

## Memory makes an assistant, governance makes it shippable

On memory, Shubham separates short-term memory (the current session) from long-term memory that bubbles up patterns, such as which repos a team works in or what a user keeps asking about. His summary: chatbots forget, assistants remember. He also traces the arc from chatbot to in-app assistant to autonomous agent, with examples like an agent that watches a PR's CI, fixes failures, and pushes until it is green.

Governance he calls the boring pillar enterprises care about most. He splits it into scoped access (do not hand an agent every tool in the GitHub MCP when it only needs a few), guardrails such as PII redaction and EU data residency, real-time content filters, and full audit trails of tool calls and model versions. Governance, in his words, is the new runtime, because it only exists while the agent is running.

## Who should watch

Engineers and leads who have a working agent prototype and a nervous security team. The context-window tricks and the "evals as benchmarks" framing are worth the time on their own. If you are still deciding whether to build an agent at all, start elsewhere.

Title: Make Kubernetes debugging deterministic with mandatory trace context
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Dell's Mridula Chilakamarri builds OpenTelemetry tracing that two engineers can't read two ways, with a nine-field allowlist.
Body:
Two engineers, one incident, two root causes. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Mridula Chilakamarri, Product Manager at Dell Technologies building microservices platforms, called that non-deterministic debugging and showed the architecture that removes it: W3C Trace Context injected at ingress, propagation that is mandatory rather than polite, a deny-by-default list of nine trace fields, and telemetry that can never take a request down with it.

## Dashboards are not a shared identity

Her example app is the usual cast: authentication, cart, payment and inventory services, each owned by a different team and deployed on its own schedule. Logs sit in one system, metrics in another, traces are partial. The trace in her slide goes gateway, auth, cart, then a gap where the payment span should be. Whoever starts from cart data concludes one thing; whoever reads the scraps of payment data concludes another.

Teams think they have solved observability because they have lots of dashboards, she says, but logs, metrics and traces are collected as three silos with no common identifier. So you grep timestamps and hop. Per-service sampling quietly drops the exact failure you needed. And under SOC 2, HIPAA or PCI, not being able to reconstruct what happened is a compliance problem, not an inconvenience. The fix is not a fourth dashboard.

## Three decisions turn a standard into a guarantee

The foundation is the W3C traceparent header: version, a trace ID that stays constant for the whole request, a span ID per hop, and flags. She picks the standard over a home-grown correlation ID so that a service with the OpenTelemetry SDK, one behind a mesh and one with a vendor agent all speak the same header.

Then three choices. Trace identity is generated at the ingress gateway, so no request starts life untraceable. Context propagation is mandatory, the one she says she will defend hardest, because optional propagation creates gaps and gaps are where the worst incidents hide. And sampling, export targets and verbosity are configuration, not code, so you can tune telemetry during an incident without a redeploy.

## Telemetry off the request path

Each service records its span into a local buffer and the request moves on immediately. Spans are exported asynchronously to the OpenTelemetry Collector, which assembles traces for whatever backend you query by trace ID. If the collector is down or the vendor's network has a bad day, you drop spans and the request still returns 200.

She is pointed about why this must be structural rather than trusted to an SDK default or a timeout: the outage where your monitoring takes down your product, export calls blocking and threads piling up, is one of the most embarrassing kind there is. Observability that causes the incident it was meant to explain is the platform equivalent of the smoke alarm starting the fire.

## Deny by default for span attributes

Rich metadata is useful, and unrestricted metadata is how a trace store becomes a queryable copy of your most sensitive data. Nobody decides to leak; an engineer adds the request body or an auth header to debug something, it works, it stays, and that repeats across dozens of teams for years.

So the default is inverted to an allowlist of nine approved fields: trace ID, span ID, parent span ID, service name, operation name, timestamps, duration, status and HTTP response code. Everything else, payloads, headers, user data, never enters the pipeline. That one structural control is what lets the same design answer SOC 2 (reproducible records), HIPAA (no PHI in traces) and PCI DSS (no card numbers riding along in attributes).

## Seven checks you can run in CI

Her claims come as seven independently testable capabilities: a unique trace ID at ingress with existing IDs preserved; correct parent-child spans, with retries keeping the original trace ID; full trace-level capture; query by ID for the end-to-end path; config-only export with multiple backends and tenant routing; trace views, dependency graphs and per-span latency; and non-blocking, PII-free tracing. Because each is testable, "are we tracing-ready?" becomes a checklist rather than a judgement call.

Her worked scenario, checkout failing intermittently under load, shows the payoff: one engineer blames the database, another a downstream API, and a single failing trace shows the auth service exhausting its connection pool, with both earlier findings as symptoms.

## Who should watch

SREs and DevSecOps engineers who own both reliability and the audit, and platform teams rolling out OpenTelemetry across services they do not control. Practical, vendor-neutral, with lessons from production; the allowlist alone is worth the time.

Title: An alert that fires too late is a log line: grading rules by deadline
Description: At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, security engineer Aleksander Kryukov replays 46 DeFi exploits to grade detection rules on timing, not just firing.
Body:
Most detection rules are tested like code: feed in a sample, check the alert fires. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Aleksander Kryukov, a security engineer working in Web3, argued that the test that matters is whether the alert fires early enough for someone to act, and built a replay harness over 46 historical DeFi exploits to measure exactly that.

## Why DeFi makes a good lab

Kryukov's reason for using blockchain incidents is evidence quality. Every on-chain step of every attack sits in a public ledger nobody can edit, with block numbers and call traces, and an archive node can reconstruct the exact state of the world at any block. You can rerun history. The one gap is the pending phase, since a transaction can travel privately until it is included.

His opening case is the Balancer V2 drain in November 2025. Monitoring flagged the first transaction. Emergency controls triggered about twenty minutes later, and pausable pools were paused, protecting over nineteen million dollars. But the older pools had outlived their pause window, so there was nothing for any alert to press. The rule worked. The outcome did not.

## Three variables decide whether an alert mattered

He breaks it down into detection time (when the rule fired, measured from the triggering event plus the detector's own processing time), response latency (alert to mitigation actually taking effect, whether a bot or humans signing a multisig) and mitigation availability (does the pause still exist). He points at the Google SRE workbook's four alert attributes, precision, recall, detection time and reset time, and notes that a unit test with one transaction measures recall and nothing else.

## The harness

The dataset starts from DeFi Hack Labs, the open collection of Foundry proofs of concept, filtered to Ethereum mainnet incidents covered by mempool archives and ranked by reported loss. Each incident becomes a manifest: fork block, setup and exploit transactions, victim contracts, attacker addresses, and a kill chain label on every event.

The key design choice is not to use the proof of concept as the replay. A PoC squeezes deployment, exploit and drain into one test at one block, which is perfect for "is it exploitable?" and useless for "when could we have known?". So the harness forks Ethereum at the block before the attacker's first setup transaction and replays the chain's own transactions block by block. A chain clock merges execution with first-seen mempool times, a visibility filter models what one telemetry profile could see, and an oracle builds the loss curve from victim balance changes. Detectors never see the oracle. Chain time is the only clock.

## Deadlines come from the loss curve, not an SLA

Replays show how different incidents are. Beanstalk lost 182 million dollars in a single transaction. Harvest Finance bled over thirty transactions in under seven minutes. Nomad took more than eight hours. A fixed "alert within five minutes" SLA is too slow for the first and pointless when nobody is watching, as with Ronin, where the theft went unnoticed for six days until a user tried to withdraw.

So each incident gets its own deadline: if you want to lose no more than a given share, the alert must fire before the loss curve reaches that share, minus your response time. For a single-transaction exploit the deadline always lands before the exploit, which is why he grades rules by kill chain stage: funding, preparation, exploitation, laundering. Euler Finance is the cautionary tale: alerts fired ten minutes and three minutes before the attack, and it still lost, because the only response was a manual multisig.

## Budget false positives by reversibility

Early rules are tempting to wire to automatic pauses. Kryukov shows why that needs care: a published early-detection approach with strong lab precision flagged 129 of more than 23,000 new contracts in live use, and 26 were real attack contracts. Attacks are rare and new contracts are plentiful, so even a small false-positive rate swamps the true ones.

His answer is a mitigation ladder from easy to undo to hard to undo: notify, throttle outflow, pause, freeze. Each tier gets a false-action budget, the harness measures each rule's alert rate on incident-free block ranges, and a rule may drive a tier only if it fits. Irreversible actions get zero budget and a human decides.

The last constraint is visibility. Private transaction routing has grown sharply, which blinds the one rule family that relies on the public mempool, pre-inclusion simulation. The others work from what lands on chain.

## It maps straight onto your SOC

The closing section is the reason non-crypto teams should watch. The archive node is your retained raw telemetry. Block-by-block replay is replaying recorded telemetry through detection-as-code rules in CI. The loss curve is time until data is stolen. The pause is auto-remediation like disabling a key or isolating a host, with the same false-positive question. The private mempool is telemetry you simply do not collect.

Detection engineers, SOC leads and anyone wiring alerts to automated response will get a reusable method. Expect a lot of named incidents and numbers; it is dense, and worth it.

Title: Flags don't find the seams in a payment monolith, DDD does
Description: Jaya Chand Bandi at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on using domain-driven design for boundaries and feature flags to route traffic out of payment monoliths.
Body:
A feature flag can move payment traffic from a monolith to a new service one merchant cohort at a time, but it cannot tell you where the service boundary should be. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, payments architect Jaya Chand Bandi (listed on the programme as an independent researcher) laid out a migration approach in which domain-driven design defines the seams, migration patterns introduce them, flags control the traffic across them, and lifecycle discipline gets the flags deleted afterwards.

The question that opens the talk is one every payments team knows: how do you modernise the platform when the business can't afford for modernisation to interrupt payment processing? His answer is one word, repeated throughout: control.

## The monolith wasn't a mistake, the coordination is the problem

Jaya starts by defending the monolith. Centralised control, transactional reliability and operational simplicity served payment businesses well for years. Then came digital wallets, new payment rails, loyalty programmes, hosted checkout and regional compliance. The problem, in his framing, is not code size but how much coordination each change now requires.

He names three things that make payment monoliths hard to split. Transactional integrity: shared database transactions keep related operations consistent, and moving code doesn't move those guarantees with it. Implicit coupling: disputes, loyalty and reporting share tables and internal calls that never appear on the architecture diagram until you try to extract something. And operational confidence: alerts, runbooks and SLOs were all built around one deployable.

## The word transaction means four things

Bounded contexts give the starting points: authorisation, settlement, disputes, loyalty, reporting. But naming a context isn't isolating it. His best illustration is linguistic. In authorisation, a transaction is an authorisation event. In settlement, a financial record. In disputes, the payment being challenged. In loyalty, an event that earns rewards. Force all four into one shared model and you've built coupling by vocabulary. Context mapping makes the differences explicit and replaces accidental sharing with intentional integration.

## Flags enforce the seam, they don't create it

Once the boundary exists, the flag becomes the migration control plane: deploy the new implementation, validate it, then expose traffic deliberately. Three controls do the work: percentage rollout, cohort targeting (specific merchants, transaction types or regions) and a kill switch back to the legacy path. He flags the limit himself: redirecting traffic doesn't undo payment actions that already completed, so fallback needs a plan for in-flight requests, data state and reconciliation.

He separates flag types by purpose: release toggles for availability, experiment toggles for shadow comparison (legacy stays authoritative, and the shadow path must never repeat a real financial action), ops toggles for incidents, and permission toggles for merchant groups or regions. They look the same in code and need different operating rules.

The patterns underneath are the classics. Strangler fig (intercept, divert, retire), with implementation, exposure and retirement as separate decisions. An anti-corruption layer that translates legacy structures at the boundary so the new domain keeps its own language. And branch by abstraction, with legacy and new implementations behind one interface and the flag choosing between them.

## Start where you can afford to learn

Sequencing is about readiness, not ambition. His proposed order runs from reporting and analytics first, through loyalty, hosted checkout and disputes, with authorisation and settlement last because of their criticality, and he is clear it's a suggestion that depends on the real platform. A readiness score supports that conversation but doesn't replace architectural judgement.

The failure modes are worth the price of admission: false decomposition (separate deployments, same shared data), over-fragmentation, flag sprawl, and organisational misalignment, where domain services still depend on layer-team handoffs and you rebuild monolith coordination in distributed form. Reaching 100% rollout isn't the finish line. The completion question is what you can now safely delete. Every flag needs an owner, a purpose, an expected lifetime and a removal task from day one.

## Who should watch

Architects and tech leads planning to break up a transactional monolith, payments or otherwise. It's a structured, pattern-level talk rather than a war story with numbers, which makes it a good shared vocabulary for a team about to start.

Title: Don't trust the agent. Trust the layers you build around it
Description: Morgan Willis (AWS) at Conf42 AI Agents 2026: layered guardrails, steering, MCP interceptors and deterministic policy for a customer service agent.
Body:
Trust is not something you give an AI agent; it's something you build into the system around it. That's the thesis Morgan Willis, Principal Cloud Technologist at AWS, works through at Conf42 AI Agents 2026, using a customer service agent for a fictional robot vacuum company and a set of very specific ways it misbehaved. Her toolkit is AWS (Amazon Bedrock, the Strands Agents SDK, Bedrock AgentCore), and she says up front that the patterns apply to any agent built anywhere.

## Model plus harness equals agent

She sorts failures into three buckets: the agent says something wrong (hallucinates, promises what it can't guarantee, leaks data), the agent does something wrong (wrong tool, wrong arguments, wrong account, deleted data), and someone deliberately tries to break it. The familiar headlines fit the buckets, from the dealership chatbot that sold a car for a dollar to the coding assistant that deleted a production database.

Her starting point: a system prompt is a suggestion. Models get better at following instructions, but you can't audit a prompt and promise the agent will never do the wrong thing. The opposite extreme, a rigid step-by-step graph, is controllable but brittle and breaks as soon as reality leaves the path. The goal is an open-ended, model-driven agent with enough layered controls that when one guardrail fails, another catches it.

## Five scenarios, five layers

**Off-task use.** A customer asks the vacuum bot to solve a LeetCode problem to save on a coding-assistant subscription, and the bot happily obliges. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails filter both directions: denied topics and injection patterns stopped before the model runs, and sensitive data such as card numbers masked on the way out.

**Not following directions.** Asked for a refund outside the return window, the agent says yes without checking eligibility or calling the refund tool. Long system prompts suffer from the lost-in-the-middle effect. Two fixes: hooks that run deterministic code at points in the agent loop (no refund call unless the eligibility tool ran first), and Strands' steering, where a second agent with its own context and rubric reviews tool calls and responses before they go out and sends them back with feedback when they're off policy.

**Wrong values in tool calls.** Asked about order 12345, the agent looked up 67890. She saw exactly this in her own testing. The problem is that the model controls the tool arguments. The fix is an MCP interceptor at AgentCore Gateway, one layer removed from the agent, which injects sensitive parameters like the customer ID from the authenticated user's token instead of trusting the model, and checks the order really belongs to that customer. The tools validate again, as the last line of defence, the same way a backend doesn't trust the frontend.

**High-stakes actions.** Policy says refunds over $500 need a human; the agent refunded $899 anyway, with the rule sitting right there in its prompt. A deterministic authorisation layer, AgentCore Policy with Cedar-family policies, permits the refund tool only under the threshold. As she puts it, no agent can think its way around that.

**Seeing what it does.** Auto-instrumented tracing, plus anomaly alerts on tool-call rates and token consumption, so a spike gets investigated before it gets expensive.

## The front door matters too

The reference architecture puts plenty in front of the agent: Cognito for OAuth (swap in any provider), AWS WAF for bot detection and IP rules, API Gateway for rate limiting. You are exposing a model to the internet, and people will try to abuse it, so you need places to shed load. Behind it, AgentCore Runtime hosts the agent in isolated sessions, tool calls pass policy and then the gateway interceptor before reaching Lambda, and IAM keeps both agent and tools on least privilege.

On shells: if you give an agent code execution, isolate it, for example in AgentCore Code Interpreter or with the open-source Strands Shell, which restricts the network addresses and files it can touch. Add egress and DNS controls, because a prompt-injected agent told to download a package is how attackers get onto your machine.

## Who should watch

Teams moving a customer-facing agent from demo to production, on AWS or not. It's an architecture talk; she ran out of time for the live demo, but the working agent with all the guardrails is in her repository. Her closing table, which labels each control as deterministic or probabilistic, is the slide worth screenshotting.

Title: When a feature flag moves a KPI, version the metric like a release
Description: Pratham Yadav of College of Southern Nevada at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026 on running old and new KPI logic in parallel, reconciling, then rolling out.
Body:
A checkout change behind a flag can move your conversion rate without a single extra order, because it quietly changed who counts as an eligible session. At Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, Pratham Yadav, Data Engineer at College of Southern Nevada, argued that data teams should treat analytics logic like a controlled software deployment: version the metric, run old and new side by side, reconcile, and only then make the new number official.

It's a short, practical talk from the side of the house that usually finds out about a flag when an executive asks why the dashboard moved.

## The denominator is where flags hide

His running example is plain on purpose. Conversion rate is completed orders divided by eligible sessions. A new checkout experience, rolled out behind a flag, changes which sessions qualify. Orders stay flat, the denominator shifts, and the KPI moves. When someone asks why the number changed, the honest answer might be that the definition changed, not the business.

And the dashboard is only the most visible consumer. The same metric feeds scheduled reports, alerts, forecasting models, planning spreadsheets, APIs and slide decks. So Pratham's question for every flag is a data question: what data contract changes when it flips? Event names, eligibility, filters, joins, aggregation, classification. If any of those move, the data team needs to know before it starts interpreting the trend line.

## Version one and version two, side by side

The core pattern is metric versioning. Instead of silently editing conversion rate, you temporarily carry conversion rate v1 and v2, each with an owner, a definition, an effective date and a description of the business rule. Before that, you map the metric as it exists today: source tables or events, filters, rules, grain, downstream consumers, owner. A definition that lives only inside a SQL file or a dashboard calculation is hard to govern, he points out, and nobody who has grepped a BI tool for a magic number will argue.

Then run both calculations over the same period and, where possible, the same population, and store enough to compare them. The dashboard should never be the first place you discover the numbers differ.

## Reconciliation explains, it doesn't just compare

What to reconcile: event and row counts, eligible population, numerator, denominator, nulls, distinct values, daily and weekly trends, then segments, because a small overall gap can hide a big one for a single product, geography or platform. In his example the new KPI runs only 0.2 percentage points higher on Monday and Tuesday, then jumps to 1.8 on Wednesday. That isn't proof v2 is wrong. It's an investigation signal: did the flag expand, did a deploy land, did the eligible population change, was there a data quality issue?

The investigation follows the pipeline (source volumes, eligibility, joins and dedup, grain, segments) and ends by tying the difference back to the flag cohort. If 20% of users got the new experience, compare flagged and unflagged groups. The flag itself becomes a lineage signal: it tells you which users experienced which business logic.

## Roll out meaning, not just code

The rollout he recommends reads like a release checklist: define v1 and v2, run in parallel, reconcile, review material differences, communicate, release to a limited audience, monitor, expand, and only retire v1 once the new definition is understood. Rollback criteria are agreed in advance. Dashboards get validated too: totals, filters, drill-downs, labels, refresh timing, the alerts tied to thresholds.

Communication is half the job. A short change notice names the metric, the rule change, the effective date, the expected impact and an owner, and says the old definition remains available for comparison. The failure modes he lists are all about lost control of the transition: silent definition changes, dashboards changed before the metric is validated, comparing totals over different populations, and deleting the old calculation too early.

## Who should watch

Analytics engineers, data platform folks and anyone who owns a number that executives quote. It's an accessible talk without heavy tooling, and the closing checklist fits on a sticky note. Feature-flag platform teams should watch it too, if only to see what their percentage rollouts look like from the warehouse.
