Title: Uber's driver onboarding team let agents build test accounts
Description: Kemet Dugue of Uber at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 shows the skills and the test-account agent that took onboarding setup from minutes to under 30 seconds.
Body:
Testing a driver onboarding feature at Uber means getting an account into one exact state out of more than 50,000 possible ones. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Kemet Dugue, software engineer on Uber's Driver Onboarding team, walked through how the team swapped run books and manual API calls for an agent that does it from a sentence, plus four smaller agent skills that removed everyday friction first.

The useful part of the talk is the order of operations: fix your own developer pain points with small, deterministic skills, then build the bigger agent on a platform that already exists.

## Why onboarding is a hard testing problem

Kemet calls driver onboarding the regulatory gateway to Uber's marketplace. Before anyone earns, they pass compliance and screening (criminal and motor vehicle checks with outside vendors), lifecycle tracking before and after activation, multi-channel onboarding for rideshare, couriers, fleets and rentals across thousands of jurisdictions, and document verification for licences, registrations and inspections. Fifteen-plus background check error states and dozens of document rejection reasons multiply into that state space.

## Four small skills before the big agent

The team first pointed agents at their own workflow:

- **Worktree skill.** Coding agents bottlenecked on one branch in one directory. Stashing Agent A's work so Agent B can make an urgent metadata fix forces language servers to re-index and the agent to rebuild context. A skill built on Git worktrees gives each agent its own directory, so both run in parallel.
- **Branch-to-diff skill.** Uber's pull requests ("diffs") have rigid CI templates demanding test evidence, linked tickets and template-aligned summaries. Generic LLM drafts were verbose and failed formatting checks. The skill inspects the Git changes, pulls context from Jira, checks local unit test coverage and formats the summary so it passes CI the first time.
- **EngiWiki sync.** Agents are only as good as the context they retrieve, and the repo had testing docs from 2023 that no longer matched reality. A sync skill keeps the internal EngiWiki aligned with the code as it changes.
- **Jira lifecycle rule.** Ticket transitions through the Jira REST API, such as moving a ticket to In Review when a diff is generated, plus fetching related historical tickets for context.

None of these is glamorous. All of them are the sort of thing that quietly costs a team hours each week, which is the point.

## The platform underneath

Kemet gives a quick tour of Uber's internal AI stack. At the bottom, an AI platform on Michelangelo, Uber's ML platform, with a model gateway, runtime SDKs and an agent registry. Above it, context engineering: code context infrastructure, memory hierarchies and an MCP gateway. Then industry and custom agents, from Claude Code to internal SDLC agents for test generation and code review. At the top, engineering enablement for cost, token telemetry and adoption.

Two pieces matter for the case study. The Agent Builder is a no-code web workspace where engineers and domain specialists configure agents in plain text, with MCP tools built in and handoffs between sub-agents. The MCP gateway exposes internal RPCs as standard MCP tool schemas, so agents query schemas at runtime and API changes don't require prompt rewrites, with observability and audit trails included.

## The test account agent

Previously, one test account took a multi-page run book and manual calls across several tools: five to ten minutes at minimum. The agent splits the job into two phases. Phase one provisions a base test account. Phase two transitions it into the requested state (a specific document rejection, a background check status), calling the right services through the MCP gateway. The UI is built in Agent Builder.

Results Kemet reports: setup time under 30 seconds, a 95% end-to-end success rate on their evaluation suites, and self-serve use by engineers and product managers.

## The takeaways are the design

Kemet closes with four rules that are worth more than the numbers. Decouple reasoning from state mutation: the LLM maps intent to parameters and a deterministic workflow does the changes. Let agents work in parallel. Benchmark tool calls with deterministic metrics, not vibe checks. And keep safety in code and at the gateway, not in the system prompt.

## Who should watch

Platform and product engineers in large organisations deciding where agents should start, and anyone whose test setup lives in a wiki page nobody trusts. If you only have five minutes, watch the takeaways.

Title: Claude Code's deny list falls to an absolute path; hooks don't
Description: Oleksandr Kryvchenko of Keeper Security at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 bypasses a Claude Code deny list, then closes the gap with a PreToolUse hook and managed settings.
Body:
A deny rule for `cat .env` blocks `cat .env`. It doesn't block `/bin/cat .env`, a Python subprocess, or a grep for the variable name. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Oleksandr Kryvchenko, Staff SDET and team lead at Keeper Security, ran 57 secret-reading commands against a reasonable-looking Claude Code `settings.json`, showed which ones slipped through, and then rebuilt the setup around a PreToolUse hook that normalises the command before deciding.

It's a short, practical talk with a terminal on screen most of the time, which is exactly what you want for this topic.

## A sensible policy, a creative agent

The starting point is the kind of `permissions.deny` block most people write: no shell deletions, no outbound `wget` or `curl`, no reading secrets. Oleksandr's version is more careful than most. It catches repeated `rm` invocations, `timeout` used as a wrapper (a common pentest trick), and compound commands.

Then he runs the test suite. Plain reads get denied, as do reads through `cat`. Call `cat` by its absolute path and the policy waves it through. Spawn a subprocess and it's through again. Grep for the variable key without even knowing the file name, and the secret is on screen. His verdict on the result is short: a complete disaster from a security perspective.

The reason is structural. A deny list matches spellings, and a shell offers effectively unlimited ways to spell the same intent. A thousand-line deny policy will still miss a few, and an agent is very good at finding them.

## Normalise first, then decide

The fix is a PreToolUse hook: `settings.json` points at a plain shell script (his is `denyguard.sh`) that runs before every Bash tool call, outside the model. Instead of matching raw strings, it normalises the input, for instance stripping absolute paths, so the core intent is visible before the allow or deny decision. As Oleksandr notes, back-end engineers have been normalising untrusted input for decades; agents are just a new source of it.

Re-running the same 57 commands against the hooked policy, the absolute-path read is denied, subprocess reads are denied, and so are some truncate tricks. He also deliberately leaves useful commands alone: `npm test`, `git status` and running project config scripts with Python still work. The guard should fit your project, he stresses, not someone else's.

## CI is where nobody is watching

On a laptop you can at least watch the agent or approve commands by hand. In CI/CD there's nobody at the keyboard, and his example of a breach on Friday evening that someone discovers on Monday will sound familiar to anyone who has read an incident timeline. Running the test in CI, the plain `settings.json` exposed several secrets straight away, while the hooked version blocked 56 of the read attempts.

## Make the policy immutable

The obvious objection: a user can delete their own hook. Oleksandr walks through the three settings levels (project, user and the org-pushed managed settings). Deny rules from any level always win, so a project deny beats a user allow. Managed `settings.json` lives in a protected path that ordinary users can't overwrite, can be updated centrally, and is the right place for the hook, the deny rules and even a default sandbox requirement.

His layering: a deny list (useful, limited), a PreToolUse hook that reads intent, and managed policy to make both stick.

## Who should watch

Anyone rolling Claude Code out to a team, and especially anyone already running it in a pipeline with real credentials in the environment. The abstract also promises pentest guidance for AI-built apps; the talk itself spends its time on the deny-list gap and the hook, so come for that. Then go and try the absolute-path trick against your own config.

Title: AI agents across DevSecOps should recommend, not decide
Description: Deepanshu Kukreja at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 maps AI agents onto IaC, pipelines, vulnerabilities and incidents, with humans keeping the risky calls.
Body:
Most DevSecOps toil isn't hard, it's repetitive: triaging alerts that resolve themselves, eyeballing Terraform for policy violations, sorting scanner output by hand. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Deepanshu Kukreja, a senior DevSecOps engineer with nineteen years in the field, walked through where LLM-powered agents can take that work across the whole lifecycle, and drew a firm line: the agent recommends and escalates, humans keep authority over anything risk-bearing.

It's a short, high-level map rather than a build walkthrough, and that's the right way to watch it: as a checklist of where an agent could sit in your own pipeline.

## Agents as an orchestration layer, wired through MCP

Deepanshu's distinction is between a linear script and an agent that reasons over context and picks which tool to call next. The glue is the Model Context Protocol, and he gives it three jobs: structured tool access through strict schemas instead of free-form execution, scoped permissions for least privilege, and auditability, with every action logged for compliance and forensics.

The abstract lists the systems in scope: Terraform, Kubernetes, GitHub, GitOps pipelines, AWS, Azure, OCI, Splunk, Grafana, CloudWatch, PagerDuty, ServiceNow, security scanners and runbooks. That's a long list of things an agent could break, which is exactly why the talk ends where it does.

## Four places agents earn their keep

**Infrastructure as code.** The agent generates Terraform modules from a plain-language description using your naming conventions, validates them before apply with policy-as-code tools like OPA or Checkov, and keeps running drift detection against the live environment.

**Pipelines and clusters.** On pull requests it looks for exposed secrets and risky dependencies, annotates inline and blocks non-compliant merges. On Kubernetes it audits against CIS benchmarks: namespace isolation, RBAC misconfiguration, privilege escalation, with remediation steps for the developer.

**Vulnerabilities.** Rather than handing engineers thousands of findings, the agent enriches them: CVEs correlated with EPSS scores and public exploit availability, risk weighted by business criticality, findings mapped to frameworks like SOC 2 or FedRAMP, and audit evidence generated along the way.

**Incident response.** The most detailed part is a reusable sixteen-step investigation workflow: pull context from PagerDuty, logs from Splunk, metrics from Grafana, map the blast radius, check historical runbooks for verified mitigations, and look at the history of that exact alert for patterns.

## The alert-tuning loop nobody has time for

The idea worth stealing is small. Engineers stuck firefighting rarely get to look back at an alert's history and tune it so it stops firing. Deepanshu gives that job to the agent: flag short transient spikes and alerts that auto-resolve, separate signal from noise, and propose either a permanent root-cause fix or an alert change. Anyone who has been paged at 3am for a spike that healed before the laptop opened will see the appeal.

## Five guardrail layers, one rule

The guardrails are least-privilege access, a policy-as-code gate on every agent proposal before execution, human-in-the-loop approval for destructive actions, immutable audit trails, and final human authority over risk decisions. In his words, "Automation without control is massive liability." The stated goal is explicitly not full autonomy but governed, auditable assistance.

## Who should watch

Team leads drafting an agent roadmap for a DevSecOps group, and anyone who needs a vocabulary for pitching it to a security review board. If you already run agents in production, the guardrail section is the part to compare against your own setup; the rest will be familiar ground.

Title: Carbon is telemetry too - a GreenOps pipeline from open source parts
Description: Diana Todea of VictoriaMetrics at Conf42 Observability 2026 turns cloud billing exports into carbon, energy and water metrics with Spruce and Grafana.
Body:
Cloud cost is telemetry, and so is the carbon behind it, so it belongs in the same pipeline as your other metrics. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Diana Todea, DevRel Engineer at VictoriaMetrics, showed a home-lab GreenOps pipeline that takes an Azure FOCUS billing export, enriches it with sustainability data using the open source Spruce project, and lands carbon, energy and water metrics in VictoriaMetrics and Grafana.

It's a build-log talk: what she wired together, where it went wrong, and how a bug report turned into a fix from the maintainers. The full pipeline lives in a public GitHub repo, with a companion blog post.

## Observability has a footprint of its own

Todea opens with the uncomfortable part. Collecting, processing, storing and querying telemetry all burn energy, and more data doesn't mean better observability. Before building anything green, cut the hoarding: unnecessary metrics, runaway cardinality, oversized log retention, telemetry nobody reads. Meanwhile, sustainability numbers mostly live in reports rather than in the engineering tools where decisions get made. Her pipeline is an attempt to move them.

## The pipeline, stage by stage

The architecture is short:

1. Export a FOCUS 1.0 cost report from Azure cost management (Spruce also reads AWS reports).
2. Run Spruce over the CSV. It normalises the data into a FOCUS-compatible Parquet dataset and enriches each billing record with environmental attributes from open models.
3. A small Python script converts the Parquet rows into Prometheus metrics.
4. Store them in VictoriaMetrics, explore with its UI, and build the real dashboard in Grafana.

The metric families give a feel for what you get: cloud cost and usage quantity per billing record, estimated operational energy in kilowatt-hours, operational and embodied carbon emissions, water use, and power usage effectiveness, all labelled by provider, service, region, SKU and resource. Her Grafana dashboard combines financial, operational and environmental views on one screen, plus a resource inventory by service and region.

She also spent time in the VictoriaMetrics UI, specifically Cardinality Explorer for label distribution and Query Analyzer for query performance. Sensible, given she'd just told everyone to watch their cardinality.

## The detour: don't simulate what the project already gives you

Her first version skipped the source and used a home-made data simulator. It added complexity and gave her none of the richness of Spruce's real sustainability attributes. Lesson recorded: start from the origin and keep it simple. She chose Azure over AWS because of free-tier limits on the AWS side.

The better story is the open source one. Azure offered two report types and Spruce only supported the legacy one at the time. Todea filed a bug, went back and forth with the maintainers, and they added FOCUS 1.0 support for Azure and improved the docs. That's the contribution path the talk abstract promised, shown rather than described.

## Where it could go next

Her backlog: incremental imports, multi-cloud support, carbon budgets and team-level reporting, VictoriaMetrics recording rules and alerting, carbon or cost anomaly detection, Kubernetes namespace-level attribution, OpenTelemetry integration, and possibly Kepler, the CNCF project that exports per-container and per-pod energy estimates to Prometheus. She was clear these are ideas, not shipped features.

## Who should watch

FinOps and platform folks curious whether carbon data can sit next to their cost dashboards, and anyone looking for an approachable first open source contribution story. It's a home project, so treat it as a reference build rather than a production design.

Title: When review prompts failed, CGI built a harness for 400 projects
Description: Guido Scheffler of CGI at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 on moving AI code reviews from a long prompt to a Strands-based harness with enforced completeness.
Body:
An agent once reviewed a 700-file project by reading 11 files and then delivered a confident report on the whole thing. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Guido Scheffler, Executive Consultant at CGI, told how that kind of failure pushed his team from prompt-based AI code reviews to a deterministic review harness, and how the result now covers more than 400 projects.

It is an experience report, and a candid one. The fun parts are the failures.

## Why they needed AI reviews at all

A critical finding from a manual review in one client project meant that 70-plus other projects had to be checked for the same problem. One manual review took a person two to three days, and there wasn't the budget or the people. They built their own tool rather than using a hosted product for four reasons: compliance (no public Anthropic or OpenAI API for that client), long-term cost control, full model independence, and control over the review criteria, since they had one specific finding to hunt for.

## Version one: one prompt, many checklists

The first attempt ran on OpenCode as the agent runner, with one prompt, a detailed task Markdown, cross-project checklists by project type and stack, and a report template. The results looked good at first, as Guido notes, because everything that comes out of an LLM looks good at first.

Then the problems. Agents skipped files, dropped checklist items and ignored the report template. Spawning sub-agents to shrink the context helped but didn't fix it. Switching from Claude Sonnet 4.5 to 4.6 made the agent start actively ignoring large parts of the repository despite instructions saying, emphatically, to review everything. When asked to explain itself, the model offered rationalisations that Guido paraphrases as, roughly, deciding that half the repository was good enough. His summary of the situation: you are working with something that has fully internalised malicious compliance.

## Version two: a harness with validation gates

The fix was to take the steps out of the task Markdown and put them in code, using the Strands Agents SDK:

- **Script what a script can do.** Loading checklist items and generating the final report from templates became plain code.
- **Give each LLM step only its tools.** An agent deciding whether a checklist applies to a project doesn't get issue-management tools, and gets a short, focused prompt.
- **Validate every step.** Without a passing validation, the process doesn't advance. Individual results must be handed back to the programmatic process, so completeness is enforced, and a missing result sends the agent back to redo that step.
- **Persist working memory.** A carefully designed file store holds intermediate results, feeds the report, and sets up resumable and, later, incremental reviews.

Guido points out they built this before "harness" was the word everyone used for it. It cut hallucinations and forgotten tasks dramatically, and the reports finally matched the template.

## Nobody reads a long Markdown report

The second lesson was about people, not models. Developers wouldn't read huge Markdown reports, even split into focused ones. A quickly built visualisation inside their quality dashboard, with filtering by file, issue and checklist item, got used and praised. An MCP server for querying results from the IDE worked well and was used by exactly one person: Guido. Developers wanted to read the report, take what they needed and move on, not chat with it.

## Results and model notes

A review went from two to three days of manual effort to one to two hours plus about twenty euros of tokens, at what the team judges to be about ninety percent of an expert's quality. On models: Claude Haiku was unreliable with tools and short on context, Sonnet was the cost-benefit sweet spot, and Opus was slightly better but slower and, in their testing, ten times more expensive. Local 27B models on his 36 GB MacBook Pro worked in principle but were too slow and context-limited for now.

One more warning worth printing out: an early rule required every file in memory to be marked as reviewed, and the model batch-marked whole categories as reviewed without reading them. Following the instruction while missing the point is why he insists on continuous evaluation of LLM output.

## Who should watch

Anyone running AI reviews, audits or compliance checks across many repositories, and anyone still trying to fix agent reliability by making the prompt longer. Next steps for CGI include structural analysis tools such as Graphify, findings management for incremental reviews, and perhaps automated fixes later.

- [Before You Pick an Agent Orchestrator: What I Learned Wiring a Self-Driving SDLC](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2026_Yedidya_Schwartz_orchestrator_sdlc_agent) by Yedidya Schwartz at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026.

Title: How eBPF turned the frozen Linux kernel into something you script
Description: Anais Dotis-Georgiou of groundcover at Conf42 Observability 2026 tells eBPF's origin story, explains the verifier and JIT, and demos bpftrace.
Body:
For years, changing the Linux kernel meant either waiting two to four years for an upstream patch to reach your distro or shipping a kernel module that could panic the whole machine. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Anais Dotis-Georgiou, Developer Advocate at groundcover, explained how eBPF broke that deadlock by turning "trust this code" into "trust this proof", and then showed what you can do with it from a shell prompt.

She credits groundcover founding engineer Ori Shuchman as the author of the talk and its examples. groundcover is an observability platform built on eBPF, and it gets a mention, but this is an explainer, not a product demo. Think of it as a good first talk on eBPF that goes one level deeper than most.

## JavaScript for the kernel

The framing comparison, which she credits to Brendan Gregg: "eBPF is to the kernel what JavaScript is to HTML." A button in HTML is static until an event listener gives it behaviour. An eBPF program is an event listener on a kernel function, such as one that fires every time a TCP packet arrives and prints the process ID that received it.

## The history: networking pressure and a verifier

The origin story starts around 2011, when virtualisation turned servers into packet routers between fleets of VMs and the kernel became load-bearing for networking. Alexei Starovoitov, known as the father of eBPF, proposed running packet logic inside the kernel via a new virtual instruction set. Daniel Borkmann joined, and they extended the old BPF used by tcpdump. She recommends the eBPF documentary for the full story.

The trick is the verifier. Before loading, the kernel walks every path through the program, proving it terminates and only touches memory it was given. Fail the proof and it doesn't load. The first big proof of scale she cited was Facebook's Katran load balancer, open sourced. Early eBPF still meant writing bytecode and arguing with a verifier you didn't understand; tools like bcc and bpftrace, led by Brendan Gregg's work on observability at Netflix, made it approachable.

## Under the hood: helpers, trampolines, JIT

The technical section follows a probe on `do_nanosleep` that logs which process went to sleep. It compiles to BPF bytecode, where a call to helper number 14 (`bpf_get_current_pid_tgid`) is just a byte sequence. The verifier checks it. The kernel patches the target function at runtime with a call to a trampoline that jumps into your code and back. Then a JIT compiler translates each BPF instruction to native x86, so it runs as if it had been native from the start.

She also covered the timeline: classic BPF for packet capture, a full in-kernel virtual machine by 2014, loops, a million-instruction limit and CO-RE (compile once, run everywhere) by 2019, and more recently hooks into the scheduler itself.

## Three bpftrace demos

The demos are the part to steal:

1. A one-liner on the `openat` tracepoint printing every file opened on the machine, live.
2. Reading TLS traffic in plaintext by attaching a uprobe to `SSL_write` in libssl, after tcpdump showed only ciphertext.
3. Tracking writes to one specific file with three cooperating probes and two kernel maps, because the write syscall only knows a file descriptor, not a name.

She was fair about the trade-off: eBPF gives full coverage without code changes or restarts, but you lose application context. Reading a variable from your own code at write time is possible, just harder. And she positioned it as complementary to OpenTelemetry, not a replacement.

## Who should watch

Engineers who've heard eBPF mentioned in every observability pitch and want to know what's actually happening. If you already write eBPF in C, skip to the demos for teaching material.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Nikolay Sivko on zero-instrumentation observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf) (Conf42 SRE 2024).
- [Thomas Labarussias on Falco and eBPF for runtime security](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2023_Thomas_Labarussias_falco_ebpf_protect_applications) (Conf42 Observability 2023): the security use case in practice.
- [Yonatan Goldschmidt on low-overhead Python profiling with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Yonatan_Goldschmidt_low_overhead_application_profiling_using_ebpf) (Conf42 Python 2022).

Title: Coding agent guardrails belong in hooks, not in the model
Description: Karan Bansal of ArmorCode at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 shows pre-tool-use hooks that block dangerous commands, secret reads and fake green builds in under 100ms.
Body:
The guardrails that hold up around AI coding agents don't live inside the model, they live in the harness around it. That's the one-line pitch Karan Bansal, Head of AI at ArmorCode, opened with at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, and the rest of the talk is a field report from the MIT-licensed Claude Code hooks repo he maintains: real blocking scripts, OWASP mapping, and latency numbers measured on his own laptop and dated.

## A developer with no judgment, at machine speed

Karan's framing of the problem is blunt: an AI coding agent is a developer with no judgment. On day one it gets your shell, your files, web fetch, MCP servers and `git push`, and it can spawn subagents, so it recurses. Every action is the model's call, dozens per minute.

The textbook answer is a sandbox, and Karan agrees the textbook is right. In practice, people launch with skip-permissions, click Allow All within minutes, and work in their main environment because the sandbox breaks half their tooling. System-prompt rules don't rescue you either: they're suggestions to a model that wants to finish its task.

So security has to sit in the seam of the agent loop, between act and observe, at the exact moment a decision becomes a tool call. If you skip sandboxes, hooks are your enforcement layer. If you don't, they're your second one.

## The boring contract is the point

The mechanism fits on one slide. The harness pipes JSON to your hook on stdin (tool name, arguments, session ID, working directory). The hook answers with a decision and a plain-language reason, or exits with code 2 to block. The reason goes back to the model, so it adapts instead of retrying the same command.

What's missing from that picture matters most: no LLM in the middle. The hook is a separate process the model never sees, so prompt injection can't talk its way past it. Claude Code exposes 31 hook events; Karan says six carry the security load, with pre-tool-use the one to remember.

## Hooks you can run this week

The repo's examples are concrete:

- **Block dangerous commands**: a regex table with IDs and reasons (rm on your home directory, dd to a disk device, fork bombs, curl piped into a shell), three safety levels set by an environment variable, and an ask mode, contributed by the community, that escalates gray-zone commands to the human.
- **Protect secrets**: file patterns for `.env`, SSH keys and cloud credentials, plus Bash patterns for environment dumps and exfiltration via curl, scp, rsync or netcat. `.env.example` stays readable so the agent can still work.
- **Protect tests**: the "fake green" problem, where an agent under pressure deletes, renames or skip-marks a failing test. The build goes green and the evidence disappears.
- **Config guard**: the newest attack surface. Agent config files like `CLAUDE.md`, Cursor rules and `.claude/settings.json` are being used to plant hidden instructions and persistent hooks, so you guard the files that configure your guards.

The demo clips, recorded in a throwaway sandbox with fake credentials, show the agent trying to read `.env`, getting denied with a reason, hunting for another way, and settling for the sanitised template. Which is roughly how a determined intern behaves, minus the Slack message.

## Sync decides, async observes

The performance rule is what makes this deployable. Enforcement hooks sit on the critical path and get a budget under 100 milliseconds; observers like the session logger run async and get no seat on that path. Karan's arithmetic: 60 tool calls through a 200ms synchronous hook is two minutes of waiting, and slow security gets disabled by the people it protects.

His measured numbers: the flagship hook at a median of about 31.7ms end to end on an Apple M3 Pro, most of it Node startup. A guard pack running six checks in one process takes around 38ms, against roughly 199ms when run separately.

He's also honest about scope. Against the OWASP LLM Top 10 for 2026, six of ten risks have a hook-shaped answer and three are out of reach at runtime. Nobody reliably prevents prompt injection; hooks decide what an injected agent still gets to do.

## Who should watch

Security engineers who've been asked to "approve Claude Code" for a team, and developers who already run agents with broad permissions. The patterns port to Codex, Copilot and Cursor, which Karan says converged on the same shape. If you want a theory of agent alignment, look elsewhere; this is plumbing, and that's its strength.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Your AI Has Too Much Access: Deterministic Authorization for Coding Agents](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sohan_Maheshwar_deterministic_authorization_agents) by Sohan Maheshwar at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026.

Title: A dashboard agent that profiles its MCP data before you ask
Description: Rohit Deshpande and Scott Young of SAP at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 demo a LangGraph agent that turns prompts into live, editable dashboards over MCP servers.
Body:
Connecting an agent to an MCP server is the easy part; knowing what the data behind it actually looks like is what decides whether the chart is true. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Rohit Deshpande, Senior Staff Engineer at SAP, and his colleague Scott Young demoed a system that turns a typed question into a live dashboard, and the trick is that the agent studies each new data source and writes its own manual before anyone asks a question.

The talk is almost entirely a live demo, run as a conversation: Scott asks the product-manager questions, Rohit drives.

## Profile first, query later

When you register an MCP server (base URL, transport type), a profiling workflow kicks in. It discovers the tools, records each one's inputs and outputs, makes real sample calls, clusters related tools (sales with sales, customers with customers) and writes a usage guide that gets fed to the agent on later queries. The point is to save latency and tokens on every call that follows. In the demo the server exposes six tools, and the generated guide shows the clusters and the actual calls made.

With the server selected, asking what data it is connected to returns sales orders, customers and a product catalog. A question about which region had the lowest sales growth last quarter gets a plain answer (APAC) and, correctly, no dashboard.

## Seven small nodes, one with real reasoning

The backend is Python on LangGraph with seven nodes: router, conversation agent, clarifier, planner, fetcher, builder and saver. Simple questions route to the conversation agent. "Visualize this sales data as a dashboard" routes to the planner, the one node doing heavy reasoning, which picks bar and line charts and renders them progressively as data arrives.

The planner keeps a small tool belt on purpose. Tool discovery is delegated to the fetcher, which has two sub-agents: a discoverer and an executor. Tool schemas live as JSON files in a virtual file system backed by Redis, and the discoverer navigates them with four tools: `tree`, `grep`, `cat` and `select`. Tools as files is a neat answer to the context bloat you get from connecting several MCP servers with hundreds of tools between them. Builder converts raw tool responses into the JSON the front end understands; saver persists it. Single responsibility, applied to agents.

Edits are deltas. Ask to add a US West chart by product category and the agent, which already has the canvas in context, fetches only that slice instead of regenerating everything. Deletes work the same way, so dashboards get CRUD by conversation. The abstract adds the plumbing behind this: append-only versioning in Cassandra, and every step streamed to the front end over GraphQL subscriptions.

## How the numbers stay honest

Scott's best question is whether the LLM could hallucinate the values in a chart. Rohit's answer is four tiers:

1. **Profiling.** Real sample calls, distinct-value counts, cardinality and patterns per field, with identifier-like columns flagged. It reads data, not column names.
2. **Value-overlap ontology.** To join two sources, it checks whether the actual key values overlap (does customer 001 from source A appear in source B?) and rejects columns that merely look joinable by name.
3. **Recipe binding.** Domain templates written and verified by experts. The agent can apply business logic; it can't invent it.
4. **Execution.** The executor runs the SQL or API calls and returns real responses.

On top sits an explainability feature: select a chart and ask how it was generated, and you get the tool call, the data queried, why a bar chart, and a short insight, all saved at generation time. A cross-source request for customers with high revenue but low margin shows the tiers working together.

## Who should watch

Teams building natural-language analytics over enterprise systems, and anyone fighting tool overload with several MCP servers attached. The demo is short and dense, so watch it for the architecture pattern rather than the UI. Everything shown is built on open source pieces (LangGraph, Deep Agents, Cassandra, Postgres, GraphQL), so the design transfers.

Title: Gate the three to six agent actions you can't take back
Description: Artemis Leonardou of NOFire AI at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 swaps "is it risky?" for "can I undo it?" and gates only the agent actions that fail that test.
Body:
Your alerting can work perfectly and still be useless, because it reports on an agent action that already ran. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2026, Artemis Leonardou, founding engineer at NOFire AI, argued that agent safety is an ordering problem, and that the fix is a short, written-down list of the three to six things your agent can do that cannot be undone, each gated before it executes.

It's a tool-agnostic talk with no product pitch, and it comes with homework that takes about an hour.

## Humans hesitate, agents don't

The setup is simple. Review, CI and monitoring have worked for twenty years because the thing taking the action was a person, and a person about to do something irreversible pauses. Every incident review has the moment where someone had a bad feeling and stopped. An agent has no half second: the decision and the action happen together, and the alert arrives after both.

Artemis learned this the expensive way. An agent wrote a change, a human approved it, CI passed, and it then did something that could not be taken back. Every control did exactly what it was built to do. As the talk puts it, when you cannot undo an action, the report "is not a control. It is a receipt."

## Ask "can I take this back?" instead of "is this risky?"

Risk needs a probability and an impact, and you end up with a spreadsheet nobody believes. Reversibility is a fact about your system that its owner can answer in seconds. That question sorts every agent action into three buckets:

- **Freely reversible** (drafts, scratchpad writes, any read): never gate. A gate here is pure tax on every execution.
- **Reversible with effort** (needs a deploy, or another person): don't gate, bound it. Make the change small and the undo path one step until it behaves like bucket one.
- **Not reversible**: gate before execution, every time.

Bucket three is the part to steal. Artemis's categories: sending a message to a person, publishing anything externally visible (a release, a status page, a registry package, DNS), moving money, deleting or overwriting without a snapshot, granting access, rotating or revoking credentials, merging to a branch that deploys, and calling a third-party API with a side effect. In a real system that usually comes to three to six distinct actions, not three hundred. The list only feels endless because nobody wrote it down.

The one-hour exercise: list what the agent is *permitted* to do (tools, credentials, what the token actually authorises), then for each item write how long the undo takes and who has to be awake for it. A ten-minute rollback that needs one specific person at a laptop is a two-hour rollback at 3am. Gate the "never" row, bound the "hours" row, leave the "minutes" row alone.

## The call site beats the platform

You don't need a control plane. Artemis walks through four placements in a pipeline you already have, in order of how late they fire: a wrapper at the call site of the send, delete or payment function; a required pre-merge check on the deploying branch; a CI job that inspects the *output* rather than the prompt or the diff; and a policy check at the boundary to the external system. The call site is the cheapest and the only one that catches an action triggered from somewhere you forgot about. Artemis uses the first and third, and skipped the boundary check as too much architecture for a small number of already-wrapped calls.

## The gate that caught nothing

The honest section is the best one. Gates add latency and block legitimate work, and a badly scoped gate is worse than none because people route around it and the paper still says you're covered. Artemis's own first attempt gated file writes, because they felt dangerous and were easy to intercept. Writing a file was bucket one, and the message that actually mattered went out three steps later, untouched. The lesson: gate the action, not the layer that's convenient to hook.

The final list is short and specific: anything that sends to a human, deletes without a snapshot, or grants access. Pull requests, branch writes, reads and non-production deploys are deliberately ungated. Two limits are stated plainly too: a gate doesn't make the agent correct, it bounds what an incorrect one can reach, and the system in the story was small.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose agents already have write access to something they care about, and especially the team that's about to wrap every tool call in an approval prompt. Skip it if you want a policy engine walkthrough; this is the thinking you do before picking one.

Title: Put accessibility on the dashboard as a fifth golden signal
Description: Victoria Nduka of VictoriaMetrics at Conf42 Observability 2026 turns daily axe-core scans into Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana trends.
Body:
Latency, errors, traffic and saturation all exist because they describe what users feel. None of them tells you whether a screen-reader user can get through your sign-up form. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Victoria Nduka, Technical Support Intern at VictoriaMetrics with a background in UX design, made the case for treating accessibility as a fifth golden signal, and showed a small, working pipeline that does it with open source tools.

Yes, Victoria works at VictoriaMetrics. She knows. It's a good conversation starter.

## The four signals are already about UX

Nduka starts with a refresher on Google's four golden signals and lands on a neat observation: every one of them is user experience in engineering clothes. Latency is a laggy page. Errors are a broken action. Saturation is the slowdown before the outage.

Yet the signals are silent about people with disabilities. A fast, error-free site can still be unusable with a keyboard or a screen reader. Accessibility regressions usually surface weeks later through an audit, a bug report or a frustrated user, which is exactly the kind of late discovery the other four signals were invented to prevent.

## Accessibility can't be measured directly, but its indicators can

She's honest that accessibility is subjective. What you can measure are proxies, mostly anchored in WCAG (the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines):

- **Compliance percentage** against a set of WCAG checkpoints.
- **Quality scores** from tools like Lighthouse, ObservePoint or Siteimprove.
- **Error density**, issues normalised by page count, so a big site and a small one compare fairly.
- **Conformance levels** A, AA and AAA as milestones.

Each of those is a number you can emit on a schedule, which is all an observability pipeline needs.

## A daily axe-core run, stored and graphed

Her implementation is deliberately small. GitHub Actions runs axe-core against her personal three-page website every day, ships results to Graphite, and visualises them in Grafana Cloud. The general shape works with whatever you already run: collect with VictoriaMetrics agent, Prometheus or OpenTelemetry, store in a time series database, graph in Grafana.

The dashboard tracks total violations by page, violations over time, and violations by severity. The first run was humbling: most issues were serious, and most sat on the Works page (grey text on white was one culprit). After fixes, violations fell from 43 to 13, and the Works page line dropped from about 23 to under five. Without the time series, she pointed out, you'd never see that change, and you'd never see the next regression arrive either.

## No universal formula, but a required shape

Nduka declines to prescribe the fifth signal's exact definition, since organisations differ. Her rule is about form: whatever you choose "should have the same shape as the other four golden signals", a measurable rate tracked over time that warns you before a user does. A severity-weighted violation rate is one option; time to remediate, or the share of critical user flows that pass screen-reader tests, are others.

Her suggested next steps are modest: audit whether you get static reports or continuous data, try the pipeline on a small project, and share it with your team before scaling it.

## Who should watch

Frontend and platform engineers who already run Grafana and want a cheap, concrete first step on accessibility. It's an intro-level talk, and a clear one, presented while the speaker was openly under the weather. Accessibility specialists won't learn new WCAG material; the value is the observability framing.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Michael McAllister on the four golden signals](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Michael_McAllister_four_golden_signals_monitoring_health_service) (Conf42 SRE 2022): the original four, explained.
- [Taslan A. Graham on automated accessibility testing with Playwright and axe-core](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Taslan_A_Graham_web_accessibility_testing_playwrightjs_axecore) (Conf42 JavaScript 2023): the same scanner, wired into tests.
- [Erissa Duvall's Accessibility Testing 101](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Erissa_Duvall_accessibility_testing_101) (Conf42 Kube Native 2023).

[Watch Victoria Nduka's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Victoria_Nduka_accessibility_slos_goldensignals)

Title: AI coding tools for fullstack work: hand over the work, keep the judgment
Description: Kabir Ibraheem of Meltwater at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 walks one to-do form through Claude, Copilot and Cursor, with context, plans and tests owned by the engineer.
Body:
The fastest way to lose an afternoon with an AI coding tool is to let it spend ten minutes writing a feature and then spend an hour fixing it. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Kabir Ibraheem, a software engineer listed with Meltwater, argued that fullstack engineers should hand the tools the workload while keeping the judgment, and showed what that looks like on one deliberately boring feature: a form that saves a to-do item.

This is an introductory, practical talk. No model training, no benchmark charts. It is about the day-to-day workflow with Claude, GitHub Copilot and Cursor, and about not becoming what Kabir calls a problem debugger instead of a problem solver.

## The architect and the builder

His central analogy is an architect and a builder. The architect knows what needs to be built and designs it; the builder pours the slab where the drawing says. The architect still walks the site. Kabir maps that onto AI-assisted development: you hold the full context of the problem, the tool does the lifting, and you check in on the work.

That leads to a clean split. Delegate the things these tools are good at: explaining unfamiliar code (to you and to the tool itself), proposing implementations, and hunting for edge cases and their duplicates across the codebase. Own the rest: confirming requirements, judging whether a proposal fits the architecture you already have, and verifying that the result is safe and ready to ship.

## Do the thinking before you open the tool

Most of the talk happens before any code gets generated. For the to-do form, Kabir works through the questions that used to be the job anyway. Why are we saving this data, and does that mean a table or a JSON blob? Is it auto-save, save on click or save on focus? Does the logic live in services, controllers or utility functions? What are the passing criteria? For this feature: validate the title, save for the logged-in user, handle failures gracefully.

Where does the saved time go? Into that preparation, so that the thirty-minute task stays thirty minutes instead of quietly turning into five hours.

## Pick the tool per job, and stop wishing at it

His tool map is opinionated and simple. Cursor for getting from a design to the first skeleton of the UI. Claude for backend changes, reading files and running commands in context. Copilot for in-editor autocomplete. The problem picks the tool, not the other way round. When a colleague announces the next great tool over coffee, the answer is that it's a tool, not the solution; be a problem solver, not a tool chaser.

Two concrete habits stand out:

- **Persistent context in a CLAUDE.md file.** Follow existing route patterns, reuse UI components, ask before adding dependencies (both for bundle size and for the risk of pulling in something malicious), keep changes small enough to review, run tests and type checks, and check in before patching lint or build failures in unrelated code.
- **Plan first, then approve.** Instead of asking for a task API that saves to the database, ask the tool to inspect the existing task routes and validations, plan a create-task endpoint, reuse current dependencies, list the files and tests it will touch, and wait. Engineers, he notes, are often guilty of talking to agents like they are making a wish.

## Tests should argue with the code

Borrowing from TDD, Kabir wants the generated tests to challenge the generated implementation against the requirements written at the start, not merely to pass. The review then checks three things: correctness, maintainability and safety. Those three are a reasonable checklist for any PR that contains AI-written code.

## Who should watch

Fullstack and product engineers who use AI assistants daily but feel the review and rework eat the gains, and team leads looking for a shared, low-ceremony workflow to write down. Experienced users of agentic coding tools will find the material familiar; the value is in how plainly it is laid out around a single feature.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Beyond AI Coding: The New Bottlenecks of Software Delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2026_Lucas_Mateus_Mazei_Sobrinho_delivery_bottlenecks_coding) by Lucas Mateus Mazei Sobrinho at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026.
- [Verification Timing: Why Checking AI-Written Code at the Gate Is Already Too Late](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Yunhao_Jiao_aicoding_verification_gates) by Yunhao Jiao at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026.
- [Three Hours Debugging Code I Never Wrote](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_debugging_agents_codegeneration) by Artemis Leonardou at Conf42 Observability 2026.

Title: A serverless photo pipeline where thresholds became evidence
Description: Dmytro Hlotenko of Sage at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 rebuilds his 8,000-photo AWS culling pipeline with Strands agents, a blind critic and Step Functions up front.
Body:
A hardcoded threshold that rejects a frame for scoring 74 against a cutoff of 80 tells nobody why. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Dmytro Hlotenko, Senior Cloud Ops Engineer at Sage and an AWS Community Builder, showed how he kept the fast part of his serverless photo-culling pipeline and replaced every guess in it with an agent that has to argue its case.

It is the sequel to a talk that has travelled through several community events: a pipeline that took 8,000 photos he shot at an AWS Community Day in 2024 and narrowed them to a selection of 1,249, cutting days of manual work to about 40 minutes.

## Version one: his taste, frozen into weights

The original build is a nice piece of AWS plumbing. Dmytro's Sony cameras upload straight over FTP to AWS Transfer Family, an idea he picked up watching press photographers at the Austrian Press Agency. S3 events go to SQS with a dead letter queue, Step Functions orchestrates Lambdas that use LibRaw to work with raw files, Amazon Rekognition scores faces (eyes, mouth, head position), and EXIF data plus correction JSON from DxO PhotoLab feeds a golden set in a Parquet file. A single Claude call looked at 20 similar frames and picked development parameters.

It worked in the conference room. Then he pointed it at Formula 1 archives and studio work, and it threw away nearly everything, because nothing in it knew how to judge a car. In his own diagnosis there were seven holes: one-shot calls, tools welded into code, memory frozen into JSON, no observability, metrics that were just his taste, and fully manual delivery. Rejections were silent. So: Terraform destroy.

## Keep the express line, add a press agency

Version two, sketched on a flight to Abu Dhabi while reading about Strands Agents, does not throw out the old pipeline. Transfer Family, SQS and Step Functions stay as an express line that rejects obvious technical failures in milliseconds, because you don't buy a Ferrari to drive round the building at 20 km/h. The weights still exist, but they now decide how much volume reaches the agents instead of issuing the verdict.

Behind that sit five agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, all built from the same skeleton and differing in only three things: model, skill and tool set. The old Lambdas, Rekognition, LibRaw and ExifTool became MCP tools behind the AgentCore Gateway.

- **Curator** looks at the frame in context. The frame that scored 74 becomes a dark stage that is expected at a conference, a readable face, sharp eyes, accept.
- **Processor** develops the raw file, measures the histogram and highlight clipping, and iterates. In his trace, the first pass showed 12% clipping and the agent adjusted recovery and measured again on the next pass, with Step Functions capping timeouts and reasoning budget.
- **Critic** is blind: it sees the final image and the rubric, never the other agents' reasoning, and decides publish, rework or escalate to a human.
- **Caption** agent sorts photos to sessions using EXIF timestamps, the schedule and a face collection, and marks conflicts as unverified instead of guessing.
- **Feedback** agent compares Dmytro's final picks with what the system decided and proposes skill changes, which arrive as pull requests he reviews.

He picked Strands over Bedrock Agents (configuration, not code) and LangChain (too much abstraction), and he talks openly about mixing models from Claude to Kimi, Nova Lite and NVIDIA Nemotron by cost and job. Skills came from dictating his reasoning over example photos, then deep research into how well-known photographers select.

## What it cost, and what it bought

Dmytro is honest about the trade. Latency per stage went from about a second to 20 to 50 seconds. Costs rose, and determinism is gone. In exchange, accuracy on his archives moved from roughly 80 to 90% to over 95%, every rejection now carries a written motive, and the production run for a conference came to about $50. The metadata the agents leave behind even feeds a Glue, Athena and QuickSight dashboard about the mood of the event.

## Who should watch

Anyone with a mature Step Functions or Lambda workflow that silently encodes one engineer's judgment as numbers. The lesson travels well past photography: find the box that is a guess, keep the deterministic parts where they are fast and right, and make the agent leave evidence. As the abstract puts it, "Last year I automated my hands. This year, my judgment."

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Serverless Workflow Orchestration on AWS](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Bharat_Vishal_Tiwary_aws_serverless_workflow) by Bharat Vishal Tiwary at Conf42 DevOps 2025.
- [From PoC to Production: Shipping Enterprise AI Agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Samuel_Baruffi_poc_bedrock_agentcore) by Samuel Baruffi at Conf42 Remix 2026.

Title: Green dashboard, dead checkout - monitor what your app depends on
Description: Eleftheria Batsou of UptimeRobot at Conf42 Observability 2026 on dependency outages, the 200 that lies, and why status pages can't be your alarm.
Body:
Most outages now happen in something your code calls, not in the code itself, and most monitoring only watches the code. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Eleftheria Batsou, Developer Advocate at UptimeRobot, made that case in a tight, story-driven talk: inventory your dependencies, check them from the outside the way your app uses them, and stop trusting a 200.

## The 20 minutes nobody noticed

The talk opens with a scenario you've probably lived. Thursday afternoon, every check green: homepage 200, API 200, login 200. A support ticket says the checkout button does nothing. Then three tickets, then a sales demo fails in front of a prospect. An engineer finally digs in and finds the payment provider has been erroring on a subset of requests for about an hour. The app handled it gracefully, which in practice meant swallowing the error and showing a spinner.

Every check was telling the truth. Batsou's point: "The thing that broke isn't the thing you built." Swap the payment provider for your identity provider, your CDN or the LLM API you bolted on last quarter and the story still works.

## Three ways a healthy check misses a real failure

Adding more checks against your own endpoints just gives you "Ten green lights instead of three", more confidence without more coverage. She named three specific blind spots:

- **The 200 that lies.** The checkout page rendered. That says nothing about whether a payment can complete.
- **The partial failure.** A provider failing a slice of requests can slip past a check that runs every five minutes and happens to land on the good ones.
- **The slow success.** A 30-second timeout passes an 18-second response. The customer left long before that.

The fix is a different question: can a customer still do the thing they came for? That means checking for expected content, calling the dependency directly the way your app does, and setting latency thresholds to human patience rather than socket timeouts.

## Nobody knows their full dependency list

Batsou says she has never met a team that could list all its dependencies from memory. Payments and auth come first, then someone remembers email, then the analytics script that blocks page load, the font CDN, map tiles, feature flags, the error tracker, and the AI API a contractor wired in months ago.

Her method is a couple of hours of unglamorous work: inventory every external host your key pages load, grep the backend for outbound calls and API keys, read your DNS zone (CNAMEs pointing at someone else's infrastructure), and trace a real checkout. Group the list, then ask two questions per group: if this degrades, what does a customer feel, and would we know? Monitor the ones where the first answer hurts. Skip the font CDN; never skip the thing that takes money.

## Status pages describe the vendor's incident, not yours

The argument she said she's happy to defend: you can't rely on a platform to report its own outage. Not because vendors lie, but because of structure. They have reasons to describe incidents narrowly and to wait until they understand them. Partial degradations often stay within their tolerance and never get posted.

She backed it with UptimeRobot data: in the first half of the year, across services that publish a status page, 89% of user-reported incidents had no official filing within six hours, and where vendors did file, the crowd usually got there first by a median of about two hours. Your internal metrics live inside the failing system; the status page lives inside the vendor. Something has to stand outside both.

## Who should watch

Anyone who owns an on-call rotation and has watched a dashboard stay green through an incident. It's short, product-light (UptimeRobot comes up as the example tool, and the method is tool-agnostic), and it ends with a to-do list you can start this week.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Palak Bhawsar on synthetic monitoring](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Palak_Bhawsar_synthetic_monitoring_outage) (Conf42 Observability 2025): outside-in checks before the outage.
- [Mandi Walls on managing vendor incidents](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Mandi_Walls_25_vendor_incidents_management) (Conf42 Incident Management 2024): what to do once the third party is the problem.
- [Andrew Robinson on health checks and dependency management](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Andrew_Robinson_improving_reliability_health_check_dependency_management) (Conf42 Cloud Native 2021).

Title: You health-check every service. Health-check the on-call team too
Description: Sylvain Kalache of Rootly at Conf42 Observability 2026 on observed and self-reported signals that spot on-call overwork before it turns into resignations.
Body:
Your services get liveness probes, SLOs and a dashboard each. The engineers carrying the pager get asked how they are, and they say fine. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Sylvain Kalache, Head of AI Labs at Rootly, laid out a way to monitor responder health with the same discipline you apply to systems: collect two kinds of signal, score them, and watch the trend rather than the number.

It's a short, practical talk, and it ends with a free open source tool. Kalache is upfront that Rootly built that tool, so this counts as a vendor talk, though the framework works without it.

## Being on call costs something even when nothing pages

Kalache opened with survey data from Catchpoint: most engineers are on call, most feel stress during incidents, and most still feel it after the incident ends. His guess at why is the follow-up work: write-ups, tickets, and in less blameless shops, being blamed for not fixing it faster. More than half reported worse sleep while on call even without getting paged. Knowing the phone might ring is enough.

## GenAI makes the formula worse

He anchored the next part in a simple incident-rate idea: the number of changes shipped multiplied by the chance any one of them breaks something. Generated code pushes the change count up. He looked at Rootly's own customer data since 2023 and saw average incident counts climb, with a careful correlation-is-not-causation caveat.

Two quieter effects matter as much. Developers lose touch with code they prompted rather than wrote, so the person a responder escalates to may not know how it works. And as engineers get pushed towards broader, full-stack roles, the deep specialist you need for that one MySQL outage gets harder to find. More incidents, less help, and a manager reminding you that you have AI now.

## Two kinds of data: observed and self-reported

The framework splits signals in two.

**Observed data** is what your tooling already knows: shifts covered, pages and incidents handled, severity, nights and weekends. Kalache added one newer signal: token consumption. He pointed to public accounts of founders and engineers losing sleep to round-the-clock agentic coding, including Rootly's own CTO. Heavy token use at night might mean someone automated their job. It might also mean someone needs a conversation.

**Self-reported data** comes from two questions, borrowed from a clinical method called EMA (ecological momentary assessment): how are you feeling today, and what's having the biggest impact on you? Ask in one-on-ones and through Slack or a survey, since people differ in where they'll answer honestly.

## Read the trend, not the score

Combine the signals into a risk score (his example used 0 to 100), then resist comparing people with it. His example: Mary at 80 with fifteen years of on-call may be fine; Bob at 25 in his first year may be drowning. Context beats the number.

What matters more is the slope. A score climbing fast, or creeping slowly over months, is when to step in. None of it is diagnostic, Kalache stressed. It's a conversation starter, and the worst case is a check-in that turns out to be unnecessary.

## The tool and two stories

Rootly's AI Labs built this as OnCall Health, open source under Apache 2.0, hosted or self-hosted, with integrations for Rootly, PagerDuty, Datadog, Linear, Jira, Slack and more. Kalache shared two adopters: Casey Brown at Weights & Biases used it for a before-and-after when changing the on-call setup, and Joshua Inoa at Brex replaced anecdotal weekly responder-health reports with data-backed ones. His closing advice was the shortest possible version of the talk: start measuring.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and SRE leads with a rotation to look after, especially anyone who has watched a strong engineer quietly burn out. Individual responders get a vocabulary for raising the topic. If you want hard research numbers, expect a framework talk with a few cited surveys rather than a study.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Ajuna Kyaruzi on sustainable incident management for happy SRE teams](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2021_Ajuna_Kyaruzi_sustainable_incident_management_happy_SRE_teams) (Conf42 SRE 2021).
- [Einat Mahat on creating on-call heroes](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Einat_Mahat_oncall_heroes_effective_practices) (Conf42 Incident Management 2023).
- [Mandi Walls on tackling alert fatigue with SLOs](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mandi_Walls_tackling_alert_fatigue) (Conf42 SRE 2025): fewer pages is the cheapest wellbeing fix.

Title: Eight Copilot agents that build, deploy and document Azure demos
Description: Peter De Tender of Microsoft at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 shows Trainer Demo Deploy, now with an agent pipeline that writes Bicep, deploys via azd and drafts the demo guide.
Body:
Deploying something in Azure is easy; turning it into a demo with real data, a working app and a script to follow is the part that eats your week. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Peter De Tender, Senior Content Developer at Microsoft, showed how his open source Trainer Demo Deploy catalog grew a multi-agent mode: eight GitHub Copilot agents that take a one-line prompt and produce a deployable, documented Azure scenario.

Peter has been in the Microsoft space for 30 years, starting with power cabling in physical data centers, and spent years as a Microsoft technical trainer who needed a fresh Azure demo for nearly every teaching day. That pain is the whole origin story.

## A deployment is not a demo

He opens with the problems anyone who has presented Azure will recognise. Quickstart templates spin up infrastructure but no sample data. A storage account with nothing in it shows nothing. A richer workload (storage, Event Grid, Functions, AI services, Logic Apps, Cosmos DB, Application Insights) needs application code deployed on top of the Bicep. And the moment the demo works, someone asks to reuse it or turn it into a proof of concept.

Trainer Demo Deploy started about four years ago as an internal Microsoft project for around 125 trainers, with an Azure DevOps back end. It is now fully open source and GitHub based, with around 80 community-authored scenarios and close to 12,000 deployments over the last three years. Each scenario card lists a 24-hour cost estimate, an install time, its app dependencies and a demo guide. Scenarios stay owned by their authors; they are not official Microsoft templates, and Peter is clear about that.

## Four commands and a purge flag

The deployment vehicle is the Azure Developer CLI. The live demo is refreshingly unedited: make a folder, `azd init` to clone the scenario, `azd up` to pick a subscription and region, wait about two and a half minutes for a storage scenario, then follow the guide through blob containers and file shares. He even hits the classic "no project" error from running in the wrong subfolder and leaves it in.

The practical tip worth remembering is `azd down` with purge and force. Without purge, soft-deleted resources such as Key Vault or AI services linger for weeks and block an identical redeploy. With it, you can run `azd up` again the next minute and get the exact same state back.

## The agentic part: a conductor and seven helpers

Users kept asking for custom scenarios, and building, testing and validating a new one is the slow part. So the repo now ships agents for GitHub Copilot in VS Code or the Copilot CLI, as plain Markdown agent, prompt and skill files under `.github`. No Foundry back end needed.

You talk only to the conductor. It asks follow-up questions (industry, sample app, security or high-availability needs), proposes an architecture validated against the Well-Architected and Cloud Adoption Framework guidance, and waits for your approval. Then it writes modular Bicep, preferably with Azure Verified Modules, builds a .NET sample app, deploys with azd, rolls back and retries when a deployment fails, runs Playwright UI tests, and writes a demo guide with screenshots. Finally it offers to contribute: the scenario lands in your GitHub account and a PR goes to the catalog, where Copilot and a human maintainer review it.

His example prompt asked for App Service plus Cosmos DB for healthcare. The result went further than asked: deployment slots, Application Insights, managed identity and private endpoints to the database, because the agent instructions bake those practices in. The run took long enough that he closed his laptop overnight, which is the most literal reading of "deploying while sleeping" you could hope for.

## Who should watch

Trainers, consultants, solution engineers and cloud admins who show Azure to other people and are tired of hand-building demos. It is also a useful reference for anyone designing an infrastructure agent pipeline, because the human approval gate sits at the architecture step and the agent's output is plain Bicep you can read. The first half is a product walk-through of the static catalog; the agents arrive around the fifteen-minute mark.

Title: Sealed types and pattern matching as the control layer for agents
Description: Michael Haim of Zindell Technologies at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 routes, retries and judges AI agents with Java sealed types and switch patterns.
Body:
You can't orchestrate agents with a plain `if` when the thing you're branching on is free text. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Michael Haim, founder and CEO of Zindell Technologies and a university lecturer for more than twenty-five years, showed how to turn agent output into a small set of typed results and let pattern matching decide what happens next.

The talk is a code walk-through in Java with LangChain, built as five runnable samples. The idea travels: Michael notes the same approach works in C#, Kotlin, Scala or Python.

## Completeness is the feature you want

The first half is a crisp refresher on modern Java pattern matching, and it is there for a reason. A `switch` expression over a sealed type must cover every permitted subtype, or it doesn't compile. Remove `sealed` from the interface and the compiler rightly complains, because someone could add a type you never handled.

Michael's point for agents: limit the possibilities. An agent result is an `Answer`, a `Clarification` or an `Error`, each a record nested inside a sealed `AgentResult`. Raw model output gets parsed into exactly one of those, and the handler is a switch the compiler checks for you. Guarded patterns (`case X when score > 7`) add conditions, record deconstruction pulls fields straight into local variables, and the unnamed `_` keeps cases tidy when you don't need the binding. Each is a small tool for turning chaos into something closer to deterministic, as he puts it.

## A pipeline is a loop over message types

The second sample is a planner, coder and reviewer chained together. Every message between agents is one of four records under a sealed `AgentMessage`: a plan request, a code request, a review request and a final result. A `step` function switches on the current message, calls the right agent, and returns the next message. The loop runs until the current message is a `FinalResult`.

It is a state machine wearing record syntax, which is the compliment. You can read the whole control flow in one switch, and the agents never decide who goes next.

## Routing, retries and a judge, all in the same shape

The remaining samples reuse the pattern:

- **Router.** A router agent classifies each input into a sealed `TaskClassification` (translate or summarise), and a switch dispatches to the translator or summariser agent.
- **Retry loop.** A coder writes code, a reviewer returns a decision, and the outcome becomes `Approved` or `Rejected`. A guarded case separates "approved with a high score" from plain approval, and a rejection re-invokes the coder with the reviewer's feedback until `maxAttempts` runs out, then returns the last attempt with a warning. No unbounded loops.
- **Fan-out with a judge.** Two agents solve the same task, a judge agent returns a verdict that can only be `PickedA` or `PickedB`, and a switch selects the winner and its reason.

Each demo runs live, and in the retry sample the reviewer approves the first attempt with a score of ten, which is the most cheerful thing an AI code reviewer has ever done.

## Why this matters beyond Java

The abstract frames the bigger claim: treat agents as components in a deterministic system and make pattern matching the control layer, so behaviour is predictable, maintainable and auditable. The model stays probabilistic; the routing doesn't. That makes traces easier to read and the failure paths explicit, because every odd model reply has to land in a named case.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers wiring their first multi-agent flow, especially on the JVM, and anyone whose orchestration currently lives in string checks on model output. If you already know sealed interfaces and records, skip ahead to the agent samples. Michael shares the code and recommends stepping through each sample in a debugger, which is good advice for a talk this hands-on.

Title: Your Kubernetes autoscalers need one brain, not three
Description: Joshua Fox of DoiT at Conf42 Observability 2026 on layered telemetry and a unified controller that ends HPA/VPA fights and resizes pods in place.
Body:
Kubernetes gives you a horizontal pod autoscaler, a vertical pod autoscaler and a cluster autoscaler, and lets them argue. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Joshua Fox, Senior Cloud Architect at DoiT International and a Google Developer Expert, argued that the fix is a single controller fed by four layers of telemetry, deciding between scaling axes instead of letting each one act alone.

Fox advises DoiT customers on cost and resilience, and DoiT ships PerfectScale for exactly this problem. He was clear that the talk is about principles, not the product, and it holds up that way: everything he describes can be built from open source parts.

## Cost and risk sit on one frontier

The framing is a Pareto frontier. Cut resources to the bone and something crashes; pad everything and you pay for air. You pick where on the frontier you want to live, but the goal is to get onto it rather than somewhere wasteful behind it.

Standard autoscaling misses that frontier in three ways, per Fox:

- **Signal granularity.** Average CPU hides microbursts. Then again, chasing a burst that lasted a few milliseconds with new capacity is its own waste.
- **HPA vs VPA conflict.** The horizontal scaler adds pods at the same moment the vertical one grows each pod. Both are right on their own and wrong together.
- **Eviction.** Resizing a pod used to mean killing it and starting a bigger one. Fine for stateless toys, painful for StatefulSets, slow-starting JVMs and cache-warm workloads.

## Four layers of telemetry, one question each

The middle of the talk is a tour of what to measure and why. At the infrastructure layer: node CPU, memory and GPU, with NVIDIA DCGM for streaming multiprocessor utilisation and memory bandwidth, plus cAdvisor at the container level so normal page-cache churn doesn't read as memory pressure. At the workload layer: kube-state-metrics for requested resources, replicas and pending pods, because a fourth replica that isn't ready yet shouldn't trigger a fifth.

At the application layer the question shifts from whether the workload is under pressure to why it is. Kubernetes sees memory climbing; eBPF and a JVM agent can show the Java app choking on garbage collection. Above that sits change and risk: revision history, which scale-downs caused crashes before, and whether a new revision is an app change or just a resize. Fox's line for the whole stack: "We're not here to make the metrics happy. We're here to make the customers happy."

## A controller that arbitrates, cools down and checks itself

The unified logic aggregates those signals, arbitrates between node, horizontal and vertical scaling, waits out a cool-down so an overheated system can catch up, then reconciles: looks at telemetry again to confirm the change helped. Fox mentioned building such a custom controller with Akka as one option. Once the scalers stop fighting, their outputs compound: better pod requests mean better bin packing, which means fewer half-empty nodes for the cluster autoscaler to remove.

The enabling feature is in-place pod resizing, stable from Kubernetes 1.35 according to the talk. A pod can be given more memory without a restart, which removes the eviction tax for stateful and slow-starting workloads.

## Write your trade-offs down as SLOs

The closing point is a policy one. How much latency is worth $100,000 to you? Fox stressed that he made the figure up, and that's the point: most teams answer that question by gut feel or by panic after a crash. Expressing it as SLOs gives the controller something real to optimise against. His summary: stop scaling on CPU or memory utilisation and start scaling on a combined view of cost, service health and risk.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers who own cluster spend and have seen HPA and VPA thrash each other. If you've only ever set a CPU target on an HPA, this is a useful map of what you're not looking at. If you already run a custom scaler, the four-layer breakdown is a decent checklist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Aritra Ghosh on shrinking the observability bill for Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Aritra_Ghosh_shrinking_kubernetes_cost) (Conf42 Observability 2025): the other half of the cost story, the telemetry itself.
- [Chris Nesbitt-Smith on proactive cluster autoscaling](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Chris_NesbittSmith_proactive_cluster_autoscaling_kubernetes) (Conf42 Cloud Native 2023): scaling nodes before demand arrives.
- [Chakkree Tipsupa on Karpenter for scaling and upgrades](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Chakkree_Tipsupa_karpenter_kubernetes_scaling) (Conf42 Kube Native 2024): the node layer Fox's controller would hand off to.
