Title: Your agent doesn't need an LLM to plan, just a graph and a search
Description: Maureese Williams of Disney at Conf42 AI Agents 2026 shows GATS, a tree-search planner that calls the model only for novel states and caches the answer.
Body:
Most agent loops ask the language model what to do next at every single step, even for steps they have already solved a hundred times. At Conf42 AI Agents 2026, Maureese Williams, AI Engineer at Disney, presented GATS (Graph-Augmented Tree Search), a planner that runs UCB1 tree search over a state graph the agent builds for itself and treats the LLM as the last resort.

The payoff is a plan you can replay. The search is deterministic, so identical starting conditions give an identical plan, which is something a sampled model call can't promise.

## The default loop has amnesia

Maureese starts with the mundane bit. A twenty-step task means twenty model calls, every run. On the second run of an identical task the agent asks the identical question and gets an answer drawn from a distribution, not a lookup table.

He counts three costs. Dollars scale with plan depth and never amortise. Latency is inference time multiplied by the number of sequential decisions. And the one he cares most about: the plan isn't reproducible, because the artifact you would need to replay it, a record of the decision procedure, never existed. If a plan fails downstream, you often can't reconstruct how you got there.

## Consult what you can prove, then what you measured

The core of GATS is an escalation ladder with three layers:

- **L1, symbolic.** Known preconditions and effects. Applicability is a set-membership test, effects are add and delete sets. Exact, nearly free, and it covers most of an agent's day.
- **L2, learned.** For actions that turn out to be stochastic, a frequency table per state-action pair, built from what was actually observed. A lookup and an increment.
- **L3, generative.** Only for genuinely novel situations does the model propose effects, and the answer is written into the graph under a canonical state key, like a transposition table in a chess engine.

That last detail is where the money goes. Two action sequences that land on the same world state by different routes collapse into one node and share statistics, cached proposals included. A novel situation costs at most one model call, ever. Episode one builds the graph and pays; later episodes mostly search a graph that already exists. Inside skills, such as writing the text of a diff, the model still does the work it is good at. It just never picks the next action.

## The numbers, with the caveats he insists on

The abstract reports a 100-task suite with 100% success, 100% optimal plans and zero model calls at plan time. In the talk he walks through PlanBench domains (Blocks World, Logistics and a harder hybrid) with 30% of the transition information masked so layers two and three actually fire. GATS solved 148 of 150 tasks; a matched control with the same budget of 2,000 expansions per task solved 65. Letting the graph persist across runs cut total model queries by 83% with no change in tasks solved. The abstract adds a sharper result: with a real local Llama 3.2 behind it, a tree-search baseline fell from 87% to under 1% and ReAct to 36%, while GATS held, because it was never calling the model at plan time.

What makes this talk worth trusting is how much time he spends narrowing the claim. Three domains, one frozen split, one masking condition. An internal review after this analysis had already found a stronger classical baseline that closes part of the gap, and he says so on stage rather than letting the slide imply finality.

## The cache saves money, the heuristic finds the goal

The ablation is the part to steal for your own systems. On 30 tasks, the full system solved 25 with 66,713 model queries. Turn off the graph memory and it still solved 25, with the same mean expansion count, but needed 231,404 queries. Turn off the heuristic instead and it solved 12 while spending even more.

So the graph is an efficiency mechanism, not a correctness one. An agent that fails hard tasks needs a better priority function, not a bigger cache. An agent that is reliable but too expensive is where the cache earns its keep. Asking whether a change moved where the system searches or only what searching costs is a useful habit well beyond planners.

## Who should watch

Engineers building agents over a structured action space (file operations, deploy steps, workflow tools) who are paying for the same decision over and over. The architecture needs a catalogue of named actions with preconditions and effects; open-ended chat with no discrete state gives you no graph, and Maureese says so. Everything shown is single-agent; shared graphs across a fleet are future work. The paper is on arXiv and the code is public on GitHub, with a deterministic backend that runs the suite in under a minute.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [You Cannot Fix a Prompt You Cannot See Fail: Debugging the Plan, Not Just the Answer](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Krishna_Chaitanya_Balusu_debugging_plan_fail) by Krishna Chaitanya Balusu at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026.
- [Beyond Sequential Agents: Orchestrating Hierarchical LLM-Based Agents for Complex Task Decomposition](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Aleksandr_Khramogin_sequential_agents_hierarchical) by Aleksandr Khramogin at Conf42 Large Language Models 2025.
- [Your Agent Failed Mid-Run. Logs Won't Replay It.](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Reza_Amini_agent_replay_logs) by Reza Amini at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Title: Six layers between an enterprise agent and a hallucination
Description: Arjun D Sureshbabu of Snowflake at Conf42 Observability 2026 on guardrails, hybrid RAG, validation and human review for trustworthy enterprise agents.
Body:
Ask an ungrounded employee assistant how to avoid tax and it will try to help, which is precisely the problem. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Arjun D Sureshbabu, who has spent three years building and productionising agents at Snowflake, walked through a layered reliability framework for enterprise AI: guardrails before generation, hybrid retrieval for grounding, validation after generation, structured human review and continuous benchmarking, rolled out in six phases.

## Why hallucinations are an enterprise problem

Sureshbabu's definition is practical. When an agent answers beyond what it is meant to answer, or answers without support, treat it as a hallucination. In a consumer chatbot that is embarrassing. In legal review, compliance, finance or HR it carries liability: an agent that explains ESPP or RSU rules from generic training data, with no citation, can create real legal exposure. Privacy is the other half. Ask an assistant for your work location and it needs to know who is asking, from a user profile loaded as context (title, manager, location), and must not answer Toronto when the right answer is San Francisco.

## Before generation: prompts as contracts

The first layer treats prompt templates as versioned, tested contracts that spell out task boundaries, permitted sources, output format and what to do when information is missing. Orchestration instructions matter more as agents gain tools: with ten tools and no routing hints, an agent will pick the wrong one or improvise. A simple rule such as sending payroll questions to the payroll search tool removes a whole class of wrong answers.

Role enforcement is the part data engineers will appreciate. Your payroll question must never return a colleague's payroll. Rather than trusting the model with that, Sureshbabu enforces it in the data layer with row-level security and row access policies, so a query resolves the current user at runtime and only ever sees that user's rows.

## Grounding with hybrid retrieval

The second layer is hybrid RAG. Sparse BM25 handles exact terms (ask about the ESPP enrollment window and it finds ESPP). Dense vector search handles meaning, so "my contribution" maps to the employee stock purchase plan. Reranking and multi-query orchestration break complex questions, such as comparing quarterly churn with customer support data, into sub-queries and combine the results.

The observability payoff is the paper trail. Every response is logged alongside the passages or SQL that supported it, which makes claims auditable and gives you data on what people actually ask. With an agent exposed to a large internal user base, the top questions by category tell you where to invest next.

## After generation: validate, then let experts score

Post-generation checks include citation enforcement, schema validation, showing the SQL for structured queries, and a second model acting as judge. Then comes human review, but not thumbs up and thumbs down. Experts score outputs on a structured rubric: factual correctness, contextual relevance (the current CEO, not one from five years ago), hallucination severity, and tone. Out-of-scope or malicious questions should get a graceful refusal, and an agent that is unsure should say it does not have enough data rather than invent an answer; he describes a confidence threshold below which the agent declines.

User feedback, including what the right answer should have been, is logged and fed back into instructions and tuning. Benchmarking then runs under stress, with adversarial prompts and missing-knowledge cases, and he describes a hybrid utility minimum Bayes risk approach that compares answers across multiple tools or sub-agents and picks the consensus. Groundedness thresholds gate releases.

## Who should watch

Teams building internal assistants over HR, finance or legal data, and data engineers asked to make those assistants safe. It is a framework overview rather than a code walkthrough, and the Snowflake features appear as one way to enforce access, not a sales pitch. The closing point is the one to keep: hallucination mitigation is not solved once at the model layer; you rerun the evals with every release.

[Watch Arjun D Sureshbabu's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Arjun_D_Sureshbabu_llms_hallucinations_nlp) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/vsYzDDZQcxE)).

Title: Green dashboards, failing checkout. An observability primer
Description: Emmanuela Opurum of SoftNet Technologies at Conf42 Observability 2026 explains, from zero, why dashboards miss customer pain and how to design for it.
Body:
Every dashboard is green, and customers still cannot pay. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Emmanuela Opurum, Solutions Architect at SoftNet Technologies, built a long, patient beginner's session around that scenario, and the answer she keeps returning to: a dashboard only answers the questions someone chose in advance, so observability has to start from the customer journey and be designed into the architecture, not bolted on later.

This is explicitly a first talk on observability. If you have never heard the word, Opurum promises you will not need to be an expert, and she means it. Experienced SREs will know most of the material; it is the talk to send to a new team member, a product owner, or an architect who has only ever seen monitoring from the outside.

## The dashboard is not lying, it is incomplete

The running example is an online shop. Servers up, errors low, CPU normal, and a stream of complaints from customers who cannot complete a payment. Opurum's point is that the dashboard is not wrong. It shows exactly what it was configured to show, and nobody configured it to show the customer's experience.

Her follow-up example makes it concrete: payments fail for customers in one availability zone while customers elsewhere pay fine, and the aggregate view stays green because whoever built it did not break it out by zone. The business does not care that the CPU looks healthy. It cares that people can pay and complete an order, so the signals have to line up with that.

## Logs, metrics and traces as clues

The middle of the talk explains the three signal types in plain terms. Logs are the system's diary, a record of events such as a payment starting and a payment service failing. Metrics are the numbers that show change over time. Traces show the journey of one request across services, which is where the most useful information about a checkout lives. Together they are telemetry, which she is at pains to say is less scary than it sounds.

She makes two points that beginners often miss. Collecting more telemetry does not automatically give you better observability; millions of log lines without a service name, version or ID will not answer a simple question during an incident. And good telemetry should never carry sensitive customer data. For cost, she suggests keeping errors and important journeys, sampling repetitive successful requests, and keeping some data, such as close monitoring of a new release, only for a short time.

She also introduces the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), SLIs and SLOs, and a rule worth repeating to any new on-call: not every change on a chart is an emergency. A CPU bump while customers keep paying is not a page. Too many unimportant alerts teach people to ignore all of them.

## Design it in, then test it on purpose

The architecture section follows the data: services emit logs, metrics and traces; instrumentation adds service name, version, IDs and timing; a collector receives and routes the data to the team's tools. OpenTelemetry gets a mention for giving teams a common way to collect telemetry without being tied to one vendor. But collection is not the goal; using it to find and fix problems before customers notice is.

Her lifecycle advice is the most practical part. During planning, pick the important customer journeys. During development, add the logs, metrics and traces they need. During testing, create a small, harmless problem on purpose and check that the metric shows it, the trace locates it and the logs explain it. After launch, alert on what affects customers. And after every incident, the system should be easier to understand next time.

## Who should watch

Newcomers to observability, students and cloud architects who want the reasoning before the tooling. It is long and deliberately repetitive, closer to a guided lesson than a conference sprint, so experienced engineers may prefer to skim. The closing advice works at any level, though: start with one critical journey, decide what success means, test the setup, then repeat for the next one.

Title: Conf42 Remix 2026: 52 talks from every corner of the series
Description: Conf42 Remix 2026 roundup: resilience, AI agents in production, Kubernetes GPUs, Go monoliths, security basics and accessible JavaScript in 52 talks.
Body:
Conf42 Remix 2026, on August 20, 2026, is the one event in the series that refuses to pick a topic. It brings together popular talks from across the Conf42 calendar, grouped into tracks named after the series' own conferences, from Rustlang and Golang to Incident Management, DevSecOps and Large Language Models. The 52 talks ranged from Spotify's scaling lessons to monitoring garden plants with IoT sensors, and the whole lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/remix2026).

Here are the threads that ran across the tracks.

## Resilience is a separate goal from uptime

Harness opened with a keynote from [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), Head of Resilience Testing and co-creator of LitmusChaos. His argument: reliability is about staying available, resilience is about how you come back when a provider fails underneath you, and SREs should push for resilience gates in the pipeline the way they already gate on test coverage. He closed with AI-generated resilience risk reports as a way to win permission for chaos testing.

[Stuart Clark](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Stuart_Clark_scale_fail_spotify) of Spotify told the story of hyper-growth in 2014 creating fragmentation that made onboarding and incident response harder, and the lesson that good abstractions teach complexity rather than hide it. [Sylvain Kalache](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_vibes_outages_writes) of Rootly looked at what LLM-assisted coding does to reliability, including AI-generated tests that mirror the bugs they should catch. [Spiros Economakis](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Spiros_Economakis_sre_experience_ai) of NOFire AI argued the real AI opportunity in SRE is customer-centred prevention rather than faster RCA, and cloud architect [Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Renato_Losio_mistakes_lessons_scaling) shared five hard lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases.

## AI agents meet production constraints

[Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Samuel_Baruffi_poc_bedrock_agentcore) of AWS addressed why so many agent projects stall at proof of concept, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore covers identity, gateway-based tool access, runtime isolation and memory. [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs) of Solo.io focused on the two questions every team running MCP gets asked: how do we observe it, and how do we keep costs down?

Two talks went after the context problem. [Roxane Fischer](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure), co-founder of Anyshift.io, showed infrastructure modelled as a graph so an LLM can follow multi-hop dependencies with Graph RAG and natural-language-to-Cypher queries instead of guessing. Lior Schejter asked what happens when an agent that copes well with one repo meets [a distributed system of 200 microservices](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Lior_Schejter_context_agents_reasoning), and how to give it a mental model of the whole. And [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Leo_Visser_governance_apis_control) of OGD ICT-diensten demonstrated API management as the leash that keeps AI usage, budget and risk under control.

## Kubernetes as a platform for everything

[Piotr Zaniewski](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Piotr_Zaniewski_sandboxes_gpu_multitenant) of vCluster spun up multi-tenant sandboxes with NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler inside them to share fractional GPUs between teams. [Christophe Gigax](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Christophe_Gigax_dapr_architectures_cloudnative) of Hager Group made the case for Dapr as an abstraction layer for state, pub/sub and more. [Peng Wang](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Peng_Wang_workloads_oceanbase_powering) of OceanBase showed one database handling RAG, semantic search and log analytics on Kubernetes, and [Alejandro Mercado](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Alejandro_Mercado_observability_kubernetes_ebpf) of Michael Page covered eBPF-powered observability for root cause analysis in clusters.

## Go and Rust, from monoliths to leaderboards

The Golang track had two strong engineering stories. [Victor Lyuboslavsky](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Victor_Lyuboslavsky_modularizing_year_monolith) of Fleet Device Management described modularising a 10-year-old Go monolith whose layers had turned into hidden coupling and unclear ownership, and was candid about the people side as well as the architecture. [Ivan Balashov](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Ivan_Balashov_engineering_high_performance) of SoftSwiss walked through a leaderboard system that suffered daily outages, and the redesign that took its core operation from O(N²) to O(log N). [Emmanuela Opurum](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Emmanuela_Opurum_building_secure_pipelines) of SoftNet Technologies used Go to build secure CI/CD automation components. On the Rustlang track, [Tashi Garg](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Tashi_Garg_cloud_ai_rust) of Juniper Networks built dynamic infrastructure UIs in Rust.

## Security fundamentals, explained well

Several talks were good introductions, and said so. [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql) of Microsoft gave a lap around GitHub Dependabot, CodeQL and the other built-in security features. [Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep) of MoEngage opened the black box of static analysis using open-source Semgrep. Security engineer [Aleksandra Drobnjak](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Aleksandra_Drobnjak_documentation_artifacts_beginners) set out a minimum viable set of ISO 42001 documents for anyone asked who approved an AI system and on what data, and [Marat Kenzhebulatov](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marat_Kenzhebulatov_vision_computer_imaging) of Booking.com showed how to bring AI agents safely into security-critical backend work like code review and threat modelling.

## The web, data and one garden

[Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Gian_Wild_accessible_easier_than) of AccessibilityOz gave concrete code for accessible forms and JavaScript, reminding everyone that a fifth of the population has a disability. [Daniel Afonso](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Daniel_Afonso_state_testing_tech) of PagerDuty reviewed a decade of change in JavaScript testing. [Alejandro Duarte](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Alejandro_Duarte_llm_vectors_semantic) of MariaDB covered RAG in production, glue-on-pizza hallucinations included, and [Maximilian Schattauer](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Maximilian_Schattauer_retrievers_documents_ranking) of Perelyn showed LLM-driven pairwise ranking beating semantic retrievers on hard document retrieval.

And for the weekend, [Marie Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics) of Grafana Labs showed how to monitor soil moisture with IoT sensors and Grafana Cloud as a project to do with your kids. The only talk of the day where the alert means water the basil.

## Sponsors

Every talk is linked from the [Conf42 Remix 2026 page](https://www.conf42.com/remix2026). The next edition, [Conf42 Remix 2027](https://www.conf42.com/remix2027), is set for August 19, 2027.

Title: Reliability keeps your job, resilience gets you promoted
Description: Uma Mukkara of Harness, co-creator of LitmusChaos, at Conf42 Remix 2026 on resilience gates, SLIs in chaos experiments and AI risk reports.
Body:
Your provider will go down eventually; the question is whether you go down with it. At Conf42 Remix 2026, [Uma Mukkara](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise), Head of Resilience Testing at Harness and co-creator of the CNCF projects LitmusChaos and OpenEBS, made the case that SREs should treat resilience as a separate goal from reliability, test it inside the delivery pipeline, and use AI to make the business case for doing so.

Uma has spent years helping teams practise chaos engineering, and he is candid about why most don't: everyone agrees it matters, but they aren't allowed to run it. Much of this keynote is about getting that permission.

## Reliability and resilience are different goals

Uma's opening distinction: reliability is about staying available, resilience is about how you behave and how fast you come back when something pushes you over. Your cloud provider, your CDN or a security agent update can all fail on a day when your own code is fine, and no number of nines on their SLA makes that impossible.

Resilience is controlling the blast radius when that happens. Does one region go down, or all of them? Do you have the runbooks, and are people trained on them? Do you understand the dependencies well enough to recover? He also had the line of the session for anyone writing a promotion packet: "If you want to keep your job, focus on reliability. If you want to get yourself promoted, focus on resilience." When a shared provider fails and you stay up while a competitor doesn't, that difference gets noticed.

## Chaos engineering is how you find weaknesses

Uma pushes back on the idea that chaos engineering means breaking things on purpose. The goal is data about weaknesses. A known weakness is already valuable: you can prepare a recovery plan, or tell your most important customer about the risk before it bites, which he argues is often enough to keep that relationship intact.

He describes an experiment as two kinds of boxes. Fault injections are one; checks that the system is still healthy are the other. Real incidents rarely come from one fault, so good experiments chain them: a network path fails over, load shifts, a memory leak starts, and the second provider slows down at the same time.

The SRE's job is defining those health checks. Observability experts know which service level indicators matter in production, and that knowledge rarely makes it back to engineering. Hand over the SLIs and the blast radius map, and pre-production chaos tests start measuring the right things.

## Put resilience gates in the pipeline

Pipelines already gate on test coverage and regressions. Uma asks why they don't gate on resilience: is this release more or less resilient than the last one? If production experiments are off the table, push for chaos tests in staging, then low-intensity game days in production, and escalate if the answer to both is no.

He offers a maturity scale to aim at. In his view most organisations have moved from level one to level two in recent years; the target is level three, where critical services go through chaos testing in lower environments and a few game days run every year. Fully autonomous resilience, he admits, nobody does yet.

## AI writes the risk report for you

The third part is about AI, and it's where the product enters. Uma calls it passive risk detection: feed deployment, incident and service data to an LLM, for example through MCP, and ask for a resilience risk report without running a single experiment. A report that says risk has grown over the last few releases is something you can take to management.

He then describes Harness doing the same from Argo CD or Harness CD data: listing likely incidents and proposing the chaos experiments to run, generated from a prompt. Active testing then confirms what the passive scan suggested.

## Who should watch

SREs who believe in chaos engineering but can't get it approved, and engineering managers deciding where resilience fits in the SDLC. If your team already runs regular game days with SLO-based checks, the AI section is the new material. Uma also gave this keynote at Conf42 SRE 2026.

- [Implementing Chaos Engineering in a Risk Averse Culture](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Kyle_Shelton_risk_averse_culture) by Kyle Shelton (Toyota), on the permission problem.

[Watch Uma Mukkara's keynote](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Uma_Mukkara_resilience_testing_enterprise).

## From Harness

Harness was the diamond sponsor of Conf42 Remix 2026. Uma leads its resilience testing product, which groups chaos, load and disaster recovery testing.

Title: LLM apps are distributed systems now, so trace the decision path
Description: Princewill Kalio of Dockie at Conf42 Observability 2026 on observing LLM apps in three layers, from system telemetry to AI execution data to quality.
Body:
The model is no longer the application. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Princewill Kalio, Senior Software Engineer at Dockie, argued that a modern LLM app (retrieval, vector database, rerankers, semantic cache, tool calls, background workers, evaluation jobs) is a distributed system, and inherits every observability problem distributed systems have, plus one more: a perfectly healthy request can still produce a bad answer.

## From one function call to many boundaries

Kalio starts with the old mental model: prompt goes to model, response comes back, done. That was roughly true for early chatbots. Today a single question may be rewritten, routed through an API service, sent to a model that decides to call a tool or another specialised agent, embedded, matched against a vector store and reranked before anything is generated. Every hop is a boundary, and boundaries are where distributed systems fail: latency, retries, a third party having a bad day.

His point is that the failures he cares about look different at each boundary. The retrieval can succeed and still hand the model the wrong context, which then answers confidently and wrongly. Or retrieval is fine and the model guesses anyway. A database can be healthy while the AI step fails; a tool can work while the request to the model never gets as far as calling it.

## A trace is a decision path

That leads to the talk's most useful reframing. In a classic service, a trace is a request path: which services were hit and how long each took. In an LLM pipeline, Kalio treats the trace as a decision path: what was retrieved, what context the model actually read, which tools it called and what they returned, and how all of that led to the final output. If your telemetry cannot show that an agent pulled the wrong year of birth from the database, he says, your observability is broken, however green the latency panel looks.

## Three layers of signal

His model for an AI observability stack has three layers.

- **System telemetry** at the bottom: latency, errors, throughput, saturation, availability. Keep all of it.
- **AI execution telemetry** in the middle: model and version (did it drift or get deprecated?), tokens, prompts in and outputs out, retrieval results, tool calls and their results, cost.
- **Quality signals** on top: groundedness, relevance, guardrail compliance, including not leaking personal data.

Traditional telemetry asks whether the request executed properly. The top layer asks whether the result was good. He notes that tools such as Langfuse and Arize Phoenix are built around roughly this philosophy, but the principle matters more than the vendor.

## Evaluate continuously, and version your telemetry

Kalio wants evaluation running all the time, not once. In practice that can be a CI job that replays a dataset through the full pipeline (tools, embeddings, vector store) whenever you change a prompt, schema, tool or index, or a scheduled job that checks outputs hourly. If you are just starting out, the CI route is the cheap one.

His closing checklist is short and worth copying: preserve causality by carrying one identity across services, tools, workers and evaluation; instrument the boundaries where retries, state mismatches and third-party failures happen; trace the decision path, not just timing; separate system health from AI quality, since a 200 with a bad answer is both healthy and wrong; and treat telemetry as a production system of its own, with sampling, access control and versioning, so you can tell whether quality is improving or regressing over time.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers inheriting an LLM feature who already know OpenTelemetry and want a mental model for what else to capture. It is a conceptual talk with no live demo, and a good one to hand to a team that still debugs its RAG pipeline like a single script.

[Watch Princewill Kalio's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Princewill_Kalio_llms_rag_distributedsystems) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/LrKiXKhgf6c)).

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Correlation Over Collection: A Layered Observability Framework for SREs](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Khushboo_Nigam_correlation_over_collection) by Khushboo Nigam (Oracle), SRE 2026.
- [Vector Embeddings and RAG Demystified](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Veliswa_Boya_rag_embeddings_vector) by Veliswa Boya (AWS), Machine Learning 2025.

Title: Put token limits, blocklists and a semantic cache in front of your LLM
Description: Leo Visser (OGD) at Conf42 Remix 2026 uses Azure API Management as an AI gateway for Foundry: token quotas, content safety and semantic caching.
Body:
A nature conservation group wanted an AI chatbot, but its donors would ask why their money was paying for GPU emissions. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Leo Visser, consultant at OGD ICT-diensten and the product lead for its AI Foundry offering, showed how he answered that brief: put Azure API Management between the app and Azure AI Foundry, and use it to throttle tokens, block topics before they reach the model, and cache answers.

The case is lightly fictionalised from a real client. They had two asks: use AI without overusing it, and keep certain politically sensitive topics out of the chatbot entirely. Leo admits it was the first time a client asked him to limit topics, and that it made him think.

## The gateway sits in the middle

API Management, which Microsoft now also calls the AI gateway, has a dedicated import for Foundry endpoints. Pick the subscription and Foundry instance, give it a base path, and it generates operations for chat completions, embeddings and image generation, with inbound processing pointing at the backend. His demo app, a small Power App, then talks only to the gateway. A small gotcha from the demo: he had to remove the max tokens parameter from the test body because GPT-5 mini doesn't support it.

## Token limits by key, not by hope

The first control is token consumption. You can cap tokens per minute and set quotas per hour, day, week, month or year, keyed either by subscription key or IP address. Subscription keys are API Management's version of API keys, so each app, each process or each monitored area can get its own budget. The resulting policy is XML; his demo uses 60 tokens per minute.

He shows a subtlety worth knowing: three parallel requests all got through before the first response came back, because the gateway only learns the real token count from the responses. The next call was refused with a retry-after. Limits are enforced, but not before the first burst.

## Block topics before the model burns energy

Content safety connects a Content Safety resource with a blocklist. There's not much to configure in the portal, so he builds the list through the REST API from a CSV (his demo blocks Azure service names like App Service and Azure Functions). With the policy attached, the "safe" request fails while the normal one gets an answer.

His argument for doing it here rather than in a system prompt is the sustainability point of the talk: the gateway rejects the request without calling the LLM at all. A system prompt or agent instruction still sends the whole thing through reasoning, burning tokens and energy to decline politely.

## Semantic caching for answers that don't change

Caching for LLMs sounds odd until you think about archives with static answers, or agents asking the same question repeatedly against data that changes slowly. API Management embeds each prompt with a small embedding model (text-embedding-ada-002 in his setup), looks for a close enough vector in a Redis cache, and returns the stored answer if it finds one. Two knobs need trial and error: the similarity threshold and the cache duration, longer for static data and shorter as you add RAG, tools or MCP servers.

The setup notes are the kind you only get from someone who did it. You need Azure Managed Redis on an enterprise tier with RediSearch enabled. Watch the instance location and used-from mapping for multi-region setups. A bug sometimes leaves the port out of the connection string. Access keys are the only supported auth for now. Most AI gateway features need the Basic v2 tier, and the wrong tier can show up as a confusing "role assignment already exists" error. He also warns that Microsoft Build had just shipped a pile of changes, so check the docs.

## Who should watch

Teams on Azure who run more than one AI app and want central budget, safety and caching policies, plus anyone who has to justify AI spend on energy grounds. If you only have one app, Leo himself says the gateway may be overkill; its value grows with MCP hosting, JWT validation and teams routing their own Foundry instances through one place.

- [Streamlining API Governance: Kubernetes Native API Management](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Pubudu_Gunatilaka_api_governance_kubernetes_api_management) by Pubudu Gunatilaka.
- [AI-Driven Rate Limiting for Scalable, Secure, and Cost-Efficient APIs](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Rehana_Sultana_Khan_rate_limiting_cost) by Rehana Sultana Khan.
- [Green DevOps: Building Sustainable Software](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Neel_Shah_green_sustainable_software) by Neel Shah.

[Watch Leo Visser's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Leo_Visser_governance_apis_control).

Title: Give AI agents system context with a Git repo of Markdown facets
Description: Lior Schejter at Conf42 Remix 2026 on the Architecture Hub, an AI-maintained Git repo of per-service docs that lets agents reason across microservices.
Body:
Drop a coding agent into one repo and it feels like magic; ask it to fix a bug that spans six microservices and it's flying blind. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Lior Schejter, Lead R&D Architect, presented the Application Architecture Hub: a plain Git repository of Markdown files, written and kept current by AI agents, that gives other agents (and humans) a system-level view of a distributed codebase.

The problem, he points out, predates AI. Tracing flows across services was always slow and unscalable, and humans are notoriously bad at keeping documentation current. What AI changed is the expectation of velocity. The same models that are hungry for context are also good at producing it, consistently and without getting bored.

## Boring infrastructure, on purpose

The design principles are the most transferable part. Zero infrastructure: no servers, nothing to monitor, just a shared repo. AI-native: agents already read and write files, grep and run scripts, so no special tooling. Diffable: Git log shows exactly what changed and when, and pull requests let humans review it. The team started out prototyping graph databases and looked at wikis, then realised they were optimising prematurely. Flat Markdown won.

The unit of ingestion is one repo, but the documentation is split into facets: domain models, exposed APIs, events, dependencies and more, each its own file. Questions tend to cut across services along one facet (events and APIs for tracing a bug, dependencies for blast radius), and the naming convention maps repo plus facet to a file path deterministically, so there's no lookup step. If you know what you want, you know the filename.

## Orchestrator, sub-agents, and a linter written in code

Ingestion runs an orchestrator agent that dispatches one sub-agent per facet. They read the same code with different instructions, run in parallel, don't pollute each other's context, and can be retried individually. Early on, the agent was told to verify its own output (paths, links, front matter), which proved unreliable, so that check became a script. His lesson, stated plainly: don't use AI where you don't need to.

Updates hang off CI: merges to main in relevant repos trigger an update and lint, opened as a PR for human review at first. Those reviews caught real gaps, such as a non-standard Kafka pattern in some repos that meant events went undocumented until the skill learned it. Once trust builds, updates can auto-merge. Cost control comes from diff-based updates rather than full re-ingestion, single-facet re-runs across all repos, rate-limit-aware batch scripts, and picking a good-enough model.

The single biggest win for reliability: requiring every claim to cite a file and line numbers. It reduced drift between runs, let humans check facts fast, and let higher-level agents jump to the real code.

## Querying is the product

The docs are the substrate; answers are the value. Query skills, distributed to developers' Cursor installs as a plugin, tell an agent how to navigate the hub, locally or through GitHub's CLI or MCP tools. An incident-analysis agent with access to logs, Jira and Slack also uses the hub to know where to look. Ready-made report prompts cover dependency maps (including implicit dependencies through shared database tables), end-to-end flow write-ups, a plain-English explainer for product managers, and repo overviews for onboarding, some as interactive HTML.

He extends it beyond engineering with a business-to-technical mapping facet, such as which service owns fees and which consumes reservations. LLMs propose the mappings, humans audit the low-confidence ones, and confirmed mappings survive future updates.

He shared rough numbers too: mostly one person built it, with an initial prototype in one to two weeks and most of the effort spent on extraction quality.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform teams with dozens or hundreds of services who want agents to do more than single-repo coding, and anyone fighting documentation drift. It's a design talk with no product to sell, and the principles (flat files, facets, citations, deterministic checks) work with any agent harness.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Context Engineering for DevOps: Turning Your Infrastructure into a Reasoning Graph](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure) by Roxane Fischer, a graph-shaped take on the same context problem.
- [Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery) by Prateek Mittal.
- [Can LLMs Understand the Linux Kernel? An LLM-Powered Approach to Understanding Large Codebases](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Yusheng_Zheng_linux_llm_codebases) by Yusheng Zheng.

Title: Lock down the role first, then let Cortex Code run your Snowflake ops
Description: Tim Spann (Snowflake) at Conf42 Remix 2026 demos Cortex Code CLI for database DevOps: skills, AGENTS.md, scoped roles, data discovery and dbt.
Body:
Before you type a single prompt, give the agent a role that can't drop your tables. That was Tim Spann's first piece of advice at Conf42 Remix 2026. Tim, Senior Solution Engineer at Snowflake, demoed Cortex Code, Snowflake's coding agent, doing database DevOps work in natural language: finding tables, profiling data quality, auditing running jobs and building pipelines, inside the same RBAC and governance as everything else in the account.

Be clear about scope: this is a Snowflake engineer showing a Snowflake product, with his own disclaimer that it's how he works, not necessarily how you're supposed to. Tim also writes a weekly newsletter on AI, data and streaming, and the talk has that same tour-guide energy (and a cat).

## Guardrails before prompts

The setup advice is the part that applies to any agent touching a database. Run it as a dedicated user or role with exactly the permissions you want: no drops if you don't want drops, one database or schema if that's the scope, read-only if that's enough. Don't hand it your own credentials. Tim runs his against a demo account behind a VPN, with a separate key-pair user and its own warehouse, so costs are easy to track.

He goes further on the host side. One of his installs is a Raspberry Pi 500 on its own network with no root access, which can do little except call Cortex Code. Lock the box down, sandbox it, or put it in a VM. As he put it, it's the internet and AI, things can happen.

Then give it context. An AGENTS.md file tells the agent your conventions, usernames and directories. MCP connections bring in other systems. Skills encode best practices so results are consistent; his install listed 102 of them, and there's a skill for writing skills.

## Two faces: Snowsight and the CLI

Cortex Code lives in two places. In the Snowsight web UI it's a helper in the corner that fixes failed queries and typos or builds a mart from a file ("like Clippy, but actually works", in his words). The main environment is the CLI: type `cortex`, reuse your existing Snowflake CLI connection, and get an interactive agent with resumable sessions, profiles, sub-agents and an auto mode that stops asking permission.

The live demo is deliberately everyday. List the five largest tables in a schema (his New York MTA bus tracking table had 22 million rows). Fetch the latest ten rows, letting the agent figure out which column is the timestamp. Load a "know your data" skill to explore and profile tables for quality and freshness. Ask what's running across services, dynamic tables, tasks and pipelines, spot jobs that ran once last year, and write the findings to a Markdown report. He also shows a procedure it wrote that sends a video in a Snowflake stage to an LLM and returns structured JSON, in his case counting 25 vehicles on a busy New York street.

## Where the DevOps part comes in

Beyond the demo, Tim lists what he uses it for: schemas following medallion or whatever architecture you specify, generated from a rough spec or even a spreadsheet; dbt projects from scratch or reverse-generated from a repo; query optimisation and debugging; tests, semantic views and Cortex Search on top; pushing everything into version control; and scheduling via Snowflake tasks, Openflow or plain cron. His typical flow, from source to tables, tests, semantic view, agent, MCP server and dashboard, takes about an hour of him approving or rejecting steps.

## Who should watch

Snowflake users curious about agent-driven admin and dbt work, and anyone designing permissions for an AI agent that touches production data. If you're not on Snowflake, the guardrail advice in the first ten minutes is the part to keep.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Schema Migrations in CI/CD: When AI Helps, When It Hurts, and How to Tell the Difference](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_postgres_mysql_scaling) by Ahmed Tariq.
- [Prompt-Driven Microservice & Database Evolution: Using LLMs for Automated Schema Migration and DevOps Delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Niraj_Katkamwar_llm_agents_delivery) by Niraj Katkamwar.
- [Codeless Generative AI Pipelines: Prompt Automation](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Tim_Spann_codeless_ai_automation), an earlier Tim Spann talk from before the agents arrived.

[Watch Tim Spann's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Tim_Spann_sql_automation_operations).

Title: Benchmarks grade the model. Production needs to grade the system
Description: Srikanth Devarakonda of Adobe at Conf42 Observability 2026 on continuous GenAI evaluation tied to observable signals and business outcomes.
Body:
A model can top a leaderboard and still give your users wrong answers, because users do not talk to the model, they talk to the whole system around it. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Srikanth Devarakonda, Software Development Engineer 5 at Adobe, where he leads GenAI capabilities for Acrobat Assistant, argued for moving from one-off model benchmarks to continuous evaluation of the complete AI system, measured with observable signals and tied to business outcomes.

## Why the benchmark score lies by omission

Devarakonda is clear that benchmarks are useful for comparing models under controlled conditions. The problem is what they leave out. A benchmark is a static, curated dataset; production is unpredictable input. A benchmark scores single transactions; production is multi-turn conversations where context piles up. A benchmark isolates the model; production adds retrieval, prompt templates, orchestration, APIs, databases, permissions, safety layers, latency budgets, and users doing things you never anticipated. A failure can come from any of those, and sometimes the model is not the problem at all.

So the question changes from how capable the model is to how the whole system behaves when real users depend on it. He breaks that into four activities: measure (define quality for your application as signals), validate (automate, with human judgment where automation falls short), monitor (catch drift and new failure modes after launch) and govern (traceability and controls).

## Four dimensions, defined by your domain

The evaluation dimensions are factual accuracy, grounding (is the answer supported by authoritative, retrieved content), safety within policy, and task completion. The last one is the easiest to forget: a factually correct answer that does not help the user finish their task is still a failure.

Which dimension matters most depends on the application. Customer support cares about resolution without escalation. Decision support cares more about evidence, traceability and confidence calibration. A generic benchmark applied to both will give you a great score for the wrong thing. Define what failure looks like and what it costs first, then pick metrics.

## Automate for breadth, send the hard cases to humans

Nobody can hand-review every production interaction, and fully automated evaluation has blind spots. Devarakonda's answer is LLM-as-judge, embedding similarity, classifiers and rule-based checks for scale, plus intelligent sampling that routes low-confidence, high-risk and policy-sensitive interactions to human reviewers. What the reviewers find feeds back into the rubric, the ground-truth dataset, the judge prompts and the system itself. A production failure is information about your evaluation method as much as about the model.

For hallucinations he describes a layered stack: entailment checks against retrieved context, self-consistency sampling across multiple generations, retrieval faithfulness, and inference-time controls such as confidence thresholds and human escalation. The aim is to intercept unreliable answers before users see them, which turns hallucination handling from an analytics job into an engineering control. Robustness gets the same treatment: perturbed and adversarial inputs, fairness checks, red teaming for jailbreaks and prompt injection, and re-evaluation when the traffic distribution shifts.

## Segment the dashboard, version everything

The observability stack he describes has three parts: real-time dashboards (hallucination rate, latency, refusals, satisfaction, task success), segmentation by model version, prompt template, user segment and environment, and full interaction tracing from input to retrieved context to output to evaluation score. Segmentation is what turns a vague five percent quality drop into one bad prompt template you can roll back. Governance belongs in the engineering process too: model versioning, evaluation snapshots, automated rollback triggers, audit logs. Added afterwards, he warns, it becomes paperwork.

The slide he calls the most important connects technical metrics to business ones. Higher task success should mean higher resolution, fewer escalations and lower support cost. That is how you tell leadership something better than a three-point bump in an evaluation score.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product owners moving a GenAI feature from pilot to production, especially if your current evaluation is a benchmark run before launch. It is a framework talk without a demo or Adobe-specific numbers, so treat it as a checklist for designing your own evaluation pipeline.

[Watch Srikanth Devarakonda's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Srikanth_Devarakonda_llms_evals_benchmarks) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/chDuQddtZyo)).

## Related Conf42 talks

- [How to evaluate your Evals?](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) by Hilik Paz (Arato.ai), LLMs 2025.
- [The Judge Problem: Why Your Agentic Verifier is Silently Rotting in Production](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Vsevolod_Voropaev_verification_agents_production) by Vsevolod Voropaev, LLMs 2026.
- [An Advanced Validation Pipeline for Summary Evaluation in High-Stakes Environments](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Liliya_Imasheva_Michael_Banf_validation_summaries_evaluation) by Liliya Imasheva and Michael Banf (Perelyn), LLMs 2026.

Title: Serverless databases remove capacity planning, not database engineering
Description: Renato Losio (cloudiamo.com) at Conf42 Remix 2026 shares five lessons from five years of Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB and DSQL: storage, cost, compatibility.
Body:
A hundred thousand single-row inserts took seconds on Aurora and about five minutes on RDS for MySQL, and serverless had little to do with the difference. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Renato Losio, cloud architect at cloudiamo.com with fifteen years on AWS, shared five lessons from five years of so-called serverless databases. His one-line summary: serverless databases "remove the capacity management, but they don't remove database engineering".

Renato has form here. He once tried to draw the New York City skyline with Aurora Serverless v2 capacity units at re:Invent, and recreated a famous Tour de France climb in DynamoDB. Before any of that, he scaled RDS up and down with CloudWatch metrics and Bash scripts, which he calls the poor man's autoscaling. Remember that script; it comes back at the end.

## Lesson 1: serverless is just an adjective

He tours AWS's history to show how loose the word is. Aurora Serverless v1 (GA in 2018, now deprecated) was roughly his scaling script with nicer packaging. DynamoDB On-Demand arrived the same year without the word in its name. Aurora Serverless v2 took a year and a half from preview to GA in 2022, which he reads as proof that transparent relational scaling is hard, and then a while longer to scale to zero. DocumentDB Serverless doesn't scale to zero; Aurora DSQL doesn't say serverless at all; S3, SQS and Athena were pay-per-use long before the buzzword. His advice: stop arguing about the label and ask whether it's elastic enough for you.

## Lesson 2: storage is underrated

On one production database he manages, monthly storage and backup costs now exceed compute, on plain gp3. So CPU elasticity may not be your biggest bill.

The second half of the lesson is the insert test: Aurora Serverless v2 at half an ACU, provisioned Aurora on r8g.large, and RDS for MySQL on the same class with 400 GB of gp3 for better baseline IOPS. Insert 100,000 rows one at a time from a stored procedure, default settings. Provisioned Aurora: two to three seconds. Serverless v2: three to four. RDS: about five minutes, maybe a minute or two with tuning. He's honest that it's an unrealistic workload, but it makes the point: Aurora's storage architecture matters far more than whether the compute is serverless.

## Lesson 3: cost needs a crystal ball

You can't forecast serverless capacity units from a provisioned cluster's baseline. His single Aurora cluster produced more than a thousand billing line items in a month: compute, traffic, multi-AZ, backup, storage type. DSQL's DPU pricing gets the same treatment. Anyone who tells you upfront that moving to serverless will save fifty percent, without trying it, is guessing. His method: put a serverless replica next to your cluster and measure.

## Lessons 4 and 5: compatible until it isn't, and which way it scales

Every managed database is "compatible" until your Postgres extension isn't supported, your MongoDB aggregation behaves differently, or your MySQL tooling doesn't work. Compatibility means wire protocol, SQL dialect, features, operational ecosystem and versions, and adverts usually cover the first two. His bet for the relational side is that things are converging on Postgres.

Finally, horizontal versus vertical. DynamoDB and DSQL shard horizontally; Aurora Serverless scales one instance vertically. Neither is "more serverless", and most workloads fit happily on a single big instance with read replicas.

The closing joke is from AWS's own Aurora Serverless v2 docs: if the database won't scale down to its minimum, stop and restart it to reclaim fragmented memory, accepting the downtime. Which is where his Bash script started. Behind every serverless database there's still a MySQL or a Postgres, and a forgotten cron job can keep it pinned at the same CPU forever.

## Who should watch

Anyone choosing between Aurora Serverless, provisioned Aurora, RDS and DynamoDB, or trying to explain a serverless bill to finance. It's funny, experience-driven and AWS-specific, with numbers you can rerun yourself.

Title: Load your cloud API output into a database and ask better questions
Description: Jason Lester (Capgemini UK) at Conf42 Remix 2026 on pulling cloud CLI and API data into tables for permission audits, history and start/stop apps.
Body:
Working out who had access to a system a month ago is a miserable job in a cloud console. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Jason Lester, Managing Architect at Capgemini UK, made a simple case: pull your environment's metadata out through the cloud APIs, load it into a database, and that kind of question becomes a SQL join.

His examples come from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure because that's where he works, but he's explicit that every idea applies to AWS, Azure and GCP.

## The console is a friendly layer over a bigger API

Consoles are built to be easy: drop-downs, calendars, a quick path to a running instance. Underneath, the providers built APIs that do the real work, and the console exposes only part of them. APIs can be chained like Lego: read details from one database, feed them into a call that builds another.

He's equally clear about the risk. Without a visual picture of what you're touching, it's easy to get lost in the data and cause damage you didn't expect, so experiment somewhere that isn't production.

REST APIs are the common form, callable from tools like Postman, and authentication is the usual pain: request a token, then use it on every call. The CLIs remove that friction by reusing a config you set up once. His example, `oci compute instance list`, returns every instance in a compartment as JSON, including plenty of metadata the console doesn't show easily, along with inventory counts, build dates, status, CPU and memory, performance statistics and cost data.

## Once it's a table, history is free

The core move is to load that JSON into tables, such as an instances table for the whole tenancy. Two examples make the payoff concrete.

Permissions first. In OCI, users belong to groups and groups get rights through policy statements. The console shows a user's groups but not the effective privileges those groups grant without reading every policy. Extract users, groups and policies, join a few tables, and you can list exactly what one user is allowed to do in a given compartment.

Then time. If you scrape permissions regularly, you can ask what someone could do last month, which is the forensic question after a suspicious change, without replaying audit logs from today backwards. And once the data sits in a database, you can also point other tools at it, including AI, to look for trends.

## Build small apps on the metadata

The third idea goes past reporting. His team built apps on Oracle APEX over that metadata. The headline use case is cost: shutting non-production environments down out of hours, say 6pm on weekdays and all weekend, with a self-service button for the developer who wants to work on a Saturday. Add a workflow and the request goes to a manager with a cost estimate attached before the environment starts.

Ordering is the subtle part. Databases should start before the application servers that depend on them and stop after them. Model environments as hierarchical groups in the same metadata, and the tool waits for the database to be confirmed up before starting the app tier. Anyone who has watched an app server crash-loop against a database that isn't up yet will appreciate this one.

## Who should watch

Cloud architects and DBAs who live in one provider's console and keep exporting CSVs to answer audit or cost questions. It's a short, practical talk, not a tour of any one API, and heavy on Oracle Cloud examples. Jason's blog, linked from the talk, has the OCI specifics.

Title: The stand-up bot that invented seven colleagues, and the fix
Description: Artemis Leonardou of NOFire AI at Conf42 Observability 2026 on an LLM bot that fabricated with 100% uptime, and why output checks beat prompts.
Body:
On its first morning in production, a Slack stand-up bot posted a digest about six people. Only one of them existed. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Artemis Leonardou, Software Engineer and DevRel at NOFire AI, told the story of that bot, why every dashboard stayed green, and why her team stopped trusting prompts and started checking outputs in code before anything reaches a human.

## Meet Duda

Duda is an async stand-up bot: it DMs each person daily, collects answers and posts a digest to the engineering channel twice a day. Leonardou, who has shipped code to production since she was 14 and started working professionally with Copilot already in the toolbox, built it in a day with Claude Code, reviewed it lightly and went straight to production. No staging, deliberately: it is an internal, low-stakes tool. Her own decision record had already noted that 18 people would treat its output as a record of what the team did.

With one person on the roster (her), the first digest described Luca, Maya, Joaquim, Priya, Chen and her. It used the same voice and level of detail for the invented people as for the real one, said it was still waiting on two more invented colleagues and on Duda itself, and flagged under Needs Attention that Artemis was blocked on Kafka ACLs from platform. She has never used Kafka. It was, she noted, the most plausible blocker a backend engineer could have.

## A hundred percent uptime, zero percent truth

Her monitoring saw nothing, because there was nothing to see: no exception, normal token count, normal latency, a 200 from Slack, a healthy pod, a clean deploy. Monitoring instincts are built around absence. A missing digest is loud. A punctual, well-formatted, false one looks exactly like success.

She spent three hours on the prompt, which already said to use only names from the roster. Rewording, moving the constraint, adding emphasis and examples gave her no signal, because the failure was intermittent and the output plausible either way. She could not tell a working fix from a lucky run.

Two more fabrications followed. The CTO, poking for fun, wrapped a request in a conditional and asked for a hashlib result; Duda has no interpreter, so it produced 64 plausible characters, while correctly refusing a direct request to run a subprocess. And asked whether Artemis was around, it said yes, from a stored flag left behind after presence data had been removed that day. Separately, a missing import crashed every non-admin DM for days, invisible because a crashed Slack handler and an idle bot both look like silence. Seventeen test suites existed; none ran in CI.

## A prompt is an instruction, not a guarantee

That sentence is now a decision record in the repository. The fixes came in three parts, each with its cost stated plainly.

First, check the output in code. The guard that catches invented names is about 20 lines: compare names in the digest to the real roster, retry once with a blunter instruction, then fall back. The guards are pattern-based and only cover failure classes already seen, which she calls a much weaker claim than being safe. One subtle trap: her first presence detector also flagged the honest answer, because saying you cannot see presence uses the same words as claiming you can. A guard that punishes honesty trains the system to be evasive.

Second, a fallback that cannot fail the same way: a digest built in code with no model involved, which announces itself as written plainly. That means two code paths to maintain forever, and steady pressure to loosen a guard when it is in your way. Her rule is never to weaken a guard just to make a test pass.

Third, gate before it lands. An alert on a false digest only tells you 18 people already read it. For systems whose failure is a confident falsehood, the check has to sit upstream of the human, even at the price of a late or plain digest.

## Who should watch

Anyone shipping LLM features or letting agents write code they are on call for. It is tool-agnostic, honest about costs, and ends with an open bug rather than a victory lap. Leonardou expands on the gating idea in her DevSecOps 2026 talk, linked below.

[Watch Artemis Leonardou's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_debugging_agents_codegeneration) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/s8DsnD_H4EY)).

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Gate the Action, Not the Alert: Checking an Agent Before It Runs](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_agents_guardrails_policy) by Artemis Leonardou (NOFire AI), DevSecOps 2026.
- [From Vibes to Outages: When AI Writes the Code You Debug](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_vibes_outages_writes) by Sylvain Kalache (Rootly), SRE 2026.

Title: RAG in production is five modules, not one prompt template
Description: Alejandro Duarte (MariaDB) at Conf42 Remix 2026 walks every RAG stage, from chunking to hybrid search and re-ranking, then demos MariaDB AI RAG.
Body:
The hello-world version of RAG fits on a slide: embed your rows, embed the question, order by distance, stuff the top three into a prompt. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Alejandro Duarte, Developer Relations Engineer at MariaDB plc, showed how fast that slide grows once real documents arrive, and laid out a modular architecture for the production version before demoing MariaDB's own implementation of it.

His running gag is the Doom Guy face from the 1993 shooter: grinning while the example is one SQL table, taking damage with every new requirement. It's an accurate health bar for most RAG projects.

## Chunking is where meaning gets cut in half

The first hit comes with PDFs. You can't embed a 300-page document as one vector, so you split it, and a naive split can turn his opening line, *I left my wife a note*, into a chunk that stops at *wife*, which says something rather different. Overlap helps for some documents. Recursive chunking tries pages, then paragraphs, then sentences until the size fits. Semantic chunking lets an LLM pick the boundaries, which is precise but adds a model call per chunk.

Ingestion brings its own list: many formats, sources from HTTP to the file system to S3, per-user directories so use cases don't trample each other, batch processing, metadata, and layout-aware extraction for multi-column PDFs that paste back as word salad. Then retries, error handling and the security questions of shipping data to an external embedder, plus CRUD and versioning for documents and chunks.

## Retrieval is a choice, not a default

Phase two opens with an architectural question: do you need a separate vector database or an extension? Every new system means licences, release cadence, drivers and operations. He makes a pointed aside about bus factor, noting that pgvector is maintained by one person, as one risk signal to weigh rather than a verdict.

Then the search itself. Vector search for meaning, keyword or full-text search for identifiers that carry no semantics, and hybrid search that merges both with reciprocal rank fusion. On top of that, a cross-encoder re-ranking step reorders candidates by relevance so you send the LLM as little as possible, with FlashRank as a local option or Cohere as a hosted one. Metadata filters discard whole documents early.

## The modular RAG blueprint

His architecture mirrors the pipeline: a document ingestion module (incremental, multi-format, layout-aware, versioned; Docling locally or LlamaParse as a service), a chunking module with fixed, recursive, semantic, sentence and token strategies, a retrieval module with vector, keyword and hybrid search plus re-ranking, and a generation module that supports several LLM providers or Ollama for data that can't leave your infrastructure, with citations and streaming. A fifth orchestration layer ties it together with async processing, retries, health endpoints, auth and multi-user support, exposed as a REST API.

He's clear that this is one way to build it, and that frameworks help but bring their own vocabulary to learn and code to maintain.

## The vendor part: MariaDB AI RAG

The second half shows MariaDB's implementation, MariaDB AI RAG, which was in beta at recording time. It runs as a Docker Compose service against MariaDB's native vector support, with an MCP server for agents. The demo ingests his book *Practical Vaadin* through the Swagger UI, chunks it recursively into around 400 vectors, and asks which dog breed appears in the examples. ChatGPT and Gemini had both got it wrong without retrieval; with hybrid search over the book, Gemini answered correctly: an English bulldog called Draco. A single "full pipeline" endpoint does the same in one call.

Treat that section as a product walkthrough. The first half stands on its own whatever database you run.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving a RAG prototype towards production who want a checklist of what they haven't built yet, and architects deciding whether to add a dedicated vector store. If you already run hybrid search with re-ranking, skim the first half and decide on the product demo.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: An AI security gate in CI/CD only works with your policy behind it
Description: Emmanuela Opurum (SoftNet Technologies) at Conf42 Remix 2026 demos a GitHub Actions gate where an LLM scans code against written policy and alerts Slack.
Body:
A hardcoded API key reached the pipeline, the pipeline stopped, and Slack got a message saying which line, why, and what to do instead. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Emmanuela Opurum, Solutions and System Architect at SoftNet Technologies, walked through a small CI/CD security guardrail in which an LLM agent scans every push against an explicit organisational policy and fails the build when it finds a violation.

Her starting point is a fair one. CI/CD makes shipping fast, and the same automation ships a mistake to production just as fast if nothing in the pipeline is looking for it.

## Why scanners and AI alone both fall short

Emmanuela splits existing tools into two camps and finds both lacking. Static analysis tools look for particular known vulnerabilities, but they don't know your organisation's rules. Standalone AI tools have the opposite problem: they're flexible, but "AI alone doesn't know your organization policy", so they don't know what to look for.

Her answer is to combine them. Write the policy down in detail, put it in the repo next to the workflow, and give the agent that document as its brief. The model supplies judgement; the policy supplies what your organisation actually cares about.

## The flow, step by step

The reference build runs on GitHub, though she stresses the same shape works on any code platform:

1. A developer pushes code.
2. The push triggers a workflow with the agent integrated.
3. The agent, backed by an OpenAI GPT model, checks the change against the policy: secret detection, pattern scanning and policy validation.
4. If nothing is found, the code continues to deployment.
5. If something is found, the pipeline fails and a detailed analysis goes to the team's Slack via the Slack API: what failed, on which line, and a suggested fix.

The demo shows two runs. The first passes. The second fails on an API key committed to a file, and the Slack message recommends removing hard-coded secrets and using environment variables. Not exotic, but a gate that explains itself gets fixed faster than a red X with a log dump.

The repository, GoCICD Security Guardrail under her cloud-architect-emma GitHub account, has the workflow, the policy file, the architecture diagram and a README for getting started.

## Two lessons, one caveat

Her lessons are deliberately modest. AI needs human input twice: someone has to write the policy, and someone has to respond to the alert. And AI speeds up the response loop, because developers get told where the problem is instead of digging through logs.

The caveat, which the talk doesn't dwell on, is scope. This is a short practitioner talk about one guardrail pattern, not a survey of supply chain security, and Go is the context (it was first given at Conf42 Golang 2026) more than the subject. Future work she suggests: multi-language policy support and wiring the same gate into cloud integrations.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who want a first, explainable AI check in their pipeline and a concrete example to fork. If you already run secret scanning, SBOMs and provenance checks, the interesting part is the policy-as-prompt idea and the Slack feedback loop, not the detection itself.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Your coding agent is a production system. Give it golden signals
Description: Elliot Gardiner of Code Telemetry at Conf42 Observability 2026 maps Google's four golden signals onto AI coding-agent sessions and trajectories.
Body:
Most teams measure AI coding assistants by tokens spent and seats used, which is roughly like monitoring a web service by its electricity bill. At Conf42 Observability 2026, Elliot Gardiner, Founding Engineer at Code Telemetry, took the Google SRE four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) and applied them to Claude Code and Codex sessions, treating each one as a production system whose trajectory you can measure.

## Why a laptop process counts as production

Gardiner has the SRE background to make the argument, with stints at Capital One, JPMorgan and Mastercard, where he worked on optimising coding assistant usage. His case: coding agents increasingly run unattended, for a long time, against your real repository, and sometimes in the cloud. They call external services (model APIs, MCP servers, package registries, test runners), consume constrained resources (tokens, context window, rate limits), retry failures on their own, carry state that degrades as the context fills, and produce consequential output in the form of commits and pull requests. That is a production system with a terminal attached.

His joke slide puts a normal service dashboard next to what you get out of the box from a coding agent: an agent started 47 minutes ago, and that is about it. He admits the slide is generous.

## The signals, translated

Traffic becomes human prompts, the count and variety of tool calls, tokens produced and the kinds of file edits, all tied to session metadata. Latency becomes checkpoints in the delivery cycle: first prompt to first file edit, to passing tests, to a reviewable change. Saturation covers context pressure, subscription rate limits, rate limits of downstream systems such as dev environments, and concurrency, since parallel agents editing the same file are a merge conflict waiting to happen. Errors are where it gets interesting.

## A failed tool call is a 404, not a 500

Gardiner's best analogy is the old SRE argument about 4xx codes. A 404 on your homepage is an outage; a 404 from a crawler guessing URLs is noise. Agent tool calls work the same way. A grep that returns a non-zero exit code during exploration is the agent learning. In one session he walks through, an early `ls` of node_modules fails, and the agent recovers with a cached `npm ci` seconds later. Not an error worth reporting. Further down the same session, though, the agent says the change still needs a benchmark against real data that it never ran. The task was to bring an API inside a two-second latency target, and nothing proved it did.

So correctness is judged against the outcome: the task intent, a relevant check, an observed result, and a comparison between them. Tool exit codes inform that verdict but do not decide it.

## Converging or stuck

The talk's most reusable slide lists failure patterns worth alerting on. Retry loops, where edit, test, fail repeats without the agent changing approach. Repeated edits with no tests at all. Tool fallback, when an MCP call fails and the agent drops to bash. Spend without progress: tokens burned, files changed, no tests, no pull request. And review rework, the extra cycles after a human or another agent reviews the PR. The summary test is whether retries produce new evidence: an agent hitting different errors and then passing is converging; one hitting the same failure after the same edits is stuck.

Each pattern points to a fix. The node_modules probe suggests a better environment bootstrap or base image. Sessions that always succeed might be running the most expensive model at full effort, a right-sizing job like picking EC2 instance sizes. Changes to agent instruction files can be checked against data instead of vibes. Frequent context overload says the tasks are too big; frequent conflicts say the code needs reorganising for parallel work.

## Who should watch

Platform and developer-experience teams paying for coding agents, and SREs who want a familiar frame for an unfamiliar workload. Gardiner builds Code Telemetry and shows its session UI, so this is partly his own product, but the signal definitions stand on their own. His closing line is the thesis in one sentence: we did not make production reliable by making software stop failing, we made failure observable.

[Watch Elliot Gardiner's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Elliot_Gardiner_agents_codegeneration_tracing) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/il86h4NsCEw)).
