Title: IoT data platforms fail on cost, not collection
Description: Bhanudeepti Chinta of Dave on lakehouse table formats, medallion layers and feature stores that keep IoT telemetry costs in line, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Collecting sensor data is the easy part; paying for it is where IoT platforms get into trouble. In a talk selected for Conf42 Remix 2026, [Bhanudeepti Chinta](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Bhanudeepti_Chinta_lakehouse_analytics_scalable), Engineering Manager for Data at Dave with 14 years of building large data platforms, argues that the cost and complexity of IoT data tend to grow faster than the value teams extract, and that lakehouse architecture is first a cost containment strategy.

The session is a compact architecture overview rather than a hands-on build. Its value is in the ordering of decisions: which choices quietly pile up storage and compute bills, and which ones keep them proportional to what the business actually uses.

## Why IoT data breaks traditional architectures

Bhanudeepti lists the traits that make telemetry different. Sensors stream continuously, often at millisecond intervals, so volumes reach petabyte scale within months. The schema never sits still: firmware updates add fields and different vendors send, in her words, "consistently inconsistent telemetry formats." And the same data has three very different audiences. Operations wants real-time dashboards, data scientists want history for modelling, and business users want aggregates.

Classic warehouses give performance and consistency but get expensive and rigid with semi-structured data. Plain data lakes are cheap but lack reliability, governance and transactions. The lakehouse sits between them: warehouse-grade guarantees on top of low-cost object storage.

## Separate storage, table format and compute

The core technologies are Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi, which add transactional semantics, schema evolution and efficient metadata to cloud storage. Without them, she says, IoT platforms accumulate hidden operational and storage costs over time.

The physical design splits three layers. Object storage holds the data with effectively unlimited capacity, the table format manages metadata and transactions, and engines like Spark or Trino scale independently. That separation lets you pay for compute only when you run it, instead of keeping fixed infrastructure warm for workloads that come in bursts.

## Most cost overruns are design decisions

Streaming sits at the centre, with Kafka, Kinesis or Event Hubs feeding Spark or Flink. The decisions that decide the bill are mundane: partition by time to match how telemetry is queried, manage hot, warm and cold tiers deliberately, and absorb schema changes without rewriting history. Bhanudeepti's view is that many IoT cost overruns trace back to getting these wrong.

The medallion pattern gives the structure. Bronze keeps raw readings exactly as received for audit and replay, silver validates and normalises, gold serves business-ready datasets for dashboards. Expensive compute only runs where there is business value. Rather than separate batch and streaming stacks, she points to a Kappa-style approach: one streaming pipeline, with incremental processing and materialised views covering both.

Machine learning is where costs creep in quietly, because feature engineering gets duplicated across teams. Snowflake feature stores are her answer: reusable, governed features that stay consistent between training and inference.

## Four places it pays off

The case studies are brief: predictive maintenance in manufacturing, route optimisation and vehicle health in connected fleets, traffic and environmental monitoring in smart cities, and smart meter analytics for utilities, including energy theft detection and peak demand forecasting. Looking ahead she expects lower-latency streaming, better time series performance, stronger governance and more edge analytics to cut bandwidth. Her closing line sums up the talk: success comes from systems that align cost with value.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects designing or inheriting an IoT pipeline, and engineering managers who need a vocabulary for why the telemetry bill keeps growing. If you already run Iceberg with a medallion layout in production, treat it as a checklist rather than new material.

Title: Teaching observability to an 8-year-old with a thirsty houseplant
Description: Marie Cruz of Grafana Labs wires a soil moisture sensor to an ESP32, Prometheus and Grafana Cloud alerts with her daughter, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
The best explanation of monitoring versus observability you will hear this year involves a houseplant and a curious eight-year-old. In this Conf42 Remix 2026 pick, [Marie Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics), Senior Developer Advocate at Grafana Labs, walks through the weekend project she built with her daughter: a soil moisture sensor on an ESP32 board, readings shipped to Prometheus, a Grafana Cloud dashboard, and a Telegram alert when the plant gets thirsty.

Marie set herself a goal for the year of no plant casualties, and used it as an excuse to teach STEM at home. The result is a beginner-level IoT build and a lesson in explaining technical ideas without jargon.

## Monitoring answers yes or no, observability answers why

The conceptual half of the talk is the gardening analogy, and it works on adults too. Monitoring is checking whether the soil is dry and watering it if so: reactive, a yes-or-no check. If the plant still looks unwell after watering, monitoring has nothing more to say.

Observability is looking at all the signals over time to understand why the plant's health changes. Does moisture drop at a certain time of day? Should room temperature and humidity be part of the picture? Is one of the dogs doing something it shouldn't? Without signals you are guessing on hunches; with them, Marie says, the black box becomes a clear box and you act before the plant suffers. Swap "plant" for "checkout service" and you have the talk most SREs give their managers.

## The hardware is cheap and the wiring is three pins

The build list is short: a soil moisture sensor, an ESP32-S3 dev kit, a breadboard, jumper wires and a USB-C cable, plus the Arduino IDE and a Grafana Cloud account on the free plan. The sensor's two metal prongs conduct better when the soil is wet, so its analog output is a number that goes up as the soil dries.

Wiring is VCC to 3.3V, ground to ground and analog out to pin 11. Marie explains each one to her daughter as parts of a battery, and explains baud rate as friends agreeing to speak at the same speed. The first program just reads the pin every five seconds and prints "dry" above 500 and "wet" below it to the serial monitor.

## From serial logs to a dashboard with alerts

Nobody watches a serial monitor all day, so the next step sends readings to the managed Prometheus that comes with Grafana Cloud. Prometheus becomes the gardener who writes every reading into a time series toolbox, and PromQL is how you ask it questions. The Arduino side needs a few libraries (Protobuf, Snappy, Loki transport and the Prometheus Arduino client), a config file with the instance URL, username, API token and Wi-Fi details, and a certificates file. Marie copied the example from the Prometheus Arduino project and adapted it; when her daughter asked whether that was cheating, she got a lesson in how programming actually works.

The dashboard uses a text panel with a picture of the plant, a stat panel for health, a gauge with the 500 threshold, and a time series. Value mappings turn green to red when the soil dries out, which made the dashboard readable for an eight-year-old. A Grafana alert rule on the same query fires to a Telegram contact point. As a last flourish Marie asks Grafana Assistant, the AI agent built into Grafana Cloud, to polish the dashboard's look.

## Who should watch

Parents and mentors looking for a first IoT project with real tooling; anyone new to Prometheus and Grafana who wants the whole metrics-to-alert path in one sitting; and engineers who need better analogies for explaining observability to non-engineers. If you run Prometheus at scale, the technical parts will be familiar, but the explanations are worth borrowing.

- [Nidal Albeiruti on feature engineering for binary IoT sensors](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2021_Nidal_Albeiruti_Feature_Engineering_Techniques_Binary_IoT_Sensors), where sensor data goes next.

Title: SAST starts with the syntax tree: a practical Semgrep primer
Description: Safeer C M of MoEngage explains how SAST parses code into ASTs and walks through open-source Semgrep rules, taint mode and CI rollout, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
Static analysis only looks like magic until you see the tree it is matching against. In a session picked for Conf42 Remix 2026, [Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep), Principal Engineer at MoEngage and an SRE for more than 20 years, takes SAST apart down to the abstract syntax tree, then rebuilds it with open-source Semgrep: YAML rules, metavariables, and a rollout plan that doesn't drown developers in findings.

It's a foundations talk and says so. If you have ever been handed a SAST report with four hundred findings and closed the tab, this is the half hour that explains why that happened and how to avoid doing it to your own team.

## Grep sees text, SAST sees structure

Safeer starts with the pipeline every static analyser shares. Source code is broken into tokens, the tokens are parsed into an abstract syntax tree according to the language grammar, and then control-flow and data-flow analysis work out how execution and data move through it. Rules are applied to that structure, not to the raw characters.

The payoff is shown with a handful of print statements that look different as text (quotes, spacing, formatting) but produce the same AST. Python's own `ast` module makes the point concrete: feed it a one-liner and you get the tree back. A variable assignment followed by a print turns into two subtrees, and you can see how a real codebase becomes a very large tree very quickly.

He is also honest about the history. First-generation SAST tools were slow, hard to set up and produced results nobody trusted, which bred alert fatigue. Later tools improved, but false positives remain, and static analysis still struggles with things like access control and authorisation logic, weak cryptography and configuration problems that live outside the source.

## Semgrep rules look like the code they catch

The name stands for semantic grep: the engine understands the language and matches code-shaped patterns against the AST. The open-source Community Edition is the engine; the commercial platform adds central rule management, reporting, supply chain and software composition analysis on top. The talk sticks to the open engine.

A rule is a YAML document with an id, a pattern, a message, languages, a severity and metadata such as CWE or documentation links. Patterns read like real code with placeholders, which matters more than it sounds: developers can review a rule without learning a separate DSL. From there Safeer layers on the combinators (`patterns` for AND, `pattern-either` for OR, `pattern-not`, `pattern-inside`, `pattern-regex`) and metavariables that capture part of the match so you can constrain it with a regex or comparison.

He then draws the line between structural matching, which finds a code shape in one place, and taint mode, which follows untrusted input from sources to dangerous sinks. The Community Edition is single-file; cross-file analysis is where the Pro engine comes in.

## The demo: three rules worth stealing

The live part runs three rules against small Python files. A `pattern-either` rule catches SQL injection in `cursor.execute` calls built with concatenation or formatting, and finds two of the three variants in the sample. A multi-line rule enforces an in-house standard: any function that processes input without calling the company's `validate_input` helper gets flagged. The last uses a metavariable regex to spot hard-coded AWS access key IDs and secret keys in variable assignments.

None of these are exotic, which is the point. The second one in particular shows how Semgrep turns a code-review comment you keep repeating into a check that never gets tired.

## Roll it out softly or it gets ignored

The adoption advice is the part most teams skip. Start with `--config=auto`, which pulls the registry's community rules for your languages and frameworks, then fork and tune those rules instead of writing from scratch. Run Semgrep in the IDE, in pre-commit hooks scanning only changed files, in CI, and as pull request comments. Begin with warnings rather than blocking builds, export SARIF or JSON to your code-scanning dashboard, scan against a baseline so you only see new issues, and add rules slowly. Noise kills adoption faster than missed bugs do.

## Who should watch

Developers and platform engineers who have been told to "add SAST" and want a mental model first; security engineers who need to explain to their teams why a finding fired. If you already maintain a custom Semgrep ruleset, you will know most of this.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Peter De Tender's lap around GitHub Dependabot and CodeQL](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql), for the GitHub-native alternative.
- [Ukanah Dean on Python security best practices](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2024_Ukanah_Dean_python_security_best_practices_protecting_common_vulnerabilities), which pairs well with the SQL injection rule.

Title: Push protection, Dependabot and CodeQL, demoed in one GitHub repo
Description: Peter De Tender of Microsoft tours GitHub's built-in security at Conf42 Remix 2026, from rulesets and push protection to Dependabot and CodeQL in VS Code.
Body:
Peter De Tender promises "full demos, no slides" and mostly delivers. At Conf42 Remix 2026, the Business Program Manager and Lead Technical Trainer at Microsoft walks through the security features GitHub ships in every repository, in roughly the order you'd turn them on: repo hygiene, secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot, and CodeQL, including running CodeQL from VS Code before code is merged.

It's a GitHub feature tour, and says so. If your code lives on GitHub and the Security tab is still mostly grey, this is the half hour that changes that.

## Start with the boring settings

The first demo is repository hygiene in a public sample repo. Collaborators are different from contributors: anyone can open a pull request on a public repo, but collaborators can manage settings and permissions, so invite carefully and limit who can review. GitHub warns when the main branch isn't protected, and Peter's recommendation is a ruleset that targets both the default branch and `main` by name pattern, since the default can be changed. The ruleset defaults block deletions and force pushes; he usually adds restricted branch creation, required code scanning and code quality results, and automatic Copilot code review.

Then the basics everyone skips: secrets go in encrypted Actions secrets, not variables, and a `SECURITY.md` file (plus code of conduct and contributing files) gives every visitor a visible security policy link. That's useful for open source and inner source alike.

## Push protection stops the secret before it lands

Secret scanning detects tokens and keys from a long list of partners and platforms, from AWS and Azure keys to API keys, connection strings and SSH keys. By default it scans what's already in the repo. Push protection goes further and blocks the push.

Peter shows both paths. Editing in the browser, he pastes a GitHub personal access token into a file and tries to commit; GitHub stops him, names the token type and line, and offers bypass reasons: false positive, used in tests, or "I'll fix it later". He's unimpressed with that last one, since it lets the secret into history. Then he repeats it from VS Code, and the push itself is rejected before it reaches GitHub. Same rule, earlier in the loop.

## Dependabot shows the CVE and the fix

Dependabot scans package dependencies against the public CVE database and GitHub's advisory database. Enabling alerts also turns on the dependency graph. In a second demo repo, alerts list the severity, attack vector and complexity, the CVE ID and a suggested version bump. His sample is a command injection issue in lodash. The dependency graph shows transitive packages too, and you can export an SBOM as JSON from it.

## CodeQL treats your code as a database

The last section is the strongest. CodeQL builds a database from your code and runs queries against it, either GitHub's and the community's standard queries or your own. Enabling code scanning generates an Actions workflow you can edit: triggers on push and pull request to `main`, or a schedule, read-only permissions, one job per language. His sample repo has C# and JavaScript, so it loops over both, and comes back clean.

Then the shift-left moment. With the CodeQL extension in VS Code, Peter downloads a database for a C# project and runs a query for the test secret he planted earlier. It's flagged by 115 different prebuilt C# queries. Even if someone clicked "I'll fix it later" on push protection, CodeQL still finds it.

## Who should watch

Teams on GitHub that haven't switched on the Security tab, and leads who want a short demo to show developers before turning on push protection org-wide. If you already run GitHub Advanced Security, Peter's later talk on going beyond it (linked below) is the better follow-up.

Title: AI can clear forensic backlogs, but a human still signs the report
Description: Victor Agboola, cyber security analyst, explains at Conf42 Remix 2026 where AI helps digital forensics, from device triage and NLP to court admissibility.
Body:
Digital forensics labs don't lack evidence, they drown in it. Victor Agboola, a cyber security analyst, opens his Conf42 Remix 2026 talk with the backlog problem: phones, laptops, cloud accounts, cars and IoT devices all hold evidence now, and investigators can wait weeks before anyone looks at a seized device. His argument is that AI is best used as a triage and pattern-finding layer, with human investigators still owning every conclusion.

It's a broad survey aimed at security and investigations people, covering techniques, tools, case studies, risks and trends.

## Three kinds of AI, three kinds of evidence

Victor maps AI families to forensic work. Machine learning flags anomalies in logs, system behaviour and network traffic, clusters artifacts into campaigns and classifies malware families. Deep learning handles image and video analysis, facial recognition and object detection, media tampering and malware behaviour. Natural language processing extracts entities from emails, chats and documents, reads sentiment and context, and summarises long threads. Commercial tools he names include Cellebrite Pathfinder, Magnet's AI features and Microsoft's GPT-based copilots.

## Triage is where weeks become days

The strongest case study is automated triage. Agencies routinely receive a pile of seized devices at once. An AI triage system scans each device as it's ingested and surfaces likely priorities: deleted messages, suspicious media, unusual communication patterns, recently accessed files, rare file types, encrypted containers and apps commonly used by known offenders. The output is a structured preview, so investigators can decide which devices need a full examination and which don't. Victor says this has cut turnaround in some agencies from three to four weeks to a few days.

## Protecting the people who review the worst material

The second case study is child sexual abuse material. Deep learning models screen and classify probable abuse content before a human sees it, and deduplicate against global databases to connect cases to known victims faster. Investigators then review only what's been flagged as relevant, which reduces their exposure to traumatic material and speeds reporting to child protection organisations. It's one of the clearest examples in the talk of AI reducing harm for the analysts themselves.

He also covers deep-learning file carving, which rebuilds fragmented or partly overwritten files that pattern-matching carvers miss, and NLP in fraud cases, where tools pull names, locations and transaction details from SMS, WhatsApp, email and social media, map relationships between suspects, and spot sudden sentiment shifts or the repeated phrasing scammers reuse.

## Evidence has to survive a courtroom

The section on risks is what separates this from a sales pitch. Models can inherit bias from training data and over-prioritise certain groups. Processing messages and location history raises privacy and warrant questions, especially across borders. Black-box models clash with courts that expect transparent, reproducible, auditable workflows, and if an investigator can't explain an output, the defence can challenge it. Models also hallucinate, so findings must be validated against raw data, with low-confidence results routed to human review. And governance has to say who may run which tools, how outputs are interpreted and what gets documented, with regular audits.

His last point is the thesis: human expertise remains irreplaceable for context, intuition and judgment.

## What comes next

Victor's trends list: LLM forensic copilots that summarise artifacts, interpret logs and draft preliminary reports; automated cloud forensics across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud; IoT and vehicle data as everyday evidence; AI that detects anti-forensic tricks like wiping, steganography and timestamp manipulation; standardised automated pipelines; and AI-driven training to address the shortage of investigators.

## Who should watch

DFIR practitioners, SOC analysts moving toward investigations, and anyone procuring AI forensics tooling who needs a checklist of questions about explainability and admissibility. It's an overview, so don't expect tool demos.

Title: Six architecture patterns that make compliance a design property
Description: Sneha Nallapu (J.B. Hunt) at Conf42 Remix 2026 on compliance-by-design with event sourcing, bitemporal data, graph lineage, CQRS, ABAC and adaptive handling.
Body:
Most compliance work arrives after the system is built, as a bolt-on report or a control that slows everything down. Sneha Nallapu, Senior Software Engineer at J.B. Hunt Transport Services, argues at Conf42 Remix 2026 for the opposite: treat compliance as a structural design principle, like scalability or security, and pick architecture patterns that make the system auditable by default.

It's a short pattern catalogue, about ten minutes, with the financial-services setting in the foreground. The title mentions robotics, but the substance is architecture for regulated systems in general.

## Reactive compliance doesn't scale

Sneha's opening is the regulatory pressure on financial institutions: anti-money-laundering rules, data privacy and risk management keep growing in complexity, and traditional methods come in late, create bottlenecks and attract penalties. Patching systems after every new rule is expensive. Her alternative is to design systems that anticipate regulation from day one, so compliance stops being a checklist and becomes a design strategy.

## Three foundations: history, time and lineage

The first three patterns give a system a memory regulators can trust.

**Event sourcing** records every change as an event and never overwrites one. Sneha's analogy is keeping a diary instead of editing yesterday's entry. Technically it's an append-only log with replayable history and cryptographic integrity, which gives full traceability and non-repudiation.

**Bitemporal data** tracks two timelines: when something was true in the world and when the system learned about it. That lets you reconstruct what was known at any point, even after corrections, which is exactly the question an auditor asks.

**Graph-based lineage** maps data flow across microservices with nodes and edges, so you can trace a number in a report all the way back to its source. Auditors get transparency; engineers get impact analysis for free.

## Separate the paths, decide access by attributes

**CQRS** splits the write side from the read side. Commands validate transactions and enforce compliance rules; the query side is optimised for audits, monitoring and reporting. Each scales on its own, which suits systems that need both accuracy and fast reporting.

**Attribute-based access control** goes beyond roles, looking at user attributes, data sensitivity and context in real time. Her example: an analyst in Europe can access European data under GDPR, while a contractor sees only masked data. ABAC policies are declarative, which makes them auditable too.

## Let exceptions teach the system

The sixth pattern is the least conventional. Compliance exceptions will happen, so Sneha proposes adaptive exception handling with reinforcement learning: detect the exception, pick a response, execute it and improve over time, so recurring issues shrink and new regulations are absorbed more gracefully. It's presented as a direction rather than a worked implementation.

## Start where the effort is low

Her implementation map is practical. Event sourcing and CQRS take significant work; ABAC and bitemporal models are lighter lifts. So adopt in phases: assess gaps and map current obligations, design around the core patterns, pilot in one domain to validate the results, then scale. The payoff she describes is moving from reactive compliance to proactive assurance and from manual reporting to automated reporting, with compliance becoming a competitive differentiator rather than a tax.

## Who should watch

Architects and senior engineers building systems in finance, logistics or any regulated domain, and teams about to choose between a CRUD database and an event log for something an auditor will eventually read. It's an overview; you'll want separate material for implementing each pattern.

Title: Robots shipped today need post-quantum crypto before quantum arrives
Description: Nehal Singh (California State University, Long Beach) explains at Conf42 Remix 2026 how hybrid TLS, Kyber and Dilithium protect robot fleets from harvest-now attacks.
Body:
A warehouse robot bought this year may still be taking commands in 15 years, long after today's RSA keys stop being safe. Nehal Singh, Senior Manager for IT Infrastructure and Productivity Apps at California State University, Long Beach, uses that gap at Conf42 Remix 2026 to argue that robot fleets should start moving to post-quantum cryptography now, and shows a migration path that doesn't wait for a forklift upgrade.

It's a short, structured talk: the threat, the NIST tools, an architecture by layer, and a five-step plan.

## Harvest now, decrypt later

The threat model is the reason for urgency. Shor's algorithm on a large quantum computer would break RSA and ECC, which secure robot command channels, telemetry and firmware today. Large machines aren't here yet, but attackers don't need them yet: they can record encrypted telemetry, maps, sensor logs and firmware blobs now and decrypt them later. Robots make good targets because they produce long-lived data and must trust updates and commands for years.

Nehal adds that robotics widens the attack surface beyond data. A breach can cause physical disruption. Control channels can be spoofed, over-the-air updates are a major entry point, cloud APIs, brokers and containerised services all sit in the path, and even lidar and camera streams need authentication, because manipulated sensor input changes behaviour.

## Kyber for keys, Dilithium for signatures

The good news is that the standards exist. From NIST's first generation of post-quantum algorithms, Nehal focuses on two lattice-based schemes: Kyber, a key encapsulation mechanism that replaces RSA and ECC for key exchange, and Dilithium, a signature scheme for command authentication and firmware signing. Open-source libraries exist, implementations are maturing, and hardware support is starting to land.

## Hybrid first, so nothing breaks

Nobody migrates a robot fleet overnight, so the practical move is hybrid cryptography: classical and post-quantum algorithms running in parallel, so if one breaks the other still protects the link. Hybrid TLS or SSH is the starting point because it keeps compatibility with legacy components.

## Put the heavy crypto where the watts are

The architecture section is the most useful part for engineers. Robots have tight compute and power budgets, so on the robot itself you use lightweight crypto for local verification and integrity checks. Edge gateways carry the heavier post-quantum operations and translate protocols. In the cloud, every API, management channel and remote debugging interface uses PQC-enabled TLS or SSH. Firmware and OTA updates are signed with Dilithium, so a robot can trust an update in 15 years just as it does today.

Layered on top is zero trust: verify every device, action and packet continuously, give robots least-privilege access and collect behavioural telemetry for anomaly detection. Post-quantum signatures make that identity layer hard to forge, even later.

## Five steps and a few traps

Nehal's plan: inventory every encryption and signing mechanism across devices, gateways and cloud pipelines; prioritise firmware, command channels and OTA; pilot hybrid TLS on one link, such as a gateway to the cloud, and watch handshake performance, latency and compatibility; check that HSMs, TPMs and secure enclaves can support PQC; and document governance and incident response.

The pitfalls are honest. Systems can quietly fall back to weaker algorithms unless policy forbids it. Legacy devices often can't run PQC, so wrap or sandbox them behind secure gateways. Not every vendor is ready, and switching vendors mid-contract is hard, so favour modular crypto APIs and clear roadmaps. And get independent testing, because cryptography is easy to implement subtly wrong.

## Who should watch

Robotics and IoT engineers, security architects responsible for long-lived devices, and anyone who has to sign off on a fleet that will outlive its current certificates. It's a planning talk with no code, so pair it with your crypto library's docs.

Title: Recommendation engines now steer inventory, content and pricing
Description: Ankita Saxena, Sr. Product Manager at Amazon, explains at Conf42 Remix 2026 how recommenders in retail, streaming and marketplaces feed business decisions.
Body:
The "you may also like" row is the smallest part of a modern recommender. Ankita Saxena, Senior Product Manager at Amazon and a Carnegie Mellon alum who works on AI-driven products, argues at Conf42 Remix 2026 that recommendation systems have become strategic infrastructure: the same signals that pick your next show now decide what gets stocked, licensed, bundled and built.

This is a product and strategy talk, not an implementation deep end. It tours four industries, sketches the architecture behind each, and keeps asking what decision the data feeds.

## E-commerce: from suggestions to supply chain

The e-commerce pipeline is the classic one: real-time capture of behaviour, transactions and context; collaborative filtering and item-to-item analysis to find purchase patterns and affinities; a personalisation engine that generates recommendations per user; and a business intelligence layer that aggregates it all for inventory, supplier and product decisions.

Ankita's examples make the second half concrete. If customers keep buying a certain reusable water bottle with fitness gear, a retailer can bundle them, increase supply or launch a private-label version. If shoppers view a jacket and don't buy, the system flags friction, and the team can test the price, the images or the messaging.

## Streaming: micro-genres and the colour of a scene

Streaming recommenders go further because discovery is the product. On top of collaborative filtering they use micro-genre tagging (not just romance, but romance with multiple couples and a Christmas theme), computer vision and audio analysis for style, pacing and mood, and NLP over plot, themes and character arcs. Her example: a viewer who prefers warm colour balance and slower pacing gets visually similar shows, even with different stories. The same signals guide production, regional acquisition and licensing decisions.

## Digital retail: fit is the expensive problem

Ankita calls digital retail her favourite case because fit uncertainty drives returns. Visual similarity models and AR try-on reduce the number of decisions a shopper has to make. She shares results from deployments she has seen: return rates down roughly 5 to 8%, conversion up 15 to 25% on average, sessions 20 to 30% longer, and order values up 8 to 12%. They're presented as observed ranges rather than a single controlled study, but the direction is clear: getting the fit right helps everyone, including the warehouse that processes the returns.

## Marketplaces: four agents with competing goals

The most complex case is the two-sided enterprise marketplace, which she frames as multi-agent reinforcement learning. A seller agent wants visibility to qualified buyers and efficient inventory; a buyer agent wants relevant suppliers and value; a platform agent protects marketplace health and liquidity; a regulatory agent enforces regional laws, logistics and payment rules. Her example: a buyer wants low shipping costs, a seller wants to clear excess stock, and the system learns to pair the buyer with a nearby supplier. Rising interest in sustainable products, likewise, flows back to product and marketing teams as a signal to expand the category.

## A foundation, not a feature

Her conclusion is that recommendation insights cross every function, from supply chain and demand forecasting to content investment, private labels and cross-selling, and that understanding customer behaviour at scale creates a competitive moat that's hard to copy.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineering leads who own a recommender and need to argue for its budget, and ML engineers who want to see how their models' outputs get used upstream. If you want model architectures and offline metrics, look elsewhere; this talk is about the business wiring.

Title: When embeddings can't tell documents apart, make an LLM pick A or B
Description: Maximilian Schattauer of Perelyn shows at Conf42 Remix 2026 how pairwise LLM comparisons re-rank retrieved documents better than one-shot ranking.
Body:
Embedding models and BM25 work until every document in your corpus looks the same to them. Maximilian Schattauer, a technical consultant in data and AI at Perelyn in Munich, hit that wall on a client project, and at Conf42 Remix 2026 he explains the fix: stop asking an LLM to rank a whole list, and ask it which of two documents better answers the question, over and over.

It's a lightning talk, around ten minutes, framed as an anecdote from one project rather than a benchmark paper. That brevity is a feature; the idea fits on a napkin.

## Retrievers are a black box with no reasoning

The conventional setup is familiar: a query goes to a retriever, the retriever searches a corpus with an embedding model (semantic relatedness) or a keyword method like BM25 (overlapping terms), and out comes a set of documents. Maximilian is specifically interested in cases where those documents go to a user or a downstream application, not just into an LLM's context.

He names two limits. The retriever always uses the entire query, so you can't tell it to focus on one aspect. And there's no reasoning step, so in a specialised domain, where documents differ only in small details, neither semantic nor keyword similarity can separate them. On his client's project, the measured retrieval quality made that plain.

## Retrieve first, then let the LLM refine

The fix keeps the classic retriever for a preliminary set of documents and adds an LLM stage to refine both the set and the order. That stage opens a second text input: you can tell it which aspects matter, add document metadata, or inject domain rules that no embedding model would capture. You can use a normal LLM or a reasoning model.

## The LLM as a binary operator

The interesting part is how they used the LLM. Putting every candidate into one prompt and asking for a ranking is fragile, especially with many documents, because of the needle-in-a-haystack problem: documents get lost. Instead, the team treated the LLM as a binary document operator. Each prompt holds the domain description, the query and exactly two documents, and asks which is more suitable, answer A or B.

Run that for every pair and you get a comparison matrix of verdicts, from which an order falls out: document two beats document one, document three loses to document one, and so on. Run each comparison several times at non-zero temperature and you get statistics, so you can count verdicts and rank by them. In their project, this was more reliable than a single LLM ranking call.

## The bill grows with the square

Maximilian is upfront about the cost. The number of LLM calls grows with the square of the number of candidate documents, so it is much slower and more expensive than an embedding lookup, a keyword search or a single re-ranking call. That's the trade: precision where similarity scores fail, paid for in tokens and latency. You'd keep the candidate set small and use this where getting the order right matters.

## Who should watch

Engineers building search or RAG over specialised corpora (legal, technical, regulatory) where retrieval scores cluster together, and anyone tempted to dump 50 documents into one ranking prompt. It's short enough to watch before your next relevance meeting. If you need recall numbers or a latency budget, the talk doesn't provide them.

Title: A lakehouse ends the warehouse-or-lake trade-off, if you zone it
Description: Richa Solanki, data management manager at Ally Bank, lays out lakehouse architecture at Conf42 Remix 2026, from raw-refined-curated zones to Data Vault and ELT.
Body:
For years enterprise data teams had to pick: a data warehouse that is governed and consistent but expensive and rigid, or a data lake that is cheap and scalable and turns into a swamp. Richa Solanki, Manager of Data Management at Ally Bank, argues at Conf42 Remix 2026 that the lakehouse removes that choice, and gives a compact blueprint for building one.

It's a short, architecture-level talk, about 15 minutes of slides with no demo. Think of it as a checklist for a design review.

## Why the old trade-off stopped working

Richa's starting point is the shape of modern enterprise data. Teams no longer handle only relational rows and columns; they get structured, semi-structured and unstructured data from many systems, and a growing share needs real-time processing. Fragmented environments make governance, security and efficiency harder, and slow down trusted insight.

The lakehouse combines warehouse reliability and governance with lake scalability and cost, and runs batch analytics, streaming and machine learning on one platform. Her summary of the goal is to build once, govern centrally and serve many use cases.

## Four pillars that make it a lakehouse

She defines the model by four capabilities:

- **ACID transactions**, so integrity holds at billions of records.
- **Schema enforcement** that supports both schema-on-read and schema-on-write as the business changes.
- **Real-time analytics** over batch and streaming data without a tangle of ETL pipelines.
- **Unified governance**: one place for metadata, lineage and compliance.

## Raw, refined, curated

The structural core is a three-zone layout. The raw zone stores data exactly as it arrived, which preserves it for audits. The refined zone is where cleansing, validation, standardisation and business rules happen. The curated zone holds analytics-ready datasets for reporting and machine learning. Nothing gets massaged on the way in, so you can always replay from the original.

Inside the lakehouse, Richa favours Data Vault modelling because it's built for change. Hubs hold core business entities and their keys, links hold relationships, and satellites hold descriptive attributes with full history. That history is what makes audit and governance questions answerable later, which matters at a bank.

## ELT, columnar files and automated governance

Performance work is familiar but well chosen: columnar formats like Parquet and ORC that compress well and read only the columns a query needs, caching for frequently used datasets, and dynamic partitioning by time or geography for pruning and parallelism. The bigger shift is from ETL to ELT, extracting and loading first and transforming in place, so there are fewer copies, fewer pipelines and fewer places to break.

Governance at that scale has to be automated: data quality checks that flag anomalies before they reach analytics, full lineage and audit trails, role-based access control and encryption. Richa reports the outcomes organisations see from the model: maintenance effort down about 60%, ETL workflows around 45% faster, and total cost of ownership down roughly 40%. The talk doesn't break down where those numbers come from, so treat them as directional.

## Start with open table formats

The implementation advice is the part to copy. Choose platforms that support open table formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg or Hudi to avoid vendor lock-in. Migrate in phases, starting with non-critical workloads to build expertise. And train people, because engineers and analysts need to understand both warehouse and lake thinking. As she puts it, it's as much about people and process as technology.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects planning a lakehouse migration, or leads who need a crisp vocabulary for zones, Data Vault and ELT before a design meeting. If you already run Iceberg in production, this is a summary rather than new ground.

Title: Security Copilot turns conditional access drift into one-click fixes
Description: Cynthia Akiotu demos Microsoft Security Copilot at Conf42 Remix 2026, from a conditional access optimization agent in Entra to DLP alert summaries in Purview.
Body:
The quietest gap in a Microsoft tenant is often the conditional access policy nobody remembered to update. Cynthia Akiotu, a cybersecurity analyst who works on identity and access management, spends her Conf42 Remix 2026 talk showing how Microsoft Security Copilot finds that drift and lets an analyst fix it by asking in plain language.

It's a vendor-specific talk: everything shown runs in Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Purview, and Cynthia, a Microsoft-certified information security administrator, uses Security Copilot as her case study. Her framing applies more broadly: attackers already use AI, so defenders have to operationalise it too.

## Defenders are drowning, attackers are typing prompts

Cynthia opens with the pressure. She cites figures of about 7,000 password attacks per second, most organisations suffering more than one breach in their lifetime, and executives worried about employees pasting sensitive data into AI tools. Add AI-written phishing and alert floods full of false positives, and her point is that the team has enough skill; what it lacks is context and speed.

Her answer is what she calls augmentation rather than automation. Instead of hunting through alerts, an analyst asks the system who the riskiest users are, and gets an answer grounded in the tenant's own data.

## Drift is how good policies go bad

The strongest section is on conditional access drift. In a large enterprise people join, change roles, pick up admin rights along the way and leave. Applications get deployed without being covered by conditional access policies. Policies pile up as duplicates, contradictions and leftovers. Each of these is a door an attacker can use, and Cynthia argues they're hard for a human to spot by eye.

The conditional access optimization agent watches for three kinds of drift: users not covered by policies such as MFA, applications not covered, and policies that should be merged.

## The demo, from risky users to an applied fix

In her Entra tenant the dashboard shows 54 high-risk user detections. The agent's page lists unprotected users it has discovered and an activity log of what it scanned in the last 24 hours. The interesting part is its suggestions. One says two users are missing from an existing policy that requires MFA for a financial application for high, medium and low risk sign-ins. The agent explains the policy; she clicks apply, and the two users are covered. One click for a gap that would otherwise wait for the next audit.

## Purview, where prompts summarise an insider's day

The second demo moves from identity to data. In Microsoft Purview's data loss prevention, Copilot summarises the existing policies by location (16 policies apply to endpoint devices in her tenant) and by data classification, such as financial and privacy data. On a high-severity DLP alert for a sensitive document, she asks Copilot to summarise the alert and then the user's activity. The answer reads like an insider-risk timeline: emails with attachments sent outside the organisation, sensitive files uploaded to cloud storage, an unusual volume of files collected, then deletions. Cynthia's guess is a disgruntled employee on the way out, and she got there in seconds instead of an afternoon of log queries.

## The prompt is now a perimeter

Cynthia doesn't stop at the upside. If prompts can configure policies, prompts are part of the attack surface. She wants every prompt and activity audited, and Security Copilot treated as a privileged access surface with its own policies, because it's now effectively a teammate with admin reach.

## Who should watch

Microsoft 365 and Entra admins, SOC analysts evaluating Security Copilot, and identity teams that suspect their conditional access policies have drifted. If your stack isn't Microsoft, the drift and prompt-governance ideas still transfer, but the demos won't.

Title: JavaScript component testing is heading back to the browser
Description: Daniel Afonso (PagerDuty) maps the 2025 state of JavaScript testing at Conf42 Remix 2026, from Jest and jsdom to Vitest browser mode, MSW and AI tests.
Body:
Ten years ago JavaScript teams ran component tests in a real browser and hated it. Then they moved everything to Node and jsdom. Daniel Afonso, Senior Developer Advocate at PagerDuty and a member of the SolidJS team, argues at Conf42 Remix 2026 that the pendulum is swinging back, and that this time the tooling is good enough to make it stick.

His talk is a survey: the State of JS pain points, eight friends' real testing stacks, a short history lesson, and a tour of where each layer of the testing trophy is going.

## Mocking hurts most, and people are only medium happy

Daniel starts with the State of JS survey. Mocking is the top pain point, ahead of configuration, performance, ESM versus CommonJS, complexity and flakiness. Satisfaction with testing tools sits at 2.5 out of four, which is roughly the score you'd give a dentist.

To see how tools are actually used, he asked friends. Eight replied, and the pattern is clear: Jest plus React Testing Library for unit and integration almost everywhere, Playwright or Cypress for end-to-end, Storybook as a catalogue. Only one counted static analysis as testing. One company migrates old Enzyme tests to React Testing Library whenever someone touches them, which is a nice low-drama migration policy.

## jsdom pretends to be a browser and ends up being neither

The history explains the present. Karma and Jasmine ran tests in a browser and were flaky, slow and painful in CI. Jest moved tests into Node with jsdom polyfilling browser APIs, which made them fast and CI-friendly. Testing Library arrived in 2018 with its user-centric philosophy, and testing got fun, but blurred the line between unit and integration so badly that every company now has its own definitions.

Then the bundler problem: Jest's TypeScript and ESM support is still experimental, while tools like Storybook 10 go ESM-only. Vitest fixed that by testing with the same toolchain that builds the app. The last step came from a blog post by Artem Zakharchenko, creator of Mock Service Worker, about jsdom's limits. His recommendation, which Daniel endorses, is Vitest browser mode: run component tests in an actual browser again.

## The migration was mostly deleting code

Daniel did the migration himself, and his notes are the most useful part of the talk. Swap two imports. Replace every `queryBy` and `findBy` with `getBy`. Drop `waitFor`, because browser mode retries assertions automatically. Run MSW in worker mode. Delete mocks for things like localStorage, since the real one is there now. The cost was two to three seconds of extra runtime, which he happily trades for tests that run where the code runs.

## End-to-end tools want to be your whole test suite

For static analysis, TypeScript and ESLint aren't going anywhere, though he suggests watching Biome and Oxlint. For end-to-end, Playwright is winning adoption, with codegen, tracing and free parallelism. The interesting trend is that end-to-end tools and Storybook now offer visual, component, API and accessibility testing too, which may redraw the testing trophy. MSW, meanwhile, has become the standard for network mocking, with REST, GraphQL and WebSocket support and a growing ecosystem.

## AI speeds you up, if you still learn the thing

On AI, Daniel is pragmatic. Copilots speed you up, but check their sources, especially for newer features like browser mode, and don't let them cover your knowledge gaps. Playwright's MCP server can explore a site and generate a test. Natural-language tools like Midscene get close to self-healing tests (a moved logout button won't break them) at the price of speed, and vision-language models like UI-TARS take terser prompts than text-based models, although GPT wrote better assertions in his experience.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers still on Jest and jsdom, leads deciding whether a Vitest migration is worth it, and anyone who has written a `waitFor` and felt bad about it.

Title: Accessible JavaScript comes down to ten principles and no CAPTCHA
Description: Gian Wild of AccessibilityOz walks through three types of JavaScript functionality and ten accessibility principles, with code examples, at Conf42 Remix 2026.
Body:
If you only take one thing from Gian Wild's talk, she tells you what it should be: don't use CAPTCHA. The founder and CEO of AccessibilityOz packs a lot more than that into her Conf42 Remix 2026 session, a dense, example-heavy tour of how JavaScript breaks accessibility and the ten principles that stop it from doing so.

It's a reference talk in the best sense. Gian moves fast, says so, and points to the AccessibilityOz JavaScript fact sheet, which has a testing checklist, correct and incorrect examples and live demos with copyable code.

## Three kinds of JavaScript, three ways to get it right

Gian sorts JavaScript functionality into three types. Type one binds behaviour to existing interactive elements like links, buttons and text fields, so assistive technologies can read their attributes; a dynamic menu built from nested lists is the example. Type two presents information without interaction, so it needs a text equivalent: a progress meter that also shows a percentage. Type three is custom components that are both interactive and informative, and they should be built from elements assistive technologies already understand. Her calendar widget has a label, a trigger button and a grid made of real table markup.

## The keyboard is the input device that matters most

Principle two (every function works with every input device) gets the most airtime, because assistive technologies like joysticks, head wands, on-screen keyboards and switches mostly mimic a mouse or a keyboard. The cardinal sin is the keyboard trap. Gian recalls the late 2000s, when video players in Firefox routinely swallowed the tab key and users had to close the browser to escape. Modal dialogs are the exception: focus should be trapped inside them, with a way out when the user is done.

Her practical rules: don't use `onfocus="this.blur()"`, keep focus indicators visible, make dynamic menus work with tab and arrow keys, and give any mouse-only feature a keyboard equivalent.

## Insert new content right after the thing that triggered it

Focus order is where well-meaning JavaScript goes wrong. Gian distinguishes three orders: source order, keyboard focus order and visual reading order. When they disagree, people get lost. Dynamic content should go into the DOM immediately after its trigger. And nothing important should live after a submit button: her examples include a ticket site that puts the accessible-tickets request below the purchase button, and an Amazon book page where the "not available" notice sits far to the right after the prices.

## Validate on submit, then send focus to the error

Forms run through several principles at once. Every field needs a coded label (she inspects Amazon's email field to show `label for` matching the input `id`), and fieldsets group fields that only make sense together, like an area code and a phone number. Errors must be described in text, not just colour, which fails screen reader users and people with red-blue colour blindness alike. Validation should run on the form's submit event rather than a button click or individual fields, then move focus to the first invalid field and put the message right after it.

## Time limits, flicker and surprises

The rest is just as concrete. Warn before a session expires and let people extend it; Gian wonders aloud why a donation form needs a 20-minute timeout at all. Flashing content shouldn't flicker faster than three times a second if it contains red, and she points to the free PEAT tool to check, with the 1997 Pokémon episode as the cautionary tale. Don't navigate on a select element's change event, don't auto-refresh or redirect on the client, give carousels a pause button, and stop animated GIFs within five seconds.

## Who should watch

Frontend developers who build forms, menus, modals or custom widgets, and anyone who has shipped a CAPTCHA and felt fine about it. Beginners can start with the accessibility basics material Gian recommends; everyone else should keep her fact sheet open alongside.

Title: Hallucinations are a symptom, missing context is the bug
Description: Sharon Yelenik (Cloudinary) shows at Conf42 Remix 2026 how MCP servers, indexed docs, Context7 and rules files make AI coding in the IDE trustworthy.
Body:
Sharon Yelenik spent a year on the Cloudinary team that turned the company's APIs into MCP servers, and she came out of it with a blunt diagnosis. At Conf42 Remix 2026, the Senior API and DevX Content Writer at Cloudinary argues that hallucinations are not the root problem in AI-assisted coding. They are a symptom; the problem is that the model doesn't know your project, your naming conventions or the API's documented rules, so it guesses.

Her fix is documentation, wired directly into the LLM client in your IDE. The talk is a practical setup guide, demoed in Cursor with Cloudinary, and it's honest about which parts are vendor-specific.

## Two jobs for the AI in your editor

Sharon splits IDE AI into two use cases. The familiar one is code generation and refactoring. The second is agentic tasks: uploading assets, configuring environments, the kind of chores that normally send you to a web console. With MCP servers handling authentication, validation and execution, those stay in the IDE.

The trust gap is real, and she says so. Only 3.8% of developers in the survey she cites report low hallucinations and high confidence, and agent adoption is still a minority. Her bet is that better context raises confidence, and confidence drives adoption.

## Four layers of context

The talk walks through four practices, in order:

1. **Connect the API's MCP servers.** Paste Cloudinary's remote MCP server config into Cursor's tools settings, authenticate, and the tools appear.
2. **Index the API's docs.** Add the documentation URL under Cursor's docs indexing and attach it to each request.
3. **Add Context7.** Its MCP server indexes code snippets and examples from API documentation, so autocomplete comes from documented examples rather than memory. Not every product is indexed yet, and she encourages users to ask vendors for it.
4. **Write rules files.** Short, example-rich files the model reads before it writes: `.mdc` in Cursor, with equivalents in JetBrains and VS Code.

## The four Cs of a good rules file

The rules section is the most reusable part. Sharon's checklist: compatibility (which parameters and SDKs work together), conventions (naming, folders, architecture), constraints (what the AI must never do, like exposing secrets or calling admin APIs from the browser) and canon (short, correct examples to copy). Keep it to one to three pages, review it often and link to the official docs.

Her Cloudinary examples are concrete: always apply `f_auto` and `q_auto`, keep text overlays legible with a set style, never combine `g_face` with `c_pad` because they're incompatible, and use named transformations for hero images and thumbnails instead of ad hoc ones.

## The demo proves the rules get followed

In the finale she asks Cursor to upload a portrait image to her Cloudinary product environment, then turn it into a wide hero image, a text-overlay variant and a face-cropped thumbnail. The agent checks for an existing named transformation, finds one that doesn't match, creates a new one and wires it into the page. The overlay comes out in white, flush to the bottom as the rules file asked, and the thumbnail uses `c_auto` with `g_face`. It even upscales on request. The thumbnail is a little big, and she points out nobody wrote a rule about size, which is the whole lesson in one frame.

She closes with a prediction: docs will stop being reference pages and become runtime components that live inside the IDE and evolve from real usage.

## Who should watch

JavaScript developers and team leads trying to get colleagues to trust AI suggestions, and anyone writing docs or rules files for an API. Cloudinary is the worked example, but she maps the same steps to Auth0, Firebase, Supabase, Slack and Shopify.

Title: eBPF gives Kubernetes observability a view from inside the kernel
Description: Alejandro Mercado, DevOps Lead at Michael Page, explains at Conf42 Remix 2026 why eBPF sits under Cilium, Falco, Pixie and the next wave of Kubernetes observability.
Body:
Kubernetes hides the Linux kernel from developers, and that is exactly where the most useful telemetry lives. Alejandro Mercado, DevOps Lead at Michael Page, opens his Conf42 Remix 2026 talk with a line he picked up at another conference, that observability is a data problem, and then spends the rest of it on the tool that collects the data at the lowest level available: eBPF.

This is a conceptual talk, not a hands-on lab. If you have heard "eBPF" in every other Cilium blog post and want the mental model behind it, it's a good half hour.

## A virtual machine in the kernel, without patching the kernel

Alejandro describes eBPF as a kernel virtual machine that runs sandboxed programs in kernel space without changing kernel source or loading kernel modules. It grew out of the classic Berkeley Packet Filter, and programs can be attached to kprobes, tracepoints, network schedulers and other kernel events. Each time the event fires, your program runs, and can observe, filter or manipulate what's happening in real time.

You have probably used it without noticing. He lists load balancing and DDoS protection on major websites, data statistics on Android devices, and most of the Kubernetes networking stack.

## Why not just do it in user space?

The middle of the talk is a short operating systems refresher, and it earns its place. User-space processes reach memory, disks and the network only through system calls, and each system call costs hundreds or thousands of CPU cycles for the switch between user and kernel modes. So if your application needs a new kernel feature (a new protocol, a smarter load balancing algorithm, traffic redirection for sidecars) you have two bad options: ship all the relevant data up to user space, which is expensive, or get the feature into the kernel itself.

The second option means convincing the kernel community. Alejandro's slide cartoons make the point: an upstream change can take a year, and by the time it lands in your distribution you may not need it anymore. With eBPF you write the program yourself, mostly in a restricted subset of C, and load it in days. Nobody has to agree with you first, which is either liberating or terrifying depending on whether you're on call.

## Powerful, sandboxed, and still your responsibility

Is eBPF dangerous? Loading programs needs admin privileges by default, which limits misuse, and the sandbox protects the kernel. But Alejandro is clear that you could still attach a program to every kernel function or block all network traffic if you tried. The tool is safe in the way a chainsaw is safe: very, when you know what you're doing.

## What the ecosystem already does with it

Most of the talk maps eBPF to tools you can run today. Cilium, the CNCF networking project, uses it for network control and visibility. Kuma and Cilium Service Mesh use it for service-to-service traffic. Falco, Tetragon and Tracee do runtime security. Pixie provides application performance visibility, and Weave Scope tracks TCP connections between containers by attaching programs to kernel probes.

He also highlights three narrower use cases: per-pod and per-container network statistics collected by attaching programs to cgroups; Landlock LSM, which lets unprivileged applications sandbox themselves; and auditing `kubectl exec` sessions by recording the exact commands typed, which matters for governance in companies of any size.

## eBPF and OpenTelemetry are a pair

The closing idea is the one to keep. OpenTelemetry sees the application layers, eBPF sees the bottom of the stack, and correlating both gives you more context than either alone. Alejandro points to projects already working on that correlation and ends with a reading list: the BCC compiler collection, a Brendan Gregg overview, the Cilium project and the eBPF Foundation's tutorials.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers who run Kubernetes but treat Cilium and Falco as black boxes, and anyone about to evaluate eBPF-based observability tools. If you already write eBPF programs, skip it; there is no code here.

- [Zero-instrumentation observability based on eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf) by Nikolay Sivko (Coroot) at Conf42 SRE 2024.

Title: Dapr's sidecar keeps your database out of your microservice code
Description: Christophe Gigax (Hager Group) at Conf42 Remix 2026 on Dapr: one sidecar, standard HTTP and gRPC APIs, and infrastructure picked in YAML.
Body:
Your order service should not need to know whether orders live in Redis or Cosmos DB. That is the pitch Christophe Gigax, Cloud Solution Architect at Hager Group and a Microsoft MVP, makes for Dapr at Conf42 Remix 2026: put a sidecar next to every service, talk to it over plain HTTP or gRPC, and let configuration decide which state store, broker or secret store sits behind it.

It's an introduction, and a well-paced one. Slides for the concepts, a live demo from the Dapr quickstarts repository, then a tour of how the same setup lands on Kubernetes.

## Microservices are easy to draw and hard to debug

Christophe starts with the honest version of microservices. Smaller, focused services buy teams autonomy and independent deployments. They also mean that fixing one bug can require running half the architecture on your laptop, and that the flows between services get hard to follow. Most languages and frameworks weren't built with this style in mind, and applications often end up tied to one hosting platform.

Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) is the CNCF project aimed at that gap. It's event-driven, portable from cloud to edge, works with any language, and ships building blocks out of the box: service-to-service invocation, state management, pub/sub, bindings and triggers, actors, distributed tracing and secrets. He mentions more than a hundred pluggable components, and you can write your own.

## The sidecar is the only dependency your code knows

The core idea is the sidecar pattern. Start a service and a Dapr sidecar comes up beside it; every interaction with the outside world goes through that sidecar. Want to save state? You call the sidecar's state URL with the name of a configured store. Want to call another service? You ask Dapr to invoke method `neworder` on app `nodeapp`, and it does service discovery for you.

The demo makes this concrete. A Node.js app exposes an orders API and stores data through Dapr on localhost port 3500, with no database client in sight. `dapr init` had already pulled a Redis container, so the default state store and pub/sub component are both Redis. A second service, a Python client, loops forever creating orders, and it never calls the Node.js app directly. It calls its own sidecar, which forwards the request. Both are launched with `dapr run --app-id ...` and the code stays free of infrastructure imports.

## Swapping Redis for something else is a YAML change

On Kubernetes, `dapr init` installs four system pods: placement (for actors), the sidecar injector, Sentry for security, and the operator. The injector adds a sidecar to every pod you deploy, and from there you configure components exactly as you did locally. Each component (state store, pub/sub broker, binding, secret store) is a YAML file holding the connection details, so the choice between, say, RabbitMQ and Azure Service Bus lives in config rather than in code.

Pub/sub works the same way: a service publishes to its sidecar, Dapr hands the message to whichever broker the YAML names, and subscribers expose an endpoint that Dapr calls when a message arrives. Telemetry follows the OpenTelemetry standard, so you can point it at Datadog or another backend and change your mind later. Christophe closes on the project's maturity: Dapr became a graduated CNCF project in November 2024.

## Who should watch

Developers and architects who keep rewriting the same Redis, Kafka and secrets plumbing in every service, or who want to see what Dapr looks like before reading the docs. If you already run Dapr in production, this is a refresher rather than new material; the talk stays at the building-block level and doesn't get into actors or failure handling in depth.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Enhancing Workflow Reliability with Dapr: Techniques to Minimize Failure Costs](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Siri_Varma_Vegiraju_workflow_dapr_failure) by Siri Varma Vegiraju (Microsoft) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2025, for the next step once the building blocks are familiar.
- [A Developer's Introduction to Service Mesh](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Rosemary_Wang_introduction_service_mesh) by Rosemary Wang (HashiCorp) at Conf42 Cloud Native 2022, the other big family of sidecars.
- [Ambient Mesh: The new sidecar less & faster Istio for zero trust](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Md_Azmal_ambient_mesh_sidecar_zero_trust) by Md Azmal (IMESH) at Conf42 Kube Native 2023, the case for dropping the sidecar.

Title: Give every team its own GPU scheduler inside a virtual cluster
Description: Piotr Zaniewski of vCluster at Conf42 Remix 2026 demos NVIDIA's KAI Scheduler inside virtual clusters for isolated, per-team GPU scheduling and upgrades.
Body:
Upgrading a shared Kubernetes scheduler is the kind of change that ruins a week: one bad version and every team's pods sit in Pending. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Piotr Zaniewski, Head of Engineering Enablement at vCluster, showed a way around it: run NVIDIA's open source KAI Scheduler inside virtual clusters, so each team gets its own scheduler version, its own fractional GPUs, and a blast radius the size of one pod.

It's a live-demo talk from the company that makes vCluster, built on a kind cluster on a laptop with an older NVIDIA card. Small hardware, but the moves are the same on EKS or bare metal.

## KAI brings GPU-aware scheduling to Kubernetes

The default Kubernetes scheduler was built for CPU nodes. NVIDIA open-sourced the Kubernetes AI scheduler, KAI, in 2025, adding what GPU workloads need: fractional GPU allocation so several workloads share one card, queue-based scheduling, and node topology awareness. Zaniewski is careful to point out that GPU workloads aren't only AI: training, fine-tuning and inference sit next to video processing, CUDA development in Jupyter notebooks and batch scientific computing, all competing for the same expensive cards.

## A whole Kubernetes in a pod

vCluster runs a certified Kubernetes distribution inside a pod: API server, controller manager, an optional scheduler and a data store (SQLite in the demo; etcd or an external database for high availability). The key component is the syncer, a reconciliation loop that copies resources between the virtual cluster and the host, handling name collisions and staying highly configurable. Teams can share host services like cert-manager or an Istio ingress, or install their own. In the demo, the virtual cluster pod used about 370 MB of memory and a sliver of CPU.

The configuration that makes KAI work is short: enable the virtual scheduler in the control plane, sync nodes from the host, and sync runtime classes so the `nvidia` runtime class and GPU node labels are visible inside. Then install KAI into the virtual cluster as if it were any other cluster.

## Fractional GPUs, A/B schedulers, 39-second rollback

The demo builds up in steps. First, a GPU-backed web app on the host generates SRE haiku from a phone via an ngrok link (the standout was about the wrong kubectl context, vanishing pods and 3am despair, which is too relatable). Then a virtual cluster with KAI inside, two pods labelled with a KAI queue, `schedulerName` set to KAI, the `nvidia` runtime class, and fractions of 10% and 20% of the GPU. They schedule as configured.

Then the real point: two more virtual clusters, "team stable" and "team beta", each running a different KAI version, while the dev team keeps using the host's default scheduler. Three scheduling setups on one physical cluster, no negotiation over a middle-ground version. When the experiment is over, the virtual cluster is deleted; in the demo that took 39 seconds.

## Why this matters more than the demo

Zaniewski's risk section is the part SREs will recognise. A shared scheduler upgrade can fail through bugs, version mismatches with features pods depend on, or slow resource leaks that only show up days later. Worse, schedulers and operators ship as CRDs, and he has seen botched CRD upgrades for operators managing databases end in data loss. With per-team virtual clusters you can test a new scheduler in production without touching anyone else, instead of standing up and paying for a separate EKS test cluster. He describes the risk as near zero, since a failing virtual cluster can just be deleted, and the pace of upgrades stops being set by the most cautious team.

One honest note: the abstract promises GPU utilisation rising from 40% to 90% with fractional GPUs. The demo shows fractional allocation working, not a utilisation benchmark, so measure that on your own fleet.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs running shared GPU clusters for ML, research and dev teams with different needs, and anyone dreading their next scheduler or operator upgrade. The vCluster docs have a dedicated KAI Scheduler guide if you want to follow along.

Title: When an outage is also a breach, run compliance in parallel
Description: Nisheedh Raveendran of LinkedIn at Conf42 Remix 2026 on incident response under HIPAA, GDPR and DMA, and building a compliance-ready playbook.
Body:
Most incident processes optimise for one clock: time to recovery. In regulated environments there's a second clock, and GDPR's runs for 72 hours from the moment you know. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Nisheedh Raveendran, Senior Staff Engineer at LinkedIn with two decades building large distributed systems, explained why ordinary incident response breaks down under HIPAA, GDPR and the Digital Markets Act, and laid out a framework that runs technical recovery and regulatory obligations side by side.

It's a methodical talk, structured like the playbook it recommends. Light on war stories, heavy on things you can paste into your runbook.

## The regulatory incident paradox

Raveendran calls it a dual mandate. Technical recovery wants speed: restore function, limit data loss, stop the cascade. Regulatory obligations want accuracy: reporting deadlines, documentation, evidence preservation, legal and forensic requirements. A small response team gets pulled between remediation and paperwork, and communication has to be timely and transparent while staying inside legal constraints on what can be shared.

Traditional incident management misses this in predictable ways. Regulatory deadlines rarely line up with recovery timelines. Documentation slows the fix. Legal, compliance and PR all join the call. And the sharpest conflict: responders often need some access to sensitive production data to act, which is exactly what the regulations try to prevent.

## Three regimes, three different clocks

The talk gives a compact summary of each:

- **HIPAA** (healthcare): incidents involving protected health information reported to HHS, and potentially the media, typically within 60 days, with direct notice to affected individuals and a risk assessment to classify severity. The hard part during an outage is deciding whether PHI was exposed while you're still restoring critical services.
- **GDPR**: 72 hours to notify the supervisory authority. Raveendran splits it into hours 0 to 24 for preliminary assessment (was personal data affected? start collecting evidence), 24 to 48 for risk assessment and drafting notices, and 48 to 72 for submission and preparing messages to data subjects.
- **DMA**: obligations on gatekeeper platforms, including transparent reporting of algorithmic failures, maintaining interoperability and continuous service during incidents, fairness in restoration priorities, and strict rules on data access during recovery.

## Documentation by design, not by heroics

The framework has three phases. Preparation means pre-approved notification templates, privacy-preserving investigation tools and a map of which regulations apply to which systems. Response means parallel tracks for mitigation and compliance, with regulatory triage, continuous documentation and evidence preservation. Recovery adds compliance verification checkpoints and progressive service restoration.

Four principles sit underneath: documentation by design (evidence collection built into the technical workflow, one source feeding several regulators' reports), decision frameworks (predefined classification criteria and automated notification triggers based on impact thresholds), privacy-preserving analysis (differential privacy and data minimisation in log collection), and parallel work streams with synchronisation checkpoints between the technical and compliance teams. Monitoring should also be compliance-aware: alerts designed to catch regulatory incidents before they become breaches, tracking of personal data flows, and timers that start the regulatory clock automatically.

His concrete tooling example is AWS Systems Manager: operators mitigate through an automated, logged tool rather than direct production access, which keeps the audit trail and masks data from on-call engineers.

## Game-day the paperwork too

The playbook section closes the loop. Document which regulations apply and build a matrix of notification requirements and deadlines. Give each incident team a named compliance liaison and train responders on the regulatory implications. Keep pre-approved templates per regulation and standard evidence procedures. Then run game days with regulated data in the scenario, testing not just recovery speed but whether the logs, audit trail and notification timelines would survive a real report.

## Who should watch

Incident commanders, SREs and platform engineers in healthcare, fintech or any company big enough to be a DMA gatekeeper. Also useful for compliance teams who want to understand what an on-call engineer is juggling at 3am.
