Title: Hurricanes are load tests; insurers need edge and serverless ready
Description: Chandra Prakash Kathroju of Citizens Property Insurance at Conf42 Remix 2026 on AI, edge computing and serverless for insurance incident response.
Body:
For a property insurer, the day of peak traffic is also the day of a natural disaster, which is exactly when the claims portal is most likely to fall over. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Chandra Prakash Kathroju, a senior software engineer at Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, laid out how AI, edge computing and serverless architectures fit together to help insurers detect incidents faster, scale through surges and stay compliant while doing it.

It's a short, high-level overview aimed at people mapping a modernisation strategy, not a deep technical walkthrough. Think of it as an architecture briefing for the insurance domain.

## Four pain points, all of them about time

Kathroju starts with the problems most insurers know: incidents that go unnoticed for hours or days, adjusters overloaded by manual claims processes, no real-time insight (so insurers react to losses instead of preventing them), and systems that collapse under demand during events like hurricanes. Each one, he argues, lands directly on customer trust and operating cost.

## Each technology answers a different one

The talk maps the technologies onto those problems:

- **AI** in underwriting (risk models using IoT sensor, driving behaviour and property data), in claims (chatbots gather details, algorithms triage severity, humans handle the exceptions) and in fraud detection, catching suspicious patterns before payout.
- **Edge computing** for decisions where the data is born. A flood sensor in a home can raise an alert immediately even when the link to the cloud is slow, and car telematics can analyse accident data locally.
- **Serverless** for elasticity. His analogy is electricity: you don't think about the power plant, you just use what you need, so claim portals don't crash in a surge and new tools ship in days.

The layered picture is sensors capturing raw data, edge processing for instant local insight, cloud analysis for patterns across sources, and the resulting actions, from claim approvals to fraud prevention. Speed at the source, depth at scale.

## Root cause and surge handling

On incident response proper, Kathroju describes AI that pulls data from multiple systems to separate weather damage from equipment failure from human error, then recommends remediation, so the fix today becomes prevention tomorrow. For large disruptions the toolkit is familiar to any SRE: auto-scaling, shifting workloads between regions, failover and backups, and load balancing to smooth spikes. Insurance just gives those patterns an unusually predictable trigger: the weather forecast.

## Compliance decides where things run

Regulation shapes the rest. Hybrid cloud keeps sensitive, regulated data in private or on-prem systems while analytics runs in the public cloud, meeting frameworks like GDPR and HIPAA without giving up scale. Logging and monitoring simplify audits, and automated governance protects sensitive data across environments. He also covers blockchain for reinsurance: smart contracts to automate settlements and immutable audit trails to cut manual steps between insurers and reinsurers.

The roadmap is four steps: assess the current state, design a strategy for where AI, edge and serverless fit, pilot in small controlled environments, then scale what works. His closing point is that this is an ecosystem decision rather than a single tool purchase.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads at insurers and other regulated businesses whose load follows real-world events. Engineers wanting implementation detail or numbers will find it light; people writing the modernisation proposal will find the structure handy.

Title: Incident dashboards should interpret the data, not just display it
Description: Priyanshi Deshwal at Conf42 Remix 2026 on AI-powered incident interfaces that rank alerts, pick the right chart and write the status update for you.
Body:
Five people on a bridge call, each staring at a different dashboard, lining up time ranges by hand while customers wait. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Priyanshi Deshwal, a senior frontend engineer at ThoughtSpot (the company behind Mode) who works on data visualisation and analytics products, argued that incident tooling should stop being a passive map and start acting like a GPS: interpreting the data, ranking what matters and suggesting where to look.

This is a vision-and-roadmap talk from someone who builds visualisation for a living. There's no product demo; the value is in the design principles and a sensible rollout plan.

## Dashboards were built for monitoring, not for crises

Deshwal's diagnosis has three parts. Data volume: telemetry arrives faster than traditional tools can process it in real time, so they sample, add latency and leave blind spots. Silos: logs in one tool, metrics in another, deployment history somewhere else, so responders swivel between systems and correlate by eye. And the dashboards themselves: reactive by design, showing history and leaving you to reconstruct the present. Twenty charts updating every few seconds is cognitive overload, and every filter click and time-window tweak during a high-severity incident is a chance for human error. Her best line on scale: nothing is worse than a dashboard that freezes when everything is on fire.

## Three capabilities that change the screen

The core of the talk is what she calls AI-powered visual intelligence, broken into three capabilities:

- **Intelligent alert prioritisation**: models trained on past incidents turn 500 alerts into a ranked handful worth attention.
- **Automated visual recommendations**: the system chooses the right representation for the problem. During a network outage it might generate a topology map with affected nodes in red, so the blast radius is visible at a glance.
- **Contextual summaries**: natural language processing turns technical data into a plain-language summary for stakeholders, so responders aren't spending 15 minutes every hour writing status updates.

In her picture of the incident view, the layout reconfigures itself: relevant metrics rise, related anomalies cluster, probable root causes show confidence scores, and predictive models warn about cascading failures while there's still time to act. Further out she sees natural-language queries ("show me all error spikes for the checkout service in the last 30 minutes"), voice, and shared views for multiple teams. The constant is the division of labour: AI crunches the data, humans own judgment, communication and decisions.

## Start in shadow mode

The roadmap is the part to take to your next planning meeting. Measure first: mean time to detection, mean time to resolution and the number of hand-offs per incident. Then integrate data into unified pipelines, because a model with half the picture is worse than none. Train on historical incidents. Design role-based interfaces, deep technical detail for SREs and business impact for executives, built for people under stress. Then keep learning from every retrospective.

Her advice on trust is the most practical bit: run the AI in shadow mode first, with recommendations shown alongside human decisions so the team can compare before relying on it. Fix data quality and logging conventions before blaming the model, and treat the rollout as change management, with incident commanders involved early. Afterwards, compare detection and recovery times before and after, check whether manual correlation steps are actually decreasing, and ask whether responders trust the system.

## Who should watch

SRE leads and incident commanders evaluating AI features in their observability stack, and frontend or data-viz engineers building incident tooling. If you want model architectures, look elsewhere; if you want a checklist for introducing AI to a war room without losing the room, this is it.

Title: AgentCore's seven primitives for getting agents off the laptop
Description: Samuel Baruffi of AWS at Conf42 Remix 2026 tours Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the managed primitives that take AI agents from POC to production.
Body:
Plenty of agent proofs of concept work beautifully on exactly one developer's laptop. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Samuel Baruffi, Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, walked through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a set of managed primitives aimed at the gap between that demo and a production agent: performance, scalability, security and governance.

This is a product tour of an AWS service, given by AWS, recorded while AgentCore was still in preview. Its most useful idea travels beyond AWS, though: you can adopt the primitives one at a time rather than buying the whole stack.

## Not the same thing as Bedrock Agents

Baruffi clears up a naming trap first. Bedrock Agents, around for a couple of years, is the opinionated way to build an agent on AWS. AgentCore is newer and lower level: building blocks that don't care which framework or model you use. Strands, LangGraph, LangChain, CrewAI or your own code; Bedrock models, Gemini or OpenAI. That framework-agnostic stance is the whole pitch.

## Runtime and identity: where it runs, who may call it

**AgentCore Runtime** is serverless compute for agents. You add a decorator, package a Dockerfile, push it to ECR and get an API endpoint. Each invocation gets true session isolation, sessions can run for up to eight hours, and billing follows consumption. It can also host a remote MCP server, for example one built with FastMCP.

**AgentCore Identity** handles both directions of auth. Inbound: who is allowed to invoke this agent, via IAM or OAuth 2.0 with existing providers such as Okta, Azure AD or Amazon Cognito. Outbound: how the agent gets credentials to call an AWS database, or Salesforce or Google Drive through API keys or OAuth flows. It works even if the agent itself is hosted elsewhere.

## Gateway: don't hand the model 360 tools

**AgentCore Gateway** is a managed MCP server. Point it at an OpenAPI schema and the endpoints become tools; point it at Lambda functions and your own code becomes tools. One gateway, many targets, many tools per target, with authentication required.

The best moment in the talk is semantic tool search. Baruffi's example gateway has 360 tools, and a plain MCP list-tools call returns all of them. Instead, the agent asks the gateway for tools that can, say, create a social media post, and gets back four. Fewer tools in context means better accuracy, lower latency and fewer input tokens: a small RAG system for your tool catalogue. Anyone who has watched a model pick the wrong one of 40 similarly named functions will appreciate it.

## Memory, browser and code: the parts agents keep reinventing

**AgentCore Memory** separates short-term memory (raw conversation turns, retained for a configurable period) from long-term memory, which is extracted asynchronously using strategies you choose: semantic facts, user preferences ("I always say colour blue" becomes a stored preference), or periodic summaries. It's built for multi-tenant use with per-customer namespaces and your own encryption keys. As Baruffi notes, models don't remember anything between calls; supplying memory is your job.

**AgentCore Browser** gives agents an isolated, serverless headless browser per session, driven through libraries like Playwright or browser-use, with live-stream URLs so users can watch, session replay for debugging and CloudTrail logging. **Code Interpreter** is a sandbox for model-generated code, with Python and JavaScript runtimes, S3 integration for large datasets and no root access.

## Observability that leaves AWS if you want

**AgentCore Observability** traces every model call and tool use. CloudWatch users get prebuilt dashboards; everyone else can export OpenTelemetry to their own backend. That last part matters for teams who don't want agent traces living in a separate silo from the rest of production.

## Who should watch

Teams on AWS with an agent POC that needs auth, memory and tracing before anyone will let it near customers. Teams elsewhere can treat it as a checklist: if you're building these seven pieces yourself, the talk shows where the boundaries usually fall. The AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, which Baruffi recommends, is the next step.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Don't Give the Agent a Shell: Tool and Identity Boundaries for AI Agents in Cloud Operations](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_identity_permissions_cloud) by Ahmed Tariq digs into the identity questions.
- [Running 50+ AI agents in production: the patterns that held up](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Muhammad_Haris_Farooq_agents_patterns_production) by Muhammad Haris Farooq, the view from after the POC.

Title: Sky computing, or how to stop picking one cloud for your AI stack
Description: Brian Irish of Ditto at Conf42 Remix 2026 on sky computing, intercloud brokers like SkyPilot, and running each ML pipeline stage on the best cloud.
Body:
Cloud repatriation is often the answer to a bill nobody planned for. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Brian Irish, Engineering Lead at Ditto and a long-time SRE, argued that going back on-prem is rarely the step forward it looks like, and that sky computing, where workloads move between clouds through a broker, deals with lock-in, data gravity and cost more directly.

The talk mixes a concept explainer with a close look at SkyPilot, the open source broker from UC Berkeley. Irish is upfront that his three pillars are his own framing, not the canon.

## Repatriation often treats the symptom

Irish starts with the promises the cloud kept (on-demand scale, pay-as-you-go, global reach) and the ones that bite: vendor lock-in, data gravity and egress fees. He cites a survey figure that 42% of US organisations are considering moving, or have moved, at least half their cloud workloads back on-premise. His suspicion is that many of them never put basic cost controls in place first: shutting down dev environments off-hours, spot instances for batch jobs, resource quotas. Abandoning the cloud is one fix; adopting it properly is another.

## Three pillars: abstraction, automation, agility

The sky computing idea comes from Ion Stoica's 2021 paper, which Irish recommends as a short read. He reduces it to three pillars:

- **Abstraction**: a compatibility layer built from tools that already exist, such as Kubernetes, Ray and S3-style APIs, so you stop caring whether data sits in S3 or Azure Blob Storage. It extends past AWS, GCP and Azure to neoclouds like Lambda Labs, CoreWeave and Nebius.
- **Automation**: intercloud brokers that place workloads based on price, availability and regulation. He calls this the largest pillar and the hardest to get right.
- **Agility**: reciprocal peering agreements between providers that make data transfer free or cheap, dissolving egress fees and data gravity.

## SkyPilot is the broker you can run today

SkyPilot, built at the Berkeley Sky Computing Lab (the same lab lineage behind Spark and Ray), is the concrete part. Irish's figures from mid-2025: over a million downloads, version 0.10, one interface to 17 clouds plus Kubernetes and on-prem, with claimed three to six times cost savings from spot orchestration and 200 GPUs provisioned in under 90 seconds. The workflow is one YAML file and one `sky launch` command, with no code changes for existing ML workloads.

He leans on two public case studies. Abridge, a former Slurm shop, got the familiar interactive experience (`sky launch` with H100s straight to an SSH shell), Jupyter notebooks on GPU clusters, managed jobs with automatic restart, and fast model evaluation by exposing models as FastAPI services, something Slurm lacks natively. Their distributed training YAML is short enough to fit on a slide, with plain PyTorch and Hugging Face and the cluster topology injected as environment variables. The other case is Covalent, which built a new AI stack around GPU scarcity.

The payoff is splitting a pipeline: training on Google Cloud TPUs, inference on AWS Inferentia, preprocessing on Azure, chosen for speed, cost and data residency. Your egress bill will want a word, which is exactly why the agility pillar matters.

## The obstacles are mostly economic

Irish is realistic about why this isn't everywhere yet. Universal standards are unlikely given competitive interests, though Kubernetes, Ray and S3 APIs are a usable bridge. Hyperscalers have little reason to sign peering agreements that undercut egress revenue; smaller providers have every reason to. Then there's inertia: existing investment, "good enough" deployments, retraining costs and the perceived risk of newer providers. He even flags a legitimacy problem: the concept's Wikipedia entry carries a reliability warning after a commercial entity tried to shape the narrative and was banned.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers fighting GPU scarcity, SREs staring at an egress line item, and anyone running research workloads on Slurm who wants to see what a broker looks like. If you're committed to one hyperscaler by contract, it's still a useful view of where the leverage is moving.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Building Robust GPU Performance Validation into CI/CD Pipelines for AI Infrastructure](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Mohit_Gupta_gpu_ci_validation) by Mohit Gupta, for checking the GPUs once you have them.
- [Governing Data Sovereignty in Distributed Multi-Cloud Machine Learning Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Sapna_Pillai_search_semantic_retrieval) by Sapna Pillai on the residency side of multi-cloud ML.
- [Self-hosted LLMs across all your devices and GPUs](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Michael_Yuan_Selfhost_LLMs_on_Macacross_devices_Fast_and_Efficient) by Michael Yuan on portable inference across hardware.

Title: Low-code for the front, public code for the core logic
Description: Anoosha Cherukuri at Conf42 Remix 2026 on pairing low-code platforms with open, auditable public code, with the governance that keeps it from sprawling.
Body:
Citizens expect government apps to work like Uber, and the government doesn't have Uber's engineering headcount. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Anoosha Cherukuri, a senior software developer with the State of Tennessee, made the case for combining two ideas: low-code for speed and access, and public code (software built in the open, auditable and reusable) for trust and sustainability.

It's an overview talk with a strong public-sector lens, best for people who have to make the low-code decision rather than people who already run a platform.

## Two answers to two different problems

Cherukuri's framing is tidy. Traditional coding is powerful, but enterprise apps can take six to 12 months to ship, by which point the requirements have moved, and skilled developers are scarce. Low-code addresses speed: visual development, prebuilt connectors for databases, APIs, authentication and notifications, prototypes in days, and business experts able to contribute directly. Public code addresses trust: openness (usually an open source licence), transparent and documented architectures, and reusability so another agency adopts the software instead of rebuilding it. In government that means citizens can see how a service works; in enterprises it means less vendor lock-in and less knowledge trapped in one team.

The talk cites a lot of analyst figures from IDC, Gartner, Forrester and Deloitte along the way. Treat those as context; the architecture is the part worth keeping.

## Where the line between them goes

The patterns section is the core of the talk:

- **Hybrid workflows**: user-facing layers in low-code, core business logic in public code. A support chatbot built in low-code, with its escalation logic coded in the open.
- **API-first design**: forms call reusable APIs rather than writing straight to a database.
- **Event-driven pipelines**: a citizen files a request, an event triggers the workflow, and the trail is logged for transparency.
- **CI/CD for low-code artifacts**: workflows stored in Git, tested automatically and deployed like any other code.
- **Observability built in**: metrics, logs and traces as part of governance, not an add-on.

In practice that looks like legacy COBOL or mainframe systems wrapped in APIs with low-code orchestrating the workflow, business units building prototypes that IT then hardens, and pipelines running through Jenkins, GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps. One example: a hospital where nurses designed the patient admission workflow in a low-code platform, integrated with the EHR system through public code APIs.

## Without governance, low-code is shadow IT with a nicer UI

Cherukuri is direct about the risks. Without oversight you get unmonitored projects, data leaks from loose access control and compliance violations. Her standards: version control for every low-code artifact, automated testing including data validation and security scans, role-based access with encryption and audit trails, and identical dev, test and production environments. Her cautionary tale is an insurer that adopted low-code widely and ended up with a sprawl of apps and no central governance, then spent months auditing and consolidating them.

The other pitfalls get a fair hearing too: some low-code platforms struggle at millions of transactions a day, proprietary tools can become cages, and non-technical users need guardrails while engineers need freedom. She points to open source low-code platforms such as Budibase and Joget as one way to reduce lock-in.

## Who should watch

Public-sector technologists, enterprise architects and IT leads being asked to "just use low-code". Engineers wary of it will appreciate that the talk takes governance seriously; those wanting a platform comparison or a demo should look elsewhere.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Empowering Digital Transformation: Using Low-Code/No-Code Platforms to Speed Up Development](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Balaji_Bodicherla_development_transformation_platforms) by Balaji Bodicherla, a wider look at low-code adoption.
- [Beyond Algorithms: Building Trust in AI-Enhanced Public Sector Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sanjiv_Kumar_Bhagat_algorithms_trust_sector) by Sanjiv Kumar Bhagat on transparency in government software.
- [Public Sector Operations with Salesforce Government Cloud](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Anirudh_Peri_salesforce_cloud_government) by Anirudh Peri on a platform route to the same goals.

Title: One database for SQL, vectors and full text, on Kubernetes
Description: Peng Wang of OceanBase at Conf42 Remix 2026 on replacing a multi-database RAG stack with one SQL engine that also does vector and full-text search.
Body:
A typical internal knowledge-retrieval app talks to MySQL for metadata, a vector store for embeddings, Elasticsearch for full text and Redis for caching, with ETL jobs gluing them together. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Peng Wang, Global Technical Evangelist at OceanBase, argued that platform teams can collapse that stack into one distributed SQL database that handles relational, vector and full-text queries, running on Kubernetes.

Be clear on what this is: a 15-minute vendor talk about OceanBase, OceanBase's own product. It's useful as a crisp statement of the "one engine" side of a real architectural debate, not as a neutral comparison.

## The problem is the glue, not the vectors

Wang's framing will be familiar to anyone who has shipped RAG. Different AI workloads want different things: Q&A and chat need low-latency semantic search with context, log analytics needs high ingestion and fast aggregation, and the core business system needs ACID transactions. So organisations stitch together a transactional database, a warehouse, a vector database and sometimes a graph or NoSQL engine. Every extra system means another thing to upgrade, another ETL pipeline, more cost, and a new way for the whole pipeline to break when one part goes down. Synchronisation between them adds latency and inconsistency.

## Four round trips become one query

His walkthrough of the conventional knowledge-retrieval flow counts at least four network round trips per user request, at around 170 milliseconds end to end, plus the work of keeping all those stores consistent. In the unified version, one query hits one platform and he cites end-to-end latency of about 50 milliseconds. For one customer team, Wang reports query latency down by over 70%, data refreshes moving from hours to minutes, and over 40% less integration code to maintain. These are the vendor's numbers, presented without a benchmark setup.

The nicest example is a hybrid query. A user asks for a coffee shop within 500 metres, average spend under a set amount, a rating above 4.5 and no queues. That mixes GIS data for distance, relational data for price and rating, and vector search for the fuzzy part. Normally it's several engines and some application-side joining; Wang's point is that it can be one SQL statement.

## Paxos, three replicas and tenants

The architecture section covers the parts a platform team will ask about first:

- Data is distributed across availability zones and scales horizontally.
- OceanBase is containerised, managed through a Kubernetes operator, with elastic scaling for compute and storage.
- Consistency comes from the Paxos consensus algorithm with three replicas across zones, with automatic failover when a node or zone fails.
- Multi-tenancy isolates workloads in separate tenants, each with dedicated resources, to keep noisy neighbours apart.

Put together, the pitch is OLTP, log analysis, semantic retrieval and AI applications on one cluster, through one SQL access layer that covers structured data, full-text search and vector search.

## The trade-off worth thinking about

The talk doesn't spend time on the counter-argument, so here it is: specialised stores exist because each one can be tuned and scaled independently, and consolidating means betting that a single engine's vector and full-text performance is good enough for your workload. Wang's argument is that for many platform teams the operational cost of the glue is the bigger risk. That's a call you make with your own benchmarks, but the talk gives you a clean list of what to test: latency per request, consistency across data types, and tenant isolation under load.

## Who should watch

Platform and database engineers running, or about to build, a RAG or semantic search service on top of several data stores. If you're already happy with Postgres plus pgvector, it's a short watch to see the distributed alternative.

Title: Use AI and platforms to cut the cognitive load developers don't need
Description: Michel Murabito of Mia-Platform at Conf42 Remix 2026 on platform engineering, reusable components and RAG assistants that reduce developer cognitive load.
Body:
In 2004, deploying a website meant dragging a folder onto a server; today the same job can mean a Jira ticket to the ops team and a wait while they're on holiday. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Michel "Mitch" Murabito, Developer Advocate at Mia-Platform and CNCF Ambassador, argued that platform engineering plus AI should target one specific kind of cognitive load: the unnecessary effort created by poor tools and clunky processes.

Murabito calls it a theoretical talk himself, and that's fair. There's no demo and no product walkthrough. What you get is a clear mental model and practical advice on where to start.

## Three kinds of load, and only one you should kill

He borrows the standard split of cognitive load. **Intrinsic** load is the real difficulty of a task; you reduce it only by learning. **Germane** load is the effort of learning itself, such as figuring out how to build a CI/CD pipeline, and it's good for you. **Extraneous** load is everything else: unintuitive systems, processes with too many steps, unclear workflows, cluttered UIs, bad docs. That third bucket is the one a platform team can cut without asking anyone to get smarter.

The complexity isn't Kubernetes as such, in his view. It's scalability, distribution, data, integration, security, privacy and now machine learning, all at once, plus a CNCF map so crowded that picking an API gateway means comparing a couple of dozen projects before you can learn one.

## A platform is more than a portal and an orchestrator

Murabito defines platform engineering through six ideas: centralise, automate, keep things simple, remove bottlenecks, raise quality, and make all of it self-service. His point is that most people stop at the internal developer portal and the infrastructure orchestrator. The interesting layer for him sits beside those: application assets such as ready-made API gateways and portals, authentication, a software catalog or marketplace, a data control plane, and AI services from LLMs to agents.

That layer enables what he calls a circular economy. A team builds a payments microservice, documents it and puts it in the catalog. The next team reuses it, adds PayPal support and releases a new version. A third team takes payments, adds an invoicing service and publishes both. Nobody starts from zero, as long as the documentation is good enough to trust.

## RAG your platform, then ask it about the logs

The AI section is the most concrete. Feed a RAG system with your platform's documentation, its centralised configuration and, crucially, the error codes for your services. Then add the logs. A developer can ask whether there are warnings or errors in their services, which ones, and how to fix them, and the assistant has both the what (logs) and the why (docs). Murabito calls this conversational DevX. It only works if the platform has centralised that configuration in the first place, which is a nice argument for doing the boring platform work before the shiny AI work.

## Start with a problem and a metric you already have

The adoption advice is the part to steal. Ask why you need a platform or AI at all and which problem comes first; large companies with several business units can't fix everything together. Don't invent new metrics: if developers wait days for an environment, time-to-environment is your metric. Look beyond deployment frequency, watch the numbers over the long run (early productivity gains can fade as the new tooling accumulates changes), and connect them to business value. Then be patient with people, because not everyone is ready for the change at the same time.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and platform leads making the case for a platform team, or deciding where AI fits into one. Teams already running a mature IDP will find the framing familiar, though the RAG-over-logs pattern is a worthwhile pitch for their next quarter.

Title: How J.P. Morgan's Athena scaled trading with deltas and dependency graphs
Description: Aroma Rodrigues at Conf42 Remix 2026 on rebuilding the Athena trading platform with dependency graphs, delta storage, geo-sharding and split compliance data.
Body:
Most systems grow; financial data also mutates, every day, in ways the schema didn't plan for. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Aroma Rodrigues, now a Software Engineer at Microsoft, told the story of Athena, the J.P. Morgan trading platform she worked on, and how it went from barely handling thousands of trades to processing millions a day. Her central lesson: in finance you optimise for change, not just for scale.

This is one of the more substantial talks in the lineup: a domain primer, an honest teardown of the monolith, and four or five architectural moves with the reasoning behind each.

## Learn the nouns before you shard

Rodrigues spends the first part on vocabulary, and it pays off. A **trade** is the atomic record of what happened in the market, written once and read many times. One trade creates multiple **deals**, mirror images in each side's books, which change constantly as markets move. **Books** are ledgers grouped by desk and product (a corporate bonds book, a CDS book) that must be aggregated in real time. Each entity has a different scaling profile, and so does each stage of the pipeline: the front office sees bursts during volatile markets, the middle office has to validate and enrich within regulatory deadlines, the back office runs settlement workflows that last days, and P&L needs real-time reads alongside heavy risk calculations.

## The monolith failed in every predictable way

The starting point was "single everything": one ingestion instance, one application node, one primary database with no replicas or sharding, synchronous blocking calls, OLTP and OLAP on the same tables, and nightly batch recalculations that ran eight to 12 hours. No back pressure meant a spike in market data feeds during major news stalled ingestion and cascaded to traders who couldn't see their positions. It was single-region, so London and Hong Kong users got latency and any regional outage was a platform outage. And audit data was just extra rows in the operational database. If you've run a growing system, you've met at least four of those.

## Recalculate what changed, store what changed

The first breakthrough was a dependency graph. Functions are marked with dependency decorators (position value depends on instrument and market data; base-currency value depends on position value and FX rates), so a price move on one instrument triggers only the calculations downstream of it. Rodrigues says this alone cut end-of-day processing from eight hours to five and made real-time P&L feasible.

The second was delta storage. A deal's full record is stored once, then only the fields that change each day, with any point-in-time view rebuilt by replaying deltas. That matters when a regulator asks for the full history of a deal through price swings, a market crash and a corporate action that converted it into a different instrument.

## Shard by legal entity, compute in isolated blocks

Data is geo-distributed with primaries in New York and London, synchronous replication within a region and asynchronous replication between regions, a deliberate trade-off she frames in CAP terms. Because trading is mostly regional and tied to legal entities, books can be processed in parallel. Cross-entity trades get a neat trick: a third deal leg stored in a separate instance, so North American and European data stay independent.

End-of-day became a dependency-aware pipeline that can restart only the failed book's job using cached reference data. Heavy maths runs in what the team calls compute building blocks: isolated nodes that load their own data, compute and return results, "like AWS Lambda, but for financial calculations" in her words.

## Compliance gets its own building

Operational and compliance data are separated physically, with every trade, price change and position update streamed to immutable audit logs. Her cautionary tale: a buggy Python analytics script once choked a queue, deals missed their regulatory window, and the firm paid a fine. She also defends Python itself: duck typing handles the diversity of bonds, swaps and CDS, with C++ compute blocks where raw speed is needed.

## Who should watch

Anyone building systems where history must be reconstructable: fintech, insurance, healthcare, ledgers of any kind. The closing pitfalls (premature optimisation without profiling, bolted-on data lineage, underestimating the operational cost of multi-region) apply well beyond trading.

Title: Rust for edge AI, from no_std operators to ARM and RISC-V builds
Description: Anushree Nagvekar of AEye at Conf42 Remix 2026 on using Rust for edge AI inference, with Candle, Burn and SmartCore and no_std patterns.
Body:
On an edge device, every byte and every CPU cycle counts, and a garbage collection pause during obstacle detection is a bug with consequences. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Anushree Nagvekar, software engineering manager at AEye, argued that Rust is the right foundation for edge AI because it gives C-level control without C's memory bugs, and she pointed at the crates that make it practical today.

This is a compact talk, closer to a well-organised briefing than a live-coding session. It's good for a team deciding whether Rust belongs in its on-device inference stack.

## The cloud can't hit an edge latency budget

Nagvekar frames the problem around latency. Sub-50-millisecond response is the target for much of edge AI, and a round trip to the cloud can't deliver that reliably. So the computation has to happen on the device, under tight memory, power and thermal limits. That's where she lines up Rust's three properties: memory safety without a garbage collector, zero-cost abstractions so clean code doesn't cost performance, and fine-grained control of the system.

She adds what she calls the secret weapons: safe concurrency across multi-core ARM chips, portable SIMD for vectorised maths without hand-written assembly, and integration with hardware accelerators from NPUs to DSPs, even in no_std environments.

## Two case studies with hard real-time constraints

The first case study is autonomous vehicles, which is AEye's world: a 15-millisecond budget for obstacle detection, with the talk reporting 12.7-millisecond inference times. The second is industrial IoT security on modest hardware, with a reported 22-millisecond response time and multi-year battery life. Her point in both cases is that predictable performance is what makes low-power devices viable, and that Rust's compile-time guarantees remove runtime errors that plague C++ code in safety-critical systems.

The abstract and slides lean heavily on percentages (a 92% performance improvement, a 73% reduction in memory use). The talk doesn't show the benchmark setup behind them, so read them as the speaker's production experience, not a reproducible comparison.

## The crates to start with

The most useful part for practitioners is the ecosystem tour:

- **Candle** (candle-core): a neural network library for inference with minimal dependencies.
- **Burn**: a deep learning framework with a strong type system and modular backends, used for training too.
- **SmartCore**: classical machine learning algorithms, compatible with no_std.

Her closing advice is direct: add Candle, Burn and SmartCore with Cargo and start experimenting.

## Patterns for custom operators

When you write your own neural network operators, Nagvekar lists the patterns that matter. Avoid heap allocations so the code stays no_std-compatible and deterministic. Lay memory out for cache-friendly access. Unroll loops manually where it helps the instruction pipeline. Use direct slice manipulation so bounds checks get optimised out in release builds while keeping Rust's safety guarantees elsewhere. For target hardware, Cargo features and `cfg` attributes switch on CPU-specific instruction sets, so the compiler emits binaries tuned for ARM or RISC-V. It's a short list, and every item is something an embedded engineer can try on Monday.

## Who should watch

Embedded and ML engineers shipping inference to cameras, vehicles or sensors who are tired of chasing segfaults in C++. If you already run Candle in production, you'll know most of it; if you're choosing a stack, it's a fast map of the options.

Title: Why HR systems, from payroll to offboarding, are a good fit for Rust
Description: Swetha Priya Sathiyam of ADP at Conf42 Remix 2026 on what Rust's memory safety, concurrency and type system offer HRIS platforms.
Body:
HR software is one of the few enterprise systems that touches every person in a company, from the day they are recruited to their last paycheck. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Swetha Priya Sathiyam, Director of Solution Design for ADP Lyric HCM at ADP, made the case that Rust's memory safety, concurrency and strict type system map directly onto the pain points of HRIS platforms: downtime, data errors and slow processing.

It's a domain talk more than a language talk. Sathiyam knows HR systems from the inside, and the value is in how concretely she ties Rust features to HR workloads.

## Modern cloud HR still chokes at open enrollment

Sathiyam walks through three eras of HR tech: paper files and physical timecards, the legacy digital era where core payroll still often runs on COBOL (reliable, but inflexible and expensive to change), and today's cloud platforms such as Workday, SAP SuccessFactors and Oracle Cloud HCM. Even the modern platforms hit bottlenecks. She describes open enrollment windows where a single benefits page took three minutes to load, and a single promotion that took seven minutes to process because thousands of employees logged in at once.

The requirements she lists explain why: employees want mobile self-service, managers want instant approvals, HR admins want compliance-ready reports, and the same stack has to scale from 500 employees to 50,000 without a rewrite. A single payroll error can mean fines and attrition.

## A job grade is a type, not a number

Her best example is small. A job grade looks like an integer but is a structure tied to pay bands, locations and the rules running behind them. Rust lets you encode those rules in the type system, so invalid states fail at compile time instead of in a pay run. The same idea applies to workflows: a state machine in which a candidate cannot be marked as hired without a completed background check.

The other features land similarly:

- Memory safety matters when the data includes social security numbers and bank details.
- Fearless concurrency matters when a fortnightly payroll run overlaps the annual performance cycle and its analytics.
- Explicit error handling forces developers to decide what happens when a tax rate file is missing or a benefits vendor's API is down.

## A reference architecture in layers

The proposed design puts Rust in modular layers: a data layer with compile-time checked SQL queries, APIs on Actix Web for employee self-service portals, role-based access control modelled in code rather than only in config files, and async background processing for payroll batches and compliance reports. Her payroll example runs tax calculations for each jurisdiction concurrently and merges the results, turning hours into minutes. Security gets its own section: tamper-proof audit logging for GDPR and HIPAA, and Rust's ownership model as a helper for retention and auto-deletion rules.

Sathiyam also cites outside case studies: a tech company that replaced a Java onboarding app that crashed during graduate hiring, a financial services firm that moved payroll from COBOL to Rust and cut processing time by 85%, and a healthcare records platform that met HIPAA without giving up speed. The companies aren't named, so file them under illustrations rather than evidence.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads on HR, payroll or other PII-heavy enterprise systems who need language-level arguments their stakeholders will follow. Experienced Rustaceans will know the language points; the HR mapping is what's new. The closing best practices (domain-driven design, consistent error handling, minimal unsafe code, auditing third-party crates) are sensible for any Rust adoption.

Title: Polling dashboards hide incidents; Rust event streams surface them
Description: Tashi Garg of Juniper Networks at Conf42 Remix 2026 on replacing polling dashboards with Rust-powered, event-driven monitoring pipelines.
Body:
A dashboard that refreshes every 30 seconds is a dashboard that is up to 30 seconds wrong, and the incident does not wait for the next poll. At Conf42 Remix 2026, Tashi Garg, Senior Staff Software Engineer at Juniper Networks, argued that static, polling-based dashboards create blind spots in cloud infrastructure, and that a Rust telemetry pipeline pushing events straight to the UI closes them.

The talk is short and structured: the cost of polling, why Rust suits real-time telemetry, a production case study, and a phased adoption plan. It's an architecture talk rather than a code walkthrough.

## Staleness and thresholds are two separate blind spots

Garg splits the problem in two. First, data staleness: widgets that collect at fixed intervals show events well after they happen. The talk cites detection delays averaging around 8.5 minutes from incident onset to the first time an operator sees it. Second, binary and threshold-based health checks simply miss the messy failures, the intermittent packet loss and slowly degrading latency that never cross a line. Put both together and the team only learns about a problem when customers do.

That pushes teams into what Garg calls the reactive monitoring trap: responding after impact, every time. The fix he proposes is architectural rather than cosmetic. Stop asking the backend for a snapshot on a timer, and start streaming events as they arrive.

## Why Rust, specifically

The argument for Rust here is about predictability under load more than raw speed. A monitoring pipeline gets hammered hardest exactly when things are going wrong, which is the worst possible moment for a garbage collector to pause. Garg's list:

- Zero-cost abstractions for high-throughput processing without runtime overhead.
- Memory safety without garbage collection, so no GC pauses during a telemetry spike.
- The ownership model and borrow checker preventing race conditions in concurrent workloads.
- Compile-time guarantees that remove whole classes of runtime errors, such as null dereferences.

He also names the crates that make it production-ready: Tokio as the async runtime for huge numbers of concurrent I/O-bound tasks, zero-copy serialization for JSON, Protobuf or Arrow payloads, Actix for low-latency web delivery, and Crossbeam for concurrency primitives when scaling across cores.

## The reference stack fits on one slide

The proposed architecture has four layers: lightweight Rust agents (the talk targets under 15 MB and under 2% CPU) sending telemetry over gRPC or WebSockets; an async streaming pipeline spread across cores; a real-time API layer pushing updates in under 50 milliseconds; and a reactive UI that listens on WebSockets or server-sent events instead of polling.

For the numbers, Garg reports that one deployment replacing static dashboards cut MTTR by 63%, from 52 minutes to 19. A case study at a global financial services provider with more than 12,000 instances across several clouds processed 3.2 million telemetry data points per second with under five milliseconds of pipeline latency, and incident detection fell from 11 minutes to 47 seconds. Those are the speaker's figures, presented without much methodology, so treat them as a direction rather than a benchmark.

## Roll it out in phases, not in one heroic rewrite

The most practical part is the adoption advice. Legacy systems get bridged with FFI or gRPC so nothing has to be replaced at once. The Rust skills gap is handled by starting with one self-contained component. Data volume is tamed by filtering and aggregating at the agent before anything goes upstream. The roadmap runs from a month auditing blind spots and baselining MTTR, through staging validation, to a production rollout wired into incident tooling, and only then ML-based anomaly detection and natural-language queries on top. AI comes last, after the pipeline is fast and trustworthy enough to feed it.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers whose dashboards lag behind their pagers, and teams weighing Rust for an observability backend. If you want Tokio internals or benchmark code, this isn't that talk; it's the case for the architecture.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Streaming Aggregation on Cloud Scale Telemetry](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2023_Shay_Lin_streaming_aggregation_cloud_scale_telemetry) by Shay Lin covers the aggregation side of a high-volume pipeline.
- [Beyond Dashboards: Deep-Dive Network Observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Uudit_Misra_distributed_systems_reliability) by Uudit Misra goes below the dashboard into the kernel.
- [Journeying through the Tales of Telemetry](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Siddhant_Khisty_journeying_tales_telemetry) by Siddhant Khisty is a tour of the OpenTelemetry framework.

Title: Conf42 LLMs 2026 roundup: context, judges and voice agents
Description: Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 in review, from agent memory and knowledge graphs to verifiers, voice pipelines under 500 ms and regulated AI.
Body:
By June 2026 nobody at [Conf42 Large Language Models 2026](https://www.conf42.com/llms2026) needed convincing that models can write code or answer questions. The 34 talks, streamed online on June 18, 2026, were about everything around the model: what context it sees, who checks its work, how fast it has to answer on a phone call, and how it behaves inside a bank's ledger. Speakers came from Harness, AWS, Revolut, Snowflake, Microsoft, Meta, Walmart, Expedia Group and a good number of startups.

## The bottleneck is context, not capability

The keynote set the tone. [Prateek Mittal](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery), Director of Product Management at Harness, argued that the next limit on AI in software delivery is context, and showed a knowledge graph of services, pipelines, deployments and owners that an agent queried to find the pipelines failing most often and why.

Three other talks attacked the same problem from different angles. [Anannya Roy Chowdhury](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Anannya_Roy_Chowdhury_memory_agents_context) (AWS) observed that agents in production rarely fail because they can't reason; they fail because they retrieve the wrong context. The talk's framework splits agent memory into working, retrieval and persistent layers. [Lior Schejter](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Lior_Schejter_context_agents_reasoning) described what happens when an agent meets 200 microservices instead of one repo: it gets lost in the middle. The fix is an AI-maintained architecture hub of APIs, domain models and events written for agents to read. [Varun Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Varun_Joshi_rag_metadata) (AWS) made the data engineer's version of the case: your schema, lineage, query history and dbt models are the context, and most teams haven't wired them into RAG yet.

## Who judges the agent?

[Vsevolod Voropaev](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Vsevolod_Voropaev_verification_agents_production) (Olo din) gave one of the sharper talks of the day: the verifier is the hardest component of an agentic system and usually the last one built. Drawing on a bandit-based verification layer routing across Claude, GPT and Gemini, he argued that verifiers should usually be smarter than the agents they watch. [Liliya Imasheva and Michael Banf](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Liliya_Imasheva_Michael_Banf_validation_summaries_evaluation) (Perelyn) showed a summary-validation pipeline that pairs BERTScore, ROUGE and BLEU with LLM-as-judge scoring on completeness, conciseness, harmlessness, correctness and readability.

Permissions were the other half of trust. [Sohan Maheshwar](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sohan_Maheshwar_deterministic_authorization_agents) (AuthZed) pointed out that letting a coding agent decide for itself what is safe is a probabilistic answer to a question that needs a deterministic one, and showed how to add enforceable permission boundaries. [Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_cryptography_compliance_pipelines) (Meta) presented RuntimeGuard-AI, which records tamper-evident, hash-chained evidence across an inference pipeline for EU AI Act compliance, and [Arunkumar Muthuramalingam](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Arunkumar_Muthuramalingam_identity_security_iam) (General Reinsurance) treated IAM as the core of AI security.

## Voice, phones and people who don't want an app

Voice agents got a strong cluster. [Bohdan Snisar](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Bohdan_Snisar_httpsyoutube5XSR13KHev4) (Solea AI) started from the classic STT, LLM, TTS chain, where every stage waits for the last and the whole conversation turn has under 500 milliseconds. He built the pipeline up layer by layer, through realtime audio transport, voice activity detection and turn detection, to show where it hits the wall, then presented an architecture that reasons in parallel while the agent talks. [Pavel Shchekotov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Pavel_Shchekotov_voice_ai_trust) (Denk Solutions) removed the app altogether and put an LLM agent behind an ordinary phone number for people who are sceptical of AI.

The most British title of the event belonged to [Anton Denisov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Anton_Denisov_british_sarcasm) (Dwelly), whose system reads emails and calls for dissatisfaction that customers soften with politeness, understatement or silence. Anyone who has heard a British colleague call a plan 'brave' will appreciate the problem. [Andrii Veremiienko](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Andrii_Veremiienko_shipping_ai_features) (Revolut) brought the mobile view: latency, inference costs, rate limits and UX design around answers that aren't deterministic. [Petras Bazdaras](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Petras_Bazdaras_reading_new_writing) argued that when generating code is cheap, reading it is the skill that matters.

## Shipping it: pipelines, modernisation and serving

[Denis Ermakov](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Denis_Ermakov_deployment_cicd_automation) (Tehpotok) presented an open-source framework for agent-driven CI/CD with retries, observability and explicit points where humans stay in the loop. [Marco Antonio Silva](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Marco_Antonio_Silva_modernization_specs_cloud) (Microsoft) shared spec-driven modernisation with Spec2Cloud and the GitHub Copilot Modernization CLI, including a large project at a Portuguese financial institution. [Tim Spann](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Tim_Spann_sql_automation_operations) (Snowflake) showed Cortex Code managing schema changes and deployments from natural language.

On the serving side, [Kosseila Haddalene](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Kosseila_Haddalene_multimodal_inference_vllm) (Cloudthrill) explained why diffusion transformers, which denoise instead of generating tokens and are compute-bound rather than memory-bound, are awkward to serve next to LLMs, and how vLLM-Omni handles both. [Sergey Speranskiy](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Sergey_Speranskiy_kubernetes_infrastructure_llms) covered the Kubernetes assumptions that break first under LLM workloads, [Kandasamy Selvaraj](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Kandasamy_Selvaraj_performance_lag_signatures) (ADP) shifted RAG performance testing left into CI/CD, and [Leo Visser](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Leo_Visser_governance_apis_control) (OGD ICT-diensten) put Azure API Management in front of models for content filtering, token-aware throttling and caching. [Andrei Shcherbinin](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Andrei_Shcherbinin_moderation_safety_platforms) (Social Discovery Group) walked through a production automoderation stack that mixes lightweight classifiers with multimodal LLMs for grey areas.

## LLMs in regulated systems

A large share of the programme dealt with finance, tax, healthcare and audit. [Abdul Basit Iqbal](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Abdul_Basit_Iqbal_compliance_agents_tax) (Amazon) turned changing tax regulations into executable compliance logic, [Karishma Velisetty](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Karishma_Velisetty_governance_audit_assistants) governed AI code assistants in SOX audit analytics, [Ravindra Rajasekhar Kavuru](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Ravindra_Rajasekhar_Kavuru_privacy_compliance_credit) (Expedia Group) built compliance into co-branded credit card apps, and [Rakesh Jha](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Rakesh_Jha_ledgers_finance_accounting) (DXC Technology) applied LLMs to general ledgers. On the people side, [Lakshmi Priya Gopalsamy](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Lakshmi_Priya_Gopalsamy_latency_reasoning_reliability) made the point that as AI speeds up execution, human decision capacity becomes the constraint, and [Susanta Kumar Sahoo](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Susanta_Kumar_Sahoo_copilots_sre_remediation) looked at LLM copilots for incident response.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/) and [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), the diamond sponsors, to the [Prompt Engineering Conference](https://promptengineering.rocks/) as gold sponsor, to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) as podcast partner, and to the media partners. The full [Conf42 LLMs 2026 playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAbZ-MTonX2gERed7dTODjm) has every talk, and the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/llms2026) lists them by track.

Next up in the series is [Conf42 Large Language Models 2027](https://www.conf42.com/llms2027).

Title: Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery
Body:
## Shipping with Context: Why Knowledge Graphs Are Becoming the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery

AI is transforming software development at an extraordinary pace. Developers can generate code, write tests, create documentation, and troubleshoot issues faster than ever before.

Yet for most organizations, the real challenge is no longer generating code.

The harder problem is understanding context.

A piece of generated code does not exist in isolation. It interacts with services, infrastructure, security controls, deployment pipelines, compliance requirements, operational processes, and business objectives. Without understanding those relationships, AI systems may be capable of producing outputs, but they struggle to make reliable decisions.

In his session *Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery*, Prateek Mittal explored why context is emerging as the next critical layer of enterprise AI and why knowledge graphs are becoming a foundational component of modern software delivery systems.

### The Next AI Bottleneck Is Not Model Capability

Over the past few years, the conversation around AI has largely focused on model performance.

Organizations compare models, benchmark reasoning capabilities, and evaluate new generations of large language models.

However, many enterprises are discovering that model quality is no longer the primary limitation.

The real bottleneck is access to organizational context.

Most enterprises operate across dozens or hundreds of systems:

- CI/CD platforms
- Security tools
- Cloud infrastructure
- Observability platforms
- Ticketing systems
- Source control repositories
- Incident management platforms
- Cost management tools

Each system contains valuable information.

The challenge is that this information remains fragmented.

An AI assistant may understand how to write code, but it often lacks visibility into which services are affected by that code, which teams own those services, what policies apply to them, and what business risks might be introduced by a deployment.

Without context, intelligence remains limited.

### Why Enterprise AI Struggles With Context

The problem is not simply a lack of data.

Most organizations already have enormous amounts of operational information available.

The challenge is that this information exists inside disconnected systems.

As Mittal explained, enterprise AI initiatives frequently encounter four common obstacles.

#### Data Silos

Critical information is distributed across numerous platforms and tools.

Even when the data exists, it is often inaccessible to AI systems or difficult to connect across domains.

#### Missing Domain Knowledge

General-purpose language models understand public information but typically lack awareness of company-specific terminology, workflows, ownership structures, and operational practices.

This creates a gap between what AI knows and what an organization actually needs.

#### Hallucination Risk

When models lack context, they compensate by making assumptions.

These assumptions can produce inaccurate recommendations, incorrect conclusions, or actions based on incomplete information.

#### Governance and Compliance Concerns

Organizations must carefully control how sensitive information is accessed and shared.

Providing AI systems with unrestricted access to enterprise data can introduce security, compliance, and governance risks.

Together, these challenges limit the ability of AI systems to operate effectively in production environments.

### The Evolution From AI-Assisted DevOps to AI-Operational DevOps

Many teams are already using AI in their software delivery processes.

Most of these implementations fall into what Mittal describes as AI-assisted DevOps.

In this model, AI helps humans perform tasks such as:

- Writing code
- Creating configuration files
- Generating documentation
- Producing runbooks
- Answering operational questions

Humans remain responsible for supplying context, validating outputs, and making final decisions.

This approach delivers productivity gains, but it does not fundamentally change how software delivery operates.

A second model is beginning to emerge.

### What Is AI-Operational DevOps?

AI-operational DevOps shifts AI from being a productivity tool to becoming an active participant in delivery workflows.

Instead of requiring humans to manually provide context, AI systems automatically retrieve information from shared enterprise models.

This allows agents to:

- Evaluate deployment risks
- Analyze dependencies
- Simulate outcomes
- Enforce policies
- Validate compliance requirements
- Recommend corrective actions

In this model, context becomes machine-readable rather than conversational.

The system itself becomes responsible for understanding relationships and applying guardrails before actions occur.

This transition requires a shared understanding of the software delivery ecosystem.

That is where knowledge graphs enter the picture.

### Understanding the Building Blocks of a Knowledge Graph

A knowledge graph is not simply a database or reporting system.

It is a representation of entities and the relationships between them.

Within a software delivery environment, entities may include:

- Services
- Pipelines
- Deployments
- Incidents
- Infrastructure resources
- Cloud costs
- Security findings
- Teams
- Applications

These entities become nodes within the graph.

The relationships between them become edges.

For example:

- A service depends on another service
- A deployment originates from a specific commit
- A pipeline belongs to a particular team
- An incident affects a specific application
- A cloud resource supports a particular workload

Individually, each piece of information has limited value.

Connected together, they create a model that describes how an organization actually operates.

### Context Is More Than Data

One of the key ideas presented during the session is that context is not merely information.

Context is information combined with relationships.

Many organizations already collect deployment events, operational metrics, cloud costs, and security findings.

The challenge is that these data points often remain disconnected.

A knowledge graph introduces a semantic layer that allows systems to understand how information relates across domains.

This transforms isolated records into an interconnected model of software delivery.

Instead of querying a single tool, AI systems can reason across multiple systems simultaneously.

### Building a Knowledge Graph for Software Delivery

Creating a useful knowledge graph requires more than importing data.

Organizations must establish a process for constructing and maintaining relationships.

The process generally includes several stages.

#### Entity Extraction

The first step is identifying important objects within the delivery ecosystem.

These may include applications, services, incidents, deployments, users, cloud resources, or security findings.

#### Metadata Enrichment

Entities become more valuable when supplemented with additional information.

Examples include:

- Ownership details
- Team assignments
- Version information
- Environment data
- Compliance classifications
- Security policies

#### Relationship Mapping

Relationships define how entities interact.

Understanding who owns a service, which deployment modified it, and what infrastructure supports it is often more valuable than understanding any individual component in isolation.

#### Query Exposure

Once the graph exists, APIs and query interfaces allow AI agents to retrieve and reason about context dynamically.

At that point, the graph becomes an operational system rather than simply a data repository.

### Why Knowledge Graph Projects Fail

Knowledge graphs have existed for years, yet many implementations struggle to deliver value.

According to Mittal, the most common failure is not technical.

It is a failure of use case definition.

Organizations sometimes invest heavily in building sophisticated graph models without clearly identifying the problems they intend to solve.

This creates several risks.

#### Over-Modeling

Teams create highly detailed ontologies that are technically impressive but provide little practical value.

The result is significant complexity with limited adoption.

#### Under-Modeling

The opposite problem occurs when relationships are not modeled deeply enough.

Data remains connected only superficially, preventing meaningful reasoning.

#### Stale Context

A graph is only valuable if it reflects reality.

Outdated relationships and stale metadata quickly reduce the usefulness of AI-driven decision-making.

Successful implementations focus on solving specific operational challenges rather than building graphs for their own sake.

### How Knowledge Graphs Enable AI Reasoning

One of the most compelling aspects of knowledge graphs is their ability to support complex reasoning across multiple systems.

During the session, Mittal demonstrated how AI could analyze software delivery pipelines across an organization and identify patterns that would be difficult to discover manually.

Rather than searching individual projects one at a time, the system was able to reason across organizational boundaries.

The AI identified:

- Pipelines with the highest failure rates
- Common failure patterns
- Missing dependencies
- Configuration issues
- Potential remediation actions

The system not only surfaced operational problems but also suggested corrective actions based on the relationships captured inside the graph.

This illustrates a broader shift in how AI interacts with enterprise systems.

Instead of responding only to direct questions, AI can begin to understand operational context and assist with diagnosis, prioritization, and decision-making.

### Shared Context Across Engineering Disciplines

The value of a knowledge graph extends far beyond DevOps.

Modern software delivery requires collaboration across multiple domains.

DevOps teams care about deployments and reliability.

SecOps teams focus on vulnerabilities and compliance.

FinOps teams analyze cloud spending and resource utilization.

Platform engineering teams manage infrastructure and developer experience.

Traditionally, each group operates within its own set of tools and dashboards.

Knowledge graphs provide a shared context layer that connects these perspectives.

When everyone operates against the same model of services, dependencies, ownership, and operational events, decision-making becomes faster and more consistent.

### Governance Becomes a Core AI Requirement

As AI systems gain access to broader organizational context, governance becomes increasingly important.

Enterprise AI cannot operate solely on trust.

Systems require mechanisms for:

- Role-based access control
- Policy enforcement
- Auditability
- Compliance validation
- Permission management

Knowledge graphs provide the contextual foundation that allows these controls to be applied consistently.

Without governance, increased context introduces risk.

With governance, context becomes a strategic advantage.

### The Future of AI-First Software Delivery

The software industry has spent years building increasingly capable AI models.

The next phase of adoption will depend less on model intelligence and more on organizational context.

The most successful AI systems will not necessarily be those with the largest parameter counts.

They will be the systems that understand services, dependencies, ownership, policies, infrastructure, incidents, and business priorities.

Knowledge graphs provide a mechanism for connecting these elements into a unified model.

As AI moves from assisting developers to actively participating in software delivery workflows, shared context will become essential infrastructure.

### Context Is the New Competitive Advantage

Software delivery is becoming increasingly complex.

Organizations operate across dozens of platforms, hundreds of services, and thousands of interconnected components.

AI has the potential to help manage this complexity, but only if it can understand the environment in which it operates.

Knowledge graphs offer a way to transform fragmented organizational knowledge into a connected, queryable system that both humans and AI can reason about.

In an AI-first future, the question will no longer be whether models can generate answers.

The question will be whether they have enough context to generate the right ones.

Title: Signed receipts, not logs, as evidence for high-risk AI pipelines
Description: Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane of Meta at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on RuntimeGuard-AI, which uses hash-chained signed records and zero-knowledge proofs for AI compliance.
Body:
If the team that built the AI system also controls the logs that describe what it did, an auditor can only trust them, not verify them. Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane, Staff Software Engineer at Meta, built his Conf42 Large Language Models 2026 talk around that gap and presented RuntimeGuard-AI, a design that turns each consequential decision in an AI pipeline into a signed, hash-chained receipt, with zero-knowledge proofs for when the details cannot be disclosed. The abstract frames it as provable EU AI Act compliance for high-risk systems.

His line for the whole talk: "immutable log is a testimony, a verifiable receipt is an evidence."

## The threats are old, the speed is new

Beshane refuses to treat AI as a brand-new risk category. The losses he sees are still credential abuse, phishing, misconfiguration, ransomware and data in the wrong place. What changes is autonomy (agents act without confirmation), velocity (thousands of actions before anyone notices) and tool access (systems humans cannot reach through normal channels). A compromised or prompt-injected agent fails faster and wider than a human would.

So the goal is not more logging. It is verifiable evidence at the moment delegated authority is used.

## It records controls, it does not replace them

He is explicit about scope. RuntimeGuard-AI does not replace IAM, patching, network isolation, prompt defenses, sandboxing or human oversight. If those are weak, the cryptography will faithfully record a badly secured system behaving badly. It runs as a vertical rail through three layers (cyber hygiene, AI and application security, governance) and asks one question at each: when a control made a consequential decision, did that decision become a structured, signed, verifiable event?

## Identity and delegation, signed at every hop

For agents, the unit of governance is the acting machine identity and its delegated authority, not the prompt. Running agents under shared accounts is fast and a dead end after an incident. His model gives each meaningful agent a distinct identity tied to an accountable human owner, a scoped delegation token tied to a purpose, risk tier, data class and expiry, and a runtime authorization check.

In multi-agent pipelines, "trust is not transitive". Identity and authorization context travel with the request, but each downstream component revalidates them, the same way microservices each authenticate a call. Every handover emits a record.

Governance documents get the same treatment. The decision-rights matrix becomes a delegation digest inside the execution token; the constraint catalog becomes a versioned policy. Asked whether a constraint was enforced on a transaction, the answer is a receipt with policy version, verdict, signer and chain pointer, not a wiki screenshot.

## Keep cryptography off the hot path

The obvious objection is latency. The design splits paths. Inline, a Rust policy engine in the gateway issues a verdict (approve, deny, escalate for human review, block); he reports a prototype latency overhead in the range of 2.3 to 4.1 percent. Then a non-blocking dispatch hands a compact record to a background attester that hash-chains it, builds the Merkle tree, signs checkpoints and generates Groth16 proofs. The roughly 1.4 seconds of prover time he quotes is compute cost in the background, not inference latency.

Receipts carry digests rather than raw prompts, customer data or model configuration. Private details sit in Merkle leaves; the root is a compact fingerprint that can be anchored externally. Edit one record and the digests stop matching: tamper-evident, which he is careful to distinguish from tamper-proof. He adds a caveat worth repeating: a zero-knowledge proof shows the encoded policy ran, not that the policy is good, fair or legally sufficient.

## Tiers, and a verifier you actually run

Not every workflow deserves the full stack. Low-risk internal assistants get distinct agent identity and a basic audit trail. Customer-facing workflows get verified actions, sandboxed tools and reviewable records. Money movement, identity changes and regulated data get mandatory human gates, signed approvals and external anchoring.

His rollout order is boring on purpose: record inference-time facts as structured evidence, sign and chain every event, anchor checkpoints outside the admin domain (WORM storage, a transparency log or a notarization service), and build and exercise the verifier before an incident forces you to.

## Who should watch

Security and platform engineers working on AI in regulated domains, anyone preparing for EU AI Act audits, and teams whose agent audit trail is currently an application log. The cryptography is explained at architecture level, so you do not need to know Groth16 going in.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [GenOps: A Governance-Driven Model for Safe, High-Velocity AI in CI/CD Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_governance_genai_velocity) from Conf42 DevOps 2026 is Beshane's own take on governance earlier in the lifecycle.
- [Adding Tamper-Evident Audit Trails to AI Agents in Production](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Joao_Marques_audit_tamper_agents) from Conf42 MLOps 2026 tackles the same receipts problem from another angle.
- [The AI Trust Triad for DevOps: Shipping Reinforcement Learning, Federated Learning, and Explainable AI Safely in Regulated Systems](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Saideepak_Kandibanda_trust_explainability_regulation) from Conf42 DevOps 2026 widens the view to regulated ML in general.
