Title: Your hiring problem is a data infrastructure problem
Description: Zeeshan Khan (STV) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on five layers from a legacy ATS to predictive hiring, with skills graphs, vector search and governance.
Body:
Every resume, interview note and candidate email is data, and in most companies it sits in a system built for compliance paperwork. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Zeeshan Khan, HRIS Manager at STV, argues that organisations which think they have a hiring problem usually have an infrastructure problem, and lays out five layers that take recruiting from an applicant tracking system (ATS) to a predictive, self-improving pipeline.

It's an architecture-and-strategy talk from the HR technology side. Expect concepts and examples rather than schemas or code.

## The ATS was never meant to be smart

Zeeshan's starting point: traditional ATS platforms were built for compliance and administrative workflow, not intelligence. Sourcing, resume parsing, interviews and compliance training each store data in a different place, and those stores rarely talk to each other. There are dashboards and reports, but no real-time insight and no prediction. Buying a newer ATS doesn't fix it, he says, because the missing piece is the data foundation, not the product.

## Five layers, each built on the last

His maturity model runs from the basics to what he calls the north star:

1. **Administrative.** The core ATS: job posts, interviews, hires.
2. **Data enrichment.** HRIS, ATS and CRM connected so the process lives in one place. Still descriptive, not predictive.
3. **NLP and embeddings.** Systems that understand the intent of a job description or a resume instead of filtering on keywords.
4. **Skills graphs and vector search.** Skills attached to jobs, employees, tasks and learning, so search works on meaning.
5. **Predictive hiring,** ending in a self-optimising ecosystem where every decision feeds the next.

## Search by meaning, not by filter

The vector search examples are the most concrete part. A keyword filter for Python, New York and a product manager title returns exactly what you typed. A query describing someone with ownership of a product from design through implementation to output surfaces people whose experience matches, even if their titles don't. His other example: an electrician can be matched to a technician role on shared skills and certifications that a title search would never connect.

The catch is the one every data engineer expects. It only works with good data, proper indexing and properly categorised records. In his words, garbage in, garbage out is real.

## From a won contract to a requisition

The predictive layer is easiest to picture through his workforce planning scenario. A company wins a project starting in six months. An agent reads the project's tasks, checks which skills exist in the organisation and who is available, finds the gap, searches internal employees for mobility candidates, then the existing candidate pool, and only then opens a new requisition. Event-driven architecture keeps it current: instead of batch jobs, signals such as a high-priority candidate losing interest trigger a notification with the reason, so recruiters can act before the offer is lost.

Skills graphs also feed internal mobility and retention. Tailored learning paths for every employee in a company of a hundred thousand are impossible by hand, he notes, but realistic when the infrastructure holds the skills data.

## Governance is not optional here

Hiring is a high-stakes automated decision area, and the abstract notes that algorithmic screening tools face active regulatory scrutiny and litigation. Zeeshan's governance list: bias detection, explainability (the system must say why it recommended a candidate, with the evidence), model auditing for accuracy and compliance, and human oversight. He is emphatic that AI supports recruiters and does not replace them. His closing line: the future of hiring is infrastructure plus judgment.

## Who should watch

HRIS and people-analytics engineers planning what to build after the ATS, and data engineers asked to support a recruiting team's AI ambitions. If you want vector database internals, pick one of the talks below.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [MLOps at Scale: Production-Ready AI Systems for HR Transformation in Enterprise Shared Service Centers](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Ramprasad_Reddy_Mittana_mlops_scale_production) by Ramprasad Reddy Mittana, running HR AI in production.
- [A gentle introduction to Vector Databases](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2023_Zain_Hasan_vector_databases) by Zain Hasan, the mechanics behind meaning-based search.
- [Leveraging Global HCM Systems for HR Digital Transformation: A Strategic Implementation Approach](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Swetha_Priya_Sathiyam_hcm_transformation_implementation) by Swetha Priya Sathiyam, the HCM foundation those layers sit on.

Title: Your LLM judge is failing silently, and it should be the strongest model
Description: Vsevolod Voropaev at Conf42 LLMs 2026 argues the verifier is an agent system's hardest part and routes cross-family judges with bandits.
Body:
When your agent is wrong, you lose a task. When your judge is wrong, you lose the ability to know anything is wrong at all. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Vsevolod Voropaev, a founding engineer at an early-stage multi-agent startup (listed as Olo din) with two years of production LLM work across three companies behind him, argues that the verifier is the hardest component in an agentic system, not the easiest, and that most teams have their intuition about it exactly backwards.

## Silence is the failure mode we can't see

The story is familiar. The agent works in the demo, someone asks how you know the output is correct, and you bolt on a second model call that rates the answer. For a while the judge and your own eyes agree, so you stop reading outputs. That's when the rot starts: a broken judge and a working judge emit the same artifact, a number.

No exception fires when a judge approves a bad answer. Logs, alerts and dashboards surface events, and a silently wrong verdict is the absence of one. The verifier, in his phrase, is the one component whose failures are invisible by construction.

## The biases are measured, and they compound

Vsevolod walks through findings from the LLM-as-judge literature. Position bias and verbosity bias appear in the original LLM-as-judge paper from Zheng and colleagues in 2023 and have survived every model generation since. Self-preference is worse: work by Wataoka and colleagues found it tracks perplexity, meaning judges favour text that reads like their own. On Arena Hard, he cites a self-preference effect ranging from -38% to +90% across judges. If agent and judge share a model family, you're getting a model nodding at its reflection.

Putting a human on top doesn't close the gap. Dietz and colleagues documented a rubber-stamp effect: people asked to check an LLM's verdict tend to agree with it, even when it's demonstrably wrong. That stacks two correlated verifiers and calls it defence in depth. None of this shows in a ten-example demo; the biases are statistical and appear at scale, exactly where you stopped looking.

## The judge should usually be smarter than the agent

The common setup puts the big model on the agent and a cheap one on the judge, because checking feels easier than doing. Vsevolod takes the verification-asymmetry argument seriously, then shows where it breaks. Checking is cheap only when there is a certificate: multiply the factors, run the code, execute the query. Most agentic tasks have none. Was the summary faithful to the contract? Will this plan reach the goal? Verifying means redoing the reasoning, and a judge can't reliably catch a mistake on a problem it couldn't solve.

His conditional rule: with a cheap certificate, a cheaper judge plus the tool can verify a stronger generator, so lean on the tool. Without one, the judge must be at least as strong as the agent.

Self-verification doesn't rescue you. He cites research showing generation and self-verification don't improve together, and that much apparent self-checking is fake verification: the model writes the words of checking with almost no effect on the answer. Real verification needs independent purchase on the problem: a different model, a tool, a ground-truth outcome.

## Route judges, don't average them

Three judges from one family averaged together give you sharper confidence, not better accuracy. Judges from genuinely different families (Claude, GPT, Gemini) disagree in systematic, measurable ways, and the cases where they split are a live map of where your risk is. Never let a model be the only judge of itself.

Since running a full panel on every output is unaffordable, he frames judge selection as a multi-armed bandit. Each judge or combination is an arm; downstream signals (spot checks, tests, escalations) are rewards. Thompson sampling, dating to 1933, explores early and concentrates on judges that keep being right per task type, and keeps relearning as models and traffic drift. The economics follow: verification at full strength can be the largest line in your inference bill, so you pay for strong judges only on the fraction of tasks near a decision boundary.

## Who should watch

Anyone running LLM-as-judge in production, or about to. The talk is dense with citations and he shares a reading list at the end, so keep the slides handy.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Who Judges the AI Agent? LLM-as-Judge for Testing Non-Deterministic Code Generation](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Liran_Yushinsky_testing_judge_codegen) by Liran Yushinsky, for judges in a code generation setting, where certificates exist.
- [Self-Signed Evidence: Why Your LLM Agent's Green Checks Prove Nothing](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Danila_Redikultsev_evidence_agent_checks) by Danila Redikultsev, a close cousin of the fake-verification argument.
- [How to evaluate your Evals?](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Hilik_Paz_evaluate_evals) by Hilik Paz, on verifying the verifier.

Title: The database risk someone saw but never said out loud
Description: Sheena Yap Chan at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on the VISIBLE framework for getting database risks to decision-makers before they get expensive.
Body:
Most postmortems ask what broke. Sheena Yap Chan wants them to ask what stayed hidden too long. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, the founder of The Tao of Self-Confidence argues that the most expensive database risks are often already known to someone on the team; they just never reach the people who can act in time.

This is the non-technical talk of the event, and it says so. There's no SQL in it. It's about the human path a signal takes from the DBA who spots it to the leader who signs off on the fix.

## The gap sits between seeing and deciding

Sheena defines the visibility gap as the distance between what the technical team sees and what decision-makers understood in time to act. Risks hide in incident response, migration planning, performance conversations, reliability reviews, postmortems and handoffs. She compares it to a child hiding a mistake from their parents: the longer it stays hidden, the bigger and more expensive it gets.

Her reframe is that visibility isn't about attention, it's about protection, for you, the organisation and the customer. And confidence isn't about being loud; it's about saying what needs to be said when it needs to be said.

## Three ways a signal dies

The most practical slide lists three failure modes:

1. **Seen but not shared.** Someone noticed, assumed someone else had it, or was afraid to speak.
2. **Shared but not understood.** The concern was raised in language the listener couldn't parse.
3. **Understood but not acted on.** No owner, no channel, no spotlight.

Anyone who has read an incident timeline with a message from three days earlier saying "this looks odd" will recognise all three.

## VISIBLE, letter by letter

Her framework spells out seven pillars. Voice: can people raise concerns early, and if speaking up is hard, are there other routes such as one-to-ones or anonymous channels? Identity: do people see themselves as part of reliability? Spotlight: what deserves attention right now? Inner work: what keeps people silent? She calls this 80% of the work and draws on her own upbringing, where she was taught to stay in the background. Belief: do people think raising a concern will change anything? If the first one went nowhere, there won't be a second. Leverage: teams working in silos, one person doing everything until burnout. Elevation: turning a technical concern into something a decision can be made from.

## Templates you can steal

The concrete takeaways are phrasing. For migrations, replace "we should be fine" with the risks, the impact and the decision needed. During incidents, people need clear updates, next steps and owners, not more noise. And a five-line visibility statement for any escalation: here is what we are seeing, why it matters, the possible impact, the options, and the decision we need.

For leaders she offers four questions: what are we not seeing yet, what are people afraid to say, where are signals getting stuck, and who needs this information sooner?

## Who should watch

Team leads, incident commanders and the engineer who always notices the slow query first but doesn't like to make a fuss. Engineers after technical depth should skip it; those whose last outage had a Slack message nobody read should not.

- [Postmortems, Continuous Learning and Enabling Blameless Culture](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2021_Julie_Gunderson_postmortem_continuous_learning_blameless_culture) by Julie Gunderson, the postmortem side of speaking up.
- [People-Powered Security: The Role of Soft Skills in a DevSecOps Culture](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Victor_Onyenagubom_security_soft_skills) by Victor Onyenagubom, the same argument for security teams.

Title: Put LLM agents in decision systems as copilots, not deciders
Description: Mazdul Choudhury (Walmart) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 lays out a three-layer architecture for LLM copilots in forecasting and planning workflows.
Body:
The hard question about LLMs in the enterprise has moved on from whether a model can answer a question. It is whether it can support thousands of business decisions a day within cost, latency, governance and stability limits. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Mazdul Choudhury, Staff Product Manager at Walmart, answers with an architecture: LLM agents as copilots inside decision workflows, with humans keeping the judgment and the accountability.

This is a product manager's framework talk. There's no code and no Walmart-specific numbers; what you get is a clean structure for taking an agent from demo to something an operations team will actually use.

## Copilot is a job description

Mazdul's definition is precise. A copilot gathers information, evaluates options, highlights tasks and surfaces recommendations. It doesn't replace people and doesn't make autonomous decisions. Humans own the call; the agent helps them process complexity faster and more consistently.

He uses forecasting and operational planning as the running example, because it mixes structured data (demand signals, operational metrics) with unstructured inputs (external events, market conditions, human expertise). The same pattern, he says, carries over to supply chain, capacity planning and risk management.

## Three layers that can change independently

The architecture matters more than the model choice, in his view, and it has three layers:

1. **Signal aggregation.** Continuously collect structured data (transactions, forecasts, metrics) and unstructured data (documents, reports, logs, communications) into one queryable context layer. Without good context, model sophistication doesn't help.
2. **Agent reasoning.** The LLM evaluates the context, generates forecasts, detects anomalies and recommends actions, and every output carries its rationale. If users can't see why, they won't act on it.
3. **Human interaction.** Users query the system, explore scenarios, validate assumptions and give feedback. This is the layer that stops the system being a black box, and where trust gets built.

Keeping the layers separate makes the whole thing more resilient and easier to deploy.

## Four production problems that tests won't show

Hallucination, decision consistency, latency and cost show up in production however well the model did in testing. His answers:

- **Grounding** is the most important hallucination fix: RAG, structured queries and authoritative internal sources, treated as an ongoing discipline around freshness and monitoring.
- **Multi-step orchestration**: retrieve context, plan, call tools, synthesise. It mirrors how an analyst works, but runs continuously.
- **Additive integration**: wrap existing systems instead of replacing them, deploy in shadow mode, and keep deterministic fallbacks.
- **Progressive maturity**: focused prototype, shadow deployment, human-in-the-loop validation, then scale with monitoring and governance. Jumping straight from prototype to production is, in his telling, why most AI initiatives fail.

His four takeaways fit on a sticky note: architecture before models, ground everything in enterprise data, integrate additively, and measure accuracy, latency, cost and human trust continuously.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineering leads scoping their first agent inside an existing planning or operations workflow, especially if stakeholders are nervous about autonomy. Engineers after implementation detail should treat this as the map and look elsewhere for the territory.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Human-in-the-Loop MLOps: Production Patterns](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Tejasvi_Nuthalapati_human_loop_mlops) by Tejasvi Nuthalapati, on the human layer in practice.
- [Transforming Inventory Forecasting with Production ML](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2026_Pallab_Haldar_orchestration_workflows_ai) by Pallab Haldar, the forecasting use case with classic ML.
- [AgentCast: Autonomous AI-Driven Time Series Forecasting for DevOps at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Premanand_Tiwari_forecasting_time_autonomy) by Premanand Tiwari, a more autonomous take on agents that forecast.

Title: Same SQL, three engines, three answers
Description: Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan (DoorDash) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on catching semantic drift across Spark, Trino and Snowflake in CI.
Body:
A query that compiles and runs on every engine in your stack can still return a different number on each one. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Muthupalaniappan Ramanathan, Senior Software Developer at DoorDash, makes the case that "SQL compatibility does not equal semantic consistency", and shows a DevOps framework for catching the difference at commit time instead of on a dashboard.

It's a compact talk, under twenty minutes, and it stays at framework level: no code walkthrough, but a clear testing strategy you can copy.

## Why you have three engines in the first place

Muthupalaniappan starts from the multi-engine reality: teams run Spark, Trino and Snowflake side by side because ETL pipelines, ad hoc exploration and real-time dashboards each favour a different runtime. That flexibility is reasonable. The cost is that the same SQL string can produce three answers, and standard SQL linting and schema tests won't notice.

## Where the divergence hides

The engines aren't buggy; they made different, deliberate design choices. He groups the differences into four:

- **Type handling:** implicit casts, numeric precision and integer overflow.
- **Null semantics:** how nulls propagate through joins and aggregations.
- **Aggregation behaviour:** floating point summation order and distinct-count edge cases.
- **Optimizer decisions:** rewrites that can silently change which rows are included or how results are ordered.

Each is small. Compounded across a few hundred pipelines and an engine upgrade or two, they become analytical drift: two teams with two "correct" revenue numbers.

## Write the meaning once

The core idea is analytical intent as a first-class abstraction. Instead of writing engine-specific SQL, you declare what the query means in engine-agnostic terms. A canonical semantic layer translates that intent into each dialect using deterministic rules, and humans never write dialect-specific SQL by hand. That removes handcrafted drift between copies and keeps one source of logical truth.

## Then make CI prove it

A semantic layer alone isn't enough, he argues; it has to be enforced. Every commit or schema change triggers a semantic diff and a cross-engine dry run, and an equivalence assertion has to pass before merge. Drift becomes a PR blocker rather than a production data incident.

The four test types are the most reusable part of the talk:

1. **Equivalence tests** assert identical results across engine pairs on a reference dataset.
2. **Null boundary tests** exercise rare but critical null paths.
3. **Precision regression tests** keep floating point aggregations within a set tolerance across engine upgrades.
4. **Translation snapshot tests** pin the generated SQL so an unintended compiler change shows up as a diff.

Merge-time checks don't end the job. In production he runs queries across engine pairs, compares result fingerprints, alerts on metric divergence and uses lineage-aware attribution to find the source of a drift. Trust in the numbers, in his framing, is an operational property you enforce, not a feature you ship once.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers running more than one query engine, and anyone planning an engine migration who wants a test harness for "did the numbers change?". If you run a single warehouse, the null and precision tests still make a good checklist for your next upgrade.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Closing the Semantic Gap with Feedback-Driven Ontology Learning](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Ravi_Chandra_llms_analytics_semanticlayer) by Ravi Chandra, another approach to keeping analytical meaning consistent.
- [Data Quality and Validation in ML Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sunil_Kumar_Mudusu_data_quality_validation) by Sunil Kumar Mudusu, validation patterns for the data feeding those queries.
- [Effective Observability in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Other SQL Databases](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Adam_Furmanek_observability_postgresql_mysql) by Adam Furmanek, for watching what the engines actually do.

Title: An AI-maintained architecture hub so agents can reason across services
Description: Lior Schejter at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on a Git repo of AI-written markdown facets that gives agents system-wide context across many microservices.
Body:
Drop a coding agent into one repository and it feels like magic. Ask it to fix a bug spanning six microservices and it's flying blind. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Lior Schejter, Lead R&D Architect, shows how he fixed that with an Application Architecture Hub: a plain Git repo of markdown files that AI agents write, keep current on every merge, and read when they need the system-level picture.

The best part is how little infrastructure it needs. No graph database, no wiki platform, no servers.

## The same AI that's hungry for context can write it

The underlying problem predates AI. In a large microservice system, tracing a flow across services, or finding where data is used and changed, is possible but slow and doesn't scale. Humans are notoriously bad at keeping documentation current. Agents raise the stakes because they need that documentation to work well, and they also happen to be good at producing it: reading code, matching semantics, doing it tirelessly.

## Flat files beat the graph database

Lior's team did prototype graph databases first, because modelling a system as a graph feels natural. Flat markdown won. Agents read it natively, Git provides versioning, diffs and pull requests for free, and there is nothing to operate. He calls the robust architecture a temptation the team decided was premature optimisation.

The unit of ingestion is one repo, but documentation is split into facets: domain models, exposed APIs, events, dependencies and more. Questions to the hub tend to cut across services along one facet. Tracing a bug wants events and APIs for a set of services; assessing blast radius wants dependencies. Facets also make ingestion parallel and retries cheap.

A strict naming convention maps a repo and a facet to exactly one file path. If you know what you're looking for, you know the file name, with no search or lookup in between.

## Agents write it, scripts check it, citations keep it honest

An orchestrator agent dispatches one sub-agent per facet. Each reads the same repo, extracts its slice, and writes its own file, so they run concurrently without polluting each other's context, and a failure retries only that facet.

Early on, the ingestion agent was asked to lint its own output. That was unreliable, and since every check was mechanical (file locations, broken links, front matter), it moved into a script. His summary is an old lesson: don't use AI where you don't need it.

A GitHub Actions workflow triggers updates on merges to main for relevant repos, and opens a pull request for human review. Those reviews caught real gaps, like a non-standard Kafka publishing pattern in some repos that left events undocumented; the skill was updated to recognise it. With confidence built up, updates can merge automatically.

The single most effective measure against hallucination and run-to-run drift: requiring every claim to cite a file name and line numbers. Structured templates helped too, and repos built on consistent frameworks such as NestJS produced noticeably better documentation than older, looser code. To control cost, an update skill diffs the code against the hub and rewrites only what changed.

## Querying is where the value is

Query skills, distributed as a plugin to the team's Cursor installations, tell agents how to navigate the hub and connect files. An incident troubleshooting agent uses the hub alongside its log, Jira and Slack tools. Ready-made reports turn common questions into one prompt: a dependency map for a repo (including implicit dependencies through a shared database), flow descriptions with a plain-English variant for product managers, and architecture overviews for onboarding.

The latest step maps business terms to the repos that own or consume them. Because those mappings can't be anchored in code, low-confidence ones go to a human audit, and confirmed mappings survive future updates.

He says the initial prototype took one or two weeks, built mostly by one person.

## Who should watch

Teams with dozens or hundreds of services who want agents to help beyond a single repo. It's also a good reference for anyone tempted to build a knowledge platform before trying a folder of markdown.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Context Engineering for DevOps: Turning Your Infrastructure into a Reasoning Graph](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure) by Roxane Fischer, the graph approach Lior decided against, applied to infrastructure.
- [Prompting Is Not the System: Engineering Context, Contracts and Reliable Agent Behavior](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Emerson_Braun_contracts_context_agent) by Emerson Braun, on context as an engineered artifact.
- [Scaling Microservices Observability with Agentic LLMs](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Nishanth_Vepachedu_microservices_observability_llms) by Nishanth Vepachedu, for the troubleshooting-agent side of a large service estate.

Title: Data engineers already own the metadata RAG needs
Description: Varun Joshi (AWS) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on four RAG uses for data teams, from schema Q&A to on-call, and why your metadata is the missing piece.
Body:
LLMs know SQL. What they don't know is your warehouse: which `orders` table is real, what grain a fact table has, why two columns with the same name mean different things. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Varun Joshi, Senior Data Engineer at AWS, argues that data engineers are better placed than anyone to fix that with retrieval-augmented generation, because they already produce the context RAG needs as a side effect of their day job.

It's a practical introduction, aimed at data engineers rather than ML teams, and it ends with a four-week plan.

## RAG is prompt engineering at scale

Varun keeps the fundamentals short. A question is embedded, a similarity search runs against a vector store of your docs, schemas and incident threads, the top chunks go into the prompt, and the model answers with that context. The model's weights never change.

That gives you three properties he cares about: it's cheap to update (re-index the docs), fast to deploy (no fine-tuning), and auditable, because you can see exactly what was retrieved and why.

## Your metadata is already machine-readable

His case for data teams rests on four assets most of them already have: schemas (DDL, column descriptions, catalogs), lineage graphs, query history (a corpus of what stakeholders actually ask), and documentation, however patchy. Lineage alone answers questions like which reports break if you deprecate a dimension table, which is otherwise a tour through hundreds of jobs.

## Four places it fits

**Schema Q&A.** New engineers spend months learning a handful of entities. Index the DDL, dbt YAML descriptions and catalog exports and they can ask what a table contains and get the current answer instead of a Confluence page last edited in 2021. His recipe: export the dbt manifest, parse DDL, chunk by table, embed, store. He sizes it as a two or three day project.

**Grounded SQL agents.** The difference between a SQL agent that invents column names and one that doesn't is usually whether it was given the real DDL. With schema retrieval, the agent finds relevant tables semantically, even ones without "customer" in the name, and can use primary key and nullability information to pick join keys.

**Incident response.** When a pipeline breaks at 2 a.m., the on-call engineer needs to know whether this happened before and what fixed it. The postmortem usually exists; nobody searches Confluence at 2 a.m. Index postmortems, runbooks and Slack threads, and his team, which already runs this, gets the earlier incident and its root cause back in seconds.

**Tribal knowledge.** His favourite example: an orders pipeline runs at 6 a.m., not midnight, because years ago someone scheduled it around a billing system window. When that person leaves, the reason leaves too. Architecture decision records and PR descriptions are underrated sources, and he recommends recorded Q&A sessions with tenured engineers on what a new hire should know when the system breaks.

## An integration problem, not a content problem

The core thesis: if your team has done data engineering for more than six months, you almost certainly have most of this content already, scattered across a catalog, Git, Confluence and Airflow logs. Building RAG looks less like an AI project and more like a new data pipeline, which is home turf.

His month plan: week one, audit your metadata without writing code. Week two, a minimal schema Q&A over the dbt manifest in Chroma. Week three, one agent use case, SQL or incident response, whichever hurts more. Week four, measure and share. He puts the first month at roughly 15 to 20 engineering days.

## Who should watch

Data engineers who keep hearing about RAG from the ML side and want to know where it lands in their own workflow. If you already run RAG in production, the use cases will feel familiar, but the point that you already own the corpus makes a good pitch to take to your manager.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Agentic Text-to-SQL in Production: What 500+ Data Marts and 30M Users Taught Us](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Vladimir_Beskorovainyi_sql_orchestration_scale) by Vladimir Beskorovainyi, the grounded SQL agent at much larger scale.
- [How to use generative AI to finally fix out-dated runbooks](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2023_Anurag_Gupta_generative_ai_fix_runbooks) by Anurag Gupta, the incident-response use case from the SRE side.
- [Vector Embeddings and RAG Demystified](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Veliswa_Boya_rag_embeddings_vector) by Veliswa Boya, if you want the retrieval mechanics in more detail.

Title: AI fixed the migration speed problem, and exposed the trust problem
Description: Muthu Saravanan (Mind-Pros) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on HAX, a framework for deciding what humans own and what AI does in database delivery.
Body:
Muthu Saravanan's story starts with a win. A database team's pipeline was too slow for migrations, they brought in an AI tool, and suddenly migrations, schemas and queries came out faster than ever. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, the Director of Experience Design at Mind-Pros explains what that win uncovered: the bottleneck moved from "can we build it?" to "should we build it this way?", and fast output isn't the same thing as trustworthy output.

His answer is HAX (Human and AI Experience), a framework he conceptualised and holds the trademark for. It's a process talk rather than a tooling one: no specific product, no benchmarks, and a clear map of who decides what.

## Experience debt accumulates where nobody looks

Muthu names the new problem experience debt: like technical debt, but more dangerous with AI because it builds up invisibly. A bad schema decision can survive for years; a poorly reviewed migration can cascade into other production systems. He lists three symptoms:

- **Inconsistency creep.** Every engineer prompts differently, assumes differently and validates differently, until the team shares no common engineering language.
- **Amplified data risk.** Generated SQL can be syntactically fine and still bring security holes, index regressions, locking issues or integrity failures.
- **Erosion of trust.** When engineers stop understanding why the AI produced something, they swing to blind trust or total rejection. Both end in failures.

## Humans decide, AI elevates

HAX splits responsibility into two layers. HX covers what stays human because the consequences are long-lived: system architecture (an AI can suggest scaling patterns but knows nothing about acquisition plans or org politics), data modelling (a schema encodes business meaning, and a naming mistake today is a reporting problem for years), governance (classification, access, audit accountability) and critical reasoning during incidents, where people weigh team history, risk tolerance and customer impact.

AX covers where AI adds the most value, in six facets: detect (anomalies, drift), predict (migration risk, capacity growth), scale (index recommendations, connection pooling, pipeline orchestration), synthesize (turning telemetry, logs and change history into usable knowledge), execute (deployments and migrations inside human-set boundaries) and ethics (transparency as part of reliability).

## Accountability first, acceleration second

The delivery method runs six stages across discovery, design and development, and it reverses the usual order where teams adopt tools first and govern later. Discovery is the most human part: interviews, system inventories, risk assessments, with AI summarising raw material. In design, engineers own schemas and architecture while AI runs validation checks, suggests index strategies and scaffolds pipelines; nothing moves without human approval. Muthu's framing is to treat the AI as a junior engineer who does the research but doesn't make the final call. In development the roles flip: AI drives migration execution, schema versioning and deployment automation, and engineers monitor with override authority at each step. Telemetry flows back so the process keeps correcting itself.

The point of the explicit boundaries is ownership. If everyone assumes the AI is responsible, nobody owns the outcome.

## The unglamorous part: shared artifacts

The section most teams can act on tomorrow is knowledge artifacts. Without standard prompt libraries, runbooks and tool-specific interaction patterns (he names ChatGPT and Gemini), every engineer invents their own prompting style and validation logic, which is inconsistency creep by another route. His closing advice follows from that: start where you are, because a shared prompt library and a validation checklist get you further than you'd expect.

## Who should watch

Engineering leads whose teams adopted AI assistants for database work bottom-up and now have five different ways of generating migrations. Engineers looking for implementation detail will find the talk high-level; its value is the vocabulary for an ownership conversation.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [I Don't Trust AI Agents (And Neither Should You): Building Production-Ready Architectures](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Morgan_Willis_production_guardrails_trust) by Morgan Willis, trust boundaries from the architecture side.
- [From Acceleration to Assurance: Governing AI Code Assistants in SOX and ICFR Audit Analytics](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Karishma_Velisetty_governance_audit_assistants) by Karishma Velisetty, governance for AI assistants under audit.
- [Gate the Action, Not the Alert: Checking an Agent Before It Runs](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Artemis_Leonardou_agents_guardrails_policy) by Artemis Leonardou, where the human gate goes in agent workflows.

Title: Conf42 Golang 2026 - Go as the boring backbone under AI and money
Description: Conf42 Golang 2026 in review, 22 talks on MCP servers in Go, monolith surgery at Fleet, O(log N) leaderboards, fallback search at eBay and GPU profiling.
Body:
[Conf42 Golang 2026](https://www.conf42.com/golang2026) aired on May 21, 2026 with 22 talks, and the language itself rarely took centre stage. Go showed up the way it does in most companies: as the dependable layer under an MCP server, a leaderboard, a search fallback, a fraud engine or an insurance core. Speakers from eBay, Fleet Device Management, METRO AG, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, General Motors, Ford, Salesforce, Walmart and SoftSwiss showed what that layer has to survive.

## Go as the plumbing for LLMs

The most hands-on AI talk came from [Shadi Elyafi](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Shadi_Elyafi_mcp_b2b_workflow) (METRO AG), who built an MCP server in Go for a real B2B workflow on a platform serving more than 1 million company profiles. It exposes tools for Claude, talks to a GraphQL backend through AWS AppSync, and draws careful read/write boundaries so mutations stay safe. He also covers how TDD with mock GraphQL clients keeps the MCP layer from turning into a fragile demo.

[Swati Kumari](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Swati_Kumari_beyond_chatbots_building) (NucleusTeq) made the case that most chatbots fail because they cannot reach CRM, order management or billing, and showed Go backend integrations that let them act. [Sanjay Basu](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sanjay_Basu_building_cognitive_commerce) (TCS) sketched Go-based architectures for LLM-driven grocery and e-commerce platforms, and [Venkat Kamma](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Venkat_Kamma_from_reactive_predictive) (StarGroup Innovations) applied the same idea to Oracle Cloud PPM, catching cost overruns before they happen instead of in the monthly report. [Rejenish Kiran](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Rejenish_Kiran_assisted_test_execution) (Citizens Property Insurance Corporation) positioned AI-assisted test execution as an augmentation layer on top of existing Go test frameworks rather than a replacement.

## Data structures still win the incident

The talk most likely to end up in a team chat was [Ivan Balashov's](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Ivan_Balashov_engineering_high_performance) (SoftSwiss). A production leaderboard was causing daily outages thanks to O(N²) updates, CPU spikes and memory pressure. The fix was an indexed skip list with span counters for O(log N) position queries plus hash-based deduplication, replacing a naive slice-based leaderboard in two days. A good reminder that your outage might be a CS201 exercise wearing a pager.

[Amol Lele](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Amol_Lele_real_time_training) (Hewlett Packard Enterprise) built a multi-layer ML training profiler in Go with 2-5% runtime overhead and walked through the three costliest failure modes he found: data pipeline bottlenecks, communication overhead in distributed training, and straggler workers in heterogeneous clusters. [Akshaya Jayaram](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Akshaya_Jayaram_ammf_attention_based) (Salesforce) presented AMMF, an attention-based fusion model for spotting the same vulnerable function across architectures, a problem Go's easy cross-compilation makes very real.

## Failing gracefully on purpose

[Hima Bindu Yanala](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Hima_Bindu_Yanala_designing_resilient_self) (eBay) treated fallback as a first-class feature of self-service search: a dedicated lightweight fallback index, circuit breakers routing traffic through closed, open and half-open states, and bulkheads protecting fallback capacity. Her point about fan-out amplification, where rare shard outliers become systemic failures, applies well beyond search.

[Yogesh Pugazhendhi Duraisamy Rajamani](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Yogesh_Pugazhendhi_Duraisamy_Rajamani_building_self_healing) (Ford Motor Company) described self-healing streaming pipelines in Go with a reinforcement-learning control plane adjusting ingestion, messaging and compute across Kafka, Pulsar and Flink. [Sudhakar Pallaprolu](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sudhakar_Pallaprolu_autonomous_cloud_infrastructure) covered self-healing infrastructure and AIOps from the platform side.

## Evolving the code you already have

[Victor Lyuboslavsky](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Victor_Lyuboslavsky_modularizing_year_monolith) (Fleet Device Management) gave the talk he says the Go community lacks: a real, open source, decade-old Go monolith mid-way to a modular design while still shipping to production. It started as an investigation into slow builds and tests and turned up oversized packages, uncontrolled dependencies and boundaries that no longer matched how engineers thought about the system. The people side gets as much airtime as the architecture.

[Sulabh Jain](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sulabh_Jain_building_cloud_native) took the same question to insurance core systems, where catastrophe-driven claims spikes punish monoliths, and [Sana Fatima](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sana_Fatima_from_code_correctness) (General Motors) argued that code which compiles and passes unit tests can still fail at system level in embedded automotive software, so behaviour validation has to move earlier.

## Compliance and money, engineered in

Regulated platforms got a strong block. [Manasa Uppula](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Manasa_Uppula_designing_defensibility_evidence) (Virtusa) designs financial platforms so that every critical customer interaction produces structured evidence by default: what was shown, how consent was captured, how a decision was made. Audits then become a query, not an archaeology dig. [Sridhar Muthineni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sridhar_Muthineni_driven_fraud_detection) (Capgemini) combined fraud detection and personalisation in Go fintech systems, and [Devi Manoharan](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Devi_Manoharan_building_high_performance) (ASTA CRS) covered AI-driven claims processing on EDI pipelines. [Emmanuela Opurum](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Emmanuela_Opurum_building_secure_pipelines) (SoftNet Technologies) showed Go-based automation for secure CI/CD across AWS, Azure and GCP.

The programme also stretched to [DOCSIS networks](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Harsha_Vardhani_Talluri_building_unified_docsis) (Harsha Vardhani Talluri), [3PL warehouse design](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Vivek_Sander_data_driven_warehouse) (Vivek Sander, Sunland Logistics Solution), [digital PMOs in retail](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_George_Job_digital_pmos_retail) (George Job, Walmart) and [design systems for analytics platforms](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Sonali_Priya_scalable_design_systems) (Sonali Priya, LB Networks).

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) and [Virtana](https://www.virtana.com/) at Gold. All 22 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCKzSYaULw7l2nLQKxk2IkS).

Next up for the gophers: [Conf42 Golang 2027](https://www.conf42.com/golang2027).

Title: When the LLM writes the code, reading it becomes the job
Description: Petras Bazdaras at Conf42 LLMs 2026 argues AI-generated code makes reading and CS fundamentals the core engineering skill, not typing speed.
Body:
If a model can produce in seconds what used to take you an afternoon, the afternoon didn't disappear. It moved to after the model stops typing. That is the argument Petras Bazdaras, an aspiring cloud engineer, makes at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026: reading and critically auditing code is now the primary engineering act, and that raises the bar on fundamentals instead of lowering it.

It's a short, opinionated talk with no benchmarks or case study. What it offers is a clear vocabulary for a problem most teams using coding assistants already feel.

## Compiled and working is not the same as good

Before AI, output was a decent proxy for skill: hours of boilerplate, scaffolding and repeated patterns. Now output is cheap, and Petras names the delusion that follows: mistaking code that compiles and runs for good engineering. Shipping code you didn't write and don't understand is a liability.

He sees it in two forms. Cargo-culting AI output means accepting code that looks right but embeds anti-patterns, security gaps or inefficient logic. Blind trust at scale means every accepted suggestion quietly adds technical debt you didn't choose and may not see until production.

His estimate is that developers now spend roughly ninety percent of their time auditing, debugging and maintaining what the model generated. Teams split into two habits: skim and accept, or read and verify, which means tracing logic line by line, testing behaviour and questioning trade-offs. Hidden assumptions and edge cases slip through the first and get caught by the second.

## The autopsy problem

The sharpest idea in the talk is what Petras calls the autopsy problem. When a system fails under load, you're performing an autopsy on logic you didn't write. Because you never built a mental model of it, the debugging intuition simply isn't there. Race conditions, resource leaks and odd edge cases tend to surface only in production, and the on-call pager doesn't care who or what wrote the code. The incident report has your name on it.

LLMs, in his framing, are pattern matchers rather than engineers. They introduce deprecated APIs and outdated library versions, write logic that scales poorly, and know nothing about your team's architectural constraints. Human review matters most on three fronts: security, performance and context.

## The basics, redefined

The fundamentals he means aren't syntax. They are the parts of computer science that let you evaluate any code regardless of who wrote it:

- data structures and algorithmic complexity, including memory layout and why trade-offs matter at scale;
- concurrency and memory management, to catch the race conditions, deadlocks and garbage collection issues that LLMs readily introduce;
- system design and secure coding, including threat modelling.

Using AI to skip learning these doesn't make you faster, Petras argues; it makes you dependent. Problem-solving is a muscle, and an unexercised one weakens. The career shift he describes runs from code typist to system reviewer, with the engineer as a managing editor who audits, secures and scales what the model drafts.

## Who should watch

Junior engineers deciding what to learn while their assistant writes the boilerplate, and leads who need words for why "it passed CI" isn't a review. Senior engineers will agree with most of it; the autopsy framing is the part worth borrowing for your next team discussion.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Low-Level Computing in a Cloud Native World](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Rob_Zuber_cs_fundamentals_fail_us) by Rob Zuber, a pre-LLM case for fundamentals that holds up well.
- [Verification Timing: Why Checking AI-Written Code at the Gate Is Already Too Late](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Yunhao_Jiao_aicoding_verification_gates) by Yunhao Jiao, on when the reading should happen.
- [Why You Don't Need That New Library: Sticking to Fundamentals](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Denis_Ermakov_library_fundamentals_need) by Denis Ermakov, the same instinct applied to dependencies.

[Watch Petras Bazdaras's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Petras_Bazdaras_reading_new_writing)

Title: Put fairness checks in CI, next to the unit tests
Description: Dharmendra Ahuja (IBM) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on embedding bias, privacy and explainability checks into the CI/CD stages of AI data pipelines.
Body:
A biased model doesn't throw an exception. It ships, passes every health check and makes the wrong call at scale. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Dharmendra Ahuja, DevOps Lead at IBM, argues that the fix belongs in the same place as your other quality gates: the CI/CD pipeline that moves data and models to production, with fairness, privacy and explainability checks at each stage.

The talk is a framework overview with a healthcare case study, aimed at teams that already run MLOps and want governance to be code rather than a review meeting.

## The cost of getting it wrong

He opens with the failure modes: a 2023 healthcare model that misclassified risk for 45% of minority patients because of biased training data, and hiring algorithms that screened out qualified candidates by repeating historical patterns. He cites an average remediation cost of $3.7 million per AI ethics failure, attributed to MIT Sloan in 2024, plus trust damage that doesn't show up on an invoice.

The four risks he wants pipelines to catch are bias in data, privacy exposure of medical, financial and biometric records, model drift after launch, and black-box models that regulators and stakeholders can't interrogate.

## Four gates, one per stage

The core of the talk maps ethics onto pipeline stages you already have:

- **Code commit:** policy-as-code rules scan for data handling violations and raise bias flags.
- **Build and test:** automated fairness tests check disparate impact across demographic groups.
- **Stage gate:** ethics thresholds block deployment if a bias metric exceeds its limit.
- **Production:** continuous drift monitoring, with automated rollback when drift appears.

Governance-as-code, in his framing, means policies expressed as machine-readable rules that block unapproved deployments, enforce fairness thresholds and require explainability documentation. It's the same idea as a failing test blocking a merge, applied to a different class of bug.

## Observability with a business layer on top

Dharmendra layers ethical observability in four tiers: infrastructure (compute, network, containers, database performance), data (freshness, schema consistency, sensitive data exposure), model (prediction quality, bias indicators, explainability) and business (user trust, regulatory compliance, stakeholder feedback). Alerts fire on prediction imbalance, demographic disparity, unauthorised data access or data corruption, and each maps to an automated action: roll back the model, quarantine a suspicious data stream, revoke access privileges dynamically, or escalate a compliance alert.

The architecture behind it is containerised validation packages for consistency across dev, staging and production, Kubernetes policy engines with network isolation and audit logging, event-driven streaming for real-time monitoring, and ethical controls embedded in infrastructure-as-code templates.

## What the healthcare client changed

The case study pairs four problems with four fixes: inconsistent clinical data quality met automated ingestion validation; patient-record privacy concerns met privacy-centred design with end-to-end encryption, automated anonymisation and role-based access; black-box diagnostic recommendations met explainability frameworks with feature importance and clinical reasoning summaries; slow incident response met continuous monitoring with automated alerts.

On the business case, he reports a 73% reduction in bias-related incidents after integrating ethics into CI/CD, regulatory audits completed 2.4 times faster with governance-as-code, and a 58% reduction in model remediation cost from earlier detection. The talk presents these as outcomes rather than walking through how they were measured.

## The trade-offs he admits

He's candid that this isn't free. Ethical checks add pipeline complexity. Too many alerts cause fatigue and erode trust in monitoring, so thresholds need continuous tuning. Different fairness metrics can conflict, and each organisation has to pick its definitions. Observability costs money and needs leadership support. His prioritisation is by risk: start with the systems that combine sensitive data, regulatory exposure and human impact, and keep human review for critical decisions in healthcare, finance and public safety.

The closing plan is concrete: this week, find your highest-risk model; this month, add fairness checks to CI and form a cross-functional ethics group; this quarter, implement governance-as-code and define thresholds and alert policies.

## Who should watch

MLOps and data platform engineers in regulated domains who need a vocabulary for turning "be fair" into pipeline stages. If you want metric definitions or tool names, pair it with the talks below.

Title: Voice AI over a plain phone call, for users who distrust AI
Description: Pavel Shchekotov (Denk Solutions) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on running an LLM voice agent over phone calls and SMS for users aged 55+, and what broke.
Body:
The easiest way to onboard someone who will never install your app is to let them call a phone number. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Pavel Shchekotov, co-founder of Denk Solutions, shares what happened when his team at Sofi Connect, where he was founding engineer, built an LLM voice agent for a dating service aimed at people aged 55 and over, delivered over ordinary phone calls and text messages.

The bet was that a concierge-style voice experience would lift retention, and that a phone call would remove app installs, accounts and registration from the funnel. It did remove them. It also surfaced a long list of problems that never show up in a chatbot demo.

## Trust is a design problem before it is a model problem

Many people don't want to talk to robots, and some react to the word AI itself. Accents tripped speech-to-text. And an unexpected call from an unknown number about a new service looks a lot like a scam.

Users also went off script: related questions, personal stories, and in a few cases flirting with the bot. Every off-script minute costs money, but you can't simply hang up on a person.

The team's responses were small and deliberate:

- A calm, pleasant voice: a neutral female voice from the latest ElevenLabs models at the time, because it sounded less robotic.
- A neutral human name, Sophie, while still disclosing up front that it is AI (US rules require it). The wording was tuned to be transparent without scaring people off.
- No picture of Sophie anywhere, for the same reason Siri and Alexa don't have faces: any face wins some users and loses others.
- Caller identification: users were asked to save the number, and calling name presentation showed who was calling even when they hadn't.
- Memory, via Mem0, so Sophie could bring back small details from earlier conversations. Pavel calls this the difference between a script and a personal experience.

Scripts were written to be heard. A sentence that looks short on screen can drag when spoken, so every phrase was replayed out loud, and a guardrail layer politely steered off-topic conversations back on track.

## The phone network has opinions

Latency at least has known fixes: optimise networking and code, move infrastructure closer to users, pick faster providers, and run speech-to-text locally if you can. Pavel's benchmark is roughly 500 to 700 milliseconds end to end, from voice activity detection to the first audio chunk of text-to-speech, on top of phone network latency.

Other problems have no clean fix. Local carriers block calls. Landlines can't receive SMS. Calls drop.

The surprise was voicemail. Undetected voicemail wastes money at best and can ruin a user's journey at worst. Twilio's built-in answering machine detection was a start but not perfect, so the team layered heuristics on top (a voice reading out a string of digits, phrases like "you have reached") and, once they had collected enough real examples, an LLM-based detector.

## SMS is billed by the segment

The text agent had its own constraints. SMS is charged per segment of about 160 characters, and some punctuation and emoji eat more space, so the agent had to count characters. Delivery rates depend on opt-out phrasing and on not looking spammy or sensitive, which is easy to trip in dating. Payment links sent by SMS had low delivery, which is understandable: a payment link in a text looks scammy. Without an app, that's an extra drop-off on top of the usual paywall.

And every interaction has a marginal cost: each minute, each message, each failed delivery.

## Who should watch

Product engineers considering voice for audiences that mainstream AI products ignore, and anyone who has only built voice agents for browsers. It's a practitioner's war story more than an architecture talk, and the voicemail and SMS details alone will save someone a sprint.

- [Scaling Conversational AI in Production: MLOps Strategies for Contact Center Transformation](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Manoj_Kumar_Vunnava_scaling_conversational_ai) by Manoj Kumar Vunnava, for running conversational AI at contact-centre scale.

Title: Serverless databases remove capacity planning, not database engineering
Description: Renato Losio at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 shares five lessons from five years of Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB and DSQL, from storage to cost forecasting.
Body:
Renato Losio once tried to draw the New York City skyline with the capacity graph of Aurora Serverless v2, on stage at re:Invent. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, the cloud architect behind cloudiamo.com turns five years of playing with AWS serverless databases into five lessons, and one thesis: "serverless database remove the capacity management, but they don't remove database engineering."

It's an experience talk, not a vendor pitch, and he's openly unimpressed by naming.

## Serverless is an adjective

Lesson one is about labels. Aurora Serverless v1 (GA in 2018) was, as he describes it, roughly an upgraded version of his old auto-scaling Bash and Python scripts, doubling capacity each time; it's now deprecated. DynamoDB On-Demand arrived the same year without the word in its name and is about as serverless as it gets. DocumentDB Serverless doesn't scale to zero. Amazon Aurora DSQL dropped the word entirely. Athena has let you pay per query on S3 for a decade. His advice: stop arguing about the name and ask whether the thing is elastic in the way you need.

## Storage is the bill and the bottleneck

Lesson two has two halves. On a production database he manages, monthly storage and backup costs now exceed compute, on plain GP3. So the CPU line that serverless optimises may not be your main problem.

The second half is a small experiment: insert 100,000 rows one at a time from a stored procedure, default settings, into Aurora Serverless v2 (minimum half an ACU), provisioned Aurora on r8g.large, and RDS for MySQL on the same instance class with 400 GB of GP3. Both Aurora flavours finish in a few seconds. RDS takes about five minutes, and tuning only gets that down to a minute or two. He's clear the workload is unrealistic, but the point lands: Aurora's storage architecture matters far more than whether the compute is serverless.

## Cost forecasting needs a crystal ball

Lesson three: you can't predict serverless cost from a provisioned baseline. One cluster's monthly bill, queried with Athena, had over a thousand line items, because you pay for everything you use: compute units, traffic, multi-AZ, backup, storage type. DSQL's DPU pricing drew the same complaint at launch. That, he argues, isn't the cloud provider being evil; pricing per query shape is hard. His method is empirical: move a replica to serverless, watch the bill, then decide. Anyone quoting you a saving before that is guessing.

## Compatible until it isn't

Lesson four walks the ladder from self-managed Postgres or MySQL on EC2 (most control, least lock-in) through RDS and Aurora to serverless, where you give up more control with each step. Claims of Postgres or MongoDB compatibility hold until your extension isn't supported or an aggregation behaves differently. Compatibility can mean wire protocol, SQL dialect, feature behaviour, the tooling ecosystem or versions, and vendors usually only talk about the first two. He also notes the relational side converging on Postgres, with DSQL Postgres-compatible from day one.

## Horizontal or vertical is a choice, not a verdict

Lesson five: DynamoDB and DSQL scale horizontally behind the scenes; Aurora Serverless scales a single instance vertically. Neither is fake serverless. Most workloads fit comfortably on one big instance with read replicas.

He closes with a line from the Aurora Serverless v2 documentation: if the database won't scale back down, stop and restart it to reclaim fragmented memory, accepting the downtime. Which is where his old scripts started. There's still a MySQL or Postgres engine under there, and a forgotten cron job can keep it awake all month while you blame the scaling algorithm.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to move a relational workload to Aurora Serverless, DSQL or DynamoDB on-demand on the promise of savings. If you already run them, the storage experiment and the billing breakdown are worth the half hour on their own.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Things Fall Apart: Navigating Managed Databases for Over a Decade as a Non-DBA](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Renato_Losio_things_fall_apart) by Renato Losio, the managed-database prequel.
- [Amazon Aurora DSQL: The Future of Scalable, Distributed Relational Databases](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_amazon_aurora_dsql) by Samuel Baruffi, the AWS view of DSQL.

Title: Voice agents that think while they talk, with a Thinker and a Speaker
Description: Bohdan Snisar (Solea AI) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 builds a voice pipeline layer by layer, then splits reasoning from speech to fit a 500 ms budget.
Body:
A voice agent gets about 500 milliseconds to answer before the conversation feels wrong, and that leaves almost no room for a model to think. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Bohdan Snisar, founding engineer at Solea AI (an AI operating system for home service businesses), builds the classic voice pipeline layer by layer, shows where it hits the wall, and then moves the reasoning off the critical path entirely.

## Voice is not a chat with audio

Text is asynchronous: you can edit before sending, and the system answers request by request. Voice is synchronous. The user hears it once, timing carries meaning, and there is no undo. Pause too long and you sound confused; answer too fast and you cut someone off.

So the simple loop of listen, understand, reason, act and speak gets hard as soon as it must happen in real time.

## The cascade, and everything before the first token

The usual production stack is three models in a row: speech-to-text, an LLM, text-to-speech. It is modular and observable, and you can swap providers per language or pick an ElevenLabs voice. Each stage waits for the previous one, so in practice everything streams chunk by chunk. Speech-to-speech models like GPT Realtime or Gemini Live cut latency but cost you control and observability.

Before any model runs, there is plain real-time engineering: WebRTC, jitter, echo cancellation, packet loss, audio arriving in 20 ms frames. Bohdan's advice is to let platforms handle most of it.

Then comes turn-taking, which he treats as one of the hardest problems. Voice activity detection only answers whether someone is speaking right now (Silero is his balanced default). Endpointing and turn detection answer the more important question: has the user finished the thought? Get it wrong and the agent talks over people, or leaves them hanging.

Tool calls make the budget worse. A CRM lookup or calendar check can take 500 ms to five seconds. His rule: never let a tool call block the conversation. Cover it with filler speech, run it asynchronously, and inject the result when it is ready. That background-then-inject pattern is the seed of everything that follows.

## Separate the Thinker from the Speaker

Fast models keep the SLA but reason shallowly; reasoning models think well but blow the budget. Voice needs both. The LTS voice agent architecture splits them into two tracks.

The foreground Speaker streams the conversation and never blocks. In the background, a semantic trigger decides when the transcript holds enough meaning to be worth thinking about, so you don't pay for reasoning on every word. The Thinker, a stronger model, maintains a structured delta-state (new address, new time, the intent of the call) and injects it into the Speaker, which steers mid-conversation.

His example: a caller starts talking about cancelling. The trigger fires, the Thinker combines intent, sentiment, account data and company policy, and the Speaker gets a state update suggesting a 20% discount offer. If the user changes topic, the coordinator kills the Speaker and keeps the Thinker's state. The Speaker is disposable; the Thinker is durable. Barge-in handling is where Bohdan locates most of the difficulty in good voice agents.

## From one Thinker to a team of sidecars

The last step replaces the single Thinker with parallel sidecars: small, cheap models that each watch the live transcript for one thing (intent, complaint detection, retrieval, notes). An expensive reducer merges their outputs and produces one compact state object with a clear next action.

The catch is freshness. Background reasoning takes time, and guidance that lands after the conversation moved on is worse than none. He lists the controls: a TTL on state, turn identifiers so state matches the turn it was computed for, and never letting a stale snapshot replace a fresh one.

## Who should watch

Engineers building or evaluating voice agents who already know the STT, LLM, TTS diagram and want the next layer. The tool survey (LiveKit, Silero, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Retell, Vapi) is a handy map, and the Thinker and Speaker split applies to any latency-bound agent. Bohdan also spoke at Conf42 earlier, on [GepAI in development processes and dev tools](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Bohdan_Snisar_gepai_development_tools).

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Whispering into the Future: Reinventing Speech-to-Text Transcriptions with Go and Whisper](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2023_Pratim_Bhosale_speechtotext_transcriptions_whisper) by Pratim Bhosale, on the first box of the cascade.

Title: LLM-generated schema migrations, shipped with their own rollback
Description: Niraj Katkamwar (Intuit) at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on a prompt-driven pipeline that generates code, migrations and rollbacks together, gated by humans.
Body:
The scariest file in most repos is a hand-written down migration nobody has ever run. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Niraj Katkamwar, Software Engineer at Intuit, presented independent research on a prompt-driven framework where an LLM turns a plain-English requirement into service code, API contracts, schema migrations and tests in one go, and where every forward migration is generated alongside its inverse.

It's a short, architecture-level talk. There's no live demo and no benchmark, so treat it as a design to borrow from rather than a product to install.

## Schema drift is a coordination bug

Niraj frames the problem as four failures that feed each other: application and database changes drift out of sync and break contracts between services; engineers still handcraft migrations, API updates and rollback scripts; business intent gets lost between stakeholders, developers and data engineers; and unvalidated schema changes pushed into distributed systems end in outages, data loss or rollbacks that don't work.

His answer moves the engineer's job from writing boilerplate to reviewing and approving generated artifacts.

## Three layers, and the first one is allowed to stop

The framework runs in sequence. Layer one interprets the prompt: the LLM extracts entities, relationships, constraints and the change type (add, modify or delete). The interesting part is ambiguity detection. Underspecified or conflicting requirements are flagged and the pipeline pauses for a human instead of guessing. Consistency checks then compare the change against the existing schema registry and cross-service contracts.

Layer two uses coding agents to generate the API contracts with versioning, data access code, scaffolded service logic and integration tests for happy paths and edge cases.

Layer three is where he spends the most care: database-aware schema transformation. Generated migrations must keep existing API contracts and consumer expectations working across service versions. Destructive operations such as column drops and type changes are blocked unless a human explicitly approves them.

## The rollback is written before you need it

The idea worth stealing even if you never let an LLM near your DDL: atomic artifact pairs. Each forward migration is generated together with its inverse, version-pinned and stored next to it, so rollback is a planned and tested action. Niraj notes that coding agents are particularly good at writing these compensation scripts, which is the part humans most often skip.

Two more mechanisms complete the safety story. The expand/contract pattern is enforced, so additive changes ship first and destructive ones only after consumers have adopted the new schema. And failed health checks after a deploy trigger the pre-generated rollback automatically, without someone hunting for a script during the incident.

## One pipeline for code and schema

He calls running application code and schema changes through separate, uncoordinated pipelines the most dangerous pattern in database DevOps. In his flow, a prompt produces all artifacts atomically. They then pass a four-layer validation pyramid: syntax parsing and linting, semantic checks against the schema registry, a dry run of the migration against a shadow database clone, and auto-generated integration tests in CI. Any failure halts the pipeline and returns structured feedback to the engineer.

Integration is meant to be incremental: a CLI and REST API to drop into Jenkins, GitHub Actions or GitLab, and compatibility with schema registries such as Confluent Schema Registry and AWS Glue. Approval gates sit at every layer. In his words, LLMs accelerate generation, but engineers still own the decision to promote to production.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers wondering where LLM code generation can safely touch the database. If your team already runs expand/contract migrations with tested rollbacks, the architecture will feel familiar, and the value is in seeing where the human gates go. If your rollback strategy is "restore from backup", the atomic pair idea alone justifies the time.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Strategies for Reliable Database Schema Migrations](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Rotem_Tamir_database_schema_reliable_migrations) by Rotem Tamir, the non-LLM foundations of safe migrations.

Title: Your agent can reason fine. It just remembers the wrong things
Description: Anannya Roy Chowdhury (AWS) at Conf42 LLMs 2026: a Harry Potter game shows agent failures are memory failures, fixed with three memory layers.
Body:
Most agent failures are memory failures wearing a reasoning costume. That is the claim Anannya Roy Chowdhury, GenAI Developer Advocate at AWS, makes at Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, and she backs it with a game her own agent kept losing: eight times out of ten, before she changed how it remembered things.

The game is a Horcrux hunt. Harry gets 50 turns to find and destroy Horcruxes across 15 locations; Voldemort spends those turns relocating them and planting decoys. Same model, same tools, same retrieval. The fix in the talk never touches the model.

## The model knew how to think

Anannya started where everyone starts: she blamed the prompt, then the model, then the architecture. Reading the failures told a different story. Harry destroyed a location after the Horcrux had already moved (stale memory). He revisited a spot already confirmed empty, because the signal was buried under tokens (retrieval failure). And the most common problem was the agent remembering everything, so each turn got slower and more expensive.

Her framing for the last one is worth stealing. A context window is less a storage limit and more a compounding tax: replay the whole history on every one of 50 turns and you are rereading the book every time you turn a page. Add more agents and the bill multiplies.

## Memory is entropy management

The lens for the rest of the talk comes from information theory. At turn one Harry knows nothing, so every location is equally likely. Each observation should lower that uncertainty; each Voldemort move raises it. Every memory decision then answers one question: does this help reduce uncertainty or add to it?

From there she builds three layers, each with one job. Working memory is what the LLM sees right now: small, expensive, precious. Retrieval memory is what the agent can pull in when it needs it. Persistent memory records everything the agent has ever experienced. The trouble starts when the layers do each other's jobs.

## Let the maths remember the probabilities

The optimisations are refreshingly unglamorous. First, stop sending the transcript. The model needs state, so she sends a compact belief map, valid actions, remaining budget and cooldowns. That alone gave 97% token compression, and the agent got better, because it stopped being distracted.

Second, keep the probabilities outside the model. A belief map updates in code, and the LLM sees something like "Chamber of Secrets, 50%", which is eight to 15 tokens instead of 5,000. Her rule of thumb: whenever memory can be structured state, use structure, because language is expensive and maths is cheap.

Third, route by uncertainty. Low entropy gets a heuristic and no LLM call at all; medium gets compressed memory; high gets richer retrieval. When Harry finds a Horcrux, Voldemort's next move is obvious, so why pay a model to predict it?

Finally, persistence: store abundantly, retrieve selectively, present minimally. The architecture diagram she asks you to remember has the LLM as a small box. Belief management, constraint solving, entropy maths and compression all live outside it.

The results on the same game: 97% fewer tokens, 75% lower latency, more than 80% lower cost, and a win rate that doubled. In Anannya's words, the LLM is not the memory system; it consumes it.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose agent gets worse the longer a session runs, or whose token bill grows faster than its usefulness. The game setting keeps it light, but the five closing principles transfer straight to support bots, coding agents and multi-step workflows. If you want a framework or a vendor product, this is a design argument with numbers from one well-instrumented toy.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI Gardening for MLOps: Managing Context, Memory, and Entropy in Agentic Systems](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Ishan_Shah_gardening_context_memory) by Ishan Shah, which reaches for the same entropy vocabulary from the operations side.
- [Reduce AI Agents Costs and Mistakes with Semantic tool Selection](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost) by Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, the same "show the model less" idea applied to tools instead of memory.
- [Make your LLM app sane again: Forgetting incorrect data in real time](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Olivier_Ruas_llm_app_forgetting) by Olivier Ruas, on the stale-memory problem from the data side.
