Title: Catching churn hidden inside polite British emails with an LLM
Description: Anton Denisov (Dwelly) at Conf42 LLMs 2026 on an LLM pipeline that spots unhappy landlords in polite emails and calls before they leave.
Body:
"Whenever you get a chance to look in the boiler, that would be great. Thank you so much for all your help." Every off-the-shelf sentiment model scores that as a happy customer. At Conf42 Large Language Models (LLMs) 2026, Anton Denisov, who leads revenue at the UK property manager Dwelly, explains why that landlord moved to a competitor about two weeks later, and how his team built an LLM system that would have flagged it.

Dwelly manages rental properties end to end for thousands of landlords on its own software. The system in the talk runs in production, reading landlord emails and phone calls and flagging dissatisfaction early enough to act on it.

## Complaints arrive with the emotion removed

Classic sentiment tools assume that stronger words mean stronger feelings. British professional politeness inverts that. "A little disappointed" usually means quite a lot. "When you get a chance" often means overdue. A note that someone would have expected a callback by now is a complaint, minus the exclamation marks. Keyword models read all of these as neutral.

NPS doesn't save you either. The people most likely to quietly leave are the ones too polite to give a low score: they give you a seven and then don't renew.

The harder half is silence. A lot of dissatisfaction came from what Dwelly didn't do: the unanswered email, the voicemail nobody returned. The triggering event is an absence, and the only trace in the data is a follow-up that is slightly shorter and cooler than the last one.

Anton is also honest about the target. Part of churn is unpreventable (landlords sell, or move back in), so the real question was narrower: can you spot the preventable, service-driven kind early, inside tens of thousands of ordinary, polite interactions?

## Read first, prompt later

The dataset was around eleven thousand interactions from roughly two thousand landlords over about seven weeks, across four channels: CRM email, direct email, outbound calls and inbound calls. About eleven hundred calls were transcribed with Voximplant. Calls were the most candid and the messiest.

Before any prompting, the team hand-labelled around two hundred borderline negative cases and wrote the label definitions as mechanical rules. Severity had four levels: amber needed one explicit signal, orange two independent strong signals, red literal termination language. Topic and intent sat on separate axes. The same set served as the evaluation benchmark and as the source of few-shot examples.

## Two cheap questions beat one expensive one

The model was Claude Sonnet, in a two-step pipeline. Step one asks only whether a message is positive, neutral or negative. Step two runs on the six or seven percent that come back negative and extracts severity, topic, intent and routing. The whole pipeline came in around a third of a cent per message.

Cost was the minor benefit. Splitting the steps let the team tune the detector for recall and the classifier for precision separately; one prompt doing both did both worse.

Three prompt fixes did most of the work. Treat courtesy as wrapping and classify the substance, anchored with polite-but-negative examples (the single biggest improvement). Put the severity rules into the prompt verbatim, so orange stopped being the default. And add an "external issue" intent, because a landlord annoyed about a contractor who says it's not your fault needs a different response from one blaming you.

## What the data said

Calls ran around 50% more negative than email. A landlord who switches from email to phone is a leading indicator of escalation. Communication failure was the largest category, about 36% of negative interactions. And one agency that looked like the top performer turned out to have most of its calls missing from the feed: coverage bounds quality.

Each intent maps to an owner and a response time, so the output is a to-do list rather than a dashboard. The communication-failure number also justified the next build: an agentic voice assistant for inbound landlord calls.

## Who should watch

Anyone classifying messy human text with an LLM, sentiment or otherwise. The British sarcasm hook is fun, but the lessons are about labelling, splitting the problem and closing the loop with action.

Title: A digital PMO makes Jira the record and Confluence the memory
Description: George Job of Walmart at Conf42 Golang 2026 on a Jira and Confluence PMO framework that replaced spreadsheet status reporting with live governance.
Body:
Status spreadsheets are where portfolio truth goes to get stale. At Conf42 Golang 2026, George Job, Principal Technical Program Manager at Walmart, presented a digital PMO framework that turns Jira and Confluence into one system of record from strategy to delivery, and reported what happened when an Automotive Care Center portfolio adopted it.

A scope note before you press play: this is a program management talk with no Go in it. It fits the conference as a governance story for engineering organisations, and it is most useful to the TPMs and engineering managers who live in those tools.

## What the traditional PMO costs

George's list of problems will be familiar to anyone who has assembled a Monday status deck. Status is tracked in spreadsheets and disconnected tools, so there is no single source of truth. Cross-team dependencies are discovered late, when mitigating them hits the timeline or the budget. Governance varies team by team.

The cost shows up in three places. Leadership makes reactive decisions because it lacks real-time data. Stakeholders work from stale reports, which erodes trust in program management. And TPMs spend their time assembling status by hand instead of managing risk and driving outcomes.

## Three layers in one system

The framework stacks a strategic layer (themes, initiatives and OKRs anchored to business outcomes), a delivery layer (epics plus delivery telemetry giving live progress and health signals), and a governance layer (risk signals and executive reporting that surface issues to leadership in time).

The division of labour between the two Atlassian tools is the practical core. Jira is execution intelligence: structured workflows, standardised custom fields so teams mean the same thing, and dashboards that update without anyone stitching data together. Confluence is living documentation fed by those Jira updates: program charter templates with owners, OKR alignment and RACI, risk and decision logs that form an auditable trail, and executive status pages built from live Jira data. The space hierarchy mirrors the portfolio structure so people can actually find things.

## Gates, conventions and a definition of done

George's workflow advice is about discipline at the edges. Gate intake so every requirement enters through one door, which stops scope creep before it reaches the portfolio. Agree on status conventions across teams so the model scales to the whole organisation. Define exit criteria and a definition of done, so finished means the same thing everywhere.

With one real-time record in place, automation follows: thresholds that raise risk signals when projects are at risk, blocked or stuck in discovery too long, dependency heat maps built from Jira components, and JQL queries embedded in Confluence so reports refresh themselves. It is the rare governance story where the paperwork writes itself, because the paperwork is a query.

## The results, and how he frames them

The abstract describes a portfolio of more than 20 cross-functional teams and around 50 initiatives per quarter, with a 30 percent reduction in PMO operational effort within six months and another 30 percent by twelve months. In the talk, George adds that the portfolio began with eight TPMs and finished the year with three, while keeping the same delivery velocity and quality. He is explicit that the point was not headcount: the effort moved from manual, ad hoc status work to strategic and tactical work.

His summary fits on a sticky note: unify your tooling, standardise before you scale, and make governance continuous.

## Who should watch

TPMs, PMO leads and engineering managers running multi-team portfolios on Jira and Confluence. Engineers looking for Go content can skip it, though anyone who has been asked to fill in a status spreadsheet might enjoy seeing it retired.

Title: CloudNativePG fails over in 11 seconds, but misses replication lag
Description: Amarachi Iheanacho of Sidero Labs at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 broke a CloudNativePG Postgres cluster six ways to test whether an operator can replace a DBA.
Body:
Kill the primary Postgres pod and CloudNativePG promotes a replica and rebuilds the cluster in about eleven seconds. Pause replication on a replica and it reports the cluster healthy while the replica falls more than 100 MB behind. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Amarachi Iheanacho, technical writer and developer advocate at Sidero Labs, ran six failure scenarios against an operator-managed Postgres cluster to answer one question: can a Kubernetes operator replace a DBA?

Her answer is the useful kind of nuanced: it replaces the routine execution, not the judgement. And because every scenario is shown with real `kubectl` output, you can see exactly where the line falls.

## No SSH allowed

The setup makes the test honest. Four nodes on AWS (one control plane, three workers) running Talos Linux, an immutable OS managed by Omni, so there is no SSH into nodes and no sneaky human fix. Kubernetes 1.35, CloudNativePG, Postgres 16 with three instances. The plan was 30 days; AWS bills shortened it to roughly 16 to 20, a constraint every homelab reader will sympathize with.

## What the operator did well

**Primary pod deleted.** CloudNativePG detected it almost immediately, promoted the most up-to-date replica, repointed the service so writes went to the new primary, and created a fresh pod. Eleven seconds, back to three of three healthy, no human. That is exactly what a DBA would do by hand (check WAL replay positions, promote, fix routing, provision a standby), only faster.

**Major version upgrade.** Patching the image from Postgres 16.13 to 17.6 triggered a coordinated shutdown, an upgrade job, the primary back on 17 in about 47 seconds, and two fresh replicas cloned from it. Amarachi notes a DBA would still plan a window, rehearse on staging and take a full backup first.

## Where it needed a human

**Node drain.** Failover worked, but the evicted replica sat in Pending for about 26 minutes. Its PersistentVolumeClaim was bound to local storage on the cordoned node, so no other node could take it. Uncordoning brought it back within the minute. A DBA would have checked storage topology and switched over deliberately before draining. Verdict: partial.

**Disk filling up.** She wrote 8.4 GB of junk to the primary (64% utilization), then about 4 GB more toward 90%. Between those points the operator said nothing. At 90% the primary crashed, failover kicked in, Kubernetes tainted the node with DiskPressure, and the replacement pod stayed Pending, with no SSH to clean up. A DBA would have had alerts at 70, 80 and 90% and a runbook. Point to the human.

**Replication lag.** With WAL replay paused on one replica and a million rows written to the primary, the replica fell about 102 MB behind while the cluster status stayed healthy, with no event or alert. Resuming replay caught it up immediately. The lesson is the clearest in the talk: the operator sees pod health, not Postgres-level replication state.

**Backup and point-in-time recovery.** A base backup to S3 via Barman finished in eight seconds. Recovery failed: WAL archiving had not been configured at cluster creation, nothing enforced it, and the recovery pod restart-looped for about an hour looking for WAL segments that were never archived. A DBA configures WAL archiving on day one and tests recovery before trusting it.

## The DBA's job moves, it doesn't vanish

The scorecard is honest: pod failover, upgrades, replica cloning and self-healing after pod failures are automated well. Storage topology, replication lag monitoring, disk-full recovery on an immutable OS, and backup architecture still need a person, or at least monitoring that a person configured. Amarachi calls it the beta of the experiment, with more to come.

## Who should watch

Platform teams deciding whether to run Postgres on Kubernetes with an operator, and DBAs asked to hand theirs over. Even if you have run CloudNativePG for years, the drain and PITR scenarios are a good checklist for your own setup. Bring your own Prometheus alerts for lag and disk.

Title: An AI security gate in CI is only as good as the policy you give it
Description: Emmanuela Opurum of SoftNet Technologies at Conf42 Golang 2026 demos a CI/CD guardrail where an LLM agent checks code against a written policy and fails the build.
Body:
Static scanners look for a fixed list of problems, and a general-purpose AI model has no idea what your organisation considers a problem. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Emmanuela Opurum, Solutions/System Architect at SoftNet Technologies, showed a pipeline guardrail that sits between those two failures: an AI agent wired into the CI workflow, told exactly what to look for by a written policy, and allowed to stop the build.

It is a short, demo-led talk aimed at teams that want a working starting point rather than a framework, and she published the whole thing as a repository so viewers can reuse it.

## Fast pipelines ship vulnerabilities fast too

Emmanuela starts from the obvious tension. CI/CD exists to get code to production quickly, and without security checks it gets vulnerabilities to production just as quickly. Her critique of the usual fixes is that static analysis tools catch particular vulnerability classes without reflecting an organisation's own rules, while a standalone AI tool fails because it does not know your policy. Neither, on its own, knows what you care about.

## The flow: push, scan against policy, ship or stop

The architecture is deliberately simple, and she notes it carries over to whatever code platform you use:

1. A developer pushes to the GitHub repo, which triggers the workflow.
2. The workflow calls an agent (she used OpenAI's GPT-4o) loaded with a policy covering security detection, pattern scanning and policy validation.
3. If the agent finds nothing that violates the policy, the code proceeds to deployment.
4. If it does, the pipeline fails and a Slack message goes to the team with what failed, on which line, why, and a suggested fix.

The demo shows two runs. The first passes. The second fails because someone left an API key in a file, and the Slack alert names the problem and recommends removing hard-coded secrets in favour of environment variables. The leaked-key example is the oldest one in the book, which is exactly why it is still worth a gate.

## Humans stay in the loop at both ends

Her main lesson is about where people fit. An AI agent cannot decide what your organisation's security rules are; a human has to write the policy into the pipeline. And when the gate trips, a human still has to respond. What the agent changes is the speed of that response: instead of digging through logs to find why a build failed, the engineer gets the reason and a starting fix in the channel they already watch.

For next steps she suggests extending the policies to cover more languages and integrating the same gate into cloud deployment flows.

## How much Go?

Honest scope: the abstract frames this as Go-based automation for CI/CD across AWS, Azure and GCP, but the recorded talk spends its time on the workflow design, the agent policy and the Slack loop rather than on Go code. The repository, which she names on screen as GoCICD Security Guardrail under her cloud-architect-emma GitHub handle, is where the implementation lives.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers who want a quick pattern for adding a policy-driven AI check to an existing pipeline, and teams starting out with DevSecOps who need a concrete first gate. If you already run secret scanning, SAST and policy-as-code in CI, this is a lightweight variation rather than a new technique, but the point about writing the policy down holds either way.

Title: Let AI review your schema migration, never approve it
Description: Ahmed Tariq at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on safe schema migrations in CI/CD, expand-migrate-contract, and a framework for where AI belongs.
Body:
The pipeline was green, the health checks passed, and production fell over anyway, because the migration behind the release locked a hot table. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Ahmed Tariq, Cloud DevOps Engineer, gave a field guide to shipping schema changes safely through CI/CD and a simple rule for AI in that pipeline: it advises, a named engineer decides.

The talk is practical rather than flashy, and Ahmed says as much: the boring part is what you want for a production database. It also includes a worked example and a two-axis matrix you can take to your next architecture review.

## Code rolls back, data doesn't

Stateless deploys are built around reversibility: immutable artifacts, blue-green, canaries, feature flags. Migrations break that, because they mutate shared persistent state. Ahmed's one line to remember: "You can roll back the code, you cannot always roll back the customer data being wrong". Point-in-time recovery and spare replicas help, but cost money and can still miss things.

His failure modes will look familiar to anyone who has been paged for one: locking DDL on a hot table that fills the connection pool, rollbacks that cannot restore a dropped column or undo a destructive backfill, environment drift (ten thousand rows in staging, four hundred million in production), big-bang changes that couple new code to the new schema, and the worst one, silent data loss from a type conversion that truncates values while the migration reports success.

## Six stages, and only one of them is a human

A good migration pipeline in Ahmed's version: lint the SQL for unsafe type changes, missing indexes and destructive operations; dry run against a production-sized clone to measure duration and locking; test the application against the new schema with both old and new code paths; approval gate with a human reviewer; deploy in a controlled way, not a manual command from someone's terminal at 11pm; then post-deploy checks of data and flows. Flyway, Liquibase or GitHub Actions all work, because the operating model matters more than the tool. Automate the mechanical checks; save the human for judgement.

## Expand, migrate, contract, in that order

The worked example adds a `customer_status` column to a table with hundreds of millions of rows and several dependent services. The unsafe version adds the column, backfills everything at once, ships dependent code and drops the old field quickly to look tidy. The safe version: add a nullable column with no default and check lock behaviour for your engine (Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server differ); dual-write old and new fields; backfill in rate-limited batches while watching replication lag; switch reads behind a feature flag, so rollback is a flag flip rather than a data revert; verify with observability; and only then drop the old field. A safe migration is a safe sequence, not a safe statement.

Observability is part of the release plan: baseline latency, replication lag, error rate, CPU and connections before, watch lock waits and p95 and p99 latency during (averages hide the pain), and let it cool down before declaring victory.

## Where AI helps and where it hurts

AI earns its keep on review prep: flagging risky type changes, likely locks and unclear rollbacks, summarizing a dense pull request into a plain risk brief, generating edge-case tests for nulls and historical rows, drafting runbooks, and summarizing timelines after an incident. The abstract's example of the failure side is a good one: hallucinated syntax such as "Postgres flags that are actually MySQL flags". The model also cannot see your traffic, data volume or which table is billing, and it can confidently suggest a rollback that makes things worse. Confident but wrong, Ahmed says, is worse than silence. The hard line: no auto-approve or auto-apply in production, because accountability cannot be delegated to a tool.

## Score every migration on two axes

The decision framework asks about blast radius, reversibility and whether business context is needed. Low risk and easy to reverse: automation with AI assistance is fine. High risk but reversible: staged rollout plus human approval. Low risk but hard to reverse: AI drafts or reviews, an engineer owns it. High risk and hard to reverse: human-led, rehearsed, explicitly approved, heavily observed. His first step for teams starting out: add a migration linter and dry-run risky migrations on production-like data.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers who ship migrations through CI/CD and are being handed AI review tools. It is a good primer for less experienced engineers, and a useful checklist for the senior ones writing the team's migration policy.

Title: Insurance cores have to survive the claims spike after a hurricane
Description: Sulabh Jain at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on decoupling insurance core systems with per-domain data, Kubernetes, IaC, events and a four-phase roadmap.
Body:
A hurricane or wildfire turns a quiet claims system into a queue overnight, and a monolith on bigger servers cannot stretch to meet it. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Sulabh Jain, a Business Applications Supervisor working on insurance platforms, laid out how to move insurance core systems to cloud-native architecture, with the database decisions front and centre.

It is a broad, well-structured modernization talk: domain decomposition, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, CI/CD, events, APIs, observability and data consistency, finished with a phased roadmap. None of the patterns are new, but seeing them mapped onto policy, claims and billing makes the case unusually concrete.

## Three pressures at once

Sulabh frames the urgency as compounding forces. Regulation: audit trails must be precise and available on demand, and change windows are shrinking, so a platform that is slow to change becomes a legal liability as well as a technical one. Competition: insurtechs built cloud-native from day one ship in days, not quarters. And catastrophe scale: a claims spike that the monolith cannot absorb becomes a backlog at the worst possible moment for customers.

All three trace back to tight coupling. A small fix to claims adjudication triggers a full regression cycle; a new underwriting rule needs a coordinated release across application, database and integration layers.

## Each service owns its data, or none of this works

The core move is data ownership. A policy service owns the policy lifecycle; a claims service owns everything from first notice of loss to settlement and scales out during a catastrophe without touching billing or underwriting; a billing service handles premiums and reconciliation, so a billing outage blocks neither policies nor claims. Share a database instead and one slow query degrades everything, one schema change breaks someone else. His warning lands well: a shared database is how a microservice migration quietly becomes a distributed monolith.

On Kubernetes he picks the capabilities that matter for insurance: horizontal pod autoscaling for claims spikes, pod disruption budgets for zero-downtime maintenance, namespaces as hard boundaries between regulated and non-regulated workloads, rolling deploys with automatic rollback, plus multi-zone clusters and StatefulSets with persistent volume claims for database pods.

## Make the audit trail a side effect

Infrastructure as code gets four stages: define networks, clusters, databases and IAM in Terraform, Pulumi or CloudFormation next to the app; review through pull requests with policy-as-code checks from OPA or Checkov; apply through CI/CD with drift tracking and rollback as a code revert; audit through Git history, so a regulator's request for the full change history is already answered. Disaster recovery becomes a drill, not a crisis.

The CI/CD pipeline adds functional tests of underwriting rules and premium calculations on every commit, synthetic load tests that simulate catastrophe-level claims volume, SAST, DAST and image scanning, and progressive delivery with automatic rollback.

## Synchronous fraud checks are the outage waiting to happen

The best example in the talk: claims intake calls fraud detection synchronously, fraud detection slows under catastrophe load, every claim waits, mobile apps time out, and one slow service takes the platform down. With events, intake publishes "claim received" and fraud scoring, adjuster assignment and notifications consume it at their own pace. Kafka suits ordered, durable claims event sourcing; EventBridge fits serverless partner routing. Event sourcing, CQRS, dead letter queues, sagas and circuit breakers round out the toolkit, with the outbox pattern bridging database writes and the event stream.

Schema changes follow expand and contract, consumer-driven contract tests, blue-green migrations for large tables, and a schema registry on Kafka topics. Partner APIs are designed spec-first in OpenAPI with versioning and deprecation timelines, secured at a gateway with OAuth 2.0 or mutual TLS.

## Foundation before decomposition

The roadmap is a strangler fig in four phases: containerize, build CI/CD, IaC and observability with no refactoring; extract high-pain domains such as claims and billing and introduce event streaming; add a service mesh, GitOps and API contracts; then tune autoscaling for catastrophes and implement SLOs. Each phase ships working software, and the whole thing is a multi-year program. His closing point is that upskilling and team ownership are prerequisites, not soft extras.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leads planning an insurance (or any regulated, spiky-load) core modernization who need a sequence they can defend to the business. Engineers already running event-sourced microservices will mostly find confirmation.

Title: Fraud detection and personalization can share one Go pipeline
Description: Sridhar Muthineni of Capgemini at Conf42 Golang 2026 on one detect, personalize and govern framework for fintech apps, with Go running real-time inference.
Body:
Banks usually split fraud prevention and personalization between different teams with different tools. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Sridhar Muthineni, Product Tech Lead at Capgemini, argued they belong in one framework (detect, personalize, govern) because they run on the same data, the same plumbing and often the same models, with Go handling the real-time path.

It is an accessible overview, pitched so that a product manager can follow it, and it covers a lot of ground quickly: model families, a streaming inference pipeline, personalization techniques, and the regulation that shapes all of it.

## Four threats, one impatient customer

Sridhar opens with the threats: account takeovers, synthetic identities built from a real Social Security number plus invented details, and money laundering through many small transactions. The fourth pressure is the customer, who wants a banking app that is both safe and as personal as the streaming service they use every evening. The talk is an attempt to do both at once.

## Pick the model for the trade-off, not the hype

There is no single best fraud model, he says; the choice depends on accuracy, response time, explainability and cost. He walks through four families:

- **Gradient-boosted decision trees** as fast pattern matchers on structured, tabular data, good for quick yes-or-no calls.
- **RNNs** for sequences, such as a spending pattern over the last ten transactions that looks off.
- **Graph neural networks** for relationships, such as several unrelated accounts all funnelling money into one hidden account.
- **Transformers** for long-range behaviour across months.

## Why Go sits in the hot path

The Go argument is about the milliseconds a bank has when you tap a card: compiled speed, goroutines handling thousands of concurrent transactions, and short, predictable garbage collection pauses. The pipeline is three steps: ingest through Kafka, pre-process (clean, format, add context such as location and how many transactions the user has made that day), then infer a fraud score. He judges the model on three metrics together: detection accuracy, false-positive rate (the card declined at the checkout for no reason) and latency, since a slow decision means a timed-out payment.

## Personal without being creepy

On the personalization side, recommendation systems suggest financial actions instead of films, such as a high-yield savings product for a consistent saver. Reinforcement learning adapts, for example by dropping alert types a user always ignores, or tuning the timing and size of credit offers. LLM agents answer questions like whether you can afford a holiday, or explain in plain English why a transaction was flagged. Adaptive credit scoring rounds it out by tracking behaviour over time instead of a dated snapshot, so the app can warn before overspending rather than punish after.

## Governance is an architecture choice

The governance pillar is the part Sridhar calls most important. Explainability, fairness and privacy are requirements: GDPR Article 22 gives people a right to an explanation of automated decisions, so he points to SHAP and LIME for human-readable reasons, and lending models get bias tests across demographic groups before deployment. Privacy techniques include federated learning, differential privacy and small models compiled with Go running on-device so transaction details need not leave the phone.

The frontier problems he lists are honest: fraudsters use AI too, real-time graph analytics on live fraud rings is computationally huge and the Go tooling is still young, and responsible AI at scale needs stronger governance. His last takeaway is the one to pin on the wall: "once AI is live, watch it like a hawk," because models quietly degrade as the world changes.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product leads new to ML in payments who want the map before the details. Experienced fraud teams will find it introductory; there are no benchmark numbers or code, and the Go material is about why rather than how.

Title: Asking Azure why it returns 503s, in plain English
Description: Sampath Rao Madarapu of Microsoft at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on Copilot in Azure for diagnostics, governance and database operations, with humans in the loop.
Body:
Diagnosing an Azure incident usually means five portal blades, a Log Analytics query and some manual timestamp matching. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Sampath Rao Madarapu, Senior Technical Advisor in Azure infrastructure support at Microsoft, presented Copilot in Azure, the AI assistant built into the Azure management experience, and focused on what it does for database and DevOps teams.

This is a Microsoft product talk from someone on the support front line, so it is an overview of capabilities rather than a hands-on demo. The most interesting part is how the human side of the system works.

## The problem is context switching

Azure has hundreds of services and thousands of resource types. A team running Azure SQL, Cosmos DB or PostgreSQL deals with interconnected configurations where a small change can cascade, and under incident pressure it bounces between portal, CLI, dashboards and docs. Sampath's sharpest point is about knowledge: the know-how that says "this error pattern means check the connection pool" lives in a few heads and does not scale across teams and regions.

## Three layers behind the chat box

Copilot combines large language models that interpret the question, Azure control plane data (live resource metadata, ARM configurations, subscription topology), and real-time telemetry such as metrics, diagnostic logs and health signals. The point of the last two is grounding: answers about your resources in their current state, not generic documentation.

The examples he gives are the kind of thing you would actually type: which VMs in a subscription are not patched, which SQL databases are above 80% DTU utilization, or why an App Service is returning 503 errors. For the last one Copilot correlates Azure Monitor, Application Insights and resource diagnostics into one summary with a root cause hypothesis and suggested next steps such as scaling or configuration changes. Sampath's claim is that what used to take an hour of investigation can now take minutes.

## Database teams get the most specific help

For data platforms the integration covers Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Synapse Analytics, PostgreSQL and MySQL. He lists four uses: query performance analysis (slow queries, missing indexes, DTU versus vCore utilization without parsing Query Store or DMV output by hand), security posture review of firewall rules, encryption and audit settings, capacity guidance for tiers, elastic pools and read replicas based on actual telemetry, and validation of backup policies, retention windows and geo-redundancy across all databases at once.

On the governance side, the same interface summarizes resources for incident triage or onboarding, finds untagged or misconfigured resources, checks RBAC role assignments at scale, and flags violations against Azure Policy and Defender for Cloud baselines.

## The AI is trained by support engineers

The section worth the watch is how Copilot's diagnostic intelligence is kept honest. Sampath describes four human stages: engineers validate that metrics map to the right diagnostic scenarios; technical advisors like him review outputs for accuracy and find edge cases; trusted troubleshooting runbooks are written into the knowledge base; and feedback from real use flows back into grounding and prompt tuning as services change.

The trust rules follow from that. Responses cite the telemetry and configuration behind them, the reasoning is shown so you can check it, and Copilot does not autonomously execute destructive or irreversible actions. The engineer stays the decision-maker, which is the right default for anything that can resize a production database.

## Who should watch

Azure database and DevOps teams evaluating Copilot in Azure, and anyone designing an internal ops assistant who wants a template for grounding and human review. If you are not on Azure, the four-stage human-in-the-loop model is the transferable part.

Title: In regulated platforms, consent is a system event, not a checkbox
Description: Manasa Uppula at Conf42 Golang 2026 on evidence-centric compliance for financial onboarding, with versioned consent, assurance levels and sagas.
Body:
When a regulator asks what a customer agreed to three years ago, the answer should be a query, not a three-week dig through logs and old Confluence pages. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Manasa Uppula, an enterprise web architect listed with Virtusa, laid out an evidence-centric compliance architecture for customer-facing financial platforms, where the system produces its own proof as a normal output.

Manasa draws on nearly fourteen years building customer-facing platforms at US financial institutions, including Bank of America, Citigroup, Fidelity and BNY Mellon, and the talk has the specificity of someone who has sat in the audit room.

## Compliance is continuous, so evidence has to be too

Her opening point: oversight is not an annual checklist. A regulator, a customer dispute or an investigation can start any day, and the expectation is an immediate, complete answer. Digital onboarding is where it matters most, because that is where the legal relationship, consent boundaries and access to regulated services are created. In her framing, a misdisclosure is not a bug; it is a compliance event.

The anti-pattern she names is compliance as an afterthought, or as a surface layer of UI checkboxes and modals. A checkbox can be skipped, broken or shipped in a version that records nothing. She has seen exactly that: the UI looked right, and when the audit question came there was no reliable record of what the customer had agreed to.

## Every obligation gets an architectural counterpart

The core of the talk is a mapping exercise. Informed consent becomes a consent step embedded in the flow, which the system cannot proceed past without. Disclosure at the point of decision becomes an API that enforces the disclosure before the action can run, not merely before it should. Explanation becomes a decision trail generated at runtime. Record retention becomes an immutable, append-only event store per interaction.

She ties this together as interaction integrity, built on three pillars.

**Consent and disclosure as artifacts.** Each consent record carries the exact disclosure version shown, when it was presented, the user's explicit response, and the system state at that moment. Disclosures are versioned and addressable, never overwritten. The sequence is strict: disclose, acknowledge, act, never in parallel. Or, in her words, "Consent is not a checkbox. It is a system event." This is the difference she draws between a log, which records what happened, and evidence, which can prove it under scrutiny.

**Progressive identity assurance.** Identity is a risk level that builds up, not a pass-fail gate. The assurance level travels explicitly in the auth context on every service call, and verification events (an ID upload, say) update what downstream services allow. For Go developers she makes it concrete: pass it as a typed value in your context, validate it at each boundary, and never assume someone upstream checked it.

**Exception handling and continuity.** Networks drop and KYC providers time out. When services disagree about where a customer is in onboarding, you get a legally ambiguous state. Her fix is saga orchestration with compensating transactions: pause the session, preserve progress, notify the customer, and log the failure, the compensation and the resolution with the same rigour as the happy path.

## Auditability and traceability are different tests

Auditability means reconstructing key events on demand from structured, immutable, complete records that auditors can retrieve themselves. Her practical test: if your auditors need an engineer to extract the evidence, you have logs, not auditability. Traceability is the link from regulation to design control to observed behaviour, so you know which controls apply when you launch a product or region.

The reference stack is named per property: Kafka and S3 Object Lock for immutable consent records, OAuth, JWT claims and SPIFFE/SPIRE for identity, AWS Step Functions, Conductor or Temporal (which she notes has excellent Go support) for sagas, and OpenTelemetry, Elasticsearch and CloudTrail for audit logs. A savings-account walkthrough runs all three pillars end to end.

## Who should watch

Architects and backend engineers in fintech, insurance or any regulated onboarding flow. Her rollout advice is sensibly small: map obligations to interactions, translate them into constraints, instrument evidence, test auditability in CI like any feature, govern changes, and start with the single flow that would worry you most if a regulator asked about it tomorrow.

Title: Treat chipset vendors as an implementation detail, in Go
Description: Harsha Vardhani Talluri at Conf42 Golang 2026 on a Go platform that hides multi-vendor DOCSIS chipset quirks behind adapters and one telemetry model.
Body:
Every cable operator runs more than one chipset vendor, and every vendor bonds channels, handles modulation and reports telemetry a little differently. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Harsha Vardhani Talluri, who introduced themself in the talk as a senior network engineer at Charter Communications, showed how a Go platform pushes those differences down into small adapters so operations can work against one model of the network.

The opener will be familiar to anyone in broadband ops: a minor firmware rollout or a local telemetry glitch turns into days of engineers debugging vendor-specific exceptions instead of building platform capabilities.

## The multi-vendor tax

Harsha splits the problem into four areas. Channel bonding groups upstream and downstream channels differently by vendor. Modulation handling diverges, because chipsets react differently to the same SNR and MER thresholds. Forward error correction varies, sometimes masking real signal degradation. And telemetry is fragmented across schemas, names and units.

The cost compounds daily: every unnormalised quirk is one more thing to remember and document, triage slows as engineers switch between vendor tools and log formats, performance under load becomes unpredictable, and firmware validation and provisioning tests get repeated per vendor.

## Contain the weirdness in adapters

The answer is a unified chipset strategy in which vendor diversity is an implementation detail. A common abstraction layer translates each chipset API into one vendor-agnostic interface, telemetry and diagnostics share a single schema, and provisioning, firmware management and rollouts run from one control plane. Onboarding a new vendor later means writing a new adapter, not rewriting the platform. Software folks will recognise ports and adapters wearing a coax jacket.

Go earned the job for the usual infrastructure reasons, which Harsha lists plainly: low latency and small memory footprint for high-volume pipelines, goroutines and channels for polling huge device populations concurrently, static binaries that behave the same in lab, trial and production, and a standard library with solid HTTP, gRPC and structured logging.

## Three layers you can adopt one at a time

The platform has three independently deployable layers. Abstraction services at the bottom hold normalisation logic and vendor adapters. Orchestration and automation in the middle handles provisioning, firmware rollouts, workflow sequencing and rollback guardrails. The observability plane on top runs unified telemetry, dashboards, alerting and fleet health. Because they are decoupled, an operator can adopt them step by step without a risky day-one overhaul.

The examples get specific. Adapters standardise channel power, timing offset and MER reporting, and the platform normalises OFDM and SC-QAM profile states, RX MER per subcarrier and bonding group membership. With that in place, a closed loop collects per-subcarrier MER, assigns OFDM profiles automatically, and the abstraction layer turns each uniform decision back into the right vendor command.

## Provisioning and firmware with guardrails

Provisioning becomes four steps: discovery over SNMP or RESTCONF at registration, config rendering from a single canonical template store, a push with retry and rollback, and an audit that the device reached its target state. Firmware gets an automated lab gate: provision test devices from a known-good baseline, run functional suites (state transitions, registration, throughput), and compare new telemetry against historical baselines with pass or fail reports wired into release workflows.

Harsha closes by looking ahead to high split upgrades and DOCSIS 4.0, arguing that the same profile management and telemetry tooling carries forward.

## Who should watch

Network and platform engineers at cable and broadband operators, and anyone building Go tooling over heterogeneous hardware fleets. There is no code on screen; the value is in the layering and the provisioning and firmware workflows.

Title: The abandoned cart won't wait for your overnight batch job
Description: Kamini Murugaboopathy of Wonderbow Analytics at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on Kafka, lakehouses, bitmap indexes and DataOps for real-time marketing analytics.
Body:
A customer adds shoes to a cart and leaves; a batch pipeline finds out tomorrow morning, after they have bought the shoes elsewhere. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Kamini Murugaboopathy, Director at Wonderbow Analytics, walked through the architecture that lets marketing act on that event within seconds, and argued that it is as much a database and DataOps problem as a data engineering one.

The talk is a well-paced architecture tour aimed at engineers who know batch ETL and want the map of what changes when everything streams. Expect clear explanations of the building blocks rather than a single system's war story.

## Freshness, not volume, is the advantage

Kamini's starting point: almost every company collects website visits, app activity, email clicks, ad impressions, CRM and purchase data. The edge goes to the one that can use it while it is fresh. Batch systems fail on three counts: latency (a 10am cart abandonment seen the next day is a lost sale), fragmentation (web, apps, Google Ads, Meta Ads, CRM, email and support tools each with their own formats and timing), and scalability (a flash sale or influencer post turns normal traffic into thousands of simultaneous shoppers).

The answer is event-driven: every page view, click, add-to-cart and purchase is an event that can update a dashboard, a profile, a recommendation model or trigger a recovery email.

## Warehouse to report, lake to store, lakehouse to do both

Her storage explanation is a clean one to borrow. A warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery or Redshift is the tidy filing cabinet for structured questions like yesterday's revenue by campaign. A data lake holds the messy, semi-structured clickstream logs, raw app events and creative assets. A lakehouse combines both, so raw events stay around for machine learning while clean campaign data answers dashboards quickly.

Apache Kafka is the "live message highway" in the middle, letting segmentation, recommendations and campaign triggers consume the same events independently, with Apache Flink, Spark Streaming or AWS Kinesis processing them in flight.

## Segmentation needs the right index

The most database-flavoured part of the talk covers real-time audience segmentation. With profile updates arriving by the thousand every second, you cannot scan every customer for everyone who viewed shoes but did not buy. Kamini covers three tools: inverted indexes that keep ready-made lists (everyone interested in shoes, everyone who clicked the discount ad) and intersect them; bitmap indexes that store yes-or-no flags like clicked, added to cart, purchased, which CPUs compare extremely fast; and materialized views that precompute the questions marketing asks every hour, such as cart abandonments today.

## No maintenance window, so ship changes like code

Streaming systems never stop for a midnight change, so DataOps applies DevOps habits to data: version control for schemas and pipeline definitions, automated data quality and regression tests, CI/CD for database migrations, and monitoring of freshness, schema failures and consumer lag. Schema changes follow expand, migrate, contract, with a schema registry stopping one team from publishing a format that breaks another's pipeline. Models get the same treatment: retrained in parallel, then shifted over with blue-green or canary traffic while performance is watched.

Scaling should be proactive: a surge in event ingestion is a leading indicator of the query load about to hit the warehouse, so scale that layer first. Observability should watch the leading signals too: consumer lag, schema failure rates, p99 dashboard latency, model drift. Consistency should be selective: strong for purchases, attribution and deduplication; eventual for click tracking and audience scores; causal where order matters, such as session stitching.

Her production lessons close it out: infrastructure as code from day one, data quality before models (bad data propagates instantly), schema registries with compatibility checks, and stress tests well beyond expected peak, because many streaming failure modes only show up under pressure.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects moving marketing or product analytics from nightly batch to streaming, and DBAs who want to know why the analytics team keeps asking about bitmap indexes. If you already run Kafka with a schema registry in production, the value is in the consistency and scaling sections.

Title: Put your cloud's API output in a database and ask it questions
Description: Jason Lester of Capgemini at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on loading cloud CLI and API output into tables for permission audits, history and start-stop tooling.
Body:
Your cloud console can tell you which groups a user belongs to; it usually can't tell you what that user could do last month. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Jason Lester, Managing Architect at Capgemini UK, showed the low-tech fix: pull the metadata out through the provider's CLI or API, load it into database tables, and let SQL answer the questions the console was never built for.

It is a short, practical talk with examples from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, which is what Jason works with, though he is clear that the idea carries over to AWS, Azure and GCP. A good one for anyone who has clicked through forty console pages to build an inventory spreadsheet.

## The console is a friendly layer over a bigger API

Hyperscaler consoles are designed for getting started fast: drop-downs, calendars, sensible defaults. Underneath, APIs do the actual work, and not every API feature makes it into the console. The upside of the API is composition: Jason compares it to Lego, chaining one call that reads a database's details into another that builds a new one.

The downside gets equal billing. Without the visual feedback of the console, it is easy to get lost in the data and break something, so he recommends experimenting in an environment where you cannot delete production.

REST APIs are the common form, callable from tools like Postman, and authentication is the usual pain: on Oracle Cloud you call an authentication API for a token before every other call. The vendors' CLIs wrap that up. Run `oci compute instance list` with a compartment and you get every instance back as JSON, with far more metadata than the console shows, using a config you generated once.

## Once it's in tables, joins do the auditing

Jason's team created an `OCI instances` table and loaded the tenancy's instance metadata into it: inventory, build dates, status, CPU and memory, plus performance and cost statistics that are hard to find in the console. With the data in a database you can point other tools, AI included, at it to look for trends and changes.

The permissions example is the strongest. In Oracle Cloud, access comes from policy statements granted to groups, and users join groups. The console shows a user's groups but not the privileges those groups inherit without reading every policy. Extract users, groups and policies into tables and a few joins tell you exactly what a user can do in a given compartment Scrape it regularly and you get history, so the forensic question of who had access to a system a month ago becomes a query rather than an afternoon of backtracking through audit logs.

## A small app beats a big console for one job

On top of that metadata the team built applications in Oracle APEX. The common customer request is shutting down non-production environments outside working hours, say dev off at 6pm on weekdays and all weekend, which saves real money. When a developer needs it on a Saturday, the APEX app lets them start it without knowing the technical steps, optionally routing an approval email to a manager with the cost of running it that day.

Hierarchical groups, stored as metadata, encode start and stop order: the database comes up before the application server, and the app server goes down before the database.

## Who should watch

Cloud and database admins who keep answering inventory, cost and access questions by hand, especially on Oracle Cloud. It is an idea talk with concrete examples rather than a tool release; Jason's blog at jasonlesterdba.wordpress.com has the how-to. If you already run a cloud asset inventory product, you will recognise the pattern.

Title: Catch the bad claim at ingestion, not at adjudication
Description: Devi Manoharan of ASTA CRS at Conf42 Golang 2026 on healthcare claims systems that pair ML scoring with staged EDI pipelines on Go and Kafka.
Body:
Healthcare claims get expensive the later a problem is found. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Devi Manoharan, Senior SDET at ASTA CRS who works in healthcare quality engineering, made the case for moving intelligence earlier in the claims workflow: score claims with machine learning as they arrive and treat EDI processing as a staged, concurrent pipeline.

It is a short, high-level talk, closer to an architecture briefing than a build log, and a useful one if you are new to how payer systems move claims around.

## Rules engines stop scaling before the claims do

Devi starts with the pressure on payers: growing claim volumes, coding standards, payer rules and compliance requirements. Rule-based validation handles the basics, but large organisations end up maintaining thousands of business rules, and a small change can ripple through several systems. Rules also cannot spot patterns they were not written for.

Machine learning fills that gap with claim classification, anomaly detection, risk scoring and intelligent routing. Her examples are duplicate claims, unusual billing patterns and high-risk claims flagged before they reach adjudication. High-confidence claims flow straight through automation, and only the complex ones go to analysts. As she points out, even small efficiency gains add up when a system processes millions of claims.

## EDI is a pipeline, so build it like one

The EDI section is the most concrete. X12 transactions, 837 claims (dental, professional, institutional) and 835 remittance files, are the backbone of claims processing. Devi breaks the workflow into stages: segment parsing, enrichment (eligibility and provider details added before the claim moves on), schema mapping and HIPAA compliance validation in line with CMS guidelines. Smaller stages scale and fail more gracefully than one big batch job.

Her reason for caring about validation up front is money. A claim that goes through wrong and is later denied or voided can leave the payer dealing with overpayments and adjustments. Catching it at the parsing and enrichment stage is cheaper than unwinding a payment. It is the claims version of the oldest rule in testing, which makes sense coming from an SDET.

## The stack behind it

The reference architecture is modular: independent services talking through Kafka topics, each scaling on its own workload and isolating faults from its neighbours. Go runs the backend services, Python and TensorFlow handle the models, and PostgreSQL with Redis covers storage and caching. Models run inside the pipeline as real-time scoring services, so claims are evaluated during processing rather than after, and Devi flags model versioning and feature consistency as requirements for trustworthy predictions.

Reliability features round it out: circuit breakers, retries, distributed tracing and audit logging, which in a regulated environment serve stability and compliance at the same time.

## Who should watch

Engineers and testers joining a payer or health-tech team who want the map of 837/835 flows, enrichment and validation in one sitting. If you already run an EDI platform at scale, expect a summary rather than new techniques; the talk does not go into model details or metrics. Her four takeaways make a decent checklist anyway: move intelligence earlier, treat EDI as a scalable pipeline, design for concurrency, and build reliability into every layer.

Title: From firefighting to forecasting, a DBA's roadmap for AI ops
Description: Ellavarasan Asokan of Capital One at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on forecasting, RL indexing and anomaly detection on the way to semi-autonomous databases.
Body:
Index maintenance, capacity planning and alert triage are still mostly manual for DBAs, even when the application around them ships through CI/CD. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Ellavarasan Asokan, Software Consultant at Capital One Bank and an Oracle DBA of fourteen-plus years, mapped the four AI capabilities he sees moving database operations from reactive to predictive, and the four stages to get there without losing control.

This is an overview talk, written from the DBA's chair rather than the data scientist's. It names techniques (LSTM forecasting, reinforcement learning for indexes, clustering for anomalies) without code or benchmarks, which makes it a good orientation for a team deciding where to start.

## The traditional DBA day is reactive by design

Ellavarasan has done the full range: installs, patching, upgrades, performance work and migrations of databases from 5 TB to around 50 TB, on-premises and in AWS and Azure. His description of the old model will be familiar: manual query profiling, manually maintained indexes and storage, threshold alerts that start the work only after something breaks, and root cause analysis as post-mortem. Continuous deployment multiplies database change, cloud workloads shift dynamically, and manual tuning cannot keep pace with DevOps velocity.

## Four capabilities, each aimed at a specific pain

- **Predictive workload forecasting.** Models such as LSTM networks learn from historical workload patterns, CPU, IO throughput, deployment schedules, traffic and seasonality, so resources are allocated before the spike. Flash sales, batch scheduling, canary planning and cloud right-sizing are the use cases he lists.
- **Automated indexing with reinforcement learning.** Static indexes age badly as a database grows from a couple of terabytes to ten. An RL agent watches query behaviour and recommends, creates and retires indexes, cutting latency and freeing the storage that redundant indexes waste.
- **AI anomaly detection.** Time series analysis, clustering and deep learning models over query latency, execution behaviour, CPU, memory, IO and transaction patterns, filtering the noise so the critical alert is not buried among a hundred harmless ones. Deadlocks, plan regressions and unusual access patterns are the catches he highlights. Anyone who has been woken at 3am by a disk alert that cleared itself will get the appeal.
- **AI in CI/CD.** Database changes validated before release, performance baselines enforced automatically, and rollback decisions that keep the blast radius small. Reliability shifts left.

## Stale models and patchy telemetry are the real blockers

The challenges section is candid. Models need regular retraining as workloads change, and a stale one produces misleading advice. Inconsistent telemetry and fragmented monitoring degrade accuracy. Legacy platforms without modern APIs limit automation without serious re-engineering. And teams will not trust autonomous recommendations without transparent reasoning and oversight.

So his position on full automation is cautious: wrong decisions in edge cases and regressions that are hard to trace are real risks. Keep a human in the loop, surface recommendations with context and confidence scores, require explicit approval for high-risk changes, test in shadow mode in lower environments, and limit the blast radius of every rollout.

## A four-stage roadmap

The plan is deliberately incremental: observability first (telemetry and baseline behaviour models across all database tiers), then AI recommendations that humans review and approve, then low-risk routine tasks automated without approval, and finally semi-autonomous operation with AI-driven scaling, self-optimizing indexes and predictive remediation inside governance guardrails. Note the word semi: his closing picture is humans setting intent and AI executing it.

## Who should watch

DBAs and database platform leads looking for a vocabulary and a sequence for introducing AI into operations. If you want implementation detail or measured results, pair it with a talk that shows a system end to end. This one tells you which questions to ask first.

Title: Modularizing an 800,000-line Go monolith is mostly a people problem
Description: Victor Lyuboslavsky of Fleet Device Management at Conf42 Golang 2026 on a failed first attempt, a pilot bounded context and the Go tools that enforce it.
Body:
It started with a 30-second test recompile on a single Go package. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Victor Lyuboslavsky, Principal Software Engineer at Fleet Device Management, told the story of moving Fleet's ten-year-old, roughly 800,000-line open source Go backend toward a modular monolith, including the first attempt that went sideways and the pilot that worked.

This is the rare architecture talk that spends as much time on pull requests nobody would review as on package diagrams, and it is better for it.

## Thirty seconds is the worst possible wait

Victor's opening diagnosis is precise. The service package was Fleet's biggest compile unit, and while Go compiles fast, linking still runs largely in series, so a huge package with many dependencies made every test recompile crawl. Thirty seconds is too long to ignore and too short to switch tasks, so it just breaks your train of thought. He also points out that AI agents do not fix this: they run the test loop far more often than humans, so slow tests slow them down even more.

## Attempt one: right idea, no buy-in

The first plan was a vertical slice for a new feature, Android MDM, mirroring the legacy structure so engineers would know where things live, with its own API and persistence layers and even a second MySQL schema. The pull request sat unreviewed despite a 24-hour review norm. Engineers felt surprised and unheard. Victor unsplit the database, and when a new ADR process arrived, the API split was approved while the persistence split was rejected as risky, confusing and too big at once.

Then delivery pressure did the rest. With no architectural oversight, the Android code seeped back into the legacy code. Some wins survived (separate Android controllers, some shared code pulled out of the service package), but the lessons are the point:

- Consensus takes real time, and early voices are not everyone's voice; ask in one-on-ones.
- Words matter. He meant architectural modules; half the room heard Go modules.
- Architecture changes slipped into feature PRs moved; standalone architecture PRs stalled. His summary: "If you don't define how your architecture is allowed to change, it changes anyway, and often it changes behind your back."
- Every endpoint needs an owner, even if it is just glue.

## Attempt two: borrow authority, start tiny

Finding no large open source Go project that had done this, Victor pointed to GitLab's documented choice of a modular monolith over microservices for its Rails codebase. That shifted the burden of proof from a crazy idea to a proven pattern. The team agreed on bounded contexts and picked the most self-contained one as a pilot: activity and audit, the record of things that already happened. The ADR stayed open for about four weeks, every related PR was reviewed by the four product-group tech leads, and a central page tracked progress. As he put it, "Surprises are great for birthdays, not for architecture."

The design rules: each context owns its controller, service and persistence layers; other contexts may call its public service API but never touch its tables; auth is injected, not owned; one shared MySQL schema stays, because the pain was ownership, not database load, and splitting a database freezes boundaries you are still learning. Cross-context calls go through small contracts owned by the provider, and legacy access goes through an anti-corruption layer outside the context.

## The glue code was the monolith

A hello-world scaffold for the new context pulled in half the codebase through utility packages and a god package where unplaced types went to live. So before modularizing the domain, they had to build a platform layer for HTTP helpers, database wiring and middleware without domain assumptions.

What made the boundary real in Go:

- An `internal` directory, so the compiler rejects outside imports. No code review rule required.
- A single `bootstrap.New` composition root for production and tests.
- The ACL interface as a coupling meter: fewer methods, less legacy dependency.
- A dedicated CI workflow for the context, which also trimmed the main suite.
- Architecture tests with per-context import allow lists, the fitness functions from Building Evolutionary Architectures, catching humans and AI agents alike.

Extracting the context surfaced old bugs, including an RBAC rule the code violated despite Fleet's public docs, and a cancelled operation that could delete past activity records. Next up are user and certificate management, which sit much closer to the centre.

## Who should watch

Anyone with a large Go codebase arguing about microservices versus just cleaning it up, and tech leads who need to sell structural work to a team shipping features. Victor's closing line is the thesis: "Modularization isn't really about modules. It's about respecting the limits of human attention."

Title: Put the AI in the control plane, not the business logic
Description: Yogesh Pugazhendhi Duraisamy Rajamani of Ford at Conf42 Golang 2026 on self-healing streaming pipelines built from Go control loops and an RL control plane.
Body:
By the time a human answers the page, the consumer lag has already piled up. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Yogesh Pugazhendhi Duraisamy Rajamani, Senior Data Engineer at Ford Motor Company, presented an architecture for streaming pipelines that detect, diagnose and recover from failures on their own, with Go supervisor loops doing the fast recovery and an AI control plane making the operational calls.

His starting point is that streaming pipelines are static while their environment is not. Nodes die mid-stream, schema changes silently break downstream consumers, bursts overload systems sized for average load, and congestion spreads backpressure across the stack. Reactive alerting plus a manual ops team means the damage is done before anyone acts: lag grows, data drops, SLAs slip.

## Three layers, one rule about where intelligence lives

The framework stacks an ingestion layer (Kafka, Pulsar, IoT telemetry, edge events), a processing layer (Go stream processors, Flink jobs, enrichment services), and an AI control plane on top that watches throughput, latency, queue depth, node health, schema integrity and error rates. The control plane acts like an autonomous operator: scale, reroute, restart, throttle.

The principle Yogesh keeps coming back to is separation of concerns. Business logic stays in the processing layer; operational intelligence lives in the control plane. It is the cleanest idea in the talk and the one most worth stealing even if you never train a model.

On the Go side, he does not expose raw broker APIs to developers. Channel-oriented abstractions wrap Kafka and friends, so consumers pull, workers process, supervisors monitor, and backpressure propagates naturally through the channels.

## Recovery belongs in a Go loop, not a round trip to Kubernetes

The self-healing cycle is detection, diagnosis, remediation. Detection uses deliberately lightweight models inline with the stream (statistical models, small anomaly classifiers, streaming feature extraction) rather than giant transformers in the hot path. Schema drift gets special attention because it fails silently: a producer changes a payload and consumers start breaking unpredictably.

For remediation, Yogesh argues for native Go supervisor loops over relying entirely on an external orchestrator. Kubernetes reconciliation, container scheduling and API propagation can make the recovery path take seconds; an in-process supervisor can react in microseconds to milliseconds. Actions include restarting workers, rerouting partitions, circuit breaking unhealthy dependencies, and replaying offsets safely.

Scaling is predictive. A reinforcement learning controller learns from bursts, regional spikes, usage cycles and deployment behaviour, and provisions capacity before saturation. Ingestion, processing and sink tiers get separate policies, with cool-down and back-off constraints so the autoscaler does not oscillate itself into a second incident.

## Exactly-once is a design choice you make early

The consistency section is refreshingly concrete. Failures can land during writes, commits, retries or checkpoints, so he combines idempotent producers, transactional consumers that commit offsets with downstream writes, and custom Go checkpoint hooks that capture state before recovery actions. The rule underneath it all: never acknowledge work until the durable downstream write has succeeded.

## Patterns you can use without the RL part

The most practical slide lists four patterns for Go engineers:

- Standardise pipeline stages behind small interfaces so the control plane can swap implementations.
- Wrap every downstream dependency in a circuit breaker and export its state as Prometheus metrics.
- Put heartbeats inside worker goroutines and let supervisor goroutines trigger recovery when they stop.
- Never over-commit offsets; commit only after the sink has persisted, so replay is deterministic.

Observability ties it together. Every goroutine pool exposes backlog, health and throughput metrics, trace context rides in Kafka headers, and the control plane logs each decision with the evidence that triggered it, which gives you auditability and training data in one go.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers running Kafka, Pulsar or Flink with Go services in between. The talk is architectural and does not show code or benchmark numbers, so treat the RL control plane as a direction and the four patterns as the immediately useful part.

Title: SAP pricing is a pipeline problem, not a condition table
Description: Sirisha Ayyagari of IBM at Conf42 Database DevOps 2026 on real-time SAP pricing with an external AI engine, streaming data and clean core BAdIs.
Body:
Enterprises moved finance, procurement and supply chain to the cloud, yet pricing often still runs on condition records, access sequences and transports that take weeks. At Conf42 Database DevOps 2026, Sirisha Ayyagari, Software Developer at IBM, laid out a hybrid design where SAP stays the transactional system of record and an external AI engine, fed by streaming data, does the price optimization.

The talk is an architecture walkthrough for SAP SD people and the data engineers who have to integrate with them. No demo, but a clear blueprint.

## Why condition records can't keep up

Sirisha names three limits of classic SAP SD pricing. Version lag: any change to a pricing table goes through change requests, testing, transports and approvals, which can take days or weeks. Context blindness: rules cannot easily use live inventory, competitor feeds or demand forecasts. And exception proliferation: special conditions and overrides pile up until the pricing logic is fragile. Pricing teams end up spending their time on approvals and overrides rather than on pricing.

Her argument, and the line worth keeping, is that pricing should be treated as a real-time intelligent pipeline rather than a static configuration exercise.

## SAP keeps the authority, AI makes the suggestion

The architecture has three layers. The SAP transactional core handles order execution, compliance validation and financial posting. An integration layer bridges SAP and the outside world through APIs and BAdI extension points. The AI optimization layer runs inference and returns pricing, discount and risk-adjusted recommendations.

The important rule: AI does not replace SAP's authority. SAP still validates and commits every final price. That is also what keeps the design inside SAP's clean core principle, since no standard code is modified. Sirisha points to specific BAdIs: `PRICING_PREPARE` for condition value determination and `PRICING_COMPLETE` for net value calculation, with manual pricing control handled at the same level. The system stays upgrade-safe and cloud-ready, which anyone who has lived through an S/4HANA upgrade with modified standard code will appreciate.

## Feed it fresh data or don't bother

The AI engine is only as good as its inputs: SAP SD order history, inventory availability, customer behaviour, competitor pricing feeds and demand forecasts. Enterprise signals leave SAP through change data capture or SAP Integration Suite, external market feeds and macroeconomic indicators come in through APIs, and Apache Kafka or IBM Event Streams carries the events. The result is continuous pricing rather than periodic updates.

## Run the model like enterprise software

Operationalizing the model gets as much attention as building it. Each model version is traceable to its feature schema and training dataset. Drift detection watches production distributions. If accuracy degrades or latency thresholds are breached, traffic reverts automatically to the last stable model.

Auditability is non-negotiable in pricing: every recommendation is logged with model version, input features, confidence score and decision context, for financial compliance and regulators. Distributed caching keeps prices identical across SAP application servers within a transaction window, and she notes modern inference frameworks can answer in under 100 milliseconds at enterprise throughput.

## Who should watch

SAP architects under pressure to make pricing responsive without breaking clean core, and data platform teams asked to plug ML into ERP. If you have never seen a condition record, the SAP vocabulary will slow you down, but the pattern of keeping the system of record authoritative while an outside engine suggests applies well beyond SAP.

Title: A 200 with zero results is still an outage. Design the fallback first
Description: Hima Bindu Yanala of eBay at Conf42 Golang 2026 on resilient self-service search in Go, with fallback indexes, circuit breakers, bulkheads and user signals.
Body:
The most dangerous search failure returns HTTP 200. At Conf42 Golang 2026, Hima Bindu Yanala, software engineer at eBay, argued that self-service search fails quietly, with empty or degraded results that dashboards call healthy, and that the fix is a fallback path designed from day one rather than patched in after each incident.

Self-service search is often the first line of customer support. When it works, people solve their own problem. When it silently returns nothing, the user just concludes the platform did not help, and every degraded query can turn into a support ticket, a lost sale or a frustrated customer. Her shorthand for it: empty does not always mean correct.

## Fallback should be engineered, not improvised

Hima describes the familiar history of fallback logic: an incident, a patch, another incident, another rule, until fallback is a pile of reactive fixes. Distributed systems surface new failure modes faster than patches keep up. Her alternative is to treat fallback as a first-class pattern with its own capacity, routing, freshness, monitoring and user experience. In her words, "fallback should be engineered, not improvised."

## Fan-out turns rare outliers into the common case

Sending one query to many shards buys parallelism and widens the failure surface. If one shard is slow, the whole response waits, which is why tail latency matters more than averages: users experience their own request, not the mean. Goroutines make fan-out easy, and that is the trap. Hima lists what a resilient Go search service needs at every fan-out boundary: context deadlines, timeout budgets, cancellation, worker limits and explicit rules for partial results.

## Four layers, none of them trusted alone

The architecture is defence in depth:

- **Distributed retrieval** sends queries to the primary shards.
- **A circuit breaker** watches latency, errors and timeouts. Closed means normal traffic; past a threshold it opens and routes to the fallback; half-open sends limited probes to check whether the primary has recovered.
- **A fallback index** built for failure, not a shrunken copy of the main one: lightweight, fast, isolated, holding enough high-confidence data (popular queries, common help articles, recent successful results, curated mappings) to keep the user moving.
- **Bulkheads** protect fallback capacity with separate goroutine pools, connection pools, semaphore limits and context cancellation. If the primary path can eat all the CPU, memory and connections, the fallback exists on the diagram and nowhere else.

The bulkhead name comes from ship design: flood one compartment and the ship stays afloat. A good metaphor for a system whose job is to stay above water while one shard is underwater.

## Zero results deserve their own defence

Before falling back, Hima layers query relaxation: loosen strict filters, correct spelling, expand terms, apply synonyms. Query logs drive the synonym work, since a query that often returns nothing, or that users immediately reformulate, is telling you about a vocabulary gap. She warns that broad synonyms cost precision, so tuning has to be careful. AI shows up here in a deliberately practical role: clustering similar queries, detecting intent, suggesting synonym candidates, not as a buzzword bolted on.

## Watch the users, not just the shards

The closing section connects two kinds of metrics. Infrastructure tells you p99 latency, timeouts, shard failures, breaker trips and resource use. Users tell you zero-result frequency, reformulation rate, abandonment, escalations and clicks. Support tickets are lagging indicators; rising tail latency, more breaker trips and spikes in zero-result rates are leading ones, and they can trigger fallback routing and alerts before customers notice. Her goal: users should not notice the incident before the system has already responded safely.

## Who should watch

Engineers who own search, recommendations or any fan-out read path in Go will get a clean checklist. It is pattern-level rather than code-level, so bring your own implementation of the breaker and bulkheads.
