Title: When every dashboard blames someone else, map the dependencies
Description: David McNerney and Daniel Raskin of Virtana at Conf42 SRE 2026 on finding root cause with a live system dependency graph and investigating agents.
Body:
Modern outages are system problems, not application problems. That is the thesis David McNerney, Director of Product Management at Virtana, and Daniel Raskin, Virtana's Chief Marketing Officer, brought to Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026. Their answer to the familiar incident where every tool points at a different culprit is a system dependency graph, discovered automatically and kept current, which both humans and AI agents can use as context while they hunt for root cause.

## The incident where every tool is right and nobody is

Every SRE has been on this call. A service slows down, the dashboards light up, application metrics say one thing and infrastructure metrics say another. Each team's view is accurate for its own layer, and none of them explains the outage, because the cause lives in the interaction between layers.

The examples in the talk are the kind that cost hours. A spike in a storage queue throttles Kubernetes pods, and the pods look like the problem. Network contention shows up as application latency, so the application team starts profiling code. A GPU pipeline stalls, but the real bottleneck is the upstream data feeding it. In each case the symptom appears in one place and the cause in another, and traditional APM, built around services, plus telemetry split across tools, makes the jump between them hard.

## A graph of how the system actually behaves

The approach Virtana presents in the talk is a System Dependency Graph: a continuously updated map of the relationships between services, Kubernetes objects, infrastructure, networks and storage, discovered from production rather than drawn from an architecture diagram. The difference matters. The diagram in your wiki shows how the system was meant to work. A discovered graph shows how it is wired today, including the dependency someone added during last quarter's migration and never documented.

Once you have that map, the question during an incident stops being which dashboard is right. It becomes what this slow service depends on, and which of those dependencies changed. Following edges from symptom to cause is what an experienced SRE does in their head. The graph makes that path explicit and gives everyone on the call the same picture.

## Agents that use the graph as context

The second half of the talk, per the abstract, is a demo of autonomous agents using the dependency graph as operational context: investigating incidents, tracing cascading failures across layers and surfacing root cause faster. This is the same pattern several Conf42 speakers arrived at in 2026. An LLM agent with access to metrics alone tends to produce plausible stories. An agent that can walk a relationship graph has a structure to reason over, so its conclusions can be checked against real dependencies instead of taken on trust.

If you are evaluating any tool in this space, the talk suggests some good questions to ask: how the graph is discovered and how fresh it stays, whether it reaches below Kubernetes into network and storage, and whether the agent's investigation can be traced edge by edge so an engineer can verify it.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers who run Kubernetes on shared infrastructure and keep losing the first hour of incidents to blame between layers. It is a vendor talk: the graph and the agents shown are Virtana's. The framing of outages as system behaviour, and the habit of following dependencies rather than dashboards, are useful whatever you run.

[Watch David McNerney and Daniel Raskin's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_David_McNerney_Daniel_Raskin_root_cause_distributed_systems) ([YouTube](https://youtu.be/z9mjbWbV8eo)).

Title: AI-written code raises the change rate, so SREs must cut the odds
Description: Sylvain Kalache of Rootly at Conf42 SRE 2026 on how AI coding multiplies changes and incidents, slopsquatting, and using AI back against the failure rate.
Body:
If incidents scale with the number of changes times the chance each change breaks something, AI coding tools just turned up the first number. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Sylvain Kalache, Head of AI Labs at Rootly and a former SRE, built his talk around that simple model: developers now ship far more change, SREs cannot control that, but they can and must drive down the probability of failure per change.

Disclosure he makes himself: Rootly sells on-call and incident management, including an AI SRE, so part of the remedies section is his own product category. The diagnosis stands without it.

## C is going up whether you like it or not

He anchors the talk in a rough formula: a constant baseline failure rate plus C, the number of changes in a time window, times P, the probability that a change causes a failure. Then he stacks the evidence on C: survey data that most engineers already use AI tools, vendors reporting large shares of their code written by AI, Cursor's founder citing a billion accepted lines a day in mid 2025, and research across 5,000 engineers at Microsoft, Accenture and another large company showing more commits and more completed tasks.

His own data point is from Rootly customers: from 2023 to the time of the talk, a three times increase in the average number of incidents per customer. And the help is thinning. Ask the author about a broken service and the honest answer may be that their agent wrote it. Specialists are getting rarer as practitioners become generalists. More incidents, less help, and a manager asking why the AI has not made you faster.

## AI fails like humans do, only faster

The catalogue of failure modes is fun and slightly alarming. Unit tests generated to match broken logic, so they pass. A test for Terraform that technically tests something but not the intent. An agent that hallucinated a GitHub repo and deployed it into a customer environment, a case he attributes to Vercel. Slopsquatting: researchers published a package under a name LLMs tend to hallucinate, a huggingface-cli package, and saw about 30,000 downloads in three months with no promotion at all. And a study where an irrelevant line about cats sleeping most of their lives doubled an LLM's error rate on a maths problem.

A friend at Airbnb gave him the counterpoint: for every AI screw-up there is a human equivalent. Slopsquatting is curl-to-bash; deleted files are a fat-fingered rm. We have also been distracted by cats for a long time. His conclusion is to extend blameless culture to LLMs: the question is still which guardrail was missing, not whose prompt it was.

## P is the SRE's job, and the fundamentals matter more

He does not list new magic. The usual tools for keeping P low (testing, review, progressive delivery, rollback and the rest) matter more than ever, because if they were weak before, more change makes it worse. Then he points AI back at the problem:

- **Mutation testing**, long a nice theory, becomes practical. He cites Meta's automated compliance hardening experiment across Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp: 9,000 mutants, 500 privacy test cases, and engineers accepting more than 70% of the generated tests.
- **LLMs as code review helpers**, the next step after linters and static analysis, since review is becoming the bottleneck.
- **MCP** to give agents the same data sources you use in an incident, and AI SRE agents that pull from GitHub, telemetry and past postmortems to propose root causes. At Rootly, he says, some lower-severity incidents are now handled fully automatically.
- **Toil**: let the agent write postmortem timelines and give the ugly internal tools some CSS.

## Who should watch

SREs and engineering leads watching change volume climb since the team adopted coding agents, and sceptics of AI in production. His advice to the latter is blunt: try it. The C times P framing alone is worth a slide in your next reliability review.

Title: Spotify learned that good abstractions teach complexity
Description: Stuart Clark of Spotify at Conf42 SRE 2026 on the abstraction paradox from 2014 hyper-growth, and how Backstage turned operational knowledge into infrastructure.
Body:
The abstraction that makes shipping easy is often the one that makes a 3am incident impossible. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Stuart Clark, Senior Developer Advocate at Spotify, told the story of how Spotify's 2014 hyper-growth exposed that paradox, and how the fix grew into Backstage, the developer portal Spotify later open sourced and donated to the CNCF.

The story is Spotify's own and so is the tool, but the talk is mostly about a design principle you can apply to any internal platform, dashboard or runbook.

## Ten pull requests in sixty days

Around 2014 Spotify was moving from a music streaming app to a personalised audio platform and hiring at breakneck speed, with a ship fast, ship often mantra. User numbers looked great. Internally, engineering productivity was sliding: the time for a new engineer to reach their tenth pull request, a milestone Spotify tracked, had ballooned to almost 60 days. Onboarding had turned into what he calls archaeological excavation.

The odd part was that the systems looked excellent. Clean APIs, documented interfaces, elegant abstractions hiding the mess underneath. Senior engineers had done exactly what was asked.

## Abstractions optimised for the 90% fail you in the 10%

Then came the incidents. A new engineer could follow the happy path, but the moment something broke, the abstraction became an opaque wall: it said something failed in the data layer, and nothing about what, where or why. The person who built it was on holiday. The tool that made development fast made recovery nearly impossible. He calls it the abstraction trap.

The diagnosis is crisp: abstractions were optimised for the 90% of normal operations, while incidents live in the 10% of edge conditions they were never designed to illuminate. The hidden cost was knowledge atrophy. Seniors were relieved juniors no longer needed them, and the understanding of how things actually worked quietly concentrated in fewer heads. Knowledge silos, disguised as good engineering.

## Abstraction is not oversimplification

The distinction he draws is the takeaway. Abstraction should reduce cognitive load while keeping the ability to dig deeper when needed. Oversimplification hides complexity until it explodes. His analogy is a good technical book: chapter one gives you the basics, the appendix is there when you need it.

So Spotify's abstractions got three layers: a happy path covering 80% of what users need 80% of the time, a context layer showing what is happening under the hood, and full system access for when things break. Each level leads naturally to the next instead of being hidden behind it.

## Treat knowledge as infrastructure

Backstage carries that idea through three components. Golden Path software templates encode operational lessons, not just boilerplate. The service catalog shows not only that service A depends on B, but the nature of the dependency, its reliability metrics and what fails downstream when it breaks. TechDocs keeps documentation next to the code. A plugin architecture lets teams customise while sensible defaults carry the collective wisdom; you can deviate, but the system shows you the implications.

The outcomes he describes are qualitative: onboarding metrics improved dramatically, seniors spent less time interrupted, juniors built understanding instead of waiting on help, and knowledge freshness kept documentation from rotting. As he puts it, "Abstractions should be bridges to understanding not solid walls around it."

## Three questions before your next abstraction

He closes with a framework for any deployment tool, dashboard or incident process: can I trace through this when something goes wrong; does it teach me something about the system, or just a rote procedure; and can I graduate from basic usage to deep understanding along a natural path?

## Who should watch

Platform teams building internal developer portals, SRE leads who keep discovering that only one person can debug a critical service, and anyone writing a wrapper that will someday be paged at 3am. It is a story-driven talk rather than a Backstage tutorial.

Title: Crisis-ready platforms should be edge-first and equity-aware
Description: Rakesh Kumar Kavsari Gopal at Conf42 SRE 2026 on AI platforms that keep health and financial services running in disasters - predictive scaling, edge, fallbacks.
Body:
Systems built for average load fail on exactly the day everyone needs them. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, technical architect Rakesh Kumar Kavsari Gopal, who brings 17 years across healthcare, banking and e-commerce, presented a reference architecture for health and financial platforms that must stay up through hurricanes, pandemics and economic shocks, and argued that keeping them up is an ethical obligation as much as a technical one.

It is a broad architecture talk covering software, hardware, SRE practice and migration, aimed at the people who would have to build such a platform rather than a single product.

## Legacy platforms are tuned for an ordinary day

He groups crisis failures into three recurring patterns: demand spikes, loss of capacity and connectivity, and compliance gaps. Hospitals in a regional disaster face surges well above baseline; payment networks and aid distribution platforms buckle precisely when vulnerable communities rely on them. The common thread is architecture designed for average load, with no ability to anticipate surges, no offline-first mode when networks degrade, no routing that prioritises the most vulnerable, and no way to reconfigure without a human in the loop.

## Predict, then reconfigure by crisis type

The intelligence layer has four parts. Predictive load balancing uses historical crisis data plus real-time signals to pre-scale capacity before demand peaks, not after things start failing. Context-aware reconfiguration reprioritises workloads by crisis type, so a hurricane, a pandemic and an economic shock each trigger a different response profile. Edge intelligence runs local inference so essential services continue when central cloud connectivity degrades or disappears. A fallback protocol engine, backed by SLAs, defines graceful degradation: critical functions stay alive while non-essential services are shed.

The design rule that holds it together is layer independence. A failure in one layer should not cascade into another, which any SRE who has watched a shared dependency take down five teams will appreciate.

## The hardware is part of the reliability story

Unusually for an SRE talk, he goes down to the metal: resilient edge clusters near hospitals, relief centres and bank branches; ruggedised servers rated for heat, humidity and intermittent power; mesh networking that picks the best path across satellite, LTE and fibre; and an offline-first sync protocol that reconciles edge state with the cloud once connectivity returns. Data is encrypted end to end and distributed across cloud and edge so a regional outage is not a single point of data loss, with HIPAA, GDPR and local data rules enforced at the infrastructure layer rather than bolted on after deployment.

## Equity as a routing rule

The most distinctive idea is the disaster equity protocol: prioritisation for elderly, disabled and low-income users encoded directly into service logic, with bandwidth and compute allocated accordingly, aid apps optimised for low-end devices and weak networks, and offline-first design so access survives infrastructure failure. Putting that into code rather than leaving it to manual decisions during a crisis is, in his framing, the right thing to do.

## Migrate in stages, let the AI earn trust

Replacing critical systems overnight is neither feasible nor safe. His three stages: offline-first modules run alongside existing platforms with no disruption; AI-driven modules take over non-critical, then mission-critical workloads with continuous validation; finally legacy systems retire and the SLA-backed fallbacks and equity protocols run fully. The talk cites outcomes from adopting organisations, including up to 60% faster service delivery during crises and 20 to 30% financial improvement, alongside a 99.9% availability target and three times provisioned headroom for surges; treat these as the speaker's reported figures rather than a benchmark you can reproduce from the talk.

## Who should watch

Architects and SREs working on public-sector, humanitarian, healthcare or payments infrastructure in disaster-prone regions. It is wide rather than deep, with no code or detailed case study, so its value is the checklist: predict rather than react, treat edge as required, model vulnerable populations explicitly, and migrate in stages.

Title: Tesla vs GM margins as a lesson in reliability trade-offs
Description: Sonali Galhotra of Sony Pictures at Conf42 SRE 2026 reads Tesla and General Motors profit ratios as telemetry for innovation speed versus stability.
Body:
Profit margins are a lagging indicator, and so is your error budget burn. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Sonali Galhotra, Senior Engineering Program Manager at Sony Pictures, compared Tesla and General Motors through their gross, operating and net profit ratios, and used the contrast to argue that organisational signals say as much about a platform's reliability as its dashboards do.

She flags it herself as slightly different from a typical SRE talk. It is a socio-technical analogy, not a finance lecture and not a tooling talk, and it is short.

## Reliability is an organisational property

Her starting point is one program leaders know well. Systems do not run in isolation; they run inside organisations that must sustain themselves. How resources get allocated, how hard the company pushes innovation, how much goes into infrastructure and how leadership balances speed against stability all shape what reliability is achievable. Program managers sit right in the middle of those tensions, which is why she wants them reading organisational signals the way an SRE reads CPU, memory pressure and queue depth.

The hypothesis is simple: financial and operational patterns can act as very high-level telemetry. She picks three ratios. Gross margin as a hint of production efficiency and architectural integration, operating margin as operational discipline and cost control, and net margin as long-term sustainability.

## Two architectures, two telemetry shapes

Tesla, in her reading, runs a tightly integrated stack: hardware, software, manufacturing and distribution closely connected. In platform terms, a vertically integrated system optimised for innovation velocity, where decisions propagate quickly. General Motors is the mature, diversified system: a large portfolio, geographically distributed operations, highly standardised processes. Closer to a stable modular ecosystem optimised for predictability over decades.

The numbers behave accordingly. According to the analysis summarised in the abstract, the gross profitability gap between the two is statistically significant, with Tesla stronger, consistent with tighter control of the value chain and fewer external dependencies. Operating and net margins show more volatility at Tesla, tied to aggressive investment and rapid scaling, and more stability at GM. Those operating and net differences were not statistically distinct, which is a nice reminder that variance and average are different questions.

## Neither shape is the right answer

The SRE translation is the payoff. Innovation-heavy architectures deliver strong top-line efficiency but introduce variability; continuous iteration creates operational fluctuation. She draws the parallel to AI platforms, where training cycles, infrastructure scaling and experimentation pipelines inject variance into production. Mature systems trade peak performance for resilience under pressure, and large enterprise platforms tend to drift toward that model as they start carrying mission-critical load.

So reliability goals have to match the organisation's risk tolerance. An AI platform in experimentation mode can accept more volatility; a customer-facing platform serving millions of users cannot experiment as freely. Setting the same SLO philosophy for both is how you end up either slow or on fire.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers, program leads and senior SREs who negotiate reliability targets with the business, and anyone trying to explain to leadership why the experimental platform and the billing system should not share an error budget. If you want tooling or incident tactics, skip it; if you want vocabulary for the speed-versus-stability conversation, it is a quick, unusual angle.

Title: Regulated systems can be up and still make the wrong decisions
Description: Shruthi Sepuri of TCS at Conf42 SRE 2026 on workflow-level reliability for insurance and finance - decision accuracy SLIs and testing that continues in production.
Body:
A rule configuration change can quietly move an approval threshold and leave every dashboard green. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Shruthi Sepuri, Software Developer Engineer at TATA Consultancy Services, showed how that kind of silent workflow failure slips past infrastructure monitoring in regulated systems, and how to extend testing into production so you catch wrong decisions, not just slow ones.

Her one-line summary is the talk in miniature: "A system can be up and still be wrong."

## The factory machine that hums while making bad parts

She opens with an analogy: a factory machine that runs perfectly, nothing overheating, panel all normal, while the parts coming out are wrong. Her first slide puts that into software. On the left, the view on-call engineers are used to: four nines of uptime, tiny error rate, low latency, CPU and memory comfortable. On the right, the business workflow: ingestion passes, the rule engine errors, the decision output is wrong, compliance validation is skipped and the audit log has a gap. The footnote says it all: a rule misconfiguration, and no infrastructure alert triggered.

Uptime, error rates and latency measure technical health. None of them measure decision correctness, and in insurance or financial services, a wrong approval at scale is a compliance event, not a minor defect.

## There is a missing layer in most monitoring stacks

She breaks systems into layers. Infrastructure and application services (servers, databases, APIs, queues, caches) are usually monitored well. The business workflow layer (claims processing, underwriting, policy adjustments, compliance validation, audit logging) is under-monitored. The compliance outcomes layer (correct decisions, audit trails, risk controls) is often not measured at all.

Her worked example is a claims system where a config change silently alters approval thresholds. Infrastructure stays green throughout, decisions drift, incorrect approvals or rejections go through at scale, and the audit trail may be incomplete. The listed causes are all mundane: rule misconfigurations, data mapping issues, threshold drift, missing compliance attributes. None of them crash anything.

## Four indicators for decision correctness

Reliability has to be defined at the workflow level, with a check at each step: is the input validated, are the right rules in use, is the outcome in the expected range, are required fields complete, is the audit record immutable and complete. From those come four indicators:

- **Decision accuracy rate**: share of automated decisions within the expected outcome range.
- **Approval and rejection deviation**: statistical drift from the historical baseline, so a sudden spike or drop becomes a signal.
- **Compliance field completion**: required audit attributes populated per transaction.
- **Rule execution correctness**: rules behaving as configured, checked against known test cases.

## Testing does not stop at the release

The bridge to QA is the part testers will appreciate. Testing feeds deployment, deployment feeds monitoring, incidents feed learning, and learning feeds better tests. Her four methods: synthetic business transactions replayed continuously against live rule engines, real-time monitoring of decision outcomes and rule execution, comparing rule engine output against expected baselines after every deployment, and alerting on statistical anomalies in outcomes rather than only on technical errors. Production decision distributions then flow back to update test cases and thresholds before the next rule change ships.

Her formula for it is testing plus observability equals workflow reliability. Neither half is enough alone.

## Who should watch

QA engineers moving toward reliability work, and SREs on rule-heavy platforms in insurance, banking or anywhere a config file can change an outcome. It is an accessible, framework-level talk with illustrative dashboards; bring your own rule engine and you will leave with a short list of SLIs to add.

Title: AI for clinical handoffs has to fail safely before it helps
Description: Abhiram Potharaju of Wells Fargo at Conf42 SRE 2026 on SBAR-aligned AI handoff summaries built with SRE habits - safe degradation, explainability, governance.
Body:
A shift change in a hospital is an on-call handover where the system being handed over is a person. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Abhiram Potharaju, Senior Software Engineer at Wells Fargo, looked at AI-augmented clinical handoffs through an SRE lens: how to build an assistant that summarises patient data reliably, stays honest about uncertainty, and leaves every clinical decision with the clinician.

It is a design and governance talk rather than a system demo, and it is careful not to oversell: the goal is fewer missed details, not automated medicine.

## Handoffs fail for three boring reasons

Communication breakdowns during handoffs are a known contributor to adverse events, and he narrows the causes to three. Cognitive overload: clinicians juggle many patients under time pressure. Fragmented EHR data: the facts exist but are scattered across notes, labs, vitals and medication lists. Variable quality: even with SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) in place, execution differs between clinicians and shifts.

Any SRE who has received a one-line handover note that says all good, watch the queue, will recognise the pattern. His point is that this is a patient safety and reliability problem, not a documentation one.

## Use the format clinicians already trust

The proposed system ingests structured data (vitals, medications, orders, labs) and unstructured notes, and produces a concise summary aligned to SBAR. That alignment is the clever, unglamorous choice: it fits a framework clinicians already use instead of inventing a new one. Situation carries current status and the immediate concern, Background the relevant history, Assessment the meaningful trends, and Recommendation the next steps that need attention.

The abstract adds the monitoring side: continuously watching vital sign trends, medication changes and lab deviations to highlight early signs of deterioration. The aim is to reduce variability and speed up situational awareness, so less time is spent searching records.

## Reliability here means degrading safely

This is where the SRE framing earns its place. In healthcare, being useful is not enough; the assistant has to stay dependable when data is incomplete, inconsistent or late. He lists the familiar toolkit (observability, fault tolerance, incident awareness, proactive maintenance) and adds the healthcare-specific requirements: safe behaviour under uncertainty and safe degradation, so that a gap in the input shows up as a gap in the summary rather than a confident fabrication.

Explainability is treated as a reliability property too. If the system flags a risk, the clinician should be able to see what drove it. That builds appropriate trust and guards against over-reliance, which in this domain is its own failure mode.

## Governance is part of the system, not paperwork around it

The deployment section reads like a production readiness review. Validate carefully before broad rollout, keep monitoring accuracy, reliability and workflow impact afterwards, train staff on how and when to use it, and set clear escalation paths and oversight for when outputs look wrong. He recommends starting with pilot programs on clearly defined use cases, involving clinicians early in workflow design, and measuring outcomes from real workflow behaviour. Adoption, in his framing, is not a one-time event.

## Who should watch

Engineers building AI features for clinical, legal or other high-stakes workflows, and SREs asked to put an LLM summary in front of people who will act on it. It stays at the level of principles, with no metrics or architecture diagrams to copy, so treat it as a framework for your design review rather than a blueprint.

Title: Green dashboards, slow humans - measure workflow latency instead
Description: Abhimanyu Narwal of Bloomberg at Conf42 SRE 2026 on silent telemetry gaps, workflow SLIs, count invariants and canaries that prove a pipeline is working.
Body:
The edge gateway said 100,000 events arrived; the analysis engine showed 90,000; every service was green. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Abhimanyu Narwal, Engineering Team Lead for security services at Bloomberg, used that gap to argue that the expensive reliability failures are often not outages but the quiet ones that slow humans down, and he left a short checklist for catching them.

He is clear about scope up front: an anonymised case study and a reusable SRE pattern, not a breach story and not a description of Bloomberg's proprietary architecture.

## The fog of war is ambiguity, not panic

The pipeline is a familiar shape: events enter, get processed, results surface in a UI, a human analyst validates them and acts. For a long time it looked perfect. Then an analyst raised a low-severity alert because counts diverged between stages.

Nothing had crashed. The question was whether the gap was expected transformation lag or a visibility hole, and in a security workflow that uncertainty is costly. Management kept asking whether threats were being missed. After a lot of digging the answer was reassuring and annoying in equal measure: processing and safety checks had worked fine, but a telemetry agent had silently failed and dropped logs before they reached the UI. Compute health was 100%. The team's confidence was not.

## The four golden signals answered the wrong question

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation were all fine. They answer whether the system is alive, and miss whether the workflow is explainable. His key distinction: service latency is milliseconds between request and response; workflow latency is the time for a human to go from seeing a signal to confidently acting on it. When telemetry drops, the second one explodes while the first stays flat.

So the team stopped treating this as a logging bug and started treating the whole human workflow like a distributed trace, human validation step included.

## Three SLIs worth stealing

- **End-to-end duration**: p50 and p95 from ingestion to visible in the UI, alerting when it is consistently worse than the workflow needs. That catches slow degradation behind healthy services.
- **Count integrity**: compare counts between stages against an explicit model of expected deltas and lag. His example: 2% divergence for five minutes is normal; 10% for an hour means the invariant is broken.
- **Liveness via canary**: a known-good synthetic event injected continuously and verified at every stage. If you take one thing from the talk, he says, take this.

## Systems should confess their own blind spots

On the design side he proposes what he calls a fifth golden signal for the system to reveal its own coverage gaps. When telemetry is missing, the UI should say so. Treat partial degradation as a first-class state instead of a binary up or down, so reduced coverage shows as reduced coverage rather than a reassuringly normal screen. And make invariants (everything received is eventually surfaced within a known window) observable contracts.

His last tactic is the most human one: if people are a reliability endpoint, measure their friction. Repeated queries, pivots, escalations and reopen rates are proxies. Before the fix, tier-one analysts did not trust the UI and escalated to engineering for manual database queries; that escalation loop was, in his words, the true error rate.

## Who should watch

SREs and observability folks supporting any human-in-the-loop pipeline: security operations, fraud review, moderation, support tooling. The checklist is deliberately small: pick one key workflow, define its invariants, add one synthetic canary, write one workflow SLO. A cheap Monday morning, and you get to stop guessing.

Title: Airline shopping traffic is mostly repeats, so cache it carefully
Description: Mukul Kumar Gaur of Accelya Group at Conf42 SRE 2026 on caching NDC airline offers at scale with freshness rules that stop pricing drift.
Body:
Many of the searches hitting an airline's offer engine are the same question asked by different robots a few seconds apart. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Mukul Kumar Gaur, Senior Principal in Product Management and Product Engineering at Accelya Group, explained how NDC shopping platforms can serve that repeat demand from cache without quoting a price the airline no longer offers.

If NDC is new to you: it is the airline industry's move to offer- and order-based retailing, where offers are built dynamically per request instead of being pulled from static fare filings. That flexibility is exactly what makes every request expensive.

## You are scaling to process repetition

The problem, in his framing, is redundancy. Requests arrive from airline websites, online travel agencies, metasearch sites and automated repricing systems, and a large share are repetitive or near-duplicate searches for the same origin and destination. Meanwhile each one now triggers real-time offer generation: fares, taxes, inventory availability and merchandising rules.

Without caching, the platform recomputes the full offer every time. His phrase for it is that platforms end up scaling infrastructure to process repetition rather than incremental revenue. The bill shows up as latency and cloud cost, and the risk shows up during traffic spikes. The fix is not a bigger engine but recognising repeat demand and reusing work already done.

## Pick the cache by how fast the price moves

The talk lays out three strategies, with the trade-off stated plainly: performance versus flexibility versus pricing freshness.

- **Full offer caching** stores the complete offer as generated and returns it instantly on a matching request. Fastest option, best for markets where prices are fairly stable or the cache window is tightly controlled.
- **Hybrid anchored caching** keeps stable parts (say, the fare structure) and recalculates the volatile parts, such as availability and dynamic price adjustments, per request.
- **Partial component caching** caches individual pipeline pieces independently, such as tax calculations, fare rules or schedule data. Less speed-up, less stale-data risk.

His recommendation is to layer them rather than choose one. Most real platforms have markets in all three categories.

## Governance is what keeps a cache honest

The obvious worry is pricing drift: a cached offer that outlives the inventory or price it was built on. The abstract also names the downstream pain, settlement discrepancies, which is the kind of bug finance finds weeks after engineering shipped it.

The controls he lists are freshness thresholds that cap how long an offer stays valid, real-time invalidation triggers that evict cached data when pricing or availability changes, special handling for high-elasticity markets, and elastic controls that hold consistency under spikes. The abstract adds request quality scoring and partner-level cache controls, so a noisy aggregator does not get the same treatment as a channel that converts.

Monitoring closes the loop: BI dashboards on cache hit rates, system performance and pricing alignment, plus automated alerts when discrepancies appear. Cache invalidation is famously one of the two hard problems; this talk is mostly about making its failures visible fast.

## Peak sales are the real test

His worked scenario is a high-demand promotion, when shopping traffic can jump within minutes. Without caching, every request hits the offer engine and performance degrades exactly when the airline most wants to sell. With layered caching, most of those requests are served from offers already computed, and the engine keeps capacity for the ones that need fresh pricing.

## Who should watch

Engineers on travel, e-commerce or any dynamic pricing system where reads vastly outnumber purchases. It is a conceptual talk with no code or benchmark numbers, so expect a clear mental model and a checklist (layered caching, explicit invalidation policy, observability on pricing accuracy) rather than an implementation.

Title: In regulatory reporting, a missed deadline is a compliance failure
Description: Bhargavaram Potharaju of Wells Fargo at Conf42 SRE 2026 on high availability, deadline-aware disaster recovery and audit replay for regulatory reporting.
Body:
When a regulatory report is late, nobody files it under operations. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Bhargavaram Potharaju, Senior Infrastructure Engineer at Wells Fargo, argued that on national-scale reporting platforms SRE directly decides compliance outcomes, and that high availability, disaster recovery and audit readiness have to be designed in from day one rather than added after the first audit finding.

It is a short, architecture-level talk with no vendor in it: a reference model, the principles behind it, and a path to adopt it one layer at a time.

## Your SLOs should be written in filing deadlines

The pressure he describes comes from two directions: data volumes grow each reporting cycle while submission windows shrink. In that world a delay is not a service issue and a wrong output is not a data issue; both can turn into penalties. So service level objectives, incident response and error budgets all need to line up with regulatory deadlines, not generic IT targets.

He names five places legacy platforms struggle: high availability, peak-load performance, data accuracy, auditable outcomes and disaster resilience. Most enterprise systems are tuned for an average Tuesday. Reporting platforms live and die in the crunch right before cutoff.

## Recovery time is measured backwards from the cutoff

The most useful idea is deadline-aware disaster recovery. Recovery objectives cannot be picked in isolation; they depend on how much time is left before submission. If an outage hits close to a deadline, the platform still needs time to recover, reprocess, validate and submit, and ideally time to validate the results before sending them. An RTO that looks fine on paper can be useless an hour before the filing window closes.

That is also why he insists failover be tested under realistic load. Availability tested only under daily traffic tells you nothing about burst traffic and peak concurrency, and a DR plan that has never run at peak is, in his framing, a theoretical design exercise.

## Prove how the number was made, not just the number

Audit readiness gets its own section. The platform has to show exactly how a submission was created: immutable logs, full data lineage and deterministic replay, so you can rerun the process and reproduce the same result when asked. The pipeline he sketches runs ingestion, validation, transformation, submission, monitoring and audit replay, with fault isolation between stages so that a problem in one stage cannot silently corrupt the next.

## Business telemetry catches what server metrics miss

Server metrics will tell you a machine is stressed. They will not tell you the deadline is at risk. He wants observability at the business-process level: record counts, validation pass and fail rates, queue depth, per-stage latency, submission timing and acknowledgement status.

The failure mode he flags as most dangerous is the silent one: records dropped, validations skipped, acknowledgements never confirmed, all while the platform looks healthy, and nobody finds out until the audit. His answer is end-to-end validation gates and explicit confirmation that each record reached a correct outcome. He also accepts that many of these platforms cannot go fully cloud native because of security, data residency or legacy integrations, so the controls have to work in hybrid setups too.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects on finance, insurance or government reporting systems, and anyone whose batch pipeline has a hard external deadline. It is high level and light on tooling; the value is the framing and the checklist: identify current failure modes, define compliance-aligned SLOs, improve telemetry, test DR in realistic scenarios, then harden submission gates step by step.

Title: CruiseKube right-sizes Kubernetes pods in place, minute by minute
Description: Shubham Rai (Truefoundry) and Raman Tehlan (Zurich Lab) at Conf42 SRE 2026 show CruiseKube, open source CPU right-sizing with in-place pod resize and PSI.
Body:
Everyone knows lower CPU requests mean a cheaper cluster, and almost nobody lowers them. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Shubham Rai of Truefoundry and Raman Tehlan, Cloud Native Consultant at Zurich Lab, presented CruiseKube, an open source controller that keeps correcting pod requests in place, using two features that only recently became usable in Kubernetes.

It is a builders' talk: the problem, the design choices, the components and a dashboard demo, closing with an honest list of where not to turn it on.

## Over-provisioning is a fear problem, not a knowledge problem

Shubham opens with why clusters stay expensive. Teams fear CPU throttling and OOM kills, because an under-provisioned pod that gets killed is a business outage. So they pad requests. Then nobody wants to keep re-analysing workloads and editing YAML. The padding compounds: inflated requests force the cluster autoscaler to add nodes that sit half empty.

His point about where to fix it is worth hearing. You cannot solve this at the node level, because node over-provisioning is downstream of request over-provisioning. Fix requests first, or the node autoscaler is just efficiently buying the wrong amount of hardware.

## Predict a little, correct often

The contrast with the Vertical Pod Autoscaler is the core idea. VPA does periodic analysis and produces a recommendation that has to hold for a long time, per workload, across whatever nodes its pods landed on. CruiseKube runs a continuous feedback loop that only needs to be right for a short window ahead, and it decides per pod, in the context of the node that pod is on.

Two things make that viable. In-place pod resource updates went GA in Kubernetes 1.35, so a request can change without a restart. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) metrics, beta in 1.34, give per-container contention data on each node, even when you set no CPU limits. CruiseKube combines CPU usage with CPU PSI to pick the request.

The node view matters because of headroom, the gap between a pod's base need and its bursts. Bursts are big and rare, so the gap between the 75th percentile and the maximum is large. Instead of every pod reserving its own worst case, CruiseKube reserves the largest headroom among the pods on a node and lets them share it. It is the same bet as a shared on-call rota: not everyone has a bad night at once.

## Two entry points and a lot of guardrails

Raman walks through the loop: observe the cluster from Prometheus, store stats, learn patterns (a peak at the same time over the last seven days), then apply. Changes land in two places. A mutating admission webhook sets requests when a pod is created, informed by history, so a pod that was OOM-killed comes back with more memory. A continuous optimizer applies recommendations to running pods in place, evicting only when a pod needs more than its node can give.

The guardrails are the part SREs will check first. Everything starts in recommend-only mode; nothing changes until you enable cruise mode per workload. Eviction respects criticality (a single-replica workload ranks higher than one with fifty pods) and you can edit priorities. OOM kills feed back into memory sizing. There is also a disruption window for Karpenter users whose do-not-disrupt annotations block node consolidation.

The demo dashboard shows monthly cost, current and untapped savings, allocatable versus requested versus recommended resources, per-workload recommendations and an event log of every change. On the demo cluster, enabling it for all workloads showed savings of about 60%.

## Where they say not to use it (yet)

Their recommendation is stateless services, dev and staging, and short-lived jobs. Latency-sensitive services, stateful apps like databases and queues, and workloads under HPA should stay in recommend mode for now; HPA support was still in progress at the time of the talk.

## Who should watch

Platform and FinOps engineers who have tried VPA, found it too slow or too disruptive, and still pay for idle cores. It is a short, practical tour with a demo; you will come away knowing whether to install it in recommend mode and look.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Kubernetes Scaling for Savings and Stability: Beyond HPA and VPA](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Joshua_Fox_kubernetes_autoscaling_reliability) by Joshua Fox.
- [The Frugal k8s Engineer: Strategies for Amazon EKS](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Piyush_Mattoo_Dariush_Azimi_karpenter_kubernetes_optimization) by Piyush Mattoo and Dariush Azimi, including Karpenter.

Title: AI personalisation fails silently, so give it circuit breakers
Description: Yury Lysak of Lionsoul Global at Conf42 SRE 2026 on proactive SRE for AI personalisation: drift signals, small-data methods and black swan circuit breakers.
Body:
A recommendation engine can be 100% available, return zero errors and still lose you a client. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026, Yury Lysak, Head of Strategic Projects at Lionsoul Global, a digital asset wealth manager, made the case that AI personalisation needs its own SRE playbook, because its failures never page anyone.

He brings a useful career arc to it: personalisation and commercial analytics for telcos at VEON and for retailers via McKinsey, now applied to wealth tech, where the client list is short and every client matters.

## Loud failures get fixed, quiet ones get quarterly reviews

His framing is the sharpest part of the talk. Traditional failures are loud: a 500, a timeout, a crash, and everyone mobilises. Personalisation failures are gradual. Features decay, embeddings go stale, recommendations get a little worse each week, and the dashboard stays green. He describes client lifetime value slipping a percent or two per month, unnoticed until a complaint or a quarterly review shows months of lost revenue.

Then there are the events no model was trained for. He cites the October 2025 crypto liquidation cascade and the February 2026 Bitcoin crash as moments when the engineering was fine and the models' assumptions about liquidity and correlation were catastrophically wrong. No latency alert catches a model that is confidently describing a market that no longer exists.

## When you have 50 clients, A/B testing is a fantasy

What transfers from telco and retail is a lot: next best action becomes fund allocation, churn prediction becomes attrition scoring, basket analysis becomes spotting which clients might fit a new strategy. What does not transfer is the sample size. With a few dozen clients you cannot A/B test or train a standard model.

His substitutes are concrete: Bayesian methods that start from priors learned elsewhere and update per client, Thompson sampling for exploration on tiny samples, transfer learning where similar data exists, and the relationship manager as a human sensor whose qualitative notes feed the loop. The architecture he shows layers this: data sources (including RM notes), an ML pipeline producing ranked recommendations with confidence intervals, an LLM layer that writes the client-facing narrative, and a guardrail layer with a rules engine and an RM review gate. The LLM drafts; it never has the last word.

## Three levels of admitting the model does not know

The circuit breaker design is the part to copy. Level one is an always-on market regime detector: volatility above twice the 90-day average, or correlations moving sharply, widens uncertainty bounds and escalates to humans. Level two watches confidence per recommendation and suppresses automation when inputs drift too far from training data. Level three, when both trip, switches off ML recommendations and falls back to conservative, pre-approved defaults. His guiding principle: silence beats a confident wrong answer.

Monitoring is tiered too: daily data quality and confidence, weekly PSI drift per feature plus the RM override rate (above 30% means the model is misaligned), monthly business metrics against a non-personalised baseline. And every alert should speak business, naming revenue at risk rather than just a threshold crossed.

## Compliance as a pipeline step

In regulated finance each recommendation is a potential regulatory event, so his pipeline logs inputs, model version and confidence at generation time, validates against concentration limits and client restrictions, has an LLM write a feature-referencing explanation, routes it through an RM, then archives it. Answering a regulator, he says, went from weeks of digging to a download.

## Who should watch

Anyone running ML in production where the feedback loop is slow and the dataset small: wealth, B2B, healthcare, anything with dozens of customers instead of millions. The business impact figures in the talk are his own, so treat them as one firm's experience; the circuit breaker and alert-design patterns stand on their own.

Title: From alerts to answers with context-driven observability and agents
Description: Savi Grover (Tekskills) at Conf42 SRE 2026 gives a quick tour of turning alert noise into context, with an agent loop that rolls back a bad canary.
Body:
SRE teams don't need more alerts, they need answers, and the gap between the two is context. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Savi Grover, Site Reliability Engineer at Tekskills, gave a brisk tour of context-driven observability and ended with an agent that notices a spike in 500s, traces it to a bad canary and rolls it back before reporting to a human.

It's one of the shortest talks of the event, closer to a lightning talk than a workshop. Watch it as a checklist, not a tutorial.

## Data rich, information poor

Savi's starting point is the paradox most on-call engineers recognize. The move from monoliths to microservices multiplied telemetry volume (she puts it at a hundred times), and SREs are now drowning in high-cardinality noise. Traditional monitoring identifies the symptom and leaves the engineer to hunt for the cause by hand.

She names four reasons the old way fails:

- **Siloed data.** Metrics, logs and traces live in separate tools with no correlation.
- **The dashboard mirage.** Flipping through dozens of dashboards during an outage adds cognitive load instead of removing it.
- **Static thresholds.** She says they lead to 80% flapping, non-actionable alerts.
- **Knowledge leakage.** Resolution depends on tribal knowledge rather than encoded patterns.

## Signal to context

Her framework shifts attention from raw data to meaningful, contextual events. Golden signals (latency, errors, traffic, saturation) are still the base, but read through SLOs rather than as raw thresholds. Distributed tracing is the backbone, with trace IDs stitching the user journey together across the mesh. And AI does dimensionality reduction: a thousand connection-refused log lines become one "database connectivity" cluster event.

The supporting practices are the ones that make all of that possible:

- consistent tags and metadata on all telemetry (application, environment, service tier, owner),
- end-to-end lineage, so you can see which downstream assets an upstream issue affects,
- anomaly detection that learns normal behaviour instead of relying only on static thresholds,
- correlation that links logs, metrics and traces to code changes, infrastructure and business impact,
- automated root cause analysis that goes past detection to triage and suggested fixes.

## The agent loop

The agentic ops part is a four-step loop. **Observe:** watch golden signals through tools like Prometheus and Grafana and notice an anomaly, say a spike in 500 errors. **Analyze:** query traces and find that a downstream API is timing out or down. **Act:** check recent CI/CD logs, identify a bad canary deployment and trigger a rollback. **Report:** tell the team in Slack or email what caused it, what was done and the details of the anomaly.

It's a clean picture of where agents fit in incident response. What the talk doesn't cover is the hard part: guardrails, how much autonomy the agent gets before a human approves, and what happens when it rolls back the wrong thing. Pair it with a longer talk if you're about to build one.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to observability who want the vocabulary in one sitting, or a team lead looking for a short talk to kick off an alert-fatigue discussion. Experienced SREs will know most of it already.

- [Tackling Alert Fatigue with SLOs](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mandi_Walls_tackling_alert_fatigue) by Mandi Walls (PagerDuty), the SLO half of the argument in depth.

Title: Three telemetry layers that answer "what changed?" in an incident
Description: Khushboo Nigam (Oracle) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on organizing traces, Kubernetes signals and CI/CD telemetry so incident triage follows evidence.
Body:
The alert already tells you something is wrong; the question you actually ask next is "what changed?" At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Khushboo Nigam, Principal Cloud Architect at Oracle, presented a layered observability framework that sorts telemetry by the investigation question it answers, so an engineer can move from user impact to platform health to the deployment that caused it without becoming the manual integration layer.

Her one-line thesis is the talk's title: correlation over collection.

## A clarity problem, not a data problem

Khushboo's diagnosis is that most teams already collect plenty: infrastructure metrics, logs, traces, deployment events, a pile of alerts. Each signal has value, but on its own it doesn't tell a story. During an incident they all compete for attention at once, and the on-call engineer ends up stitching them together by hand under pressure.

She draws the usual line between monitoring and observability, and it's a useful refresher. Monitoring catches known failure conditions: CPU above 90%, latency above 500 milliseconds, the known knowns. Observability is for the unknown unknowns, the failures nobody wrote an alert for. Neither helps if the telemetry has no shared context linking a latency spike, a timeout in the logs, a slow span and last night's release.

## Organize signals by the question they answer

The framework has three layers, each tied to one question:

1. **Application traces: where is it failing?** Follow the request across services and find the slow or failing span.
2. **Kubernetes metrics and events: is the platform healthy?** Node resource pressure, pod restarts, crash loops, scheduling problems.
3. **CI/CD telemetry: what changed?** Deployments, version bumps, configuration changes, pipeline results.

The order matters. You narrow from the whole system to one component, then decide whether the platform or the application is at fault, then look for the change.

## Enrich spans so you can pivot

The demo uses a retail microservices app on managed Kubernetes: a load balancer, a web frontend, an API backend with a payment operation, and an external database. Telemetry flows through the OpenTelemetry Collector plus cloud-native services into separate backends for application monitoring, logs and metrics.

The key move is in the collector: it enriches application spans with Kubernetes metadata, so the payment span that shows the error and high latency also carries the node name, pod name and pod IP. That's the pivot from layer one to layer two; you jump straight to that node's resource usage and that pod's events. Further down the same span sits the service version and the error message from the application's instrumentation. If the platform looks healthy and errors began right after a deploy, the version in the span tells you which release to look at.

Put together, telemetry becomes what she calls a structured hierarchy of evidence, with each layer narrowing the search rather than adding more noise.

## Know what your provider owns

One aside is easy to skip and shouldn't be. On managed Kubernetes, the control plane (API server, etcd) is usually the cloud provider's responsibility, while nodes and workloads are yours. Khushboo's advice: read your provider's policy, find out which metrics and logs they expose for the parts they manage, and know in advance when to escalate rather than debug.

## Who should watch

SREs whose incident response still starts with opening five dashboards, and platform teams setting up OpenTelemetry who want a reason to enrich spans with Kubernetes and deployment metadata. The framework is platform-agnostic and clearly explained; it's not a vendor pitch.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Practical introduction to OpenTelemetry tracing](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Nicolas_Frankel_opentelemetry_tracing) by Nicolas Frankel (Apache APISIX), if layer one needs work first.
- [Deterministic Kubernetes Diagnostics with OpenTelemetry](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Mridula_Chilakamarri_kubernetes_opentelemetry_diagnostics) by Mridula Chilakamarri (Dell Technologies), on the layer two side.
- [Optimizing Observability with OpenTelemetry Collector for Budget-Friendly Insights](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Bruno_Ferreira_observability_opentelemetry_collector) by Bruno Ferreira (TheyDo), for the collector doing the enrichment.

Title: Watch the business workflow, not the service, to detect faster
Description: Rohit Wadhwa (Walmart) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on Predictive Workflow Integrity, which models workflows as state machines and cut detection time below a minute.
Body:
A burnt pizza alarm fires after the damage is done; a better system checks the oven temperature and the dough on the way. That analogy opens the talk by Rohit Wadhwa, Senior Software Engineer at Walmart, at Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026. His model, Predictive Workflow Integrity (PWI), moves observability from individual services to end-to-end business workflows, and he reports mean time to detection dropping from about 12 minutes to 58 seconds.

It's a short talk, more of a model and results summary than an implementation guide, but the reframing is worth the time.

## Service signals miss workflow failures

Event-driven microservices across regions bring three problems Rohit sees in practice. State divergence, where services stop agreeing about what's going on. Latency variability, where one slow service compounds across the whole call path. And cascading failures, where one failing component ripples into a wide outage. Service-level dashboards can look fine while a business workflow is stuck halfway, and with a 12-minute detection time you're only starting to fix things after customers have noticed.

## Workflows as state machines

PWI models each workflow as a distributed state machine and keeps evaluating its transitions. It looks for three red flags:

- **Delayed convergence.** The workflow doesn't reach its expected state within the expected time, a sign some service didn't follow its instructions.
- **Conflicting ownership.** Several teams acting on the same workflow or platform, which slows down resolution.
- **Abnormal execution paths.** A service routes the workflow down an unexpected path, which leads to degraded performance and then failure.

None of these are visible from a single service's latency graph, which is the point.

## Autonomous triage on a causal graph

To act on those signals, PWI correlates logs, metrics and traces into one map of the system (the abstract calls it an event-driven causal graph) and applies machine learning on top to prioritize incidents by severity. From there it moves to automated remediation. Rohit claims it predicts likely issues and fixes some before they surface, which reduced incident creation and level-two escalations. He doesn't walk through the models themselves, so treat this part as the outline of an approach rather than a recipe.

The numbers, from the talk and its abstract: MTTD went from roughly 12 minutes to under one minute (58 seconds in his example), mean time to mitigation from about 45 to 50 minutes down to 10 to 12, and false-positive alerts from around 18% to about 4%. That last one matters most for on-call morale.

## Rings by geography

The second idea is Ring-Based Geolocation Routing. If users are on the East Coast and servers on the West Coast, you pay latency on every call, and a regional failure can take down the whole application. Rohit's team localized event processing and decisions into rings per region. He reports edge-to-cloud latency falling from about five seconds to under one, roughly an 80% improvement, and says PWI runs across thousands of nodes at edge and cloud.

## Who should watch

SREs whose dashboards are green while customers report stuck orders, and teams thinking about workflow-level SLIs. If you want implementation detail (which models, how the state machines are defined), you will need to follow up with the speaker; the value here is the reframing and the before/after numbers.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Enhancing Workflow Reliability with Dapr: Techniques to Minimize Failure Costs](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Siri_Varma_Vegiraju_workflow_dapr_failure) by Siri Varma Vegiraju (Microsoft), workflow reliability at the runtime level.
- [Optimize end user connectivity for multi-region architectures](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Christian_Elsen_Lerna_Ekmekcioglu_reliable_multiregion_arch) by Christian Elsen (AWS), on the routing side.
- [AIOps: New Approaches to Reduce Alert Noise](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Birol_Yildiz_aiops_alert_noise) by Birol Yildiz (Ilert), for the false-positive problem.

Title: Moving a message broker to AWS: rehost, replatform or refactor
Description: Ran Tao (AWS) at Conf42 SRE 2026 compares lifting RabbitMQ to EC2, Amazon MQ, and refactoring clients for SQS and SNS, with Python code.
Body:
Lift-and-shift is the fastest way to move a message broker to the cloud and the one that keeps the most work on your team. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Ran Tao, Cloud Support Engineer at Amazon Web Services, compared three migration paths for on-prem messaging (rehost on EC2, replatform onto Amazon MQ, refactor for SQS and SNS) and showed Python client code for RabbitMQ and SQS side by side.

He calls it an introductory session, and it is: a structured map of the options on AWS, from an AWS engineer, useful if you're about to make this decision.

## Two kinds of messaging

On one side sit traditional message brokers such as IBM MQ or RabbitMQ, dedicated infrastructure connecting producers and consumers. On the other sit cloud-native serverless services: on AWS, SQS for queueing and SNS for broadcasting. Ran notes how requirements differ by industry: retail needs elasticity for peaks and quiet nights, while financial and government customers care most about durability and recovery during incidents.

Running brokers on-prem means paying for capacity up front, provisioning more to scale, and keeping engineers with specialist skills to run and monitor them.

## Three paths and who owns what

**Rehost.** Mirror the OS, broker engine and configs on EC2. Few application changes and full control, but you still own patching, broker monitoring and security configuration, and native integration with IAM or CloudWatch is limited.

**Replatform.** Move to Amazon MQ, a managed broker. Configuration shrinks to deployment mode and instance size; CloudWatch metrics (connections, channels, memory, per-queue message counts) and broker logs come enabled. Scaling up is a bigger instance size and a reboot instead of editing RabbitMQ config files. TLS is enforced, data at rest can be encrypted with a KMS key, and patching happens in a weekly maintenance window you pick, for example midnight for a retailer. Single-node brokers live in one Availability Zone and suit proofs of concept; for production Ran recommends cluster mode, which mirrors messages across three nodes in three AZs so losing one doesn't lose data.

**Refactor.** Rewrite clients for SQS and SNS. Scaling and capacity become the provider's problem and pricing is per API call, so a retailer isn't paying for an idle broker fleet at night. Your team's responsibility shrinks to business logic.

## What the code actually changes

The RabbitMQ example uses Pika: set TLS 1.2 connection parameters, open a connection and channel, declare a queue, publish, then close the connection. Ran stresses closing connections, because leaked ones show up as broker memory and CPU creeping up over time. Consumers must call `basic_ack`, or the broker eventually treats them as inactive.

The SQS version has no connection management at all. Create the queue, get its URL, send and receive messages through API calls, and delete each message after processing using its receipt handle; skip that and the message reappears after the visibility timeout.

## The refactor checklist

- **Separate producers from consumers** so they scale independently; draining a backlog shouldn't require more producers.
- **Know your delivery model.** A broker does point-to-point and publish-subscribe in one place. On AWS they split: SQS is point-to-point, SNS is publish-subscribe.
- **Protocols change.** AMQP and other persistent-connection protocols become HTTPS API calls.
- **Ordering versus scale.** SQS FIFO queues keep strict order; standard queues give best-effort ordering and scale much further.
- **Payload limits.** Messages are capped at one megabyte by default; AWS extended client libraries for Java and Python store the body in S3 and send a pointer, up to two gigabytes.
- **Auth and audit.** SQS and SNS use IAM and can log requests in CloudTrail, whereas RabbitMQ, even on Amazon MQ, may need something like an LDAP server.
- **Lost knobs.** Managed services remove some settings; you can't turn TLS off on an Amazon MQ RabbitMQ broker.

## Who should watch

Teams running RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ on-prem with a cloud migration on the roadmap, and SREs who want to know what they will still own after each option. If you already run SQS in production, you can skip it.

- [Migrating to Multi Cluster Managed Kafka with 0 Downtime](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Natan_Silnitsky_migrating_multi_cluster_managed_kafka_0_downtime) by Natan Silnitsky (Wix), a messaging migration story at scale.

Title: Why HTTP/2 sent all our Kubernetes traffic to one pod
Description: Mariem Sboui (gridX) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on an incident where kube-proxy's connection-level balancing pinned HTTP/2 traffic to a single pod.
Body:
One pod at full CPU, its siblings idle, plenty of cluster capacity, and the autoscaler perfectly happy: that was the picture after Mariem Sboui's team switched some critical services to HTTP/2. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Mariem, Senior Site Reliability Engineer at gridX, walked through the incident and its cause: Kubernetes Services balance TCP connections, not requests, and HTTP/2 puts many requests on one long-lived connection.

It is a short, focused incident review, and the kind of talk that saves someone a very confusing afternoon.

## The symptoms didn't add up

External users saw extra latency, which Mariem put at more than 300 milliseconds. Not catastrophic, but real. Looking at the backends, one pod was serving essentially all incoming traffic while the others sat idle.

What made it confusing was everything that looked fine. Nodes and pods had idle capacity. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler was working normally. And killing the hot pod didn't help: the traffic simply landed on another single pod, with no redistribution. Mariem is candid about the team's mistake. They assumed HTTP/2 would behave like HTTP/1.1 inside Kubernetes, without knowing what happens one layer down.

## Layer 4 balancing meets multiplexing

By default a Kubernetes Service does Layer 4 load balancing. When a new TCP connection arrives, kube-proxy picks a backend pod and every request on that connection goes to that pod. Nothing looks at individual requests.

That works for HTTP/1.x because clients typically open many short-lived connections, and each new connection can land on a different pod. HTTP/2 changes the deal: a client multiplexes many requests over a single connection, and those connections tend to stay open for a long time. So kube-proxy makes one choice and the whole stream follows it. One pod gets everything, its CPU spikes and throttles, and latency climbs for users.

## A quick patch, then a six-month fix

The short-term changes were all at the application level: tuning keep-alive settings, reducing connection reuse in the HTTP/2 clients, and increasing the number of active connections. That spread traffic out enough to stop the bleeding, and Mariem is clear that it was only a stopgap.

The permanent fix is Layer 7 routing: a service mesh, an HTTP-aware proxy, or an API gateway or ingress that routes per request. Her team chose a service mesh, specifically Istio, and the rollout took about six months. The proxy inspects each HTTP request and decides per request, taking into account paths, headers, routing rules, backend latency and health. Distribution afterwards isn't perfectly equal, but it is far better than the default.

That six-month number is worth remembering. The incident fix took days; the architectural fix took two quarters.

## The takeaways

- Don't rely on default kube-proxy load balancing for HTTP/2-based traffic. That includes gRPC and anything else that keeps connections open.
- Put Layer 7 load balancing in front of those services.
- Run enough backend pods that capacity can actually absorb the distribution.

## Who should watch

Anyone about to enable HTTP/2 or gRPC inside a Kubernetes cluster, and anyone staring at one hot pod with an autoscaler that sees no problem. Platform teams debating whether a mesh is worth the cost will find a concrete reason here. It's short, practical, and has a real incident at its centre.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [A Developer's Introduction to Service Mesh](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Rosemary_Wang_introduction_service_mesh) by Rosemary Wang (HashiCorp), if Layer 7 routing is new territory.
- [Developing custom Load Balancer using Envoy](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Sandeep_Bhat_custom_load_balancer_envoy) by Sandeep Bhat (Harness), for the proxy-level view.
- [gRPC in Python. Build fast scalable APIs for your services](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2023_Aditya_Mattos_grpc_fast_scalable_apis) by Aditya Mattos (Kandji), the protocol most likely to trigger this.

Title: Run VMs as Kubernetes resources to cut hybrid on-call pain
Description: Shruthi Rajashekar (Broadcom) at Conf42 SRE 2026 on VM Service in VCF, which manages virtual machines and containers through one Kubernetes control plane.
Body:
If your on-call rotation covers containers in Kubernetes and VMs in a separate virtualization stack, you are on call for two platforms with two sets of alerts, dashboards and runbooks. At Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2026, Shruthi Rajashekar, Engineering Manager at Broadcom who leads VM Service in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), argued for managing both through one Kubernetes control plane, with VMs declared and reconciled like any other resource.

To be clear about scope: this is a talk about a Broadcom product, VM Service in VCF, from the team that builds it. Shruthi has spent a decade at VMware and Broadcom and worked on vMotion, so the hybrid problem is home turf.

## Two worlds, one pager

The pain she describes is operational fragmentation. Containers live in Kubernetes-native tooling; VMs live in another stack with different APIs and consoles. During an incident, SREs correlate alerts from different systems and switch context to troubleshoot, and automation is hard to standardize when every workload type has its own lifecycle model. Most enterprises still run critical workloads on VMs while newer services run in containers, so this split isn't going away on its own.

## A VM as a first-class Kubernetes resource

VM Service makes a virtual machine something you declare, deploy, scale and manage with the same Kubernetes primitives as a pod or a deployment. You write the desired state in a manifest; the platform provisions it and keeps reconciling. That brings the usual Kubernetes benefits to VMs:

- VM specs can live in Git next to application code, so GitOps workflows apply to them too.
- Provisioning becomes repeatable and auditable instead of a console click or a one-off script.
- Engineers stop asking which system owns a workload during an incident; they interact with Kubernetes either way.

The same automation, policies and playbooks then apply across both workload types.

## Where reliability actually improves

Shruthi's list of reliability gains is concrete enough to test against your own setup:

- **Consistent alerts and metrics.** When VMs and containers sit under the same orchestration layer, alerts are generated the same way and metrics follow the same patterns, so incident response becomes predictable.
- **Capacity planning as one pool.** Instead of reasoning about separate resource pools for VMs and containers, teams can plan holistically.
- **Policy-driven rollouts and isolation.** Rollout safety, resource isolation and security policies can be enforced programmatically for VMs, and Kubernetes scheduling and policy help limit blast radius.
- **Unified telemetry.** Correlating CPU pressure, network anomalies or latency spikes across VMs and containers in one view, rather than across two monitoring pipelines.

## Modernize without rewriting

Her closing point is the most persuasive for teams with real legacy estates: you don't have to containerize everything to adopt cloud-native operations. Bring existing VM workloads under Kubernetes governance, keep newer services in containers, and modernize incrementally. The legacy application that nobody wants to rewrite gets declarative management and safer rollouts without a migration project.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE teams on VMware or VCF who run mixed VM and container estates and are tired of two operational models. If you're not in the VMware world, the talk still frames the case for unifying control planes, but the mechanics are specific to VM Service. It is an overview talk; expect architecture and benefits rather than a demo or incident numbers.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [KubeVirt Alchemy: Transforming VMs into Kubernetes Workloads](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Koray_Oksay_Batuhan_Apaydin_kubevirt_vms_kubernetes_workloads) by Koray Oksay and Batuhan Apaydin (Kubermatic), the open-source route to the same idea.
- [Debugging cluster issues as an on-call SRE](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Pravar_Agrawal_debugging_cluster_oncall) by Pravar Agrawal (IBM).
