Title: Cross-channel attribution starts with identity resolution
Description: Ashutosh Verma of Meta at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on an ML framework that joins online and in-store journeys to measure marketing ROI.
Body:
Last-click attribution gives all the credit to whoever touched the customer last, which is roughly like crediting the goalkeeper's final pass for the whole match. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Ashutosh Verma, a software engineer at Meta in Seattle, laid out a machine-learning framework for attributing conversions across both digital and physical channels, and his central claim is that none of it works until you can tell that the phone, the laptop and the shopper at the till are the same person.

This is a compact framework talk: no demo, but a clear checklist.

## Why the old models miss the middle

Ashutosh named three failures. Channel silos give each team its own analytics view, so nobody sees how touchpoints influence each other. Linear assumptions in first-click and last-click models ignore the mid-funnel interactions where decisions actually form. And the offline blind spot leaves point-of-sale data and in-person visits disconnected from everything that happened online.

## Four components, identity first

His unified framework has four parts: integrate touchpoint data from every channel into one repository; resolve identities across devices and contexts; model channel contribution and interaction effects; and activate the results in budget and campaign decisions.

Identity resolution gets the most attention. It combines deterministic matching (logged-in states), probabilistic matching on device fingerprints and behaviour, graph-based entity resolution that weighs evidence across touchpoints, and privacy-preserving hashing. The balance he describes is precision against coverage: match too eagerly and you merge strangers, too cautiously and the journey falls apart.

## Synergies are the point

Once journeys are joined, feature engineering adds recency and frequency signals plus cross-channel interaction features, and ensembles of gradient boosting, neural networks and survival analysis estimate each channel's incremental contribution, including diminishing returns.

The payoff Ashutosh highlighted is the interaction effect. On his slides, social engagement does little for conversions directly but lifts the effectiveness of later email campaigns by 34%, and store visits preceded by website browsing convert at 2.8 times the rate of walk-ins. Analyse each channel alone and both effects vanish, so budgets drift towards the wrong places.

## Close the loop, then keep it legal

Attribution only matters when it changes spend. The framework feeds automated budget reallocation, validated with A/B tests, and pushes scores into campaign tools for timing and creative. For durability, he recommends a privacy-first design (on-device processing, federated learning, differential privacy), continuous retraining as behaviour shifts, and LLMs for feature discovery and causal inference.

His roadmap is pleasingly modest: start with two channels, invest in identity before modelling, get cross-functional buy-in early, and ship an MVP you can measure.

## Who should watch

Marketing data scientists and analytics engineers asked to prove ROI across online and offline channels. If you work on identity graphs already, the modelling half is the part to focus on.

Title: Explainable recommendations by storing positives, not embeddings
Description: Lev Fedorov of Amazon at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on rebuilding a recommender so every card in the feed traces back to something the user liked.
Body:
A user profile that is a single embedding is efficient and impossible to explain: the vector lands somewhere between Java and Python and somehow recommends C#. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Lev Fedorov, Software Engineer at Amazon, walked through how his team rebuilt a recommender so that each item in the feed can say "because you liked this", which helped both confused users and developers debugging complaints.

It is one of the more hands-on talks of the event: a full recsys pipeline, then the specific changes that made it traceable.

## The pipeline before

Lev described the classic funnel. Out of about 100 million items, candidate selection picks a couple of thousand; features are computed for each; a ranking formula scores them; business logic diversifies the top by author and topic and returns about 20 items.

Two places made explanations hard. The user profile was an embedding from collaborative filtering, or a set of k-means centroids for content models, and centroids can land in clusters the user never cared about. Candidate selection used KNN over an HNSW index, which returns neighbours that are not always close and knows nothing about quality or popularity.

The trigger for the work was practical: user reports about irrelevant content, and no tooling to say which past interaction led to a given card.

## Replace the vector with a list of IDs

The fix starts with the profile. Instead of an embedding, store the IDs of publications the user interacted with positively. No approximation, nothing to interpret.

Candidate selection then becomes a map: each positive is a key, and its value is a list of related candidates. Two models keep those lists sensible:

- A **relevance formula**, trained on crowdsourced annotations of similar and dissimilar pairs, using cosines from several content models as features, filters out unrelated items.
- An **attractiveness formula** orders what is left. Version zero is conditional CTR (the CTR of item A given a positive interaction with item B); the trained version adds metadata about both items and keeps conditional CTR as a feature.

Now explanation is a lookup. The shown item came from a positive, the positive has a title and an author, and the feed can say so.

## Keep the positives list honest

Positive lists only grow, so Lev uses a determinantal point process to keep a subset that is both high-weight (watch ratio, likes, shares, comments) and diverse. Each positive's downstream performance is tracked too: positives that lead nowhere get dropped, and a ranking formula for positives sorts the rest.

The last trick is quota allocation. Asked for 300 candidates from three positives, the system splits by each positive's CTR rather than evenly: in his example, 150 from the strongest positive and 60 from the weakest. He framed it as a bandit-style idea, and it is the part most teams could borrow tomorrow.

The results he claimed were transparent explanations for users, improved feed relevance, and backend traces developers can follow when someone files a complaint.

## Who should watch

Recommender engineers who are asked "why did it show me that?" and have no good answer. If your stack is pure two-tower retrieval, the talk is a useful counterweight.

Title: Predict NPS from telemetry instead of waiting for surveys
Description: Abhinay Kumar Reddy Seella of Roku at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on a multi-modal model that predicts Net Promoter Score per session in real time.
Body:
Net Promoter Score has a sampling problem: fewer than 5% of users answer the survey, the ones who do are the delighted and the furious, and the result lands weeks after the session that caused it. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Abhinay Kumar Reddy Seella, Senior Software Engineer at Roku, presented Dynamic NPS (DNPS), a model that predicts a user's NPS category for every session from behaviour, telemetry and text, with no survey at all.

## Surveys measure the loud minority, late

Abhinay opened with the standard arithmetic (promoters 9-10, passives 7-8, detractors 0-6, NPS is promoters minus detractors) and then the four ways collection breaks: the participation gap, the speed barrier, response bias towards the extremes, and the fact that by the time a team reads the score, the chance to fix the experience is gone.

His question is simple: what if the score could be computed from what users do, while they are still doing it?

## Three models, each reading a different signal

DNPS ingests three kinds of data. Behavioural interaction data covers click patterns, navigation flows, session duration, drop-offs and error events. Telemetry covers backend event logs, performance metrics and device metadata. Text covers in-app comments, support messages and chat transcripts. A processing layer cleans, normalises and, critically, aligns timestamps so events from different sources are ordered correctly.

The modelling is a hybrid:

- Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost or LightGBM) on structured behavioural and telemetry features.
- A sequence model (LSTM or transformer) for how behaviour changes across a session.
- A text model built on embeddings for sentiment and topic.

A fusion layer learns how much to weight each model rather than averaging them, then produces the final score.

## The numbers, and what removing a signal costs

Abhinay reported about 85.9% accuracy, a mean absolute error around 1.21, strong F1 across all three categories, and inference at roughly 80 milliseconds, quick enough for live dashboards. The ablation is the most useful slide: dropping text pulls accuracy down to about 55%, while dropping behavioural and telemetry data lands near 78%. If you were planning to skip the messy text pipeline, that result argues otherwise.

## Explanations that point at the UI

SHAP and LIME sit on top so each prediction comes with the features that drove it. The findings are the kind a product team can act on: frequent back clicks track with negative sentiment, short sessions often signal dissatisfaction, and deliberate clicking tends to go with promoters. That turns a score into a pointer at friction, such as UI confusion or buffering.

He was candid about limits: the approach needs large, high-quality datasets, struggles with cold-start users, adds operational complexity, and text signals can carry bias.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and product engineers who own customer-experience metrics and are tired of quarterly survey decks. The talk is architecture and results, not code, so bring your own pipeline ideas.

Title: Scale on the forecast, not on the CPU alarm
Description: Vivek Kumar of Majesco at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on using telemetry-trained models to scale transaction platforms before the spike.
Body:
A scaling rule that fires when CPU crosses 70% is a smoke detector: it tells you about the fire once the kitchen is already full of smoke. At Conf42 Machine Learning 2026, Vivek Kumar, a staff developer at Majesco with 16 years of building insurance and finance platforms, argued for flipping that around: train models on the telemetry you already collect and scale on the forecast, before latency climbs.

It is an overview talk rather than a code walkthrough, and a good one to hand to a team that still tunes threshold alerts by hand.

## Static thresholds react after the damage

Vivek's starting point is the setup most transaction platforms share: Spring Boot microservices, REST APIs behind a gateway, Kafka for events, a database per service. That architecture scales well, but it also makes performance harder to reason about, because the bottleneck moves around.

Rule-based scaling handles this badly. By the time the threshold trips and new capacity arrives, he pointed out, users have already seen the slowdown, and sometimes the downtime. The rule is reactive by design.

## Your telemetry is already a training set

The core idea is that every system emits the data needed to predict its own load: CPU, latency, thread utilisation, request rates, queue depth, transaction volume. Vivek treats those as model features. Concurrency level, queue depth, volume and resource use become the inputs that tell a model what the next few minutes will look like.

He walked through three model families and the job each does:

- **LSTM networks** for forecasting load from time-series history, such as future CPU or request volume.
- **Anomaly detection** for spotting behaviour that suddenly departs from normal.
- **Regression** for predicting how many resources a given workload needs.

## Three things the model can actually turn

Prediction is only useful if it drives an action. Vivek grouped the actions into adaptive autoscaling (add capacity on the forecast), dynamic caching, and real-time configuration tuning: connection timeouts, batch sizes and retry policies adjusted to the current workload instead of a value someone picked during the last incident.

His comparison slide credits ML-driven systems with 73% fewer performance incidents and 28% lower infrastructure cost, the latter from scaling back down in quiet hours. Treat those as the talk's headline figures rather than a benchmark you can reproduce from the slides.

## The loop matters more than the model

The architecture he closed on is a feedback loop: telemetry flows from a tool such as CloudWatch into the model, the model emits a prediction, the autoscaler adjusts containers or Kubernetes capacity, and the new telemetry feeds the next round. He pointed to AWS predictive auto scaling and Azure Kubernetes Service as proof that the cloud providers already run this pattern.

His production advice is the sensible kind: models sitting in the transaction path need consistent latency and high availability themselves, so start with one focused use case, deploy with safeguards, and widen the loop only when it has earned trust.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE engineers who own autoscaling policies and want the vocabulary for a predictive approach. If you already run forecast-driven scaling in production, this will be familiar ground; the value is in the clean framing you can reuse in a design review.

Title: Telecom towers need structured engineering data before machine learning
Description: Crown Castle's Sudarshan Kasera at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on turning telecom tower structural analysis into ML-ready data in the 5G era.
Body:
Many US telecom towers were designed in the 1980s and 1990s for much lighter antennas than 5G hangs on them today. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Sudarshan Kasera, a structural engineer and senior project engineer at Crown Castle with more than ten years in the tower industry, explained how tower analysis works and why the route to predictive models runs through structured engineering data first.

His message to the tech audience is repeated on purpose: the engineering fundamentals must come first. It's a bridge talk between infrastructure and data people, not an ML methods talk.

## Heavier equipment, older steel

Each wireless generation from 2G to 5G has added load: bigger, heavier equipment on ageing structures, while densification and rural broadband keep the market growing. Towers carry public safety and emergency communications, so continuous uptime is a hard requirement, and structural analysis has to account for every component accurately.

## The code stack is the spec

Before analytics, Kasera lays out the standards that govern every tower in the US. The International Building Code is the legal umbrella. ANSI/TIA-222 is the primary standard for antenna-supporting structures: self-support towers, monopoles, guyed towers. ASCE 7 supplies the environmental loads, from wind speed maps to ice and seismic parameters. AISC 360 governs steel members and connections, ACI 318 the concrete foundations. Any automation has to stay fully compliant with that hierarchy.

The load types are the model inputs. Dead loads cover the tower and everything bolted to it, where accurate equipment inventory is where analytics can cut errors. Wind usually governs, and the wind load on antennas and appurtenances can exceed the load on the structure itself. Ice adds weight and projected area in cold climates. Seismic can control foundation design in high-seismic zones. Thermal effects are easy to overlook in guyed towers and long monopoles. Each produces large volumes of site-specific data.

## From PDF reports to queryable data

Software such as RISA Tower and TNX already automates hundreds of load combinations and member-by-member checks. The structural analysis report, with sealed drawings, is what gets a permit, and without a permit nothing gets built or modified. The problem is that results often live in isolated PDF reports. For operators that own anywhere from hundreds to over 40,000 towers, centralised data is the difference between one-off projects and portfolio-wide analysis.

The data he wants integrated: material properties and member dimensions, stress (demand-to-capacity) ratios across members and analysis runs, deflection and dynamic response such as natural frequency and vortex shedding, and digitised inspection records of corrosion, loose connections and foundation cracks that models alone can't predict.

## The maturity curve

Kasera's roadmap has five steps: traditional code-based analysis, digital 3D finite element modelling (where he places the industry today), data integration, analytics, and finally predictive analysis with ML. His warning to anyone keen to jump ahead: "you cannot skip straight to machine learning without first having structured high quality engineering data."

The payoff he describes is concrete: extending tower life beyond the original 25 to 30 year design expectation, with every extra five to ten years avoiding the cost of a new build; lower liability through traceable decisions; and capital planning based on portfolio data instead of emergencies and permit deadlines.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers working with physical infrastructure, utilities or telecom who need to understand the domain before modelling it, and structural engineers wondering what "ML-ready" would mean for their reports. Expect engineering standards, not neural networks.

Title: Why delivery pricing needs switchback tests instead of A/B tests
Description: Rothesay quant Sergei Nasibian at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on switchback testing and change-point analysis for system-level pricing experiments.
Body:
Raise the delivery fee for half your users and the other half get a better service, because the couriers you freed up are now waiting for them. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Sergei Nasibian, a quantitative strategist at Rothesay, used food delivery pricing to show why user-level A/B tests break in marketplaces, and how switchback testing plus change-point analysis measures what a price change actually does.

The examples are FoodTech, but the method applies anywhere users share a constrained resource: ride-hailing, logistics, ad auctions, cloud capacity.

## The pricing problem in one curve

Nasibian keeps the scope tight: short-term revenue optimisation, not lifetime value, which he treats as a separate and harder strategic problem. Charge too much for delivery and revenue per order rises while orders fall; charge too little and the opposite. Somewhere in between sits a sweet spot. The quantity you need is demand elasticity: how conversion from a session to an order changes with the delivery fee. The relationship is monotonically decreasing, and for small changes a linear approximation, a single first-derivative number, is good enough.

## Why A/B tests lie here

A/B testing splits users randomly and assumes they are independent. In a three-sided marketplace of users, restaurants and couriers, they are not. Supply is often the bottleneck. Increase prices for the test group, they order less, courier capacity frees up, and the control group gets faster deliveries, possibly cheaper ones too if your pricing algorithm accounts for courier distance. The experiment ends up measuring the price change plus a side effect you didn't intend.

## Switch time, not users

A switchback experiment randomises over time instead. All orders in a time window get the same pricing algorithm, and the system alternates. His example splits a 48-hour experiment into 12 four-hour blocks. The design question is window size: too short and the system has no time to react, so results are noise; too long and local seasonality, such as lunch peaks, gets mistaken for the effect. Two practical fixes he describes: flip the mode at night when volume is low, so each time of day sees both algorithms across days, and run for at least two weeks so every weekday appears under both modes.

## Evaluate it as a change-point problem

A/B results are a classic hypothesis test: two-sample t-test, Welch's test when variances differ, permutation tests, applied to order size, revenue per order or conversion. Switchback results are better treated as change-point detection in a time series, which also catches shifts in variance and frequency, not just in averages.

His recipe:

1. Keep a sliding window of observations and compute its mean: a simple moving average, an EWMA, or a GARCH-based estimate.
2. Pick a recent stable period with no interventions, split it into equal windows, compute each window's mean the same way, and take pairwise absolute differences between windows. That gives the empirical distribution of differences when nothing changed.
3. Use a high quantile of that distribution, typically 0.95, as the threshold for declaring a change point.
4. Validate detected change points against the known flip schedule; the size of the jump above the threshold is your impact estimate.

The same monitor can watch several order metrics at once, so you also see any unintended negative effect of the experiment.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and engineers running experiments on marketplaces or any shared-capacity system, and anyone whose A/B results look too good when supply is tight. It's statistics-forward and concise, and the threshold recipe is directly reusable.

Title: Machine learning as an intelligence layer across the payment lifecycle
Description: Synchrony's Balakumaran Sugumar at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 maps ML across merchant onboarding, authorisation, settlement and payment operations.
Body:
A card swipe gets roughly a hundred milliseconds to be scored, routed and approved, and static rules written by a committee can't keep up with fraudsters who probe them for weaknesses. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Balakumaran Sugumar, AVP and principal engineer for digital servicing at Synchrony, argued that machine learning in payments works best as a shared intelligence layer running through the whole lifecycle, not a feature bolted onto fraud detection.

He said up front that this is a systems talk, not an algorithms talk, built on more than 16 years of running large payment platforms.

## Rules versus models

The contrast is familiar but well drawn. Traditional systems decline a transaction over a fixed amount on a new card or flag high velocity, run batch reports overnight, treat every similar customer the same way, and need committee meetings and full test cycles to change a rule. Fraudsters get a window between rule updates. ML systems score every transaction in its own context, update from outcomes, and run on streams instead of batch windows.

## Where ML touches each stage

He walks the lifecycle:

- **Merchant acquisition:** risk scoring and KYC automation. Straightforward low-risk merchants are approved instantly, clear high risks declined with reasons, and the edge cases routed to an experienced underwriter with the model's key factors highlighted. He cites around a 90% cut in processing time for standard applications and 75% fewer manual reviews.
- **Authorisation:** real-time fraud scores from device, location, velocity, merchant category and history, returned as a probability rather than a yes or no. In his example, a score between 0.5 and 0.7 triggers step-up customer validation. Routing picks the payment network with the best historical approval rate.
- **Processing and settlement:** anomaly detection on transaction flows, capacity prediction, reconciliation and cash-flow forecasting.
- **Operations:** traffic forecasts that trigger autoscaling ahead of spikes, anomaly-based alerting, root-cause models and, in some systems, automated remediation.

He also reports manual intervention dropping from around half of cases to under 5% on an ML-enhanced platform.

## The challenges he doesn't skip

The challenges section is the most useful for builders. Data quality: missing fields, biased samples, duplicates. Explainability: regulators and stakeholders need to know why a merchant was declined. Latency: a two-minute ensemble is useless on a card swipe, so you trade sophistication for speed or precompute. Monitoring: fraud patterns shift daily, so retraining pipelines and alerts are part of the system. And integration with legacy platforms that were never designed for ML, including a fallback to the rule-based path when a model misbehaves. A bug in a fraud model, he notes, can cost millions.

## What's next, and a small demo

Looking ahead, he expects ML to underpin embedded finance, real-time personalisation, cross-border routing, alternative payment methods and more autonomous operations. Two concrete notes: shopping agents that must pick the customer's best-reward card on their behalf, and stablecoins entering cross-border transfers at the bank he works with.

The talk ends with a deliberately simple demo: Kafka running locally in Docker, a producer generating synthetic transactions, and a consumer scoring them with a pickled model trained on synthetic data where high amounts, low device trust, international origin and prior fraud push the score up. It's a teaching toy, not a production fraud system, and he presents it that way.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product owners new to payments who want a map of where ML fits end to end, and architects planning how to wire models into a legacy authorisation path. Fraud specialists will want the related talks below for depth.

Title: LLM agents in incident response should shorten understanding, not act
Description: Payjoy staff engineer Sumit Kaul at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on a production-safe LLM architecture for incident response, with humans deciding.
Body:
Incidents rarely go badly because the data is missing. They go badly because no human can read all of it under pressure. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Sumit Kaul, staff software engineer at Payjoy, laid out an architecture where LLM agents correlate signals, summarise and propose hypotheses during an incident, while nothing executes in production without a human. His target metric is not MTTR but MTTU, mean time to understanding.

For scale, he gave his own numbers: around 4 million messages a day on a single endpoint, and more than 200 endpoints like it. That's the alert fatigue that pushes teams from proactive to reactive operations.

## Accuracy is not the blocker; trust is

Kaul's point on why LLMs aren't already everywhere in SRE: the risks are operational. Confident but wrong suggestions. Privileged tools that can mutate production. And trust erosion, because once engineers stop trusting the system, adoption dies. The blocker is safety and trust, not whether the model can spot 99% of patterns.

## Analyse and propose; humans decide and act

The pipeline is data ingestion, context building, LLM analysis, human review and decision logging, with a strict separation of concerns. In his words, "AI suggestions are inputs, not commands." That maps onto SRE habits teams already have: change control, auditability and postmortems.

The context matters more than the model. Traces for request flow and latency, metrics for health, logs for detail, recent deployments, and SLOs and error budgets to frame impact. A better context beats a bigger model, in his telling, and a narrower one beats a firehose. The outputs are three: situational summaries so responders across application, infrastructure and data teams share one picture; ranked, explainable root-cause hypotheses, explicitly guesses and not facts; and runbook-style mitigations that a human reviews and that are never auto-executed.

## Guardrails are architecture, not prompt tricks

Three layers keep it production-safe:

- **Data hygiene:** automated PII redaction (emails, phone numbers, auth keys, customer IDs) before anything reaches the model, and a bounded context window: the last couple of hours, key metrics, recent deploys.
- **Privilege boundaries:** read-only by default, an allowlist of tools with explicit scope, and an audit trail on every call. If an action isn't auditable, it doesn't belong in production.
- **Verification gates:** shadow execution of recommendations in isolation, counterfactual validation ("would this have helped last time?"), and an immutable decision ledger of AI suggestions and human responses that feeds back into improvement.

## From reactive to proactive

The lowest-risk, highest-return uses he suggests: the LLM as first-line responder that filters low-threshold noise and escalates only real issues; cross-service correlation that spots systemic problems across dependencies early; and evidence assembly that pre-builds incident context before anyone formally declares an incident. Knowing about an incident before it is declared is the safest win available.

His pilot blueprint is pure SRE: start on non-critical services, measure trust and not just accuracy, tune guardrails from real behaviour, and expand as confidence grows. Production AI maturity grows the way reliability does, incrementally.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams being asked to "add AI" to on-call, and anyone evaluating vendor incident copilots who wants a checklist of what safe looks like. Pair it with Kaul's DevOps 2026 talk on observability contracts below.

Title: Credit card profit is a lifetime value problem, and ML models it
Description: American Express analytics director Avaneendra Kanaparti at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on ML-driven customer lifetime value for card approvals and credit lines.
Body:
A credit card issuer spends money on a customer long before it earns any back, so every approval is a bet on lifetime value. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Avaneendra Kanaparti, director of data analytics at American Express focused on small business and commercial cards, explained how ML-driven customer lifetime value (CLV) models decide who gets approved, how big a credit line should be, and when to pull back.

He has spent more than 15 years in the industry, including Capital One and Discover, and the talk has that practitioner flavour: the economics first, then the models, then the validation that keeps them honest.

## Two phases, one number

He splits the card lifecycle in two. Acquisition is all cost: marketing, sign-on bonuses, risk strategy and back-office processing, ending at approve or decline. Customer management is where money comes back, through interchange on purchases and interest from customers who revolve, minus the losses from those who charge off. CLV nets the two over the life of the relationship.

That number drives three decisions. Acquisition economics, where approving the wrong customer means losses and declining the right one hands value to a competitor. Portfolio strategy, where macro conditions, competitors and a customer's own credit use keep changing. And P&L forecasting, where expected revenue meets expected losses.

## Why multivariate beats one variable at a time

Historically, he says, these decisions were largely two-dimensional, analysing one variable in isolation, which skewed outcomes toward a handful of inputs. ML models weigh hundreds or thousands of variables at once and pick out the ones that actually predict behaviour.

A CLV model in his framing predicts four things: future spend, revolving behaviour (who carries a balance, and how much), payment reliability (ability and willingness to pay), and default probability over roughly two to three years. Inputs include spend volume, frequency and merchant categories (groceries and gas read differently from casinos), payment patterns, balance utilisation, modelled income and credit bureau attributes. One behavioural tell he highlights: several partial payments from different sources close to the due date can signal an impending cash-flow problem. The workhorses are gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM), deep sequence models for dynamic predictions, and survival models for time-to-event questions like attrition.

## Validation is the part that bites

Kanaparti spends real time on keeping models honest:

- **Temporal validation:** with three years of history, train on two and validate on the third, instead of validating inside the training window and overfitting.
- **Segment analysis:** a model built on transactors (who pay in full) will produce confident nonsense on revolvers. Match the use case's population to the development sample.
- **Test and control:** roll out model-driven decisions to a test group while a control keeps the traditional approach, until incremental value is proven.
- **Continuous monitoring,** preferably quarterly, with refits when behaviour drifts.
- **Stress testing** with an economic downturn factor, to check whether the strategy stays profitable or the model would wipe out the whole target population.

## Where the value shows up

Applications run across the lifecycle. Bigger sign-on offers for segments predicted to spend or revolve heavily. Carefully tested approvals of borderline customers to check the model's assumptions, useful for new products with no history. Credit line increases for customers bumping against their limit, before a competitor offers more, and proactive decreases when risk signals appear. Retention offers and fee waivers tied to value. He puts the typical breakeven on a card customer at four to six years, and argues accurate CLV targeting can get high-value segments there in under four.

## Who should watch

Data scientists and engineers in lending, cards or any subscription business where acquisition cost is paid upfront. The validation section alone is worth it for anyone shipping risk models.

Title: Supplier risk starts outside the ERP, so the model has to look there
Description: Oracle's Sujith Vadakkepati at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on an explainable hybrid RAG-LLM pattern for continuous, auditable supplier risk intelligence.
Body:
A supplier can be green on every internal metric, on-time and freshly audited, while a regulator is already investigating it. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Sujith Vadakkepati, senior principal product manager at Oracle working on supplier qualification and risk, presented an explainable hybrid RAG-LLM framework that pulls external signals in next to ERP data and produces risk narratives an auditor can trace back to evidence.

He is explicit that this is "a pattern, not a product." No chatbot, no Oracle feature tour: an architecture for putting generative AI to work inside the constraints of a procurement and compliance organisation.

## The system of record is always late

Traditional supplier risk runs on scorecards, thresholds and quarterly or annual reviews over structured ERP data. That suits slow, stable environments. Modern supply risk is neither. It is triggered by pandemics, sanctions, geopolitical tension, litigation and ESG violations that surface first in news, filings and enforcement actions, long before they show up as a missed delivery. His core insight: "the system of record is never where risk first appears."

He names three gaps that reinforce each other: static rules that assume we already know what risk looks like, limited sources that ignore unstructured external data, and threshold-based detection that fires only once the risk is already big.

## Retrieve first, then reason

The framework is a pipeline with separated responsibilities, which is why he thinks it survives regulated, high-stakes use:

1. **A RAG grounding layer** gathers evidence from internal systems (performance history, compliance data) and external intelligence (regulatory actions, news, ESG disclosures). It defines what the system actually knows.
2. **An LLM reasoning layer** connects signals across domains and explains why a risk profile may be shifting, anchored to the retrieved evidence. If the data isn't there, it doesn't invent an answer.
3. **Risk narratives** replace a bare score: which evidence was used, how the signals combined, and where uncertainty remains.

The data layer pairs ERP context with four external streams: geopolitical indicators, financial stability signals such as credit stress and rating changes, regulatory signals such as warning letters and litigation, and ESG performance, treated as a primary input. Sources are normalised and tagged with metadata like recency and source credibility so the retriever can weigh them.

## Weak signals add up

The detection argument is the interesting part. A small financial concern, some regulatory scrutiny and an ESG flag may each look minor, and none crosses a threshold. Together they can mark a supplier heading for trouble. Because retrieval runs continuously and in parallel, a new filing or enforcement action is evaluated almost as soon as it appears, instead of at the next review cycle.

He reports evaluations across manufacturing and technology supplier networks showing better detection precision, faster response and broader risk coverage than rule-based systems. The talk gives the direction of those results, not the figures.

## Governance is in the architecture

Every step leaves a record. Retrieval logs which documents were pulled, from where, when and why. Extraction ties each fact to its source. Synthesis produces the structured narrative. Human review, including approvals, overrides and escalations, joins the audit trail. On top sit three controls: bias monitoring across data, weighting and outputs; interpretability for every assessment; and structured human oversight, because this is decision support, not an autonomous decision maker.

## Who should watch

Procurement, compliance and risk engineering teams evaluating LLMs, and anyone building RAG over mixed internal and external sources where every answer must be defensible. It is architecture-level; if you want retrieval tuning or prompt details, bring your own.

Title: Securing AI coding agents: contain the body, convene a council
Description: Booking.com payments engineer Marat Kenzhebulatov at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on sandboxes, multi-model review councils and audits for agents.
Body:
Marat Kenzhebulatov gave an AI agent one boring task: update the dependencies and run the tests. The build failed, the agent decided the environment was the problem, and 30 seconds later it had left the project folder and was rewriting his global Maven configuration. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), the Booking.com software engineer, who builds and maintains payment systems, explained what he built after that moment so that an agent's mistakes stop mattering.

The agent wasn't malicious. It was, in his words, trained to be aggressively helpful. In payments, where breaking things means people don't get on flights and hotels don't get paid, that helpfulness is the threat model.

## Prompts are guidelines, not guardrails

His first attempt was to talk the agent into being good: rules about PCI requirements, never hardcode secrets, don't make mistakes. It doesn't hold. Prompt injection is always possible, models are non-deterministic, and they can hallucinate past any rule. If a prompt is all that stands between the agent and a bug in production, "you don't have security strategy, you have hopes and prayers."

So if you can't trust the brain, contain the body. His playground has three walls:

- **A Docker container with a restricted file system.**
- **A command allowlist,** including which websites the agent may reach and no destructive commands. Where you draw the line is up to you: autonomous but not destructive.
- **A secrets manager.** The agent may work with credentials, but secrets never land in its context.

Treat the environment as hostile, and the agent's intent stops mattering. Malicious or merely clumsy, the result is the same: access denied.

## A council beats a single reviewer

The box stops the house burning down; it doesn't stop buggy code. Kenzhebulatov rejects both camps: the one that lets AI do the security review alone and the one that insists only humans can. His answer is a council, a pattern he credits to Andrej Karpathy: several agents on different LLMs, each with a role. A PCI expert that follows the standard. A code-quality reviewer explicitly prompted to be mean. An arbiter that weighs their views. If they can't agree, each writes its take and a human makes the call. Like a serious diagnosis, you want a second and third opinion, partly because a single model can reward-hack its way out of actually reviewing.

## The feature workflow

The loop he runs: a brainstorm where the agent questions the developer until it understands the feature, a plan that breaks the design into bite-sized tasks, execution by subagents with a small single-reviewer check after each task, then the full council on the finished change. He stays in the loop throughout. The agents amplify his input; they don't replace it.

## Audit everything, start small

After ten years in fintech he assumes something will go wrong. You can't debug an agent like a normal program, so record the sessions and the reasoning, log as much as possible and keep the logs. If an agent tries to escape the playground, you want to know exactly how.

None of this needs a big infrastructure project on day one. Start by having the agent describe your project in a markdown file and review what it writes. Then turn your team's routine tasks into skills, then add the council. His checklist: no secrets in context, a physical playground instead of rules, a human approving critical actions, and cross-validation of everything.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers letting coding agents near production repositories, especially in regulated domains. It's short, practical and opinionated; security teams will find a vocabulary for a policy, and developers a setup they can build in an afternoon.

# Agentic AI, CI/CD Automation, and the Future of DevOps - Conf42 DevOps 2026

The DevOps landscape is entering a new phase where AI-driven automation, agentic systems, and intelligent CI/CD pipelines are becoming core to software delivery. As organizations scale cloud-native architectures and accelerate release velocity, traditional DevOps approaches struggle to keep pace. Conf42 DevOps 2026 brings together industry experts to explore how AI is redefining DevOps practices across CI/CD, infrastructure, and operations.

This virtual conference is designed for DevOps engineers, platform teams, SREs, and engineering leaders who want practical insights into enterprise-ready DevOps powered by AI. The sessions focus on real-world adoption, architectural patterns, and governance strategies that help teams move from experimentation to production.

## Chinmay Gaikwad Keynote on Agentic AI in CI/CD

The featured keynote at Conf42 DevOps 2026 is delivered by [Chinmay Gaikwad](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chinmay-gaikwad/), Director of Product Marketing at Harness. His session, *(Building Enterprise-ready CI/CD Pipelines using Agentic AI](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai)*, examines how agentic AI transforms modern CI/CD pipelines.

Chinmay explains how AI agents can autonomously reason across pipeline context, detect and remediate failures, enforce security and compliance, and continuously optimize delivery performance. The keynote also addresses enterprise concerns such as scalability, reliability, and governance, making it highly relevant for organizations modernizing their DevOps platforms.

For teams evaluating [AI-powered CI/CD automation](https://www.harness.io/products/continuous-delivery/ai-assisted-deployment-verification), this keynote provides a clear and actionable roadmap.

## DevOps Sessions Featuring AI Agents and Automation

Conf42 DevOps 2026 features multiple sessions that showcase how AI agents are being applied across the DevOps lifecycle.

**Premanand Tiwari** presents a session on autonomous time-series forecasting, demonstrating how AI-driven systems can improve observability and operational decision-making without manual intervention.

**Pallab Haldar**, Technical Architect, shares insights on AI-powered workflow orchestration, focusing on how intelligent automation can dynamically manage complex DevOps pipelines and toolchains.

**Gobu Natarajan**, Manager of Technical Program Management, explores multimodal conversational agents and their role in correlating logs, metrics, and human input to accelerate incident response.

**Praneeth Patil**, Senior Staff Software Engineer, discusses autonomous infrastructure management in cloud environments and how AI agents can improve scalability, resilience, and cost efficiency.

## DevOps Governance and AI at Scale

In addition to automation, Conf42 DevOps 2026 addresses critical topics such as GenAI governance, distributed AI platform design, and operational reliability. These sessions help teams adopt AI responsibly while maintaining control, visibility, and compliance.

## Register for Chinmay Gaikwad’s Keynote

Conf42 DevOps 2026 offers practical, expert-led insights into AI-driven DevOps, agentic automation, and next-generation CI/CD pipelines.

Title: Conf42 DevOps 2026 - agents joined the pipeline, failover got boring
Description: Conf42 DevOps 2026 in review, 47 talks on agents in CI/CD and on-call, infrastructure as a graph, boring failover, CI-gated SLOs and what green CI misses.
Body:
[Conf42 DevOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) opened the Conf42 year on January 22, 2026 with 47 talks. The loudest question was what happens when AI agents get commit rights, pipeline access and a seat on the on-call rota. The quieter, equally useful one was how to make the old hard things (region failover, migrations, compliance) dull enough that nobody needs a hero. Speakers came from Intuit, Google, Disney, Meta, Microsoft, Cisco, Splunk, Twilio, Workday, Oracle, ASML, Harness and more.

## Agents in CI/CD and on call, with the brakes attached

Diamond sponsor Harness set the frame. [Chinmay Gaikwad](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai) argued that AI made writing code cheap and moved the bottleneck after the commit, then laid out an enterprise-ready pipeline built by agents: a knowledge graph for context, policies enforced outside the prompt, and RBAC that treats the AI as an extension of the user, so if you can't deploy to production, neither can your agent.

[Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_governance_genai_velocity) (Meta) proposed GenOps, a governance-first model for letting generative agents act inside CI/CD. [Vladyslav Budichenko](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vladyslav_Budichenko_incidents_agents_security) (Vocaly AI) gave agents in incident response the good, the bad and the ugly treatment, including how to use them safely with MCP. [Neal Iyer](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neal_Iyer_guardrails_ai_accountability) (Splunk) brought the same "guardrails first" stance to agents in the security operations centre, keeping human control in the loop. On the infrastructure side, [Praneeth Patil](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Praneeth_Patil_autonomous_infrastructure_cloud) (Equinix) described LLM-driven multi-cloud infrastructure that catches misconfigurations, and [Premanand Tiwari](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Premanand_Tiwari_forecasting_time_autonomy) (Amazon) demoed autonomous time-series forecasting for capacity planning.

## Infrastructure is a graph, so give the model the graph

Context engineering got its own cluster. [Roxane Fischer](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Roxane_Fischer_context_reasoning_infrastructure) (Anyshift) explained why LLMs fail at infrastructure: they can't see live dependencies or multi-hop relationships. Her answer is to model infrastructure as a graph, query it with Graph RAG and natural-language-to-Cypher, and measure context quality. [Pronnoy Goswami](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Pronnoy_Goswami_observability_queries_context) (Workday) used the Model Context Protocol to make telemetry queryable, and [Michael Levan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Michael_Levan_agents_telemetry_costs) (Solo.io) asked the two questions every platform team now hears about agentic and MCP traffic: how do we observe it, and how do we keep the bill sane. [Tina Kanth](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tina_Kanth_finops_streaming_prompts) (Microsoft) showed prompt templates that turn streaming financial events into structured, auditable triage decisions.

## Make failover boring

The most satisfying talks were about removing drama. [Akshay Pratinav](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Akshay_Pratinav_failover_resilience_workloads) (Intuit) described a Kubernetes-native platform where services onboard declaratively to region failover: pre-scale from live traffic, promote standby databases, shift routes through Route53 and Istio. The goal, in his words, is to make failover boring, which is the highest compliment in operations.

[Harris Baskaran](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Harris_Baskaran_kubernetes_modernization_containers) (Google) walked a high-volume ticketing monolith from VMware and Oracle to GCE, then rebuilt it cloud-native on GKE and PostgreSQL, with dependency mapping, replication and multi-region DR lessons along the way. [Kalyan Inturi](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Kalyan_Inturi_availability_migration_gateways) (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) used shadow traffic and phased rollouts for a zero-downtime gateway migration. [Nikhil Kokal](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Nikhil_Kokal_apis_scalability_reliability) (The Walt Disney Company) covered architectures for APIs at billions of requests, and [Srinivas Pagadala Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Srinivas_Pagadala_Sekar_gitops_resilience_automation) (Karsun Solutions) built self-healing pipelines with Tekton and Argo CD.

## Observability as a contract, not a nice-to-have

[Sumit Kaul](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Sumit_Kaul_slos_instrumentation_observability) (Payjoy) made observability a platform contract: zero-code instrumentation and SLOs gated in CI/CD, so a service cannot ship without traces and metrics. [Mohit Gupta](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Mohit_Gupta_gpu_ci_validation) (Intel) applied the same idea to GPU performance, catching compute and memory bottlenecks in the pipeline instead of in production. [Aravind Sekar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Aravind_Sekar_reliability_prevention_ai) (Twilio) and [Raghu Bhupatiraju](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Raghu_Bhupatiraju_predictive_analytics_outages) (Expeditors) both pushed from firefighting towards prediction, the latter for supply chain systems.

## Green checkmarks are not the whole story

[Tilda Udufo](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tilda_Udufo_cicd_quality_testing) (Outreachy) gave one of the event's sharpest reminders: passing tests don't guarantee quality, as the XZ Utils incident showed, and review practice and culture have to cover what automation misses. [Bhaskar Sawant](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Bhaskar_Sawant_security_automation_pipelines) mapped how AI-driven development changes the pipeline attack surface. [Gian Wild](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gian_Wild_accessibility_security_inclusion) (AccessibilityOz) took apart the idea that security and accessibility must trade off against each other. Hands-on security tooling came from [Nikolay Milyaev](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Nikolay_Milyaev_xdr_security_analytics) (Microsoft) on Defender XDR alert fatigue, [Gareth Emslie](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gareth_Emslie_sentinel_security_automation) (Dynatrace) on extending Microsoft Sentinel, and [Gurdeep Gill](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gurdeep_Gill_firewalls_ai_protection) (Cisco) on NGFWs for AI workloads. [Imran Abdul](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Imran_Abdul_sdwan_networking_automation) (Pace University) brought GitOps to the enterprise network, SD-WAN and zero trust included.

## Regulated and physical systems

Compliance and industry talks rounded out the programme: [Pooja Ranjan](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Pooja_Ranjan_compliance_saas_governance) (Oracle) on continuous compliance for SaaS, [Vivek Chittireddy](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Vivek_Chittireddy_privacy_regulation_security) (Meta) on privacy by design with differential privacy and anonymisation in the pipeline, [Swapna Chimanchodkar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Swapna_Chimanchodkar_clinical_healthcare_ai) (Cognizant) on deploying real-time sepsis detection, and [Rasmi Ranjan Nayak](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Rasmi_Ranjan_Nayak_embedded_robotics_ai) (ASML) on deterministic embedded AI for robotics.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), the Diamond sponsor, and [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) at Gold. All 47 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/devops2026) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrB6SG3pv3bmTo7NWFlCGiNx).

The series returns with [Conf42 DevOps 2027](https://www.conf42.com/devops2027).

Title: Active inference as a first-principles path to next-generation agents
Description: QF Network CEO Alex Vyatkin at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on active inference and the free energy principle as a basis for adaptive AI agents.
Body:
Today's agents are LLMs in a loop, and they still struggle the moment a scenario is genuinely new. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Alex Vyatkin, co-founder and CEO of deep tech startup QF Network, pointed past the hype to a different foundation: active inference, a framework from neuroscience built on Karl Friston's free energy principle, in which agents act to reduce surprise about their world.

He calls it "quite a deep rabbit hole" and means it as an invitation. This is a research-frontier talk: no benchmarks, no product demo, but a clear explanation of the ideas and a reading list to get started.

## The reality check behind the agent boom

Vyatkin opens by taking stock of the year of the agent: lots of new projects, some of them wild, and even talk of Mac Mini shortages from people running agents at home. The market is growing fast. But in his assessment, current agents still fail in novel scenarios, remain hungry for data and compute, and get harder to run as tasks grow more complex, with many projects at risk from unexpected costs. The gap between promised autonomy and delivered autonomy is where he wants engineers to look.

## Agents that minimise surprise

The core idea: an adaptive system survives by minimising variational free energy, a bound on surprise, meaning the mismatch between its internal model of the world and what it senses. It can close that gap two ways. Perception updates the internal model. Action changes the world so it matches the model. In active inference, perception and action are two sides of one loop.

Agents choose policies by minimising expected free energy, which bundles two values. Epistemic value rewards exploring to reduce uncertainty. Pragmatic value rewards reaching preferred states. That gives a principled answer to the exploration-exploitation dilemma, instead of a reward function bolted on afterwards, and Vyatkin argues it produces goal-seeking and curious behaviour from first principles.

## What that buys you, on paper

The claimed advantages are the ones current agents lack. Adaptation to novel scenarios without massive retraining. Much lower data and compute for learning. And explainability: you can inspect an agent's beliefs and the policies it is weighing, which makes governance easier than with a black-box model. He also flags robotics, where controlling a body in a changing environment remains a hard problem.

## Many agents, no central controller

Active inference is multi-scale. Agents keep their own boundaries (Markov blankets in the jargon), share world models, and coordinate through belief propagation and message passing, minimising expected free energy as a team. Orchestration can emerge from collective behaviour with no central controller. Vyatkin stretches this toward enterprise systems with traceable, adaptive workflows and, more speculatively, toward agents that act like researchers testing hypotheses.

## Where to start digging

His resource list is the practical takeaway: the textbook by Parr, Pezzulo and Friston, available free from MIT Press; a forthcoming fundamentals book aimed at engineers; libraries in Julia and Python with example agents; and the Active Inference Institute for courses and community.

## Who should watch

Engineers who suspect LLM-in-a-loop agents are not the end state and want a serious alternative to read about, and anyone in robotics or control looking for a principled take on exploration. If you need something to ship next sprint, this is background reading, not a recipe.

Title: Shipping faster without losing sleep
Description: This is the practice
Body:
# DevOps, but now it thinks for itself

DevOps has always been about automation.

In 2026, the automation talks back.

Conf42 DevOps 2026 is a very clear signal that agentic AI has moved from experiments to infrastructure. CI/CD pipelines are making decisions. Compliance is running in real time. Incident response is increasingly autonomous. And somehow, it all still needs to be observable, secure, and affordable.

This conference is packed. The agenda spans agents, AI, architecture, compliance, data, FinOps, MLOps, observability, security, SRE, and sustainability. If DevOps touches it, it’s probably here. Often with an AI-powered opinion.

AI agents are everywhere. From enterprise-ready CI/CD pipelines and autonomous cloud engineering to self-healing operations and AI-driven incident response, many talks focus on what happens when systems stop waiting for humans to intervene. There’s excitement, but also a lot of healthy caution.

Compliance and governance get serious attention. Compliance-as-code, continuous regulatory validation, privacy-by-design pipelines, and real-time compliance copilots show how DevOps is adapting to regulated environments like finance, healthcare, and critical infrastructure. This is DevOps where audits are not theoretical.

Data and FinOps show up in force. Medallion data lakes, blockchain-driven BI, read-intensive architectures, streaming financial events, and cost-aware observability all point to a world where DevOps teams are responsible not just for uptime, but for economics and trust.

Observability and SRE round things out. AI-powered observability, predictive reliability, agent traffic monitoring, and multi-workload failover reflect how complex systems have become. The focus shifts from reacting faster to preventing problems before users notice.

If DevOps is your job, your craft, or the thing that quietly connects everything else you do, this one’s for you. In 2026, DevOps isn’t just shipping software anymore. It’s running intelligent systems at scale.

Title: Machine learning as the layer that lets automation adapt
Description: Amazon BI engineer Aditi Namdeo at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on ML as the intelligence layer for self-optimising factories, fleets and grids.
Body:
Rule-based automation works until the world changes, and then it is the thing causing the downtime. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Aditi Namdeo, a business intelligence engineer at Amazon, made the case for machine learning as the intelligence layer that sits on top of industrial automation and lets it adapt: learning from new data, catching faults early and tuning itself against the KPIs that matter.

This is an introductory, framework-level talk. It doesn't walk through code or a single system in depth. What it gives you is a clean mental model of where ML fits in automation, and a checklist for making it trustworthy.

## From static rules to systems that learn

Namdeo frames the shift as moving from static, rule-based automation to dynamic systems that keep improving. She cites the figure that 70% of unplanned downtime is linked to inflexible automation, which is the problem statement in one number.

Three techniques do most of the work in her model. Reinforcement learning lets a system learn from interaction and trial and error in changing environments. Predictive modelling uses history to forecast what comes next so processes can be tuned ahead of time. Anomaly detection spots irregular patterns in real-time data so the system can respond before a small fault becomes an outage.

## Three places it pays off

She walks through manufacturing, logistics and energy:

- **Manufacturing:** data-driven workflow optimisation, higher throughput and less downtime through predictive maintenance.
- **Logistics:** route planning on real-time data to cut fuel and delivery time, and smarter load balancing to use vehicle capacity better.
- **Energy:** predictive load management to forecast demand, distribution tuned to predicted usage, and real-time anomaly detection across the grid.

The common thread is self-healing automation. Manual anomaly detection means delays and extended downtime; ML-driven detection allows immediate identification and, in her framing, autonomous corrective action.

## Keep the AI and the OT apart

The architectural advice is the part engineers will recognise. Separate the AI layer from the operational technology layer so either can change without destabilising the other. Manage the data flow between them for real-time responsiveness. Build modular so the system grows incrementally instead of being redesigned.

Explainability gets equal billing. In critical industries, people need to understand why a model made a call before they let it act. She argues for explainable pipelines, standardised model validation against benchmarks, cross-functional teams that pair data scientists with operations experts, and continuous feedback so human reviews and corrections flow back into the model. The balance she describes is honest: overly complex models hurt interpretability, overly simple ones miss the patterns that matter.

## Measure the right things

Her closing advice is to pick KPIs tied to operational goals, not model metrics in isolation. Throughput, downtime reduction and energy efficiency are the three she highlights, because they map straight to revenue, cost and sustainability targets.

## Who should watch

Engineers and analysts new to industrial or operations ML who want the big picture before picking tools, and managers who need vocabulary for a predictive-maintenance proposal. If you already run anomaly detection on plant telemetry, the related talks below go deeper on implementation.

Title: Multi-cloud ML meets data sovereignty law, and governance has to adapt
Description: EY's Sapna Pillai at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 on keeping multi-cloud ML compliant with GDPR, the CLOUD Act and data localisation rules.
Body:
Running machine learning across several clouds is the easy part now. Doing it while every jurisdiction tightens the rules on where data lives and who can reach it is harder. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), Sapna Pillai of EY's Technology Consulting practice gave a compact tour of where governance breaks down in distributed, multi-cloud ML systems, and the four tools she reaches for to fix it: sovereign cloud zones, zero trust, compliance automation and unified cross-region governance.

It's a short talk and an overview, not a build-along. Its value is the map: which laws pull in which direction, which standards give you a shared vocabulary, and where in the ML lifecycle the gaps open up.

## Why multi-cloud makes compliance harder

Pillai starts with the case for multi-cloud ML: best-of-breed services, less vendor lock-in, better disaster recovery and the ability to shift resources with demand. The cost of that flexibility is governance complexity. Governments increasingly assert control over where data is stored, processed and accessed, especially when it crosses borders, and that collides with workloads designed to move freely.

She names three recurring problems. Keeping data residency lawful across several providers. Keeping full auditability of data movement when lineage spans clouds. And staying consistent when the laws themselves disagree.

## Three laws that pull in different directions

The examples are the ones that keep architects awake. GDPR sets strict data protection standards in the EU and has shaped governance practice well beyond it. The US CLOUD Act lets law enforcement reach data held by US-based companies even when that data is stored overseas. China's Cybersecurity Law imposes strong localisation and cross-border transfer requirements. Put a training pipeline, a feature store and an inference endpoint in three regions and you can trip over all three.

For a common language across platforms she points to ISO 27018 for personal data in public clouds, the Cloud Security Alliance STAR programme for evaluating and certifying cloud controls, and NIST 800-53 for security and privacy controls in regulated and government-aligned systems.

## Visibility first, then controls

The gap she keeps returning to is visibility. Many organisations can't say how data moves between providers, and without that, unauthorised access, accidental cross-border transfers and failed audits become likely. Her toolkit, in order:

- **Sovereign cloud zones** keep storage and processing inside a jurisdiction while still giving you cloud scale, and they help with trust from local customers and partners.
- **Zero trust** assumes no implicit trust and verifies every access request, so data stays protected as it moves across clouds and regions, with least-privilege access throughout.
- **Compliance automation** covers real-time monitoring of regulatory requirements, consistent policy enforcement across providers and automatically generated audit trails, because manual compliance doesn't scale across clouds.
- **Cross-region ML governance** means one framework for residency, access and security from training to inference to retraining, not a separate patchwork per region.

Her balancing rule is worth pinning above the architecture board: "Compliance should enable the business not slow it down." Governance has to bend with new regulations instead of freezing the platform.

## Who should watch

Platform and ML engineers who have just been told the next model must serve EU and US customers from shared infrastructure, and architects who need a quick refresher on which regulations and standards matter before a design review. If you already run sovereign regions in production, this one will mostly confirm your checklist.

Title: Treat climate risk models for food systems like software
Description: Poshan Kumar of Kyndryl at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on generative AI climate scenarios, adaptation advice and stakeholder briefs run as GitOps pipelines.
Body:
A climate model that informs a planting decision should be versioned, tested and rolled back like any other production service. That's the thesis [Poshan Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Poshan_Kumar_climate_modeling_food), Senior Lead and Managing Consultant at Kyndryl, brought to the sustainability track at Conf42 DevOps 2026: generative AI can simulate climate risk, propose local adaptations and write briefs for decision-makers, and DevOps practice is what makes those outputs reliable enough to act on.

The talk is short and dense, a reference architecture packed with dataset and model names rather than a demo. Kumar describes himself as an analytics architect working where enterprise platforms meet climate resilience, and the talk sits at that crossing.

## The operational backdrop changed

He opens with 2024, likely the first calendar year above 1.5 degrees over the pre-industrial baseline, with compounding floods and heat stress hitting production, storage and transport. Food insecurity stays high, with around 2.3 billion people facing moderate or severe food insecurity in the figures he cites. The engineering takeaway he draws is that data and ML systems for food have to anticipate extremes, quantify uncertainty and keep adapting.

## The inputs are better than most teams realise

The convergence he describes has three parts. First, data: ERA5 reanalysis gives hourly global data back to 1940 at roughly 31 km with uncertainty estimates; Sentinel-2 provides multispectral surface imagery at 10 to 20 m, useful for vegetation stress; CMIP6 scenarios define possible futures for stress testing. Second, ML weather and climate models: GraphCast for 10-day global forecasts, NeuralGCM as a hybrid physics-ML model that runs stably over decades, and generative downscaling to kilometre scale for precipitation and near-surface fields, which is what a farm-level decision needs. Third, DevOps maturity: containers, GitOps and policy as code.

## Three capabilities, one pipeline

The core of the talk is three generative capabilities. Climate scenario generation builds synthetic extreme-event ensembles conditioned on emissions pathways, downscales them, and validates them against historical analogues from ERA5. Adaptation strategy generation uses LLM agent workflows to suggest local interventions, such as crop rotation, irrigation timing tied to soil moisture and seed selection for drought, conditioned on hydrology, soils and economics. Automated brief generation writes stakeholder-specific briefs for farmers, buyers and NGOs, including uncertainty bands, scenario IDs and data provenance so the output can be audited.

Between them sit the unglamorous steps: ingest from the Copernicus data APIs and soil databases, link weather stress indices such as heat degree days to yield models, and render farmer-friendly maps.

## The DevOps stack is the familiar one

The architecture uses Argo Workflows for the container DAG (ingest, generate, downscale, evaluate, brief), Kubeflow Pipelines v2 for reusable ML components and experiment tracking, KServe for autoscaled inference with canary rollouts for both predictive models and LLM endpoints, Argo CD for cluster state and drift detection, and a model registry (Azure ML or SageMaker) for promotion, lineage and approval gates. Pipelines fail on significant data or prediction drift, and dataset and model version IDs travel in metadata. Nothing in that list will surprise an MLOps engineer, which is the point: the climate part is new, the plumbing is not.

## Governance built in

For trust, Kumar maps the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (govern, map, measure, manage) and its 2024 generative AI profile onto pipeline stages, and wants a model card for each climate and LLM component. His closing advice: integrate AI into pipelines, treat climate LLM artifacts like versioned, tested software, promote them through GitOps, and keep outputs practical.

## Who should watch

MLOps and platform engineers working with geospatial or agricultural data, and climate-tech teams that need a production architecture rather than a notebook. The auto-generated captions struggle with the dataset names, so keep the slides at hand.

Title: ISO 42001 for beginners: the 16 documents an AI audit asks for
Description: Security engineer Aleksandra Drobnjak at Conf42 Machine Learning 2026 maps the minimum ISO 42001 paperwork that makes an AI management system auditable.
Body:
Sooner or later someone asks who approved a model change, what data went into it, and whether anyone can explain it. At [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026), security engineer Aleksandra Drobnjak answered that question with a short list: the 16 documentation artifacts an ISO 42001 auditor expects to see before concluding that an organisation manages its AI systems in a controlled, repeatable way. She calls it "Minimum Viable AIMS", and the point is clarity about risk, ownership and change, not perfect paperwork.

Drobnjak comes at this from both sides of the table. She has spent more than ten years in engineering roles across multi-cloud and container security, supported ISO and SOC 2 audits, and trained as an ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 lead auditor. So the talk reads less like a summary of the standard and more like a walk through what an auditor actually opens first.

## The standard in one paragraph

ISO 42001 was published in 2023 and is the first certifiable standard for managing AI at the organisational level. It doesn't tell you which models or tools to use. It has ten clauses, with clauses 4 to 10 holding the auditable requirements, plus Annex A with 38 controls across nine control objectives. Not every control is mandatory: you pick them by risk, scope and context. It follows the plan-do-check-act cycle, so it sits comfortably next to ISO 27001. Certification runs as a stage one documentation audit, a stage two effectiveness audit, then annual surveillance audits inside a three-year cycle.

A nice practical aside: you can pull the ISO 42001 certificates behind AWS services such as Amazon Bedrock, Transcribe and Textract from AWS Artifact, then check the certificate number yourself on IAF CertSearch. Drobnjak says it takes a couple of minutes.

## Scope is where shadow AI gets caught

The first artifact, the AIMS scope (clause 4.3), sounds dull and does the most work. Her MLOps example is familiar: a model starts in a notebook, someone wires it into a pipeline, and it is influencing real workflows before anyone decided whether it belongs inside governance. The same gap covers engineers pasting company material into personal AI accounts whose default settings may let the vendor train on it.

She also points at ordinary infrastructure mistakes: Jupyter, Kubeflow or MLflow instances left reachable from outside or from production networks. A written scope forces the question of which ML tools may run in production and which environments need authentication, logging and approvals.

## Risks that never become tickets don't count

The planning artifacts (clause 6) exist because risks get discussed, even documented, and then nothing changes. Each risk or opportunity needs an owner, a decision and a concrete next step that lands on someone's board. A repeatable risk assessment method stops one team calling a model change low risk while another blocks the same change outright. She treats model artifacts as executable components, not just data, which is why promotion shouldn't be "just another commit".

The statement of applicability example she shows is control A.5.5 on societal impact, and she makes it concrete: energy use and carbon footprint, who gains or loses access to tools, whether a decision can be understood and challenged, and effects on health and wellbeing.

## Operations, audits and the closing loop

The rest of the list follows the lifecycle: competence records (7.2), the documentation your teams actually rely on (7.5, the place for release notes and prompt changes that otherwise live in Slack DMs), operational controls (8.1), the risk register, treatment plans (8.3), AI system impact assessments (8.4), monitoring results (9.1), internal audit (9.2), management review (9.3), and nonconformities with corrective actions (10.2). She explains the difference between a minor nonconformity, such as a missing approval record, and a major one that signals a systemic breakdown and can delay or suspend certification.

Her strongest takeaway is the one engineers tend to nod at: "advanced models rarely cause problems by themselves." Missing ownership, missing traceability and missing feedback loops do. She is also frank that certification costs time, attention and budget, so a risk-based approach beats trying to do everything at once.

## Who should watch

Watch it if you run ML platforms or security and someone has just said the word "audit" in a meeting, or if you need a checklist to start an AIMS without boiling the ocean. It is a beginner-friendly talk by design; if you have already been through an ISO 42001 stage two audit, you'll mostly be checking your own list against hers.
