Title: Supply chain outages give warnings hours ahead if you read the weather
Description: Raghu Bhupatiraju of Expeditors at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on predictive observability, blending telemetry with weather and carrier signals to act before outages.
Body:
In a global supply chain, a small delay becomes a missed pickup, which becomes a missed flight, which becomes a customer on the phone. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Raghu Bhupatiraju, a senior software engineer at Expeditors, made the case for predictive observability: combine your own telemetry with signals your monitoring never sees, such as weather, carrier status and traffic, and act hours before the failure instead of minutes after it.

His one-line summary of the difference: it is a smoke detector versus fire prevention. The goal, he says, is fewer incidents, not better dashboards.

## Why application monitoring is blind here

Raghu lists the usual gaps of threshold monitoring (alerts after performance has already dropped, root cause hunted during customer impact, cascading failures that hide the original cause) and adds one that is specific to logistics: external signal blindness. A storm over a transit corridor or a struggling carrier API does not show up in your CPU graphs until it is already your problem.

## Five layers, and prediction kept off the critical path

The architecture has five layers: real-time signals (metrics, logs, traces, events), historical pattern analysis in time-series stores, external intelligence (weather APIs, carrier status feeds, traffic data), a predictive engine of ML and statistical models, and action orchestration that triggers alerts and remediation playbooks.

The design rule worth stealing is the separation. Events flow through a streaming backbone such as Apache Kafka or Amazon Kinesis, and the prediction services run as independent microservices. Prediction systems are allowed to fail; production systems are not. A broken model produces a missed forecast, not an outage, and data science teams can ship models without touching business logic.

## Three scenarios

The examples make the idea tangible:

- **Weather and transport.** A severe storm forecast for a major corridor is matched against traffic patterns and carrier routes on the same path, and backup carriers are lined up early. Raghu describes three to six hours of early warning and up to a 90% cut in the resulting delay.
- **A carrier API slowly degrading.** Response times trend upwards and error rates accelerate well before failure. The model forecasts full degradation within about 45 minutes, so a circuit breaker trips, a caching layer switches on and backup routes are prepared. Users see brief delays instead of an outage.
- **A cold chain sensor drifting.** Rate-of-change analysis on refrigeration temperatures, cross-checked against other sensors, gives a 15 to 30 minute warning before the threshold is breached, enough to divert the vehicle and save the cargo.

## Different horizons need different models

One model does not fit every alert. Raghu splits them into short-term (15 to 60 minutes, live data and rapid out-of-control detection), medium-term (one to six hours, combining weak predictors with seasonality, used for transport delays and API degradation) and long-term (days to weeks, feeding capacity planning).

## Nobody acts on a black box

The trust section is the most useful part for anyone building this. Operators will not reroute freight on an unexplained score, so each prediction carries its reasoning: SHAP values for per-feature contribution, feature importance across past incidents, attention views for neural models, and counterfactuals, such as telling the operator the alert would not have fired had API response time stayed below 500 milliseconds.

Automation is then tiered by risk. Low-risk, reversible actions such as cache warm-up, throttling and circuit breakers run automatically at high confidence. Medium-impact moves like carrier rerouting or inventory relocation need a human to approve. High-stakes calls such as vendor escalations or customer communication are alert-only. Actions graduate to automation as accuracy earns trust.

## Who should watch

Anyone whose systems depend on the physical world: logistics, delivery, IoT fleets, travel. The specifics are supply chain, but the explainability and risk-tiered automation patterns apply to any team trying to get operators to trust a model. The talk is architecture and scenarios rather than code.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Transforming Supply Chain: Smart Logistics & Fleet Management through Event-Driven Microservices](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Venkata_Anil_Kumar_Nilisetty_logistics_chain_services) by Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty covers the event-driven backbone from the logistics side.
- [Operating Predictive Analytics at Scale: Reliability Engineering for Data-Driven Education Finance](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Prajakta_Talathi_operating_predictive_analytics) by Prajakta Talathi looks at running prediction systems reliably in a different domain.
- [From Reactive to Predictive: Building an AI-Embedded Project Financial Governance Framework with Go](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Venkat_Kamma_from_reactive_predictive) by Venkat Kamma applies the same reactive-to-predictive shift to project finance.

Title: Let AI suggest the rollback before you let it run the rollback
Description: Aravind Sekar of Twilio at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on AIOps for reliability, from alert grouping and predictive scaling to remediation that earns its autonomy.
Body:
When a region goes down, every threshold monitor on every host fires at once, and the on-call engineer gets hundreds of pages about one problem. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Aravind Sekar, director of engineering at Twilio, walked through where AI and ML actually help with that kind of reliability work, and where they still need a human holding the keys. His model is a staged handover: AI recommends a mitigation, a human approves it, and only after that loop has run many times does AI execute on its own.

## Why the old monitoring model buckles

Aravind's diagnosis is about scale. Monoliths became many microservices, dependencies multiplied, and deployments went from monthly or quarterly to several a day, so each outage cascades further and each release is another chance to ship a regression.

Against that, most teams still run threshold-based monitors on 5xx counts, CPU or heap. The results are alert storms, root cause analysis across telemetry volumes no human can read, tribal knowledge that leaves with the people who hold it, and on-call burnout from always fighting the fire instead of preventing the next one.

He also opens with a reminder of stakes, citing the AWS us-east-1 outage of October 20 and an often-quoted estimate of around $5,600 of lost revenue per minute of downtime.

## Where ML genuinely helps

His framework rests on four capabilities: pattern detection, predictive analytics, intelligent automation and augmented insight over large data. In practice that means anomaly detection across all signal types, seasonal awareness (his example is pizza orders on Super Bowl weekend), correlation across metrics, logs and traces, and a push towards causality rather than coincidence.

The build advice is pragmatic:

- stream the right telemetry first; without it nothing else works
- tier the models, with lightweight ones on the stream and heavier ones on aggregates
- keep inference near real time, since a detection 30 minutes late is not useful
- validate models continuously and keep a safe way to roll a model back when false positives rise, the same way fraud models are retrained as fraud changes

## Two quick wins: scaling and paging

Capacity is where Aravind sees an easy return. Teams know a peak is coming, over-provision because scaling up takes minutes, then forget to scale down. Predictive, just-in-time scaling addresses both; he cites 92% SLO adherence and 35% cost reduction for that approach.

The most concrete result is from his own on-call experience. Using PagerDuty's alert grouping, related alerts from many tripped monitors were folded into one incident pointing at the likely area, which he says cut pager noise and alert storms by 60%. He notes that most monitoring and incident tools, from Datadog and Dynatrace to Splunk and BigPanda, now ship similar AIOps features, so phase two often means switching on what you already pay for.

## Remediation on a leash

The remediation section is where the talk is most careful. Many fixes are the generic mitigations from Google's SRE book: roll back the recent deploy, replace the bad host, pull it from the load balancer, limit traffic. Because the set is small, it can be automated. The question is trust.

Aravind's human-AI collaboration loop: AI spots elevated 5xx on a version deployed an hour ago and suggests rolling back; a human agrees and either does it or hands the action to the AI; the outcome is captured and the loop repeats until humans can step out for that class of issue. He is also frank that automated root cause identification is still in its early stages and depends on the quality of the data you feed it.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and SREs deciding where to start with AIOps, especially if alert storms are the main pain. It is a strategy talk rather than a build tutorial, with a clear phased plan: emit good telemetry, then correlate and map dependencies, then automate and predict, then optimise.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AIOps: New Approaches to Reduce Alert Noise](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Birol_Yildiz_aiops_alert_noise) by Birol Yildiz zooms in on the alert grouping problem.
- [AI-Assisted Incident Response Using LLMs and MCP in Distributed Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Makarand_Gujarathi_assisted_incident_response) by Makarand Gujarathi shows the LLM side of the suggest-then-act loop.
- [AI-Powered Anomaly Detection and Self-Healing Systems for Resilient and Efficient Supply Chains](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Venkata_Anil_Kumar_Nilisetty_ai_powered_anomaly) by Venkata Anil Kumar Nilisetty applies detection and self-healing to one industry.

Title: Make observability part of the paved road, then fail builds without it
Description: Sumit Kaul of PayJoy at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on zero-code instrumentation, SLOs as version-controlled contracts and CI/CD gates that enforce them.
Body:
Observability that depends on each team remembering to add a span is observability with holes in it. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Sumit Kaul, staff software engineer at PayJoy, argued for turning it into a platform contract: the platform guarantees traces, metrics and logs to every service on the paved road with no instrumentation code, SLOs live next to the manifests as version-controlled agreements, and CI/CD fails a build that breaks the contract, the same way it fails one with low test coverage.

## The problem: coverage only where someone remembered

Sumit's starting point will be familiar to anyone who has bought Datadog, New Relic or a Grafana stack and still had blind spots. Every tool needs manual instrumentation. In a codebase with millions of lines, retrofitting it is a daunting job, so coverage is inconsistent, debugging turns reactive the moment an incident hits an uninstrumented corner, and teams split along an unhelpful line: platform says it does not know the application's context, application teams say observability is platform's job.

The contract model resolves the silo by changing who owns what. The platform owns collection. The service gets observability as an outcome of shipping on the paved road. The contract defines the expectations in between.

## Zero-code instrumentation has three parts

The architecture section is concrete:

- **Automatic instrumentation** with OpenTelemetry agents and framework configuration, across Java, Python, Node, Go, .NET and others, with no code changes from developers.
- **Runtime sidecars** that capture network traffic, database queries and message interactions, so a web request can be correlated with the middleware call and the query behind it.
- **Base container images** shipped by the platform team with the agents, ports and signal configuration already baked in. Merge the PR, the pipeline picks up the base image, and the service is instrumented.

Portable containers and standardised collectors keep it consistent across EKS, AKS and GKE. Sumit says his organisation instrumented more than 200 services across three clouds this way, with service coverage above 99%.

## SLOs as a contract the pipeline can check

The contract has a signal requirement (the few high-signal, low-noise indicators that say whether a service is healthy) and an SLO specification, such as availability targets and p95 latency, stored as a manifest beside the deployment config. That turns "the site feels slow" into a number someone agreed to.

Enforcement sits in CI/CD. On commit, contract validation checks the schema and API contracts, an instrumentation check confirms the hooks and the pre-baked image are present, and a failure stops the pipeline. Sumit's mental model is explicit: treat it like a coverage threshold or a critical vulnerability gate.

## Canaries judged against the SLO

On release, the pattern is to capture the current SLI baseline, send a small slice of traffic (he uses 5% as the example) to the new version, compare its metrics against the baseline and the burn-rate policy, then promote to 50% and 100% or roll back. Degraded SLIs are tied to the deployment's version tag, so tracing a bad release down to the span, the database query and the commit becomes a short walk instead of a war room.

## Results and the adoption path

The before-and-after numbers he shares include mean time to respond dropping from 45 to 12 minutes, failed deployments falling to 12% from 30 to 40%, and 78% fewer manual rollbacks. He also cites examples from financial services, retail Black Friday traffic and logistics, where he says 450-plus microservices were instrumented with zero code changes.

The adoption advice may be the most transferable part. Pilot with two or three services over four to six weeks, expand to 10 to 20, then scale. Run workshops for two or three teams at a time, built on their own metrics and traces rather than generic training, and let early wins spread.

## Who should watch

Platform teams building golden paths, and SREs tired of being the instrumentation police. The numbers are from Sumit's own environments, so treat them as one organisation's results rather than benchmarks; the contract-plus-gate pattern is what travels.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Zero-instrumentation observability based on eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Nikolay_Sivko_zeroinstrumentation_observability_ebpf) by Nikolay Sivko gets to "no code changes" by a different route.
- [Techniques for SLOs and Error Budgets at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2023_Fred_Moyer_slos_error_budgets_scale) by Fred Moyer goes further into the SLO math the contract depends on.
- [Optimizing Observability with OpenTelemetry Collector for Budget-Friendly Insights](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Bruno_Ferreira_observability_opentelemetry_collector) by Bruno Ferreira covers the collector side of a platform-owned pipeline.

Title: Your LLM writes good Terraform but cannot see your infrastructure
Description: Roxane Fischer of Anyshift at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on why AI fails at infrastructure without context, and how a live knowledge graph of cloud, code and state fixes it.
Body:
Ask a coding assistant for a Terraform VPC peering connection and you get clean, idiomatic code that references a VPC that does not exist. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Roxane Fischer, co-founder of Anyshift, used that small example to make a large point: LLMs are now good at writing infrastructure code, and they still fail at infrastructure because they cannot see the live dependencies around it. Her fix is to model infrastructure as a graph and give the AI that graph as context.

Anyshift builds AI on-call engineers for root cause analysis, but Roxane says up front that the talk is about the technology underneath, the graph, and not a product tour. That makes it useful whether or not you ever touch their tool.

## Three ways to write one peering connection

The opening example is the best part of the talk, because it shows the failure mode step by step.

First, a developer with no AI writes the peering by copying VPC IDs out of the AWS console and hardcoding them. It works today, and it quietly breaks dependencies as the estate grows.

Second, GitHub Copilot does better on style. It knows hardcoded values are bad practice and reaches for references instead. But it does not know where your VPC is defined, so it creates a new one, which is complete as code and completely unrealistic as infrastructure.

Third, an AI IDE like Cursor that can read several repositories should, in principle, wire the reference to the VPC in another repo through remote state. Except that the junior developer's hardcoded ID from the first step only points at a cloud resource, not at any code. Cursor cannot reconcile cloud data with code, so the dependency link never gets made. The missing ingredient each time is the same: context about what actually exists.

## Infrastructure already is a graph

Roxane's argument is that a graph database is the natural shape for this context. Nodes are VPCs, IAM roles, pods, containers and accounts; edges are relationships such as an IAM role attached to an EC2 instance, or an instance belonging to a VPC. Layer on metadata (where a resource is defined in code, who owns it, who last committed to it, its timeline) and you can ask questions like which instances or pods have run hot on CPU over the last 24 hours and what depends on them.

She notes that at Anyshift, once versioning is included, such a graph can reach tens of millions of nodes. Every answer depends on that density.

## Building one is mostly ontology and plumbing

The recipe she gives is honest about where the effort goes:

- **Pick a graph database.** Anyshift uses Neo4j internally; she mentions Amazon Neptune as an option.
- **Define the ontology.** Decide what nodes and edges exist, with a common model across AWS, GCP and Azure so the AI treats equivalent resources as equivalent despite different definitions.
- **Populate and keep it fresh.** Each integration differs: scan AWS APIs for resources, and use CloudTrail for live updates.

Clean, structured data is the slow, expensive part, she says, and also what makes the context good.

## Where MCP servers are enough, and where they stop

For smaller estates, Roxane suggests a lighter route: connect MCP servers for your cloud providers to your AI tools and query live data directly. It is quick to set up and useful. The limit is that each MCP call is an API call returning a bounded slice of data, so a question that needs every dependency, relationship and bit of history in one go needs a prebuilt graph behind it.

## Drift detection as the worked example

She closes with a concrete subset: reconcile AWS resources, Terraform state and Terraform files into one graph. Parse all three, match entities by their IDs across cloud, state and code, then load the links into the graph and keep it updated. The result shows what is correctly defined in code, what has drifted, and what is shadow IT.

The abstract also promises natural language to Cypher querying and measuring context quality; the recorded talk runs to its 15-minute limit before getting there, so expect the graph-building half rather than the evaluation half.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers evaluating AI assistants for infrastructure work, and anyone wondering why their copilot keeps inventing resources. If you already run a CMDB or asset graph, the ontology section will feel familiar and the AI angle gives it new reasons to exist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Shipping with Context: Knowledge Graphs as the Backbone of AI-First Software Delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery) by Prateek Mittal makes the same case for graphs one level up, across the delivery process.
- [Stop AI Agents from Making Up Facts: Graph-RAG for Reliable Data Retrieval](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_graph_rag_retrieval) by Elizabeth Fuentes Leone covers the Graph RAG side the abstract mentions.
- [From Ghost Assets to Infrastructure Drift - Don't Get Spooked](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2022_Naor_Paz_ghost_assets_infrastructure_drift) by Naor Paz is a good pairing for the drift and shadow IT example.

Title: Self-healing deploys start with Git as the only source of truth
Description: Srinivas Pagadala Sekar of Karsun Solutions at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on self-healing CI/CD with Tekton, Argo CD and Argo Rollouts, plus an airline case study.
Body:
The 3am page about a deployment gone sideways usually starts the same archaeology dig: what changed, who deployed it, where did it drift. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Srinivas Pagadala Sekar, senior site reliability manager at Karsun Solutions, laid out how to write a different ending with GitOps: Tekton for CI, Argo CD for continuous reconciliation, Argo Rollouts for canaries that roll themselves back, and observability feeding every decision.

It is a long, structured talk that goes from GitOps basics to a reference architecture, six failure scenarios, an airline case study and a careful take on where AI fits. Treat it as a blueprint walk-through rather than a live demo.

## Git is the rollback button

Srinivas starts by grounding GitOps in four principles: Git as the single source of truth, declarative desired state, automated reconciliation and full auditability. The resilience payoff follows directly. Rollback is a `git revert`, every change goes through a pull request, and drift is detected because the cluster is constantly compared with the repository.

His stack has four parts: a Git repo holding code, infrastructure and manifests; Tekton pipelines, themselves Kubernetes resources, for build, test, scanning and image promotion; Argo CD as the reconciliation engine; and a cluster with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry built in.

## Six ways a deploy goes wrong, and the GitOps answer

The scenarios are the most practical section, because each one is a real failure most teams have seen:

- **A slow memory leak** that passes testing. Argo CD health checks spot the degradation and roll back to the last good version in under two minutes, instead of a 30-minute human loop.
- **A hotfix made with kubectl** and never committed. The drift is detected within seconds, and Argo CD either alerts or reconciles back to Git.
- **Works in staging, fails in prod.** The same commit is promoted through environments, so the manifests match.
- **An exhausted database connection pool**, where pods look healthy but requests fail. Watching error rates and latency, not just pod status, catches it.
- **A canary that degrades.** Promotion halts automatically and traffic stays on stable.
- **A network partition** that leaves state inconsistent. Once it heals, reconciliation brings everything back to what Git says.

## The canary config that does the work

The Argo Rollouts walkthrough is the bit to copy. Start with 5% of traffic on the new version, watch error rates, latency and resource use, then step up through 10%, 20% and 50% with analysis at each stage. Analysis templates point at Prometheus queries for success rate. Two settings carry the safety: auto-promotion off, so a step only advances when analysis passes, and rollback on failed health checks. A slow problem that only shows under load still gets caught before the whole user base sees it.

The same layer extends to autoscaling with HPA, VPA or KEDA, and to traffic shifting with Istio or Linkerd, with every remediation written back to Git so the audit trail stays complete.

## An airline that could not take maintenance windows

The case study is a flight booking system with strict uptime commitments, holiday peaks around ten times normal load, multiple regions and heavy regulation. Before GitOps they deployed in planned windows, rollbacks took 15 to 20 minutes, and regions drifted apart.

The fix was one Git repository with an Argo CD instance per region, blue-green deployments with traffic switched on real-time metrics, automatic regional failover, and self-healing for connection pool pressure, latency spikes and memory leaks. Srinivas reports MTTR falling from 20 minutes to 90 seconds and no manual rollbacks over six months.

## AI as an advisor first

The AI section covers anomaly detection that learns normal patterns, predictive rollback based on similarity to past failed deployments, canary analysis that stretches its window when traffic is unusual, and automated root cause hypotheses. The guidance is sensibly cautious: build observability before automation, start with a manual gate, add auto-rollback to the most critical services first, test it with chaos engineering, and let AI suggest while humans decide until trust is earned.

## Who should watch

Teams running Argo CD who have not yet wired health-based rollback into it, and anyone pitching GitOps to a reluctant ops team. If you already run Argo Rollouts with analysis templates, the first half will be review; the scenarios and the adoption advice are still worth the time.

Title: Driver assistance works best when AI and the driver share authority
Description: Alagar Raja Govindasa (Dorman Products) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on human-AI collaboration, driver-state monitoring and safe rollouts for automotive control.
Body:
Rule-based driver assistance is excellent at the scenarios its authors predicted and poor at the rest. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Alagar Raja Govindasa, Senior Manager of Electronics R&D at Dorman Products, presented a human-centred alternative: AI and human cognition as complementary partners, with control authority shifting between them based on the road, the risk and how ready the driver actually is.

The talk is short and moves through its framework slide by slide, so think of it as an annotated architecture rather than a story. The architecture is worth knowing if you work anywhere near ADAS.

## What traditional automation misses

Govindasa names three limits. Rule-based systems handle predictable scenarios but struggle with dynamic real-world conditions. Static decision logic can't adapt to real-time perception and prediction. And classic systems have limited context: they lack situational awareness and don't monitor the state of the driver.

## Three pillars of the collaborative architecture

His solution framework has three parts:

- **Multi-sensor perception**: camera, radar and lidar fused for environmental awareness. Cameras give high-resolution data for lane markings and object classification, radar gives all-weather velocity and distance, lidar gives a precise 3D map for obstacle detection and path planning. Fusion, he reports, significantly outperforms single-sensor approaches across conditions.
- **Driver-state monitoring**: gaze tracking, physiological signals and behavioural analysis. The monitoring system he presents achieves 90% accuracy in detecting critical cognitive states: fatigue, distraction and readiness.
- **Dynamic authority allocation**: continuous assessment of environmental complexity and risk, real-time evaluation of driver capability, and adaptive handoff that preserves both safety and driver agency.

The third pillar is the interesting one. Instead of a binary "autopilot on or off", authority is a variable that depends on context and on the person.

## Control and feedback for a human who might be tired

Underneath sits model-predictive control running at millisecond-scale loops, optimising competing goals: safety constraints and collision avoidance, passenger comfort and ride quality, energy efficiency, and regulatory compliance.

The feedback side is designed to reduce cognitive load during transitions, using several channels at once: visual (head-up displays and dashboard indicators), auditory (spatial audio cues and voice notifications for time-critical information) and haptic (steering-wheel and seat vibrations for directional guidance). A buzz in the left side of the seat is faster to understand than a dashboard icon.

## Validated three ways

Govindasa describes a three-stage validation methodology: simulation testing across thousands of edge cases and failure modes, controlled experiments on instrumented test tracks, and naturalistic driving across varied conditions, driver populations and traffic. The results he reports are qualitative but specific: fewer lane-departure events, lower collision rates in simulation and the real world, smoother takeovers, better-calibrated driver trust with less over-reliance, improved situational awareness and lower cognitive load.

Applications include intent-aware adaptive cruise control that predicts driver intentions and adjusts following distance, and cooperative vehicle-to-vehicle coordination that extends perception beyond the car's own sensors.

## The DevOps part

The link to this conference is the deployment strategy for safety-critical software: continuous validation pipelines with automated testing to keep updates regression-free and maintain safety certification, fleet-wide observability with real-time telemetry and anomaly detection, and human-centred rollout with gradual enablement driven by driver feedback and acceptance. His closing theme is augmentation over automation: machine precision combined with human intuition, not a machine replacing the human.

## Who should watch

Automotive and embedded engineers, and anyone designing systems where a human and an automated controller share the wheel, literally or not. It is an overview with few implementation details. If your on-call tooling ever had to hand control back to a tired human at 3am, the authority-allocation idea will feel familiar.

- [Introduction to ADAS and Autonomous Driving](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Rajesh_Reddy_computing_software_vehicles) by Rajesh Reddy (ECARX) is a good primer on the systems this talk builds on.

- [Human-AI Symbiotic Robotics](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Rajarshi_Tarafdar_human_ai_symbiotic) by Rajarshi Tarafdar (JP Morgan Chase) explores human-AI collaboration in robotics.

Title: Treat GPU performance like a failing test, not a production surprise
Description: Mohit Gupta of Intel at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on putting GPU performance gates into CI/CD, and why mixed compute and memory workloads must be tested together.
Body:
Most teams find their GPU performance regressions the expensive way: after deployment, on shared hardware, with several other teams' jobs running next to theirs. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Mohit Gupta, a staff GPU performance verification engineer at Intel, argued for moving that discovery into the pipeline, with GPU counters as build artefacts and performance gates that fail a build the same way a broken unit test does.

It is a short talk, around ten minutes, and it reads like a checklist from someone who verifies GPU behaviour for a living. If you run a platform that hands out GPUs to AI teams, it is a cheap way to sanity-check your own approach.

## Why post-deployment testing breaks down on GPUs

Mohit's framing is simple. GPUs are expensive, shared and performance sensitive, so a regression burns money directly, and the feedback loop from production is slow. He gives three reasons the validation belongs in CI/CD: cost (a regression wastes compute you already paid for), reliability (training and inference need predictable performance) and early detection (catching it in the pipeline keeps it out of the incident queue).

The shared part matters most. When one GPU pool serves many workloads and teams, a post-deployment test tells you something got slower, but not whose change did it.

## Classify the workload with counters, not opinions

The core of the method is a split most GPU engineers will recognise: compute-bound workloads, dominated by math and expected to show high ALU utilisation with few memory stalls, and memory-bound workloads, limited by data movement, cache misses, bandwidth saturation and access patterns.

What Mohit adds is discipline about how you decide which is which. The framework classifies workloads from measurable GPU counters: ALU utilisation, cache hit rates, memory stall cycles, bandwidth use and coalescing efficiency. That replaces "it feels memory-bound" with numbers you can store per build and compare across builds.

The benchmark suite has three families:

- dense linear algebra for compute-heavy AI work
- irregular memory access, such as graph and sparse operations
- hybrid workloads that mix both, to look like real production systems

In his compute-bound results, sustained ALU utilisation sat around 85% with strong L1 locality and few memory stalls. On the memory-bound side, bandwidth utilisation reached about 75%, with a clear gap in coalescing efficiency between structured and irregular access patterns. That gap is where he points the optimisation effort.

## The regression your isolated benchmark never sees

The finding he calls critical is the mixed-workload one. When compute-bound and memory-bound workloads run at the same time, cache contention and resource interference cause slowdowns that testing each workload alone completely misses.

This is the GPU version of the noisy-neighbour problem, and it is why a green isolated benchmark proves less than it looks. If your production GPUs are shared, your validation has to share them too. His takeaway list ranks this as the most important item: test mixed workloads, not just isolated benchmarks.

## Performance becomes code

The implementation side is familiar CI/CD practice applied to a new signal: define performance gates in the pipeline, run benchmarks automatically in a controlled environment, and capture GPU metrics as part of every build. In Mohit's words, performance becomes "version, repeatable and enforceable."

The same metrics then feed observability. GPU utilisation trends, bandwidth saturation, cache degradation alerts and the workload mix give SRE teams data for capacity and reliability planning, so the numbers collected for gating do double duty.

## Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers who own shared GPU clusters, and anyone who has been asked why training got slower this week and had no good answer. There is no code or tool demo, so if you want a specific product walkthrough this is not it; if you want a clear model for what to measure and gate on, it is a quick, focused one.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Which Workload Owns This GPU Metric?](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Nishant_Modak_gpu_workload_metric) by Nishant Modak takes on attribution, the natural next question once you are collecting GPU counters.
- [Running vLLM Inference on Kubernetes Across Clouds: A Production-Ready GPU Blueprint](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Kosseila_Haddalene_vllm_kubernetes_gpu) by Kosseila Haddalene covers the kind of inference platform these gates would protect.
- [Instant KAI Sandboxes with vCluster: Multi-Tenant, Multi-Scheduler GPU Sharing](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Piotr_Zaniewski_sandboxes_gpu_multitenant) by Piotr Zaniewski looks at the sharing that makes mixed-workload testing necessary.

Title: Embedded AI should aim for predictable, not maximum, intelligence
Description: Rasmi Ranjan Nayak (ASML) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 presents a real-time embedded AI framework that keeps inference inside hard deadlines.
Body:
In a hard real-time system, an AI decision that arrives late is a wrong decision, however accurate it is. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Rasmi Ranjan Nayak, a senior software engineer at ASML working on real-time embedded systems, argued that the supposed choice between deterministic behaviour and AI-driven intelligence is a false trade-off, and presented a framework for getting both on constrained hardware.

He sums up the design goal in one line: "The goal is not maximum intelligence. The goal is predictable intelligence." Everything else in the talk follows from that.

## The embedded AI paradox

Nayak's constraints will be familiar to anyone who has written firmware: limited compute because the device is built for one job, tight memory budgets because more RAM costs money and complexity, and millisecond latency requirements. Traditional AI optimises for accuracy and throughput; real-time systems optimise for predictability. That mismatch is the paradox.

He offers a handy distinction for the non-embedded audience. In a hard real-time system, a task due in two milliseconds must finish in two milliseconds. In a soft real-time system, a text message that arrives twenty minutes late is annoying but fine.

## Three layers on one control loop

The framework is hierarchical, with three layers running in a synchronised control loop:

- **Perception**: deterministic sensor acquisition and pre-processing, with sensor fusion making sure all data is time-aligned.
- **Cognition**: AI inference with models that are quantised and hardware-accelerated to keep latency bounded.
- **Execution**: every actuation is scheduled and verified.

The principle is that AI must adapt to the real-time constraints, never break them.

## C++ for the core, Python for the lab

The obvious question, why not Python everywhere, gets a straight answer. Python is excellent for rapid development, model training, pipelines and analytics, but not for hard real-time work. In his framework C++ forms the deterministic core: control loops, scheduling, sensor fusion, memory management and hardware access, with modern C++ standards making that safer to write. Optimised bindings connect the two worlds with minimal overhead.

## Every optimisation protects a deadline

The optimisation list is concrete. Quantised CNNs cut memory use by up to four times while preserving accuracy. Hardware acceleration on ARM NEON and GPUs brings up to ten times faster inference. Compile-time scheduling removes runtime uncertainty. Lock-free queues eliminate priority inversion and synchronisation bottlenecks.

He takes a moment to explain priority inversion: a low-priority task holds a resource that a high-priority task needs, and the usual fix is priority inheritance, temporarily lifting the low-priority task so it can finish and release the resource. As he puts it, every optimisation exists to protect the real-time guarantee.

Energy gets the same treatment: dynamic voltage scaling during low-demand periods, hibernating idle subsystems without hurting wake-up latency, and memory pooling to avoid fragmentation. A robot that hits every deadline but needs charging every hour has only solved half the problem.

## Where it runs

For manufacturing he cites vision-guided precision assembly at sub-millimetre accuracy with a 99.7% success rate, real-time inspection with 35% higher throughput and fewer false positives, and predictive maintenance cutting unplanned downtime by 60%. For defence, he describes autonomous navigation in GPS-denied environments via sensor fusion, and swarm coordination from distributed deterministic decisions, evaluated against dynamic obstacles and bandwidth limits. On implementation, he mentions sensor fusion loops at up to one kilohertz and inference under eight milliseconds.

Looking ahead, he points at federated learning, neuromorphic hardware, formal verification and smarter splitting of work between edge and cloud.

## Who should watch

Embedded and robotics engineers adding ML to control systems, and ML engineers about to deploy onto hardware that has never heard of garbage collection. The delivery is informal and wanders occasionally, but the architecture is clear. If your inference latency is reported as an average, this talk will make you want a worst case.

- [Optimizing Real-Time AI Inference at the Edge](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Murali_Krishna_Reddy_Mandalapu_ai_inference_edge) by Murali Krishna Reddy Mandalapu (Renesas Electronics) looks at edge inference for vehicle safety.

Title: Student-risk models only help if they reach an advisor's task list
Description: Venkatesan Kandavelu (HCLTech) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on MLOps for education analytics - models, metrics, drift, fairness and FERPA-ready governance.
Body:
Plenty of universities have a notebook that predicts which students are at risk; far fewer have that prediction turning up as a task for an advisor the same week. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Venkatesan Kandavelu, a senior project manager at HCLTech, focused on that gap: how DevOps and MLOps practices turn predictive analytics in education from proof-of-concept into a reliable, monitored and ethically governed production system.

It is a structured, introductory talk. The first half is an ML toolkit for education data; the second half is the pipeline and governance that make it safe to run.

## The data is there; the production system usually isn't

Kandavelu's starting point is that digital learning platforms generate far more than grades and attendance: behavioural, performance and engagement data in large volumes. Raw data on its own delivers no insight, and institutions struggle to move models out of notebooks and sandboxes into production. MLOps, in his framing, brings the three things that gap lacks: reproducibility, scalability and governance.

## A toolkit matched to the questions

He walks through the model families that fit common education problems:

- **Binary classification** such as logistic regression for pass/fail or at-risk/not-at-risk.
- **Ensemble methods**: random forests reduce variance by averaging many trees; gradient boosting reduces bias by adding weak learners in sequence, and is his pick for forecasting final outcomes early in a term.
- **LSTMs and recurrent networks** for multi-semester performance trajectories.
- **Unsupervised clustering** (k-means, hierarchical methods) to group students by similarity without a target label.
- **NLP sentiment pipelines** for unstructured text.

The accuracy drivers he lists are the classics: data quality and completeness (impute numeric gaps, label missing categories as unknown, normalise), feature engineering, correct temporal alignment, sample size and class balance, and the trade-off between model complexity and interpretability. In education, interpretability is not optional, because someone has to explain to a student why they were flagged.

## Metrics, versioning and the pipeline

Evaluation gets a proper section: confusion-matrix-based metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC) for classifiers, and MSE, RMSE and R-squared for regression. On the DevOps side he recommends DVC for dataset versioning and lineage, MLflow for tracking and packaging models, feature pipelines that keep training and inference logic consistent, and CI/CD with automated testing and validation gates.

His reference architecture has six layers: data management, model development, model deployment, model monitoring (which he calls the most important), infrastructure and automation with containers and autoscaling, and governance and compliance. For cost, he points to serverless and spot instances for batch work, keeping GPUs and autoscaling for real-time inference.

## Fairness, FERPA and model cards

Governance is where the talk is most specific to education. Fairness means validating models across student subgroups and applying bias mitigation. Transparency means explainability tools such as SHAP and LIME so stakeholders can see why a prediction happened. Privacy means role-based access that complies with FERPA, the US federal law protecting student records, and GDPR in the EU. Model cards document how each model was built and its intended use, automated validation checks fairness, privacy and performance before deployment, audit trails log predictions and outcomes, and humans stay in the loop at key decisions.

## Close the loop with the people who act

The final step is the one that justifies the rest: integrating predictions with student support services. API-driven architecture pushes model output to dashboards and turns it into task lists for advisors and tutors. Then deploy, monitor, collect feedback, retrain, because production ML systems are never finished.

## Who should watch

Data teams in universities and edtech who have models but not a platform, and engineers new to MLOps who want a well-organised tour of the standard pieces. Experienced MLOps practitioners will know the tooling; the FERPA and fairness framing is the part worth their time.

Title: The sidebands you filter out as noise can predict motor failure
Description: Avinash Sista (MongoDB) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on four-layer, vectorised motor health monitoring that turns sensor data into predictive maintenance.
Body:
Run the current feeding an AC motor through a Fast Fourier Transform and you get the expected harmonics plus small sidebands that most people discard as noise. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Avinash Sista, a principal at MongoDB who manages system-integrator partnerships in IoT and AI, argued that those sidebands are a signature, and that combining them with design data, sensor reactions and a vectorised learning loop lets you predict which part of a motor is failing before it fails.

Sista is an electrical engineer with a master's in mechanical engineering, and it shows: this is an electro-mechanical reliability talk first and a data platform talk second. It is based on his own research into AC motors, with brushless DC and switched reluctance motors also in scope.

## Commodity parts, expensive failures

Motors are everywhere: dishwashers, washing machines, HVAC, and in industry compressors, conveyors and robotics. They are also commodities, often bought by weight with limited per-unit R&D. When one fails, you get downtime and sometimes catastrophic damage.

Today's protection is mostly threshold alarms (temperature, emergency stop) plus the intuition of an engineer who has listened to motors for years. Sista's critique is that these inputs live in silos. Nobody stitches design specs, electrical signals, temperature, vibration and experience into one model that says when, where and how a motor will fault.

## Four layers of diagnosis

His approach is a multi-layer decision process, mapped onto the motor as an input-process-output block:

1. **Design signature analysis.** How should this motor behave? Torque, RPM, 50 or 60 Hz supply, four-pole or six-pole, no-load versus full-load thermal behaviour. Traditionally checked with circle diagrams in the lab; here digitised as a baseline.
2. **Current signature analysis.** Feed the supply current through an FFT and you expect spikes at 60, 120, 180 Hz and so on. Because every motor is also a generator, back EMF distorts the wave and sidebands appear around those spikes. That pattern is specific to the motor's design, and as the motor ages the sidebands change in amplitude or width. That change is the anomaly to watch.
3. **Reaction analysis.** The output side: heat, vibration, noise and efficiency. His analogy is the kitchen blender in India that you knew was overloaded by its sound and how hot it got, with a sensor doing the listening instead of a person. A rattle in your car is the same diagnostic instinct.
4. **Aging signature analysis.** Combine layers one to three against the baseline to spot the trend, and attribute it: bearing wear, winding losses, resistance changes, insulation breakdown.

## Fix the bearing, not the compressor

His worked example is a motor driving a compressor whose output values started skewing and hampering plant operations. The old response is to swap the compressor, the motor or both. With current signatures describing motor health, reaction data pointing at the application, and design conformance defining expected behaviour, the aging trend tells you which component is degrading, so you can do targeted predictive maintenance before anything breaks.

## Vectors and a learning loop

The data side uses the sensors motors already have, plus soft sensors, and vectorises temperature, vibration and electrical inputs to relate cause and effect. Sista is careful that vectorisation alone doesn't give early detection: it comes from matching against similar measurements and known defects, and gets better as the system learns more failures. That continuous learning loop leans on a document database to store unstructured data, including photos and video, feeding vector models. Given his employer, the document-model choice is unsurprising, but the talk doesn't turn into a product pitch.

He frames the outcome in DevOps terms: data-driven decisions, continuous monitoring and resilient operations, with preventive rather than firefighting maintenance. Research is continuing on purely resistive and more complex loads.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on industrial IoT, predictive maintenance or any telemetry pipeline where domain physics should shape the features. Software people get a clear, friendly explanation of motor-current signature analysis. If your anomaly detection treats every sensor as an anonymous time series, this is a good argument for learning what the signal means.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Transforming Manufacturing Through AI-Driven Predictive Maintenance](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Muruga_Angamuthu_transforming_manufacturing_ai) by Muruga Angamuthu (Techtronic Industries) covers the plant-floor rollout side.

Title: Sepsis detection AI needs clinical gates, not just a good model
Description: Swapna Chimanchodkar at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on DevOps for clinical AI - streaming vitals, EHR integration, shadow and canary rollouts, SRE for sepsis alerts.
Body:
With sepsis, every hour of delay raises the chance of death by roughly 8%, so a prediction model that is down or late is a clinical failure. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Swapna Chimanchodkar, an IEEE Senior Member and Osmania University alumna who works as a senior consultant and manager at Cognizant Business Consulting, walked through the DevOps and SRE practices that get real-time sepsis detection from a trained model into hospital workflows safely.

The talk frames sepsis as the case study, but she says explicitly at the end that the same approach applies to any mission-critical domain: fraud detection, predictive maintenance, autonomous vehicles.

## Why this is a platform problem

Chimanchodkar opens with the scale: sepsis claims approximately 11 million lives, around 20% of all mortality by her figures. AI can improve outcomes, she argues, but only when it is embedded into redesigned care workflows and backed by an always-on platform.

The complexity is familiar to anyone who has integrated enterprise systems, with higher stakes. Data comes from distributed hospital systems, vendor systems such as labs, and legacy electronic health records. It must stream in real time, feed a validated model, stay compliant and keep an audit trail. And a correct alert that no clinical process acts on is useless, so the workflow has to be designed alongside the pipeline.

## The pipeline, from monitor to alert

Her reference architecture processes patient vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, lab values) through cloud-native, event-driven microservices aiming for sub-second latency. Apache Kafka and cloud streaming services ingest data from monitors, lab systems and nursing platforms, and do feature engineering, aggregation and EHR enrichment before the model sees anything.

Two details stand out. Back-pressure management protects downstream services during peak demand. And EHR integration is a real engineering job: extract via HL7 FHIR APIs or custom interfaces, normalise heterogeneous data and terminology, handle missing values, and validate quality. Her example of an outlier blood pressure reading is a good reminder that normalising is not the same as averaging away the signal.

## Shadow mode before a clinician ever sees it

The rollout sequence is the most transferable part of the talk:

1. Algorithm development on retrospective data.
2. Retrospective validation on held-out data across patient demographics.
3. Shadow deployment, generating predictions without acting on them.
4. Clinical review of those results.
5. Canary release to small cohorts with continuous adverse-event monitoring.
6. Full production with ongoing performance and drift detection.

She calls these CI/CD with clinical gates: validation, performance and bias checks run continuously, alongside Kubernetes orchestration with autoscaling and health checks, and infrastructure as code for reproducible, recoverable environments.

## Observability is clinical, not just technical

Uptime is not enough. Her observability list covers prediction performance (sensitivity, specificity, alert rates), dashboards segmented by demographic and clinical unit to catch uneven drift, end-to-end latency from ingestion to alert delivery with thresholds tied to intervention windows, and automated data-quality alerts for missing values.

Drift is expected: patient populations change, practice changes, seasons shift. Statistical tests compare live prediction distributions against training baselines, and a breach triggers automated retraining or a data-science investigation, with actual clinical outcomes feeding back into supervised updates.

## SRE with patients in the loop

The SRE section translates directly: error budgets aligned with clinical impact (she cites a 99.95% uptime target for sepsis detection with strict latency percentiles), structured on-call with escalation paths to DevOps engineers, data scientists and clinical informatics, runbooks for common failures, and blameless postmortems. A pager rotation that includes a clinical informatics team is one most SREs have never had to design.

## Who should watch

Platform and ML engineers in healthcare, and anyone running models where a late answer is a wrong answer. It is a well-structured overview rather than a system tour from a specific hospital, so expect patterns, not war stories.

Title: Route agent traffic through a gateway and the LLM bill gets a dashboard
Description: Michael Levan (Solo.io) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 demos agentgateway on Kubernetes plus Prometheus and Grafana to track LLM tokens and cost per gateway.
Body:
Agents call LLMs, MCP servers and other agents, and the first question finance asks is who spent what. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Michael Levan, AI architect and solutions engineer at Solo.io, answered it with a live terminal demo: route all that traffic through agentgateway on Kubernetes, scrape its metrics with Prometheus, and read token usage and cost per gateway off a Grafana dashboard.

This is a vendor-adjacent demo talk: Levan works at Solo.io and the demo uses agentgateway end to end, built step by step with kubectl, curl and Grafana.

## Three gateways, one model, on purpose

After installing agentgateway, Levan creates a Kubernetes secret holding an Anthropic API key. Any LLM provider would do; Anthropic is simply where he has a subscription.

He then creates three gateways. The number is arbitrary, chosen so the dashboard has something to break down. Each one is three objects:

- a **Gateway** from the Kubernetes Gateway API CRDs, using the agentgateway class, accepting routes from all namespaces for testing;
- an **agentgateway backend**, which tells the gateway where to send traffic, here a Claude model, though it could just as well be an MCP server;
- an **HTTPRoute** that references both and gives you an endpoint to hit.

A nice detail for anyone who has typed it too often: the route rewrites the OpenAI-style chat completions path to a short `/anthropic` prefix. Levan also heads off the obvious question about why a Claude backend uses the chat completions path at all: Claude supports the OpenAI API format, so it works as expected.

## Generate traffic, then make it visible

With the three gateways up, he exports their load balancer IPs into environment variables and curls each one. The point is partly to prove routing works and partly to generate metrics.

For observability he installs kube-prometheus, his usual choice because it ships Prometheus and Grafana with a set of Kubernetes dashboards already in place, instead of an empty Grafana. Then come pod monitors, one per gateway, each scraping the gateway's metrics endpoint every 30 seconds. There's a small live fix along the way: the gateways now deploy into the `agentgateway-system` namespace rather than the older `kgateway-system`, so the monitors needed updating. Demos that include the namespace rename are the honest kind.

## Cost per gateway, tokens per request

The payoff is a custom Grafana dashboard, published on Levan's GitHub, that shows cost per gateway and for all gateways combined. In his case the spend was small enough that he was still in budget.

Below the dashboard, the raw agentgateway metrics in Prometheus are where the useful slicing happens. Token usage can be broken down by which gateway received the request, which model served it and where it originated. That is the attribution a platform team needs before it can set budgets or rate limits per team.

## Why the gateway pattern matters

The demo is small, but the shape is the useful part. Put every agent-to-LLM, agent-to-MCP and agent-to-agent call through a gateway you control, and cost tracking becomes a metrics problem you already know how to solve, using the Prometheus and Grafana stack most Kubernetes teams run anyway. Splitting traffic across gateways (per team, per product, per environment) is what turns one big invoice into numbers someone can own.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have been asked to put guardrails on agent spend and want to see the moving parts in a terminal. If you already run the Kubernetes Gateway API, most of this will feel familiar, which is rather the point. If you were hoping for a deep comparison of AI gateways, this is a hands-on walkthrough of one.

Title: AI subscriptions turn model freshness into the product you sell
Description: Chandan Kumar (Adobe) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on the foundations of AI subscription platforms - metering, MLOps, drift monitoring and compliance.
Body:
When customers pay monthly for an AI feature, they expect it to get better every month, and that makes continuous delivery of models a commercial obligation. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Chandan Kumar, Senior Engineering Manager at Adobe, laid out what an AI subscription platform has to stand on: the infrastructure foundations, the MLOps practices that keep models fresh, and the operational and compliance work that comes with running them at scale.

It is a strategy-level overview rather than an implementation talk, and Kumar says so in effect by moving quickly across architecture, operations, customer success and market trends. Its usefulness is as a map of the moving parts.

## Three forces that reinforce each other

Kumar's starting point is a convergence. DevOps and continuous delivery are the backbone of modern software cycles. The subscription economy raises expectations of ongoing value. And AI only stays good when it is continuously updated and retrained. Each one pushes the others, which is why companies are moving to the model.

## Four foundations, including the one people forget

He names four foundations a platform must rest on: cloud infrastructure for training and inference, model management with versioning, rollbacks, audits and experimentation, robust data pipelines, and service metering. Metering is the one engineers tend to treat as somebody else's job, but in a subscription business it underpins predictable billing and capacity planning. Without all four, he argues, the platform cannot scale sustainably.

## MLOps is DevOps with more things to version

The engineering core is MLOps as an extension of DevOps. CI has to integrate data and model artifacts as well as code. Testing goes deeper, into edge cases and adverse scenarios. Deployment is gradual, with canary rollouts and automated rollbacks.

Kumar separates two kinds of decay worth monitoring: data drift, where inputs change, and concept drift, where the real-world relationship the model learned changes. Either way, continuous observability of AI pipelines is in his words non-negotiable. Continuous learning pipelines then keep models fresh, with retraining schedules that weigh cost (training is expensive) and human feedback loops structured so they don't reinforce bias.

## Data quality, privacy and the right to be forgotten

On data, he stresses validation, anomaly detection, stream processing to catch problems in real time, and provenance tracking for traceability in regulated settings. On security he lists differential privacy, federated learning for training without moving data, and adversarial defences against input manipulation and model extraction.

The compliance section includes an item more teams should plan for: machine unlearning, removing a specific piece of data's influence from a trained model. Combined with GDPR and CCPA and audit trails, it is a reminder that "delete my data" gets harder once the data is in the weights.

## Operations, customers and the money

Operational challenges at scale are cost management, debugging across tightly coupled data, algorithms and infrastructure, capacity planning that balances training against real-time inference, and getting data scientists, ML engineers, DevOps and domain partners to share tools and language. Customer success, in his framing, means translating technical performance into business outcomes, good onboarding and usage analytics that spot friction before churn.

The abstract quotes figures of 37% higher accuracy, 31% cost reduction and 61% faster deployment; the talk itself stays with frameworks and does not walk through a case study behind those numbers.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and platform leads planning or inheriting an AI feature sold on subscription, who want a checklist of what the platform needs beyond the model. Hands-on MLOps engineers will find most of the techniques familiar. If your team ships models but billing has never heard of your inference costs, the metering section is the one to watch.

- [From DevOps to MLOps: Scaling Machine Learning Models](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2024_Chinmay_Naik_devops_mlops_scaling) by Chinmay Naik (One2N) is a hands-on counterpart on serving models at scale.
- [AI Model Monitoring: Building Reliable Alert Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Muddassar_Sharif_ai_model_systems) by Muddassar Sharif (Virtuans.ai) goes further into drift and alerting.

Title: Past a thousand nodes, more hardware stops buying read throughput
Description: Ivan Sinitsin (Ozon) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on tail latency, connection storms, binary formats, CQRS projections and sharded in-process caches.
Body:
The standard Kubernetes, microservices and sharded-cache stack scales linearly right up until it doesn't. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Ivan Sinitsin, Golang tech lead at Ozon, explained what goes wrong in read-intensive systems once you cross roughly a thousand nodes, why the usual painkillers only mask it, and how his target architecture ends up serving most reads from local memory with only about 1% reaching the databases.

This is a dense, opinionated systems talk. It moves from network math to CPU cache lines to data-locality routing, and it ends with an honest bill for the complexity.

## The tax nobody puts on the diagram

Sinitsin's list of large-scale failures starts with tail latency. A single search query might fan out to 50 database shards, and the response is only as fast as the slowest one. At scale, the rare anomaly becomes daily statistics.

Then there is the orchestration tax. Control planes, service discovery and gossip-style protocols eat a growing share of CPU and network, until management traffic competes with users. His example: add 20% more hardware and get only about five percent more performance.

The memorable bit is the connection math. With 1,000 application pods each opening a pool to each of 100 cache nodes, you have around 100,000 open connections, enough to exhaust file descriptors and hammer the top-of-rack switch. The system, as he puts it, chokes itself.

He also reminds SREs where to live on the latency-versus-throughput curve: the linear zone, with enough margin to absorb spikes, well before the inflection point where queues form.

## Painkillers help you survive, not scale

The first response he describes is the familiar one: graceful degradation, circuit breakers, soft timeouts and serving stale data. If a database doesn't answer within 20 milliseconds, kill the connection and serve a partial response. After that comes zonal isolation, duplicating the whole stack per availability zone so a zone failure stays local, at the cost of roughly tripled resources and harder synchronisation.

Sinitsin's warning is that a dashboard full of green after all this is an illusion of stability. The symptoms are masked; the inefficiency underneath is untouched.

## Make the bytes cheaper

The cure starts at the lowest level. He sees waste in three places: processing (CPU spent deserialising more than running business logic), transfer (keys and metadata repeated in every request) and storage (reading a whole row to get one column). His prescriptions are binary formats over text, zero-copy access that maps data straight into memory and skips garbage collection pressure, reading only the fields you need, and stripping schemas and field names out of payloads via a central registry.

He goes one layer further, to memory layout: grouping data into developer-friendly objects often pollutes CPU cache lines. No layout wins everywhere, so profile and pick the one that fits your access pattern.

## Projections, local caches and smart routing

Architecturally, he reaches for CQRS: keep one source of truth and generate read projections tailored to each consumer, carrying only the fields and format that consumer needs. Then move those projections into the service's own memory, where access costs nanoseconds instead of a network hop.

Caching everything in every pod would blow up memory, so pods become shards. Service discovery tracks topology in real time, client-side balancing skips the extra hop, and consistent hashing ensures that requests for a given ID always land on the same pod. Storage formats differ by tier: compact and backward-compatible for external storage, native runtime structures in process. FlatBuffers on the wire, native objects inside, is one of his examples.

## The bill

The result in his comparison: instead of every request hitting external caches, about 85% are served from local memory and only 1% reach the databases, which means far fewer servers and much lower cross-AZ traffic. The cost is a system that is harder to maintain, with a thinner safety margin and monitoring that needs surgical precision. His closing advice is the right one: make sure you are fighting physical hardware limits, not suboptimal code.

## Who should watch

Engineers running high-fanout read paths in Go or any runtime where serialisation shows up in profiles. Small services can skip it with a clear conscience. If you have ever doubled a cache cluster and watched p99 stay put, this explains why.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [High-Load Systems: Overcoming Challenges in Social Network Development](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Alexandr_Kolobov_highload_systems_development) by Alexandr Kolobov (VK) covers similar scale from a social network.
- [Architectural Caching Patterns for Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2021_Rafal_Leszko_architectural_caching_patterns_kubernetes) by Rafal Leszko (Hazelcast) is a good primer on where a cache can live in a cluster.
- [Building Self-Healing Cache Infrastructure](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Shailin_Saraiya_cache_millions_latency) by Shailin Saraiya (Roku) treats the cache layer as a platform of its own.

Title: Ad hoc prompts fail in ops; version-controlled templates don't
Description: Tina Kanth (Microsoft) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on template-driven prompt engineering for triaging streaming financial events.
Body:
Two engineers paste the same error into the same model and get different answers, because only one of them knew which context to add. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Tina Kanth, a software engineer at Microsoft on the team behind the company's financial engine, argued that this is why ad hoc prompting breaks down in operations, and that the fix is templates: versioned, modular prompts that carry the senior engineer's troubleshooting knowledge into every request.

The setting is a high-throughput financial platform: millions of events, microservices and Spark engines, Cosmos DB and Redis in between, on Azure or AWS. Low outages, high availability, minimum latency and auditability are the non-negotiables.

## The real problem is context, not wording

Kanth's diagnosis starts with fragmentation. Transactions, metrics and application logs live in different tools, so a developer or SRE tracing why a transaction didn't process has to hop between systems. Copilots help, but she is direct that prompt engineering and context engineering go hand in hand and neither substitutes for the other. You can write the best prompt in the world and still get a bad answer if the model lacks the context.

Ad hoc prompts fail in four ways in her account: missing context, inconsistent output from probabilistic models, poor auditability (how do you measure a platform nobody prompts the same way twice?) and latency overhead.

## A template is operational knowledge written down

Her template anatomy has four parts: operational knowledge, policy constraints, event context and schema reference, plus a defined output format.

Operational knowledge is the part that usually lives in a few senior heads: when you see this log message, which fields matter and what is the next action. Writing it into a template is, as she puts it, a great leveller, because a junior engineer's triage then starts from the expert's steps. Policy constraints spell out what the model must not do, which matters a lot with production financial data. The output format has to be machine-actionable so one agent's output can feed the next.

She draws the parallel with GitHub's Spec Kit, which keeps developers inside a project's design guardrails; templates do the same for ops prompts.

## The plumbing around the prompt

The framework she sketches is concrete. Events are ingested, then routed with Semantic Kernel plugins to the right templates. A corpus of docs, designs and code is embedded into a vector database for context injection. An output validator checks results and feeds a dashboard of model effectiveness. The output is an action item, such as replaying orders or deleting duplicates, either automated or sent through an approval process.

Because templates live in source control, every change goes through reviewers and approvers. She recommends modular templates over one big file, and a separate pipeline to re-vectorise documentation as teams update it so the model doesn't work from stale docs.

The abstract cites accuracy gains of 10 to 15 points from this approach; the talk itself spends its time on the architecture and the rollout advice.

## Start with the 80/20 cases

Her rollout advice is pragmatic: pick frequent problems that cause the most toil for on-call engineers, connect to the observability platform, keep fallback mechanisms until performance evaluation is done, and set up a feedback loop, even an informal one at first. Beyond triage she points at compliance checks against the AWS and Azure Well-Architected frameworks and capacity forecasting as extensions.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers building LLM-assisted triage for any high-volume system, not only finance. It is architecture and practice, no live demo. If your team's prompts live in a Slack thread titled "useful prompts", this is the argument for moving them into a repo.

Title: Shipping AI models is solved; operating them safely is the hard part
Description: Saideepak Kandibanda (DISH Network) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 presents the AI Trust Triad, RL plus federated learning and explainable AI with DevOps guardrails.
Body:
Kubernetes, CI/CD and infrastructure as code already get models into production; the trouble starts the day after. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Saideepak Kandibanda of DISH Network, who leads AI and automation engineers, presented what he calls the AI Trust Triad: a framework for running reinforcement learning, federated learning and explainable AI in regulated systems with the same traceability and rollback you expect from any critical software.

The examples lean towards finance and supply chains, but the pipeline advice is domain-neutral. Think of it as a checklist for what your MLOps platform should track once models start making decisions that auditors care about.

## Treat the learning process as something you deploy

Reinforcement learning gets the most operational attention. Kandibanda's examples are portfolio optimisation that reallocates assets within risk constraints, automated circuit breakers that react to volatility, and supply chain routing driven by live demand signals. In every case the policy changes as it learns, which means a static model-approval process does not fit.

His four operational requirements:

- **Policy versioning**: every reward function, exploration policy and constraint is version-controlled.
- **Safe exploration**: new policies run in shadow mode before they touch real users or assets.
- **Reward monitoring**: check continuously that learned behaviour matches business goals instead of exploiting loopholes.
- **Meta-risk detection**: watch for second-order failures such as reward hacking and emergent behaviour.

The underlying idea is that the learning process itself must be observable, governable and reversible.

## Federated learning needs a DevOps-grade pipeline too

For industries where data cannot leave its boundary (banking, telecom, healthcare, e-commerce), federated learning trains locally and shares only encrypted updates, combined through secure aggregation. Kandibanda's production requirements are model versioning with cryptographic verification of every update, secure aggregation via homomorphic encryption or secure multi-party computation, drift detection to catch local models diverging or malicious updates arriving, and performance validation so the global model behaves fairly across participants. Private is necessary; he also wants it auditable and reproducible.

## Explanations can drift, and that is a signal

The third pillar, explainable AI, serves three audiences: regulators who need transparency, engineers who need fast debugging, and customers who expect fairness. In the pipeline he wants three checks: pre-deployment checks that each model version keeps stable, interpretable feature attributions; runtime explanations stored for every live prediction; and explanation monitoring over time.

That last one is the sharpest idea in the talk. If feature importance suddenly shifts, it is an early warning of drift or data problems, often before accuracy metrics move. Your model can keep its score and quietly change its reasoning, which is exactly what an auditor will ask about.

## Governance as code, lineage as default

The wrap-up is familiar DevOps applied to models: policy as code for approval workflows and explainability thresholds, drift dashboards with automated alerts and rollbacks, and progressive rollouts (canaries, A/B tests) that validate fairness and interpretability as well as accuracy. Reproducibility means versioning every dataset, hyperparameter and code dependency, containerised deterministic training, and end-to-end lineage from data ingestion to deployment.

He closes with three hidden risks to monitor in production (reward hacking, data poisoning through federated nodes, explanation drift) and a four-step blueprint: start with pipelines, layer in drift and explainability checks, monitor meta-risks proactively, release progressively.

## Who should watch

MLOps and platform engineers in regulated industries who already have a deployment pipeline and now need to prove that a model still behaves. It is a framework talk with no code, so it pairs well with something hands-on. If explainability in your shop is a SHAP plot someone made once for a slide, the explanation-monitoring section alone is worth your time.
