Title: Healthcare compliance works better as a pipeline than a report
Description: Sai Hanumara (L.A. Care Health Plan) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on cloud-native pipelines and analytics for provider network governance.
Body:
In health insurance, a wrong phone number in a provider directory is a compliance problem, a claims problem and a member problem at the same time. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Sai Hanumara, Lead SQL Developer at L.A. Care Health Plan, made the case that provider network governance should run like any other software system: version-controlled rules, automated tests and continuous monitoring, instead of manual reporting assembled before each audit.

It is a short talk and it stays at the architecture level. Its value is the framing, and the framing is one a lot of regulated teams need.

## The regulator moves faster than the legacy stack

Hanumara starts with the pressure: CMS requirements have grown significantly in recent years, while expectations on cost control and member experience keep rising. Many health plans have already moved workloads to the cloud and seen efficiency gains, but compliance itself often stays manual and fragmented.

He names three challenges: regulations change continuously, legacy systems struggle to provide audit-level transparency, and when compliance is manual and spread across tools, risk and operational drag grow together. On-premise systems are slow to scale and expensive to maintain, so keeping up with rule changes becomes a staffing problem.

## Unify the rules, then let pipelines check them

The architecture he describes has two halves. First, interoperability: regulatory data from CMS, state mandates and internal rules gets unified into one data layer. Second, cloud-native pipelines run continuous updates and real-time validation across environments, with analytics turning that data into something people can act on.

The point is a shift from reactive reporting to proactive governance. When validation runs all the time, an out-of-date provider record shows up as a failing check, not as a finding in next quarter's audit.

## Credentialing is the big win

Of the use cases, Hanumara singles out provider credentialing as one of the biggest wins. Automated intake, parallel verification and real-time compliance checks shorten the path from a provider's application to network activation, with fewer hand-offs along the way. Directory accuracy gets similar treatment: cleaner, continuously validated data means fewer claim denials, less administrative friction and members who can actually reach the doctor listed.

## DevOps is what makes it last

The DevOps layer is where the talk earns its slot at this conference. Compliance changes are version-controlled, automated testing protects data integrity during regulatory updates, and continuous monitoring detects compliance drift before an auditor does. Anyone who has watched a schema migration break a downstream report will recognise the pattern: treat a rule change like a code change, review it, test it, roll it out.

He also describes the shared-truth benefit. Regulators get real-time dashboards, providers get self-service visibility into their own records, and members get accurate information, all from the same source.

For the migration itself, he recommends phases: assess, design a scalable architecture, migrate incrementally, then optimise, minimising disruption along the way.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers at payers, providers or any organisation where a regulator reads your data. It is high-level and light on implementation detail, so treat it as a framing talk to share with stakeholders rather than a build guide. If your compliance process includes a spreadsheet emailed around before audits, this one is time well spent.

Title: Privacy by design belongs in the pipeline, not the audit
Description: Vivek Chittireddy (Meta) at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on k-anonymity, differential privacy, tokenization and DPIA gates baked into CI/CD.
Body:
Zip code, date of birth and gender are enough to re-identify about 87% of Americans, which is a good reason to stop treating privacy as a checkbox at the end of a project. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Vivek Chittireddy, a data engineer at Meta who works on privacy-centric data architectures and real-time streaming, argued that privacy controls belong in every stage of the data pipeline, and then walked through the techniques that make that practical.

He is clear up front that the talk reflects his own experience and nothing about his employer's internal systems. What you get is a compact tour of the toolbox, aimed at DevOps and data engineers who own pipelines rather than lawyers who own policies.

## The stakes are already high enough

Chittireddy opens with the numbers he uses to justify the effort: more than 140 countries with active privacy laws, and an average data breach cost of around $5 million in 2024. Add the re-identification figure and the conclusion is blunt: anonymous-looking data often isn't.

Privacy by design, in his framing, means building protections into the architecture from the client-side collection step through storage, analytics, processing and deployment. Bolting it on later is how you end up with PII in places nobody remembers creating.

## Four principles, one of them inconvenient

He lists four principles: be proactive, default to privacy, make privacy part of the design, and keep full functionality. The second one is the uncomfortable test. If users have to change a setting to become private, he says, you are doing it wrong.

The third principle comes with practical advice that is cheaper than any cryptography: collect as little data as you possibly can, and ask up front whether each field would cause harm in the wrong hands. The fourth keeps the whole thing honest, because a pipeline that is private and broken helps nobody.

## Anonymization has levels

The technical core is a ladder of techniques:

- **K-anonymity** makes every record indistinguishable from at least k minus one others. He cites k of 50 as typical for decent private systems, which suits demographic analytics.
- **L-diversity** adds variety of sensitive attributes inside each group, which matters for healthcare data where a whole group sharing one diagnosis leaks it.
- **Differential privacy** adds calibrated noise to query results so nobody can tell whether a given person is in the data. He suggests epsilon values between 0.1 and 1 for strong privacy without wrecking the statistics, and points at Opacus as a way to implement it, including local differential privacy in the browser.
- **Pseudonymization and tokenization** swap identifiers for pseudonyms or random tokens and keep the real values in a separate, locked-down store. Analytics never touches PII, and re-identification is a deliberate join done only for legitimate reasons such as customer support.

For teams that want to go further, he sketches homomorphic encryption (computing on encrypted data without decrypting it) and secure multi-party computation, where systems each process their share without pooling raw data.

## DPIAs as pipeline gates

The most DevOps-flavoured idea is treating the data protection impact assessment as a continuous process instead of a one-time document. Chittireddy suggests automatic privacy scans that stop sensitive data reaching code commits, pipeline gates that require DPIA approval before deploying changes that process personal data, and privacy metrics tracked daily next to performance and security. Counting how often PII nearly slipped into a pipeline is a metric most teams have never looked at.

His closing checklist is short: minimise data, encrypt wherever possible, role-based access for the people who need it, and compliance that runs automatically rather than by hand.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers who build pipelines touching personal data and want a vocabulary for talking to their privacy team. It is an overview, not a code walkthrough, so if you already run differential privacy in production you will mostly be nodding along. If "anonymised" in your org means dropping the name column, watch it twice.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Privacy by Design for JavaScript Data Systems](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2025_Vivekananda_Chittireddy_privacy_design_building) is Chittireddy's earlier take on the same theme, aimed at JavaScript data systems.

- [Anonymize application logs in DevOps way](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Leonid_Yankulin_structured_logging_google_cloud) by Leonid Yankulin (Google) tackles the PII that hides in logs.

Title: Compliance belongs in every stage of SaaS delivery, not just the audit
Description: Oracle engineering manager Pooja Ranjan at Conf42 DevOps 2026 maps where compliance lives in each SDLC stage of SaaS delivery and what to automate.
Body:
The gap between 99.95% and 99.99% availability looks like a rounding error on a contract. In practice it is the difference between a few hours of downtime a year and under an hour. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Pooja Ranjan, an engineering manager at Oracle America, used that gap as the entry point to a stage-by-stage tour of where compliance actually lives in SaaS delivery, and why automating it is how you keep promises like that without burning out your engineers.

It is a broad overview from someone with over a decade in B2B cloud software, good as a first talk on the topic.

## The SLA is the first compliance artefact

Ranjan starts before any code exists. In feature planning, product managers (increasingly with data-science tooling, including LLMs mining structured and unstructured data) decide what to build, and the legal side signs NDAs and contracts that fix the service level agreement: availability, scaling, and what happens financially when you miss. Everything downstream exists to keep that promise.

## Design and code reviews are compliance too

At architecture review, compliance means checking that every third-party component is either open source or properly licensed, and sending the design to an internal security team for a full posture review against things like denial of service and cross-site scripting. Findings send the design back to the architecture board.

In development, it means good coding practice, generated unit tests, design-doc revisions when something proves infeasible or risky, and a CI/CD gate stack: AI code-review bots, linters, and scanners that catch outdated or vulnerable package versions before merge, plus human reviewers.

## Tests are what auditors read

The testing stage is where her talk is most concrete. She describes a coverage bar of 95% or above as standard practice, black-box functional tests run continuously and touchlessly against production from Kubernetes or cron, white-box tests that catch infinite loops and null pointer exceptions, and load tests with Locust or JMeter to confirm that latency targets (such as requests completing within 500 milliseconds) actually hold.

Two US standards get a closer look. SOX requires documented acceptance criteria for every ticket and evidence of how they were met, kept ready for audit (Jira fields will do). VPAT, the Voluntary Product Accessibility Template, matters for federal customers: you test the UI with tools like screen readers, document results in an accessibility conformance report with screenshots, and redo it every year.

## Production is where governance never ends

After deploy, compliance becomes data handling: access control, isolation between customers' data, audited logging, constant dependency upgrades, and alarms (CloudWatch, Grafana) feeding scaling decisions. Ranjan notes that engineers at cloud providers can spend over 30% of their time just maintaining software, which is the argument for automating everything that can be. Her closing link is sustainability: less wasted engineering time and better-optimised code mean less hardware and a smaller carbon footprint.

## Who should watch

Engineers new to regulated SaaS delivery, and managers who need a map of where compliance work happens to explain it to a team. If you already run SOC 2 or FedRAMP programmes, the overview will be familiar; the VPAT section may still be news.

Title: GitOps for the network turns router changes into reviewed pull requests
Description: Imran Abdul at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on infrastructure as code for enterprise networks, with SD-WAN templates, canary rollouts and zero trust segmentation.
Body:
Push a security patch to 500 network devices the traditional way and you SSH into each one, paste the config, and do it again 499 times, starting over when you make a typo. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Imran Abdul (listed with Pace University, New York) showed how the same Git, CI/CD and canary habits application teams take for granted apply to enterprise networks, drawing on deployments across nuclear, solar and wind sites and enterprise data centres. His reported result: changes that took three to five days now finish in about 15 minutes across 500-plus sites, with a 95% success rate.

## Configuration drift is the silent outage

The problem statement is one every network engineer knows: devices drift from their intended state, troubleshooting gets close to impossible, a one-minute change takes days of coordination and approval windows, and rollback means digging out an old backup. Meanwhile the business wants global changes in minutes, consistent security policy, and connectivity across on-prem and several clouds.

## Templates in Git, pushed through a controller

Abdul uses Cisco Viptela as the worked example: vManage as the central brain for policy and configuration, vSmart as the control plane, vEdge routers as the data plane at every site. Change a policy once in vManage and it reaches every vEdge with no SSH sessions.

The IaC layer replaces hundreds of lines of CLI per device with a YAML template per site type: nuclear sites with strict security requirements, solar sites with isolated SCADA, wind sites with remote monitoring. Templates live in Git, every change has an explanation, and pull requests are reviewed by senior engineers.

## The pipeline, step by step

His GitOps workflow for adding, say, a new VLAN:

1. Branch, edit the YAML, commit with a descriptive message, open a pull request.
2. Automated syntax and policy-compliance checks, plus simulation in a virtual environment that mirrors production, with results posted on the PR.
3. Peer review of the business justification, security and approach, which catches design errors automation misses.
4. Canary deployment to one or two test sites, monitored for 30 to 60 minutes, then 10%, 50% and 100% of sites, with automatic rollback if anything fails.
5. Production rollout with dashboards and continuous health checks.

He credits pre-deployment validation with catching about 80% of errors before they go live.

## Zero trust you can enforce from code

The second half covers zero trust: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach. The concrete examples land well. SCADA systems at a wind site talk only to their control server and cannot reach corporate email, HR or other sites. Web tiers reach databases only through approved APIs. Access depends on identity, device posture, location and time, so the same engineer on a managed laptop during business hours gets in, and on public Wi-Fi at night is challenged. QoS keeps SCADA and voice traffic first even under attack.

He also covers routing automation that raises link costs on latency or loss, Cisco ACI's application-centric spine-leaf fabric with VXLAN, and defining one policy (SCADA on port 502 to its control server only) that is translated into AWS Transit Gateway, Azure Virtual WAN and on-prem firewall rules alike.

## Who should watch

Network teams who want to borrow DevOps practice without a big-bang rewrite, and DevOps engineers who keep getting blocked by manual network changes. His starting step costs nothing: put the existing configs of one device type into Git, and make every change go through it.

Title: Lift and shift first, then Kubernetes, so you change one thing at a time
Description: Google staff SRE Harris Baskaran at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on moving a ticketing monolith from VMware and Oracle to GCE, then GKE and PostgreSQL.
Body:
Change your infrastructure, your runtime and your database in one go, and when latency jumps you will not know whether to blame the network, a pod limit or a rewritten stored procedure. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Harris Baskaran, a staff SRE at Google, made the case for doing it in two phases, using the migration of a two-decade-old ticketing monolith that handles more than a hundred thousand tickets a day: first lift and shift onto Google Compute Engine, then rebuild cloud-native on GKE with PostgreSQL.

It is a grounded case study, including the parts they would do differently.

## Phase one buys a baseline

The starting point: a tightly coupled monolith on ageing VMware with a very large Oracle database, globally deployed, untouched for about a decade, where even patching was risky. Phase one moved it to GCE as is, to exit VMware quickly and, more importantly, to measure how the unchanged app behaves in the cloud before adding containers.

Four steps made that safe. Dependency mapping with discovery tools on the network, not just the code (he notes how many zombie services and undocumented API calls a ten-year-old monolith hides). A parallel cloud environment that mirrored production. Continuous replication with Oracle's native tooling, so the data was already there at cutover. And a cutover by DNS and load balancer redirects that took minutes, with an easy fallback.

The measured latency, throughput and resource utilisation then became the bar phase two had to meet or beat.

## The database was the real migration

Phase two moved the workload to GKE and the data from Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Baskaran calls the database the hardest hurdle: rewriting custom PL/SQL packages, time zone conversions, character sets and data types, kept in sync with change data capture, and many rounds of performance tuning and load testing. Terraform made it cheap to spin up a full load-test environment and tear it down again.

## Zero trust replaces the perimeter

On-prem security was a hard perimeter. On GKE it became layers: Workload Identity instead of long-lived service account keys, so pods get short-lived rotated tokens; network policies across more than 200 distinct communication paths, started loose and tightened as traffic was observed, with default deny; image scanning and Binary Authorization in the build; and automated mTLS plus customer-managed encryption keys. The phase-one dependency map is what made those fine-grained policies possible.

## DR went from recovery to resilience

Legacy DR meant manual backups and recovery times measured in hours or days, rarely tested. Phase one brought automated persistent disk snapshots; phase two brought multi-region deployment and Backup for GKE. Before go-live, the team ran Google's "wheels of misfortune" exercises to test RTO and RPO for real. His line on untested DR plans: a system only theoretically ready for disaster is a liability.

## What they would change

Two honest regrets. Start the schema simplification for Postgres much earlier, even during phase one. And add distributed tracing to the monolith before the lift and shift, not after; it would have made latency jitter far easier to find.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform teams with a big, old, business-critical system and a mandate to modernise it. His four takeaways work as a checklist: map dependencies, measure baselines, plan for database complexity, test DR.

Title: Four layers and a few algorithms keep APIs up at billions of requests
Description: Disney's Nikhil Kokal at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on edge caching, request coalescing, distributed rate limiting, sharding and tail-based tracing.
Body:
Ten thousand requests for the same uncached item arrive in the same instant. Without help, that is ten thousand database queries and a database that will not be answering the ten thousand and first. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Nikhil Kokal, a software engineering manager at The Walt Disney Company (previously Google and Salesforce), walked through the architectures and algorithms that keep APIs fast past the billion-request mark, drawing on ad platforms that handle over 200 billion annual impressions.

It is a dense, well-organised survey, closer to a reference card than a war story.

## Scaling hits a coordination wall

His starting point: vertical scaling has physical limits, and horizontal scaling done naively adds coordination overhead. Past some node count, service discovery, health checks and state sync start costing more than the work. He nods to Netflix's edge caching and adaptive streaming, Uber's geo-sharding to keep one city's surge from becoming everyone's noisy neighbour, and RevenueCat's request coalescing.

## The edge: the fastest request never reaches you

Layer one is the edge, and the main lever is cache key design. Too specific and your hit rate collapses; too broad and you serve stale data. Segment keys by user class, geography or device type. Use stale-while-revalidate so an expired entry is served immediately while a background fetch refreshes it, and adaptive TTLs that stretch when the backend is under load. Kokal says the combination can cut origin traffic by 95%.

## Coalescing and rate limiting are reliability tools

Back to that thundering herd: the single-flight pattern marks the first miss as in flight, queues every later request for the same key, and broadcasts the one database result to all of them. One query instead of ten thousand. He calls it a reliability insurance policy, and it is the cheapest one in the talk.

At the gateway layer, the token bucket allows bursts (handy when a web app loads 20 resources at once) while the leaky bucket enforces a smooth rate for fragile legacy downstreams. The hard part is global: a 1,000-requests-per-minute limit across 50 data centres. His answer is local-first counting with periodic sync to a central Redis-style cluster, trading a little accuracy for local speed.

## Data and services: shard well, break circuits early

Multi-region active-active beats active-passive: geo-DNS sends users to the nearest healthy region, each region keeps enough data to serve requests if the cross-region link is cut, and CRDTs merge concurrent profile updates without human help. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes lets you add or remove database nodes without remapping everything, and geographic sharding often doubles as data-residency compliance. A service mesh such as Envoy or Istio handles mTLS, retries with exponential backoff and circuit breakers that stop the death spiral of retries hammering a failing service.

## Observe failures, not everything

At this volume, logging everything would cost more than compute. Tail-based tracing buffers each trace and keeps it only if the request failed or ran slow (he uses 200 ms as the example), giving full visibility into failures while storing a fraction of the data. Predictive autoscaling then pre-provisions capacity from historical traffic, because reactive scaling at 70% CPU arrives after the spike.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers whose traffic is growing faster than their architecture, and anyone preparing for a live event or a viral moment. If you already run all of this, the closing look ahead (energy-aware elasticity, chasing P99.99 rather than P99) is still worth the last few minutes.

Title: One shared cluster, a namespace per branch, only changed services
Description: NetApp architect Ravi Babu Dasari at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on a shared-cluster dev platform that deploys only changed services per feature branch.
Body:
If your SaaS product has a hundred microservices, a dedicated test cluster per feature branch means a hundred copies of services you did not touch, idling on your cloud bill. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Ravi Babu Dasari, a senior lead software engineer and architect at NetApp, showed the platform his team uses instead: one shared cluster holds a baseline of every service, and each feature branch gets its own namespace containing only the services it changed.

He calls it SDDP, a scalable development deployment platform, and he ends with a live demo on Rancher Desktop.

## Why canaries are not a dev environment

Dasari dismisses the two usual options quickly. Dedicated clusters are slow to provision and expensive to keep around, especially the ones nobody deleted. Canary builds are designed for production rollouts: you typically get one, not one per developer, and they get awkward fast with stateful services.

## Baseline plus overlays, stitched by ingress

When a developer pushes a branch, the platform creates a namespace, applies Helm or Kustomize overrides and gives the branch its own URL. Only modified services (and anything that must come along) are deployed there; everything else is served from the shared baseline, which CI keeps current from staging or production.

Three things hold it together:

- **Dynamic wildcard ingress rules**, so a request to a branch URL hits the branch's version of a service where one exists and the baseline otherwise.
- **Network policies**, so feature namespaces cannot talk to each other, only to approved baseline services. Without that, branches collide in ways that are miserable to debug.
- **Resource quotas**, so one runaway branch cannot slow the cluster for everyone.

A web portal sits on top for developers, QA and product owners to create sandboxes, pick baselines and share previews. In the demo, one branch deploys a new frontend and API while using the baseline backend; another deploys only the backend; calling the endpoints shows which version answered each hop.

## State is the hard part

Stateless services share easily. Databases, caches and blob storage do not: one branch adding a column another branch does not expect is how a shared environment corrupts itself. His answer is change analysis on the branch diff. A new endpoint with no schema change shares the database; a migration gets a replicated database in the branch namespace. Connection strings are injected per namespace, caches are isolated by key or instance. He suggests an LLM agent reading diffs across repositories is now good enough to make that share-or-replicate call automatically.

## Who should watch

Platform teams fielding a steady stream of own-environment requests for a large microservice estate, and anyone whose preview environments cost more than production. Dasari says he has been running and maintaining the platform at NetApp for years, and that the production version is a lot more complex than the demo. His adoption advice is incremental: start with easy stateless services like the UI, replicate stateful ones until you can share them safely, automate, then scale.

Title: GenOps treats the AI in your pipeline like a supervised junior engineer
Description: Meta staff engineer Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on GenOps, a governance model with blast-radius scores and signed AI changes.
Body:
Ask an LLM to optimise the same Dockerfile three times and you get three different Dockerfiles. In a CI/CD pipeline, that variance is a bug. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Neeraj Kumar Singh Beshane, a staff software engineer at Meta whose career runs through Wayfair, JPMorgan Chase and American Express, presented GenOps: a governance-first way to let generative agents act inside pipelines by giving them the same supervision you would give a new hire.

## Faster coding, shakier delivery

He frames the problem with industry numbers: high reported AI adoption, the promised productivity boost from coding assistants, and the 2024 DORA finding that delivery stability dropped for teams rushing to adopt AI. His metaphor: a faster car with the seat belts taken out.

Then a near miss from his own experience. An AI agent working through Terraform looked at a legacy authentication handler, saw no recent commits, decided it was unused and tried to delete it. That service authenticated 20 million users. A human caught it, and he admits it kept him up for a week.

## From helper to pipeline actor

The mental shift is the core of the talk. A chatbot or coding assistant is an external helper with zero accountability: if its suggestion breaks the build, you broke the build. In GenOps the AI is a pipeline actor with a service account and permissions, it triggers builds and opens its own pull requests. That sounds terrifying until you compare it with onboarding a junior engineer: sandbox first, every PR reviewed, no unsupervised production deploys at 5pm on a Friday.

## Four pillars of governance

- **Context.** RAG over build history, incidents, postmortems and Slack threads. Before the AI prepares a deployment, the prompt is intercepted and the relevant recent builds plus current infrastructure state are injected, so it knows that the last time someone touched this config it leaked memory.
- **Blast-radius scoring.** Before a merge, the dependency graph is analysed: a README change scores low and auto-merges, a change to a core auth library used by dozens of services scores high and needs a human. Scores map to error budgets per service, enforced with Open Policy Agent as a pass-or-fail gate, not a PDF.
- **SLO-based canaries.** Deploy to 1% of traffic, watch latency, error rate, CPU, memory and IO, and roll back automatically if latency drifts by two standard deviations. No waiting for a customer tweet or a PagerDuty alert.
- **Runtime assurance.** Every AI-generated change is cryptographically signed with the exact model version, prompt and injected context, so you can later query every service touched by a given model. Auditors, he suggests, will like this better than human changes.

## The 14.4% that would have been outages

His headline result is a protection rate: in 14.4% of cases, despite all the context and prompting, the AI tried something dangerous (an SLA-violating change, a vulnerable dependency) and the governance layer blocked it. He also reports a 55% faster cycle time and a Meta tool that turned a multi-hour onboarding task into a five-minute automated flow. The blocks are fed back into memory, so the system learns from its near misses.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps leads being asked to put agents into CI/CD, and security teams being asked to approve it. If you want a vocabulary for that negotiation (blast radius, error budgets, signed provenance), this talk has it. His Formula One line sums it up: the brakes are there so the driver can go fast.

Title: Replay production traffic to migrate a gateway with zero downtime
Description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure's Kalyan Inturi at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on moving a Ruby monolith gateway to Kong using sampled shadow-traffic parity checks.
Body:
Synthetic tests only check the behaviour you remembered to write down. A legacy gateway is mostly behaviour nobody wrote down. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Kalyan Inturi, a principal member of technical staff at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, walked through how his team replaced a monolithic Ruby gateway with Kong without a customer-facing incident, by replaying sampled production requests against the new gateway and diffing everything.

This is a case study with a reusable trick at its centre, and it is the trick that makes it worth the watch.

## The monolith in question

The old gateway was Ruby and Sinatra, with session management, authentication, authorisation and routing all in one service. A routing change could break the auth stack. It could not make good use of multi-core machines, scaling one concern meant scaling all of them, Ruby expertise was getting scarce, and security vulnerabilities kept piling up. The obvious plan (write unit and integration tests against the old system, run them on the new one, cut over when green) fails exactly because of the undocumented behaviour and tribal knowledge baked into years of changes.

## Shadow traffic without double writes

The core of the talk is a five-step replay mechanism, and it solves the problem that makes most shadow-traffic schemes scary: executing a write twice.

1. The legacy gateway handles the request normally and answers the client.
2. Asynchronously, a processor on the legacy side assigns a parity ID and stores the downstream request, downstream response and client response in a NoSQL store.
3. It fires the same request at Kong with the parity ID added as a query parameter.
4. Kong does what the legacy gateway should do and forwards downstream. There, an interceptor spots the parity ID and, instead of executing the call again, returns the stored downstream response from the cache.
5. The processor compares both sides and records every difference.

Two comparisons come out of it: what each gateway sent to the backend, and what each sent back to the client. Inturi calls this a store-and-forward pattern that decouples validation from real backend state. Reads would have been safe anyway; the interceptor is what makes writes safe.

## Sample, then roll out in phases

Replaying everything would double load on downstream systems, so they sampled roughly one fifth of requests with a random function over the request ID, on the assumption that over time every route and function would be covered. The full plan had eight phases, from Terraform-provisioned infrastructure with routes captured as YAML for Kong, through load testing, shadow validation and offloading authentication into its own microservice, to incremental traffic shifting, final cutover and retiring the old gateway.

## What it bought

Inturi reports zero customer-facing incidents across millions of requests and around a 20% reduction in compute cost, mostly from independent scaling: no more scaling the whole Ruby stack to serve lightweight auth checks. A vendor-supported gateway took over security patches, and mean time to recovery dropped with automated deployments and rollbacks.

## Who should watch

Anyone facing a project to replace the thing everything goes through: gateways, auth services, API layers. His closing point is that the pattern is not gateway-specific; it applies to any backend REST migration where the old system's behaviour is the only real spec.

Title: AI agents on call multiply your speed and your mistakes
Description: Vladyslav Budichenko of Vocaly AI at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on where AI agents help incident response, where they go wrong, and prompt injection via logs.
Body:
Here is an incident nobody budgets for: an attacker writes a prompt into a request, it lands in your logs, and during the next investigation your helpful AI agent reads it and does what it says. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Vladyslav Budichenko, a senior software engineer at Vocaly AI with a background in platform and observability engineering, sorted AI agents for incident response into the good, the bad and the ugly. His verdict: use them as a force multiplier, and remember that they multiply your mistakes too.

It is a practitioner's talk with no product pitch, from someone who uses Claude Code, Cursor and custom agents day to day.

## The good: gathering and correlating, fast

The slow part of most investigations is not the fix. It is pulling the alert context, checking the playbook, gathering logs and metrics from several systems and correlating them: the service is failing, and CPU is high. That is exactly what an agent does well. Budichenko points to the commercial wave (Datadog, PagerDuty, Honeycomb's MCP, New Relic) and to the open-source route: wire Claude, Cursor, Codex or your own agent into Loki, Tempo or an ELK stack.

The enabler is MCP, the Model Context Protocol, which replaced everyone writing their own API glue. One agent can search Slack for a similar discussion from a year ago, check the Jira ticket behind a deployment, read telemetry in Datadog or Grafana, look up the page in PagerDuty and open the code in GitHub.

## The bad: rabbit holes, garbage in, context limits

Agents can dig without end: fetch, analyse, fetch more, try a change, crash, repeat. You have to bound them. Garbage in, garbage out still applies: without good alerts, decent telemetry and access to it, the agent has nothing useful to reason over. And even million-token windows run out when you pour raw logs into them, so you scope by time (the incident window plus or minus about ten minutes, widened only if needed) and reduce log volume with tooling first.

His structural fix is a swarm rather than one generalist: narrow agents that collect logs, metrics or events, an analytical agent working from a playbook, and an orchestrator on top. Focused agents give better answers.

## The ugly: rubber stamps and prompt injection

The worst failures are human. Engineers approve agent output without reading it, so human-in-the-loop quietly stops being a loop. Senior skills erode, and juniors lose the chance to learn because some companies decided seniors with AI were enough.

Then security. Budichenko compares prompt injection to SQL injection two decades ago, and the log vector above is the scary version: data you investigate becomes instructions. The mitigations are the ones you would expect, applied without exceptions: restrict which tools an agent can call and what it can reach on the internet, run read-only by default, and require approval for everything else.

## Who should watch

SREs and on-call leads deciding how much autonomy to hand an investigation agent, and anyone already running one in YOLO mode. The takeaway is a clear split: trust agents for data gathering, aggregation, pattern recognition and first-pass analysis; verify everything else; never let them take high-risk actions unapproved.

Title: Beyond LLM template generators to a RAG-aware infrastructure agent
Description: Equinix's Praneeth Patil at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on an autonomous multi-cloud infrastructure agent built on RAG, staged verification and tight IAM.
Body:
Asking an LLM to write Terraform gets you a template. It does not get you the right values, an awareness of what is already deployed, or any idea whether the change will break the network three clouds away. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Praneeth Patil, a senior staff engineer at Equinix, argued for the next step: an autonomous infrastructure agent that knows your multi-cloud estate through retrieval, checks its own work in stages, and runs under least-privilege identities.

It is a short, opinionated talk. Expect a vision and a build order, not a product demo.

## Multi-cloud is a stitching problem

Patil's starting picture is familiar to anyone at a company of any size: training in Nvidia's cloud, data pipelines in AWS, inference in GCP, sensitive data on-prem, and a constant need to connect them. Every provider names the same thing differently (direct connect, express connect, cloud routers), and the tooling has multiplied: Terraform and Terraform Cloud, Pulumi, Kubernetes operators, Crossplane for reconciliation, CloudFormation.

What all that produces, in his words, is fear of change. State files that disagree with what someone clicked in the console. Opaque state. Cognitive overload from a pile of DSLs and APIs. And tribal knowledge: the one engineer you hope never leaves.

## LLMs as glorified template generators

His critique of today's "AI for IaC" is blunt. LLMs speed you up, but the output is only as good as your prompt, they have no context about your real infrastructure, you still verify correctness, security policy and syntax by hand, and there is no operational intelligence at all. The agent he describes turns a passive code generator into a system that keeps an up-to-date picture of your infrastructure, reasons about changes, acts, and self-corrects.

## RAG in three parts, then a verification pipeline

The architecture centres on a purpose-built retrieval layer, split three ways:

- **Specialised retrieval:** a domain-specific vector store of infrastructure metadata, configuration templates, provider schemas, relationship indices and historical change logs, so the agent can see why a past decision was made.
- **Real-time sync:** cloud feeds, activity logs and drift detection streaming into the agent, so it reasons on today's state rather than last year's provider docs.
- **Guardrail workflows:** mandatory checkpoints, with human-in-the-loop escalation.

Every proposed change then runs through a multi-stage verification pipeline: syntax, semantics (relationships and organisational constraints), security (no stray open ports, no overwritten security groups) and compliance checks from InfoSec.

## The risks get their own slide

Patil does not pretend this is safe by default. He names context-window limits (mitigated by specialised retrieval and summarisation), identity boundary failures (least privilege, service accounts), hallucination (multi-stage verification and dry runs) and the scariest one, a compromised agent manipulating production (immutable audit trails and anomaly detection on agent behaviour). Agents should get time-bound permissions, MFA through their service accounts, segregated execution environments and continuous permission monitoring in case they try to grant themselves more.

## Who should watch

Platform and cloud networking teams drowning in multi-cloud glue, and anyone pitching an agent that runs Terraform to a security team. His build order is sensible: RAG foundation first, then the verification pipeline, then agents on low-risk, high-repetition tasks, scaled up only with governance. If you want benchmarks or a working repo, this talk will not give you one.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Kevin Brown on why your agent can write Terraform but can't feel what it breaks](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2026_Kevin_Brown_agent_terraform_break) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2026, the sceptic's companion piece.

Title: Taking multimodal voice and vision agents from demo to production
Description: Amazon's Gobu Natarajan at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on fusion trade-offs, task-level evals, cross-modal tracing and fallbacks for multimodal agents.
Body:
"Find a comedy movie for family night" sounds like one request to the person on the sofa. To the system behind a voice-enabled TV it is speech recognition, on-screen context, personalisation and live content availability, all of which have to agree within a latency budget. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Gobu Natarajan, a technical program management manager at Amazon, turned that example into a production checklist for multimodal conversational agents.

He says up front that this is a framework, not a low-level design. Think of it as the questions to answer before your impressive demo meets real traffic.

## Users go multimodal without being taught

Natarajan cites field studies across 250 households that saw about a 30 percent improvement in task completion when people could combine modalities instead of using voice or text alone. The more interesting finding: within roughly three weeks, users drifted to multimodal commands on their own. So the question he poses is not whether multimodal works, but how you operate it at scale.

## Four stages that must fail separately

His reference pipeline has four stages: ingestion, fusion, reasoning and action. They are split so each can scale, fail and be observed independently. When teams blur the boundaries, debugging in production becomes close to impossible.

Ingestion is where things go quietly wrong. Audio, video, touch and sensor data arrive at different frequencies and latencies, and if timestamps are not aligned, perfect models still reason about the wrong moment. He wants strict synchronisation, back-pressure handling and observability hooks from day one.

## Pick a fusion strategy by its failure mode

Early fusion combines signals immediately: fast when everything is in sync, brittle when one modality goes missing. Late fusion processes each modality on its own and merges decisions later: better fault isolation, more latency, and lost cross-modal nuance. Most production systems, he says, end up hybrid. The choice is driven by five constraints: latency budget, where GPUs live (device or cloud), streaming versus batch, degradation paths, and cost controls including data transfer. In production those matter more than theoretical model accuracy.

## Text metrics do not grade a system that looks at your room

For evaluation he proposes four multimodal metrics: task success rate (did the user get what they wanted, end to end), grounding accuracy (did it identify the right objects and spatial context), modality agreement (do voice, vision and touch line up) and temporal alignment (were the signals in sync over time).

Observability gets three tools: cross-modal tracing with correlation IDs to follow one interaction across audio, video and touch; per-modality compute attribution, because one modality often quietly eats most of the GPU budget; and drift detection on inputs, behaviour and model performance. Safeguards complete the set: fall back to a single modality such as voice when fusion fails, degrade gracefully under load, and treat audio and video privacy (encryption, retention limits, consent) as a requirement.

## Who should watch

Teams shipping voice or vision features on devices, cars or wearables, and DevOps engineers inheriting an ML system they did not design. The closing advice is the kind you can paste into a design review: architecture matters most, measure real task success, observe everything, plan for failure before it happens. Roll out behind feature flags and keep runbooks and an on-call rotation.

Title: AgentCast lets an agent pick, tune and retrain your forecasting model
Description: Amazon applied scientist Premanand Tiwari at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on AgentCast, an agent that chooses, tunes and retrains capacity forecasting models.
Body:
Capacity planning usually needs a data scientist, a planner and an ops engineer in the same room, and none of them are cheap. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Premanand Tiwari, an applied scientist at Amazon who builds forecasting models for capacity and inventory planning, presented AgentCast: an agent that looks at your time series, picks the model family, tunes it, deploys it and retrains it when accuracy slips, with no human choosing anything along the way.

It is a design walkthrough of a system he built, not a tutorial. If you want to know what an "autonomous forecaster" has to decide on your behalf, it is a tidy map.

## The model zoo is the point

The core argument is that no single model wins on infrastructure data, so the agent carries a whole toolkit and chooses per dataset. Tiwari lists the shelves: statistical models (ARIMA, auto ARIMA, Holt-Winters) for simple series, gradient boosting such as XGBoost when you have many independent variables and a short or medium horizon, and deep models (Temporal Fusion Transformers, N-BEATS, DeepAR, LSTMs and GRUs) when the horizon is long and the dependencies stretch across months.

The agent trains candidates, runs hyperparameter search itself (he notes it builds the search grid from the data rather than asking you for one), scores them on MAE, MAPE, RMSE, WAPE or a custom metric you supply, and can ensemble two or three models when no single one is best. Anyone who has hand-tuned a Holt-Winters model at midnight will see the appeal.

## Probabilistic forecasts beat a single line

A design choice worth copying even without the agent: AgentCast emits P10, P50, P70 and P90 rather than one point forecast. For capacity, the spread is the useful part. A wide band tells you demand is volatile and you need headroom; a narrow one says you can run closer to the line. The same horizon knob covers sub-minute operational views up to monthly, quarterly and multi-year planning.

## Forecasts as a cheaper autoscaler

The most DevOps-flavoured idea in the talk is a jab at reactive autoscaling. Tiwari's point is that autoscaling works, but the bill at the end of the month can be painful. His alternative is to feed the agent's forecasts into your scaling configuration, so pods, CPUs or GPUs are added ahead of a predicted spike (holiday traffic is his example) instead of after the CPU graph has already gone vertical.

He also describes the operational wrapper you would want around any model in production: daily or weekly retraining, live tracking of error metrics against an acceptable band, automatic re-selection of the model when the data changes shape, versioning with rollback, and A/B testing one deployment against another.

## Honest scope

The abstract promises live demos; the recording is a slide walkthrough of the architecture and the expected workflow (CPU, memory and network traffic forecasts), not a screen-share. There are no accuracy numbers either, so treat it as the shape of a system rather than proof that it beats your current planner. The questions it raises are the good ones: what does the agent do when the data is sparse or intermittent, and who signs off when it swaps the model under you?

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE folks who own capacity planning and keep losing arguments with the finance team. ML engineers thinking about how far AutoML-style selection can be pushed into an agent loop will get a useful checklist. If you already run a mature forecasting service, you can skim.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Piotr Stepinski on forecasting time series with Polars and Deno](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2024_Piotr_Stepinski_forecasting_timeseries) at Conf42 Machine Learning 2024, a hands-on counterpart to the model zoo.
- [Pawel Skrzypek and Anna Warno on advanced ensembling for time series forecasting](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2022_Pawel_Skrzypek_Anna_Warno_ensembling_techniques_time_series_forecasting), for the ensembling step AgentCast automates.
- [Vasuki Uday Kiran Vudathala on turning observability signals into peak readiness](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Vasuki_Uday_Kiran_Vudathala_loadtesting_performance_capacityplanning) at Conf42 Observability 2026, the capacity side of the same problem.

Title: Predictive CI/CD scores each pipeline run for risk before it ships
Description: Cognizant architect Pallab Haldar at Conf42 DevOps 2026 on predictive DevOps with telemetry, anomaly detection and risk scores that gate CI/CD runs.
Body:
Most pipelines learn about a bad release from the alert that fires after it lands. At Conf42 DevOps 2026, Pallab Haldar, a technical architect at Cognizant, laid out a reference architecture for predictive DevOps: collect CI/CD and runtime telemetry, model it, score every pipeline execution for risk, and let a decision engine proceed, pause or block the stage before anything reaches production.

The talk is a layer-by-layer architecture tour rather than a war story, so come for the blueprint, not for benchmark numbers.

## Why reactive pipelines break

Haldar opens with the failure list most teams will recognise: monitoring that alerts after the damage is done, failures detected late because logs and batch jobs surface them hours afterwards, and humans doing the heavy lifting at every trigger. His framing is simple: a pipeline that only reacts is always one incident behind.

## Six layers from commit to gate

The architecture he walks through has a clear order, and it is the most reusable part of the talk:

1. **Data sources and ingestion.** Agents and collectors pull logs, metrics and events from CI/CD and infrastructure, through both streaming and batch paths, then normalise them into one model-ready schema with context tags.
2. **Feature engineering.** Raw signals become trends, windows and baselines, plus change-level features such as code complexity and dependency analysis.
3. **Model layer.** Time-series forecasting and outcome prediction trained on pipeline history.
4. **Anomaly detection.** A baseline of normal log patterns and expected metric ranges, so weak signals show up before they turn into failures.
5. **Risk scoring.** Forecasts, anomaly scores and historical signals combined into one risk view per pipeline run.
6. **Decision engine.** Policies and thresholds that decide whether a stage proceeds, pauses or is blocked, and escalate to a human only when needed.

The pleasant surprise is how conservative the integration story is. Haldar insists this sits beside your existing tooling: no CI/CD replacement, existing pipelines unchanged, lightweight hooks, no retraining of the team.

## The loop is what makes it predictive

The last piece is the feedback loop: when the actual outcome differs from the prediction, the error goes back into the model, run after run, until predicted and actual outcomes converge. He calls it predicting smarter with every cycle. That is ordinary supervised learning, but applied to deploy outcomes it means your gate thresholds should improve with each release instead of staying frozen at whatever someone guessed in the first sprint.

He also extends the idea to predictive maintenance: cluster capacity and node failure prediction, so you fix tomorrow's outage today. Every on-call engineer would sign that petition.

## Who should watch

Platform teams sketching an AIOps layer for their delivery pipeline and wanting a checklist of components and their order. Architects who need a diagram to argue with will find plenty. If you want concrete tooling, model choices or before-and-after metrics, the talk stays at the reference-architecture level, so pair it with something hands-on.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Saranya Jena and Sarthak Jain on chaos engineering inside CD pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2024_Saranya_Jena_Sarthak_Jain_embracing_resilience_power_cd_pipelines) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2024, another way to find risk before production does.

Title: Conf42 IoT 2025: from houseplants to Kafka, edge AI and payments
Description: Conf42 IoT 2025 roundup - Grafana-monitored houseplants, IoT data pipelines and lakehouses, edge AI cameras, supply chain security and device payments.
Body:
Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025 ran online on December 18, 2025, with ten talks that followed sensor data from the moment it is measured to the moment someone pays for it. The data track was the strongest, with four talks on moving and storing device telemetry at scale. Around it sat edge AI, supply chain security, payments, and one talk about keeping houseplants alive that may be the best introduction to observability Conf42 has published.

Every session is on the [Conf42 IoT 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/iot2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrAoyYvqm9wESh0loKTsm84Y).

## Observability, explained to an eight-year-old

[Marie Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Marie_Cruz_sensors_gardening_analytics), Senior Developer Advocate at Grafana Labs and co-author of Contract Testing in Action, declared 2025 the year of no plant casualties. She teamed up with her eight-year-old daughter on a beginner-friendly project: a soil moisture sensor that reports to Grafana Cloud and tells them when to water.

The project is fun, but the real value is the vocabulary. Marie explains IoT, monitoring, and observability through gardening analogies: each plant gets a little helper in the soil that detects moisture and tells you when it needs water. If you have ever struggled to explain your job at a family dinner, take notes. If you have ever killed a house plant, you are the target audience; Marie asks for a show of hands on exactly that.

## The data track: streams, lakehouses, feature stores

Four talks dealt with what happens after billions of devices start talking.

- [Rehmat Kharal](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Rehmat_Kharal_streaming_scalability_governance) of Conduktor looked at making IoT streams on systems like Kafka reliable, secure, and usable, covering messy pipelines, outages, and governance. The hard part, as the talk frames it, is the move from devices producing data to data producing value.
- [Ketul Dusane](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Ketul_Dusane_messaging_latency_throughput), a Software Development Engineer at AWS, covered messaging at scale with three pillars: low latency, high throughput, and operational resilience, using caching, load balancing, and anomaly detection.
- [Bhanudeepti Chinta](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Bhanudeepti_Chinta_lakehouse_analytics_scalable), an Engineering Manager for data, made the point that organisations rarely fail at IoT because they cannot collect data. They struggle because the cost and complexity of managing it grow faster than the value extracted, which is where lakehouse architectures that unify telemetry, device logs, and analytics come in.
- [Manmohan Alla](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Manmohan_Alla_warehousing_featurestores_optimization) of Apple showed how Snowflake plus a structured feature store turns raw sensor data into ML-ready features, with examples from manufacturing, utilities, energy grids, and smart monitoring.

Watched back to back, these four make a decent reference architecture for device data, from broker to model.

## Edge AI: make the camera think

[Madhu Niranjan Reddy Puduru](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Madhu_Niranjan_Reddy_Puduru_vision_edge_processing), a Software Engineering Manager at Synchronoss Technologies, made the case against cloud-only smart cameras. Streaming raw video costs bandwidth, adds latency that real-time safety alerts cannot afford, raises GDPR and CCPA privacy questions, and gets expensive across hundreds of cameras. Running the model next to the sensor and sending only events like "person detected" fixes all four. The abstract promises neural networks on $10 hardware, which is the kind of constraint that makes edge work interesting.

[Ramakrishna Ambati](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Ramakrishna_Ambati_maintenance_predictive_medical), an Enterprise Solutions Architect at Visby Medical, applied edge computing, machine learning, and zero trust security to medical diagnostic devices, moving maintenance from reacting to failures to predicting them, with results from a real deployment.

## Security: the attack comes in the box

[Gresshma Atluri](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Gresshma_Atluri_security_supplychain_defense), a cybersecurity risk analyst, opened with a story from a hospital she consulted for, where a vulnerability planted during manufacturing put patient safety at risk. Supply chain attacks do not break in through the front door; they arrive in trusted updates and embedded components. She also recalled the Mirai botnet built from baby monitors and cameras with default passwords, and a logistics company whose smart scanners were hijacked through compromised firmware. The defences: hardware attestation, network segmentation, and behavioural analytics.

## Money moves at the edge too

Two talks looked at finance. [Silpa Potluri](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payments_microservices_architecture) of GoodLeap, with more than ten years in the payments industry, explained how payment gateways moved from monoliths to microservices to handle transactions initiated by connected devices acting on our behalf. [Swetha Lakkaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Swetha_Lakkaraju_banking_modular_modernization), with more than 18 years in mainframe-based core banking, argued for modular core architectures that let banks decouple from legacy systems without a big-bang rewrite.

## Partners and what's next

Conf42 IoT 2025 was supported by the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners listed on the event page.

For earlier editions of the series, see [Conf42 IoT 2024](https://www.conf42.com/iot2024). And if the data track was your favourite part, the [Conf42 Robotics 2025](https://www.conf42.com/robotics2025) lineup covers similar ground with more moving parts.

Title: From sensors to cities, iot is taking over
Description: Everything is connected
Body:
# Your devices are talking. A lot.

IoT used to be about connecting things.

Now it’s about securing them, scaling them, analyzing them, and explaining why they’re generating so much data at such inconvenient times. Sensors are everywhere, and they’re not shy.

Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025 is a look at what IoT actually looks like once it leaves the lab.

This conference brings together nine talks across two tracks, focused on real-world IoT systems running in production. From smart cameras and medical devices to payment systems and connected supply chains, these sessions are about devices that matter and data that can’t be ignored.

Edge computing plays a big role. You’ll hear about running AI directly on devices, real-time image processing without cloud dependencies, and building IoT architectures that keep working even when connectivity doesn’t. Because sometimes the cloud is far away, and decisions still need to be made.

Security and trust show up everywhere. Talks cover IoT supply chain defense, securing connected ecosystems, and designing edge architectures that can survive cyberattacks without grinding everything to a halt. When devices are deployed at scale, “we’ll patch it later” stops being an option.

Data is the other half of the story. IoT data lakehouses, messaging at scale, low-latency pipelines, and cost-aware analytics all feature prominently. These sessions explore how to turn massive device streams into something useful, reliable, and affordable.

And yes, there’s room for fun too. From monitoring plants with sensors to using Grafana dashboards to keep things alive, IoT still has a playful side, even when the systems get serious.

If your world involves connected devices, edge systems, or figuring out what all that data is trying to tell you, this one’s for you. IoT is messy, powerful, and very much alive.

Title: One feature pipeline for six teams, not six for one
Description: Manmohan Alla of Apple at Conf42 IoT 2025 on cutting IoT ML costs with a Snowflake feature store, incremental processing, dbt tests and right-sized compute.
Body:
The same rolling average, computed three different ways by three teams, is how IoT machine learning gets expensive and untrustworthy at the same time. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Manmohan Alla, a member of technical staff at Apple, showed how a structured feature store on Snowflake brings IoT telemetry under control, and where the cost savings in his title actually come from.

The talk draws on deployments in manufacturing, utilities, energy grids and smart monitoring. It is an architecture and practices talk, built around Snowflake.

## Temporal context is the feature

Manmohan's first point is that a single sensor reading means almost nothing. A vibration value is only interesting compared with the last hour, last week or the seasonal pattern. So useful IoT features are rolling windows, lags, trend acceleration and seasonal behaviour, and he says that in many real deployments over 70% of model accuracy comes from that temporal context.

Doing that consistently across thousands of sensors and dozens of models is where ad hoc scripts collapse. Sample rates differ, smart meters report every few seconds while vehicles send irregular bursts, and the resulting temporal misalignment breaks simple SQL analytics.

## Fragmentation is the real cost

IoT data quality problems such as null values, network gaps and calibration drift are unavoidable. The danger, in his telling, is inconsistent handling: data engineers clean at ingestion one way, scientists write their own transforms, ops builds BI aggregates, and the same metric ends up computed three different ways. He has seen three to six copies of the same logic in real pipelines because there was no central feature store.

A feature store fixes that with canonical, versioned, reusable feature definitions and optimized serving. He reports feature reuse cutting engineering effort by 60 to 80%, and frames it neatly: instead of six teams building six pipelines, one pipeline serves six teams.

## Where Snowflake earns its place

He highlights three Snowflake capabilities. VARIANT ingests semi-structured sensor JSON without schema gymnastics. Time Travel keeps historical training data reproducible even if it changes. Streams with materialized views give incremental change capture, so only new sensor data is processed; he says this routinely cuts compute by 40 to 60% because nobody reprocesses history that has not changed.

The layering is raw (truth, timestamps, device metadata), transform (windowing, smoothing, health metrics) and a denormalized serving layer for fast lookups. dbt turns the transforms into software, with dependency graphs, reusable macros for rolling statistics and automated tests that catch bad upstream sensor data before it reaches dashboards or models. SQL handles about 80% of the work; Python running inside Snowflake, with libraries such as pandas and SciPy, covers the remaining spectral analysis and anomaly scoring inside Snowflake, so data never leaves its governance boundary.

## Right-size everything

The cost section is the most directly reusable. Match warehouse size to the job: small for simple aggregations, medium for wide joins, large only for parallel work, which he says commonly saves over 50% of compute in production. Tier storage from granular recent data to downsampled older data to a cold compliance archive. Lean on caching for repeated inference lookups. Denormalized serving tables trade a little storage for two to five times better serving latency in many deployments, and he notes that predictable latency matters more than raw speed for IoT ML.

Operations close it out: monitor data quality, pipeline health and feature drift (he has seen unnoticed drift cost 20 to 30% of model accuracy within a month), use RBAC with row-level security, run multiple feature versions side by side, and tag cost per model and team.

## Who should watch

Data and ML engineers feeding models from device telemetry, especially teams already on Snowflake or arguing over who owns feature logic. If you are not on Snowflake, the principles transfer; the specific features do not.

Title: IoT messaging at scale needs proactive scaling, not reactive
Description: Ketul Dusane of AWS at Conf42 IoT 2025 on a three-pillar framework for IoT messaging, covering latency, throughput and operational resilience.
Body:
Reactive autoscaling works fine until a firmware rollout makes a million devices reconnect in the same minute. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Ketul Dusane, Software Development Engineer at AWS, argued that IoT messaging needs proactive, data-driven scaling and offered a three-pillar framework (latency, throughput, resilience) for getting there.

It is a framework talk: patterns and principles drawn from his work on high-performance messaging pipelines, rather than a walkthrough of a specific AWS service.

## A perfect storm of volume, latency and connections

Ketul sets the stakes with three constraints that arrive together. Data volume is enormous, with projections he cites of 175 zettabytes generated by IoT systems in 2025. Real-time workloads such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, industrial automation and medical devices need responses under 100 milliseconds. And even moderately large deployments in smart cities or industrial plants carry over a million concurrent device connections.

The traditional pattern, wait for metrics to spike and then respond, fails on all three. By the time the system reacts, latency budgets are blown and backlogs are building.

## Pillar one: remove the waiting

Latency work is about taking friction out of every hop. Multi-tier caching at edge, regional and central layers cuts lookup overhead. Asynchronous, event-driven communication between microservices avoids blocking. Intelligent prioritization makes sure an actuator command or safety alert never queues behind routine telemetry. His summary of the biggest cause of slowdowns is unnecessary waiting in the system, which is also a fair description of most meetings.

## Pillar two: scale before the spike

Throughput comes from three mechanisms. Load balancing picks nodes by health and capacity rather than round robin. Predictive autoscaling uses ML on historical traffic patterns to prepare for surges before they arrive. Queue partitioning separates messages by priority or destination so they process in parallel.

Spikes are a fact of IoT life: firmware rollouts, sensor storms, mass reconnections after a network blip, ordinary daily peaks. The architecture he describes absorbs threefold traffic surges without downtime through early horizontal scaling, circuit breakers that stop cascading failures, and buffering that prevents message loss.

## Pillar three: notice before users do

Resilience rests on continuous monitoring across components, anomaly detection that surfaces early warning signals, and ML-driven tuning that learns from past incidents and adjusts parameters. He puts the target at 99.9995% uptime, even in resource-constrained environments, and stresses that in IoT uptime translates directly into safety and business continuity.

The recurring patterns he sees in deployments are familiar but worth listing: event-driven microservices, clustered message brokers for high availability, regional failover for geo resilience, and protocol optimization with MQTT and CoAP for constrained devices. Looking ahead he expects self-healing systems with AI agents that detect and fix performance issues, more edge processing to avoid cross-continent hops, and energy-aware algorithms he says can cut consumption by up to 30%.

## Do one optimization at a time

The most practical advice comes near the end: optimization has to be balanced, because complexity breeds fragility. Start simple, change one thing at a time and measure its impact. Monitor everything and wait for real data before deciding. Keep iterating as traffic patterns evolve. The goal is sustainable scalability, not over-engineering.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers running MQTT brokers, device gateways or event pipelines that need to survive reconnection storms. It is a high-level framework, so treat it as a checklist to compare your architecture against rather than a build guide.

Title: Taming IoT streams on Kafka starts with trusting the data
Description: Rehmat Kharal of Conduktor at Conf42 IoT 2025 on why IoT streaming data is hard to trust and how governance, quality gates and self-service tame Kafka.
Body:
The hard part of IoT streaming is not moving the bytes; it is knowing whether you can believe them. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Rehmat Kharal of Conduktor laid out three hidden challenges of IoT data pipelines, unreliable sensors, device heterogeneity and data provenance, and the governance controls a Kafka platform needs to keep them from turning into outages.

Honest scope: Rehmat works at Conduktor, which builds a control plane for Kafka, and the second half describes that kind of tooling. The talk does not do a product demo, though, and the problem framing applies whatever you run.

## Bad data rolls downhill

Sensors produce noisy, inaccurate or irrelevant readings because of temperature swings, vibration, hardware limits or plain malfunction. Because one device's data feeds many business applications, the damage multiplies.

Her manufacturing example sticks: robotic arms placing windows, painting and fitting tyres on cars. If the window count reported upstream is off by a factor of ten, the other robots, procurement, shipping and the exchange with the manufacturer all inherit the error. Calibration drift becomes a supply chain problem. Missing data and packet loss from flaky connectivity do the same thing, leaving an incomplete picture that can end in production halts or quality and safety issues. She poses the uncomfortable question for teams that moved off legacy ETL: which is worse, data that gets stuck, or data that flows fast and is wrong?

## Heterogeneity and provenance

The second challenge is making very different devices cooperate without the least capable one becoming the bottleneck. That means standard interfaces and protocols, assigning work to the right processor, and coping with uneven performance, power constraints and a larger attack surface. Integrating many sources also brings schema mismatches and inconsistent data.

The third is provenance. As companies spread across regions, languages, deployment types and entry points, it gets harder to establish a chain of custody: who gathered the data, when and where, which servers and systems touched it, who transformed it, and who touched it last. In regulated environments, that is what audits and liability hinge on.

## Guardrails at the source, not after the incident

The remedy is a single view across the whole streaming estate: topics, schemas, consumer groups and Kafka Connect in one place, with labels and metadata so resources are discoverable, and real-time cluster and broker monitoring. Developers get self-service tooling so they can build, test and debug against Kafka without being Kafka experts.

The security controls she lists are concrete: fine-grained role-based access integrated with SSO and LDAP or Active Directory, immutable exportable audit logs, end-to-end message encryption including field-level and schema-based encryption, and dynamic data masking so sensitive fields are visible only to authorized users.

Data quality is enforced before data lands: quality gates, mandatory schemas and validation rules, with non-compliant messages blocked at the producer. An enterprise catalog makes streams, topics and schemas searchable, supports sharing with partners and tracks usage for chargeback.

Cluster protection rounds it out. Topic creation and changes go through a governed approval workflow, and topics can be renamed without breaking producers or consumers. Producer policies require valid schemas and rate-limit runaway producers; consumer group policies limit membership, join rates and offset commits so one misbehaving consumer cannot destabilize the cluster. The aim is moving Kafka operations from firefighting to prevention.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who run Kafka for teams ingesting device data, and data owners who have to vouch for that data in an audit. If your Kafka estate is one cluster and one team, the governance half may feel early; the sensor reliability half will not.

Title: IoT data platforms fail on cost, not on collection
Description: Bhanudeepti Chinta of Dave at Conf42 IoT 2025 on lakehouse architectures for sensor telemetry, from Iceberg and Delta Lake to medallion layers.
Body:
Collecting sensor data is the easy part; paying for it a year later is where IoT platforms come apart. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Bhanudeepti Chinta, Engineering Manager for Data at Dave, with 14 years on high-volume data platforms, argued that the lakehouse is as much a cost containment strategy as an architecture for connected device analytics.

Her opening observation sets the tone: organizations rarely fail at IoT because they cannot collect data, but because the cost and complexity of managing it grow faster than the value they get out.

## Three audiences, one firehose

IoT telemetry arrives at millisecond intervals and can reach petabyte scale within months. The same data then has to serve operations teams who want real-time dashboards, data scientists who need history for modeling, and business users who want aggregates. On top of that, schemas keep moving: firmware updates add fields and vendors produce consistently inconsistent formats. Any architecture has to ingest continuously, absorb schema changes gracefully, and keep years of history without rewriting it.

## Why the lakehouse wins the middle ground

Warehouses give performance and consistency but get expensive and rigid with semi-structured telemetry. Data lakes are cheap but weak on reliability, governance and transactions. The lakehouse puts warehouse-grade guarantees on cheap cloud object storage.

The enabling layer is the open table format: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi add transactional semantics, schema evolution and efficient metadata management to object storage. Without them, she warns, IoT platforms quietly pile up hidden operational and storage costs. Physically, storage, table formats and compute are separated, with engines like Spark or Trino scaling only when there is work, instead of paying for fixed infrastructure around the clock.

## The decisions that decide the bill

Bhanudeepti points at where IoT cost overruns usually start: architectural choices made early.

- **Streaming at the core.** Data flows through Kafka, Kinesis or Event Hubs and is processed in real time with Spark or Flink.
- **Time-based partitioning** that matches the temporal nature of telemetry.
- **Lifecycle management** across hot, warm and cold tiers.
- **Schema evolution** without rewriting historical data.

The medallion layout organizes the rest. Bronze keeps raw sensor data exactly as received, for audit and replay. Silver validates, normalizes and standardizes. Gold exposes business-ready datasets for reporting and dashboards. The cost argument is that expensive compute only runs where business value sits, and nothing gets reprocessed twice for no reason.

For real-time versus batch, she favours a Kappa-style approach where one streaming pipeline feeds both, with incremental processing and materialized views lowering long-term cost. On the ML side, feature engineering tends to get duplicated across teams; a governed feature store such as Snowflake's keeps features consistent between training and inference and cuts the repeated compute.

## Use cases, briefly

The case studies are short sketches rather than deep dives: predictive maintenance in manufacturing from early failure signals in telemetry, connected vehicle fleets doing route optimization, driver scoring and vehicle health, smart city traffic and environmental monitoring with open data, and utility smart meter analytics for theft detection, peak demand forecasting and grid optimization across millions of households. Looking ahead, she expects lower-latency streaming, better time series performance, stronger governance and more analytics pushed to the edge.

Her closing line is the one to keep: the platforms that last will be cost aware by design, not merely data aware.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and platform owners sizing an IoT analytics stack, or inheriting one whose storage bill grows faster than its users. It is an architecture overview rather than a hands-on build; pair it with a talk that goes deep on a single table format if you want the mechanics.
