Title: Secure by Default: Why AI-Driven Delivery Needs a Rethink
Description: Why fast, AI-powered delivery demands secure-by-default pipelines.
Body:
# Secure by Default: Why AI-Driven Delivery Needs a Rethink  
By Dewan Ahmed

Software delivery has been accelerating for more than a decade, and the arrival of AI has pushed us into an entirely new velocity class. Code generation, configuration scaffolding, infrastructure suggestions, remediation hints, and deployment decisions now involve AI. It participates in every stage of the delivery pipeline.

On the surface, this feels like progress. Faster delivery, fewer bottlenecks, happier teams.  
But a closer look reveals something more complicated.

## The Gap Between Speed and Safety

Most modern pipelines were designed for a world where humans made the important decisions, such as writing code, reviewing changes, crafting configurations, and evaluating risks. AI changed that dynamic. It introduced automation that moves faster than traditional security practices can respond to.

The result is a widening gap between the speed at which we can ship and the safety at which we can ship.

Here are a few of the challenges teams are already feeling today.

### 1. AI is amplifying existing weaknesses

If your base images are outdated, your tests barely cover your codebase, or your deployment strategy lacks guardrails, AI does not fix these issues. It accelerates them.

Pipelines automate mistakes with the same enthusiasm they automate features.

### 2. The threat surface has shifted

The most common AI failures today are not the classic vulnerabilities we are used to scanning for.

Instead, organizations are seeing issues such as:

- prompt injection  
- model jailbreaking  
- vulnerable AI-generated code  
- behavior-driven exploits  
- configuration drift caused by AI tools  

These attacks target behavior and reasoning, not code structure.

### 3. Delivery is faster, but security has not kept up

AI-assisted workflows generate code, configurations, and infrastructure definitions at machine speed. Most security models still rely on manual reviews, point-in-time scans, or human approval gates.

This mismatch means misconfigurations are no longer slow, human-scale mistakes. They have become automated hazards.

### 4. Developers are not set up for AI-era security

Most developers have little or no training in AI security or AI threat modeling, yet we expect them to recognize model manipulation, unsafe outputs, and subtle behavioral failures in AI-generated artifacts. The expectations do not match the support we give them.

---

These challenges will define the next era of DevSecOps. If you want to hear about a practical four-pillar framework for secure-by-default AI-driven delivery, [join my keynote at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2025).

Title: Conf42 DevSecOps 2025: securing pipelines that AI now writes into
Description: Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 roundup: 26 talks on AI in the delivery pipeline, SBOMs and provenance, safer deployments and security in finance and healthcare.
Body:
Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 ran on December 4, 2025, with 26 talks and one question underneath most of them: what happens to security when AI writes code, generates configuration and makes decisions inside the pipeline? Speakers from Harness, AT&T, Chevron, JPMorganChase, Microsoft, Dropbox, Cisco and others answered from the pipeline, the supply chain and some of the most regulated industries around. Everything is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2025), and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCMXkZdQESvj8M_clmevDME).

## AI is in the pipeline, so secure the pipeline

Harness's keynote from [Dewan Ahmed](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Dewan_Ahmed_secure_ai_delivery), Principal Developer Advocate, set the tone. Pipelines automate whatever you feed them, and AI makes them faster at shipping mistakes as well as good code. His framework for secure-by-default delivery has four pillars: contextual intelligence about what a change means, automatic verification of provenance and drift, behaviour-based anomaly detection, and continuous learning from every deploy and rollback.

Others took the same problem from different angles. [Rajkumar Sukumar](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Rajkumar_Sukumar_ai_ml_ethics) of AT&T showed how to embed security, privacy-aware training, policy as code and audit-ready steps into machine learning pipelines. [Baradwaj Bandi Sudakara](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Baradwaj_Bandi_Sudakara_ai_ml_secure) of Ascension Health covered AI-driven testing and defect prevention. [Alex Shershebnev](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_cloud_mcp_secure) of Zencoder demonstrated MCP workflows that let an LLM trigger CI jobs, query Grafana or debug from Sentry inside the IDE, and the risks to check before plugging that into your stack. [Murali Koney](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Murali_Koney_ai_risk_llm) of Cox Automotive tied LLM adoption to governance, risk and cost, starting from his observation that most enterprise AI projects fail before production.

## Supply chain: know what you ship

[Bhaskar Bharat Sawant](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Bhaskar_Bharat_Sawant_supply_chain_ci) of Cornerstone Building Brands gave the most hands-on supply chain session: automated SBOMs, SLSA provenance and attestations, hermetic builds and artifact verification at deploy time, so every release is traceable by default. [Gresshma Atluri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Gresshma_Atluri_supply_chain_threats) of Chevron built a proactive defence framework from real-world supply chain incidents.

For teams starting closer to the code, [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql) of Microsoft toured GitHub Dependabot, CodeQL and the other built-in security features, and [Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep) of MoEngage explained how static analysis actually works using open-source Semgrep. Together they make a good afternoon for anyone whose SAST stage is a box nobody opens.

## Deploying without seeing red

[Rayenn Hamrouni](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Rayenn_Hamrouni_deployments_aws) of Lenstra had the best title of the day, "From Blue to Green Without Seeing Red", and a real case study behind it: implementing blue/green deployment for a web application on AWS using Lambda@Edge, with the trade-offs spelled out. [Meenu Venkataarangam](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Meenu_Venkataarangam_migration_cloud_auto) of Recode Solutions covered automation for enterprise migrations that closes security gaps along the way, and [Nishanth Sirikonda](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Nishanth_Sirikonda_risk_secure_system) of First Day Foundation argued for risk-driven DevSecOps with compliance as code. [Raghavendra Reddy Kapu](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Raghavendra_Reddy_Kapu_resilient_system_secure) brought fault-tolerance patterns and chaos engineering into the security conversation.

## Where the stakes are regulated

Finance had its own track. [Swamy Biru](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Swamy_Biru_finance_rag_ai) of JPMorganChase covered DevSecOps patterns for RAG and agentic systems in financial operations, [Janardhan Chejarla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Janardhan_Chejarla_trading_cloud_scale) of Calypso Technology secured event-driven order management for high-frequency trading, and [Silpa Potluri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payment_api_secure) of GoodLeap described keeping PCI compliance while moving a payment gateway to microservices with daily releases.

Healthcare and education followed. [Mahendar Ramidi](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Mahendar_Ramidi_health_cloud_scale) of the Maryland Health Benefits Exchange shared how he built a HIPAA-compliant mobile platform for cancer patients with zero-trust architecture and compliance automation, and [Raghav Sai Cheedalla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Raghav_Sai_Cheedalla_ai_ethics_edu) of Meta looked at secure, ethical personalisation of learning for students with special needs. [Mallikarjun Bussa](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Mallikarjun_Bussa_data_access_secure) of Dropbox addressed self-service BI that doesn't leak data.

## People are part of the system

Two talks were about the humans who run all of this. [Kuldeep Deshwal](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Kuldeep_Deshwal_culture_teams_secure), Director of Engineering at Proofpoint, unpacked the productivity paradox in DevSecOps culture and how to avoid burning out the people expected to ship securely. [Sanjeevani Bhardwaj](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Sanjeevani_Bhardwaj_health_secure_cloud) of Salesforce proposed a four-dimension technical health index to move teams from reactive to proactive security work. On the infrastructure side, [Nazim Khan](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Nazim_Khan_ethernet_ai_infra) of Cisco explained how Ethernet with RoCEv2 and Ultra Ethernet standards competes with InfiniBand for AI training networks.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [Harness](https://www.harness.io/), our diamond sponsor, to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/) as gold sponsor, to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter and to [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) for the podcast partnership.

## What's next

All 26 talks are linked from the [Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2025). The next edition, [Conf42 DevSecOps 2026](https://www.conf42.com/devsecops2026), is set for October 1, 2026. Plenty of time to make the security stage the one that can't be skipped.

Title: Where code, infrastructure, and risk meet
Description: And nothing ships blind
Body:
# Security at scale is a lifestyle now

DevSecOps used to be about shifting security left.

Now it’s about making sure security doesn’t quietly break everything while AI, automation, and cloud platforms move at full speed. Small difference.

Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 is where those conversations get real.

This conference brings together twenty five talks across eight tracks, covering AI, cloud, data, infrastructure, finance, security, and transformation. The focus is not on adding more scanners, but on building systems that are secure by default, even as pipelines get smarter and faster.

AI is front and center. From AI-driven DevSecOps and autonomous cloud security to embedding security and ethics directly into machine learning pipelines, many sessions explore what happens when intelligence becomes part of the delivery process. There’s a clear theme here: automating insecurity at scale is very easy, and very expensive.

Supply chain security gets serious attention. SBOMs, SLSA, provenance, dependency management, and defending against modern software supply chain attacks show up across multiple talks. These sessions dig into what it actually takes to trust what you’re shipping, and where it came from.

Real industries feature heavily. Finance, healthcare, payments, and enterprise platforms all appear, with talks on securing high-frequency trading systems, payment gateways, clinical platforms, and large-scale migrations. These are environments where “we’ll fix it later” is not an option.

Culture and sustainability round things out. Developer productivity, DevSecOps health frameworks, and avoiding burnout while raising security standards are treated as first-class concerns, not side notes.

If your job sits somewhere between shipping fast and not ending up on the news, this one’s for you. DevSecOps is no longer a phase in the pipeline. It’s the system.

Title: Predicting medical device failures before the lab goes dark
Description: Ramakrishna Ambati of Visby Medical at Conf42 IoT 2025 on a zero trust IoT edge architecture and ML for predictive maintenance of diagnostic devices.
Body:
When a diagnostic device fails in a hospital, the cost is not just a repair ticket; it is delayed results for patients. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Ramakrishna Ambati, Enterprise Solutions Architect at Visby Medical, walked through a secure IoT edge architecture that moves medical device maintenance from fixing failures after the fact to predicting them from telemetry.

The talk is architecture-first: a pipeline, a zero trust layer, an ML approach shaped by regulation, and a phased rollout plan. The abstract cites results from a deployment of 157 medical devices, including 97.8% uptime and 91.3% failure prediction accuracy; the talk itself spends its time on how the system is built.

## Reactive maintenance is an expensive habit

Ramakrishna frames the status quo plainly. Healthcare operations typically respond after a device fails, which means downtime, delayed diagnostics and higher costs, plus scheduled maintenance that is not tied to actual device condition. That mix wastes technician time and still hurts patient care. The goal is data-driven intervention that anticipates failures before they reach clinical operations.

## Five hops from sensor to recommendation

The pipeline has five stages:

1. **Device telemetry.** Continuous monitoring of operational parameters on the diagnostic devices.
2. **Edge processing.** Local analysis and filtering that spot critical patterns and anomalies and cut the volume sent upstream.
3. **Secure transport.** Data moves to the cloud over HTTPS and MQTT.
4. **Time series storage.** A database tuned for telemetry and later analysis.
5. **Analytics engine.** ML models that generate predictive insights and maintenance recommendations.

The edge layer earns its keep twice: less data to ship, and anomalies caught close to the device instead of minutes later in a dashboard.

## Zero trust, because these are medical devices

Security is not a bolt-on here. Every device conversation uses mutual TLS. Certificates rotate on an automated schedule, compromised credentials can be revoked in real time, and every change to a device leaves an audit trail for compliance reporting. Combined with HIPAA requirements, the architecture is designed so that the security story is in place before any patient-adjacent data is collected, which is also his first implementation rule.

## ML that a regulator can read

The machine learning section is shaped by the domain. Feature engineering turns raw telemetry into predictive indicators using signal processing (frequency analysis, filtering, transforms), statistical measures such as trends, variance and correlation, and clinical plus engineering knowledge about which signals actually matter. Failures are rare events, so class imbalance gets dedicated sampling and weighting. Models must be interpretable, because software as a medical device has to satisfy FDA expectations, and they keep learning from technician feedback as device behaviour drifts.

Predictions only help if someone acts on them, so the system plugs into an automated ticketing workflow and real-time dashboards that clinical and technical teams share. A model that predicts a failure into an inbox nobody reads is just a very expensive horoscope.

## Roll it out small, then scale

His rollout runs in five steps: assess existing infrastructure and pick critical devices, design the secure architecture, pilot edge units on an initial set of devices, collect telemetry and train models with validation protocols, then expand to the full fleet with continuous learning. Looking ahead he mentions embedded MEMS sensors inside devices, federated learning across fleets without centralizing sensitive data, and digital twins for testing maintenance scenarios and training.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform teams building IoT for healthcare or any regulated equipment fleet, and maintenance leaders making the case for predictive programs. The talk is a blueprint rather than a code demo; come for the sequencing and the compliance-aware ML choices.

Title: When a security bug can delay chemotherapy, DevSecOps is the design
Description: Mahendar Ramidi at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on securing a HIPAA-compliant cancer patient app with zero trust, offline-first encryption and policy as code.
Body:
In most apps a security failure is an embarrassing incident. In a symptom tracker for cancer patients it can mean a wrong medication or a missed treatment. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Mahendar Ramidi](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Mahendar_Ramidi_health_cloud_scale), a mobile architect in health technology listed with Maryland Health Benefits Exchange, described how his team applied DevSecOps to My Story, a mobile platform for cancer patients that supports active clinical trials.

According to the abstract, the platform serves 450+ patients across 12 cancer centres with a 92% completion rate. The talk spends its time on the architecture rather than those outcomes, so treat it as a blueprint for regulated mobile apps.

## Why healthcare raises the stakes

Ramidi's starting point is that there's no margin for error. A patient's chemotherapy schedule depends on precise data transmission, clinical trial results depend on data integrity, and the information is deeply personal. He sees three forces. Regulatory complexity: HIPAA sets the baseline, clinical trials add FDA oversight, states add their own rules, and international work brings GDPR. Attractive data: medical records sell for more than credit card numbers because you can't change your medical history. And patient safety, where a security failure can have physical consequences.

Mobile makes it harder. Data moves between personal devices and cloud services, phones join untrusted networks next to other apps with broad permissions, and patients need their information offline, in hospitals with poor reception, while travelling or in rural areas.

## Zero trust, from enrolment to idle timeout

His zero-trust model has four layers. Patients can't just sign up; they're provisioned through a secure enrolment that requires multi-factor authentication with verified health-system credentials. After authentication, the patient's identity is cryptographically bound to their device so stolen credentials alone aren't enough. Biometrics (fingerprint or face) add another factor on enrolled devices. And verification is continuous: short-lived tokens refresh every few minutes, and idle sessions are killed, so the user has to log in again.

Encryption is data-centric. Data is encrypted on the device before it leaves, transmitted with certificate pinning, stored encrypted with hierarchical key management, and decrypted only on authorised devices.

## Offline-first is a security problem

The offline section is the most distinctive part. Full-device encryption is only the baseline; on top of it the app adds application-level encryption with keys derived from patient credentials, plus secure element integration and hardware-protected keys. Because patients edit data offline, sync needs conflict resolution: vector clocks track modification history, operational transformation keeps eventual consistency, and every offline change lands in an audit trail. Anyone who has debugged a mobile sync bug will appreciate doing that under HIPAA.

## Compliance as code and a five-layer pipeline

Ramidi treats regulations as requirements that automation can verify continuously. HIPAA requires encryption at rest and in transit, so the infrastructure code refuses to provision storage or networks without it, and policy-as-code tools check infrastructure against compliance rules before deployment. Try to deploy an unencrypted database and the pipeline rejects it, naming the requirement it would violate.

The CI/CD pipeline has five security layers: static analysis for hard-coded credentials, SQL injection and insecure crypto; dependency scanning that blocks deployment on known vulnerabilities; dynamic testing against running builds for authentication bypass; container image scanning; and API security tests for unauthorised access and rate limits. He names Sonar among the scanners in that pipeline.

## Monitoring and response

Production gets application and infrastructure monitoring, audit log analysis for suspicious patterns in authentication, data access and configuration changes, and behaviour analytics that learn typical patterns for patients and clinicians. His incident response follows detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident analysis. The closing argument: patients trust the app with data that could save their lives, so robust security isn't optional, and it doesn't have to cost the user experience.

## Who should watch

Mobile and backend engineers building regulated health apps, and anyone designing offline-capable apps that handle sensitive data. It's a broad architecture walk-through, not a code demo.

Title: Breaking up a payment monolith moves PCI from network to service
Description: Silpa Potluri of GoodLeap at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on keeping payment gateways PCI-compliant while migrating from monoliths to microservices.
Body:
A payment monolith is slow to change and, for the same reason, easy to fence in. Split it into dozens of services and the fence disappears. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Silpa Potluri](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payment_api_secure) of GoodLeap, who brings two decades in software and more than ten years in payments, explained how DevSecOps keeps payment gateways secure and PCI-compliant through a monolith-to-microservices migration, and why compliance has to move from the network to the individual service.

It's a clear overview talk, good for teams at the start of such a migration. It names the right patterns rather than showing implementations.

## Why payments left the monolith

Potluri starts with the business pressure. Payment systems were built as large monoliths, stable and predictable but slow and risky to modify, with long development cycles. Real-time payments, international commerce, mobile-first users and round-the-clock demand pushed processors towards microservices for agility, independent scaling, faster updates and better fault isolation. The catch is that the same architecture makes security and compliance much harder.

Her framing of DevSecOps is the familiar contrast: security used to arrive at the end, after development and QA, which caused delays and friction. With several deployments a day that model can't keep up, so security moves into design, build, deployment and operations.

## PCI DSS stops being a perimeter

The core of the talk is what changes for PCI DSS, which sets rules for protecting cardholder data, access control, network segmentation, encryption, logging and monitoring. Monolithic setups leaned on perimeter controls: isolated networks, firewalls, DMZs. In microservices, data moves across many services, the perimeter blurs and the attack surface grows. So compliance has to go from network-based to service-based, and it becomes a constant priority rather than an annual exercise.

She names three shifts. The attack surface expands, from one app to many entry points. Infrastructure becomes dynamic, with containers scaling up and down constantly. And security responsibility becomes shared across every team and service.

## The architecture that replaces the fence

Her answer comes in layers. A service mesh provides mutual TLS, authorisation and traffic policies automatically, so developers aren't hand-coding them. An API gateway acts as the secure front door with authentication, rate limiting, threat detection and input validation. Zero trust means every service authenticates and authorises every request, internal ones included.

For the data itself: tokenisation replaces card data with tokens to shrink PCI scope, data at rest is encrypted with keys in a secure vault, everything in transit uses TLS, and secrets live in vaults rather than code, environment files or repos. Defence in depth, applied to the thing attackers want most.

## Automation keeps security at deployment speed

To the obvious objection, that all these checks will slow releases, her answer is to automate them: static analysis early, dynamic testing against running applications, container image scanning. Infrastructure as code gives consistent, version-controlled environments, and compliance as code turns PCI requirements into automated checks, so compliance is validated on every deployment instead of waiting for the quarterly or annual audit.

In the pipeline she lists source control protections (secret detection, required reviews), dependency scanning in the build, artifact signing so images and binaries are trusted and unmodified, deployment gates that block insecure builds, and quick rollbacks. After deployment, detection matters: a SIEM to correlate logs, real-time fraud detection models, distributed tracing to follow a single transaction across services, and anomaly detection. On cloud platforms she reminds teams of the shared responsibility model: the provider secures the platform, you still own code, configuration and access.

## How migrations succeed

Her success strategies are practical: migrate in phases, start small and iterate; appoint security champions on each team; threat model before writing code; and keep test environments close to production so real vulnerabilities show up. The abstract mentions a drop in security incidents alongside daily releases; the talk itself focuses on the patterns that get you there.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects planning or in the middle of a payments migration, and compliance owners who need to understand what changes when the cardholder data environment becomes a mesh of services.

- [IoT Payment Systems: Microservices Architecture for Connected Devices](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Silpa_Potluri_payments_microservices_architecture) is Potluri on payment microservices for connected devices.
- [AI-Powered Fraud Detection in Cloud-Native Digital Payments](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sandeep_Katuri_fraud_detection_digital_payments_security) expands the detection layer.
- [Distributed Transactions in Service Mesh](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Alparslan_Avci_distributed_transactions_in_service_mesh) tackles consistency once payments span services.

Title: Smart cameras that think locally and only send the verdict
Description: Madhu Niranjan Reddy Puduru of Synchronoss at Conf42 IoT 2025 on running quantized neural networks on IoT cameras to cut bandwidth, latency and battery drain.
Body:
A camera that streams every frame to the cloud so a server can say "person detected" is paying a lot of bandwidth for one sentence. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Madhu Niranjan Reddy Puduru, Software Engineering Manager at Synchronoss Technologies, made the case for edge AI on smart cameras: optimize the model, run inference next to the sensor, and ship only events.

This is one of the denser talks of the event, a full pipeline from model compression to frame buffers to joules per frame, with case studies at the end.

## The cloud-first camera does not scale

Madhu lists the bottlenecks of cloud-only vision: bandwidth that climbs with every camera added, latency from the network round trip, privacy exposure from shipping raw video, and compute plus storage bills that become unsustainable across dozens or hundreds of devices. Construction sites and rural deployments make it worse, since good connectivity is the first thing they lack.

Moving inference onto the device flips that. In his numbers, sending only events cuts bandwidth use by about 85%, battery life improves four to five times because the radio does less, and local processing gets frames done in under 50 milliseconds. The raw video never leaves the camera, which matters for homes, public spaces and regulated industries.

## Shrinking the model is a three-stage job

The optimization pipeline is the core of the talk:

1. **Architecture selection.** Start from families built for constrained hardware, such as MobileNet V3 and SqueezeNet, or lightweight encoder-decoder networks with residual connections that land at a few megabytes.
2. **Quantization and compression.** Convert FP32 weights to 8-bit integers for a fourfold size reduction and faster, lower-power inference, with accuracy loss he puts usually under 2%. Knowledge distillation and pruning trim further.
3. **Platform-specific compilation.** TensorFlow Lite for ARM, the Edge TPU compiler for Google Coral, Qualcomm's toolchain for Hexagon, with graph optimization, operator fusion and memory layout tuning so each operation lands on the best available CPU, NPU or TPU.

He is blunt about why CPUs alone fall short: general-purpose chips are not built for the matrix math, while NPUs and TPUs bring parallel multiply engines and optimized memory paths. Hardware support spans 512 MB to 1 GB ARM Cortex boards, Raspberry Pi 3 and 4 in the middle, and Coral, Hexagon and NVIDIA Jetson at the top.

## The real-time loop, budgeted in milliseconds

To hold 30-plus frames per second, frames land in a ring buffer so a busy processor never drops them. Preprocessing (resize, colour adjustment, normalization) uses SIMD and should stay under about 10 milliseconds. Inference on mid-range hardware takes roughly 30 to 45 milliseconds. Post-processing filters noise, applies thresholds and turns raw outputs into something an app can act on.

## Memory, not math, eats the battery

The energy section has the most surprising detail: he notes that a DRAM access costs on the order of 100 to 200 times more energy than the arithmetic itself, so compressing models and reusing buffers pays off more than people expect. Add adaptive scheduling (run inference more often when there is motion, idle the radio otherwise) and he reports 60 to 70% energy savings against cloud-based setups. Per frame, an ARM CPU uses 0.5 to 0.8 joules, accelerators drop that to 0.1 to 0.2, while continuous cloud streaming can reach 3 joules. The optimized model itself is around 600 KB, with 4 to 8 MB of total memory including buffers.

The case studies make it concrete: a smart doorbell on a Raspberry Pi 3 with 72% less bandwidth and 4.25 times the battery life, and an industrial defect detection prototype with 50-plus cameras flagging anomalies in under 100 milliseconds while cutting transmitted data by over 90%. He closes with federated learning and cameras that share workloads as next steps.

## Who should watch

Embedded and ML engineers shipping vision on battery-powered or bandwidth-starved devices, and product owners deciding between cloud and edge inference. If you have never quantized a model, this is a good map of the steps; if you have, the energy and memory numbers are the part to steal.

- [Chiara Civardi and Petr Aubrecht on robotic applications at the edge](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chiara_Civardi_Petr_Aubrecht_robotics_applications_edge) at Conf42 IoT 2024.
- [Tim Spann and David Kjerrumgaard on the FLiPN stack for edge AI](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Tim_Spann_David_Kjerrumgaard_flipn_stack_edge_ai_flink_nifi_pulsar) at Conf42 IoT 2023.

Title: Good SAST matches the shape of your code, not the text
Description: Safeer C M of MoEngage at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 explains how SAST works via abstract syntax trees and how to write and roll out Semgrep rules without drowning devs.
Body:
Grep finds strings; a SQL injection is a structure. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Safeer C M](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Safeer_C_M_sast_open_source_semgrep), principal engineer at MoEngage, opened the black box of static application security testing: how tools turn source into abstract syntax trees, why that beats text matching, and how to write and roll out rules with the open-source Semgrep engine without burying developers in false positives.

Safeer brings 20-plus years in SRE, infrastructure and platform engineering, and the talk has that flavour: less about vulnerability taxonomy, more about building a tool developers will actually keep turned on. It's a foundations talk, so start here if SAST has always been somebody else's dashboard.

## Why SAST, and why it got a bad name

Manual security review of every change doesn't scale, so shifting left is the only way. Because SAST is white-box testing with full access to the source, it can cover the whole codebase before anything is built, and catch classics like SQL injection, exposed secret keys and buffer overflows.

Safeer is candid about the history. First-generation tools were clumsy: slow scans, complex setup, results nobody could act on, and developers who decided the tools were useless. Later tools improved, but false positives remain the big problem, and SAST still struggles with authentication and authorisation flaws, weak cryptography and configuration issues, since it only reads code.

## Abstract syntax trees are the whole trick

Under the hood, source is tokenised, parsed by the language grammar into a hierarchical tree, and then analysed for control flow and data flow before rules are applied. The tree is abstract because it drops what doesn't change meaning: comments, whitespace, formatting. His slide shows four print statements that look different as text but produce the same tree. He uses Python's built-in ast module to show the structure, then compares a direct call with one that goes through a variable assignment to show how quickly trees grow.

## Semgrep rules look like the code they catch

Semgrep, the name a blend of semantic and grep, works directly on source, no compiled artefacts needed. Rules are YAML, and patterns look like ordinary code with placeholders. Even rules are parsed into trees, so matching stays deterministic. A rule carries an ID, the pattern, a message for the developer, target languages, severity and metadata such as CWE links or internal docs, which lets a rule set double as your organisation's coding standard.

He walks through the combinators: pattern, patterns (all must match), pattern-either (any can match), pattern-regex, and nestable operators like pattern-inside and pattern-not. Metavariables capture part of the code so later conditions can inspect it, for example a URL passed to a requests call. He also distinguishes structural rules from data-flow and taint analysis, noting that the community edition focuses on rules within a single file while the commercial Pro engine adds cross-file and deeper taint support.

The demos keep it concrete: a hello-world rule, an SQL injection rule with three alternatives (variables concatenated, interpolated or percent-formatted into a cursor's execute call) that flags two of them in a sample, a rule that checks that functions call the company's standard input-validation helper before processing input, and an AWS credentials rule that uses metavariable regexes for the 20-character access key ID and the 40-character secret.

## Roll it out softly or nobody will look at it

The adoption advice is the part teams usually get wrong. Start with the community registry, which Safeer puts at more than 3,000 open-source rules, using the auto config that detects your languages and frameworks, then fork and tweak rules locally. Integrate in layers: IDE plugins so the tool teaches rather than gates, pre-commit hooks scanning only changed code, CI with SARIF output into GitHub code scanning or other dashboards, and PR comments that turn tribal knowledge into rules over time.

Begin with warnings rather than blocks, except for critical issues. Scan the baseline, focus on new findings, use ignore files to cut noise, and don't switch on every rule at once. Work with security engineers to tune rules as you go.

## Who should watch

Developers and platform engineers about to introduce SAST, or stuck with a scanner everyone ignores. AppSec veterans will know the theory but may like the rollout playbook.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Why We Need to Think of Adopting Static Analysis in Dependency Tools](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Joseph_Hejderup_going_beyond_metadata_adopting_static_analysis_dependency_tools) applies the same idea to dependencies.
- [Vulnerability Management that developers won't hate](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Anthony_Laiuppa_vulnerability_management_developers) shares the developer-experience-first view.
- [Purple Teaming with OWASP PurpleTeam](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Kim_Carter_owasp_purpleteam) covers the dynamic testing SAST can't do.

Title: GitHub ships most of a DevSecOps toolchain in the Security tab
Description: Peter De Tender of Microsoft at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 demos GitHub rulesets, secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot and CodeQL in VS Code.
Body:
Before you buy another scanner, check what is already sitting in your repository settings. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Peter_De_Tender_github_dependabot_codeql), lead technical trainer at Microsoft, gave a demo-heavy tour of GitHub's built-in security: repository best practices, secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot for vulnerable dependencies and CodeQL for code scanning, including running CodeQL on your own workstation.

It's an introductory talk and says so, built from live demos on public sample repos you can inspect afterwards. By his own account at the end, every demo worked, which in a live security demo is a minor miracle.

## Start with the repo you already have

De Tender begins with hygiene. Decide who collaborates versus who merely contributes to a public repo (not the same thing), limit who can do code reviews, and protect the main branch. GitHub nags when a branch is unprotected, and his advice is to protect both the default branch and branches matching a pattern such as main, since the default can be changed. He admits that after years on Azure DevOps he still calls rulesets branch policies.

Rulesets restrict deletions and block force pushes by default. He usually also restricts branch creation and requires code scanning and code quality results; with GitHub Copilot you can request an automatic AI code review too. Secrets used by Actions belong in encrypted repository secrets rather than plain variables, and a SECURITY.md file gives every visitor a visible link to your security policy.

## Secret scanning, then stop secrets before the push

Secret scanning checks repositories against a long list of known secret formats from partner platforms: AWS and Azure keys, API keys, connection strings, SSH keys. He commits a GitHub personal access token through the web editor and gets blocked with options: mark it as a false positive, as used in tests, or "I'll fix it later". He's not a fan of the last one, since it lets the secret land in the repo anyway.

Push protection moves the check earlier. He pastes the same token into a file in VS Code, tries to sync, and the push is rejected because it contains a secret. If it never reaches the repo, there's nothing to scan for.

## Dependabot reads the CVE feed so you don't have to

Dependabot works on public and private repos, using the public CVE database plus the GitHub Advisory Database. Enabling alerts also enables the dependency graph, and you can add custom rules, security updates as pull requests and version updates. On his pre-scanned demo repo it flagged a command injection issue in lodash with attack vector, complexity, severity, the CVE ID and a suggested package upgrade. The dependency graph can also export an SBOM as a detailed JSON file.

## CodeQL treats your code as data

CodeQL builds a database from your code and runs queries against it, from GitHub's research team, the community or your own. Enabling code scanning generates a GitHub Actions workflow under .github/workflows that you can edit: change triggers, run it on a schedule or fold it into your build pipeline. He also points out the permission settings in that workflow, so the scanning job can read but not change code.

The bit worth the watch is shifting it further left. With the CodeQL extension for VS Code, or the CLI, developers run the same queries locally before merging. His example query hunts for the token from the secret-scanning demo; out of the CodeQL database it was flagged by 115 different prebuilt C# queries. Secrets are just the relatable example, he notes, since CodeQL can query for far more.

## Who should watch

Teams already on GitHub who haven't switched these features on, and anyone setting a baseline for repository security. Experienced AppSec engineers will know the features but may pick up the local CodeQL workflow.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [DevSecOps beyond GitHub Advanced Security](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2026_Peter_De_Tender_github_codescanning_sast) is De Tender's follow-up on what to add beyond the built-ins.
- [Why you should never use static shared secrets in GitHub Actions](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2023_Kenneth_DuMez_static_shared_secrets_github_actions) tackles the pipeline secrets problem head on.
- [Open-source vulnerability management? Use the source, Luke!](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2022_Henrik_Plate_opensource_vulnerability_management_source) asks what dependency alerts miss.

Title: Enterprise LLMs stall between the pilot and the AI gateway
Description: Murali Koney of Cox Automotive at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on why enterprise LLM projects stall and a framework of deployment models, TCO and an AI API gateway.
Body:
The gap between an LLM demo and an LLM in production is mostly governance, security and an invoice nobody can forecast. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Murali Koney](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Murali_Koney_ai_risk_llm), technical team lead at Cox Automotive, laid out why enterprise AI projects stall before production and a three-pillar framework for getting past that: pick the right deployment model, do the economics honestly, and put an AI API gateway between your users and the model.

It's a structured, slide-led talk aimed at DevSecOps and platform leads who have been handed an AI roadmap. No demos, a lot of checklists, most of them useful.

## Why pilots don't graduate

Koney lists four reasons initiatives fail. Infrastructure gaps: traditional systems struggle with AI compute and storage needs. A governance vacuum: no clear policies on model selection, data handling or decision accountability, with compliance frameworks lagging behind. Security teams unprepared for AI-specific threats such as prompt injection, model poisoning and data exfiltration through model outputs. And cost uncertainty, because token usage is hard to predict and that makes return on investment hard to argue beyond the pilot.

## Pick a deployment model on purpose

The first pillar is choosing between infrastructure, platform and software as a service. IaaS gives full control over model selection, fine-tuning and infrastructure, which suits highly regulated environments, at the price of a heavy operational burden, slower time to market and deep ML expertise. PaaS runs on managed infrastructure while you keep model development and tuning, trading some vendor lock-in for much less operational complexity. SaaS, with Amazon Bedrock as his example, is the fastest path for standard use cases but gives the least control over model behaviour and raises compliance questions because you depend on a third party.

## Do the five-year maths before the launch

The economics pillar is a five-year total cost of ownership: infrastructure (compute, storage, networking, scaling), licensing and API costs, operational overhead (monitoring, maintenance, security, compliance), talent and training, and ongoing optimisation. He ties investment to three performance metrics: time to first token, which shapes user experience in chat-style apps; tokens per second, which decides how many concurrent users you can serve; and utilisation, which he calls the fastest path to better return on infrastructure spend.

## The AI gateway is the control plane

The part most teams can lift directly is the AI API gateway, which Koney treats as the security control plane. It does five jobs:

- Authentication and authorisation with role-based access.
- Token-based rate limiting and quotas, so neither abuse nor a runaway loop blows the budget.
- Input sanitisation to detect and block prompt injection.
- Output filtering to scan responses and redact sensitive data before it reaches the user.
- Semantic caching, so similar queries are answered from cache instead of paying for a fresh completion.

That list maps neatly onto his four operational risks: prompt injection, data exfiltration, hallucination (mitigated with confidence scoring and human-in-the-loop review where the stakes are high) and cost overruns, which he wants handled with token limits and budget alerts so the bill is never a surprise.

## LLMOps habits for production

His LLMOps lifecycle runs from prompt engineering, model selection and fine-tuning, through adversarial, bias and performance testing (essential because the models are non-deterministic), to controlled rollouts with A/B testing, then monitoring of quality and cost. Production best practices include version-controlling prompts, configuration and policies as code so you can roll back instead of hot-fixing; fallback models for graceful degradation when the preferred one is down; and decision logs for compliance and debugging. For regulated industries he points to domain-specific models, naming BloombergGPT and Med-PaLM.

He closes on where it's heading, from text-only models to multimodal and agentic systems, and on embedding AI into the DevOps toolchain itself: code review in CI/CD, incident triage, anomaly detection and root cause analysis, and knowledge base generation.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevSecOps leads writing the business case or the guardrails for an internal LLM platform. Practitioners who already run a gateway will find it a checklist to compare against.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [GenOps: A Governance-Driven Model for Safe, High-Velocity AI in CI/CD Pipelines](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Neeraj_Kumar_Singh_Beshane_governance_genai_velocity) takes the governance pillar into pipelines.
- [Reduce AI Agents Costs and Mistakes with Semantic Tool Selection](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Elizabeth_Fuentes_Leone_tools_semantic_cost) attacks the cost problem from the agent side.
- [Transforming Cybersecurity Governance with GenAI](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2024_Akshay_Sekar_Chandrasekaran_cybersecurity_governance_genai) covers risk and compliance from the security team's seat.

Title: Strangle the banking mainframe one domain at a time
Description: Swetha Lakkaraju at Conf42 IoT 2025 on modernizing legacy core banking with the strangler pattern, domain-driven design, API-first and microservices.
Body:
Most banks are not short of ideas; they are short of budget left over after keeping the core running. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, independent researcher Swetha Lakkaraju, who has spent over 18 years in mainframe core banking with Systematics and Vision Plus, argued that modular core architectures are how incumbents get their release cycles from months back down to weeks or days.

A heads-up on scope: despite the event, this one has nothing to do with sensors or devices. It is a strategy talk about core banking modernization, aimed at the people who have to fund and sequence it.

## Where innovation goes to die

Swetha opens with the money. In her account a large share of bank IT budgets, sometimes 60 to 80%, goes to simply keeping legacy systems alive, leaving little for anything new. Every change drags through long testing cycles and carries high risk, so traditional banks ship in months or years while fintechs launch something every few weeks. Her point is that the legacy core stops being a technical burden and becomes a strategic one.

The underlying cause is coupling. Core banking, payments, customer accounts and card systems are so interdependent that touching one means retesting all of them. Breaking the monolith into modules that each own a business capability lets teams update one piece without risking the rest, and keeps a failure in one area from taking down the whole core.

She grounds the case in her research comparing institutions across several countries over multiple years: speed, cost efficiency, innovation output, digital adoption and customer experience. The pattern she reports is that banks that went modular outperformed those that did not.

## Four pillars, and the order matters

The strategy section is the most reusable part of the talk:

- **Strangler pattern.** Replace legacy components in small increments while the business keeps running, instead of betting the bank on a big bang migration.
- **Domain-driven design.** Make the technical boundaries match the business ones, so teams own and evolve their domains independently.
- **API-first.** APIs become the standard layer between internal systems, partners and fintechs.
- **Microservices.** Fine-grained scaling, flexible deployment and better fault isolation.

Operationally, she ties decoupling to fewer cascading failures, fewer integration defects thanks to explicit API contracts, and smaller audit scopes that make compliance quicker. Less firefighting, more building.

## The roadmap starts somewhere boring

Her modernization roadmap has four stages. Assess the current architecture, name the pain points and get leadership aligned early. Validate on a small, non-critical domain to build skills and test assumptions. Then scale into the core domains such as lending, payments and customer systems, with governance, automated testing and refined deployment. Finally, expand into an ecosystem of partner integrations, where APIs let a bank add things like digital KYC or loyalty programs without modifying the core.

She is candid about what gets in the way: people resisting change, regulators who need early engagement and detailed documentation, legacy code with little documentation and tangled logic, and budgets. Her answer to the budget problem is phased execution that reinvests the savings from each step into the next.

## Who should watch

Architects and engineering leaders in banks or insurers sitting on a mainframe core, and anyone writing the business case for a modernization program. If you are here for IoT, skip to the next talk; if you have ever tried to change one field on a COBOL copybook, stay.

Title: Circuit breakers, backoff and chaos tests are security controls too
Description: Raghavendra Reddy Kapu of Akshaya Inc at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on fault-tolerance patterns, chaos engineering and queueing maths for secure enterprise systems.
Body:
A retry storm and a DDoS look a lot alike from the database's point of view. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Raghavendra Reddy Kapu](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Raghavendra_Reddy_Kapu_resilient_system_secure), quality performance engineer at Akshaya Inc, walked through the classic fault-tolerance toolkit (circuit breakers, exponential backoff, redundancy, chaos engineering) and argued that it has to be designed together with security, because a resilience mechanism nobody watches can be turned into an attack.

This is a broad, practical survey rather than one deep idea. If you already run a service mesh with circuit breaking and a chaos programme, much of it will be a refresher. If you are building that muscle, it's a well-organised map with worked numbers.

## Three pressures, one design rule

Kapu names three pressures on distributed systems. Security threats aimed at microservice boundaries, where controls are inconsistent and one vulnerable service can expose the mesh. Cascading failures, where a pool exhaustion or a memory leak in one service turns into timeouts and aggressive retries everywhere. And performance demands, with Black Friday traffic far above baseline and security incidents creating their own spikes.

His design rule is to assume the service will fail and ask how the system handles it, what stops the cascade, and whether recovery is automatic.

## The patterns, with the numbers attached

The circuit breaker gets the most attention. Closed means normal flow. After five consecutive failures, in his example, it opens and callers get a fast "temporarily unavailable" instead of hanging on a dead database. After 30 seconds it goes half-open and lets one or two test requests through; success closes it, failure keeps it open. His before-and-after: without a breaker, a five-minute outage plus a long recovery; with one, the failure is recognised in seconds and recovery happens automatically.

Retries use exponential backoff with jitter. His example doubles the wait from 100 milliseconds upwards, so by the fifth attempt a client has backed off 1.6 seconds, and jitter stops every client retrying at the same instant, the thundering herd. Redundancy comes in active-passive form (primary and standby) and active-active (three payment processors each taking a third, so losing one means slower service, not an outage), plus multi-region deployment for near-zero recovery time.

He also covers the CAP theorem in enterprise terms: partition tolerance isn't optional, so you choose per domain. Money stays consistent even if that means refusing requests; social feeds stay available and tolerate slightly stale data.

## Break it on purpose, one radius at a time

The chaos engineering section is hypothesis-driven. State an expectation, for example that the API keeps serving from the database, more slowly, if the cache cluster goes down; then kill the cache, observe, fix the gap and rerun. His schedule widens the blast radius week by week: a single node, then a network partition between regions, then multiple critical services, and finally a simulated security incident to check that malicious traffic gets detected and blocked. Netflix gets the expected credit for pioneering the practice.

## Observability and maths make the arguments objective

Kapu wants security and performance signals in one place: metrics, centralised logs with security correlation (multiple failed logins from one IP), distributed traces across a checkout that touches seven services, and anomaly-based alerts rather than static thresholds, so a jump in error rate or traffic from an unusual geography gets flagged as a possible attack.

He then brings in Markov chains to model service state transitions and queueing theory to size capacity, so teams can say how many servers a traffic pattern needs instead of guessing. His worked cost example right-sizes an over-provisioned platform while checking availability, p99 latency and error rate after each step.

## Security and resilience have to be designed together

The closing point is the one worth remembering. Fault tolerance has to work in harmony with security controls: an attacker can exploit retry behaviour to amplify a DDoS, so watch your circuit breakers and treat unusual trip patterns as a security signal. His defence-in-depth stack layers network controls, rate limiting, circuit breakers, retries with backoff, health checks with automatic failover, and chaos tests that validate the lot. Blameless post-mortems close the loop: ask why it failed, not who.

## Who should watch

Engineers and SREs moving a monolith-shaped team into microservices, and security engineers who want to understand how reliability patterns change the attack surface.

Title: Your GPUs are only as fast as the Ethernet between them
Description: Nazim Khan of Cisco at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on building lossless Ethernet fabrics for AI clusters with RoCEv2, ECN, PFC and Ultra Ethernet, plus how to secure them.
Body:
The expensive part of an AI cluster is the GPU, and the most common way to waste it is a network that makes it wait. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Nazim Khan](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Nazim_Khan_ethernet_ai_infra), technical solutions architect on Cisco's data center and AI infrastructure team, explained how plain Ethernet becomes a lossless, GPU-to-GPU fabric with RoCEv2 and congestion control, and where security fits as the clusters grow.

Khan brings 23 years in networking and a dual CCIE, and it shows: this is a clear, well-paced primer, with the occasional joke. His line about buying the fastest GPU and putting it on a congested network is that you are driving a Ferrari in a traffic jam.

## The network is part of the computer

He starts with the silicon. The CPU orchestrates, the GPU does the heavy parallel maths, and the DPU takes over what he calls the infrastructure tax: at 400G and 800G, packet processing, encryption and inspection eat CPU cycles, so the DPU offloads them and leaves the CPU and GPU to their workloads.

An AI cluster, in his framing, is a group of GPUs acting as one supercomputer, which makes the network part of the compute fabric rather than plumbing. During training every GPU computes a gradient and they all have to exchange results together, using topology-aware patterns such as rings and trees. If that collective communication lags, training time explodes.

Training and inference need different networks. Training wants high node-to-node bandwidth and is measured in time to train; inference cares about latency and reliability and can run on smaller, more distributed clusters that look much like a regular data center network.

## Lossless Ethernet is the trick

Training uses RDMA, remote direct memory access, so the NIC writes straight into GPU memory and skips the CPU. His joke: with human RDMA you could sit in the room and have his networking knowledge copied into your head by the end of the session.

RDMA assumes no packet loss. If a packet drops, the collective operation stalls or restarts. So AI designs split into a front-end network (storage, management, user access, ordinary data center traffic) and a dedicated back-end network for GPU-to-GPU traffic only.

For that back end you choose InfiniBand or Ethernet. InfiniBand runs RDMA natively and has better latency, but it's proprietary and expensive. Ethernet is standard, widely understood and cheaper, but best effort. RoCE closes the gap by carrying RDMA inside Ethernet frames. RoCE v1 was limited to layer 2; RoCEv2 adds UDP/IP headers so RDMA can route across layer 3, which is what lets clusters span racks, rows and whole halls.

Two mechanisms keep it lossless. ECN, explicit congestion notification, marks packets instead of dropping them when queues build, so endpoints slow down. PFC, priority flow control, pauses specific traffic classes under congestion. Khan stresses that tuning PFC headroom, pause thresholds and queues is critical to a successful RoCEv2 deployment. Get it wrong and you've built a very fast way to stall.

Looking ahead, the Ultra Ethernet Consortium is standardising better congestion control and lower latency for AI back ends, aiming to replace proprietary approaches.

## Security for the fabric

The security section is shorter and higher level. Khan lists the AI-specific risks (data poisoning, model extraction, privacy violations, insider threats) and the core strategies: encryption in transit and at rest, secure design, continuous monitoring for anomalies in traffic flows and user behaviour, and access control. DPUs enforce encryption and isolation at the server edge so the GPU can stay fully on training.

## Who should watch

Platform, SRE and security engineers who are suddenly responsible for GPU clusters and want the networking vocabulary fast. Network veterans will know the material; everyone else gets a clean mental model in one sitting. Don't expect a deep security architecture; the talk is mainly about the fabric.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: When the toll booth pays itself, monoliths stop working
Description: Silpa Potluri of GoodLeap at Conf42 IoT 2025 on microservices for IoT payments, from device auth and fast authorization to aggregating micro-transactions.
Body:
Payment systems were built for a human tapping a card a few times a day, not for a smart meter that wants to bill thousands of fractions of a cent before lunch. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Silpa Potluri, a software developer at GoodLeap with over two decades in software and more than ten years in payments, explained why IoT breaks monolithic payment platforms and how a microservices design carries the load.

It is an architecture overview rather than a code walkthrough, and a tidy one: each service in the pipeline gets its slide, in the order a device transaction actually flows.

## IoT breaks the assumptions payments were built on

Silpa's starting point is that devices now make decisions and trigger transactions on our behalf: smart meters reporting energy use, vehicles paying tolls automatically, appliances reordering supplies. Traditional payment systems assumed human interaction, infrequent transactions and relatively large amounts. IoT flips all three.

The monolith fails in predictable places. Vertical scaling cannot absorb thousands of devices joining at once. Waiting weeks to deploy a security fix is untenable when devices are already in the field. Legacy stacks struggle to adopt modern cryptography or machine learning. A failure in one corner cascades across the platform, which for connected vehicles or city infrastructure is not an acceptable outage. And a single database was never designed to juggle real-time telemetry, micro-transactions, fraud signals and settlement records at the same time.

## The pipeline, one service at a time

The fix is the familiar split by business capability, with four principles: single responsibility, independent deployment, technology flexibility per service, and fault isolation, so an analytics failure never stops payments.

The device side is where IoT payments get unusual. Devices must authenticate themselves, often with little processing power and flaky connectivity. That means cryptographic credentials embedded at manufacturing, secure elements for tamper resistance, and full lifecycle management including ownership changes and decommissioning. A dedicated service lets you rotate credentials without anyone physically touching the device.

Authorization then has milliseconds to check balances, subscriptions and usage limits, score risk, validate location to catch impossible scenarios, and enforce idempotency so a retrying device is not charged twice. Anyone who has debugged a double charge will nod at that last one.

## Aggregate the pennies, keep the receipts

The cleverest piece is micro-transaction aggregation. Many IoT charges are tiny fractions of a cent, so processing each individually makes no sense. A smart meter's thousands of daily usage records are accumulated, aggregated on thresholds or schedules, and settled as a single payment, while the detailed logs are kept for transparency.

Settlement is the strictly consistent, heavily regulated core, with multi-stage flows, continuous reconciliation and banking network integration. Machine learning fraud detection runs alongside it, analysing device behaviour and coordinated attacks without slowing normal transactions.

## Events in the middle, a gateway at the edge

Services talk through events rather than direct calls: a device authenticates, an event is published, and fraud detection, analytics and notifications each consume it. Silpa points to Kafka as the backbone for millions of events a day. At the front, an API gateway translates the zoo of device protocols (MQTT, CoAP, HTTP and automotive protocols), enforces security, applies rate limits and shields the backend from spikes and malformed requests.

Her smart city example ties it together: parking meters, vehicles and charging stations paying automatically, with revenue split across agencies that each have their own rules. Distributed tracing, metrics and alerting, plus layered security (secrets management, service authentication, tokenization, segmentation), keep it operable and compliant.

## Who should watch

Engineers designing payment or metering backends for connected devices, and fintech teams wondering what changes when the customer is a machine. Seasoned microservices folks will know the patterns; the device authentication and aggregation sections are where the IoT-specific value sits.

Title: Your MCP server is safe. The web page it fetched isn't
Description: Alex Shershebnev of Zencoder at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on wiring MCP into DevOps workflows and a live prompt-injection demo that wrote a file to disk.
Body:
The scary part of giving an LLM tools isn't the tool. It's whatever text the tool brings back. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Alex Shershebnev](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_cloud_mcp_secure), ML/DevOps lead and developer advocate at Zencoder, showed how the Model Context Protocol lets an assistant solve Jira tickets, open pull requests and inspect Kubernetes from your IDE, then hijacked his own agent with a web page that looked harmless to a human.

The demos run inside Zencoder, his company's AI coding assistant, so expect some product on screen. The MCP concepts and the attack apply to any client.

## LLMs need context, so we gave them hands

Shershebnev starts from why MCP exists. Models predict probable tokens and live somewhere in the cloud, with no access to your servers, your logs or your in-house frameworks. Ask a chatbot for Google's response time and it suggests running ping; it can't run it. Tools fix that by letting the model gather extra context.

MCP, introduced by Anthropic around December 2024 and since adopted by OpenAI too, is the common way to do it. It's based on JSON-RPC 2.0 and has two main roles: the host (your IDE or LLM client) and the server, which advertises a list of tools and executes them. He shows the GitHub MCP server's create-branch tool, whose short description and parameter list are exactly what ends up in the prompt so the model can decide which tool to call.

Writing your own server is cheap. In Python with FastMCP he circles three lines: import the library, instantiate the server, decorate a function. His example turns a function that runs bash commands into a tool any MCP-compatible model can call, which is also a nice preview of the security half of the talk.

## The useful part: tickets to pull requests, pods to answers

The first demo chains Jira, Git and GitHub servers. He tags a ticket, asks the agent to solve it, create a branch, push and open a pull request. The agent explores the repository, edits files, runs commands to regenerate an OpenAPI schema and opens a PR under his token, touching 110 files with a tidy description. He jokes that a well-documented PR is now a sign it was written by AI.

The second gives the agent the Kubernetes MCP server and asks whether any pods in a namespace are unhealthy. He also runs through the servers he finds most useful day to day: Postgres for databases, Grafana and Sentry for monitoring, Slack, Context7 for up-to-date library docs, and Playwright MCP to drive a browser.

## The attack lives in the context, not the protocol

Then the security part. Shershebnev serves pages that look identical to a human reader but carry hidden instructions, fetched through the fetch MCP server. The first page is a clean control. The second hides an injection, and Anthropic's prompt injection detection catches it. The third, more elaborate one asks the model to list every function it can access, then introduces a fake function and asks it to test that function and simulate the output. The model said hi as instructed, listed 17 functions and, instead of simulating, actually called its write-file tool and created a file on his machine.

His point is precise: the MCP fetch server did exactly what it was built to do. The attack came through the page content. He ties it to the publicised GitHub MCP exploit, where an issue in a public repository asked the agent to collect information from private repositories and post it publicly, and the agent, holding a token that allowed both, obliged.

## What to lock down

His recommendations are practical:

- Allowlist which MCP servers developers and agents may use, and manage configs organisation-wide.
- Store the tokens servers need, such as GitHub personal access tokens, in a proper secrets system.
- Keep agents away from sensitive systems like production databases, or at least make access read-only.
- Use server permission flags where they exist. The Kubernetes MCP server, he notes, has one to enable read-only tools and another to disable destructive ones.
- Put an intermediary in front of untrusted content: a search or summarising proxy instead of piping raw web pages into the model.

## Who should watch

Anyone who has added an MCP server to their IDE this year, and platform or security teams deciding what agents may touch. The injection demo is worth the time on its own.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Don't Give the Agent a Shell](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Ahmed_Tariq_identity_permissions_cloud) draws tool and identity boundaries for agents in cloud operations.
- [Building an MCP Server in Go for a Real B2B Workflow](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2026_Shadi_Elyafi_mcp_b2b_workflow) is the build-your-own side in more depth.

Title: In high-frequency trading, every security control has a latency bill
Description: Janardhan Chejarla of Calypso Technology at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on securing event-driven trading systems without paying the sidecar latency tax.
Body:
A service mesh sidecar is a reasonable price for security in most microservices. In high-frequency trading it is the whole budget. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Janardhan Chejarla](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Janardhan_Chejarla_trading_cloud_scale), senior technical consultant at Calypso Technology, made the case that trading platforms have to move security into the application and eventually into the hardware, because every check added on the hot path is measured in microseconds and money.

It's a short, high-level talk, closer to an architecture sketch than a demo. The value is in how cleanly it lays out the trade-offs.

## The latency tax

Chejarla starts with three goals that pull against each other: speed, scale (millions of orders per second) and security. Focus on one and you usually sacrifice another. He calls the cost of security checks the latency tax. His illustrative example: if a traditional firewall adds something like 50 microseconds, you are losing money.

His comparison chart makes the point sharper. A sidecar, the default security pattern in modern microservices, adds about 150 microseconds, which he calls too much for HFT. The alternative is to bake security into the application through an in-process library and keep the overhead to around five microseconds or less. The lesson isn't that sidecars are bad. It's that the security architecture should follow the latency tier of the component it protects.

## Bypassing the kernel means bypassing its protections

The fastest trading paths skip the operating system entirely. Chejarla describes kernel-bypass networking with DPDK or RDMA so the application talks directly to the network card. The catch, which he states plainly, is that this also skips security measures the OS would normally give you. So the controls have to move closer to the hardware.

For the order matching core he uses Aeron, which he describes as reliable, encrypted, near-instant messaging for machines, with Raft consensus so all trading nodes agree on the order of trades even if one fails. Slower, high-volume work such as market data analysis and trade settlement goes over Kafka, kept separate so record-keeping never slows the matching engine. Two tiers, two latency budgets, two security designs.

## Observe with eBPF, prove with event sourcing

You still need to see what happens, and standard agents cost too much. Chejarla's answer is eBPF: hook into the kernel to observe packets and system actions for compliance without adding latency to the trading path.

The second half of his compliance story is determinism. Every action in the system is captured as an immutable event, so you can replay a trading sequence after something goes wrong and reconstruct exactly what happened in a given window. That matters for post-mortems and for regulators, who increasingly ask for proof of best execution. His rule of thumb: if you can't replay it, you can't prove it. He folds this into what he calls compliance as code, and points to the London Stock Exchange as an example of speed and reliability improving together.

On resilience he offers one memorable principle for HFT: a system that cannot recover in milliseconds has already failed.

## The next step is the wire itself

The forward-looking part goes below software. Chejarla wants firewalls, risk checks and encryption implemented in FPGA gates as bump-in-the-wire devices, so bad packets are dropped before they ever reach a CPU, giving zero CPU overhead for those checks. He also wants these patterns to work on public clouds, not only private infrastructure, which is the harder half of the problem.

## Who should watch

Engineers on trading, market data or other microsecond-sensitive systems, and anyone who has been told to add a sidecar to a hot path and suspected it was the wrong tool. It's an overview, so expect pointers (Aeron, DPDK, eBPF, FPGA) rather than implementation detail.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Observability in Modern Treasury Trading Platforms](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Ganesh_Marimuthu_trading_treasury_platforms) covers monitoring high-frequency systems at scale.
- [True Kubernetes Observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Shahar_Azulay_kubernetes_observability_ebpf) goes deeper on the kernel-level observation Chejarla relies on.
- [Ambient Mesh: the sidecar-less Istio for zero trust](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Md_Azmal_ambient_mesh_sidecar_zero_trust) is another answer to the sidecar overhead question.

Title: Round robin is too polite for banking traffic
Description: Raghunadha Dornala of Miracle Software Systems at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on ECBA, a hybrid ensemble load balancer for secure cloud banking transactions.
Body:
Round robin treats every server as equal and every request as the same size, which is a generous assumption for a bank on payday. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Raghunadha Dornala](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Raghunadha_Dornala_banking_load_cloud), senior cloud architect at Miracle Software Systems, presented the Ensemble Cloud Banking Algorithm (ECBA): a hybrid of weighted round robin and adaptive load balancing that routes transactions on live metrics and forecasts, with security hooks built in.

It's a short research talk that walks from the problem to a simulation-based evaluation. Dornala notes his own day job is mostly pharmacy, retail and food, so this is a cross-industry idea brought to banking rather than a production story from a bank.

## Why the classic algorithms fall short

Dornala's diagnosis is short and familiar. Round robin hands requests out in sequence without looking at server capacity or current load, so utilisation gets uneven. Least connections looks at open connections but ignores processing power and response times. Under dynamic banking workloads both lead to bottlenecks, idle capacity next to hot nodes, and degraded service quality.

Digital banking makes that worse. Transaction systems have to be fast, secure, compliant with regulation and continuously available, all at once, and the traffic is anything but uniform: payments, fraud checks and analytics don't cost the same.

## ECBA routes on what the servers are actually doing

ECBA watches server capacity, transaction types, latency and throughput, and routes each request using real-time metrics plus predictive analytics. AI forecasting and reinforcement learning let it anticipate spikes before they arrive instead of reacting after queues build. The weighted round robin half keeps distribution fair; the adaptive half shifts load when the numbers move.

He lists the side effects that make it more than a scheduler: fraud detection, predictive routing, compliance monitoring and self-healing. That's where the DevSecOps angle comes in.

## Security travels with the traffic

In Dornala's design the balancer sits inside the DevSecOps framework rather than in front of it. Transactions are encrypted end to end, AI-driven compliance monitoring scans continuously for anomalies and regulatory risk, audit trails are generated as traffic flows, and threat detection flags suspicious traffic patterns in real time through behaviour analysis and automated risk scoring. He positions it alongside a zero-trust architecture.

The appeal is that the component already looking at every request is a natural place to notice when requests look wrong. The trade-off, which the talk doesn't go into, is that your load balancer becomes a much bigger piece of software to secure and operate.

## How it was tested

The evaluation is Python-based simulation, not a live bank. Dornala ran workloads from a thousand up to ten thousand transactions, compared ECBA against round robin, least connections and a standalone adaptive balancer, and measured response time, throughput and utilisation using real-world banking transaction patterns, with anomaly detection integrated to check behaviour under unexpected load.

He reports ECBA posting the lowest response times of the group and, at 5,000 transactions, holding 36.9 requests per second at 83.3% utilisation. Future work is to feed historical transaction data into models that predict workload spikes. Read the numbers as a simulation benchmark: useful for comparing algorithms, not a promise about your traffic.

Deployment, in his outline, starts with an infrastructure assessment, then metric configuration, then rigorous testing, followed by continuous tuning. Use cases run from payment processing to fraud detection.

## Who should watch

Engineers who own traffic management for payment or core banking platforms, and anyone weighing whether a smarter balancer is worth the operational cost. If you want production incident data, this isn't it; if you want a clear argument for capacity-aware, predictive routing, it's a quick watch.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Developing custom Load Balancer using Envoy](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2024_Sandeep_Bhat_custom_load_balancer_envoy) shows what building your own balancing logic looks like in practice.

- [Cloud-Driven Reconciliation for Financial Accuracy](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2025_Jaya_Krishna_Vemuri_investment_banking_accuracy) covers another cloud-scale banking workload.
