Title: Conf42 Robotics 2025: the software and rules around the robots
Description: Conf42 Robotics 2025 roundup - post-quantum robot networks, DO-178C for electric aircraft, compliance-by-design, and AI in clinics and disaster response.
Body:
Conf42 Robotics 2025 ran online on November 20, 2025, with nine talks, and almost none of them were about motors or grippers. The lineup was about everything that has to be true around a robot before anyone lets it loose: how its network survives quantum computers, how its flight software gets certified, how its decisions are audited, and what data infrastructure feeds it. If you build the systems that robots plug into, this was your kind of robotics conference.

All talks are on the [Conf42 Robotics 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/robotics2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDUt9JKK5BDogRgpbqPK4wc).

## Robots outlive their cryptography

The sharpest framing of the day came from [Nehal Singh](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Nehal_Singh_robotics_quantum_security) of California State University, Long Beach. The robots deployed today in manufacturing, healthcare, defence, and logistics will still be running five, ten, even fifteen years from now. Large quantum computers are not here yet, but a fleet with that lifespan has to assume they will arrive while it is still in service. Robotic systems combine long-lived hardware, sensitive operational data, and real-time autonomy, which makes them an attractive target.

The talk walks through post-quantum cryptography based on the NIST standards, with the constraint robotics engineers care about most: securing the network without breaking real-time performance. A useful one if your hardware refresh cycle is measured in decades rather than sprints.

## Certification is the long pole

[Charles Antony Raj](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Charles_Antony_Raj_avionics_certify_flight), Senior Manager of Systems and Software Engineering at Collins Aerospace, brought about two decades of aerospace experience to a problem most software engineers never meet: certifying flight software under DO-178C when it runs on multicore processors. Multicore chips are what electric aircraft programmes want for performance, and they are also what makes interference between cores hard to bound and hard to prove safe.

The talk covers the certification paths and strategies for cutting the delays they cause. It is a rare look at what "shipping" means when the regulator, not the CI pipeline, is the final gate.

## Compliance as an architecture choice

Two talks treated regulation as a design input rather than paperwork bolted on at the end.

[Sneha Nallapu](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Sneha_Nallapu_compliance_design_finance) of J.B. Hunt Transport Services made the case for compliance-by-design in automated financial systems. The patterns are ones backend engineers will recognise: event sourcing, bi-temporal data so you can answer what you knew and when, graph lineage, CQRS, and adaptive workflows. Audit trails stop being a report someone generates and become a property of the system.

[Vinaya Nadig](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Vinaya_Nadig_governance_banking_robots), a Principal Engineer at Amazon, opened with the 2008 financial crisis: algorithms making decisions with opaque logic and incomplete data, long before generative AI. Today AI approves loans, flags fraud, and advises on investments in real time. The argument is that a unified AI data governance framework is what keeps banking automation from repeating that history at machine speed.

## AI and robotics where the stakes are human

[Srinivasa SKN Ambati](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Srinivasa_SKN_Ambati_healthcare_analytics_ai), an Engineer Lead at Anthem, looked at how advanced analytics and AI are changing clinical robotics, with an emphasis on building systems that are scalable and compliant enough for patient care.

[Vivek Karnam](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Vivek_Karnam_cloud_response_robots) of Surge Technology Solutions started from the shortcomings of traditional emergency response and showed how cloud computing, robotics, and predictive analytics can combine into faster, smarter disaster response frameworks.

## The infrastructure underneath

The remaining talks went one layer down, to the data and even the walls that robotic systems depend on.

- [Adithya Sirimalla](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Adithya_Sirimalla_oracle_azure_cloud) of Enliven Technologies gave a practical framework for tuning Oracle and SQL Server on AWS and Azure, on the premise that in automation every millisecond of database latency can shape a real-time decision.
- [Ankita Saxena](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Ankita_Saxena_ai_insights_industry), a Senior Product Manager at Amazon, traced recommendation systems from a "you may also like" widget to strategic infrastructure, including in robotics-enabled marketplaces.
- [Rahul Pingale](https://www.conf42.com/Robotics_2025_Rahul_Pingale_iot_materials_smart), Technical Director at Wallquest, gave the most unexpected talk of the day: PVC-free non-woven wall surfaces with embedded sensors and connectivity, turning something as ordinary as a wall into part of a smart environment. Proof that the edge can be quite literal.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to [LLMday](https://llmday.com/), the in-person LLM engineering conference series, which joined as a gold sponsor, and to the newsletter, podcast, and media partners listed on the event page.

Robotics 2025 was the first Conf42 event dedicated to the topic. For more hardware-meets-software talks, the [Conf42 IoT 2025](https://www.conf42.com/iot2025) lineup is the closest neighbour, and the [full robotics playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDUt9JKK5BDogRgpbqPK4wc) is there whenever you have an evening and a soldering iron cooling down.

Title: IoT supply chain attacks come in through the trusted update
Description: Cybersecurity risk analyst Gresshma Atluri at Conf42 IoT 2025 on defending connected devices from supply chain attacks with secure by design and zero trust.
Body:
The scariest IoT attacks do not break down the front door; they ship inside the box. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, cybersecurity risk analyst Gresshma Atluri laid out how supply chain attacks reach connected devices through firmware, components and trusted updates, and the governance-heavy playbook she uses with regulated industries to push back.

Gresshma comes at this from GRC work rather than exploit research, and the talk reads that way: a structured walk from threat to roadmap, built on her research and consulting in heavily regulated sectors. It is a strategy talk, not a hands-on hardening lab.

## One component, one mistake

She opens with a story from a hospital she consulted for. A small pump from a trusted vendor carried a vulnerability in its firmware, introduced during manufacturing, which allowed unauthorized access. Nobody checked, because the vendor was trusted, and patient safety was suddenly on the line.

That is the core of her argument: trust is implicit across the IoT supply chain, so attackers aim for the parts nobody inspects. She lists the attack surface in layers. Microcontrollers and chips sourced from many countries, third party and open source code that may be outdated or malicious, contract manufacturers who do not follow security processes, update servers that can push malware as a legitimate update, and cloud backends whose compromise hands over every connected device at once.

The examples are familiar but still sobering: Mirai turning default passwords on baby monitors and cameras into a global DDoS, and a logistics firm she worked with where smart scanners were hijacked through compromised firmware to gain a foothold in backend systems. Her line about a toaster talking to the light hub, and both talking to the Wi-Fi, is the most concise threat model of a smart home you will hear.

## Secure by design, then trust nothing

The defensive half starts with building security in rather than patching it on later. Her analogy is earthquake-proofing in California: you reinforce the structure before the quake, not after. The must-haves she lists are threat modeling when a product is designed, hardware features such as secure boot, vetting suppliers the way you would vet a new hire (including their breach history), and maintaining a software bill of materials so you always know what is running on a device.

On top of that comes zero trust. Every device, request and update must prove it is legitimate. Each device gets a unique identity, talks only to the services it actually needs, encrypts all communication and receives only the access it requires.

## Behaviour beats signatures

Signature-based detection loses the race, she argues, because attackers change faster than signature databases. Behaviour modeling catches the device that suddenly sends far more traffic than usual at 2 AM. Her comparison is a fitness tracker that knows your resting heart rate and flags an unexplained spike.

Incident response gets its own IoT-flavoured checklist: detect both digital and physical anomalies, contain by segmenting smartly instead of shutting down a whole network, investigate with IoT-specific forensic tools, remediate by distributing clean firmware securely, then feed the lessons back into controls.

## Start with the boring wins

The roadmap is refreshingly unglamorous. Begin with a maturity assessment, kill default passwords, tighten password policy, and do basic segmentation. Then build cross-functional teams spanning security, supply chain and product, and track live metrics such as time to detect and time to fix. Her closing ask is aimed at manufacturers and buyers alike: do not trade security for the cheapest part, push for transparent supply chains, and expect more regulation and lightweight cryptography for constrained devices.

## Who should watch

Security, risk and procurement folks who need a shared vocabulary for IoT supply chain risk, and product teams starting a connected device who want a checklist to argue from. If you are after firmware reverse engineering or attestation code, this is the wrong half hour.

Title: When software gains hands and eyes
Description: Automation becomes tangible
Body:
# Robots have paperwork now

Robotics used to be about movement.

Arms, wheels, sensors, maybe something that could bump into a wall and recover gracefully. These days, robots also deal with compliance, security, data governance, cloud platforms, and regulations that very much do not care how cool the hardware is.

Conf42 Robotics 2025 sits right in that reality.

This is a focused conference with six talks, all centered on how robotics is evolving into a serious, enterprise-grade discipline. AI-powered recommendation systems, secure robot networks, compliance-by-design, and data governance all feature prominently. These are robots that operate in finance, healthcare, aviation, and critical infrastructure.

Security gets real attention. There are sessions on post-quantum cryptography for robot networks, protecting real-time systems without breaking performance, and preparing robotics platforms for a future where cryptography itself is changing.

Regulation and compliance are not treated as side notes. Talks on compliance-by-design, auditability, and regulatory-resilient architectures explore how robotics systems can be built to survive scrutiny in finance, aviation, and other tightly controlled environments.

Healthcare, emergency response, and sustainability round things out. Clinical robotics powered by advanced analytics, AI-driven emergency response systems, and IoT-enabled materials show how robotics is expanding beyond factories into spaces where reliability and trust matter deeply.

If robotics is part of your work, and that work involves more than just motion control, this one’s for you. Robots are no longer experimental. They’re operational, regulated, and increasingly critical.

Title: Bank-grade AI agents need consensus, not just guardrails
Description: Swamy Biru of JPMorganChase at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on securing RAG pipelines and multi-agent systems in investment banking middle-office operations.
Body:
Traditional security controls assume the system makes the same decision twice. AI agents in a bank don't. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Swamy Biru](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Swamy_Biru_finance_rag_ai), a vice president at JPMorganChase & Co, walked through a security-first architecture for agentic AI and retrieval-augmented generation in investment banking middle-office operations, built on one rule: every component of the AI pipeline is a potential vulnerability, so design for that from day one.

## The problem: probabilistic decisions in a deterministic compliance world

Biru frames the challenge as two questions the industry hasn't fully answered. How do you secure a system where decisions come out of probabilistic models instead of deterministic code? And how do you stay compliant when agents autonomously pull and synthesise information from huge knowledge bases?

His answer is that security has to be embedded in the architecture, not bolted on afterwards. The rest of the talk is that idea broken into layers.

## Retrieval is a security boundary, not just a search call

The first layer is knowledge retrieval. The knowledge base is multi-tiered and segmented by domain, with encryption and a security posture that tightens with the sensitivity of the information. Every retrieval passes through validation before anything is released: verify the identity and credentials of the caller, sanitise the query to block injection, apply role-based access control to limit what can come back, log every interaction for compliance, and protect the response in transit.

If you have ever built a RAG prototype that happily returned whatever the vector store found, this is the list of things your prototype skipped.

## Agents get narrow scopes and have to agree with each other

The second layer is orchestration. Biru describes multiple specialised agents (validation, compliance, risk assessment, communication, exception handling, operations), each confined to a strictly defined scope under least privilege, talking over a zero-trust model with end-to-end encryption between agents.

The interesting bit is the consensus mechanism, which he calls blockchain-inspired. High-stakes decisions need agreement from several specialised agents: an execution agent proposes an action, and the compliance, risk and operations agents must approve it independently before anything runs. It's four-eyes review, automated, with the eyes being models that don't share a context.

The third layer is isolation of model processing: sandboxes with no direct access to production, multi-stage input sanitisation and output validation, and what he calls an air-gap approach so a compromised model can't reach the systems that matter.

## The DevSecOps plumbing around the models

Around those layers sits fairly familiar DevSecOps: automated security testing from the earliest stages, continuous automated penetration testing and fuzzing, infrastructure as code that carries security policies, access controls and encryption settings, and secure coding templates so the safe path is also the easiest one for engineers.

Model security gets its own lifecycle. Training data is curated, training runs in isolated environments without network access, models are benchmarked for consistency with previous versions, and deployment needs approval from security and compliance teams. After release, drift is monitored and regular back-testing checks the model still behaves under current conditions.

Threat detection combines statistical baselines, deep learning for attack signatures, graph neural networks for unusual relationships across systems, and reinforcement learning to adapt. Responses are tiered: low-severity events trigger automated defences such as extra authentication or rate limiting, while medium-severity ones keep operations running under closer monitoring and escalate to senior security staff.

## Lessons worth stealing

Biru's closing lessons are short. Retrofitting security into an AI architecture is far harder than building it in. Human oversight stays critical, with a clear line between what the AI handles alone and where it escalates when uncertain. And the defence has to keep learning, through regular red-team exercises.

He also covers the compliance side (transaction reporting, Dodd-Frank, GDPR, model risk management) and explainability tailored to auditors, engineers and business users. The abstract mentions efficiency gains; the talk itself is mostly architecture, so watch it for the design, not for benchmarks.

## Who should watch

Architects and security engineers putting RAG or agents near regulated data, especially in finance. The consensus pattern and the retrieval checklist travel well outside banking.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [RAGged and Compromised: Hacking Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Blaize_Stewart_rag_security_injection) shows the attacks this architecture defends against.
- [I Don't Trust AI Agents (And Neither Should You)](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Morgan_Willis_production_guardrails_trust) builds production guardrails around agents.
- [Leveraging AI in Fintech](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Sudeep_Meduri_ai_fintech_security) covers AI for security and compliance automation in financial DevSecOps.

Title: Risk-driven DevSecOps starts outside the CI/CD pipeline
Description: Nishanth Sirikonda at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on ranking security work by business impact and mapping the SaaS, identity and API layers pipelines never see.
Body:
Most DevSecOps programmes guard the pipeline and call it a day, while the real exposure sits in a SaaS admin console nobody scans. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, [Nishanth Sirikonda](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2025_Nishanth_Sirikonda_risk_secure_system), a Workday solutions architect at First Day Foundation, argued for risk-driven DevSecOps: find the assets that would hurt most if they failed, protect those first, and let risk decide where the automation goes.

It's a short, slide-driven talk, closer to a playbook than a war story. That makes it a good fit for anyone who has to explain to a steering committee why the security backlog is ordered the way it is.

## The pipeline is a small part of the attack surface

Sirikonda's starting complaint is about scope. Classic DevSecOps concentrates on CI/CD: scanning, gating, blocking releases. The gaps he lists are everywhere else. SaaS platforms, identity and access management, and the integration layer between systems mostly live outside any pipeline, so they never get the scanner's attention.

He adds two more failure modes. Security turns into a downstream checkpoint instead of a design principle, and findings arrive scattered across tools with no central view of risk, so nobody can say which fix matters most. His summary line is the old one, and it still holds: you cannot protect what you cannot see.

So step one is a map of the whole ecosystem. He names four layers to cover: cloud misconfigurations (storage buckets, network rules, encryption settings, resource permissions), third-party risk (API connections, vendor access, data sharing), identity surfaces (service accounts, grants, privilege escalation paths), and the data flows and dependencies that tie systems together.

## Compliance as a continuous signal, not an audit season

The second idea is to stop treating compliance as an annual event. Sirikonda describes three moves: set baselines and guardrails for the usual failure points across cloud, SaaS, identity and API configuration; run automated policy checks continuously so drift gets caught when it happens instead of at the next audit; and feed the results back into engineering decisions.

His key point is that monitoring here is a discipline, not a shopping list. More tools don't help if nobody runs validation as a routine operational practice. Anyone who has inherited three overlapping CSPM dashboards will recognise the problem.

Inside the pipeline he keeps it practical: automate early checks in developer workflows, audit and update third-party dependencies consistently, and hold custom scripts and integration glue to the same security standard as product code. That glue is often where the shortcuts live.

## Least privilege is a boring superpower

The access governance section is the most concrete. Sirikonda wants RBAC roles that map to real job responsibilities rather than generic templates, regular reviews that keep permissions in line with current duties, conditional access (device health, location, risk signals, behaviour) as the default rather than an exception, and tamper-evident audit logs. He frames audit data as a strategic asset: it supports accountability and tells you where to improve.

## Speak in business impact, report in risk metrics

The last part is about getting leadership to care. Translate findings into revenue loss, compliance violations and reputational damage instead of raw CVE identifiers, plug DevSecOps into the existing enterprise risk framework and board reporting, and track metrics executives understand: mean time to remediate critical exposures, attack surface reduction, control effectiveness.

He closes with a cadence: quarterly security reviews, annual API penetration tests, a seven-day target for remediating critical risks, SCA and SAST in CI/CD that halt critical flaws, policy as code and configuration as code with auto-fixes, plus monthly risk meetings and leadership dashboards. Treat those as his suggested targets, not results from a measured rollout.

## Who should watch

Security leads and platform owners building a risk register, and architects who own SaaS-heavy estates (Workday, CRM, ITSM) where the pipeline tooling stops at the API boundary. If you want deep tooling demos, this isn't that talk. If you need a framework to argue priorities with, it's a quick watch.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Securing the software supply chain: beyond SBOM](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Marek_Najmajer_Aleksander_Baranowski_beyond_sbom_risk_assessment) turns vulnerability findings into risk assessment.
- [AI-Driven Risk-Aware Decision-Making for Scalable Reliability Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_Oreoluwa_Omoike_driven_risk_aware) brings the same risk lens to reliability work.
- [Cloud MCP Servers Under Fire](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2026_Aleksandr_Pinaev_security_vulnerabilities_compliance) looks at a newer integration layer that pipelines rarely cover.

Title: Teaching an 8-year-old observability with a thirsty house plant
Description: Marie Cruz of Grafana Labs at Conf42 IoT 2025 builds a soil moisture monitor with an ESP32, Prometheus and Grafana Cloud alongside her daughter.
Body:
A house plant makes a surprisingly good on-call rotation: it fails silently, nobody notices until it is too late, and the postmortem always blames too much or too little water. At Conf42 Internet of Things (IoT) 2025, Marie Cruz, Senior Developer Advocate at Grafana Labs, showed how she and her 8-year-old daughter wired a soil moisture sensor to an ESP32, shipped readings to Prometheus in Grafana Cloud, and got a Telegram alert whenever the plant was thirsty.

The project is deliberately beginner-level, and Marie says so. The interesting part is less the hardware than the way she explains monitoring and observability to someone with zero jargon, which is a skill most of us could use at work too.

## Monitoring is a yes or no, observability asks why

Marie's framing for her daughter: each plant gets a little helper, a sensor in the soil, and the internet of things is just a way to connect objects like that so they can report, communicate and sometimes act on their own.

Monitoring, in her version, is checking whether the soil is dry and reacting. Useful, but it only answers yes or no. If the plant still looks sad after watering, monitoring has nothing more to say. Observability means looking at the data over time: does moisture drop at a certain hour, should room temperature and humidity be in the picture, or is one of the family dogs up to something? Without signals you are guessing; with them the black box becomes a clear box. That is the same pitch you would give a VP about distributed tracing, just with more chlorophyll.

## The bill of materials fits in a shoebox

The hardware list is short: a soil moisture sensor, an ESP32-S3 dev kit, a breadboard, DuPont jumper wires and a USB-C cable. Software is the Arduino IDE plus a Grafana Cloud account on the free tier, which conveniently comes with a managed Prometheus instance.

Marie walks through the wiring pin by pin (VCC to 3.3 V, ground to ground, analog out to pin 11) and how she explained it: VCC is the plus side of the battery, ground is the minus side. The sensor itself is two metal prongs; wet soil conducts better than dry soil, so a high analog reading means dry and a low one means wet. Her first program reads the value every five seconds and reports dry soil above 500. She explains the 9,600 baud rate as a group of friends who all agree to speak at the same speed, which is honestly a better definition than most serial port docs offer.

## From serial monitor to dashboard to alert

Staring at the Arduino serial monitor around the clock is nobody's idea of observability, so the second iteration pushes readings to Prometheus. Prometheus became a gardener who collects every value and keeps it in a time series toolbox with timestamps; PromQL is the language you use to ask the gardener questions. The team used the Prometheus Arduino libraries, a config file with the instance URL, user and API token plus Wi-Fi details, and a certificates file copied from that project. When her daughter asked whether copying the example code was cheating, Marie had to break the news that this is just programming.

The Grafana dashboard has a text panel with a photo of the plant, a stat panel and a gauge with a threshold at 500, and a time series panel. Value mappings turn the stat and gauge from green to red when the soil dries out. Finally, a Grafana alert rule fires above 500 and sends the message to a Telegram contact point. She also tried Grafana Assistant, the AI agent built into Grafana Cloud, to tidy up the dashboard's look.

## Who should watch

Parents and teachers looking for a weekend STEM project with real tools, and anyone who has to explain monitoring versus observability to non-engineers. It is also a compact, honest tour of the Prometheus and Grafana Cloud path for a single ESP32 device. If you already run Grafana in production, the value is in the explanations, not the stack. Marie's full project lives in her plant monitoring GitHub repo, linked from the talk.

- [Guillermo Ruiz on building the largest Raspberry Pi Kubernetes PostgreSQL cluster](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Guillermo_Ruiz_raspberrypi_kubernetes_postgresql) at Conf42 IoT 2024, for when the hobby project gets out of hand.

Title: Counting commits won't make developers productive; context will
Description: Kuldeep Deshwal of Proofpoint at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on the pitfalls that drain developer productivity and four pillars for keeping it sustainable.
Body:
Pull requests, commits, deploys, lines of code: measure them without context and you get exactly the behaviour you did not want. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Kuldeep Deshwal, Director of Engineering at Proofpoint, walked through the pitfalls that quietly drain developer productivity in DevSecOps organisations and proposed four pillars for keeping it sustainable.

It is a short, manager-to-manager talk, and it starts from a simple premise: for any company shipping software, developers are the most important asset, and setting them up for success is how the company succeeds.

## Start with what developers value

Before any framework, Kuldeep asks what developers actually want. His answer, drawn from study after study: meaningful impact. They want to understand the big picture and see how their work drives long-term outcomes. Everything that follows is measured against that.

## Pitfalls, grouped by where they come from

**Management.** Micromanagement tops the list; he calls it a massive anti-pattern for productivity. Close behind is metric obsession. Activity counts like PRs, commits, deploys, lines of code and velocity are easy to collect and easy to game, and without context they drive unintended behaviour. Goodhart would like a word.

**Tooling.** The DevOps, DevSecOps and observability movements each added to the average developer's plate. The result is constant context switching across many tools, which he names as possibly the biggest drain on productivity, depending on whether tooling and culture were set up with empathy for how developers work.

**Prioritisation.** Shifting security left needs proper processes and automation, or developers spend their days playing catch-up across an ever wider range of tools, vulnerability types and attack surface. Tech debt left alone snowballs; everyone knows how long a small change to a legacy app takes.

**Organisation.** The pace of change opens learning gaps and silos. His current example is AI code generation tools, which improve so quickly that developers are always catching up. Forums and processes for collaboration help, and so does designing teams with developer wellbeing in mind.

## Four pillars

His alternative rests on four pillars:

- **Context-based measures.** Keep metrics, but tie activity to outcomes, and pair quantitative data with qualitative signals.
- **Autonomy and trust.** Development is creative work, and trust is at its heart.
- **Clarity.** None of it works unless goals and the business outcomes behind them are spelled out.
- **Continuous learning.** The tooling keeps moving, so investment in growth has to be ongoing.

## Making it practical

Execution, he admits, is easier said than done. His practical steps: build a context-rich picture of productivity by combining qualitative and quantitative data; study the specific triggers of context switching across the organisation and fix them; and set up platform tooling and automation to put minimal cognitive load on developers delivering customer features. The order matters too: clarity of goals first, then autonomy in execution, then measurable outcomes to track progress, with continuous investment in people underneath.

He closes on a single principle: empathy and respect for developers and their workflow should sit at the centre of culture, planning and customer value delivery.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and directors who have just been handed a productivity dashboard, and platform teams deciding how much tooling to put in front of developers. It is brief and conceptual, so watch it as a framing for the next planning conversation rather than as a metrics playbook.

## Related talks

- [Health Checks for Systems. What About Your Team?](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2026_Sylvain_Kalache_burnout_oncall_sre) by Sylvain Kalache, on burnout.

Title: Supply chain security should be the default path in CI, not a checklist
Description: Bhaskar Bharat Sawant of Cornerstone Building Brands at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on automatic SBOMs, SLSA, provenance and deploy-time verification.
Body:
When Log4j hit, one team needed almost a full week just to find the affected services. After they built supply chain defence into their pipeline, a simulated vulnerability event took minutes. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Bhaskar Bharat Sawant, Lead Engineer at Cornerstone Building Brands and an IEEE senior member, explained how automatic SBOMs, SLSA, provenance and deploy-time verification make the secure path the default one.

His stance is practical from the first minute: no theoretical frameworks, no checklist documents nobody reads, and no late-night heroics that depend on someone remembering a manual step.

## CI/CD is trusted most and verified least

Attackers used to aim at SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Now they go upstream, at open-source dependencies, package managers, build systems and artifact repositories. Bhaskar's line about pipelines is pointed: in many organisations CI/CD is the most trusted system and the least verified. His three cautionary tales: SolarWinds was a build system compromise, Log4j was a visibility failure, and the XZ backdoor showed that even long-standing open-source maintainers can become attack vectors. The shared lesson is that you cannot secure a supply chain you cannot see.

## The pieces of defence by default

**SBOMs.** An ingredient list for your application, but only useful if generated automatically on every build and stored with the artifact. Then the Log4j questions (are we affected, where, which versions) have instant answers. He calls them operationally lifesaving rather than paperwork.

**Provenance and attestations.** A chain of custody for each artifact: who built it, when, from which source, with which pipeline, in what environment, with signed attestations as proof. Missing or wrong provenance should make an artifact undeployable, and a system, not a human, should enforce that.

**SLSA as a ladder.** Start where you are: logged builds, then builds from version-controlled scripts, then provenance and signing, eventually hermetic and reproducible builds. He frames it as strengthening each link rather than chasing perfection.

**Hardening controls.** Keyless signing with short-lived CI identities instead of stored private keys, ephemeral runners destroyed after each run, immutable artifacts that cannot be silently swapped, and hermetic builds with no network access that rely on pre-approved pinned components. Reproducible builds mean the same input always gives the same output, so tampering shows up immediately.

**Dependency hygiene.** Pin versions, review new libraries, avoid floating versions and stop automated updates from bypassing review. Dull, and one of the most effective things you can do.

## The before and after

The example team deployed microservices to Kubernetes with a fast but unverified pipeline: developers could push local images to the registry, SBOMs were inconsistent and provenance was not enforced. After adoption, every build was signed automatically, every artifact came with an SBOM, Kubernetes enforced signature verification and dependency metadata was centralised. Security went up and, he stresses, velocity did not drop.

Deployment is the point of no return, so that is where enforcement belongs: a missing signature or provenance means a hard fail, not a warning email. Roll it out in phases: SBOMs first, then signing and provenance in CI, verification in staging, enforcement in production once it is stable.

## The culture shift

His closing argument is about mindset: from "we trust our pipeline" to a pipeline that proves it can be trusted, from hoping dependencies are safe to knowing what you ship, and from security slowing you down to security preventing the emergencies that do.

## Who should watch

Platform and release engineers who own CI/CD and the Kubernetes admission path, and security teams who want a phased SLSA story to bring to developers. If you already enforce signed images at deploy time, the talk is a good sanity check; if you do not, it is a plan.

Title: Emergency response needs predictions before the water arrives
Description: Vivek Karnam of Surge Technology Solutions at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on combining ML, computer vision, NLP, cloud and robots for faster disaster response.
Body:
Most emergency systems still find out how bad a flood is by watching it happen. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Vivek Karnam, Senior QA Automation Engineer at Surge Technology Solutions, proposed an emergency response framework that forecasts the flood extent first, using machine learning, computer vision and NLP on a cloud-native platform, with robots for the places people can't safely go.

It's a conceptual architecture talk built around a simulated scenario rather than a production system, and it says so.

## Legacy response is reactive by design

Vivek opens with two problems. Climate change is making disasters more frequent and more severe, while response systems built on legacy infrastructure and manual coordination can't keep up. And the vulnerabilities are systemic: fragmented data sources that prevent a shared picture, slow information flow, weak prediction and poor coordination across jurisdictions. Decisions wait on humans reading separate feeds under pressure.

## Three models, three kinds of signal

The intelligence layer uses three technologies, each matched to a data type:

- **Machine learning** on historical disaster data to predict likelihood, severity and the best intervention.
- **Visual deep learning** on satellite imagery, drone footage and surveillance feeds to assess damage and spot hazards.
- **NLP** on emergency calls, social media and news to pull actionable signal out of the noise.

The pipeline runs data collection, AI processing, then actionable output: resource deployment, evacuation routes, situational awareness and decision support. Vivek is honest that merging streams with different formats, update rates and reliability is the hard engineering problem.

## Serverless for spikes, Kubernetes for survival

The platform design is cloud-native. Serverless functions handle bursty stream processing without infrastructure overhead, and Kubernetes provides high availability through automatic failover, load balancing and multi-region deployment, so the system keeps running when local infrastructure doesn't. Add elastic scaling for demand spikes, geographic redundancy and data sharing across agencies. A disaster system that goes down in a disaster is just an expensive dashboard.

## A flood, simulated

The worked example is a metropolitan area facing record rainfall and rising rivers. The traditional approach relies on manual gauge readings, weather forecasts and historical flood maps, all interpreted by coordinators. The AI version combines rainfall patterns, soil saturation, river flow and tide schedules to forecast flood extent before the water arrives, uses computer vision to watch for drainage blockages, and mines social posts for real-time flooding reports.

On top come dynamic evacuation planning that updates routes as traffic and flood paths change, a unified dashboard for emergency managers, and ML-driven resource allocation that pre-positions crews before the peak. Geospatial simulation lets managers test interventions, such as opening flood barriers or ordering evacuations, and see the cascading effects.

## Collect less, explain more

The privacy section is the part many such talks skip. Vivek's three principles: data minimization, with automatic purging of personal details once the crisis resolves; algorithmic transparency, with explainable recommendations and decision audit trails for post-crisis review; and community consent and oversight, with the public involved in system design.

Looking ahead, he points to digital twins for stress-testing plans, edge computing for when cloud links fail, federated learning so cities can train shared models without sharing sensitive data, and ground and aerial robots for delivery and rescue where humans can't safely go. The rollout plan: assess capabilities, build data infrastructure, develop models, integrate and simulate, train people, iterate.

## Who should watch

Public-sector technologists, civic and smart-city engineers, and SREs curious how their resilience patterns translate to the physical world. It's a framework overview without production metrics, so watch it for the architecture and the privacy checklist.

Title: Attackers stopped hitting your app and started hitting your pipeline
Description: Gresshma Atluri of Chevron at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on defending CI/CD and third-party supply chains with shift-left, RASP, vendor risk and zero trust.
Body:
A clean repository can still ship malware if the build runner is compromised. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Gresshma Atluri, Cybersecurity Risk Analyst at Chevron, laid out a five-pillar defence framework for software supply chains, drawing on more than eleven years across investment banking, oil and gas, energy and consulting. Her abstract credits these strategies with reducing supply chain attacks by 57%.

The thread through all of it: it is rarely your own code that gets you into trouble. It is the dependencies, the pipelines and the third parties wrapped around it.

## Why the supply chain is the soft spot

A modern application is open-source libraries, third-party SDKs, cloud services and CI/CD tooling, with hundreds of components, many of them transitive dependencies nobody knows they use. Compromise one trusted delivery channel, such as a build pipeline, a popular package or an update mechanism, and you reach hundreds or thousands of organisations at once. She notes that the OWASP Top 10 and the OWASP CI/CD Top 10 now read like a description of the problem: vulnerable components, integrity failures, dependency chain abuse, poisoned pipeline execution and weak identity management.

Her case studies cover each failure shape. SolarWinds was a build system compromise that pushed a malicious update to around 18,000 customers. Log4j showed how a single buried library becomes a global emergency for teams that did not know they ran it. The 2024 CrowdStrike Falcon content update was not an attack, but from a resilience view it behaved like one: one update pipeline, global impact. And the Snowflake incidents showed attackers abusing stolen credentials at a third-party data platform.

## The attack vectors, in plain terms

She names three modern vectors. Dependency confusion: your CI pulls a public package with the same name as your internal one. Typosquatting: a tired developer mistypes one character and installs the wrong library. CI/CD compromise: the source is perfect and the payload is injected at build or packaging time.

Traditional security misses these, she argues, for three reasons: perimeter thinking assumes the inside is safe, checks happen at the end of the lifecycle while attacks happen mid-pipeline, and signing only proves origin, not safety. A signed artifact from a compromised build is still malicious.

## Five pillars

- **Shift-left DevSecOps.** Security in planning, coding and build, with IDE and pre-commit checks, continuous dependency scanning and SBOMs.
- **Secure CI/CD.** Least privilege for build agents and service accounts, secrets in vaults, ephemeral runners destroyed after each job, network segmentation, and a review process for third-party plugins and actions, since each plugin is code running in your pipeline.
- **Advanced detection.** Behavioural monitoring for odd events, like a pipeline suddenly pulling many new dependencies from unfamiliar sources, using SIEM and user and entity behaviour analytics. Runtime application self-protection (RASP) sits inside the app and can block a compromised dependency that tries to run a suspicious command.
- **Vendor risk management.** SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS reviews where relevant, questions about the vendor's own SBOMs, signing and incident notification, and continuous monitoring rather than a one-time questionnaire.
- **Zero trust.** Strong authentication everywhere, every repo, agent and service proving its identity continuously, hardware-anchored signing and micro-segmentation to limit lateral movement.

## A phased roadmap

Foundation (three to six months): dependency scanning, SBOMs for key apps, code signing for critical artifacts, basic vendor assessment, MFA on platforms. Enhancement (six to twelve months): RASP for critical external services, behavioural monitoring of pipelines, SAST, DAST and container scanning, continuous vendor monitoring. Optimisation (ongoing): tune detections, streamline governance, add attestation and provenance tracking inspired by SLSA. Her closing point is that you do not have to choose between agility and security; you just have to design for both on purpose.

## Who should watch

Security engineers responsible for CI/CD, third-party risk teams who want the engineering view, and anyone who still thinks a signature means safe. It is broad rather than deep, which makes it a good map before picking the first control to build.

## Related talks

- [Supply Chain Attacks: Focused on NPM attacks](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2023_Danish_Tariq_Hassan_Khan_Yusufzai_supply_chain_npm_attacks) by Danish Tariq and Hassan Khan Yusufzai, for the dependency confusion and typosquatting details.

Title: More security tools, less clarity; a four-part health index fixes that
Description: Sanjeevani Bhardwaj of Salesforce at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on a four-dimension DevSecOps health framework that tells you whether a pipeline is healthy.
Body:
Pipelines can pass every scan and still be brittle. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Sanjeevani Bhardwaj, Director of Product Management at Salesforce, presented a four-dimension framework for DevSecOps health that answers the one question leadership keeps asking: is our pipeline actually healthy today? Her abstract reports 42% fewer incidents and 2.8 times faster secure development across 15 enterprise implementations.

## The DevSecOps health paradox

Organisations have more tools, more scans and more dashboards than ever, and somehow a less clear picture of their security posture. Security checks boxes, developers push code, operations keeps the lights on, and none of them share a language of health. When everything is measured separately, she says, nothing is understood collectively. Her bottom line: more tooling does not equal more clarity.

Her research found three gaps across industries: no standard way to turn raw scan output into health signals, inconsistent thresholds between teams (one group's acceptable build delay is another's emergency), and no remediation guidance once a problem is found. Is it a config fix, a redesign or a backlog item?

## Four dimensions instead of forty metrics

The framework distils health into four pillars:

- **Platform efficiency.** Pipeline performance, provisioning speed, resource utilisation and reliability. Her reasoning is behavioural: slow builds make developers bypass gates, and teams in permanent firefighting mode never get round to proactive security.
- **Customisation resilience.** How safely you diverge from vendor and community defaults. She calls it one of the most underestimated sources of incidents, with three maturity levels from everything customised and nothing tracked up to clear owners, lifecycle management, deliberate deprecation and real security reviews.
- **Observability.** Application instrumentation, infrastructure telemetry, security event aggregation and trace propagation across microservices, which buys earlier detection, faster investigation, empirical proof that controls work, and post-mortem learning.
- **Security guardrail adherence.** Preventative, detective and corrective controls, where the differentiator is operating them consistently with clear exceptions and feedback loops. When adherence is high, she argues, the secure path becomes the fastest one.

## Measure with layers and stable thresholds

Each dimension needs different data (monitoring tools, config repos, logging and tracing, scanners, policy engines), so collection is layered and automated, with data quality validation. Missing data often reveals infrastructure problems nobody knew about, which is a finding in itself.

Thresholds come in three tiers (baseline, target, excellence) rather than one magic number, and they must stay stable over time so you can tell real improvement from noise.

Industry adaptations get a short tour: healthcare guardrails tied to patient safety, retail's seasonal elasticity and strict payment thresholds, financial services' heavy customisation governance, and manufacturing's legacy systems and long deployment cycles.

## Start with the quick wins

Her rollout: a baseline assessment of all four dimensions, cross-functional health review forums, building skills such as root cause analysis plus DevSecOps health champions, then phased implementation. Platform efficiency and guardrails come first as quick wins; customisation resilience and observability follow because they need more instrumentation. Use the tools you already have, review regularly, and version the framework itself. Next on her list: AI-driven operations, confidential computing, third-party risk and supply chain security.

## Who should watch

Engineering and security leaders who have to report on pipeline health upward, and platform teams tired of arguing about whose dashboard is right. The talk is framework-level; the specific metrics behind each tier are left for you to define.

## Related talks

Title: Adaptive learning for students with disabilities needs DevSecOps first
Description: Raghav Sai Cheedalla of Meta at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on building AI learning pathways for special-needs students that stay private, fair and accessible.
Body:
More than 7.5 million US students receive services under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, and traditional instruction was never built to adapt to each of them. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Raghav Sai Cheedalla, Senior Software Engineer at Meta, showed how adaptive AI can personalise their learning, and argued that in education the pipeline around the model (security, privacy, accessibility and bias checks) matters as much as the model itself.

His core belief, stated at the start: AI in education has to be secure, transparent and equitable if it is going to change lives.

## Three ways a system adapts

Raghav describes three mechanisms for personalised learning. **Modality adaptation** works out whether a student learns best visually, by ear or another way. **Difficulty calibration** keeps tasks in the student's optimal zone so skills come faster. **Scaffolding intelligence** gives hints, examples and explanations at the right moment and fades them out as mastery grows, which he says reduces learned helplessness and builds confidence.

The outcomes he cites are large: skill acquisition up 41%, engagement up 35%, and reading challenges detected as early as seven months. With accessible design such as screen readers and speech-to-text, he reports close to a 50% increase in independent task completion.

## The threat model is a child's file

The security section is what earns this talk its slot at a DevSecOps event. AI in education carries particular risks: exposure of sensitive student data, model inversion attacks, biased outcomes, spoofing of assistive technology interfaces and insider threats. Those risks, he says, define the guardrails you have to build from day one.

His design rules: meet FERPA and GDPR, encrypt the data, use zero-trust security, and continuously monitor both access and model behaviour, so students never have to trade privacy for personalisation. For the data lifecycle: collect minimally, encrypt thoroughly, get consent, keep logs only for a set period, and let families revoke consent.

## Explainable, audited, and still the teacher's call

Trust, in his framing, needs interpretable models, audits, dashboards for teachers and clear explanations for families, so no decision feels like a black box. Bias in educational AI has real consequences, so he wants diverse training data, fairness metrics, routine audits and inclusive design, all built into the development lifecycle as a continuous responsibility rather than a checkbox.

He is clear that AI should not replace educators. Automating grading and content adaptation frees teachers for the emotional connection, context and individual support that only humans give.

## The pipeline that makes it real

The DevSecOps blueprint is concrete: infrastructure as code, automated security and accessibility testing, model signing and tamper detection, continuous monitoring and feedback-driven iteration. In the ML pipeline he adds secrets scanning, FERPA and GDPR checks, fairness tests for bias and drift, and model behaviour monitoring. Compliance checks for FERPA, GDPR, the ADA and WCAG run directly in CI/CD, so compliance becomes proactive instead of reactive.

One lesson stands out for anyone in a regulated sector: treat accessibility issues as severity one. For this audience, an inaccessible feature is a broken feature.

## Who should watch

Engineers building edtech, health or any product where users are vulnerable and regulated, plus accessibility advocates looking for language that lands with platform teams. The numbers come from the speaker's slides rather than a study he walks through, so treat them as his summary of the field.

Title: Banking AI ships at the speed of its data lineage
Description: Vinaya Nadig of Amazon at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on a unified data governance framework that makes AI in banking traceable from source data to decision.
Body:
Banks already run fleets of automated decision-makers, and the thing slowing new ones down is rarely the model; it's proving where the data came from. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Vinaya Nadig, Principal Engineer in Amazon's Last Mile Transportation organization, made the case for a unified AI data governance framework that bakes lineage, quality and access control into the model lifecycle.

Vinaya calls governance the least exciting word in AI, then spends the talk showing why it decides what reaches production.

## Machines decide in milliseconds, reviews take months

The setup starts with 2008: opaque algorithms on incomplete data, long before generative AI. Today AI approves loans, flags fraud and suggests investments in real time. Vinaya cites survey figures that most financial institutions call governance their main barrier to scaling AI, and puts the typical deployment delay from compliance review at six to nine months. The talk's best line sums up the gap: "AI moves at milliseconds, but our controls move at human speed."

The war stories carry it. When GDPR arrived, banks paused projects to trace how customer data flowed into ML pipelines; one European bank found 30 versions of the same data set across models, with no consistent consent tracking. After the LIBOR scandal, regulators asked for lineage in risk models and most banks couldn't produce it.

## Four pillars, one catalogue

Legacy governance tools came from the 1990s warehouse era: batch, monthly reports, Excel exports, blind to model lineage. The proposed framework embeds governance from feature engineering through deployment and monitoring, on four pillars:

- **Metadata management**, a central catalogue for every data asset and model.
- **Lineage tracking**, every transformation and dependency visible end to end.
- **Quality monitoring**, automated checks for drift, anomalies and bias.
- **Cloud-native oversight**, with targets of sub-200 ms query response while tracking thousands of model updates a day.

Security is the other half: role-based access for tens of thousands of users, a full audit trail for every access, integration with enterprise identity. Vinaya flags data-lineage hijacking, tampered upstream data silently corrupting models, as the AI version of the SolarWinds supply-chain lesson. The frameworks on the checklist are GDPR, CCPA, Basel III and BCBS 239, whose demand for accurate, complete and timely risk data is close to impossible without automated lineage.

Vinaya's analogy for the framework: less a gatekeeper, more an air traffic controller for thousands of models.

## A weeks-long trace became one query

The case study is a tier-one global bank, unnamed, that adopted the framework in 2025. Vinaya reported 30% faster AI deployment, 40% stronger audit readiness and full compliance across GDPR, Basel III and BCBS standards. The anecdote that sticks: a regulator asked to trace a fraud model back to its 2019 training data, a job that used to take weeks, and the answer came from one governance query in 0.3 seconds. We only have the speaker's account of the bank, but the shape of the win, lineage as a query instead of an investigation, is the point.

## Governance first, not governance later

The rollout is foundation (cloud-native with governance built in), integration (wire ML lifecycle tools into governance pipelines), automation (continuous bias, drift and compliance monitoring), then scale. Vinaya's comparison is Netflix building observability into its cloud migration from day one.

## Who should watch

Data platform and ML engineers in financial services, risk and compliance technologists, and anyone who has watched a finished model sit in review for a quarter. Engineers outside banking will still recognise the lineage problem; regulated industries just make it louder.

- [Bhanu Maryala: Automating AI Ethics](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Bhanu_Maryala_automating_ai_ethics) builds MLOps-native data governance for generative AI.

Title: Self-service BI works when security is neither too tight nor too loose
Description: Mallikarjun Bussa of Dropbox at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on letting everyone query data with AI-powered BI while least privilege, masking and lineage keep it safe.
Body:
Everyone wants answers from the data, and nobody wants to wait a week for a report. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Mallikarjun Bussa, Lead Business Intelligence Engineer at Dropbox, made the case that self-service BI and DevSecOps belong together: give people direct, AI-assisted access to data, and build the security in from the start so that access does not turn into a leak.

It is a short, plain-spoken talk from someone with 18 years in BI and data, aimed at the balance point rather than at any one tool.

## Too much data, too few answers

Mallikarjun's diagnosis is familiar to anyone who has owned a reporting backlog. Companies have more data than ever and still struggle to answer simple questions, because the data sits in too many systems and silos and every report takes too long. Self-service BI is his answer: marketing, HR, finance and operations open a dashboard and get the insight in minutes instead of filing a ticket and waiting.

The catch is obvious. Hand more people access and you widen the blast radius. That is where he brings in DevSecOps: build security into development, deployment and daily operations instead of patching it on at the end. His analogy: you put the seatbelt on before driving, not after.

## Why most BI projects fail

He cites studies saying 70% of BI projects fail, and the reasons he lists are about people and governance rather than technology: no governance, untrained users, access that is either too open or too restricted, and systems too complicated to use. The 30% that succeed balance security with easy access. Too tight and people route around it; too loose and you end up in an incident review.

## AI makes it easier, which raises the stakes

Natural language querying changes who can ask questions. Instead of SQL, users ask for this month's revenue or for the top reasons for churn, and the system finds patterns, predicts outcomes and guides them. He likens it to a small data analyst sitting on your shoulder. The more powerful the tool, he warns, the more the security matters.

His two examples keep it grounded. A marketing team using AI-powered BI saw campaign reporting drop from hours to minutes, cut costs and improved ROI while staying compliant with privacy law. An HR team used predictive analytics to spot employees likely to leave so it could offer help early, which only worked because the sensitive details were visible to HR alone and every access was audited.

## The controls are simple on purpose

The security baseline he recommends is deliberately unexciting: least-privilege access, masking sensitive data for people who should not see it, multi-factor authentication, and sessions that time out automatically. On top of that sits lineage, the story of where a number came from, what transformed it and who touched it, so that when a leader asks about a figure on a dashboard, you have an answer, and the auditors stay happy.

He closes on culture: leadership support, trained users, clear policies, continuous improvement. His roadmap is four steps (assess the current state, design the architecture with security and automation in mind, enable and train users, monitor and optimise), and he says it works for small teams and large enterprises alike.

## Who should watch

Data platform and analytics engineers rolling out self-service tooling or natural-language querying, and security teams asked to approve it. It is an overview, so treat it as a checklist for the conversation rather than an implementation guide.

Title: AI promises to end the speed-versus-security standoff in DevSecOps
Description: Venkatesh Kata of CGI at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on moving cloud security from manual gates to predictive, AI-driven and eventually autonomous protection.
Body:
Developers want to ship today; security wants to read the diff first. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Venkatesh Kata, Senior Middleware/DevOps Engineer at CGI, argued that AI resolves that old standoff by turning security from a final checkpoint into something predictive and continuous, built into every stage from design to operations.

It is a vision talk from someone with more than twelve years in DevOps and middleware automation: short on demos, long on where the field is going and what teams need to get there.

## The security velocity paradox

Venkatesh calls the core tension the security velocity paradox. Teams want fast releases; security teams want precision and deep analysis. The result is manual gates, slow scanners and security teams buried in thousands of alerts, while compliance delays stall whole releases. With threats evolving faster than ever, he says, you cannot give up either side.

His answer is to change the nature of the work. Instead of reacting to vulnerabilities, AI predicts them. Instead of waiting for reports, it analyses continuously. Instead of humans sifting false positives, it triages, prioritises and fixes common issues automatically. The abstract claims 40% fewer production vulnerabilities and 25% faster deployment cycles for this shift-left approach.

## From procedural automation to adaptive intelligence

He traces the history in four steps: security bolted on at the end, early shift-left that improved timing but stayed manual, tool sprawl that multiplied alerts without context, and now AI that adds prediction and reduces noise.

The technical core is a short tour of the models. Machine learning trained on large code corpora spots vulnerability patterns. Neural networks look at cloud configurations as a whole instead of resource by resource. Reinforcement learning improves decisions with each iteration. Graph neural networks get special attention: attackers do not compromise one resource, they chain misconfigurations to move laterally, and GNNs can find those multi-step attack paths at a scale humans cannot.

That leads to his most practical point: settings that each look fine on their own can be dangerous together, and AI analysis of those interactions is how many organisations find issues they had missed for years.

## Remediation in minutes, explained decisions

Traditional remediation runs scan, ticket, developer rework, review and retest, a loop that can take weeks. AI shortens it by fixing common vulnerabilities automatically while keeping controls in place. Predictive security reads behaviour patterns, commit histories, deployment trends and infrastructure changes to guess where the next vulnerability will appear, which he frames as moving from firefighting to foresight.

He insists AI decisions be explainable, naming adversarial training, differential privacy, federated learning and explainability frameworks such as LIME and SHAP.

## People and the road there

Two closing sections matter for anyone planning adoption. Security engineers need ML basics, ML engineers need security, and cross-functional teams become the default; AI is framed as augmentation, not a threat to jobs. The roadmap: assess maturity, start with high-value pilots, decide build versus buy, measure outcomes, scale what works. The endpoint he sketches is autonomous security operations, with AI agents investigating threats and generating policies while humans own strategy, ethics and the hard calls.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders building a case for AI in their security programme and engineers curious where graph-based cloud analysis is heading. If you want code, a reference architecture or vendor comparisons, this one stays at strategy level.

Title: Blue/green on AWS with Lambda@Edge, cookies and a cache that cooperates
Description: Rayenn Hamrouni of Lenstra at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on cookie-based blue/green routing with Lambda@Edge, SSM and CloudFront caching.
Body:
Rollbacks that take ages are the tax you pay for release days you dread. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Rayenn Hamrouni, DevOps Engineer at the Paris cloud consultancy Lenstra, showed how his team built cookie-based blue/green deployments at the edge with Lambda@Edge, and then made it survive CloudFront caching. Since adopting it, he reports zero production incidents during releases and promotions or rollbacks in under a minute.

This is a field report from a client project, which makes it one of the more hands-on talks of the event.

## The starting point was ordinary

The architecture is textbook AWS: CloudFront serving a static front end from S3 and forwarding API calls to an Application Load Balancer in front of ECS on Fargate. It looked fine on a diagram, but production releases kept causing incidents, rollbacks were slow and painful, and deployments sometimes meant downtime.

Blue/green fixes that in principle: two identical environments, test the new release on green, switch traffic, flip back if it breaks. Rayenn is upfront about the costs too: you run two environments for a while, state and database schema changes need careful thought (his project had no database to manage, which helped), and routing gets more complex.

## Five ways to switch, one that fit

He walks through the AWS options before revealing the one they picked:

- **Route 53**, including weighted routing. Simple and works with any architecture, but DNS caching means the switch is never instant and you cannot route per request.
- **API Gateway**, flexible per header or cookie, but no help for a static S3 front end.
- **ALB weighted target groups**, fast to switch and roll back, again no S3 and less routing logic.
- **CodeDeploy**, a full blue/green workflow with health checks and automatic rollback, at a real setup cost.
- **Lambda@Edge**, functions that run in CloudFront edge locations and can rewrite the origin or S3 prefix before a request hits your backend.

They chose Lambda@Edge for per-user control and low latency.

## Cookies decide who sees which colour

Each colour gets its own ALB and ECS cluster, and the front ends live under different prefixes in the same bucket. A cookie, holding something hard to guess like the release commit hash, pins a user to a version so they do not bounce between releases mid-session. No cookie, or a full reload of the app, assigns the currently active release. A developer override cookie always wins, so QA can force a version in their browser.

The catch: changing the active version in the function code meant redeploying Lambda@Edge to every edge location, which is slow and unpredictable. Iteration two moved the active version to SSM Parameter Store and cached it in memory for a short time, so a switch is a parameter change, not a deploy.

## Make the cache work for you

The best part of the talk is the caching explanation. CloudFront has four hook points (viewer request, origin request, origin response, viewer response) and the cache sits between viewer and origin. If an object is cached, the origin hooks never run, so where you put your logic decides whether blue/green works at all.

Their final flow: at viewer request, a developer cookie injects a unique identifier to bypass the cache. On a miss, origin request routes to the right prefix using the cookie or the active release from SSM. Origin response sets the release cookie when the app loads. Every switch triggers a cache invalidation, so the next load reaches the origin hooks and gets assigned correctly. Getting caching right is half the design here.

He flags what the talk leaves out: coordinating colours across multiple backends and databases, progressive rollout to a subset of users, and CI/CD automation of promotion and rollback.

## Who should watch

Anyone running a CloudFront-fronted app on AWS who wants safer releases without adopting a full deployment platform. If your stack is all API Gateway or ALB, the comparison of options is still useful.

Title: Surgical robots need a data pipeline before they need a smarter arm
Description: Srinivasa SKN Ambati of Anthem at Conf42 Robotics 2025 on a five-layer analytics architecture that feeds clinical robots real-time patient data.
Body:
A surgical robot is only as good as the data reaching it, and hospital data lives in systems that rarely talk to each other. At Conf42 Robotics 2025, Srinivasa SKN Ambati, Engineer Lead at Anthem, laid out an architecture that connects EHRs, IoT devices and robotic telemetry into one pipeline, so clinical robots and the clinicians beside them act on the same near-real-time picture.

The talk is a wide overview, from history to ethics, with a clear technical spine in the middle.

## From reactive care to closed loops

Srinivasa frames the shift as moving from treating illness to predicting and preventing it, powered by a mix of imaging, genomics, wearables, IoT and electronic health records. He sketches the robotics timeline too: PUMA 560 and later the da Vinci surgical system for minimally invasive surgery, robotic rehabilitation in the 2010s, AI-assisted robotics across surgery, pharmacy and hospital logistics by 2020. What comes next, he argues, is an integration era where robotic data feeds patient analytics and the loop closes.

Analytics follows the same arc: descriptive (what happened), predictive (what will happen), and now prescriptive (what to do next).

## Five layers between a sensor and a surgeon

The core of the talk is a five-layer framework:

1. **Acquisition** from robots, EHRs, IoT sensors and medical devices.
2. **Processing** that turns raw feeds into structured, usable records.
3. **AI and analytics**, where statistical and ML models produce insight.
4. **Integration** through APIs and middleware, so the pieces combine.
5. **Presentation**: dashboards, alerts and decision support at the point of care.

In motion, that is Apache Kafka streaming robotic telemetry and patient vitals, Apache Spark processing across a cluster, Hadoop HDFS storing structured and unstructured data, SAS Viya for modelling and forecasting, and HL7 and FHIR for talking to hospital EHR systems. Srinivasa calls the result the digital nervous system of modern healthcare, which is a fair description of a Kafka cluster nobody is allowed to restart.

## The model zoo has a job for everyone

The ML infrastructure runs on an automated lifecycle, a hybrid cloud that keeps sensitive PHI under tighter on-prem control while bursting to the cloud for scale, GPU clusters for imaging and containerized deployment. Models are monitored for drift, fairness and performance, with retraining triggered on drift. The algorithm map is tidy: CNNs for images, RNNs for patient time series, transformers for clinical text and reinforcement learning for robotic control.

Governance is non-negotiable here: HIPAA controls with role-based access, AES-256 encryption and audit logging, GDPR-style consent tracking, MFA, network segmentation and lineage. His one-liner: "trust is the ultimate currency".

## Before, during and after the incision

The clinical walkthrough covers preoperative 3D maps for planning, intraoperative tissue classification and postoperative models that flag complications early. The talk cites a 23% cut in operating times, roughly a third fewer complications, and predictive maintenance on robotic components at over 90% accuracy with downtime down nearly 40%; it doesn't name the studies behind them, so treat them as the speaker's figures.

Srinivasa is candid about the limits: inconsistent data quality, interoperability gaps, compute cost, clinician resistance, algorithmic bias and the need for real-world validation. His advice is to pilot small, adopt HL7 and FHIR, monitor for bias, set up ethics committees, and keep clinicians, engineers and patients in the same conversation.

## Who should watch

Data engineers moving into healthcare, architects designing PHI-heavy pipelines, and robotics teams who need to know what clinical data integration really involves. Expect breadth over depth; it's a map rather than a build guide.

- [Swapna Chimanchodkar: DevOps Pipelines for Clinical AI](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Swapna_Chimanchodkar_clinical_healthcare_ai) deploys real-time sepsis detection at scale.
- [Rajarshi Tarafdar: Human-AI Symbiotic Robotics](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Rajarshi_Tarafdar_human_ai_symbiotic) looks at precision in collaborative robots.
- [Aishwarya Pai: MLOps in Healthcare](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Aishwarya_Pai_mlops_healthcare_scaling) covers deploying and monitoring clinical models.

Title: Stop running migrations as projects and build a migration platform
Description: Meenu Venkataarangam of Recode Solutions at Conf42 DevSecOps 2025 on automating discovery, transformation, orchestration and compliance in migrations.
Body:
The dependency nobody mapped is what usually sinks a migration. At Conf42 DevSecOps 2025, Meenu Venkataarangam, Program Manager at Recode Solutions, showed how an automation framework built on DevSecOps principles turns enterprise migrations from risky one-off projects into a repeatable, compliant capability.

Meenu leads enterprise-scale migration programmes covering data platform modernisation and transformation pipelines, and the talk is a compact, structured overview: why manual migrations fail, the four automation components every framework needs, where security fits, and what comes next.

## Lift and shift was the easy era

Migrations used to be physical-to-virtual moves with minimal transformation. Today they span mainframes still carrying mission-critical workloads, AWS migrations with multi-account governance and containerisation, Hadoop estates being replatformed to cloud-native systems, and consolidation into Snowflake. Hybrid ecosystems, compliance constraints and cross-team alignment all come along. Her verdict on the manual approach: long timelines, coordination failures, security gaps and compliance trouble. It simply cannot keep up.

## Four components, one backbone

Meenu's framework has four building blocks:

- **Discovery tools** that automatically map applications, data flows, security policies and performance baselines. She calls unknown dependencies the biggest cause of migration setbacks, which is why discovery is where automation pays off first.
- **A data transformation engine** in four stages: parallel extraction with minimal load on the source, automated schema conversion and cleansing, real-time reconciliation to stop data drift, and optimised loading with rollback.
- **Workflow orchestration** that sequences dependencies, runs tasks in parallel, handles exceptions and shows progress live, removing the manual hand-offs that cause most delays.
- **Automated testing** to verify accuracy and integrity at every stage.

## Security as a gate, not a sign-off

The DevSecOps part is the security and compliance layer. Encryption, access control and vulnerability scanning live inside the pipeline. Continuous compliance monitors against SOC 2, HIPAA and GDPR in real time. Validation gates stop the process from moving to the next stage until security and compliance criteria pass. The point is to avoid finding out about a GDPR problem the night before cutover.

## Where migration automation is heading

Three trends close the technical part: AI-driven planning that predicts risk from historical migrations, adaptive orchestration that adjusts to live system behaviour, and zero-downtime cutovers through traffic routing and real-time replication. Organisations adopting automation, she reports, finish up to three times faster than manual migrations, with fewer data integrity issues and fewer mid-migration failures.

## Migration as a capability

Her strongest idea is organisational. Move from project-based to platform-based migrations: embed the automation in DevOps pipelines, capture the knowledge in playbooks, and every future migration gets cheaper. Done that way, a migration becomes a reusable capability instead of a painful cyclical event.

## Who should watch

Programme managers and platform leads facing a multi-platform modernisation, and engineers who keep getting pulled into the "just one more migration" project. It is a short, high-level talk; the value is the checklist structure, not deep implementation detail.

## Related talks

- [AI-Powered Mainframe Modernization](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sanath_Chilakala_ai_powered_mainframe) by Sanath Chilakala, on the reliability side of legacy transformation.
