Title: Use JavaScript and AI to take paperwork off clinicians, not patients
Description: Rakesh Kumar Yadav at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on Node.js and React systems that use AI to augment healthcare scheduling, inventory and billing.
Body:
Clinicians are not burning out on patient care; they are burning out on everything around it. That was Rakesh Kumar Yadav's starting point at Conf42 JavaScript 2025. Speaking from 13 years in IT and his current work at a medical college, he argued that a Node.js and React stack with AI behind it can absorb the scheduling, inventory and billing busywork, while people keep the decisions.

The tone is practical and the scope is broad: four impact areas, an architecture, and a phased rollout plan. It is aimed at teams starting such a project rather than those deep into one.

## Augment, don't replace

Rakesh is explicit that the goal is not to replace staff. Updating records, managing billing and juggling disconnected legacy systems eat the time clinicians should spend on judgement and empathy, and the opportunity is to automate the repetitive part.

His case for JavaScript is reach and speed: it runs on the browser, the phone and the tablet in a hospital room without heavy installs, it has a huge module ecosystem for visualisation and API integration, and it is good at the real-time alerts and live dashboards operations depend on. Node.js microservices let scheduling, billing and analytics evolve separately; React keeps the interface consistent. Hospitals can pilot one service and grow from there.

## Four places it pays off

- **Scheduling.** Rosters must balance availability, skill mix, demand, regulation and endless last-minute changes. A JavaScript interface processes the constraints and suggests assignments, with the human scheduler making the final call. Rakesh reports one pilot that cut overtime by 25% and schedule revisions by 40%.
- **Inventory.** React dashboards give every department real-time visibility, with predictive usage forecasts, automated restock alerts and supplier-cost suggestions, replacing fragmented systems and guesswork.
- **Financial workflows.** AI flags missing information, validates billing codes and tidies claims before submission. He reports up to 35% faster claim processing and nearly 18% higher revenue capture, which he attributes to consistency and error prevention rather than magic.
- **The human side.** Less rework means less burnout, and the talk keeps returning to that as the real measure.

The figures come from his own projects; the talk doesn't detail the baselines.

## Architecture and design rules

Interfaces in healthcare must be clear, contextual and safe: visual clarity for complex tasks, actions that match each person's role and moment, and proactive validation that catches errors before they reach a patient. Technically, Rakesh names three pillars: microservices to decouple domains, state management with Redux or the Context API, and real-time sync over WebSockets or server-sent events. For integration, abstraction layers tame inconsistent legacy APIs, event-driven updates keep systems in sync, security means end-to-end encryption, role-based access and audit logs, and lazy loading, pagination and caching keep big datasets responsive.

## A four-phase rollout

Foundation (assess systems, define success metrics, check compliance), development (modular microservices, React components, thorough tests), deployment (a pilot in one department, then refine) and scale. He closes with example use cases: symptom-triage chatbots, real-time vitals dashboards, appointment cancellation forecasting and AI-assisted image labelling for radiology.

## Who should watch

Developers and IT leads in hospitals, clinics or medical colleges planning a first AI-assisted operations tool, and JavaScript teams wondering whether their stack is ready for healthcare. It's a strategy-level talk without code or model details; bring your own compliance team for the hard parts.

Title: CO-STAR prompts turn generic LLMs into e-commerce seller tools
Description: Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy (eBay) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on CO-STAR prompts for personalization, forecasting, pricing, listings and shopping chatbots.
Body:
The model every seller can rent is the same one their competitors rent; the difference is in what you tell it. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy of eBay walked through prompt engineering for e-commerce seller tools, built around the CO-STAR checklist, and applied it to personalization, demand forecasting, dynamic pricing, product listings and conversational commerce, ending with a view of seller tools in 2030.

It's a broad survey talk with a practical core: the prompt patterns are concrete enough to copy, while most of the business numbers are industry figures he cited rather than results from one system.

## CO-STAR is a checklist, not magic

The prompt-writing section is the most reusable part. CO-STAR stands for context, objective, style, tone, audience and response format, and Sureshkumar uses it as a pre-flight check: did you give background, say what outcome you want, set the voice, name who the answer is for, and specify a list, paragraph or JSON?

Around it he adds habits that apply well beyond retail. State constraints up front (length limits, content to avoid). Treat prompting as iteration, not a one-shot. Give the model a role and the context it needs. His before-and-after example: instead of asking what product to recommend, tell the model it's a virtual assistant helping a customer who likes outdoor activities, based on their browsing history, and ask for a recommendation with a reason. And show an example of the output shape you want. The model can only do what you ask, so ask precisely.

## Personalization is context injection

His personalization example is a prompt that carries the customer's recent history: they bought running shoes and have been browsing trail-running gear, so suggest three more products with a one-sentence rationale each. That's the whole technique. The model doesn't know your shopper; the prompt does. He paired this with industry figures on revenue, retention and order value from good personalization.

## Forecasting and pricing want more signals

For demand forecasting, the argument is that AI can mix unstructured signals (social media buzz, weather, news) with historical sales. His sample prompt asks for next month's demand per category given last year's sales data plus recent social media mentions. He cited forecast accuracy rising from around 60% to 80% and stockouts falling by up to 65% in AI-driven setups.

Dynamic pricing applies the same idea: inventory levels, market trends, competitor prices and review sentiment feed a suggested price. Overstocked and slow? Discount. Scarce and in demand? Hold steady or nudge up.

## Listings, reviews and chatbots that sell

Content generation gets the most vivid example: one small business reportedly cut listing creation from 60 minutes per item to 15, and a retailer saw more organic traffic after switching to AI-written listings, because the copy naturally included relevant keywords. AI review summaries turn thousands of reviews into a highlight reel of pros, cons and recurring themes.

On conversational commerce, he's clear that a good shopping bot needs two things: well-designed prompts and access to real-time data such as product details, order status and customer profile. His techniques: inject relevant data into the prompt, use system roles and personas, give the bot a conversational blueprint rather than letting it wing it, and keep feeding the conversation history so context survives. The example of a bot finding a science kit for a 10-year-old niece shows the shift from support desk to sales assistant.

## The 2030 bet

His outlook: natural-language interfaces replacing dashboards, digital twins of individual shoppers, autonomous workflows, AI coworkers for operations teams, and prescriptive analytics that say what to do next, not just what happened. The competitive edge, he argues, is your proprietary data plus a library of prompts refined over time.

## Who should watch

Product managers and engineers building seller-facing or shopper-facing AI features, and anyone who wants a clean, copyable prompt checklist with retail examples. If you're after evaluation methodology or a production architecture, look elsewhere; this one is about framing and use cases.

Title: Regional Keycloak hubs keep global SASE logins close to users
Description: Vivek Koodakkara Shanmughan of Aryaka Networks proposes at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 a regional hub model for Keycloak to scale SASE identity worldwide.
Body:
In a zero trust world, the login page is part of the network path, and a slow one is an outage with extra steps. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Vivek Koodakkara Shanmughan, Senior Engineering Manager at Aryaka Networks, laid out a regional hub model for Keycloak: autonomous identity clusters in each major region, kept in step with each other, so users authenticate near where they are.

The talk is framed as a design proposal ("we could") rather than a production war story, and it is honest about the trade-offs.

## Identity is the new perimeter

Shanmughan starts from the end of the castle-and-moat model. With remote workers, apps spread across cloud and edge, and regional regulation, the network perimeter is gone, and SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) merges networking and security into a cloud-delivered service built on zero trust. In that model, identity is the passport: every access decision hangs on who you are, on what device, under what conditions.

His analogy is airports. Instead of routing every traveller through one central hub, you check in and clear security locally.

## Why one central IdP hurts

Centralised identity looks tidy on a diagram and causes four problems in practice. Latency: he puts a Singapore user authenticating against a US-based identity provider at 200 to 300 milliseconds of delay per request. Availability: one outage locks out users worldwide. Data sovereignty: GDPR and CCPA can require identity data to be processed and stored locally. And throughput: a central IAM system may simply not be built for global traffic.

## A hub per region, synchronised

The proposal is one autonomous Keycloak cluster per major region (for example the Americas, EMEA and APAC), each authenticating local users on its own. A hub has a standard shape: the Keycloak cluster for authentication and SSO, a database for users and configuration, a load balancer across Keycloak nodes, directory synchronisation with corporate accounts, and an observability layer.

Keycloak fits because it is open source and Kubernetes-native, supports multi-tenancy through realms, speaks OIDC, SAML and WebAuthn, and can be extended through SPIs and event listeners.

Placement is driven by data: map where users are, align hubs with existing SASE points of presence, group regions with similar compliance rules, pick cloud regions with strong service, and test latency from real user locations. He suggests starting with three or four hubs. Sync goes through shared directories such as AD or LDAP or database replication, with GitOps workflows for policy, cross-cluster token validation, Infinispan distributed caches or token exchange between hubs.

## Automate it or don't do it

Several Keycloak clusters by hand is a recipe for drift, so automation carries the design: Keycloak configuration as code through GitOps, the Keycloak Operator on Kubernetes, canary rollouts and per-region observability of login flows, latency and errors. He lists the costs too: data consistency across regions (define authoritative sources and conflict rules), more operational complexity, tricky failover (health-aware global load balancers, tested regularly), higher spend and harder compliance.

His suggested first step is modest: map your users, find the hotspots, and pilot a two-region deployment.

## Who should watch

Identity and platform engineers running Keycloak for users on more than one continent, and anyone designing zero trust access who has only planned for one region. If you want Keycloak 101, start with the docs; this assumes you know realms and clients.

Title: RLHF at scale is a networking and data problem on Kubernetes
Description: Jyotirmoy Sundi, CTO of Votal.ai, maps at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 how RLHF training runs across multi-GPU Kubernetes clusters, and where it breaks.
Body:
The models get the headlines, but the hard parts of reinforcement learning from human feedback are moving weights between GPUs fast enough and getting enough good human labels. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Jyotirmoy Sundi, co-founder and CTO of Votal.ai, walked through how RLHF systems run on multi-GPU Kubernetes clusters, which frameworks people reach for, and where the bottlenecks really are.

It is a survey talk with a practitioner's checklist, not a code walkthrough. Good as a map if you are about to stand up your first distributed training cluster.

## From MDPs to transformers

Sundi starts with the theory in one breath: classic RL comes from Markov decision processes, an agent maximising cumulative reward step by step. Swap the policy for a transformer and the same loop can learn far richer functions over text, images, audio and video. Policy optimisation algorithms such as PPO, GRPO and DDPO, plus actor-critic setups, do the learning; which one wins depends on your data and how you define the reward.

He spends real time on that last point. A sloppy reward function invites reward hacking, where the model finds a way to score well that you didn't intend. If you remember one warning from the talk, make it that one.

## Data parallel, model parallel, and the checkpoint that saves your week

On the distributed side, the two shapes are data parallelism (the same model on every pod, the data split across them, gradients gathered by a coordinating server and sent back) and model parallelism for models too large for one GPU, where the network itself is split across pods. Training runs can take weeks, so checkpointing is not optional: a pod failure at 50% should resume from the last checkpoint, not from zero.

Kubernetes handles the orchestration, resource management and failure recovery, plus the state for replay buffers and terabytes of training data. It doesn't do GPUs out of the box: you install NVIDIA's device plugins and typically request four, sometimes eight, GPUs per pod.

## The network is the bottleneck you pay for

Sundi keeps returning to communication overhead. Every step means sharing policy or weight parameters across the cluster, and slow links turn into idle GPUs and a bigger bill. NVLink for GPU-to-GPU traffic and NVIDIA's NCCL library for collective communication are the baseline. On frameworks he names IMPALA, Ray, Lightning AI, DeepSpeed (for models that must be split), PyTorch DDP, Ray Train from Anyscale, and Kubeflow's PyTorch and TensorFlow job operators.

In production, watch GPU utilisation closely: badly sharded data leaves some GPUs underused while others work flat out, and finding the right distribution takes trial and error. He also recommends circuit breakers for unstable policies and robust failover, so one bad pod doesn't sink the run.

## Human feedback is the golden dataset

The bigger long-term constraint, in his view, is labels. Supervised fine-tuning depends on expert-made data (doctors, physicians, maths olympiad winners), and feedback loops can take months. Labelling companies such as Scale AI help, but he expects the next two to three years to be about collecting specialised human data. His bets for easing it: reinforcement fine-tuning, where a good reward function lets the model generate new training data from a small seed; feedback captured inside products; and federated RLHF that learns on edge devices and syncs weights centrally.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers asked to run RLHF or fine-tuning on Kubernetes, and infra folks who want to know why the ML team keeps asking for faster interconnects. Researchers after new algorithms won't find them here.

Title: Platforms should ship LLM-powered observability built in
Description: Srinivas Pagadala Sekar of Karsun Solutions argues at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 that PaaS providers should offer LLM-driven diagnostics as a native service.
Body:
A dashboard that says "latency is high" during an outage is a smoke alarm with no map of the building. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Srinivas Pagadala Sekar, Senior Site Reliability Manager at Karsun Solutions, made the case that platform-as-a-service providers should ship LLM-driven observability as part of the platform, so every tenant gets correlated, explained incidents without building their own AI stack.

It is a framework talk drawn from 14 years in cloud and SRE work: the argument, the implementation steps and, usefully, how to prove it works before you roll it out.

## Alerts without context slow recovery

Sekar's starting point will be familiar to anyone on call. Microservices on a PaaS fail in tangled ways: one service falters, a cascade follows, and the SRE team gets a flood of alarms with no correlation. Pods scale in and out within seconds and IPs change, so yesterday's troubleshooting assumptions stop holding. He walks through examples from fintech trading, healthcare records and e-commerce on a busy sale day to show how small changes ripple.

Observability grew from CPU graphs to the three pillars of metrics, logs and traces, but those still need a human to stitch them together. His claim is that LLMs can do the stitching: link a recent deployment, a memory spike in one service and an odd error pattern in another, then suggest the rollback or scale-up.

## Start with the alerts you already have

The implementation path is incremental. Feed existing monitoring signals to the model and enrich them with context so alerts read like narratives. Fine-tune on your own telemetry, deployment history and failure patterns. Add predictive checks for failing nodes and bottlenecks. Give engineers a chat interface to ask why latency is spiking. Correlate apparently unrelated signals (API errors, pod churn, config changes) before they cascade.

The technical framework below that is plain engineering: ingest and normalise metrics, logs, traces and CI/CD events; pick and tune models for platform workloads; keep inference latency low; deliver different outputs to SREs, developers and managers; and expose it all through APIs and the platform console. He also suggests storing cleaned telemetry in vector databases as the baseline the model works from.

## Prove it before you scale it

The section worth the watch is the evaluation method. Build a staging environment that mimics production, multi-tenant Kubernetes and service mesh included, then inject pod crashes, cascading degradation and traffic surges. Run your current stack and the LLM-enhanced one through the same failures. Measure MTTD, MTTR, false positives and root-cause accuracy. Survey the SREs on alert clarity and trust. Then apply statistical tests, A/B comparisons and effect sizes so the improvement isn't one lucky incident. That is the bar more AIOps pitches should clear.

He pairs it with guardrails: collect only the telemetry you need, anonymise, comply with HIPAA and GDPR, keep critical remediation human-verified, and make outputs explainable so engineers trust them.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running a multi-tenant PaaS, and SRE leads evaluating AI-assisted incident tooling who want a way to test vendor claims. If you want a demo of a specific product, this talk doesn't name one.

## Related talks

- Birol Yildiz on the noise half of the problem: [AIOps: New Approaches to Reduce Alert Noise](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Birol_Yildiz_aiops_alert_noise).
- Nishanth Vepachedu takes it agentic in [Scaling Microservices Observability with Agentic LLMs](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Nishanth_Vepachedu_microservices_observability_llms).
- When the telemetry itself misleads: David McNerney and Daniel Raskin in [When the Stack Lies: Finding Root Cause in Distributed Systems](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2026_David_McNerney_Daniel_Raskin_root_cause_distributed_systems).

Title: Fast campaign dashboards start with small, honest payloads
Description: Sruthi Erra Hareram at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on a cross-cloud analytics pipeline that feeds a React dashboard built for speed and trust.
Body:
Two dashboards that disagree do more damage than one slow dashboard: people stop trusting both. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Sruthi Erra Hareram walked through an end-to-end campaign analytics stack, from a partitioned data lake and Azure Databricks to a React front end, built around one goal: shrink the distance between a marketer's question and a trustworthy answer.

The talk covers the whole path rather than one layer, which is its strength. The JavaScript part only works because of decisions made three hops upstream.

## Every layer optimises for something different

Sruthi's pipeline runs ingest, transform, serve, visualise, and she gives each stage one job. Storage is about cost and durability: a lake partitioned by day and source, lifecycle rules that push cold data to cheaper tiers without breaking lineage, and manifest files that surface missing partitions and record-count mismatches early. Orchestration, here Azure Data Factory, runs parameterised batch and micro-batch pipelines so one pattern covers many feeds, and its alerts name the failing step, the affected partition and a link to the run.

Compute in Azure Databricks owns correctness: columnar tables with constrained schema evolution, deterministic transforms, and attribution and deduplication done there, not in the browser. Aggregates come out at the grain product managers actually use, like daily by geography, channel and creative. Row-level security is applied at query time from identity claims. The serving API caps and compresses payloads and keeps short caches on hot endpoints so a traffic surge doesn't stampede downstream systems.

Why cross-cloud at all? Storage sits where the economics are best, transformation where the managed Spark and governance are, and because the contract to the front end stays fixed, workloads can move later without rewriting the product.

## React patterns for big data on ordinary laptops

On the front end, data state and presentation stay separate. Chart components share one grammar for titles, axes and empty states. Filters for date, geography, channel and creative live in a central store with memoised selectors. Requests carry authentication, retry carefully and are cancelled when the user changes direction. The interface responds to a filter change immediately and the data fills in a moment later, so every click feels acknowledged.

For large data sets: virtualise long tables, send a summary first and fetch detail on intent, run small roll-ups in a Web Worker to keep the main thread free, and debounce rapid filter changes so only the final intent triggers work. Existing Power BI reports are embedded with single sign-on and two-way filter sync, so nobody has to leave the app.

## Charts should state the conclusion

The storytelling advice is the part analysts will steal. A chart title should state the finding, not the category, with benchmarks for context and annotations tying movements to business decisions. Views differ by role: executives get a compact ROI and pacing summary, campaign managers a tactical cross-channel view with a next step, analysts the freedom to slice and export, all from one source of truth.

Performance is treated as a promise: code splitting, server and browser caches with lifetimes matched to data freshness, server-side pagination with prefetch, and tracking of time to interactive, first contentful paint and p95 API latency, with regressions handled as product bugs.

Her closing answers are crisp. Keep joins and heavy aggregation on the server and give the worker only small roll-ups. Enforce tenant filters on the server, never trust client-provided ones.

## Who should watch

Front-end engineers building analytics products, data engineers who hand them APIs, and anyone whose dashboards are slow or contradict each other. It is architecture-level, with no code on screen, but the server-versus-browser split is a checklist you can apply directly.

Title: Insurance underwriting in seconds, not weeks, on Kubernetes
Description: Gurucharann Visagamurthy of Humana shows at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 how Kubernetes-native pipelines move insurance underwriting and enrollment to real time.
Body:
If a fintech app can approve a loan in seconds, why does buying insurance still involve a PDF, a scanner and a week of silence? At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Gurucharann Visagamurthy, Lead Digital Product Owner at Humana with 16 years in healthcare, argued that insurers who keep underwriting on monoliths and paperwork are handing the market to cloud-native insurtechs, and walked through what a Kubernetes-native underwriting and enrollment flow looks like.

This is a strategy-level talk from the product side: patterns, outcomes and anonymised case studies rather than manifests and code.

## The pain is measured in days

Visagamurthy lists the familiar failures. Underwriting cycles of five to 15 days. Up to 30% of applications delayed or rejected for missing information. Human underwriters buried in repetitive checks instead of the hard cases. Applicants who give up halfway, and compliance work that is manual and reactive. Each one is an automation, integration or scaling problem, which is his argument for cloud native.

## Underwriting as a pipeline

The core idea is to treat underwriting as a data pipeline. Credit scores, medical history, pharmacy data, lifestyle attributes and even wearable data feed a Kubernetes cluster where models score risk and return approve, deny or review. He claims the cycle can shrink to under 60 seconds and underwriting time by 95% or more, with monitoring for bias, compliance breaches and data drift running alongside.

Kubernetes earns its place on the boring days and the busy ones. Open enrollment is the stress test: when thousands of users log in at once, autoscaling absorbs it; when a component dies, it restarts; and every deployment through the pipeline leaves an audit trail regulators can read.

## Enrollment is where customers drop out

Underwriting is half the journey. Enrollment is where people finish or abandon, so the talk's second half is about removing friction: automated ID verification against government and other data sources, e-signatures inside the workflow, and validation APIs that catch errors before submission. Visagamurthy credits this with up to 70% fewer errors.

The integration patterns are standard and sensible: an API gateway in front of internal engines and external data sources, Kafka-style events so a changed medical score mid-application updates the decision, hybrid cloud to keep sensitive data on-prem, and zero trust for every call.

## Automation with an exception desk

He is clear that automation doesn't remove underwriters. In his model about 85% of applications go straight through, and the edge cases and high-risk profiles go to expert review, which also reassures regulators that a human is still in the loop.

The two case studies are anonymised. Insurer A cut underwriting from five days to 45 seconds for 85% of applications, with completion rates up 40% and satisfaction up 35%. Insurer B fixed enrollment, cutting manual overhead by 60% and smoothing broker relationships.

## Who should watch

Architects and product owners in insurance or healthcare who need the business case for re-platforming, and engineers who want to know which parts of a regulated workflow can be automated safely. If you want Helm charts and code, look elsewhere; this is the "why" and the shape.

Title: What the pandemic taught Zensar about automating partner supply chains
Description: Kunal Dixit (Zensar Technologies) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on order automation, direct shipping and remote field operations built during COVID.
Body:
"Plan A always worked" is a fine strategy until a lockdown closes the office, the warehouse and the customer site in the same week. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Kunal Dixit, a delivery manager at Zensar Technologies, told the story of how partner and field automation kept a supply chain running through COVID, and why the remote-first changes outlived the crisis.

This is a case-study talk from the delivery side, light on code and heavy on what was changed, in what order, and what it bought.

## What broke first

Kunal's list of pandemic failure points is a useful audit for any operations team. Paper-based order processing, email coordination and spreadsheet tracking all became bottlenecks the moment people worked remotely. Field operations, equipment installation and partner training needed physical presence that lockdowns made impossible. Inventory visibility was limited, so information arrived late and decisions arrived later. And a centralised, inflexible network meant one failing node could take the environment down. In his words, there was no plan B because plan A always worked.

## Automate the order, end to end

The first fix was splitting order handling into three automated stages. Capture: partners submit orders through API integration, removing manual data entry. Processing: a new middleware layer validates the order, checks inventory and routing options, without a human in the loop. Fulfilment: shipping is triggered, systems are updated on delivery status, and notifications go out in real time. He described orders that used to take days now taking hours, with remote teams keeping full operational capability.

## Ship direct, track everything

Next came distribution. Rather than routing equipment through a central warehouse, Zensar shipped directly to partner locations, using GPS and IoT sensors for real-time shipment visibility and automated notifications at every milestone (dispatch, transit, delivery). Exceptions could be handled proactively instead of discovered by an angry phone call. Internal teams stopped babysitting shipments and went back to strategic work.

## Field work without the field

The third piece is the one that stuck: technicians configured equipment remotely using automated configuration templates, digital audits kept compliance documentation paperless, and a virtual training platform gave partners on-demand modules with automated assessment of knowledge gaps. Expensive site visits disappeared from many workflows, and Kunal says the shift to remote operations became permanent, with cost savings lasting beyond the crisis.

## Resilience is a design choice

The architectural lesson is explicit. Zensar's resilient design framework rests on modular, component-based architecture that can be reconfigured or replaced quickly, automated health monitoring, simulation testing of crisis scenarios, and comprehensive documentation so knowledge survives staffing disruption. Kunal cited a chart showing organisations with mature automation recovering 15 times faster than traditional peers, and real-time inventory visibility cutting stockouts by 60%. His takeaway: recovery speed correlates directly with digital maturity, and that maturity came from deliberate choices, not luck.

His practical sequence: start with the most painful high-friction process, make the architecture modular, integrate the partner ecosystem, invest in training, then test and iterate regularly. The next disruption, he closes, is inevitable; the question is whether you're ready.

## Who should watch

Delivery and operations leaders in hardware or partner-driven businesses, and architects who need a concrete before-and-after story to justify modularity and automated monitoring. Engineers looking for implementation detail on the middleware itself won't find it here.

Title: LLMs that audit healthcare data pipelines, not just generate text
Description: Manikesh Iruku of Amazon presents at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 an LLM framework that audits EHR pipelines with hierarchical, chain-of-thought prompts.
Body:
A broken join in a healthcare ETL job doesn't throw an exception; it quietly drops a medication from a safety alert. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Manikesh Iruku, Business Intelligence Engineer at Amazon, presented research on using LLMs to audit electronic health record (EHR) pipelines for exactly those silent, semantic errors, using a layered prompting strategy rather than a bigger model.

It is a research presentation: architecture, method and reported results, with no live demo.

## Manual audits see a third of the logic

Hospitals move EHR records, lab results, imaging, prescriptions and admin data through systems such as Epic and Cerner, and every hop is a transformation someone has to trust. Iruku cites research that manual audits examine only 35% of transformation logic and catch 52% of known pipeline issues in controlled settings. Rule-based checks scale better but mostly validate structure and syntax. Neither reliably catches the expensive kind of bug: logic that runs fine but contradicts a clinical guideline or business rule.

## Three tiers of prompts

The framework's core is a prompt hierarchy:

- **Structural prompts** look at SQL syntax, ETL connectivity and data type consistency.
- **Semantic prompts** check clinical appropriateness: guideline adherence, temporal logic, cross-domain consistency.
- **Comparative prompts** compare components across versions and reconcile between systems.

Chain-of-thought workflows break each audit into steps that mirror how an expert reviewer reasons, while keeping track of dependencies across domains. Compared with standard prompting, he reports a 42% improvement in error detection sensitivity and a 35% cut in false positives.

Around the prompts sit five components: read-only data extraction from existing systems, a prompt generation engine fed with guidelines and organisation rules, an LLM orchestration service, an interpretation module that turns outputs into findings, and an audit management system that tracks remediation.

## The reported results

Iruku's numbers: an 87% detection rate against 52% for manual audits and 63% for rule-based systems; annual audit effort down 70%, from 2,400 to 720 hours; pipeline coverage up from 35% to 92%; and around $340,000 in annual savings. On complex logic specifically, 94% accuracy versus 34% for manual review. The figure that stuck with me is guideline update lag, down from 47 days with rule-based systems to two, which matters when a protocol changes and the pipeline should follow.

The case studies are concrete about the bug types: incomplete medication reconciliation logic feeding patient safety alerts, a sepsis bundle dashboard whose calculations didn't match its specification, and heart failure protocols that hadn't caught up with updated AHA/ACC guidelines.

## Humans still sign off

He closes on governance: human oversight with clear responsibility, transparency about model limits, equity in pipeline coverage, and HIPAA-compliant privacy assessments. The quickest return, in his account, came from running the audits inside CI/CD. Next steps include streaming audits, domain fine-tuning and shift-left checks at design time.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and analytics leads in healthcare or any regulated industry, and anyone who suspects their "data quality" checks are really schema checks. The Kubernetes angle is light, so platform folks hunting for cluster detail can skip it.

Title: Cloud telematics moves fleets from fixing breakdowns to foreseeing them
Description: Preeti Sali (Ford Motor Company) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on telematics architecture, hybrid connectivity, predictive maintenance and routing.
Body:
A fleet manager used to find out a brake was failing when the truck stopped on the hard shoulder. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Preeti Sali, a senior technical program manager at Ford Motor Company, walked through how cloud-based telematics changes that: every vehicle becomes a data source, the cloud learns what normal looks like, and maintenance, routing and driver coaching shift from reactive to predictive.

It's an overview talk, not a prompt-engineering talk despite the event; think of it as a well-organised map of the connected-fleet stack from someone who leads that kind of platform work.

## The stack, end to end

Preeti lays out the architecture in layers. IoT modules in each vehicle track performance, GPS and environmental data. That data is encrypted, authenticated and verified end to end. Connectivity is hybrid: cellular for fast, low-latency updates in cities, satellite for rural highways, deserts and remote mining sites, with algorithms choosing the network by signal strength and cost so no vehicle goes dark. In the cloud, scalable analytics engines apply machine learning to detect anomalies and optimise operations.

The point she keeps returning to: none of the clever analytics matter if the data stops flowing. Connectivity is the unglamorous foundation.

## Predictive maintenance is a cultural shift

The headline use case is predictive maintenance. Sensors on engines, brakes and other components stream performance data; cloud models learn the normal operating envelope and flag deviations early. She cited maintenance cost reductions of up to 25%, fewer emergency repairs and longer vehicle life. Her phrase for it is a shift from fixing to foreseeing, which is a decent summary of the whole talk.

## Routes and drivers are where the fuel goes

Intelligent routing combines real-time traffic, weather and load parameters, reroutes around congestion or storms, and balances loads. Preeti cited fuel savings of up to 20%, with emissions falling alongside cost.

Driver behaviour gets its own section, and it's the most human one. Telematics tracks speeding, harsh braking and idling, and feeds that back to drivers in real time. The results she quoted: 30% fewer harsh driving incidents, a 40% improvement in safety scores and 15% longer vehicle life. Gamification and coaching (dashboards, recognition, incentives) turn the data into a feedback loop rather than surveillance. Nobody enjoys being told they brake like a cartoon character, but a leaderboard helps.

## One dashboard, then digital twins

The operations dashboard pulls it together: live location, health status and ETA for every vehicle, alerts when maintenance is due or performance drifts, and automated reporting. Overall, she cited 15% total cost savings and 20% better utilisation for organisations running cloud telematics.

Her look ahead covers four ideas: edge computing to process data in the vehicle and cut latency, more autonomous AI decision-making, V2X (vehicle-to-everything) communication for coordinated traffic flow, and digital twins of whole fleets to simulate routes, maintenance strategies and energy use before trying them for real.

## Who should watch

Engineers and product people new to fleet or mobility platforms who want the whole architecture in one sitting, and IoT folks from other industries curious how hybrid connectivity and predictive maintenance fit together in vehicles. If you already run a telematics platform, it will confirm more than it surprises; the related talks go deeper into specific layers.

Title: eBPF gives Kubernetes observability from inside the kernel
Description: Alejandro Mercado, DevOps Lead at Michael Page, explains at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 why eBPF sits under Kubernetes networking, security and observability.
Body:
Kubernetes hides the Linux kernel from you on purpose, which is great right up until the problem lives in the kernel. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Alejandro Mercado, DevOps Lead at Michael Page, made the case that eBPF is how you get that visibility back: small sandboxed programs attached to kernel events, reporting what really happens to your pods.

This is an introduction, and a good one. If you've heard "eBPF" in every other CNCF talk and nodded along, this is the half hour that explains why.

## Observability is a data problem first

Mercado opens with a line he picked up at another conference: observability is a data problem. Getting the data, cleaning it and acting on it in real time is the hard part, and the closer you collect it to the source, the less you have to guess. For Kubernetes, the source is the kernel, because everything the orchestrator does rests on Linux primitives underneath.

## User space pays a toll on every syscall

The middle of the talk is a clear tour of kernel space versus user space. Applications can't touch hardware; they ask the kernel through system calls, and each call costs hundreds to thousands of CPU cycles because of the mode switch. So when an application needs a new kernel-level capability (a protocol, a load-balancing algorithm, traffic redirection for sidecars) there are two bad options: ship all the data up to user space and pay for it, or get the feature into the kernel itself.

Mercado's slides include a cartoon about the second path: the kernel is run by committee, a change can take a year, and by the time it ships your application may no longer need it. eBPF is the third option. You write a constrained program, usually in C (Rust is possible), load it into the kernel's virtual machine, and attach it to kprobes, tracepoints, network events or cgroups. A feature can arrive in days instead of a release cycle.

## Is it dangerous? Only as dangerous as you are

He takes the obvious question head on. eBPF runs in a privileged context, and loading programs needs admin rights by default, which keeps casual misuse out. You still could attach a program to every kernel function or drop all network traffic, he notes, but the sandbox and verifier make the kernel harder to crash by accident, not easier. The responsibility sits with whoever writes the program.

## Where you are already using it

The tools list is the useful bit for anyone mapping their own stack: Cilium for networking and its service mesh, Kuma, Falco, Tetragon and Tracee for runtime security, Pixie for application visibility, Weave Scope tracking TCP connections between containers. He also walks through concrete use cases: per-pod and per-container network statistics via cgroup-attached programs, Landlock LSM letting unprivileged apps sandbox themselves, and auditing `kubectl exec` sessions down to the exact commands typed.

His closing pitch pairs eBPF with OpenTelemetry. OpenTelemetry sees the application layers, eBPF sees the low layers, and correlating the two gives you both sides of the same incident.

## Who should watch

Platform and SRE folks who run Cilium or Falco without quite knowing what's under them, and anyone deciding whether eBPF-based tooling belongs in their cluster. Kernel hackers already writing BPF programs can skip it. Mercado ends with a reading list: the BCC tools, Brendan Gregg's talks, the Cilium project and the eBPF Foundation.

## Related talks

- Pranshu Srivastava goes deeper on the networking side in [The Power of Cilium For eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pranshu_Srivastava_cilium_ebpf_networking).
- Shahar Azulay's [True Kubernetes Observability with eBPF](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2023_Shahar_Azulay_kubernetes_observability_ebpf) applies the same idea to tracing applications without code changes.
- For the security tools Mercado lists, Thomas Labarussias shows [Use Falco and eBPF to protect your applications](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2023_Thomas_Labarussias_falco_ebpf_protect_applications).

Title: An AI copilot for Agile should spot risk early and leave decisions to people
Description: Hema Yalamancheli (Tyler Technologies) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on AI for sprint forecasting, hidden dependencies and burnout signals, with guardrails.
Body:
Sprints rarely fail on day one; they fail on day eight, when a dependency nobody mapped finally shows up. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Hema Yalamancheli, a release train engineer and Agile coach at Tyler Technologies, made the case for AI as a copilot to Agile teams: forecast capacity better, surface dependencies and technical debt earlier, catch burnout before it lands, and keep every final call with humans.

It's a short talk from someone who runs release trains for a living, so the problems are the familiar ones rather than hypothetical, and the AI is framed as decision support, not a robot Scrum Master.

## The reality gap

Hema starts with the gap every enterprise Agile team knows: the plan says one thing, delivery says another. Her list of pain points is a retro board in miniature: sprint overruns and missed commitments, inaccurate estimates, hidden dependencies that surface late, and resource allocation that doesn't match the work.

Her pitch is that AI can do more than automate tasks around this. Used well, it becomes a planning partner that augments the humans making delivery decisions.

## Forecast from your own history

The planning half of the talk is about capacity modelling. Machine learning looks at historic velocity, seasonal productivity patterns, skill alignment and past success rates, and helps refine the backlog and forecast what a sprint can really hold. She adds multi-dimensional prioritisation (business value, technical dependencies, risk and resource availability weighed together) and AI-assisted estimation and dependency mapping to shorten planning without losing accuracy.

The detail that matters most to her: graph-based backlog intelligence. AI can analyse relationships between user stories and spot cross-team dependencies that a human planner misses. The same lens applies to technical debt, which in her experience teams often discover only after it has quietly shaped several sprints.

## Read the team, carefully

The riskier half is real-time risk detection. Hema describes NLP over stand-up notes, comments and team communication to detect sentiment shifts and collaboration problems, velocity tracking to spot declining trends sprint over sprint, and meeting-participation signals. She's candid that poor communication is the most common Agile dysfunction she sees, and half-jokingly calls the AI a spy, helper or coordinator.

Burnout prevention is the most humane use case in the talk: if one person carried a heavy load this sprint and is planned for the same next sprint, the system flags it before they break.

## Guardrails are part of the design

This is where the talk earns its title. Monitoring a team's chat and meetings is exactly the kind of thing that destroys trust if done carelessly, and Hema treats it that way. Her responsible-adoption rules: document how AI recommendations are generated so teams can challenge them; set ethical boundaries around team monitoring to protect privacy; require explainable suggestions; and keep humans in the loop, with final decisions staying with the team. Successful integration, she argues, should strengthen psychological safety, not erode it.

Her playbook is four steps: assess the current state, start with pilot projects, train and enable teams, then iterate.

## Who should watch

Release train engineers, Scrum Masters and delivery leads who want a structured list of where AI can help planning, and engineering managers thinking about the ethics of team analytics before they buy a tool that does it. It's conceptual rather than a tool demo, so don't expect a working setup at the end.

Title: A swarm of specialist LLM agents reads the market on Kubernetes
Description: Kiran Purushotham of JPMorgan Chase presents SAFSO at Conf42 Kube Native 2025, a swarm of specialist LLM agents with a consensus oracle and federated learning.
Body:
One generalist model reading every headline, tweet and SEC filing is a bottleneck with a good vocabulary. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Kiran Purushotham, Executive Director and Head of Architecture at JPMorgan Chase, presented a different shape: a swarm of specialist LLM agents on Kubernetes, each reading one kind of source, with a consensus layer deciding what the market is telling you.

The system is called the Self-Adapting Financial Sentiment Oracle (SAFSO). The talk is short and dense, closer to an architecture briefing than a tutorial, and it leans on results the speaker reports from the system.

## Most market data is text, and text is slow

Purushotham starts with the scale problem: he puts the daily volume of market data at 2.5 quintillion bytes, around 80% of it unstructured (news, social chatter, analyst reports, filings). Traditional models can't keep up with the volume or the variety, and in trading the latency of analysis is the cost: a signal you find after the move is trivia.

## Specialists plus a referee

SAFSO pairs two models. FinBERT extracts domain-specific sentiment from financial texts such as earnings calls; RoBERTa-large adds broader context from news and social media. Around them sit specialist agents: news agents on breaking stories and press releases, social media agents on investor conversations, regulatory agents parsing filings, and market data agents tying sentiment to price action and order flow.

The interesting piece is the referee. A consensus oracle uses a 16-head attention mechanism to weigh the agents' predictions, scores its own confidence and recalibrates as conditions shift. Think of it as an ensemble that learns which expert to trust this week.

He reports the swarm handling about 1,200 documents a second with end-to-end latency from ingestion to insight measured in milliseconds, even during volatile markets.

## Federated learning so banks can share without sharing

Data privacy is the other half of the design. Institutions train locally on private data and send only encrypted model weights to a central orchestrator, using homomorphic encryption. Purushotham says the setup ran across 47 financial institutions and improved accuracy by almost 15% compared with isolated models, while keeping raw data where regulators want it.

The reported performance numbers are bold: about 95% directional accuracy, 87% magnitude accuracy, 21% annualised returns over five years of backtesting and a Sharpe ratio of 1.67. Treat them as the speaker's results; the talk doesn't go into the backtest methodology. He also describes an early-warning use, flagging market stress events up to 36 hours ahead and spotting coordinated manipulation campaigns on social media.

## Kubernetes is the boring, essential part

The platform layer is deliberately standard: each agent in a lightweight container, HPA for surges, Istio for service-to-service traffic, Prometheus for health and performance. The challenges he lists will sound familiar to anyone running ML in production: latency versus model complexity, GDPR and CCPA compliance, model drift, and tuning clusters for cost.

## Who should watch

Architects designing multi-agent LLM systems who want a reference shape (specialists, consensus, federation), and fintech engineers curious how a large bank frames the problem. If you want code or a reproducible benchmark, this talk doesn't carry one.

## Related talks

- Sunny Guntuka's [Algorithmic Trading with Python](https://www.conf42.com/Python_2025_Sunny_Guntuka_trading_algorithmic_python) is the hands-on counterpart.

Title: REST, SOAP or GraphQL? Pick by workload, then secure every layer
Description: Darshini Jayaprakash of Driscoll's at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on choosing API styles, middleware, layered API security and event-driven integration.
Body:
SOAP is not dead; it just moved to the parts of the economy where a failed transaction makes the news. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Darshini Jayaprakash, a senior application developer at Driscoll's, gave a broad tour of enterprise API integration: when REST, SOAP and GraphQL each make sense, what middleware platforms take off your plate, and why security has to be in the design from day one.

This is a fundamentals-and-strategy talk. It suits developers moving from building single services to owning integrations between many, and it stays at the level of patterns rather than code.

## Three paradigms, three jobs

Darshini's comparison is the backbone of the talk:

- **REST** stays dominant because it is simple, uses the HTTP verbs every developer already knows, and is stateless, so each request carries everything the server needs and it scales well in cloud-native systems. The tooling ecosystem around it is vast.
- **SOAP** is heavier, built on XML and strict schemas, but still the backbone in banking, healthcare and government, where WS-Security, reliable messaging and formal contracts between services are requirements, not preferences.
- **GraphQL** lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need, which cuts round trips and suits front ends and mobile apps with nested data and tight bandwidth.

Her summary is pragmatic: SOAP for strict enterprise transactions, REST for general-purpose APIs, GraphQL where flexible, efficient fetching matters.

## Middleware turns integration into configuration

As the number of connected systems grows, point-to-point code becomes fragile. Darshini makes the case for enterprise middleware platforms: prebuilt connectors for systems like Salesforce, SAP, AWS and databases; elastic scaling for seasonal spikes; real-time monitoring of metrics, logs and alerts; and visual, low-code design tools that let technical business users take part. The shift she describes is from writing integration code to configuring and optimising it.

## Security is not a phase at the end

Her strongest point is that security bolted on after the API is finished is the wrong order. The model she recommends is defence in depth: OAuth for token-based access, API gateways for rate limiting, validation and threat detection, and lifecycle management for versioning, deprecation and continuous auditing. Combined, those layers reduce endpoint exposure while keeping the API usable for legitimate clients.

For production, she adds three habits: consistent naming and predictable resource hierarchies, rigorous automated integration, performance and security testing before release, and documentation with interactive explorers, multi-language examples and a clear changelog.

## Where it is heading

The forward-looking section covers event-driven architecture (producers emit events, brokers such as Kafka or RabbitMQ route them, consumers react independently, so failures stay isolated) and AI-assisted testing that generates test cases and predicts failure points. She also sketches ideas still on the horizon, such as self-healing APIs and usage-aware rate limiting.

## Who should watch

Developers and junior architects who need one map of API styles, middleware and security before designing integrations, and teams arguing about whether to retire a SOAP service. Experienced platform engineers will find it familiar; the comparison section is the bit to forward.

Title: Ballerina writes your Kubernetes YAML so you don't have to
Description: Anupama Pathirage of WSO2 shows at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 how Ballerina turns integration code into Docker and Kubernetes artifacts with one build.
Body:
Integration code has an awkward habit: the business logic takes an afternoon, and the Dockerfile, the Deployment, the Service and the resource limits take the rest of the week. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Anupama Pathirage, Director and Head of Engineering for Integration at WSO2, showed how Ballerina, the open-source language WSO2 started in 2016, closes that gap by building the container and Kubernetes artifacts straight from the source code.

It is a product-focused talk from the team that builds the language, and it says so. What makes it worth the time is the live demo: a small REST service goes from VS Code to a running Kubernetes deployment without anyone typing a line of YAML.

## Integration is a data, network and concurrency problem

Pathirage frames integration as three jobs: moving data around in many shapes, talking over many protocols, and doing all of it concurrently. Ballerina gives each one a first-class abstraction. Services and clients are part of the language syntax rather than a framework bolted on top. A resource function looks like an ordinary function whose name maps to the resource path, with typed input parameters and return types, so the network plumbing stays out of the business logic.

Data lives in records, Ballerina's canonical representation for whatever arrives over the wire, whether that is JSON or something else. If you've written a C-family language (C, C++, Java, Go), she argues the syntax will feel familiar; the new parts are those integration constructs.

## Every program is also a diagram

The feature that gets the most screen time is code-and-diagram parity. Every Ballerina program has an equivalent flow or sequence diagram, kept in sync automatically by the VS Code plugin. In the demo she adds an `if` node in the diagram and the matching code appears in the source file; edit either side and the other follows. The same idea extends to a service designer for HTTP and GraphQL, a visual data mapper with an AI-assisted auto-map for records with many fields, debugging from diagram nodes, and an ER-style view of your types.

There is also tooling for contract-first work: point the OpenAPI tool at a spec and it generates the service and client code in one command, with similar tools for other formats.

## Code to cloud, minus the YAML

The demo app checks the weather for a location, maps the weather to a mood and asks Spotify for a matching playlist. Two APIs, one service, three resources. She runs it locally with `bal run`, tries a couple of cities, then moves on to the part the talk is named for.

A `bal build` with the cloud option set to Docker produces the image and a Dockerfile in the target folder. Set it to Kubernetes and the compiler emits the deployment YAML too, reading the port and other settings from the source and filling in default CPU and memory values that you override with a config file. Then it is plain `kubectl`: apply, check the deployment, expose the service. She mentions the same approach for serverless targets such as AWS Lambda and Azure Functions, and OpenTelemetry-based observability on the operations side.

## Who should watch

Integration developers who live between APIs and SaaS connectors, and platform teams who are tired of reviewing hand-written manifests for small services. If you need a Kubernetes primer, this is not it; if you want to see how far a language can absorb deployment concerns, it is a tidy half hour.

## Related talks

- Pathirage covered the deployment side in more depth a year earlier in [From Code to Cloud: Mastering Kubernetes Deployments with Ballerina](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Anupama_Pathirage_kubernetes_ballerina_deployments).
- Anuruddha Liyanarachchi looks at the network side in [Simplify Network Services for Real-World, Cloud Native Applications with Ballerina](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Anuruddha_Liyanarachchi_network_services_realworld_ballerina).
- For the gateway in front of all those services, Roman Rastiehaiev compares open-source options in [Navigating the World of API Gateways](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Roman_Rastiehaiev_api_gateways_comparison).

Title: Post-quantum crypto for Kubernetes should start at the ingress
Description: Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb (Broadcom) at Conf42 Kube Native 2025 on where Kubernetes depends on RSA and ECC and how to phase in hybrid PQC.
Body:
Every trust relationship in a Kubernetes cluster, from kubectl to the API server to pod-to-pod mTLS, rests on RSA or elliptic-curve keys that a large enough quantum computer could break with Shor's algorithm. At Conf42 Kube Native 2025, Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb, Principal R&D Engineer at Broadcom, mapped where that exposure sits and laid out a phased migration to post-quantum cryptography (PQC): hybrid handshakes first, external ingress next, then the service mesh, then etcd and the control plane.

It is a planning talk, not a demo, and it is refreshingly specific about the costs.

## Kubernetes is PKI all the way down

Derek's inventory of what breaks is the useful part. API server traffic is protected by TLS. Service mesh mTLS between microservices relies on RSA and ECC key exchange. Ingress terminates external TLS with classical certificates. Registry pulls and pushes are authenticated by classical signatures. If the PKI falls, so does the rest: man-in-the-middle attacks become easy, secrets such as database passwords and API tokens become readable, malicious pods can impersonate services, and backups encrypted today become tomorrow's plaintext.

His summary: without a secure PKI, trust inside the cluster becomes impossible to establish or maintain. Harvest-now, decrypt-later makes that a problem for today's traffic, not just tomorrow's.

## NIST has picked the algorithms

The answer comes from NIST's completed post-quantum project: lattice-based key encapsulation (ML-KEM, the Kyber family) for key exchange, Dilithium-family signatures for authentication, and hybrid modes that combine classical and post-quantum algorithms so upgraded and legacy systems can still talk. With standards final, Derek argues the transition has moved from optional to inevitable.

## Four places to put it, in order

PQC has to land everywhere Kubernetes uses classical crypto, and he gives the order:

1. **Ingress controllers.** The most exposed surface and the easiest win. Clients negotiate a hybrid TLS handshake, the ingress swaps in post-quantum key exchange while staying backward compatible, and pods behind it receive traffic over a quantum-safe hop. Support is emerging in OpenSSL post-quantum branches, Envoy and NGINX.
2. **The service mesh.** Istio and Linkerd depend on mTLS, so PQ-enabled crypto libraries go into the Envoy sidecars, the mesh CA issues hybrid certificates, hybrid mode keeps old and new workloads talking, and latency gets watched closely.
3. **Secrets and etcd.** Post-quantum certificates are much larger, which stresses etcd storage and replication. Use PQ-safe key management such as Vault or a cloud KMS, and rotate long-lived secrets automatically.
4. **Core control plane.** Last, once the rest is proven.

Throughout: keep rollback paths, canary deployments and feature flags.

## The bill comes due in the handshake

Derek doesn't oversell it. His figures put the PQ handshake at about 3.2x the cost of classical algorithms, certificates around 10x larger, and production-grade library maturity at roughly 60%. His comparison has RSA-2048 at a 1x handshake with universal compatibility, and the Kyber-768 option at 3.2x with limited compatibility. Early adopters, he notes, should budget for two to four times the handshake latency and plan capacity accordingly. Polyglot microservices add another snag: PQC support differs across languages and frameworks.

His operational suggestions are very Kubernetes: manage PQ policy with operators and custom resources, ship it via Helm charts, and make cryptographic health an observability signal. Track which algorithms handshakes actually use, the share of connections on PQ, and the latency and error impact.

## Who should watch

Platform security teams, anyone running a service mesh, and compliance-minded orgs in finance where, he notes, early adopters are already experimenting. The call to action is achievable this quarter: inventory your cryptographic dependencies, stand up a PQ-enabled ingress and mesh in staging and measure it, and use hybrid crypto for new deployments.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Preparing for the Impact of Quantum Computing on Cloud Security](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pavan_Nutalapati_quantum_cloud_security) takes the same threat to cloud security broadly.
- [Ambient Mesh: The new sidecar less & faster Istio for zero trust](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Md_Azmal_ambient_mesh_sidecar_zero_trust) explains the mesh layer you would be upgrading.
- [Encrypting Your Way to Safety: Data Security in Kubernetes](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2024_Victor_Onyenagubom_data_security_encryption_kubernetes) covers encryption at rest and in transit as it stands today.

Title: Riddles show where ChatGPT predicts instead of understanding
Description: Aroma Rodrigues (Microsoft) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 probes GPT-3-era ChatGPT with riddles, translated Hindi puzzles and word problems to test AGI claims.
Body:
Ask ChatGPT "when is a door no longer a door?" and it gives you a dictionary answer. Tell it the question is a riddle and it says: when it's ajar. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Aroma Rodrigues of Microsoft used dozens of riddles like that one to probe what a pure language model actually does, and her conclusion is blunt: ChatGPT is not AGI, and the places it fails tell you why.

The experiments were run on the GPT-3 version of ChatGPT on a free personal account, which she flags up front. That's the point rather than a weakness: before retrieval and tool layers were bolted on, you could watch the language model think without it looking things up.

## Riddle mode is a context, and it sticks

Once ChatGPT decides it's in a riddle conversation, it stays there. It answers classic riddles well (all twelve months have at least 28 days; a hole makes a bucket lighter; today comes before yesterday in a dictionary) and Aroma suspects most of those were simply in the training data. The interesting part is what happens off the beaten path. Asked what has a bottom at the top, it said a staircase. The answer is legs. Prompted for another answer, it invented a second, equally confident story. She describes the model spinning an imaginative narrative and then bending the answer to fit it.

The same sticky context breaks maths. Asked how many apples ten rabbits eat in ten minutes if five eat five in five, it stayed in riddle mode and produced reasoning she calls incredibly weird. A bus-passenger word problem fell apart as the model lost track of its own running total, which she compares to young children losing count across multiple steps.

## Translated riddles strip away the memory

Her best methodological move: to get riddles the model probably hadn't seen, she took riddles from Hindi and regional sources with no common English translation. The results got much stranger. One crude translation produced the claim that ducks give both milk and eggs. A riddle about ants (two ants ahead, two behind) got the wrong answer, and she bets the classic version with ducks would have got the right one. A question about ten birds on a wall, one shot with an arrow, got the arithmetic answer of nine, as if birds were inanimate objects that don't fly away.

The pattern she draws out: the model handles a familiar surface form, and stumbles when the same logic arrives in unfamiliar words. Your parents have six sons and each has a sister; it added six and six, twice.

## What would count as AGI, anyway

The second half takes the historical definitions one by one: the Turing test, the coffee test, the robot college student test, the employment test. Her view is that several of them are either already passed or not very meaningful, which says more about the tests than about the models. Her own definition leans on observation. Humans learn by perceiving the physical world, not only by reading about it; the model relies on available knowledge, from training or from search.

She closes with her own heavy ChatGPT use: good at context-linked creative writing in theory, but in practice it loses the thread, and a travel itinerary it wrote assumed she could cover a half-hour cab ride in about ten minutes. Retrieval helps today's versions answer her riddles correctly, but she calls that cheating in the riddle-game sense: looking up the answer isn't solving it.

## Who should watch

Anyone building on LLMs who wants an intuitive feel for failure modes before reading the papers: context lock-in, multi-step arithmetic drift, surface-form matching. It's a long, conversational talk built on examples rather than benchmarks, so treat it as a field notebook, not a study. People who want rigorous evaluation methods should pair it with the related talks.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [The Secret Language of Models: Prompt Psychology & Behavior](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2025_Shashank_Shivam_models_psychology_behavior) by Shashank Shivam at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025.
- [Measuring hallucinations in RAG](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2024_Ofer_Mendelevitch_rag_measuring_hallucinations) by Ofer Mendelevitch at Conf42 Large Language Models 2024, for the retrieval side of the story.
- [How you can trick your company into hiring ChatGPT](https://www.conf42.com/Prompt_Engineering_2024_Daniel_Pries_chatgpt_hiring_trick) by Daniel Pries at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2024.

Title: Ship AI features as micro frontends, not monolith releases
Description: Linga Annela at Conf42 JavaScript 2025 on Module Federation, edge-side composition and WebAssembly for adding AI features to large web apps.
Body:
Adding a chatbot to a big monolithic front end usually means touching shared code, rerunning the whole regression suite and waiting for the next release train. At Conf42 JavaScript 2025, Linga Annela argued that micro frontends let teams ship AI features (a chatbot, a recommendation widget, a predictive dashboard) as independent units with their own stack and schedule, and walked through the techniques that make that practical.

It is an architecture overview rather than a hands-on demo: one pattern per slide, explained at the level you would use to brief a team before a migration.

## Micro frontends are microservices for the browser

Linga's definition is the familiar one: split one big JavaScript app into smaller, independently deployable pieces, each owned by a team or domain, each free to pick React, Vue, Angular or plain JavaScript. The AI angle is that a feature team can put a conversational assistant or a personalisation engine live without touching the core application, and run experiments in isolation. The talk also cites industry figures for faster delivery and A/B testing; it doesn't name the studies, so treat them as directional.

## The toolkit, one technique at a time

- **Module Federation in Webpack 5.** Applications, even ones built with different frameworks, share code at runtime. You expose a component, say the recommendation widget, from one project and consume it in another without rebuilding or redeploying, and share common dependencies like React to keep bundles down.
- **Edge-side composition.** Instead of assembling micro frontends in the browser, the CDN stitches together only the pieces each route needs, which helps time to interactive and lets each piece cache independently.
- **WebAssembly for inference.** Compile models from TensorFlow or PyTorch to WebAssembly and run predictions, image classification or sentiment analysis on the client, with no server round trip and sensitive data staying on the device.
- **API patterns.** Plain REST endpoints owned by each micro frontend, so teams can update models independently, or GraphQL Federation, where each micro frontend contributes a subgraph to one typed schema.

## State is the hard part

Linga flags state management as the most important piece of distributed front ends. The layered approach in the talk: keep state local to each micro frontend where possible, use custom events or a lightweight shared store for what must be shared, and use optimistic rendering so the UI stays consistent when AI features are loaded or swapped at runtime. Anyone who has watched two micro frontends disagree about who the logged-in user is will appreciate the emphasis.

Performance comes next: lazy-load components on demand, share common dependencies instead of duplicating them, cache API responses and predictions in service workers, and deploy to edge runtimes.

## Start with one widget

The roadmap is sensible and modest. Find where the monolith blocks AI work, draw boundaries around business domains, set up Module Federation with shared dependencies and pipelines, then ship one small AI feature, like a chatbot or analytics widget, as a proof of concept before scaling. Linga mentions applying the approach to an e-commerce project with customer, admin and driver apps, still in progress at the time of the talk.

## Who should watch

Front-end leads with a large single-page app and a queue of AI feature requests, and architects weighing micro frontends for team autonomy. If your app is small and one team owns it, the coordination problem this solves may not exist for you yet.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Maksim Zemskov of Yandex on scaling an application without micro frontends](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2023_Maksim_Zemskov_glorious_monolith_scaling_application_microfrontends) at Conf42 JavaScript 2023.
- [Konstantinos Leimonis of Bit.dev on web bundling with Rspack](https://www.conf42.com/JavaScript_2024_Konstantinos_Leimonis_34_rspack_bundling_webdevelopment) at Conf42 JavaScript 2024.

Title: Treat migration as a standing capability, not a one-off project
Description: Meenu Venkataarangam (Recode Solutions) at Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025 on four automation pillars and AI that make enterprise migrations repeatable.
Body:
Most enterprises run a big migration, swear never again, and then start the next one with the same spreadsheets. At Conf42 Prompt Engineering 2025, Meenu Venkataarangam, a program manager at Recode Solutions, argued for the opposite: make migration a continuous, automated capability, built on four pillars (discovery, transformation, orchestration and testing) with AI on top for prediction.

It's a short, framework-level talk aimed at people who plan and run migrations rather than at engineers looking for tool configs. Think of it as a checklist with a spine.

## From lift-and-shift to a permanent muscle

Meenu traces migration's history in three steps. It used to be lift and shift: move the workload, done. Today it involves many teams, tools and compliance frameworks. The future she describes treats migration as a strategic capacity, where systems keep evolving without disrupting the business.

Manual migrations, in her framing, fail in predictable ways: long timelines, unpredictable results, high error risk. Automation's job is to shorten delivery, raise predictability, improve data quality and free specialists from repetitive migration work. Her line is that this is about reliability, consistency and governance as much as speed.

## The four pillars

**Discovery automation.** Automatically map dependencies, data lineage and system interconnections. What used to take weeks or months of documentation becomes a visual map of how every data source and service affects the others, so the plan starts from reality.

**Transformation engine.** Schema conversion, code refactoring and bulk data movement at scale. Her examples: converting an Oracle schema to PostgreSQL, rewriting stored procedures, and moving terabytes with validation built in. She names three common patterns: cloud migration to AWS, Azure or GCP; Hadoop to modern cloud platforms; and data warehouse modernisation onto platforms like Snowflake with automated schema and query translation.

**Intelligent orchestration.** Even fully automated steps need sequencing and monitoring. Her metaphor is an air traffic controller: define the workflows, execute them, adapt to conditions in real time, validate each stage.

**Automated testing.** Differential testing compares source and target systems to catch hidden logic or data issues early, and real-time monitoring plus automated rollback lets teams recover quickly when something slips. This is the pillar that turns a migration from a leap of faith into something you can measure.

## Where the AI comes in

The AI layer is modest and sensible. Machine learning looks at previous migrations to predict effort, cost and risk. AI-driven automation adjusts workflows when issues appear. Predictive analytics forecasts bottlenecks before they arrive. If your organisation has done five migrations and kept the data, the sixth one should be easier to estimate, and that's the whole idea.

She also covers zero-downtime strategies: continuous replication, intelligent routing and instant rollback, so the migration happens while the business keeps running. No weekend cutover, which anyone who has spent a Saturday night watching a progress bar will appreciate.

## Start small, then compound

Her roadmap is four steps: assess your current migration process, define a target automation vision, implement gradually starting with high-impact use cases, and measure and optimise continuously. The enterprises that get this right, she argues, adapt to new technology faster because moving is no longer an event.

## Who should watch

Programme and delivery managers planning a portfolio of migrations, and architects who need a vocabulary for pitching migration tooling as an investment rather than a project cost. Engineers after deep detail on, say, stored procedure translation will want to pair it with something more hands-on, like the talks below.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Zero-Downtime by Design: High-Availability Migration Patterns for Modern Gateway & Platform Engineering](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Kalyan_Inturi_availability_migration_gateways) by Kalyan Inturi at Conf42 DevOps 2026, with shadow traffic and microservice extraction.
- [De-Risking a Legacy CRM Migration in Life Sciences](https://www.conf42.com/Feature_Flags_2026_Jaymin_Sutarwala_crm_migration_salesforce) by Jaymin Sutarwala at Conf42 Feature Flags 2026, a feature-flag-driven Salesforce rollout.
- [Modernizing Legacy Systems: Achieving Innovation and Stability for Future-Ready Enterprises](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sasidhar_Reddy_Somula_systems_legacy_modernizing) by Sasidhar Reddy Somula at Conf42 Machine Learning 2025.
