Title: SiriusXM cut model deployments from 45 days to four hours
Description: Jimmy Katiyar of SiriusXM at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on validation gates, CI/CD, monitoring and Kubernetes behind a jump from MLOps level one to three.
Body:
Machine learning projects rarely fail because the model is bad; they fail when someone tries to run it in production at scale. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Jimmy Katiyar, Senior Product Manager at SiriusXM, showed how his organisation went from MLOps maturity level one to level three in 18 months, bringing model deployments down from 45 days to four hours while serving millions of daily transactions.

It is a product manager's view of an ML platform, which is a feature: the talk spends as much time on shared KPIs and team habits as on pipelines, and the numbers come with the organisational changes that produced them.

## Months to production is a business problem

Jimmy started with the familiar enterprise picture: deployments done by hand, environments that don't match between development and production, teams in silos, frequent incidents and painful compliance. When a model takes 60 to 90 days to reach production, competitors who iterate faster win. He framed maturity in four levels, from fully manual and ad hoc (level zero) through partial automation and continuous delivery to level three, where everything is automated and systems heal themselves.

## Four pillars, and the gate that mattered most

SiriusXM's architecture rests on four pillars: automated model validation, CI/CD pipelines, monitoring, and scalable infrastructure. The validation framework is the part worth copying. Every model passes three gates before going live: statistical performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and business KPIs), operational readiness (latency, scalability, throughput) and compliance (explainability, bias detection, regulatory alignment). Jimmy credited those gates with a 94% reduction in production issues.

The CI/CD pipeline versions data sets, configurations and artifacts alongside code. Build and test covers containerisation, performance benchmarks and security scanning. Staging runs shadow deployments and A/B tests under load, and production relies on canary releases, automated rollbacks and audit logs. That pipeline is where 45 days became four hours.

## Monitoring that pays for itself early

Monitoring spans four dimensions: model performance, data quality, system operations and business impact, the last measured in revenue or conversion. In its first year the system caught 28 critical drift incidents before customers felt them. On the infrastructure side, Kubernetes handles orchestration and autoscaling, Apache Spark does distributed data processing, and load-balanced inference services sit behind strict access controls, encryption and audit logging. He reported 3.5 million inference requests a day at 99.99% uptime and under 50 ms latency.

## The hardest pillar is the one without a diagram

Jimmy was candid that technology doesn't solve mismatched skills, fragmented tools and inconsistent success metrics. Data scientists and engineers often don't speak the same language. SiriusXM unified development environments, standardised workflows and created shared KPIs, and he relayed that their VP of AI engineering considered getting both sides speaking one language the biggest win.

His roadmap has four phases: foundation (standard environments, version control, basic pipelines), automation (CI/CD, validation dashboards, model registry, metadata tracking), scale (Kubernetes orchestration, drift detection, automated rollback), and optimisation (feature stores, self-healing infrastructure, governance). The pitfalls are the ones every platform team has hit at least once: tool obsession, underestimating culture change, and over-complicating the first step. Start with one high-value use case.

## Who should watch

Product and engineering managers building an internal ML platform, and teams stuck at level one wondering what level three looks like in practice. Engineers wanting pipeline code will find the outline here and the details elsewhere.

Title: Why most ML models never ship, and the MLOps pillars that fix it
Description: Bharath Reddy Baddam of New York Life at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on orchestration, infrastructure, monitoring and CI/CD that move models from lab to production.
Body:
Only about one in five ML models makes it to production, according to the research Bharath Reddy Baddam opened with, and his takeaway at Conf42 MLOps 2025 was to treat machine learning as a product, not a project. Bharath, a Senior Salesforce Developer at New York Life Insurance Company with nine years in Salesforce cloud and AI work across finance, healthcare and real estate, organised the talk around five pillars that close the gap between a notebook and a service.

This is an introductory-to-intermediate roadmap. If you are new to MLOps or need a structure to explain it to a team, it is a tidy one; if you already run Kubeflow in anger, skim to the testing section.

## Proofs of concept die of the same causes

Bharath's list of barriers will be familiar: reproducibility, a gap between research and engineering, no standard deployment process, weak monitoring and maintenance, testing methods that don't fit ML, and poor integration with enterprise systems. He then walked the maturity curve from isolated notebooks and one-off deployments, through basic training automation, to CI/CD for ML and finally full maturity with monitoring, drift detection, retraining and rollback. Mature organisations, he said, cut deployment time by 80% and sustain 95% accuracy in production, and he stressed that the shift is cultural as much as technical.

## Pick orchestration tools for the team you have

The orchestration section compares three tools fairly. Kubeflow is Kubernetes-native with strong model serving, a fit if you already live on Kubernetes. MLflow is lightweight for experiment tracking and a model registry. Apache Airflow is a general workflow engine that handles complex, data-heavy processes without being ML-specific. Many organisations mix them, for example MLflow for tracking with Kubeflow for deployment. His test for any tool: does it fit our workflow and skills, or are we adding complexity for its own sake?

## Real-time inference is an infrastructure problem

Infrastructure as code with Terraform, Docker to kill the works-on-my-machine bug, CI/CD across dev, test and prod, and Kubernetes autoscaling form the base. For real-time use cases like fraud detection, chatbots and recommenders, he added horizontal scaling, load balancing with health checks, Redis caching for frequent queries, and GPUs where they earn their keep. His example: a healthcare client's real-time insurance eligibility checks went from minutes to milliseconds on an optimised autoscaling setup.

## Monitoring and testing keep the model honest

Monitoring covers three layers: data drift (statistical checks such as divergence measures and the population stability index), model performance (accuracy, F1, AUC against benchmarks) and operational metrics (latency, throughput, resource use). When drift shows up, retraining can trigger on a performance threshold, a schedule, or a significant distribution shift. New models then go out as shadow deployments running silently in parallel, canaries starting at 5% of traffic, A/B tests that measure business impact, and automated rollback when the newcomer underperforms.

The CI/CD-for-ML test suite is the most reusable slide: data validation (schema checks, missing values), model performance tests that block regressions, integration tests over the whole pipeline, load and performance tests, and security and compliance checks for GDPR and HIPAA.

## Who should watch

Engineers moving from application development into ML platforms, and leads who need a shared vocabulary for an MLOps roadmap. It is a map, not a deep implementation guide.

Title: Black Friday-proof retail: design for failure, migrate by strangler fig
Description: Maruti Pradeep Pakalapati (Capital One) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on autoscaling, circuit breakers, real-time inventory and strangler-fig migration for retail.
Body:
When the product detail service slows down on Black Friday, the right answer is a cached page and a completed checkout, not an error. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Maruti Pradeep Pakalapati, Software Engineer Technical Lead at Capital One, laid out the cloud-native patterns retailers lean on to survive their biggest weekend, and tied each one back to incident response: how fast you detect, how small the blast radius stays, and whether revenue keeps flowing while you fix it.

The framing is retail-wide rather than a single company's case study, and it moves from why to how in a tidy order: autoscaling, microservices, personalisation, inventory, resilience, security, incidents, observability and migration.

## Peak weekends make every outage expensive

Pakalapati opens with the stakes. Black Friday and Cyber Monday can account for more than 20% of a retailer's annual revenue, customers expect sub-second responses on every channel, and inventory has to be accurate in real time across web and stores. The old answer was to buy servers at three to four times normal demand and let them idle most of the year. Elastic autoscaling, guided by demand forecasts and live monitoring, replaces that.

## Contain the blast radius

Monoliths fail as a unit: one checkout bug and the site is gone. Splitting catalogue, cart, checkout and payments into independent services lets each one scale, fail and deploy on its own. He pairs that with the classic resilience patterns: circuit breakers against cascading failure, bulkheads to isolate resources, back-pressure to stop overload, and async communication to loosen coupling.

The most useful example is graceful degradation. If the product detail service is slow, serve cached or simplified content instead of an error. The shopper still buys, revenue still flows and the incident stays small. Fallbacks and rate limiting are part of the design from day one, not something bolted on after the first bad Black Friday.

## Inventory as an event stream

Legacy inventory relied on batch updates that could lag by 15 to 60 minutes, which is how you sell the last pair of shoes twice. The cloud-native version publishes every sale as an event to Kafka or Kinesis, fans updates into Redis caches across regions and serves them through a GraphQL layer. He describes inventory visibility in under 200 milliseconds across digital and physical channels, enough to support buy-online, pick-up-in-store.

Personalisation gets a similar treatment: recommendation engines isolated as their own services, scaled separately on GPUs for inference and backed by session caching, so they don't drag down the rest of the site at peak.

## Observability tied to revenue

On incidents, he contrasts typical pre-cloud-native numbers (detection over 45 minutes, recovery over four hours) with what SRE practices deliver: detection in under a minute through automated alerting, and much faster resolution thanks to canary analysis, automated rollbacks and playbooks for partial failures. The figures he cites across the talk are industry-level claims rather than measurements from one system, so treat them as targets.

The sharper point is about what to watch. Metrics, structured logs with trace IDs and end-to-end traces are table stakes. Leading retailers also track cart abandonment against service latency, watch revenue impact during incidents and run synthetic shopping journeys that exercise checkout continuously. Recovery means the customer can buy again, not that the pods are green.

## Strangle the monolith, don't swap it

For legacy platforms he recommends the strangler fig pattern: an API gateway routes traffic to either the old system or new services, traffic shifts as each new service proves itself, and the monolith is retired quietly. Team structure matters too: product-aligned squads owning domains end to end, platform teams providing self-service infrastructure, SRE practices embedded in squads and security as code in CI/CD, with short-lived secrets and scanned immutable images.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects at retailers planning for peak season, or partway through a monolith migration. It is a broad, well-organised overview rather than a deep implementation talk, and the graceful-degradation and observability sections are the most reusable.

- [Feature Flags as a Migration Engine](https://www.conf42.com/Feature_Flags_2026_Jaya_Chand_Bandi_migration_payment_platforms) by Jaya Chand Bandi shows another way to decompose a monolith safely.
- [Leveraging AI-Driven Insights for Incident Management: Enhancing Customer Retention](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Anandakumar_Kumaravelu_4_ai_retention_personalization) by Anandakumar Kumaravelu links incidents and personalisation to customer loyalty.

Title: Human-in-the-loop MLOps treats reviewer feedback as first-class data
Description: Tejasvi Nuthalapati of Amazon at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on tiered autonomy, observable models and feedback loops that put human judgment into retraining.
Body:
Most ML teams pick a side: automate everything and watch drift creep in, or put a human on every decision and watch throughput collapse. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Tejasvi Nuthalapati, a software development engineer at Amazon, argued for a third design where the pipeline treats humans and models as first-class participants, and showed four patterns for building it.

This is a patterns talk, told through short case examples rather than code. The 40% in the title is his summary of the improvement in effective performance across organisations that adopted these patterns, and he was careful to say it came from architecture, not from a better algorithm.

## Both extremes fail the same way: trust evaporates

The full-automation pipeline looks clean until false positives pile up and nobody can say why the system decided what it did. The manual pipeline looks accurate but becomes slow and expensive, and reviewers burn out on repetitive cases. Tejasvi's opening story was a fintech fraud system drowning in false positives. Tuning the model barely helped. What worked was structured human review whose decisions were logged, versioned and tied into retraining cycles, and false positives fell by 40%.

## Autonomy is a dial, not a switch

The first pattern is tiered autonomy. Low-risk, high-confidence transactions get auto-approved. Medium-risk, uncertain ones go to an analyst who brings context. High-value cases go to full human review, with AI-generated insights attached so the reviewer starts with evidence. He listed several ways to implement the routing: a service mesh, CI/CD branches keyed on confidence thresholds, or Kubernetes operators that decide which requests need intervention. In one deployment this cut analyst workload by 60% because people stopped spending time on trivial cases.

## Models deserve the observability services get

Pattern two is the observable model. Nobody ships a service without logs, metrics and traces, yet models go to production as black boxes. Tejasvi's fix is structured decision logging, dashboards for confidence distributions, drift indicators and feature stability, and explanations layered for engineers, business stakeholders and end users. Imagine a recommender that quietly starts suggesting stale products: without confidence scores and drift signals you find out from the complaints.

## Corrections should reach retraining in days, not months

Pattern three is the one he cared about most. In many organisations a human spots a mistake, files a ticket, and the correction might reach a training set months later. He wants every correction logged against the model version that produced the error and fed automatically into retraining. In a content moderation system he observed, this loop lifted production F1 from 0.72 to 0.84 within three training cycles. His point that follows is the interesting one: as models improve, human input becomes more valuable, because what remains are the ambiguous, ethically loaded cases no model handles well.

## Oversight has to grow slower than the system

Pattern four is scalable oversight: stratify risk, sample intelligently, and design escalation paths. In a supply chain anomaly detection example, the team oversampled low-confidence cases for human review, caught 90% of novel anomalies and halved the human workload.

He closed with metrics for the whole human-plus-machine system: reduction in false positives, time to drift detection, how fast feedback reaches retraining, and operator confidence, because a system people trust is one they actually use.

## Who should watch

Anyone running fraud, moderation or anomaly detection with a review queue, and platform teams designing where humans plug into ML pipelines. Short on implementation detail, long on design patterns you can argue about with your team.

Title: Your runbooks have a half-life, so let the incidents write them
Description: Mahmood Nawaz (LTIMindtree) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on four-layer AI knowledge systems that surface past fixes while an incident is still open.
Body:
The engineer who knows why the queue backs up every second Tuesday is a single point of failure with a notice period. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Mahmood Nawaz, Senior Specialist in Data Engineering at LTIMindtree, built a talk around the idea of knowledge half-life: in cloud-native systems, troubleshooting know-how goes stale within months, and the fix is an AI-driven knowledge system that captures what each incident teaches and puts it in front of the next responder.

## Why tribal knowledge stopped scaling

Nawaz's diagnosis has three parts. Cloud providers keep shipping new services and features that change how existing systems behave and create new failure modes. Small changes cascade, so one tweak can mean updates to monitoring, alerting, deploy scripts and procedures. And continuous delivery means the system you documented last quarter has already moved.

Meanwhile, most incident frameworks were designed for slower monolithic systems, and experienced engineers are scarce. Organisations keep paying for training and documentation whose value decays faster each year. That is the treadmill he wants off.

## Four layers

The architecture he proposes stacks four layers:

- **Foundation.** Fast, highly available knowledge storage, built on a vector database for similarity search and an event-driven design so knowledge updates in real time.
- **Processing.** The cognitive core, where NLP extracts structured information from unstructured sources: log files, incident reports and the communication threads where the real diagnosis usually happens.
- **Interaction.** Conversational interfaces for natural-language questions mid-incident, visual timelines and dependency views, explanations pitched to the user's experience level (more detail for new joiners, terse summaries for veterans), and context-aware delivery that surfaces relevant knowledge from active alerts without anyone asking.
- **Integration.** APIs into incident management, monitoring and collaboration tools; workflow automation that extracts and distributes insights when an incident is resolved; and real-time sync so the same knowledge appears everywhere.

The integration layer is the one that decides whether this works. A knowledge base that needs its own tab during an incident is a knowledge base nobody opens during an incident.

## Matching today's incident to last year's

Where the system earns its keep is solution generation. Instead of rediscovering a fix someone already found, machine learning matches the characteristics of the current incident against historical ones and suggests troubleshooting steps that worked before. Each resolved incident feeds back in, so the base gets more complete as more teams contribute. Nawaz calls these network effects, and adds cross-team surfacing: an insight from one team is pushed to others who are likely to hit the same issue.

He presents figures for implementations, including 99.8% processing accuracy for knowledge extraction, a 90% reduction in the time to deliver relevant information compared with manual searching, and a 75% cut in the mental effort engineers need to find and apply it. The talk doesn't detail how these were measured, so treat them as directional.

## Culture is the other half

His closing point is that the technology is necessary but not sufficient. These systems only work in organisations that value knowledge sharing and collaborative problem solving, and the benefits he lists (faster resolution, expertise that survives turnover, operations that scale without proportional headcount) depend on people writing things down in the first place.

## Who should watch

SRE leads and platform teams whose postmortems vanish into a wiki, and anyone sketching an internal RAG assistant for on-call. It is an architecture-level talk without a demo, so expect a blueprint rather than a product walkthrough.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Building Production-Ready RAG Systems for Enterprise Knowledge Infrastructure](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Srinivas_Chennupati_knowledge_rag_strategies) by Srinivas Chennupati covers the retrieval plumbing.
- [Transforming Knowledge Systems with Embedded Analytics in Cloud-Native Architectures](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Harshita_Dubey_knowledge_analytics_architectures) by Harshita Dubey looks at knowledge systems from the analytics side.
- [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2020_Yury_Nino_postmortem_culture) by Yury Niño is about producing the knowledge worth capturing.

Title: HR AI at 10 million interactions a month scales with the HR calendar
Description: Ramprasad Reddy Mittana of NSF at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on running production ML for HR shared services, from privacy pipelines to blue-green deploys.
Body:
HR traffic has a calendar: onboarding spikes in January, performance reviews in December, benefits enrollment in the fall. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Ramprasad Reddy Mittana, Senior Manager HRIS at NSF (NSF International), laid out the MLOps architecture behind AI in an HR shared services centre handling over 10 million interactions a month for about 50,000 employees, and his one line to remember was to align your scaling with the HR calendar.

Ramprasad brings 20-plus years across NSF International, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Oracle. The talk is an architecture walkthrough with the speaker's reported results attached, aimed at people who run ML where the data is personal and the audit trail is mandatory.

## HR is a hard place to run models

He listed why standard MLOps falls short here. The data is sensitive and crosses national and legal jurisdictions. Volume swings with mass hiring, review cycles and open enrollment. The models have to answer a wide spread of query types consistently. Compliance is non-negotiable. And all of it runs at the 10-million-a-month scale, so manual babysitting is off the table.

## Containers, canaries and retraining on a schedule

The production setup is containerised models on Kubernetes, with GPU acceleration where training or inference needs it. New models roll out through automated A/B testing and canary deployments to a small slice of users first, gated by statistical significance tests. Scheduled retraining pipelines keep accuracy at or above 92% as query mix and data distributions drift.

Monitoring is HR-specific: real-time dashboards for chatbot response accuracy, resolution time and satisfaction, plus drift detection that he said spots degradation 73% faster than before. Every interaction, response and satisfaction rating feeds a supervised retraining loop, which he credited with a 28% accuracy gain overall.

## Privacy and the feature store do the heavy lifting

The data engineering section is the strongest. Automated PII detection and tokenisation built for GDPR and CCPA, schema enforcement and anomaly detection for data quality, and streaming feature engineering to keep inference fast. At the centre sits an HR feature store serving the same features to training and real-time inference, with point-in-time correctness to prevent leakage in time-series HR data, sub-10ms serving, and versioning and lineage tracked with Spark and Flink. He tied it to a 65% latency reduction and 40% lower compute cost.

Point-in-time correctness is the detail to steal. HR features like tenure or internal mobility change over time, and training on today's value for last year's label is a quiet way to build a model that looks brilliant offline and disappoints in production.

## Multi-tenant, blue-green, and spot instances

For scale, a multi-tenant architecture isolates business units on shared infrastructure. Blue-green deployments give zero-downtime updates and instant rollback. Autoscaling absorbs traffic spikes up to ten times normal during busy seasons, and spot instances plus right-sizing cut infrastructure spend by 40%.

Governance closes the talk: end-to-end audit trails for every AI decision, multi-jurisdiction compliance monitoring, HR-tailored explainability, and bias checks on both training data and every retraining cycle. He reported an 89% drop in discriminatory outcomes and made the point that bias is a continuing responsibility, not a one-off fix.

## Who should watch

HRIS and people-tech engineers putting chatbots or classifiers in front of employees, and anyone building a feature store for time-dependent personal data. If you need the Kubernetes specifics, this stays at the architecture level.

Title: Retail incident response on AWS, built for the Thanksgiving spike
Description: Mahesh Yadlapati (Haliburton) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on using AWS forecasting, Lambda remediation and DR drills to keep retail sites up at peak.
Body:
Retail outages don't stay internal for long: a checkout that falls over on Thanksgiving is on social media before the pager finishes ringing. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Mahesh Yadlapati, Senior DevOps Engineer at Haliburton, made the case for cloud-native incident response in retail, with AWS as the toolkit, and argued that the goal is customer experience during the bad moment, not just uptime.

This is an introductory, AWS-centric talk. It spends its first half on why cloud beats traditional data centres for this job and its second on which AWS services fill which role, sprinkled with a few incidents from his own work.

## Think like the customer, then size for the holiday

Yadlapati's starting point is that retailers should judge incidents by what the shopper sees: customer experience, revenue lost during peak periods, and brand reputation once complaints go public. He then compares traditional IT with cloud across infrastructure, scalability, recovery, monitoring and cost.

The core argument is about peaks. On-premises, you size for the holiday season and carry that hardware all year. In the cloud, autoscaling and elastic load balancing run normal capacity most of the time and scale up when traffic arrives. The same logic applies to recovery: rather than a duplicate physical DR site, you replicate across regions and fail over with tools like AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery. He mentions once recovering from DR within minutes, which is what sold him on the approach.

## Forecast the spike, automate the fix

On the AWS side, three services do most of the customer-facing work in his design:

- **Amazon Forecast** looks at previous years' data to predict how much traffic a holiday will bring, so you can scale ahead of it, manually or by automation.
- **Amazon Personalize** keeps recommendations working as a fallback when primary systems are degraded.
- **Amazon Connect** routes customer inquiries during incidents so support quality holds up under pressure.

Underneath, CloudWatch watches infrastructure and applications, alerting application owners for app issues and invoking Lambda for infrastructure ones. His example: in a pool of four servers, one runs hot on CPU and memory. Lambda either adds a server to share the load or spins up a replacement and removes the sick one, and health checks keep traffic away from it in the meantime. He also lists X-Ray and OpenTelemetry for tracing, Rekognition for watching visual content for anomalies and IoT Core for in-store devices.

## Small incidents teach the most

The most relatable story is not about a region failing. After the team installed new antivirus software, monitoring flagged abnormal CPU spikes across servers. They traced it to the antivirus, uninstalled it and switched to one that used less CPU. Monitoring that knows what normal looks like catches the change you made yourself, which is where a lot of incidents come from.

## Practise the failover

His best-practice list is short and sensible. Design for failure, with graceful degradation that keeps core shopping working when non-essential services break. Automate detection, escalation and first response, keeping humans for complex decisions. Monitor customer-facing metrics, not just technical ones. And practise: run chaos exercises and actually switch to the second region to check it has the data and works. A DR plan you have never exercised is a hypothesis.

## Who should watch

Teams moving retail platforms from on-premises to AWS, and engineers who need a map of which managed services cover which part of incident response. If you already run multi-region active-active with automated failover, most of this will be familiar; the customer-first framing is still worth the time.

- [Securing the Future: How AIOps Drives Operational Resilience on AWS](https://www.conf42.com/DevSecOps_2024_Indika_Wimalasuriya_aiops_resilience_aws) by Indika Wimalasuriya adds the AIOps layer on AWS.
- [Disaster Recovery preparedness using Chaos Engineering](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Kyle_Shelton_disaster_recovery_preparedness) by Kyle Shelton shows how to drill the failover.

Title: Predictive maintenance pays, so why do most factory pilots fail?
Description: Muruga Angamuthu of Techtronic Industries at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on AI predictive maintenance, its tech stack, and the reasons most initiatives stall.
Body:
A machine that breaks without warning costs far more than one you fix on your own schedule, and almost everyone in manufacturing knows it. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Muruga Angamuthu, BI Manager and Data & Analytics architect at Techtronic Industries (TTI), made the case for AI-driven predictive maintenance and then spent a good part of his talk on the less glamorous question: why roughly 60% of these initiatives fail anyway.

It is a compact, overview-style talk from someone with 23 years across data engineering, BI and manufacturing. Expect a structured tour (stack, models, failure modes, roadmap) rather than code.

## Maintenance has four eras, and most plants are stuck in the first two

Muruga framed the problem as an evolution. Reactive maintenance fixes things after they break, with unpredictable cost and big production disruption. Preventive maintenance follows a fixed calendar and replaces parts too early or too late. Predictive maintenance services equipment based on its condition. The fourth stage, the one he argued for, is ML that predicts failures and keeps getting better as it learns.

The numbers he cited for the destination are the industry-report kind: up to $50,000 lost per hour of unplanned downtime, reactive repairs three to ten times pricier than predictive ones, and organisations reporting around half the downtime, roughly a third lower maintenance cost and a 385% return on investment. The figure that matters most operationally is the warning window: models giving eight to twelve days of advance notice, enough time to order spare parts and schedule the outage instead of discovering it.

## The stack: sensors, edge, cloud, and four model families

The architecture section is a useful checklist. IoT sensors on industrial machines capture temperature, vibration and pressure, and he put the volume at 1.5 to 2.3 terabytes a day per setup. Edge computing pre-filters that stream on site and handles instant alerts. A cloud data platform keeps the history and runs training, deployment and cross-facility benchmarking.

On top sit four techniques, each with a job: autoencoders that learn what normal looks like and flag deviations, random forest classifiers that name the specific failure mode, recurrent neural networks that read long time series for slow degradation, and digital twins that simulate the equipment to sharpen predictions. Nobody wins with a single model here; the anomaly detector says "something is off" and the classifier says what.

## Failure is mostly data and people

This is the part worth the watch. Muruga gave three reasons pilots die. Data integration first: legacy machines without sensors, siloed IT systems and inconsistent data quality, which he said trips up nearly 80% of deployments. Scope second: projects that run 30 to 40% over budget because the proof of concept was too wide or too weakly validated. People third: technicians who resist because they fear for their jobs or simply don't trust the model's recommendations.

His blueprint answers each one. Start with the equipment whose failure costs the most. Link maintenance, production and quality systems into one data architecture. Bring technicians in early so the tools fit their workflow. Scale in phases, proving ROI at each step. The roadmap that follows is concrete about timing: one to three months of foundation work, four to six months of pilot on the highest-impact assets, seven to twelve months of expansion with ERP integration, and a second year for digital twins and a predictive maintenance centre of excellence.

He also pointed at explainable AI as the fix for the trust problem: a technician who can see why the model flagged a bearing is far more likely to act on it.

## Who should watch

Title: How MLOps cut insurance policy issuance time by 99%
Description: Sameer Joshi of Cognizant at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on feature stores, model registries and compliance pipelines behind AI in insurance operations.
Body:
Insurance used to issue a policy in three to four days and assess a claim in weeks. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Sameer Joshi, Senior Manager Projects at Cognizant and a technical architect on Duck Creek cloud platforms, walked through how MLOps practices compress those cycles, and why the plumbing (registries, feature stores, validation pipelines) matters more than any single model in a regulated industry.

The talk is a brisk, slide-driven survey across the main insurance use cases. Treat the headline percentages as the speaker's reported results rather than a benchmark you can reproduce; the value is in seeing where ML lands in an insurer and what infrastructure each use case leans on.

## The before picture is paperwork

Sameer started with the traditional carrier: paper applications and manual data entry, underwriting that depended on who was looking at the file, claims assessments stretching for weeks and risk evaluated once a year. The cost of that is long cycle times and a customer experience that varies by desk. His figure for adoption was that carriers went from about 18% experimenting with AI to 54% once MLOps practices made models operable.

## Four components do most of the work

The architecture he described is standard MLOps, applied to an industry where every decision may need defending to a regulator. GitOps-style automated deployment pipelines. Monitoring for real-time drift detection. Experimentation platforms for A/B testing. Centralised feature stores with versioning, which he credited with cutting feature engineering time by 67%, and model registries for traceability.

Data integration sits underneath: eight to twelve sources joined per decision, from customer and property records to IoT, telematics, credit scores and satellite imagery. Policy issuance is where it pays off most visibly: a three-to-four-day process cut by a reported 99%, the figure in the title, at 93.6% accuracy.

## Three use cases with very different shapes

Catastrophe modelling swapped static data and quarterly updates for live weather feeds, satellite imagery and ensembles that mix physics models with ML. Computer vision for property and casualty runs on drones with edge-deployed models, so an inspection that used to take days finishes in minutes, with champion/challenger frameworks keeping the models honest. Telematics pulls more than 300 driving features from OBD-II devices and smartphones through Kafka-based streaming pipelines into containerised inference that scales with traffic.

Each is a different MLOps problem: batch retraining on fresh climate data, edge deployment, and high-throughput streaming. Seeing them side by side is the most useful part of the talk.

## Compliance belongs in the pipeline

The section on fairness is short but pointed. Automated adversarial testing before deployment catches bias early, validation pipelines generate the documentation regulators ask for, and LIME and SHAP explanations make individual decisions explainable. In insurance, a model nobody can explain is a model nobody can ship.

His roadmap is three phases: foundation (registries, versioning, pipelines) over three to four months, operationalising training and monitoring over two to three, then optimisation with automated retraining, A/B testing and compliance automation. Under a year from proof of concept to production, by his estimate. The next step he gave the audience is refreshingly practical: assess your ML maturity, pick high-value use cases, and build compliance in from day one.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects at carriers or insurance software vendors who need a map of where MLOps fits, and anyone pitching feature stores to a compliance team. If you want implementation detail on any one use case, pair it with a deeper talk.

Title: Twilio's Slack bot that writes the incident update for you
Description: Gandhi Mathi Nathan Kumar (Twilio) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 demos a Windmill + OpenAI Slack bot for customer summaries and status page drafts.
Body:
Most AI-for-incidents talks are about detection. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Gandhi Mathi Nathan Kumar, Principal Incident Commander for Platform Engineering at Twilio, spent his slot on the part customers actually experience: communication. He demoed a Slack bot his team built in a Twilio hackathon that turns the chaos of an incident channel into customer-ready summaries and status page drafts in well under a minute.

It is refreshing to see a talk pick the unglamorous problem. As he points out, there is plenty of content on resiliency and detection and very little on how incident response communication happens.

## Working the tools instead of the incident

Kumar starts by listing what a Twilio incident touches: FireHydrant to declare and run incidents, PagerDuty to alert, Zoom for the bridge, Slack for async chat (where around nine in ten incidents are run), Datadog dashboards, Atlassian Statuspage for customers, Google Docs for retrospectives, Confluence holding 15-plus years of product knowledge, and Slack canvases for action items. You can trim that list, he says, but you can't collapse it into one tool.

The trouble starts, in his words, when you end up "working the tools instead of working the incident". An incident commander's job is to keep people on mitigation, ask the right questions and push back when the discussion drifts. Every tab switch to gather data or draft an update takes attention from that.

He pairs this with the customer's view of the same incident: something is broken, the status page is still green, nobody has said anything, so they file tickets, call account managers and assume the worst. Each poorly communicated incident spends some trust, and trust is slow to earn back.

## Three Slack commands

The bot is a Slack app built on Windmill that calls OpenAI and is wired into the incident tool, Slack and Zoom chat and voice, and the Confluence and wiki knowledge base. Each command carries a persona describing who the answer is for:

- **A technical customer summary** for an incident number, phrased the way you would brief a technical customer.
- **A status page post**, generated as the usual title plus body.
- **An open question command** for anything else, including the questions people hesitate to ask on the triage bridge because interrupting the engineers who are fixing things costs time.

In the demo, he asks what Twilio's core products are and gets an answer drawn from the internal help centre; asks what a customer's 503 errors on all services might mean and gets causes plus pointers to internal troubleshooting articles; then queries a test incident for a technical summary and its start time. During a live incident the bridge audio is transcribed and fed in, so the answers keep up with what is being said. Responses came back in around 20 to 30 seconds in the demo.

## The next step is the risky one

The team is prototyping automatic posting to the status page, which needs the model to reliably separate internal detail from what customers should see. Kumar is clear that this is still being tested. He also mentions generating retrospective drafts from the same context. Both are the right order of operations: let humans review drafts until the filter has earned trust.

## Who should watch

Incident commanders, support leads and anyone who has typed "any update?" into a busy incident channel. It is a practitioner's talk with a real demo and an honest scope: a hackathon tool, a handful of commands and a clear problem. If you run Slack-first incidents, you could prototype the same thing with a workflow engine and an LLM API in a week.

Title: Fraud ML has to decide before the customer leaves checkout
Description: Naresh Karri (Intuit) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on running fraud, credit and ledger ML at transaction scale, with drift handled by shadow deployments.
Body:
A card authorisation has to finish while the customer is still standing at the checkout, and in that fraction of a second the system also has to run KYC, KYB and sanctions screening. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Naresh Karri, Group Product Manager for the Money Platform at Intuit, used that moment to explain what production MLOps looks like in finance: pipelines built for latency, compliance in every layer, and drift handled with shadow deployments and gradual traffic ramps.

## Every dropped checkout is lost revenue

Naresh's framing is the product manager's view of ML infrastructure. Financial institutions process enormous transaction volumes with tight response budgets, under GDPR, CCPA and FCRA, while keeping critical systems at 99.99% uptime. If the decision is slow or wrong, checkout conversion drops, and a lost sale is lost revenue. That turns latency and false positives from engineering metrics into business ones.

He groups the work into three applications: real-time fraud detection, credit assessment (where a loan or card decision takes seconds but covers prospecting and underwriting behind the scenes) and automated financial management, from portfolio optimisation to personalised guidance.

## Fraud detection is a pipeline, not a model

The fraud architecture starts with channels: point of sale, online and mobile, each with its own stream. Those feed pipelines and a feature store, then low-latency inference, decision engines with rules, and finally monitoring and audit with telemetry and retraining. His key line is that fraud detection "isn't just about a model", it is a pipeline that has to handle massive scale.

The hard parts he lists: sub-10-millisecond latency while processing more than 100,000 transactions per second at peak, feature freshness as fraud tactics evolve, rapid adaptation to new patterns, and false positives. Flag too many legitimate transactions and you lose good customers, so the balancing act has to be precise.

## Debits and credits still have to match

The financial management section has the most memorable engineering point. Money cannot be created or destroyed in a ledger; debits and credits must always reconcile. Naresh describes streaming each transaction to a Kafka topic, with consumers recording it in the ledger and driving reconciliation, settlement and clearing. Without that automation, tracking transactions becomes, in his words, super tricky. ML or not, the accounting identity always wins.

## The layered architecture

His reference stack goes bottom to top: data infrastructure with separate governance policies for structured and unstructured data; a training and validation pipeline that automates compliance checks and testing; a feature layer serving both batch and real-time features; a model registry with versioning, A/B tests and controlled rollouts; and a high-performance serving API on top for time-sensitive flows like checkout and loan applications.

Deployment runs on Kubernetes with separate clusters for training and inference, GPU nodes for deep learning, demand-based autoscaling, dedicated or isolated nodes for compliance-critical models, hot standby replicas and geo-distributed deployments. Monitoring spans latency, throughput, resource use and error rates, plus model accuracy and drift, plus business KPIs like approval rate, false positives and revenue impact.

## Drift is unavoidable, so plan the response

Naresh treats drift as a given in high-stakes systems. Detect it with statistical tests and segment-based analysis. Respond with shadow deployment comparisons, gradual traffic ramps up or down, and a human-in-the-loop approval fallback when in doubt, with an audit trail through every transition. A/B testing gets the same discipline: a clear hypothesis tied to a business metric, statistical rigour, controls for adverse effects, segment-level analysis and progressive rollout.

His takeaways: design for scale from day one, integrate compliance throughout, automate everything but keep fallbacks and humans in the loop, and invest in monitoring and response.

## Who should watch

Payments and lending engineers, and product managers who own ML-backed decisions with a latency budget. It is an architecture-level talk with a strong product lens.

Title: In regulated finance, MLOps is how responsible AI actually ships
Description: Narasimha Rao Vanaparthi (State Street) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on ethical guardrails, data lineage and continuous validation for AI in finance.
Body:
You cannot deny someone a mortgage and then shrug when they ask why. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Narasimha Rao Vanaparthi, Assistant Vice President at State Street, made the case that in financial services MLOps is the framework that makes responsible AI possible, and walked through the guardrails, data governance and validation loops that let a bank innovate without losing the regulator's trust.

Narasimha brings over 19 years in fintech, focused on modernisation and regulatory compliance, and the talk is aimed squarely at people who have to answer to auditors.

## MLOps means more than pipelines here

When people hear MLOps they think of pipelines and automation. In finance, Narasimha argues, it carries four jobs: automation that makes every model reproducible with an audit trail, monitoring that catches drift and anomalies before they cause damage, governance that bakes approvals and documentation into the process, and explainability, which is critical when decisions affect credit and fraud flags.

The challenges come in two flavours. Technical: real-time fraud checks that cannot wait even a second, legacy integration and extremely sensitive data. Regulatory: complete audit trails for every decision, rigorous validation before launch, and a stack of overlapping regimes from GDPR to CCPA plus sector-specific banking law. His comparison: building AI in finance is like building an aircraft engine.

## Who is doing it

He grounds the argument in public examples. Mastercard uses AI to monitor transactions at very large scale while reducing false positives. JPMorgan Chase has applied ML to credit scoring with explainability built in. HSBC has tested NLP systems for parsing regulatory filings. And predictive models can spot early signals of customer financial distress. The common thread: success comes from the MLOps framework around the model, not just the model.

## Guardrails across the whole lifecycle

The ethics section is the heart of the talk. Models can be highly accurate and still unfair; lending algorithms have been shown to penalise certain groups unintentionally. So the guardrails run end to end: representative datasets, fairness constraints during modelling, transparent documentation of how decisions are made at deployment, and monitoring for fairness as well as accuracy. He reports that some institutions cut bias by more than 70% without sacrificing performance.

Data governance sits underneath. Narasimha compares data lineage to a supply chain: you need to know where each dataset came from, how it was transformed and how it flows into the model, or regulators will not sign off. Automated tools detect and anonymise PII, differential privacy adds protection, quality is validated continuously, and access is logged. His argument is that good governance accelerates innovation because it builds trust.

## Validation never stops

Before deployment, models go through testing, statistical checks and compliance review. After deployment the real test begins: continuous monitoring for drift and degradation, with automated responses that retrain, alert or switch to a fallback model. Compliance documentation, once a heavy manual process, becomes automated so regulators get transparency in minutes. He cites a retail bank whose model-related incidents dropped 64% after adopting continuous validation.

## Start with the low-risk work

The best-practice advice is practical. Design modular platforms that separate data, model and serving layers. Use infrastructure as code. Keep every model version trackable. Start with low-risk use cases like compliance automation before moving into lending. Build reference architectures, set up a centre of excellence for governance, and bring compliance in from day one, because building it in is far easier than bolting it on later.

## Who should watch

Engineering and risk leaders in banks and asset managers who need a framework for responsible AI that maps onto real platform work. It is strategic and example-led rather than hands-on.

Title: If your AI triages the breach, it has to show its working
Description: Vasanth Mudavatu (Dell Technologies) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 on four pillars that make AI-driven security incident response explainable and auditable.
Body:
An AI system that flags an intrusion and can't say why is a pager with opinions. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Vasanth Mudavatu, Senior Principal Software Engineer for Gen AI, ML and Application Security Products at Dell Technologies, argued that once AI makes split-second calls in security operations, transparency stops being a compliance checkbox and becomes part of how fast you can respond. He offered a four-pillar framework for getting there.

The talk sits on the security side of incident management: breaches, threat validation, forensics and regulators, rather than latency spikes.

## Opacity costs you time at the worst moment

Mudavatu gives three reasons transparency is non-negotiable. Threats are evolving fast, so defenders need AI they can verify. Regulators in sectors like financial services increasingly require explainable decisions rather than suggesting them. And in the middle of an incident, a black-box recommendation creates hesitation: the analyst stops to second-guess the model, and a small anomaly gets time to become an organisational crisis.

That last point is the useful reframe. We usually talk about explainability as a governance cost. Here it is a speed feature.

## Four pillars

**Explainability, at three levels.** An executive summary for leaders with the high-level risk, analyst detail covering feature importance and the specific decision pathway, and a technical view of model weights and algorithmic logic for the people who own the model. Same decision, three audiences.

**Accountability.** Granular attribution, meaning you can point to the exact inputs, model components and pathways behind each decision. Oversight, giving human operators real-time insight and escalation protocols so they can step in when model confidence drops. And a tamper-proof record of inputs, outputs and human interventions that works as a chain of custody.

**Bias mitigation.** Curate representative training data so the model doesn't have blind spots, monitor live models for emerging bias, and validate threat assessments with objective fairness metrics. In security, bias shows up as threats you never see plus false positives you can't stop seeing.

**Auditability.** Trace each decision from input to recommendation so you can reconstruct why something was flagged, or missed. Version every model so you can roll back when an update raises false positives or opens a gap. Generate compliance reports automatically from decision traces and version history, so post-incident reviews start with evidence instead of archaeology.

## Where it pays off

His examples are critical infrastructure: power grid operators validating network anomalies faster, explainable models catching subtle malicious control patterns in water treatment SCADA systems, and transit security teams coordinating better because everyone can see the AI's reasoning.

He also takes on the objections. Worried that explanations leak proprietary models? Use layered explanations that give insight without exposing IP. Worried that interpretable models detect less? Pair a high-performance model with a dedicated interpretability module. Worried the transparent model goes stale? Run continuous learning while keeping the explanations intact.

Success is measured in faster triage, higher analyst confidence in recommendations, better cross-team coordination and fewer false positives.

## Who should watch

Security engineers and SOC leads evaluating AI triage tools, and anyone writing the procurement checklist for one. It is a framework talk with no tooling demo, so use it to sharpen the questions you put to a vendor: can it show the decision pathway, can it roll back a model, and can it produce the audit trail without a week of log-diving?

Title: Most finance ML dies after training. MLOps gets it into BI dashboards
Description: Mallikarjun Ramasani (Barclays) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on the ML lifecycle for finance and wiring model output into Tableau and Qlik.
Body:
The bottleneck in financial ML is rarely the model. It is everything that happens after. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Mallikarjun Ramasani, a software engineer and BI developer at Barclays, walked through the ML lifecycle as it plays out in finance and finished where a BI developer naturally would: getting predictions into the Tableau and Qlik dashboards people already trust.

## The maturity gap

Mallikarjun opens with a figure meant to sting: 83% of ML models in finance never make it to production. That is talent and platform spend with no business value. His reasons are familiar to anyone in a bank: complex requirements that slow deployment, legacy systems that resist integration, and real-time performance needs most pipelines cannot meet.

The fix he proposes is MLOps as the bridge between model development and business impact: automated deployment, logging, compliance checks, versioning and monitoring, so a risk review that took weeks can happen in days or hours.

## The lifecycle, with a financial twist at each stage

Each stage gets a finance-specific note. Ingestion is not pulling CSV files; it is streaming market data, payment data and alternative datasets. Feature engineering is where risk signals live: rolling windows, credit utilisation ratios, liquidity metrics. Training needs hyperparameter tracking and regulatory documentation, because every decision must be explainable. Deployment is containerised and runs through CI/CD. Monitoring covers drift, performance, compliance auditing and financial impact.

For market data he highlights temporal features (how price and volume evolve, short-term versus long-term trends) and market microstructure features like bid-ask spread, order book depth imbalance, transaction costs and slippage.

## A tool for every stage

The stack slide is a useful shopping list: Apache Airflow, Spark and Kubeflow for pipelines; DVC for data versioning; MLflow for experiment tracking and the model registry, with Neptune.ai for comparing runs; Docker and Kubernetes for scalable deployment, plus BentoML and Amazon SageMaker; and Evidently AI for drift detection and metrics.

CI/CD in his framing is a governance framework as much as a DevOps practice. New data passes quality and bias checks, the training pipeline generates documentation and risk reports automatically, canary releases reduce rollout risk, and compliance reviews are built into the pipeline as gates instead of email threads.

## Drift, measured

The drift section is concrete. Monitor input features and predictions over time, watch for training-serving skew, check pipeline health, backtest continuously, and alert on unexpected changes. For detection he names population stability index and KL divergence, with recalibration or retraining on recent data when drift is flagged. Governance rests on model cards aligned with SR 11-7, SHAP and LIME explainability reports, immutable logs and reproducible environments, with encrypted pipeline components, strict role-based access and container scanning.

## The BI bit

The part that sets this talk apart is integration with BI tools. Mallikarjun describes four approaches: APIs exposing model predictions as endpoints, embedded Python for in-dashboard computation, pre-computed feature stores for low-latency access, and custom visualisation extensions for model insights, across platforms like Tableau, Power BI, Looker and ThoughtSpot. The pay-off is predictive analytics and automated insights sitting inside tools business users already open every morning.

His takeaways: design the pipeline with financial requirements in mind from day one, integrate early with the BI tools users trust, and build compliance into the workflow rather than adding it later.

## Who should watch

BI developers and analytics engineers in finance who want to bring ML into their dashboards, and MLOps engineers who need a stage-by-stage tool map. It is a broad survey, so expect breadth over depth.

Title: A four-phase roadmap from threshold alerts to AI remediation
Description: Mallikarjun Ramasani (Barclays) at Conf42 Incident Management 2025 maps the AI/ML incident stack, from anomaly detection to RL-driven auto-remediation.
Body:
Threshold alerts tell you the CPU crossed 90%. They don't tell you the database will saturate in twenty minutes. At Conf42 Incident Management 2025, Mallikarjun Ramasani, Software Engineer at Barclays, gave an overview of how AI and machine learning move incident management from reacting to outages toward predicting and auto-remediating them, and offered a phased plan for getting there without betting the platform on day one.

This is a survey talk: broad, well-structured and short, aimed at teams deciding where to start rather than teams already running models in production.

## Reactive, responsive, predictive

Ramasani frames the history in three stages. First came threshold monitoring, where an alarm fires on CPU or memory and a human digs through logs. Then came the responsive era of correlation engines, automated runbooks and structured postmortems. The leap he cares about is the third: models that forecast failures before users feel them. He name-checks LSTM networks for time-series forecasting, causal inference to pin down dependencies, and reinforcement learning agents to handle remediation.

The motivation is the familiar one. Downtime in distributed systems cascades across dozens of services, human error and alert fatigue still cause a large share of incidents, and manual triage doesn't scale with microservice counts.

## Four capabilities, one pipeline

The core of the talk is four capabilities:

- **Predictive alerting**, with models trained on baselines that catch early warning signals before static thresholds trip.
- **Automated root cause analysis**, using graph-based models of service dependencies to isolate where a fault started.
- **Autonomous remediation**, where RL agents restart services, reroute traffic or scale clusters.
- **Intelligent escalation**, routing incidents to the right engineer by expertise, context and availability.

He then sketches the architecture that carries them: telemetry collected with OpenTelemetry or native agents, a unified observability layer such as Elastic or Datadog, an AI processing layer on Spark ML or TensorFlow Serving, orchestration into ServiceNow or PagerDuty to trigger runbooks, and a feedback loop that retrains continuously. Each major cloud has its own version of the loop: SageMaker with CloudWatch and Lambda on AWS, Azure ML with Log Analytics and Logic Apps, and Vertex AI with Cloud Operations and Cloud Functions.

## Garbage telemetry in, false positives out

The section worth slowing down for is about training data. Metrics give latency, throughput and saturation; logs can be parsed with NLP to pull out error codes and correlation IDs; past postmortems become labelled training sets for root cause models. His warning is blunt: a model trained on noisy, inconsistent telemetry produces false positives, and false positives are how you lose the on-call team's trust. Clean and normalise the pipeline before you train anything.

His one concrete example comes from financial services: a predictive model spotted database saturation about twenty minutes ahead of failure and scaled the cluster automatically, avoiding the outage.

## Phase it, and keep humans in charge

The roadmap runs in four phases: data readiness (centralised telemetry, normalised logs, baseline anomaly detection), augmentation (AI alert correlation and runbooks), proactive intelligence (graph-based RCA and RL remediation), then optimisation (predictive capacity planning, expanding across regions and teams). Start with one service, prove value, then scale. Explainability matters because engineers won't adopt recommendations they can't follow, and the end state he describes has engineers moving from firefighting to design and governance rather than disappearing.

## Who should watch

Engineering managers and SREs building a business case for AIOps, or looking for a sequence that doesn't start with "train an RL agent". If you already run anomaly detection in production, the later phases are where the value is.

Title: Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 - paved roads, self-healing and sane thresholds
Description: Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 in review, 83 talks on developer platforms, SCM at 50K engineers, ML inference, self-healing infra, zero trust and thresholds.
Body:
[Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025](https://www.conf42.com/platform2025) ran on September 4, 2025 with 83 talks, one of the biggest line-ups of the Conf42 year. The common thread: a platform is a product with internal customers, and its job is to remove decisions developers shouldn't have to make, whether that is which Git permissions to request, where an ML model gets served, or what the alert threshold should be. Engineers from Meta, Google, Microsoft, Qualcomm, eBay, Roku, Starbucks, Intuit, Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks, JPMorgan Chase, Fidelity and AWS showed their versions.

## The platform is a product, and DevEx is the metric

[Vasdev Gullapalli](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Vasdev_Gullapalli_scm_git_policies) (Qualcomm) gave the clearest example of platform thinking applied to something most companies treat as plumbing: source control. Managing GitHub, GitLab and Gerrit for more than 50K engineers, his team treats SCM as a platform with governance built in. Licence activation, deactivation and reactivation are all self-serve and automated, because a developer waiting on a licence is a developer not writing code, and an unused licence is opex nobody wants.

[Anil Kumar Veldurthi](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Anil_Kumar_Veldurthi_internal_ops_impact) (US Bank) covered how to build internal developer platforms that move delivery speed, and [Michel Murabito](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Michel_Murabito_practical_elevate_strategies) (Mia-Platform) focused on using AI in platform tooling to cut developer cognitive load. [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Mohamed_Najaaf_developer_gitlab_level) (AWS) demoed GitLab with Amazon Q Developer for modernising legacy Java and generating merge requests and reviews. [Rajani Jayantha](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Rajani_Jayantha_monolith_microservices_decision) (Wayfair) offered a decision framework for the eternal microservices versus monolith argument, and [Jayant Tyagi](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Jayant_Tyagi_development_ides_performance) (Salesforce) looked at cloud IDEs as a platform concern, security and performance included.

The most unexpected platform: design. [Pallav Laskar](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Pallav_Laskar_design_tokens_multi) (Zscaler) treats design tokens as infrastructure, run through GitOps workflows, with automated theming across platforms.

## Thresholds are maths, not vibes

[Emmanuel Bakare](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Emmanuel_Bakare_math_exploring_thresholds) (Twilio) gave the most quietly nerdy talk of the day. Static thresholds are easy to estimate and diagnose but noisy, single-variable and blind to organic growth. Dynamic ones adapt and produce fewer false positives, but need more data and a model of the system up front. He walks the numerical process for static thresholds step by step: filter outliers with IQR or z-scores, choose an aggregate, then reduce the error. If your alert thresholds were picked because a round number felt right, this one is for you.

## Self-healing is the new uptime

A whole cluster of talks tried to take humans out of the 3am loop. [Sureshkumar Karuppuchamy](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Sureshkumar_Karuppuchamy_defense_dashboard_large) (eBay) went beyond dashboards to adaptive rate limiting, auto-rollbacks, circuit breakers and closed-loop pipelines for a high-scale listing platform. [Shailin Saraiya](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Shailin_Saraiya_cache_millions_latency) (Roku) described self-healing cache infrastructure built to scale with a fast-growing user base. [Konstantin Berezin](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Konstantin_Berezin_context_agents) (Rapyd) used AI agents to tag anomalies in logs and traces so engineers are paged only for the outliers that matter, and [Lakshmi Srinivasarao Kothamasu](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Lakshmi_Srinivasarao_Kothamasu_firefighting_manual_pipelines) (Fidelity Investments) applied the same thinking to self-healing data pipelines. [Ajay Averineni](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Ajay_Averineni_observability_healing_intelligent) (IBM) tied AI-driven observability to automated remediation.

## Platforms for ML, data and money

ML infrastructure is now a platform team's job. [Gangadharan Venkataraman](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Gangadharan_Venkataraman_inference_orchestration_kubernetes) (Starbucks) shared patterns for Kubernetes-native ML inference platforms that keep data scientists productive, drawing on production systems at Starbucks and eBay. [Bhaskar Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Bhaskar_Goyal_container_paradise_chaos) (Google) went from container chaos to production-ready AI platforms, and [Peng Wang](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Peng_Wang_workloads_oceanbase_powering) (OceanBase) ran many workloads, AI included, on one database on Kubernetes. [Srinivas Chennupati](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Srinivas_Chennupati_knowledge_rag_strategies) (Fannie Mae) treated production RAG as enterprise knowledge infrastructure.

Financial systems got a strong showing. [Tapan Vijay](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Tapan_Vijay_card_planet_resilience) (Meta) covered the distributed systems and zero-downtime strategies behind planet-scale card processing, [Karthickram Vailraj](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Karthickram_Vailraj_sharding_replication_database) (Charles Schwab) went into database sharding and replication for fintech, and [Tarun Chataraju](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Tarun_Chataraju_modernizing_fixed_index) (JPMorgan Chase) modernised fixed-income index systems cloud-native.

## Security and the network underneath

[Naveen Kumar Birru](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Naveen_Kumar_Birru_perimeters_zero_trust) (Palo Alto Networks) laid out zero trust at enterprise scale, [Naresh Yelkoti](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Naresh_Yelkoti_transforms_code_bulletproof) (U.S. Bank) made the case for security as code in the pipeline, and [Anjan Kaleru](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Anjan_Kaleru_governance_identity_secure) (Sony Interactive Entertainment) used data to drive identity governance.

Then there was the network trivia question you didn't know you had. [Srinivas Shamkura](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Srinivas_Shamkura_ditched_multicast_challenge) (SADA) explained why the big clouds don't offer native multicast: forwarding-state explosion in software-defined networks, a protocol designed for one administrative domain colliding with multi-tenancy, dynamic routing that is hard to automate, and packet processing costs in virtual environments that can eat the bandwidth savings. The radio-station analogy alone is worth the click.

## Where to watch

All 83 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/platform2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrBMHyARfX-JY_7WHoF5qmDh). The series returns with [Conf42 Platform Engineering 2026](https://www.conf42.com/platform2026).

Title: An MLOps primer for fraud and risk models in banking
Description: Dileep Kumar Kanimetta (Microsoft) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 gives an intro to MLOps for bank fraud and risk models, from IaC and CI/CD to drift and governance.
Body:
If your fraud model takes weeks to reach production because someone sets up servers by hand, the fraudsters are iterating faster than you are. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Dileep Kumar Kanimetta, Advanced Cloud and Customer Experience Engineer at Microsoft, gave an introductory tour of how MLOps helps financial institutions run fraud detection and risk models reliably, with infrastructure as code, CI/CD, drift-triggered retraining and governance as the four load-bearing pieces.

This is a first talk on the subject rather than a deep technical one, and that is how to approach it.

## What breaks without MLOps

Dileep draws on more than 19 years in IT, including work on SWIFT integration onto Azure, which gave him a view of how ML can help with fraud and risk in payment processing. The problems he describes are the classic ones. Deployment is manual, so a team spends weeks standing up systems and installing code instead of improving models. Models are poorly tracked, so they drift and lose accuracy without anyone noticing. And governance gaps create compliance problems in an industry where regulators are watching.

His one-line definition: MLOps is to machine learning what DevOps is to software development, with the promise that deployment can happen in hours instead of the old, slow way.

## Four building blocks

The core of the talk is a blueprint of four components:

- **Infrastructure automation**, with the whole environment defined as code. He names Terraform and stresses isolated development environments so new projects cannot disturb current ones, and a separate, secured production environment.
- **CI/CD pipelines**, which he describes as an assembly line for AI: automated testing, pre-deployment checks and post-deployment validation.
- **Monitoring and alerting**, watching data accuracy, model metrics and feature importance, so drift is caught early.
- **A governance framework**, starting with documentation of models, data and process steps so compliance becomes part of the flow rather than an audit scramble.

## Retraining on a trigger, not a calendar

The retraining section is the most actionable. Drift detection watches for changes in incoming data; when a shift is detected, the training pipeline updates the model and it goes back through validation before serving. Dileep's claim is that with this automated, leading firms deploy models in hours rather than days.

He adds A/B testing to validate each change before full launch, automated bias detection so the system treats customers fairly across backgrounds and ages, and auto-scaling serving infrastructure because fraud attacks do not wait for business hours. In finance, as he puts it, every second matters and 24/7 availability is the expectation.

## Cloud choice and team shape

On platforms, Dileep is pragmatic: Azure, Google Cloud or AWS can all host an ML platform, and the choice comes down to your needs. On people, he argues for cross-functional MLOps teams where data scientists, engineers and operations actually talk to each other, because the pipeline crosses all their boundaries.

His closing advice is to start by measuring where you are and what needs to improve before building anything.

## Who should watch

Engineers and managers in financial services who are new to MLOps and want the vocabulary and the main components in one sitting. If you already run drift-triggered retraining in production, pick one of the more detailed finance talks below.

Title: Financial MLOps needs point-in-time features and segment monitoring
Description: Parul Purwar (IMC Trading) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on why finance needs its own MLOps stack, from point-in-time feature stores to segment-level drift checks.
Body:
A credit model can look healthy in aggregate while quietly failing one customer segment, and in finance that is the kind of failure a regulator finds before you do. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Parul Purwar, Strategy Leader at IMC Trading, laid out how financial MLOps differs from the standard playbook and closed on four rules: compliance is infrastructure, segment-level everything, explainability by design, and resilient architecture.

## Why finance is not just another ML domain

Parul frames the market first: she cites 85% of financial institutions deploying AI and a projected $78.6 billion market by 2030, with modern systems processing thousands of credit variables in real time. Then she lists what makes the domain hard:

- **Regulatory compliance** under FCRA, ECOA, GDPR and Basel standards, with full audit trails.
- **Explainability**, because customers and regulators are entitled to know why, including adverse action notices.
- **Market volatility**, which degrades models fast when the economy shifts.
- **Adversarial threats**, since fraud models face attackers actively trying to get around them.

## Standard MLOps, upgraded line by line

The clearest slide is a side-by-side. Standard MLOps has basic model versioning, simple A/B tests, general feature stores, standard CI/CD and basic dashboards. Financial MLOps needs immutable audit trails with regulatory metadata, champion-challenger testing with segment isolation, time-series feature stores with point-in-time correctness, compliance-integrated deployment workflows, segment-level monitoring with drift detection, and isolated infrastructure with controlled access.

Point-in-time correctness deserves the attention she gives it. If your feature store can leak tomorrow's data into a backtest, your model's historical performance is fiction, and regulators reviewing that backtest will not find it amusing.

## The components, stage by stage

On the data side: a financial feature store supporting thousands of versioned variables per customer with lineage and both batch and online serving; a secure access layer with fine-grained role-based controls, tokenised PII and encryption at rest and in transit; and a data quality framework with schema enforcement, anomaly detection and drift checks.

For model development: experiment tracking that records regulatory metadata, fair lending analysis, disparate impact assessment and model cards, plus an explainability toolkit with adverse action code generation, SHAP and LIME, and counterfactual explanations.

Deployment and operations run through a validation gateway (champion-challenger analysis, stress testing across market scenarios, sensitivity on key segments), compliance-integrated CI/CD with an immutable deployment trail, segment-aware monitoring, and retraining that is scheduled or triggered by events like a COVID-style market shock, with validation-gated promotion and versioned training sets.

## Four phases and four pitfalls

The rollout runs in four phases: foundation (feature store with compliance, experiment tracking, secure environments), production pipeline (compliance-integrated CI/CD, validation gateways, model registry), operational excellence (segment-aware monitoring, drift alerting, automated retraining), and advanced capabilities like multi-armed bandits for model selection, shadow-mode testing and adaptive per-segment thresholds.

The pitfalls are the useful bit for anyone starting out. Underestimating regulation, so compliance gaps show up late and force expensive rework: involve compliance from day one. Bolting on explainability afterwards. Monitoring only the aggregate and missing degradation in critical segments. Building for steady-state markets that collapse during shocks: stress-test against historical scenarios and wire up responsive retraining triggers.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers in banking, trading and fintech who need to explain to their team why the generic MLOps template is not enough, and data scientists who have never had to answer an adverse action request. It is architecture and process, not code.
