Title: Low-level control, high-level guarantees
Description: Rust changes expectations
Body:
# Rust: safe, fast, and somehow everywhere

Rust has a reputation.

Memory safety. Performance. Fearless concurrency. A compiler that cares deeply about your life choices. Naturally, it’s now being used to build some of the most intense systems out there.

Conf42 Rustlang 2025 is a showcase of exactly that.

This conference goes all in on real-world Rust. Ultra-low latency 5G systems, high-performance cloud platforms, data lakes, data meshes, financial APIs, and mission-critical emergency response systems all show up. If it needs to be fast, correct, and not crash at the worst possible moment, Rust is probably involved.

Cloud, data, and infrastructure get plenty of attention. From Rust on AWS and multi-cloud environments to edge cloud orchestration and distributed systems, the talks focus on how Rust is being used to replace bottlenecks and simplify complexity without sacrificing performance.

AI is everywhere too. Rust-powered machine vision, edge AI, predictive telecom systems, fraud prevention, multi-agent AI platforms, and ethical AI frameworks all make an appearance. It’s less about hype and more about building systems that need to run fast, safely, and continuously.

Security and regulation are a big theme. Zero trust architectures, DevSecOps pipelines, secure networking, regulatory environments, and memory-safe security tooling all feature heavily. Rust’s guarantees are put to work where mistakes are expensive and downtime is not an option.

You’ll also find plenty of Rust fundamentals in action. Concurrency patterns, cross-language libraries, zero-copy networking, performance tuning, and designing systems that stay maintainable as they scale.

If you like building serious systems and sleeping slightly better because the compiler has your back, this one’s for you. Rust isn’t just a language choice anymore. It’s an architectural one.

Title: FinTech databases need different consistency for different money
Description: Karthickram Vailraj of Charles Schwab covers sharding, replication and consistency choices for FinTech platforms at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025.
Body:
In most systems, eventual consistency means a like count is briefly wrong. In finance it can mean a balance is briefly wrong, which is a very different support ticket. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Karthickram Vailraj, Senior Manager at Charles Schwab, walks platform engineers through how distributed databases in FinTech are sharded, replicated and given different consistency guarantees depending on what the data is for.

The talk is a structured survey: foundations, sharding, replication, consistency, architecture patterns, security and a few case studies. It is a good refresher for anyone about to design storage for payments, trading or digital banking.

## Why finance is a special case

Vailraj sets the requirements first. Calculations allow zero margin for error and regulators require comprehensive logging. Load spikes come from market events, product launches, tax season and heavy trading days. Data residency laws vary by country while customers still expect low latency everywhere. High-frequency trading wants microseconds, digital banks want millions of concurrent users, and payment processors settle across currencies and jurisdictions. Monolithic databases do not stretch that far, which is how the industry ended up with distributed ones.

## Three ways to slice the data

Sharding enables linear scaling, and the hard part is keeping transactions intact across shard boundaries. He describes three strategies:

- **User-based sharding** keeps all of one customer's data on one shard, so most operations stay local. The catch is the operation finance exists for: moving money from one account to another, which may cross shards and needs distributed transaction management.
- **Geographic or regulatory sharding** aligns data placement with residency law. Cross-border payments then need routing logic and coordination protocols.
- **Time-based sharding** partitions historical transactions by date range, keeping recent data on fast shards while statements, tax records and archives live elsewhere.

He flags rebalancing as one of the hardest operational problems, because user bases grow unevenly and transaction patterns shift.

## Synchronous where it hurts, asynchronous where it doesn't

Replication gets the same trade-off treatment. Synchronous replication means every replica confirms before a transaction completes, so any replica can take over without data loss, at the cost of latency, especially across regions, and with extra conflict-resolution pain in multi-master setups. Asynchronous replication commits to the primary and propagates later, cutting write latency and enabling geographic read distribution, but you must monitor replication lag and handle conflicts.

The pattern he recommends is hybrid, based on data classification: critical financial data replicates synchronously within a region and asynchronously across regions, while less critical data can be asynchronous throughout. Consistency follows the same logic. Strong consistency for core banking, trading and payments; eventual consistency for analytics, reporting and customer-facing views; and causal consistency as a middle ground for multi-step workflows where related operations must stay ordered but unrelated ones need not.

## Patterns that come with an audit trail

On architecture, he groups event-driven design with Kafka at the centre, microservices with domain-driven boundaries and a service mesh, and CQRS paired with event sourcing. The FinTech-specific selling point of event sourcing is that the event log is the audit trail regulators ask for, and you can rebuild new read models from history later. Security covers encryption at rest and in transit, hardware security modules for keys, role- and attribute-based access, MFA and row- and column-level security.

The case studies are anonymised: an investment bank combining synchronous replication within a region and asynchronous across regions, a digital bank sharding by geography and account type with event sourcing, and a payment network sharding by geography and merchant with real-time fraud detection.

## Who should watch

Backend and platform engineers designing or reviewing storage for anything that moves money, and SREs who want the vocabulary to argue about replication lag with their DBAs. It is an overview rather than a deep implementation talk, so pair it with something hands-on.

Title: Blockchain in healthcare works best as a trust layer, not a database
Description: Brahmanand Reddy Bhavanam of Info Way Solutions shows at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 how blockchain, IaC and FHIR fit into medical platforms.
Body:
The quickest way to lose a room of engineers is to say blockchain and patient records in the same sentence. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Brahmanand Reddy Bhavanam of Info Way Solutions, a Java developer working with the US Department of Veterans Affairs, makes a more careful argument than the title suggests: keep sensitive medical data off-chain, put permissions, proofs and audit trails on-chain, and run the whole thing with the same infrastructure as code and DevOps discipline as any regulated platform.

## Why centralised health data keeps failing

Bhavanam starts with the shape of the problem. Healthcare systems were built decades ago around centralised databases and proprietary technology, back when data volumes were small. Today hospitals produce enormous volumes from electronic health records, imaging, wearables and remote monitoring. His example will be familiar to anyone who has moved house: a patient relocating from North Carolina to California does not bring their history with them, because it is fragmented across providers. Centralised systems are also attractive ransomware targets, and he points to attacks on US hospitals increasing sharply in recent years.

## Off-chain data, on-chain proof

The architecture has four layers: a distributed ledger for immutable, transparent records; a consensus mechanism, where he notes proof of authority suits healthcare because trusted institutions validate transactions faster than proof of work; smart contracts that automate agreements such as processing insurance claims once clinical data arrives or tracking trial consent; and a hybrid data architecture. That last layer is the key design decision. Because of privacy law, patient data stays off-chain and only cryptographic proofs and metadata go on-chain. For EHRs, he is explicit that blockchain does not replace the record system; it acts as the trust and access layer, verifying identity, recording permissions and proving provenance, with FHIR keeping it compatible with existing health IT.

The patient-centric piece follows: smart contracts let a patient grant temporary access to a specialist, an insurer or a research team, such as an oncologist in one hospital and a trial team in another, without bulk copying records between institutions.

## The platform engineering part

What earns this a slot at a platform conference is the delivery story. Docker and Kubernetes give consistent environments, Terraform provisions across clouds, Ansible enforces security and compliance baselines, and GitOps puts every change under version control with rollback. In a HIPAA world where audit trails and reproducibility are non-negotiable, that is a compliance tool as much as an engineering one, and it means a data centre failure becomes a redeploy rather than a rebuild.

His DevOps pipeline for this domain adds specialised testing (smart contract vulnerability checks, HIPAA compliance, simulations of clinical workflows), feature flags to try new features with limited patient groups first, continuous static and dynamic analysis, and release management that includes clinical sign-off and regulatory notification. It is a safety-first pipeline, which is a sensible frame for any system where a bad deploy has a patient on the other end.

## Beyond records

He covers several more use cases: immutable audit trails and automated consent and milestone payments for clinical trials; drug supply chain verification with per-product digital fingerprints, IoT cold-chain monitoring for vaccines and targeted recalls; privacy techniques such as zero-knowledge proofs, differential privacy and secure multi-party computation; scaling via optimised consensus, side chains and state channels; and federated networks that keep records in-country while allowing cross-border verification. The future-directions slide flags quantum-resistant cryptography and energy-efficient consensus.

## Who should watch

Engineers in health IT weighing distributed ledgers, and platform teams in any regulated sector who want a worked example of IaC and release management under compliance constraints. It is a broad survey rather than a production case study, so expect breadth over depth.

Title: Generative AI can turn a plain-English request into an ETL pipeline
Description: Achyut Kumar Sharma Tandra of Amazon explains at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 how LLM-driven ETL parses intent, plans execution and generates pipelines.
Body:
The number of pipelines a data team can ship is capped by the number of data engineers it has, and every analyst in the company knows it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Achyut Kumar Sharma Tandra, Data Engineer at Amazon, describes how generative AI changes that equation: users describe the data they need in plain English, and a system parses the intent, plans the work and generates, deploys and monitors the pipeline.

It is an architecture and adoption talk, not a product pitch. He does not name a specific tool; he describes the components such a system needs and the results he attributes to organisations that built one.

## Three bottlenecks of traditional ETL

Tandra names the familiar trio. Manual coding means every pipeline needs a specialist, so throughput equals headcount. The learning curve means the analysts and business users who need data most cannot get it themselves, so they file tickets and wait. Operational overhead means pipelines are never done; maintenance and troubleshooting eat the time that should go to new work. If your data team's roadmap is mostly a list of other teams' reports, you have met all three.

## Four components between a sentence and a Spark job

The core of the talk is the architecture, and it is the part worth stealing for a design review:

1. **Natural language interface.** Users type or speak a request, with contextual help to sharpen vague ones.
2. **Semantic parser.** Maps the request to real data entities, relationships and transformations. Ask for sales by product and it knows which tables hold sales and products and how they join.
3. **Execution planner.** Decides how to run it given data size, available resources and governance policies.
4. **Runtime engine.** Emits executable code for the target framework, whether a Spark job or a series of SQL queries.

Intent recognition is the step that separates this from keyword search. His example: a request about sales trends should become a time-series analysis with the right aggregations, not a single query. In a fuller walk-through, a marketing user's request for total sales by product category and the top ten customers turns into a sum, a group-by and a ranking, plus a time comparison, scheduling, output formatting, monitoring and notifications.

## The unglamorous foundation

To get from demo to enterprise, Tandra lists what has to sit underneath: metadata discovery that catalogues every source so the model knows what exists; credential management on zero-trust principles; caching to avoid recomputing frequently run reports; stream support for time-sensitive work such as fraud detection; data lineage tracking for audits and debugging; and API orchestration across systems. Lineage is the one regulated industries will care most about, because a pipeline nobody wrote still needs a paper trail.

## Results, and the caveats he gives

He shares two case studies from unnamed companies. A financial services firm with over 300 data sources went from an average of three weeks per new pipeline to hours, with most common integration tasks done without code and a smaller engineering backlog. An e-commerce company cut customer-behaviour pipeline builds from five days to 30 minutes, and its marketing team built over 75 pipelines on its own. He also cites aggregate benchmarks from a dozen enterprise implementations showing large drops in pipeline creation time and errors.

To his credit, he is realistic about limits. Complex transformations may still need hand-written code extensions, large volumes may need tuning of generated pipelines, and legacy systems without modern APIs need connectors. Governance must adapt to many user-generated pipelines, and data engineers shift from writing code to architecture and oversight. His rollout advice: discovery, a pilot on two or three low-complexity, high-value use cases, validation against the old method, then scale.

## Who should watch

Data platform leads drowning in report requests, and engineers designing an LLM-to-SQL or LLM-to-Spark layer who want a component checklist. If you are sceptical of no-code claims, watch for the limits section; it is more candid than most talks on this topic.

Title: A single pane of glass for the place you live
Description: Sheela Kakanur Shivayogi at Conf42 MLOps 2025 sketches an AI platform that pulls a residential community's scattered services into one personalised dashboard.
Body:
Your HOA probably runs on a WhatsApp group, a notice board and a property manager's inbox, and something important is always buried in one of them. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Sheela Kakanur Shivayogi, a systems QA engineer with more than 18 years in software, proposes fixing that with an AI-powered single pane of glass for residential communities: one dashboard that gathers services, communication and bookings and personalises them for each household.

She is upfront that this is a vision talk. The goal, in her words, is to spark ideas about what is possible, so treat it as a product concept with an ML angle rather than a production case study.

## The cost of a fragmented neighbourhood

Sheela starts with scenarios most residents will recognise: missing the last day of school registration because the reminder was lost in a chat thread, spending hours finding a plumber and regretting the choice, or never learning that the clubhouse was free. She cites figures that roughly 23% of the US population, about 77 million people, live in some form of community association such as HOAs, condos and housing cooperatives, and that more than 80% of new homes sold in 2023 were part of one.

Her list of costs is broader than inconvenience. Residents lose time across many apps and threads. Poor communication erodes trust. Shared assets like green spaces and courts go underused. Property managers stay stuck in manual workflows instead of building a connected community, which she argues eventually shows up in property values.

## Personalisation is the product

The core idea is a dashboard that knows who you are. A parent with a 7-year-old sees school updates, kids' activities and tutoring, not everything for ages 5 to 18. School reviews are aggregated from several sources. High-schoolers get academic clubs like debate, coding and leadership. The system refines its recommendations as families engage with them, which is the familiar feedback loop of any recommender.

Beyond education, the platform builds a vetted service-provider marketplace (plumbers, electricians, handymen with ratings, prices and availability), automates recurring upkeep like lawn care, snow removal and pest control, and points residents to mortgage refinancing, home insurance and healthcare referrals with faster appointment booking.

## The ML under the hood

Sheela names three building blocks. Predictive analytics anticipates demand, for example preparing maintenance resources if requests usually spike at a certain time. Natural language processing powers chatbots so residents can ask questions in plain language. Computer vision monitors facilities and opens maintenance tickets when it spots a problem. On top sit facility reservations without booking conflicts, rental matching, play-date coordination for families with children of similar ages, and real-time property valuation insights with suggested upgrades.

Her roadmap goes further out: predictive maintenance for shared areas in the near term, and longer-range ideas like shared autonomous shuttles for residents and programmes connecting toddlers, youth and seniors.

## Who should watch

Product engineers and ML practitioners looking at consumer or proptech applications, or anyone who sits on a residents' board and has wondered what the tooling could look like. If you came to an MLOps event for pipeline internals, this one sits at the application layer: it is about what to build, with the operations side left for later.

Title: In healthcare, an accurate model nobody trusts never ships
Description: Nikitha Edulakanti (Fresenius Medical Care) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on governed MLOps pipelines that let healthcare AI scale past the pilot.
Body:
A model that predicts ICU admissions with 95% accuracy on paper is worthless if clinicians and regulators cannot see how it got there. That is the opening example from Nikitha Edulakanti, Manager of Data and AI Solutions at Fresenius Medical Care, at Conf42 MLOps 2025, and her whole talk follows from it: in healthcare, governance is the part of the pipeline that turns a clever model into a used one.

Her framing line, taken from her deck, is that healthcare AI does not just need to be powerful, it needs to be trusted. The rest of the talk is about how you build that trust into the plumbing instead of bolting it on at the audit.

## Pilots die on data formats, not accuracy

Nikitha's diagnosis of why healthcare AI stalls is practical. Fragmented pipelines, data silos and compliance risk mean a model that works brilliantly at one hospital cannot move to the next. Her example is a pneumonia detection model trained on chest X-rays that performs well and then fails to expand because data formats differ across sites and nobody can sign off on compliance. A readmission-risk model piloted in one hospital needs standards, automation and monitoring before it can run in fifty.

She groups the obstacles into four: data governance (HIPAA in the US, GDPR in Europe, PHI protection at every stage), model trust (bias, drift, explainability), integration into clinical workflows, and operational scale. The integration point is the one engineers underrate. A triage tool that makes doctors log into a separate portal tends to fail; the same tool inside the EHR, with no extra clicks, has a chance.

## Compliance belongs in every stage of the lifecycle

Her definition of healthcare MLOps is DevOps practice plus the ML lifecycle, with governance embedded at ingestion, preprocessing, training, deployment and monitoring rather than reviewed at the end. Everything flowing through the pipeline must be traceable and auditable.

Because she works at a dialysis company, her examples come from kidney care. A kidney disease progression model ingests EMR data, masks PHI in preprocessing, trains with bias checks, deploys behind secure APIs and is monitored for drift quarterly. In another, IoT devices on dialysis machines stream patient vitals into the pipeline, and a sudden drop in blood pressure alerts clinicians before the patient deteriorates.

Her reference architecture is easy to steal: ingestion from EMRs, IoT devices, imaging and claims; a governance layer with data catalogs, access controls and audit trails; training with validation and explainability checks; containerised deployment across hybrid or multi-cloud; and continuous monitoring with a human in the loop.

## Generative AI explains the score, governance keeps it honest

The generative AI section is grounded. Rather than handing a clinician a bare risk number, a GenAI layer can explain that a patient is at elevated risk because of abnormal creatinine levels, a history of hypertension and two prior admissions in six months. Nikitha also lists documentation, coding workflows and data curation as places GenAI helps, and she is clear that without governance it can hallucinate or amplify bias.

Her closing metaphor works: governance is the steering wheel rather than the brake, the same way seat belts and traffic lights are what let cars go fast safely.

## Who should watch

ML and data engineers in healthcare or life sciences, and anyone who has watched a promising pilot die in compliance review. It is a framework talk with concrete clinical examples rather than a code walkthrough, which makes it useful for aligning engineers, clinicians and compliance teams on one picture.

Title: Stop guessing alert thresholds and derive them with statistics
Description: Emmanuel Bakare of Twilio shows at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 how IQR, the law of large numbers and curve fitting turn thresholds into math.
Body:
Every on-call engineer has a threshold they did not choose and do not trust: CPU over 80%, error rate over 1%, numbers somebody picked years ago and nobody has dared to move. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Emmanuel Bakare, Senior DevOps Engineer at Twilio, takes that problem apart with numerical methods: how to derive a static threshold you can defend, and when to switch to dynamic thresholds that follow the system as it grows.

This is the rare platform talk with actual maths in it, delivered in a friendly walk-through style. Bakare also builds CostCraft at Baseline HQ Cloud, which applies similar methods to right-sizing Kubernetes requests and limits; he mentions it, but the talk is about the methods, not the product.

## Static versus dynamic, honestly compared

Bakare starts with definitions. A threshold is an upper or lower bound at time t, and you act when a metric crosses it for long enough. Static thresholds are a fixed line through the noise: easy to set and easy to diagnose, but prone to noise, blind to organic growth, and usually tied to a single variable. Dynamic thresholds move with observations, rely on past and present data in a feedback loop, can combine signals such as CPU and memory, and produce fewer false positives, at the price of needing more data and more understanding of how your system behaves.

## Clean the data before you trust the line

For static thresholds he gives a three-step recipe. First, filter outliers, because a static threshold never adapts, so whatever skew you bake in stays there. The interquartile range method is his suggested starting point: compute Q1 and Q3, then set bounds at Q1 minus 1.5 times the IQR and Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR. Z-scores and standard deviation are the next step up. Second, pick an aggregate: a percentile or a plain mean. Third, reduce the error.

## The law of large numbers does the arguing for you

That third step is the heart of the talk. Take a percentile over rolling windows (p99 over each five minutes, say) and average across many windows. Outlier windows still happen, but the average converges towards the true value as samples accumulate. Bakare demonstrates it with a cron job that runs health checks three times a minute, enumerates the pass and fail combinations, and simulates one versus ten jobs over many iterations. Comparing p90 with p99.999, the p90 shows far more deviation, which suits a spiky system, while the tight percentile fits strict SLOs. Watching the standard deviation fall as iterations grow tells you the estimate is converging; watching it rise tells you it is not.

The payoff is a threshold you have proven over many iterations rather than guessed. Bring that to the next argument about whether the alert is too sensitive.

## Curve fitting for systems with a rhythm

Dynamic thresholds are anomaly detection under another name. Bakare covers supervised methods (logistic regression, KNN, naive Bayes, support vector machines), unsupervised ones (isolation forests, DBSCAN, PCA) and spends his time on the one he has used most: curve fitting. With simulated hourly sales data that rises and falls in a wave, he fits a sine-style function by iterating over amplitude, phase and constant within sensible bounds, and judges the fit with a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test, which he prefers over standard deviation because it accounts for sample count.

## Who should watch

SREs tuning noisy alerts, platform engineers building autoscaling policies, and anyone who has ever eyeballed a Grafana panel and typed a number into a YAML file. Bakare's own closing advice is fair: sometimes eyeballing is enough, but when systems behave strangely, statistics can save months of headache.

Title: An ML inference platform succeeds when deploying a model is boring
Description: Gangadharan Venkataraman of Starbucks covers Kubernetes ML inference at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, from CRDs and canaries to feature stores and caches.
Body:
A model that works in a notebook needs one pod. The same model serving a marketing use case in production might need a thousand, depending on latency targets and the features it pulls. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Gangadharan Venkataraman, Technical Lead for the AI/ML Platform at Starbucks, walks through how to build a Kubernetes-based ML inference platform that scales to that kind of load while keeping the developer experience simple enough that shipping a model feels routine.

It is a long, practitioner-flavoured talk, full of examples from retail and e-commerce, and it covers the whole path from orchestration to team structure.

## Three layers that have to agree

Venkataraman's architecture has three pillars. The orchestration layer is Kubernetes doing scheduling, resource allocation, container lifecycle, service discovery and GPU scheduling. The model serving layer loads and routes models, batches where it helps, and reformats responses into whatever the calling application expects. The data pipeline layer supplies features at three speeds: offline historical data, near-real-time features from Kafka streams, and true real-time checks just before a response goes out. His example: a model may pick ten items for a customer, but something has to confirm they are still in stock before the customer sees them.

## Teach Kubernetes what a model is

The orchestration detail is custom resource definitions. CRDs let teams talk in ML terms (a model deployment, a feature pipeline, an experiment run) instead of raw Deployments and Services, and custom operators handle the lifecycle: deployment workflows, autoscaling on inference load, and integration with feature stores and model registries. He points to Databricks as an example of the end-to-end pattern, with training, a feature store and connectors to managed Kubernetes on Azure and AWS.

The developer experience goal follows from that. Check code into a branch and it deploys to a dev namespace automatically. Merge to main and CI/CD tests, validates and deploys to production. No hunting through consoles.

## Rollouts in percentages, rollbacks without a meeting

The CI/CD section is where the platform pays for itself. Automated regression, integration, sanity and smoke tests run on every model change, and if they fail, the deployment never happens. After deployment, monitoring triggers automatic rollback when failures cross a threshold, which only works if artifact management keeps the last few stable versions ready. Canary deployment means one pod gets the new model first; gradual traffic shifting moves through 1%, 5%, 10% and then all traffic. He adds the pragmatic exception: for a hotfix, you need the option to go straight to 100%.

## Cold starts and caches

Serving gets three topics. Container images for ML need multi-stage builds to keep large artifacts and GPU dependencies out of the runtime image. Autoscaling keeps a minimum pod count warm and scales up with request rate. Cold-start optimisation covers model preloading, lazy initialisation and shared model caches; when a pod restarts its local cache is gone, so a persistent shared cache tier keeps latency in milliseconds instead of falling back to the database. He comes back to caching later for model chaining, where each cache hit saves a call to another model.

Monitoring rounds it out: accuracy metrics, prediction distribution and feature drift detection, so retraining happens when the data moves rather than on a fixed schedule.

## The people part

Unusually for an infrastructure talk, Venkataraman spends real time on organisation: a platform team that owns the infrastructure, scientists who build on it, domain teams that consume model output, and the business that defines the problem. His Starbucks example is a store where coffee wait times run long and a model helps rebalance baristas. Governance means design reviews, pull-request reviews and security scans that block merges, plus communicating platform migrations early so consuming teams are not surprised. Security for sensitive data, audit trails and data lineage get their own section.

## Who should watch

Engineers building or inheriting an internal ML serving platform on Kubernetes, especially the ones fielding complaints from data scientists that deployment takes too long. If you already run KServe or Seldon in production, the organisational and caching sections are the fresh material.

Title: AI can take the toil out of platform teams if humans stay in the loop
Description: Anbarasu Aladiyan of Compunnel maps AI-driven provisioning, scaling and self-service for platform teams at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, plus a phased rollout.
Body:
Platform teams are meant to make developers faster, and most of them spend their week answering tickets instead. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Anbarasu Aladiyan, Lead Java Full Stack Engineer at Compunnel, argues that AI-driven automation, in provisioning, scaling and self-service, is how platform teams climb out of reactive mode, and he lays out a four-phase plan for getting there without betting the cluster on it.

## The cost of the ticket queue

Aladiyan's problem statement is about time. Microservices multiply instances, every instance needs managing, and the platform team sits in the middle of thousands of developers and applications. He cites research figures that will feel familiar to anyone who has run an internal platform: developers losing several hours a week to infrastructure chores, a large share of feature delays traced back to platform bottlenecks, and platform engineers spending most of their time reacting and troubleshooting while the improvement backlog grows. Slow provisioning then shows up downstream as slower release cycles.

Treat the precise percentages as industry survey numbers rather than one team's measurement; the shape of the problem is the point.

## Three generations of scaling

The clearest part of the talk is a progression. Manual scaling means people adjust resources by anticipated need, so you get over-provisioning, performance issues and hours of response time. He adds a detail worth checking in your own cluster: instances idling at zero percent CPU and memory, and several low-utilisation copies of the same service, while other services wait for capacity.

Rule-based automation, with fixed thresholds and predetermined scaling rules, is where most teams live today. It helps, but it does not adapt and still needs frequent human intervention. The third stage is AI-powered orchestration that learns usage patterns, predicts needs and adjusts infrastructure in real time, turning scaling from an hours-long job into minutes.

## Where AI touches Kubernetes

For Kubernetes specifically he lists intelligent pod placement based on historical performance data, node scaling that anticipates workload changes, self-healing that shortens time to respond, and proactive detection of cluster-level problems. The headline claims are better utilisation, lower infrastructure cost and handling around three times the workload on the same hardware.

On the developer side, the vision is a self-service platform: infrastructure requested in natural language and translated into properly configured resources, configuration drift detected and corrected before it reaches production, developer portals that surface relevant docs based on project context, and continuous scanning of infrastructure as code with suggested fixes. His case study is a global financial services firm with roughly 2,800 developers and strict compliance needs, which rolled out self-service provisioning first, then anomaly detection, then automated compliance validation for every deployment, and reported a big drop in production incidents.

## Start with a human in the loop

The best section is on what goes wrong. Aladiyan lists poor-quality training data, skills gaps, resistance from operations teams, legacy integrations and worries about opaque AI decisions. His mitigations are practical: improve observability first and use synthetic data while real datasets build up, run education programmes and clear upskilling paths, put abstraction layers with well-defined APIs in front of legacy systems, keep comprehensive logs, use explainable approaches, and start with a human-in-the-loop model before letting automation act on its own.

The rollout runs in four phases: assess capabilities and pain points and define KPIs, build the foundation (observability, standardised IaC, API-first services), deploy targeted capabilities such as predictive scaling for critical workloads and a self-service portal, then scale across platform services and into CI/CD.

## Who should watch

Platform leads writing the case for AI-assisted operations, and teams still on rule-based autoscaling wondering what comes next. It is a strategy talk with survey numbers rather than a technical demo, so bring your own implementation details.

Title: Low-code ships fast; public code and governance keep it honest
Description: Anoosha Cherukuri (State of Tennessee) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on pairing low-code delivery with open, auditable public code and real engineering standards.
Body:
Low-code gets you speed, public code gets you trust, and you need both if the software belongs to citizens. That is the argument Anoosha Cherukuri, a senior software developer with the State of Tennessee, makes at Conf42 MLOps 2025: let business experts build the user-facing layer visually, keep the core logic open and auditable, and treat every drag-and-drop artifact like source code.

It is a short, structured talk, closer to an architecture primer than a war story. If you have ever inherited a pile of unversioned workflows built by someone who left, the premise will feel personal.

## The bottleneck is people, not tools

Anoosha opens with the pressure every government IT shop knows. Citizens expect public services to behave like the apps on their phone, regulators want transparency, executives want a return on every technology dollar, and there are not enough skilled developers to go around. She cites an IDC forecast of a global shortage of 4 million developers and the familiar Standish Group finding that a large share of software projects arrive late, over budget or not at all.

Her answer splits the problem in two. Low-code addresses speed and access: visual builders, prebuilt connectors to databases, APIs and authentication, and prototypes in days. Public code addresses trust and sustainability: software built in the open, documented so it can be audited, and reusable so the next agency does not pay for the same thing twice. Her example of public code done at national scale is Estonia, which runs nearly all government services on open standards.

## Put the forms in low-code and the rules in the open

The most useful section is the set of architecture patterns for making the two coexist. In a hybrid workflow, the user-facing layer lives in the low-code platform while business logic sits in public code. A customer-support chatbot might be assembled visually, but its escalation logic is coded and published.

API-first design keeps that split clean: forms call reusable APIs instead of writing straight into a database, so the same rule serves the portal, the back office and whatever comes next. Event-driven pipelines give you audit trails as a side effect, because every request is an event someone can trace later.

## A drag-and-drop workflow is still code

Anoosha's governance list is where the talk earns its place at an MLOps event. Every low-code artifact goes into version control. Workflows stored in Git get tested in CI with Jenkins, GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps, the same as anything else. Security is designed in through role-based access, encryption and audit trails, and dev, test and production must be identical, or the designer preview becomes the new works-on-my-machine.

She is candid about how this goes wrong. Low-code platforms can buckle under millions of transactions a day. Proprietary tools turn into cages. Citizen developers produce workflows nobody monitors. Her cautionary tale is a global insurer that adopted low-code widely and, a year later, had hundreds of apps with no central governance and months of auditing ahead of it.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevOps engineers in the public sector, healthcare or any regulated shop being asked to enable citizen developers without losing control of the estate. It is also a decent briefing for architects who need language to explain to leadership why low-code still needs pipelines. If you want deep ML content, this one is about the delivery plumbing around it, not models.

- [Sanjiv Kumar Bhagat on building trust in AI-enhanced public sector systems](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sanjiv_Kumar_Bhagat_algorithms_trust_sector), the trust half of the same problem.

Title: AI observability should tell you where the fire started
Description: Ajay Averineni of IBM shows at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 how AI on metrics, logs and traces cuts alert noise and drives self-healing remediation.
Body:
It is 3 a.m., the dashboards say CPU and memory are fine, the logs run to millions of lines and the traces are missing half the context. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Ajay Averineni, Lead Application Developer at IBM, opens with that scene and spends the talk on how to make it rarer: use AI on observability data to find the one cause behind a thousand alerts, then let the platform fix the common failures itself.

His background is the useful part. Averineni has worked on enterprise hybrid cloud platforms at IBM and on telecom-scale services at AT&T, where millions of customers expect service around the clock and the alert volume grows with the microservice count.

## More data, less insight

The problem statement is one most SREs will nod at. Traditional observability works when you run tens of services. At thousands, metrics spike constantly, logs are mostly noise (he estimates 90% of them do not matter), traces are fragmented, and every service raises its own alarms, most of them false positives. He describes teams at AT&T drowning in alerts, to the point where observability became a distraction instead of a help.

## What AI changes on each signal

Averineni's breakdown is per signal, which keeps it concrete:

- **Metrics:** models look for subtle drift, seasonality and predicted spikes instead of crossing a fixed line.
- **Logs:** NLP models sift millions of lines for unusual error patterns.
- **Traces:** graph analysis connects transactions across services and points at causality rather than mere correlation.

The architecture behind it is a straightforward pipeline: streaming ingestion of API, network log and metric data; a processing layer built on tools like Kafka and Spark handling millions of events per second; models that detect anomalies, forecast demand and correlate incidents; and integration back into dashboards, incident management and CI/CD. The CI/CD hook is the clever bit. Running anomaly detection against new builds flagged regressions before deployment instead of after customers found them.

His telecom example shows why thresholds alone fall short: a signalling service might show a latency increase so small no human would notice it, but a model trained on historical outages can flag it as the precursor to a major incident.

## Root cause in minutes, not bridge calls

The section that will sell this to your manager is root cause analysis. The traditional version is hours on a bridge call with networking, database and application teams arguing over whose graph is red. Dependency mapping with AI highlights the one failing node that triggered the downstream alarms. Averineni says that at AT&T this cut RCA from hours to minutes, which he frames as the difference between a four-hour outage and a twenty-minute hiccup.

## Self-healing, with guardrails

Detection is half the loop. The self-healing cycle he describes is detect, diagnose, decide, remediate and learn, feeding results back into the model. The examples are deliberately unexotic: restart a failed container, scale APIs ahead of a peak event such as an Apple launch, isolate a misbehaving dependency before it takes the system down. He insists on guardrails, with thresholds, approvals and audit logs, because automation that can scale your fleet can also scale your mistakes.

The roadmap is incremental: assess observability gaps, pilot on one critical service, scale across services, then keep refining models from real incidents. Start where the pain is greatest; no big-bang transformation.

## Who should watch

SREs and platform engineers buried in alert noise, and anyone pitching AIOps internally who needs a sober framing with an RCA story attached. It is an architecture-level talk with no code, and the forward-looking part on reinforcement learning for operations is brief.

Title: Cascading timeouts - every layer gives up before the one above it
Description: Madhavi Bhairavabhatla (Mastercard) at Conf42 MLOps 2025 on cascading timeouts, shorter limits inward so failures surface fast and threads stay free.
Body:
Most outages that start slow end badly, and a lot of them start with a timeout someone copied from another service. At Conf42 MLOps 2025, Madhavi Bhairavabhatla, Director of Software Engineering at Mastercard, makes the case for cascading timeouts: every upstream call waits longer than its downstream dependency, so the innermost layer fails first, releases its resources, and the error travels up while the client is still listening.

It sounds like a config detail. In a highly transactional system it decides whether one sick database becomes one bad minute or a full outage.

## Three anti-patterns you probably have

Madhavi starts with the timeouts she sees in the wild. Uniform timeouts use the same value at every layer regardless of who calls whom. Inverted timeouts let an outer service give up before the inner one, so the client gets an error while a downstream thread keeps working on a request nobody is waiting for. Excessive timeouts, the 30-seconds-plus kind, hold threads and connection pools hostage during exactly the incident where you need them back.

The symptoms are the familiar ones: thread pool exhaustion, database connection starvation, slow failure detection and, eventually, cascading service degradation. Her advice before changing anything is to go through incident and latency data and work out how many of your major incidents a bad timeout actually contributed to.

## Shorter as you go in, with a buffer at each step

The rule itself is simple. Timeouts get progressively shorter from the outermost edge inward, and Madhavi's implementation gives each downstream layer at least 500 milliseconds less than the layer above to absorb network latency and processing overhead.

Her worked example runs the whole stack. At the edge, the proxy route gets 3,000 ms and the backend proxy 2,500 ms, with circuit breakers and custom response codes for timeouts. The API gateway gets 2,000 ms with one retry and exponential backoff, enough for a second chance without a retry storm, plus caching of known failure responses. The application layer gets 1,500 ms, sized thread pools and a circuit breaker. At the database, she sets statement timeouts at the connection pool level (HikariCP in her example) and separate query timeouts for reads and writes.

The payoff is predictability. When something breaks, the system fails in a controlled way, which, as she puts it, is what engineers want most in the middle of chaos.

## ML inference needs its own budget

This is where the talk earns its MLOps slot. Model serving does not behave like a CRUD endpoint, so Madhavi separates model loading from inference with distinct timeout strategies, gives batch prediction jobs longer limits than real-time inference, and adds a fallback model for when the primary one times out. A cache of recent predictions keeps the service answering in a degraded state, and each model type gets its own circuit breaker tuned to its resource profile. A GPU-heavy model and a tiny classifier should not share one breaker.

## Measure first, then tune iteratively

Her rollout plan is refreshingly unglamorous. Baseline response times, error codes, thread pool and JVM usage under normal load. Assign preliminary values starting from the innermost layers (databases, caches) and work outward, adding buffer at each step. Deploy incrementally, run performance and chaos tests, then keep adjusting from real production data and incident reviews. Setting the numbers lower is not enough; each layer still needs time to do its real work.

## Who should watch

SREs and backend engineers running multi-tier services, especially anyone putting model inference behind an API gateway. If your timeouts were last reviewed when the service was created, this is a good evening's audit checklist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Suraj Modi (Uber) on exponential backoff for system resilience](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Suraj_Modi_system_resilience_backoff_computing), the retry half of the same design.
- [Yamini Rathamsetty and Karthik Akula on the retry storm that ate their budget](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Yamini_Rathamsetty_Karthik_Akula_cost_loops_tokens), what happens when retries in agentic AI go unbounded.
- [Nick Hodges (Rollbar) on self-healing systems](https://www.conf42.com/Chaos_Engineering_2022_Nick_Hodges_self_healing_systems) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2022.

[Watch Madhavi Bhairavabhatla's talk](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2025_Madhavi_Bhairavabhatla_fail_fast_recover) and then go and check what your load balancer timeout is.

Title: Fairness, privacy and explainability for CRM AI, with Rust underneath
Description: Ketankumar Patel of Wind River Systems at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on building ethical CRM AI in Rust, with privacy, bias checks, explainability and governance.
Body:
A lead-scoring model that keeps favouring New York and San Francisco is not malicious; it is just faithfully copying where deals closed before. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Ketankumar Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Ketankumar_Patel_memory_safety_zero), Senior Architect for Business Applications at Wind River Systems and holder of 13 Salesforce certifications, presented a framework for building CRM AI that is private, fair, explainable and governed, with Rust as the foundation.

Honest scope: the talk is mostly about ethical AI practice, explained through Salesforce examples such as Einstein GPT and lead scoring. Rust's role is the safety net under those practices rather than the source of the fairness itself.

## Great power, the usual caveat

Patel frames it with Uncle Ben: "with the great power comes with the great responsibility." AI writes the emails, forecasts the pipeline and handles service chats. Without ethics, he argues, it invades privacy, treats groups unfairly and makes mistakes at scale. Regulation is pushing the same way, with GDPR, CCPA and the EU AI Act requiring clear consent, the right to say no and proof that the system behaves.

His case for Rust is that memory safety, ownership and a strong type system mean fewer data leaks and fewer bugs in the code enforcing those rules, so the rules can be built into the code instead of added later.

## Four privacy techniques, explained with CRM examples

Each technique comes with a plain-language example:

- **Differential privacy:** a sales-trend dashboard where no individual customer can be identified.
- **Homomorphic encryption:** computing on data without decrypting it, like calculating a bill without seeing the numbers.
- **Secure multi-party computation:** two companies measuring customer overlap without revealing their lists.
- **Federated learning:** models learn inside each local Salesforce org and share only what they learned.

## Bias, explainability and governance

For bias, the framework adds detection metrics, fairness rules and continuous monitoring. His second example is a chatbot that answers faster in English than in Spanish because the training data was lopsided.

The explainability section is practical. Local explanations answer why this lead scored 92 (five emails opened and a demo scheduled). Global explanations show what drives sales overall, say webinar attendance more than website clicks. Counterfactuals ask whether one more support ticket would change a churn prediction.

Governance runs through four phases: ethics rules coded into the design, audit trails that cannot be erased during development, real-time monitoring at deployment, and continuous testing in operations, because AI is never set-and-forget.

## The case study

A multinational needed a CRM recommendation engine that was fair, private and transparent. Built in Rust with federated learning, differential privacy, fairness rules and per-recommendation explanations, it achieved, he reported, full GDPR and CCPA compliance, 93% less demographic bias, 27% higher customer trust scores and zero privacy leaks over 18 months. The company is not named.

## Who should watch

Salesforce and CRM architects starting to ship AI features, and engineers who need a clear vocabulary for privacy and fairness techniques. Rust developers expecting compiler-level fairness guarantees should adjust expectations: this is a practice framework with Rust underneath.

Title: Real-time computer vision needs a platform that heals itself
Description: Manoj Sai Jayakannan of George Mason University lays out a containerised, observable, self-healing platform for computer vision at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025.
Body:
Computer vision is where ML platforms stop being forgiving. Video frames do not wait for a slow model, and a GPU node falling over mid-stream is a gap in the footage, not a retry. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Manoj Sai Jayakannan of George Mason University presents a playbook for AI platforms that serve real-time vision workloads: containerised pipelines, careful model rollout, three layers of observability and infrastructure that recovers without a human.

The talk is a compact reference architecture. It reads like the design doc you wish you had before your first GPU cluster went into production.

## Split the pipeline into pods with one job each

Jayakannan starts from three principles: infrastructure as code (Terraform or CloudFormation, so GPU-enabled environments can be replicated and versioned), GitOps with Git as the single source of truth and automated rollbacks, and testing that covers data validation and model validation, not only code.

The pipeline itself is modular. Ingestion pods pull video streams from IoT sensors. Preprocessing pods normalise and augment. Training pods use distributed GPUs. Inference pods serve predictions over REST or gRPC. GPU access comes through the NVIDIA container runtime and Kubernetes device plugins, builds are tied to Git commits so they are deterministic, and node pools are tuned for each stage. Horizontal autoscaling applies to inference, where load actually varies.

## Ship models like risky code, because they are

Model rollout gets three patterns, each for a different appetite for risk. Blue-green runs the new version beside the old and switches traffic. Canary releases expose a slice of users first. Shadow deployments run the new model on production traffic without showing its output to anyone, which is the cheapest way to find out that your new detector thinks every shopping trolley is a person.

Serving performance comes from three optimisations: request batching to keep GPUs busy, keeping hot models in memory to avoid cold starts, and accelerated serving frameworks such as TensorRT, Triton Inference Server and TorchServe. Jayakannan says these typically give a three- to five-fold throughput gain and quotes latency dropping from 200 ms to 15 ms.

## Watch the model, not only the machine

Observability spans three layers: infrastructure (CPU, GPU, memory, network), pipeline (success rates, queue latency, data integrity checks) and model (prediction drift, latency, error rates, fairness metrics). The tooling is mostly what you would expect: Prometheus and Grafana for infrastructure, OpenTelemetry for tracing through ML pipelines, and ML-specific monitoring tools for drift and bias detection. Tie those signals to alert thresholds and the system can respond to GPU saturation or falling accuracy before users see it.

## Recovery is a feature you test

Self-healing comes from ordinary Kubernetes mechanics used deliberately: liveness and readiness probes restart failing containers, cluster autoscaling adjusts compute, and chaos engineering with Chaos Mesh injects failures to prove the recovery actually works. To remove single points of failure he adds distributed processing across nodes and regions, geo-redundant clusters for disaster recovery and lower latency, and event-driven rerouting when a node dies.

The outcomes he reports from organisations doing this are 99.9% uptime, model updates in hours instead of weeks, and 20 to 40% lower cost from better GPU scheduling. He notes the same practices carry over to NLP, recommendation and generative AI.

## Who should watch

ML platform engineers moving vision models from notebooks to production, and SREs who have just been handed a GPU cluster. It is a checklist talk rather than a single case study, but nearly every item on it is concrete and nameable.

Title: AI projects stall in pilots when the infrastructure comes last
Description: Bharath Reddy Baddam of New York Life gives Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 a map of AI-native platforms, from GPUs and feature stores to observability.
Body:
Plenty of companies have an AI pilot. Far fewer have an AI product, and the gap between them is usually infrastructure nobody budgeted for. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Bharath Reddy Baddam, Senior Salesforce Developer at New York Life Insurance Company, lays out what an AI-native platform needs underneath it, from GPU scheduling to model observability, and why treating infrastructure as an afterthought keeps models stuck in experiments.

This is an orientation talk, a structured tour rather than a war story. If you are the platform engineer who just got told the company is doing AI now, it is a tidy checklist of the layers you will be asked to own.

## Training and inference are different animals

Baddam's first point is the one teams most often get wrong: training and inference have opposite shapes. Training is massively parallel and GPU-hungry. Inference, for recommendation engines, chatbots or fraud detection, is about millisecond responses and scaling out. Build one environment for both and you get the classic trio he names: over-provisioning, under-utilisation and costs that spiral.

The scheduling consequence is mixing CPUs and GPUs on purpose. Lightweight preprocessing runs on CPUs, heavy training goes to GPUs, and a scheduler that knows the difference saves real money. For scaling training itself he points to Kubernetes and container orchestration, distributed data parallelism across GPUs, network topology that can carry the traffic, and fault tolerance so one failed node does not kill a multi-day run.

## Data pipelines decide whether the model is any good

The data section leans on two components. Feature stores let teams reuse features across models and keep training and serving consistent. Stream processing adds real-time signals alongside batch pipelines over historical data. His fraud example makes the latency point well: if the pipeline lags by even a few cycles, the window to stop the fraudulent transaction has already closed.

## Observe three layers, not one

AI platforms need monitoring at the infrastructure level (GPU utilisation), the data level (pipeline health) and the model level, which he calls the most important: accuracy, precision, recall and fairness indicators, tracked continuously so drift, bias and degradation show up before they become an incident. Performance tuning gets practical notes too: managing GPU memory, NVMe storage, batching inference requests and caching frequently accessed features.

## No single blueprint

The implementation-patterns slide is a useful reality check. High-frequency trading needs ultra-low latency and real-time pipelines; content recommendation needs per-user personalisation at scale; healthcare puts compliance, accuracy and ethical safeguards first. One architecture will not fit all three, so the platform has to follow business goals rather than a reference diagram.

Governance closes the technical part: defending models against adversarial attacks, data privacy, role-based access, and explainability that holds up under regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA. The roadmap is phased: short-term wins like feature stores, observability in the medium term, and longer-term bets such as edge AI.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers and architects about to inherit ML workloads, and engineering managers who need a shared vocabulary with their data science teams. Seasoned MLOps practitioners will find it familiar ground; the training-versus-inference framing is still a good one to borrow when arguing for separate clusters.

Title: Design tokens are platform infrastructure, not a style guide
Description: Pallav Laskar of Zscaler argues at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 that design tokens belong in build pipelines, with schemas, reviews and versioned releases.
Body:
Most design systems die the same way: a beautiful Figma file, a PDF style guide, and fifty hand-copied hex codes that drift apart one pull request at a time. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Pallav Laskar, Principal Software Engineer at Zscaler (and eleven years at Adobe before that, on Adobe Sign, Acrobat and Adobe Experience Manager), makes the case that the fix is to treat design tokens as infrastructure: versioned, validated, built by a pipeline and shipped to every platform from one source.

It is a short talk, closer to a lightning session than a full hour, and it moves fast. That makes it a good one to send to the frontend lead who keeps saying the design system is just CSS.

## One definition, many outputs

The core idea is a token hierarchy run through a build. Raw values sit at the bottom, global and semantic tokens on top of them, and component tokens at the end. Each layer adds meaning, so a button does not know it is `#0057FF`; it knows it is the primary action colour, and the primary action colour knows which blue that is this quarter.

Tokens live in a source format and a pipeline transforms them into whatever each platform eats: CSS variables for the web, Swift for iOS, Android XML for Android. Laskar's summary is one definition, many outputs. Theming falls out of the same structure: multiple brands, light and dark modes and accessibility-driven themes come from composing token sets, not from copying definitions.

If that sounds like infrastructure as code with nicer colours, that is exactly the point.

## The numbers from Zscaler's Nimbus

The concrete part is Zscaler's own design system, Nimbus. Laskar describes consolidating repositories and moving to tokens, which by his account took about 240 kB off the bundle and improved First Contentful Paint by roughly 18%. Those are web-vitals numbers, which is a nice change from the usual feel-good outcomes of design system talks.

He also summarises a Fortune 500 rollout across seven product lines and three acquisitions, quoting around 40% faster feature development and fully automated WCAG compliance checks. Acquisitions are the interesting detail: three companies' worth of buttons is where hand-maintained style guides go to die.

## Governance is what makes it a platform

The section platform engineers will recognise is governance. Token changes go through schema validation, automated contrast testing guarantees accessibility rules hold, peer approval keeps design and engineering in the loop, and documentation updates itself. Tokens get a formal lifecycle: creation, review, distribution, monitoring and a structured deprecation, so old values can be retired without breaking every app that still references them.

For developers, the before-and-after is the familiar one from any good platform: scattered hard-coded values on one side, type-safe tokens with IDE autocomplete on the other.

## Adoption is the hard part, and he says so

Laskar is candid that rollout is never smooth. Teams resist, legacy systems complicate integration, and governance can look like extra risk. His answer is codemods to migrate existing code, a phased rollout (audit and standards, a foundation repo, a pilot, then scale and automate), schema validation and early proof points. His closing line frames tokens as the API contract between design and development, which is the sentence to steal for your next architecture review.

## Who should watch

Frontend platform teams, design system owners, and anyone running a multi-brand or multi-platform product where the blue has five definitions. If you already ship tokens through Style Dictionary or similar, the governance and deprecation parts are the bits worth your time.

Title: An AI pricing platform is only as good as its fallback price
Description: Amaresh Sahoo of Xometry on real-time AI pricing at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, from cached predictions to circuit breakers and fallback prices.
Body:
Most ML systems can be wrong for a while before anyone notices. A pricing system cannot: a bad number shows up on the invoice. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Amaresh Sahoo, Vice President of Pricing, Sourcing and Analytics at Xometry, walks through the architecture of real-time AI pricing platforms, and his recurring theme is that the model is the easy part; low latency, consistent data and a sane fallback when things break are what keep revenue intact.

## Why pricing is a hard platform problem

Sahoo lists the constraints up front. Every decision has direct revenue impact. Inputs come from many places at once: competitor prices, inventory and sourcing data, customer behaviour. Customers expect an instant quote, not a spinner. And the system has to behave consistently across geographies while meeting each region's regulations.

The infrastructure answer is familiar but well assembled: edge computing to put pricing compute near each market, container orchestration that scales with demand, CDNs and dedicated links between data centres to trim API latency, and stream processing that ingests and validates data continuously. The detail worth noting is real-time data quality checks that catch anomalies without adding processing delay, because a stale competitor feed is how you end up underpricing a whole catalogue.

## Cache the common case, infer the edge case

The sharpest idea is about where models run. Rather than calling a model on every request, Sahoo describes caching predictions for common scenarios and reserving real-time inference for the edge cases, with memory allocated deliberately so the hot models answer fast. It is the pricing version of the read-heavy cache you already have in front of your database, with the twist that the cache needs to know when its inputs have gone stale.

Around that sits the model lifecycle: ensembles where models sit behind other models, weighting each by its strengths and controlling for its biases; strict version control so you can compare a new model against the old one and roll back; continuous training on fresh feedback; and monitoring that looks at customer and financial outcomes together, not only technical metrics. He also notes that off-the-shelf APM tools miss what matters here, so teams need custom tracking of prediction latency, model performance and business impact.

## Experiments need automatic brakes

Pricing has to be tested constantly, and Sahoo covers A/B tests, multi-armed bandits and contextual bandits. The platform lesson is the guardrail: automated rollback triggers tied to KPIs, so a pricing experiment that starts hurting the business reverts without waiting for someone to read a dashboard on Monday.

## Degrade to a boring price, not to an error

The reliability section is the one to bookmark. Circuit breakers isolate a failing data source or a degraded internal service before it drags everything down. Graceful degradation means serving cached prices, a simplified pricing algorithm or default pricing rules when the AI service is unavailable. Replication is split: synchronous for critical data, asynchronous for less time-sensitive information. Health checks go beyond a ping and verify that models actually loaded and predictions look sane, and disaster recovery plans have to account for rebuilding model state and warming caches, not only restoring data.

Security and compliance get their turn too: regional rules for European, North American and Asian customer data, federated learning where data cannot move, and role-based access with fine-grained authorisation.

## Who should watch

Engineers building any real-time decisioning system where an outage costs money directly: pricing, quoting, bidding, fraud scoring. It is an architecture overview from the business owner's chair, not a code walkthrough, which makes it a good primer for the platform team that will run such a system.

Title: Security as code turns the release-day gate into pipeline checks
Description: Naresh Yelkoti of U.S. Bank lays out at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 how scanning, policy as code and secrets detection move security into CI/CD.
Body:
If your security review happens the week before release, you have not got a security process, you have a scheduling problem. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Naresh Yelkoti, Senior Information Security Engineer at U.S. Bank, argues for security as code: scans, policies, data protection and compliance checks written down, versioned and run inside the pipeline, so security stops being the last gate and becomes something every commit passes through.

## The story every platform team has lived

Yelkoti opens with an example from his own pipelines. Releases used to depend on a manual security sign-off at the end of the cycle, so problems in Terraform and container images surfaced when the code was already nearly production-ready. Fixes landed late, release dates slipped, and both developers and security engineers ended the quarter annoyed with each other.

He frames it as the dual mandate of platform engineering: the business wants faster delivery, regulators and customers want secure, compliant, resilient platforms, and those pulls collide exactly at the release gate. Security as code is his bridge between them.

## Five pillars, one pipeline

The framework has five parts: automated security integration, serverless security, infrastructure security, intelligent risk management and secrets management. The useful bit is that each comes with concrete tools rather than vibes.

- **Automated integration** means scanning in the CI/CD system you already have: GitLab security scanning, Azure DevOps security tooling, AWS Inspector.
- **Serverless and infrastructure** means checking Lambda and Azure Functions before release and enforcing policy as code on cloud configuration during deployment.
- **Secrets** means scanning for hard-coded credentials before they ever reach production, with tools such as GitGuardian, Snyk and AWS Secrets Manager.

He quotes plenty of industry figures along the way (vulnerability reductions, faster time to market, prevented misconfigurations). Treat those as the sales case for your leadership deck; the architecture is the part to take home.

## Alert fatigue is the failure mode of shift-left

The most practical section is about what happens after you add all those scanners: a flood of findings that nobody reads. Yelkoti's answer is contextual risk scoring and smarter alerting. His example: GitGuardian detected hard-coded secrets in GitLab repositories, the findings flowed into a ServiceNow workflow, and contextual prioritisation let the team fix critical exposures immediately while parking the low-risk noise. That is the bit most shift-left talks skip, and the bit that decides whether developers keep the scanner on.

He also shares an audit angle: automating container and code scanning with Prisma meant compliance teams spent far less time on audit preparation, because the PCI evidence was always current instead of assembled by hand.

## A roadmap in four phases

The rollout plan is sensible and unglamorous. Phase one is pipeline scanning, baselines and training. Phase two adds policy as code, secrets detection and feedback loops. Phase three brings risk dashboards and automated remediation. Phase four is maturity: continuous improvement, threat modelling automation and even chaos engineering. Looking forward, he points at AI-assisted vulnerability prediction and zero trust pipeline architecture, and mentions piloting anomaly detection on API traffic to separate normal behaviour from suspicious calls.

## Who should watch

Platform and DevSecOps engineers who own a CI/CD system in a regulated shop (PCI, HIPAA, SOC 2), and security teams trying to get out of the release-blocker business. It is an overview rather than a hands-on demo, so experienced AppSec folks will know most of the tools; the alert-triage and audit-evidence examples are what earns the time.

Title: Rust from wearable to hospital, a health platform for older travellers
Description: Raphael Shobi Thomas at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on a Rust healthcare AI stack for senior travellers, from no_std biosensors to WebAssembly translation.
Body:
By 2030, about 703 million travellers worldwide will be 60 or older, and many carry chronic conditions into places where they do not speak the language. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Raphael Shobi Thomas](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Raphael_Shobi_Thomas_memory_safety_code), a senior software engineer and independent researcher, presented a health and safety platform for those travellers with Rust at every layer: biosensor firmware, data pipelines, risk models, in-browser translation and medical records.

## One language from the sensor to the cloud

The pitch for Rust is the usual trio (memory safety, native performance, compile-time thread safety) plus one that matters a lot here: cross-compilation to Windows, Linux, embedded targets, iOS and Android. A single language across devices is a real simplification when the same health record moves from a wrist to a hospital.

He described the platform handling 2,847 concurrent users, each with more than 47 health variables, at sub-millisecond latency, operating under GDPR across 34 countries.

## Firmware that survives bad connectivity

The embedded layer runs `no_std` Rust with embedded-hal on biosensors, which means no standard library, no OS services and tight memory. On top sits a custom protocol built for poor or intermittent connectivity: data is buffered locally and forwarded when the link returns, end-to-end cryptographic checks guard against tampering, and medical data gets priority. That is the right design for a traveller who walks out of mobile coverage mid-arrhythmia.

## The data and ML pipeline

On the server side, Tokio handles continuous health streams, zero-copy parsing reads biosensor data straight from byte buffers, and a custom Serde serialization pipeline processes medical records about 340% faster than a comparable Python implementation, by his measurement. Schema evolution relies on Rust's type system to keep old and new data formats compatible.

Risk assessment uses Candle and the tch-rs bindings, plus ONNX Runtime for pre-trained models on CPU or GPU. The predictor shares the model across threads behind `Arc` and `Mutex`, a deliberately simple pattern for safe concurrent access, and evaluates around 150 risk factors per assessment.

## Translation that never leaves the device

The WebAssembly piece is the most interesting design choice. Medical terminology translation runs as Rust compiled to WebAssembly in the browser or on the device, covering 23 languages at a reported 94% accuracy, with about 60% lower latency than server-side translation. Sensitive health data never goes to a server just to be translated.

Records use the Substrate framework to log every access on a blockchain, with patients managing permissions on chain and smart contracts enforcing consent.

## The Portugal scenario

His case study ties it together: a 72-year-old traveller in rural Portugal, a sensor detecting an irregular heart rhythm and elevated blood pressure, the model flagging a potential cardiac event with 92% confidence, the system finding the nearest medical facility, translating the medical history into Portuguese and sharing verified records with the receiving hospital.

## The honest part

He is upfront about the costs: few medical-domain crates compared with Python or Java, FFI work to reach existing healthcare systems, slow certification under GDPR, HIPAA and MDR for new tech, long early build times, and the ownership learning curve. His answers were custom domain crates, type-safe bindings, compliance checks in CI/CD, build tuning and team training.

## Who should watch

Engineers building health, wearable or edge-AI systems who want to see one Rust stack stretched from firmware to the browser. Compliance-minded teams will appreciate the challenges section.
