Title: Secure multi-tenant platforms for banks start at the admission controller
Description: Nageswara Rao Nelloru at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on securing multi-tenant Kubernetes for finance with mTLS, admission control and policy as code.
Body:
A financial platform team has two jobs that pull in opposite directions: satisfy the regulator and let developers ship. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Nageswara Rao Nelloru of Marquee Technology Solutions, a technology lead with 20 years mostly in financial services, walked through the controls that let a multi-tenant cloud-native platform do both.

His abstract frames the stakes with results from platform teams securing financial operations across 530+ organisations, including incident detection cut from 21 days to 4 hours. The talk itself is a layered tour of the controls rather than a breakdown of those numbers.

## The threat list is long

Nageswara opens with the threats financial services face: increasingly AI-assisted attacks, phishing and social engineering, ransomware, insider threats, and third-party and supply chain risk. His goal is a multi-tenant platform that balances heavy security demands with rapid innovation as institutions move to cloud-native architectures. The platform evolves from managing infrastructure to running a self-service ecosystem with zero trust built in.

## Isolation and encryption by default

Multi-tenancy in finance means careful isolation boundaries, data segregation and access control, implemented as micro-segmentation for defence in depth at every layer. Service mesh does a lot of the work: fine-grained traffic control, mutual TLS for all service-to-service traffic, and security policies that travel with the workload so protection is consistent wherever it runs.

## Admission control is the gate

The Kubernetes section covers the container lifecycle: image scanning and vulnerability management, secure configuration, and runtime monitoring that flags anomalous behaviour. The piece he dwells on is admission controllers, the gatekeepers that check everything from resource limits to security context before a workload is admitted. Non-compliant workloads are rejected automatically, with clear feedback on how to fix them, and every decision is logged for compliance reporting and later investigation. A rejection with a fix-it hint beats a pentest finding six months later.

## GitOps and policy as code

GitOps treats infrastructure changes with the same review rigour as application code. Policy as code captures security requirements in a form machines can enforce and humans can read. Progressive security gates validate changes before they land, and vulnerability and compliance scanning run throughout the pipeline. Repeatable deployment patterns eliminate configuration drift.

Identity gets its own section: automated provisioning and de-provisioning from authoritative sources, attribute-based access that considers context beyond roles, and proper management of non-human identities such as service accounts, API keys and secrets. Observability ties it together with distributed tracing, SIEM correlation of platform events with security signals, automated response that contains threats while preserving evidence, and continuous compliance evidence collection instead of manual documentation.

## Secure has to be usable

His most important line of argument comes late: the most secure platform delivers no value if developers can't use it. Self-service with policy enforced automatically, templates and examples, and watching where developers hit friction are what keep teams on the paved road. He closes with chaos-style security experiments to find weaknesses before attackers do, and a reminder to design controls that can be updated as threats and regulations change.

## Who should watch

Platform and security engineers in regulated industries, especially anyone writing the admission and policy layer for a shared Kubernetes estate. The transcript is dense with terminology; the slides help.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Ashish Dibouliya on Kube-native AI data governance for banking compliance](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Ashish_Dibouliya_banking_compliance_governance) covers the data side of the same problem.
- [Peter O'Neill on Terraform apply secured by Open Policy Agent](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_2022_Peter_ONeill_terraform_apply_secured_open_policy_agent) is policy as code in practice.
- [Piotr Zaniewski on multi-tenant GPU sandboxes with vCluster](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Piotr_Zaniewski_sandboxes_gpu_multitenant) shows another approach to tenant isolation.

Title: Containers, Terraform and GitOps turn AI deploys into a non-event
Description: Google's Bhaskar Goyal at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on AI-aware Docker builds, Kubernetes GPU pools, Terraform modules and GitOps for model deploys.
Body:
"It works on my machine" is funnier when the machine has a GPU and the model is several gigabytes. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Bhaskar Goyal, a software engineer at Google, laid out a four-part path from chaotic AI deployments to boring, reliable ones: AI-aware containers, Kubernetes, Terraform and GitOps, with a 30-day and 90-day plan to get there.

None of the pieces are new. The value is in how each one is tuned for AI workloads, and in the order he suggests adopting them.

## Three ways AI deploys go wrong

Bhaskar groups the pain into environment inconsistency (libraries, dependencies and hardware differ between a data scientist's laptop and production), manual deployment that depends on one person who might be on holiday, and the production fires that follow. The cost is deployment cycles stretching from days into weeks or months, and teams losing faith in AI projects.

## Docker patterns built for models

Containerisation fixes the laptop problem, but AI adds GPUs, huge artifacts and unusual scaling. His three Docker patterns:

- **Multi-stage builds** for smaller, more secure production images with faster pulls.
- **Hardware-aware base images**: CUDA-enabled for GPU workloads, CPU-optimised for CPU inference, instead of one generic base for everything.
- **Layer caching by change frequency**: stable system packages first, frequently changing code and model artifacts last.

He quotes a principal engineer at a Fortune 500 financial services company crediting containerisation with a 65% cut in model deployment failures.

## Kubernetes for expensive hardware

On Kubernetes, the AI-specific bits are horizontal pod autoscaling on custom metrics such as prediction requests per second, GPU node pools with resource quotas so costly GPUs are shared fairly across teams, and canary deployments that roll a new model version to a small slice of users before going wide.

## Terraform and GitOps keep it reproducible

For infrastructure as code he recommends Terraform modules for common AI components (model registries, inference clusters, feature stores), separate directories or workspaces per environment so promotion through CI/CD stays consistent, and remote state in S3 or Google Cloud Storage with locking, encryption and versioning turned on. The disaster recovery payoff: rebuild the platform in hours instead of days.

GitOps ties it together. Git is the single source of truth for infrastructure and application config, a pull-based operator such as Argo CD or Flux syncs the cluster, drift is detected and corrected, and a rollback is a git revert.

## The numbers and the plan

The results he cites from organisations adopting these patterns: 85% less deployment time for complex AI workloads, 73% fewer production incidents, 40% infrastructure savings and three times more models in production.

The plan is the most useful slide. In 30 days, containerise one high-value AI workload with multi-stage builds, write basic Terraform modules for the key components, and set up a GitOps repository. In 90 days, run Kubernetes with GPU support, add canary releases for model updates, and build monitoring tailored to AI workloads.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who just inherited the ML team's deployments, and ML engineers who want production to stop being a surprise. If you already run Argo CD with GPU node pools, it is a confirmation, not a revelation.

- [Graziano Casto on managing AI workloads in cloud environments](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2025_Graziano_Casto_workloads_cloud_environments) covers the operational challenges from another angle.
- [Kosseila Haddalene on running vLLM inference on Kubernetes across clouds](https://www.conf42.com/MLOps_2026_Kosseila_Haddalene_vllm_kubernetes_gpu) is a production GPU blueprint.

Title: Put AI inside the platform loop, and keep a rollback for the model
Description: Praveen Kumar Guguloth at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on AI-driven platforms, four architecture patterns, guardrails and gradual adoption for CI/CD.
Body:
Monitoring that tells you what broke is useful; a platform that scales before the Black Friday spike is better. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Praveen Kumar Guguloth (listed with State University of New York, and introducing himself as a VP of engineering in financial technology with over 14 years in IT) argued that AI should move from a tool developers use to a layer inside the platform itself, closing the loop between observing and acting.

It is a short, strategic talk. The abstract leads with headline results (47% faster CI/CD across 150+ enterprises); the talk itself spends its time on patterns and guardrails rather than walking through those numbers, so treat them as the framing, not the content.

## Complexity beyond human scale

Praveen's diagnosis: traditional platforms rely on manual configuration, monitoring explains failures after the fact, and developers spend more time debugging infrastructure than writing features. With hundreds of interacting microservices, no human team can model all the relationships intuitively. That is the opening for AI: spotting patterns humans miss and automating routine pain.

He describes AI as a closed optimisation loop. Observe system data in real time, learn from history, act proactively (scale before the traffic arrives, rebalance before the bottleneck, adapt to business criticality), and get smarter with every cycle.

## Four architecture patterns

The core of the talk is four patterns:

- **Federated AI models** keep decisions close to where the action is and avoid a central bottleneck.
- **AI orchestration layers** act as the platform's brain, seeing the whole system and making optimisations no single service could.
- **Event-driven intelligence** responds to context in real time, for example triggering auto-healing on a predicted anomaly instead of on downtime.
- **Edge-based processing** pushes AI into the developer workflow for faster code review and CI/CD feedback.

His two domain examples show different priorities. In e-commerce it is about surviving peak days: pre-emptive scaling, prioritising critical fixes, rolling back a bad release automatically. In finance it is continuous compliance auditing, secure provisioning and predictive risk detection, where intelligence is about avoiding catastrophic mistakes as much as speed.

## Guardrails before autonomy

The best section is the least glamorous. Praveen insists on progressive adoption: start with service meshes that learn anomaly patterns, then add automated performance tuning gradually, then developer-workflow assistants. Build trust in the algorithms and with the engineers who rely on them.

He wants AI-driven systems to avoid becoming black boxes: careful data pipelines, rigorous model deployment workflows, and the ability to roll back a model just like application code. Security covers the models too, since they can be poisoned, and regulation demands explainability. If the platform denies a transaction or reconfigures resources, someone must be able to say why. Without those guardrails, in his framing, AI becomes a liability.

He closes looking ahead to largely self-adjusting platforms, which he compares to a self-driving car for infrastructure.

## Who should watch

Engineering leaders building a roadmap for AI in their platform, and SREs who want a vocabulary for where predictive automation fits. Hands-on engineers looking for implementation detail will want to pair it with something more concrete.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Chinmay Gaikwad on enterprise-ready CI/CD pipelines with agentic AI](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Chinmay_Gaikwad_cicd_agentic_ai) is the hands-on version.
- [Debosmit Ray on a GitOps and automation approach to developer platforms](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2024_Debosmit_Ray_gitops_automation_efficient_platforms) covers the declarative foundation AI would sit on.

Title: When friend-of-a-friend breaks SQL, build a graph platform
Description: Muthuselvam Chandramohan of Intuit Mailchimp at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on real-time graph platforms, partitioning, query tuning and backups.
Body:
Find every friend of a friend who shares at least three interests with a user, and your relational database starts guessing how many joins you meant. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Muthuselvam Chandramohan, senior software engineer at Intuit Mailchimp with more than 20 years in data engineering, walked through the architectural decisions behind a graph platform that serves both real-time and analytical queries.

It is the most thorough talk of its kind at the event: partitioning, replication, storage tiers, query tuning, memory, integrations, monitoring and backup, each with the trade-off spelled out.

## Relationships as first-class citizens

The case for graph is multi-hop analysis when you don't know the number of hops in advance. Relational databases force you to assume a depth and write the joins; a graph database stores the relationship itself, so traversals follow edges whose next step depends on the previous result. Social networks, supply chains, fraud and knowledge graphs all look like this.

The platform challenges are threefold: sub-second responses for fraud and cybersecurity, integration with very different producers (microservices, batch pipelines, packaged apps), and scale. Vertical scaling hits a ceiling, so horizontal it is.

## Event-driven in, partitioned underneath

Muthuselvam favours an event-driven architecture with Kafka or another streaming platform feeding the graph. Many graph databases ship Kafka connectors, updates route to the right partition, and you get replay after an outage plus multiple consumers. One stream can feed a fraud graph and a marketing graph, each tuned for its own audience.

For horizontal scale he splits the decision in two. Partitioning (vertex-cut or edge-cut) should follow your query patterns, not your data shape, and not every graph database supports both. Replication ranges from quorum-based eventual consistency, which he considers reasonable because a graph is usually a system of reference rather than the system of record, to leader-follower and Raft-style consensus.

## Storage tiers and query tricks

Storage depends on latency needs: in-memory options such as RedisGraph for sub-second lookups, persistent stores such as Neo4j or Amazon Neptune when durability and recovery matter more, or a graph layer on a NoSQL store you already run.

The query optimisation section is where the graph-specific ideas shine:

- **Early termination**: stop traversing once you have the answer.
- **Bidirectional search**: start from two anchors (a country and an age group) and meet in the middle.
- **Cost-based starting points**: check vertex degree and avoid starting a traversal at a supernode.

Memory tuning follows: vertex and edge pooling to calm the Java garbage collector, compressed representations such as CSR adjacency lists, and splitting hot partitions onto more compute.

## Integration, monitoring, backup

Integrations come in three flavours: change data capture from existing databases, GraphQL as the schema layer in front of the graph (the graph does the heavy traversal, GraphQL presents it), and Spark or Trino connectors for analytics. Monitoring watches query complexity, hot vertex heat maps, and graph-shape metrics such as degree distribution and clustering coefficients. For backup he recommends full graph backups over incremental ones, because interconnected data doesn't split cleanly into change logs.

His closing caution is worth framing: not every use case needs a graph. Know the use case and the target users first.

## Who should watch

Data and platform engineers evaluating graph databases for fraud, identity, recommendations or knowledge graphs. It is long and dense, so it rewards a second screen with notes open.

- [Prateek Mittal on knowledge graphs as the backbone of AI-first software delivery](https://www.conf42.com/Large_Language_Models_LLMs_2026_Prateek_Mittal_knowledge_graphs_delivery) shows the knowledge-graph angle.
- [Sasidhar Reddy Somula on real-time fraud prevention at scale](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sasidhar_Reddy_Somula_real_time_fraud) covers the sub-second fraud requirement from the SRE side.

Title: Chakra UX maps seven human needs onto product design
Description: Pratyush Tewari of Blue Book Services at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 uses the seven chakras as a checklist for designing for the whole user.
Body:
If your product crashes, nobody cares how delightful the onboarding animation is. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Pratyush Tewari, head of UX design at Blue Book Services and a human-computer interaction specialist in New York City, used the seven chakras of Hindu tradition as a framework for "conscious design": a checklist that starts with reliability and climbs to flow and purpose.

He is clear that this is a metaphor, not a belief system you need to sign up for. The chakras are a map of human needs, built up the way Maslow's hierarchy is, and the map is the useful part.

## Beyond clicks and conversion

Pratyush opens with a question every designer recognises: have I covered all my use cases? His answer is to focus on the edge cases of the human experience, not only the happy path. Engagement, conversion and retention metrics, he argues, can push teams towards addictive patterns and digital anxiety. Conscious design asks what the product does to the person emotionally and intellectually, not just what it does for the funnel.

## The seven checks, bottom to top

Each chakra becomes a core need plus UX principles you can test against:

1. **Root (Muladhara), security**: is it usable, reliable and safe with my data? His example is a banking app. If it fails here, no other feature matters.
2. **Sacral (Svadhisthana), pleasure**: aesthetics, micro-interactions, moments of delight, room for creativity, like Instagram's filters.
3. **Solar plexus (Manipura), control**: undo, customisation, efficiency, the feeling of a tool rather than a maze. Notion and Asana are his examples.
4. **Heart (Anahata), connection**: empathy, community, and support that feels human. He notes that getting stuck with a bot when you need help fails this one.
5. **Throat (Vishuddha), honesty**: clear copy, transparent pricing, accurate feature descriptions, and system feedback that shows real status rather than a fake spinner.
6. **Third eye (Ajna), intuition**: smart defaults, personalisation, continuity across devices, anticipating needs. A playlist that seems to read your mind.
7. **Crown (Sahasrara), flow**: the tool disappears and the user achieves something meaningful, like a distraction-free writing app.

The lower three are about the individual; from the heart up, the needs turn social. A good product, he argues, activates several at once. The music recommendation example hits intuition, pleasure and connection together.

## Why it is at a platform conference

The talk barely mentions infrastructure, which is the point. Internal platforms are products too, and developers are users with the same needs: a portal that crashes fails the root check, error messages that hide what broke fail the throat check, and a golden path that remembers your context passes the third eye. Swap "user" for "developer" and the closing questions still work: is it reliable, enjoyable, empowering, connecting, clear, intuitive, transformative?

## Who should watch

Designers and product managers, and platform teams who treat their internal developer platform as a product. Engineers who want architecture diagrams should skip it; anyone who has shipped a technically perfect tool nobody liked should not.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Jessica Wirt on why UX unicorns do not exist](https://www.conf42.com/Mobile_2022_Jessica_Wirt_ux_unicorns_myth_of_oneperson_usability_team) is about building the team that can do this work.
- [Gian Wild on why security and accessibility can be friends](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Gian_Wild_accessibility_security_inclusion) pairs with the root and throat checks.
- [Vignesh Kuppa Amarnath on AI-powered cognitive support for digital accessibility](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Vignesh_Kuppa_Amarnath_accessibility_support_cognitive) extends designing for the whole person.

Title: Keep React, move the math, Rust and WebAssembly for BI dashboards
Description: Shahzeb Akhtar of UnitedLex at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on fast BI dashboards, with heavy computation in Rust compiled to WebAssembly and the UI left in JavaScript.
Body:
Everyone has opened a dashboard and watched it think. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Shahzeb Akhtar](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Shahzeb_Akhtar_memory_security_rust), Director of IP Strategy and Technology at UnitedLex, argued that the fix is not a new frontend framework: keep React or Vue for rendering and move the aggregation, filtering and heavy calculations into Rust compiled to WebAssembly.

Akhtar leads the IP data science team behind Vantage for IP, a patent intelligence platform that runs natural language processing over very large patent collections, so dashboards that crunch a lot of data in the browser are his day job.

## Why dashboards are slow

His diagnosis has three parts. Heavy data processing done in JavaScript leads to slow rendering. JavaScript's dynamic nature, and untrusted code running in the browser, widen the attack surface. And inefficient code with frequent data transfers wastes CPU on both the client and the server.

## WebAssembly as a compilation target

He spends a moment on what WebAssembly actually is, which is useful if you have only heard the name. It is not a language but a low-level binary format for a stack-based virtual machine. "Think of it as the assembly language of the web." Modules run close to native speed in a sandbox, so a buggy or malicious module cannot reach the rest of the page.

## Rewrite only the hot path

The workflow is deliberately selective:

1. Identify the performance-critical parts of the dashboard and write only those in Rust.
2. Compile to a `.wasm` module plus the JavaScript glue, with wasm-bindgen handling the calls between the two.
3. Import the module from the existing frontend like any other library.
4. Keep rendering in your existing UI framework.

He maps this onto three layers: a data layer (SQLx for database access, Polars for data frames), a processing layer (Rayon for parallelism, ndarray for numerics) and a visualization layer. For charts in Rust he lists Plotters, Charming (a Rust API over Apache ECharts) and Plotly, plus Tauri for desktop apps.

## The evidence he picked

Akhtar's examples are public ones rather than his own benchmarks. Figma rewrote its multiplayer engine in Rust and reported a 3.8x reduction in memory and 6x reduction in CPU usage; he admits it is not a dashboard, but the real-time sync problem is similar. A graph visualization of related Spotify artists went from under 10 frames per second to 60 after moving its calculations to Rust and WebAssembly. And Databento uses Polars, which he cited as outperforming pandas by 8 to 15x on benchmarks.

## Fast and useless is still useless

The second half is a reminder that performance is not the product. His design principles: know your audience (a CEO and an analyst need different dashboards), keep it simple, provide context through benchmarks and targets, use visual hierarchy, allow customization and drill-down, choose the right chart type, and design for colour blindness, keyboards and screen readers. He closes with a chart-selection infographic as bonus material.

## Who should watch

Frontend and data engineers whose dashboards stall on client-side computation, and teams wondering whether WebAssembly is worth the build complexity. If you already ship Rust to the browser, the design half is the part with new material.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Beyond Static Dashboards: How Rust-Powered Dynamic UIs Transform Cloud Infrastructure Management](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Tashi_Garg_cloud_ai_rust) by Tashi Garg (Juniper Networks) at Conf42 Remix 2026.
- [Using Rust and WASM](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Andrey_Makarov_wasm_assembly_code_web) by Andrey Makarov (Islamic Coin) at Conf42 Rustlang 2024.

Title: One SQL query instead of four databases for RAG and search
Description: OceanBase's Peng Wang at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on running SQL, full-text and vector search in one Kubernetes-native database for AI apps.
Body:
A typical RAG backend asks MySQL for metadata, a vector store for embeddings, Elasticsearch for full text and Redis for the cache, then hopes they all agree. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Peng Wang, global technical evangelist at OceanBase, argued that platform teams can collapse that stack into one database, and showed how OceanBase does it on Kubernetes.

Honest scope first: this is a vendor talk about OceanBase, and the numbers are OceanBase's customer results. The architectural argument travels further than the product, though.

## AI workloads are now normal workloads

Peng starts with the demand side. Citing IDC, he says over 92% of global data is unstructured, and he points to surveys showing most enterprises already run AI infrastructure platforms and are embedding agents in core applications. His point: RAG and semantic search have left the lab, so platform and database teams inherit their operational problems.

Those problems differ by workload. Q&A chatbots want low-latency semantic search with context. Log analytics wants high write throughput, search and aggregation. Core business systems want ACID transactions and strong consistency. Teams usually answer with one specialised database per need, and then spend their weeks maintaining the ETL between them.

## Count the network round trips

The clearest slide compares two request paths for AI-powered knowledge retrieval. In the conventional design, one user query fans out to MySQL, a vector database and Redis, adding up to at least four network round trips and about 170 milliseconds end to end, plus the job of keeping all of them consistent. In the OceanBase version, the same request is one query against one engine, at about 50 milliseconds, with strong consistency maintained throughout.

His hybrid-query example makes it tangible: a coffee shop within 500 metres, average spend under a set price, a rating above a threshold, and no queues. That mixes GIS, relational and semantic data. In a stitched stack it is several queries and some glue code; in OceanBase it is a single SQL statement.

From the customer case he cites, query latency dropped by over 70%, data that used to take hours to refresh became available in minutes, and the integration code to maintain shrank by over 40%.

## Under the hood

The architecture section covers what platform engineers will ask about. Data is distributed across availability zones for horizontal scale. OceanBase is containerised with operator-based management and elastic scaling of compute and storage. Consistency comes from a Paxos-based consensus protocol with three replicas across zones and automatic failover.

Multi-tenancy is the other half of the pitch: different workloads share a cluster but run in isolated tenants with dedicated resources, so the log-analytics tenant doesn't become the noisy neighbour of the transactional one. A single SQL layer covers structured data, full-text and vector search.

## Who should watch

Platform teams running a vector database next to a relational one and tired of syncing them, and anyone designing RAG infrastructure who wants a counterpoint to the reflex of adding another specialised store. If you need a neutral comparison of databases, look elsewhere; this is one vendor's well-argued case.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Alejandro Duarte on RAG in production](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Alejandro_Duarte_llm_vectors_semantic) covers the challenges on the retrieval side.
- [Amarachi Iheanacho asks whether a Kubernetes operator can replace a DBA](https://www.conf42.com/Database_DevOps_2026_Amarachi_Iheanacho_postgres_k8s_tuning), a good reality check on operator-managed databases.

Title: Predictive maintenance is a platform problem before it's a model
Description: Muruga Angamuthu of Techtonic Industries at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on cloud-native platforms for industrial IoT predictive maintenance.
Body:
A model that predicts a bearing failure is worthless if the sensor data never reaches it. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Muruga Angamuthu, BI manager and data and analytics architect at Techtonic Industries, laid out the cloud-native platform that sits under AI-driven predictive maintenance for factories, drawing on 23 years in data engineering, BI and manufacturing.

His thesis: data scientists should focus on the model, not the plumbing, and platform engineers are the ones who build the plumbing.

## From fix-it-when-it-breaks to eight days' notice

Muruga walks the maintenance ladder: reactive (fix after failure, pay for unplanned downtime), scheduled (often too early or too late), condition-based (better, still no foresight), and AI-driven predictive maintenance. The figures he cites for the last rung are 8 to 12 days of advance warning with around 90% prediction accuracy, and implementations reporting roughly half the downtime they had before.

Getting there, he notes, takes infrastructure plus organisational change, technical and cultural.

## Four architecture choices that decide the rest

The patterns are sensible and battle-worn:

- **Multi-tier processing**: edge devices for fast local decisions, cloud for heavy analysis, hybrid where you need both.
- **Event-driven architecture**: handle data as events happen so sudden surges from many sensors don't queue up.
- **Kubernetes auto-scaling** for peak loads.
- **Tiered storage**: hot storage for real-time access, cold storage for history used in training.

Then the layers: ingestion over industrial protocols such as OPC UA, MQTT and Modbus, streamed through Kafka or Pulsar; time-series databases and data lakes such as Snowflake and Databricks; ML orchestration with Kubeflow or MLflow and a feature store; and GraphQL and REST APIs feeding dashboards and alerts. Loose coupling is the rule, so each layer can change without dragging the others along.

## The edge needs its own checklist

The edge computing section is the most practical. Handling critical alerts locally is much faster, sending only important data saves bandwidth, and the plant keeps working when connectivity drops. The platform engineer's list: deploy models onto devices with little memory, update them remotely without a truck roll, use mutual authentication, and keep data consistent between edge and cloud over unreliable links. Anyone who has tried to OTA-update a gateway on a factory floor will nod along.

## Case study and roadmap

His case study is a global manufacturer with 37 facilities and 12 equipment vendors. The platform used a hybrid AWS and Azure architecture, Snowflake analytics, Kubeflow pipelines and custom adapters for the vendor mix. Reported results: 42% less downtime, $4.3 million in annual savings, a 93% model deployment success rate and a 2.5x productivity gain for the data science team.

The roadmap is phased: foundations (connectivity, basic pipelines, governance) over three to four months, ML deployment over two to three, scale and optimise with edge integration over four to six, then ongoing expansion as an internal platform service. Start with one high-ROI use case and grow from there.

## Who should watch

Platform and data engineers in manufacturing, energy or any asset-heavy business, and MLOps folks who have only ever deployed models to clean cloud APIs. It is an architecture overview with a full ML lifecycle (collect, process, train, validate against real failures, deploy, monitor for drift), not a code walkthrough.

- [Mohan Kumar Dalai on AI maintenance platforms for power plants](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2026_Mohan_Kumar_Dalai_maintenance_power_plant) applies the idea to energy.

Title: Use AI on your platform to cut the cognitive load nobody needs
Description: Mia-Platform's Michel Murabito at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025: cut extraneous cognitive load with self-service, reusable components and RAG over docs and logs.
Body:
In 2004 you could deploy a website by dragging a folder onto a server. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Michel "Mitch" Murabito, developer advocate at Mia-Platform, used that memory to make a sharp point: the job got harder faster than our ability to manage it, and the only kind of cognitive load a platform team can really remove is the unnecessary kind. AI, used well, is one more tool for removing it.

Mitch co-organises Cloud Native Days Italy and co-founded the Developer Life and Green Software Italia communities, so this is a talk from someone who spends his days listening to developers complain.

## Three kinds of load, one you can delete

The framework is cognitive load theory. Intrinsic load is the task itself being hard; you reduce it by learning, not by tooling. Germane load is the effort of learning something new, like figuring out how CI/CD pipelines work, and that is the good kind. Extraneous load is everything else: poor tools, clunky UIs, workflows with too many steps, unclear docs. That third category is the target, because it is the only one you can cut without a trade-off.

His example is painfully familiar. A developer needs a new environment, files a Jira ticket, and waits while an ops colleague configures resources, variables, networking and security, possibly from another building, possibly from a beach. The platform's job is to make that a self-service click.

He also takes a swipe at the idea that Kubernetes is the hard part. It is just a tool; the real complexity is scalability, distribution, data, integration, security, privacy and now AI, plus choosing between twenty API gateways in the CNCF catalogue.

## Platform engineering is more than a portal

Mitch argues that most people picture platform engineering as an internal developer portal plus an infrastructure orchestrator. His picture is wider: application assets such as ready-made API gateways, API and event portals, a software catalog or marketplace of reusable microservices, a data control plane, and AI services.

That catalog enables what he calls a circular economy. Team one builds a payment microservice and documents it well. Team two reuses it and adds PayPal support as a new version. Team three takes the payment service, adds invoicing, and publishes that too. Nobody starts from zero, which is the whole point, and good documentation is the price of entry.

## RAG over your docs and your logs

The AI section is concrete. Put your LLM behind a RAG layer that holds the platform's documentation, the configuration of your services, and the logs. Now a developer can ask whether the logs show any warnings, which errors they are, and how to fix them, and the assistant can answer with your error codes and your docs in context. That only works if configuration and documentation are centralised in the platform first, which is a nice argument for doing platform work before AI work.

## Start with a problem and a metric you already have

The closing advice is the most transferable. Ask why you need a platform at all, pick a couple of problems rather than everyone's problems, and reuse metrics you already have. His favourite: how long a developer waits for a new environment. Track it over the long run, because tools that help in month one can drag in month twelve, and tie it to business value.

## Who should watch

Platform leads making the case for their roadmap, and anyone told to "add AI" to an internal platform without a clear use case. Mitch himself calls it a theoretical talk; the RAG-over-logs idea and the environment-wait metric are what you walk away with.

Title: GitLab Duo with Amazon Q: from issue to merge request in a slash command
Description: AWS's Mohamed Najaaf at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 demos GitLab Duo with Amazon Q: code from issues, Java 17 upgrades and security reviews.
Body:
Type `/q dev` in a GitLab issue and a merge request comes back. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Mohamed Najaaf, a solutions architect at AWS, demoed GitLab Duo with Amazon Q, the integration that puts Amazon Q Developer inside GitLab so the AI help happens where the code review already lives.

To be clear about scope: this is a vendor product walkthrough by AWS, built around three recorded demos, and at the time of the talk it was only available to GitLab Self-Managed Ultimate customers.

## Why put the assistant inside the DevSecOps platform

Mohamed opens with a figure from GitLab's Global DevSecOps report: 74% of organisations using AI for software development want to consolidate their toolchain. The pitch follows from that. Developers already juggle an IDE, a chat assistant, a scanner and a CI system; putting the assistant in the issue tracker and merge request cuts down the tab switching and the confusion.

He lists four jobs for the integration: turning an idea into code, optimising code by generating unit tests from a merge request, security code review, and modernising legacy Java.

## Demo one: issue to merge request

The first demo starts with a TypeScript sample project and an issue: add a signup flow with email, password and username, plus a sign-in flow for existing users, linked from the home page. A `/q dev` comment kicks off Amazon Q, which replies that it is generating code and will open a merge request when done. A few seconds later, it does.

The interesting bit is the loop afterwards. The reviewer notices there is no logging, comments asking for logging, invokes `/q dev` again, and Q adds a new logger file to the same merge request. Mohamed stresses that a human still reviews every change; the tool shortens the path, it doesn't remove the reviewer.

## Demo two: Java 8 or 11 to Java 17

The modernisation demo is the one most teams will care about. An issue titled "Upgrade project to Java 17" with `/q transform` in the description triggers a GitLab CI job that uploads the code, produces a transformation plan (lines of code, dependencies to replace, files to change), transforms the code and opens a merge request. The traceability is the selling point: what was upgraded, what was removed, and what you should check is all documented in the merge request.

Mohamed is candid that upgrades like this used to take weeks or months depending on code size, and that you may still need to make small fixes by hand afterwards.

## Demo three: review, then fix

The last demo runs `/q review` on a merge request. Q flags a likely SQL injection, highlights the offending code inline, and a follow-up `/q fix` proposes the patched version for the developer to review and apply. Think of it as a second reviewer who never gets bored of reading string concatenation.

## Who should watch

Teams on GitLab Self-Managed Ultimate with an AWS footprint, especially anyone sitting on a pile of Java 8 services. If you are on GitLab.com or another forge, it is still a useful look at how slash-command AI workflows can live inside merge requests, but check current availability before planning around it.

Title: Platform engineering is the glue between network and app teams
Description: Sunil Jorepalli of JPMorgan Chase at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on service meshes, API gateways, zero trust and IaC as one network platform.
Body:
Developers want to ship to AWS, Azure and the on-prem data centre without learning how packets get between them. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Sunil Jorepalli of JPMorgan Chase, who has spent around 16 years in networking, security and automation, argued that the platform team is where that wish gets granted: it hides the network plumbing behind self-service, and it bakes security in so nobody has to remember it.

It is a short, structured talk (he promises 15 minutes and keeps to it), and it works best as a map of the tools a network-aware platform needs rather than a build log.

## Friction is a security problem

Sunil's framing starts with four pressures: hybrid and multi-cloud complexity, zero trust demanding verification at every layer, latency-sensitive apps (payments, gaming) that expect milliseconds, and developer experience. The last one is the sneaky one. When the official path is slow, he says, developers bypass the security controls or build shadow infrastructure just to move faster. A platform that is pleasant to use is also a platform people don't route around.

So his definition of platform engineering is practical: abstract the complexity, automate the repetitive operations, and give teams a secure self-service way in. It is the bridge between developers, operations and security, and it should feel the same whether the workload lands on-prem, in a cloud, or at the edge.

## Four tool sets, one job each

The core of the talk splits the stack into four layers, each with a clear responsibility:

- **Service mesh** (Istio, Linkerd) for east-west traffic: retries, observability, and mTLS between services, so developers don't hand-roll any of it.
- **API gateways** (NGINX, Apigee, Kong and open-source options) for the north-south edge: ingress security, authentication, and a clean front door for consumers. He notes a drift towards open-source gateways that teams can extend themselves.
- **Zero trust** with identity-aware proxies and policy-driven access, citing SPIFFE/SPIRE for service identity and Google's BeyondCorp model for enterprise access. The perimeter firewall as the only line of defence is, in his words, all gone.
- **Programmable infrastructure**: Terraform plus GitOps with Argo CD or Flux, so every change is versioned, reviewed and reproducible.

He is explicit that the names are examples, not endorsements. Pick what fits the business; the layering is the point.

## The forgotten firewall rule

The most relatable part is about repetition. A new app needs an IP address, a DNS name, firewall rules, security config. Done by hand through tickets, someone eventually skips a step, and the missing firewall entry shows up in production. Encoding those steps once, in code that a reviewer approves, turns a checklist into a pipeline. Fewer tickets, fewer 2am "where did I miss it?" moments.

His design rules follow from that: abstract without hiding so much that developers lose visibility when they need it, keep environments consistent, and be secure by design with policies from day one and continuous measurement.

He closes with one anonymised case: a multi-cloud microservices shop that adopted a mesh, a gateway and IaC together, and saw both recovery time and platform adoption improve. Start small, automate incrementally, measure continuously.

## Who should watch

Network and security engineers moving into platform roles, and platform teams who treat networking as somebody else's problem. If you already run Istio behind Kong with SPIRE identities and Argo CD, this is a recap you could have given; if you are deciding where each of those belongs, it is a tidy 15-minute orientation.

- [Md Azmal on Istio ambient mesh for zero trust](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2023_Md_Azmal_ambient_mesh_sidecar_zero_trust) goes deeper on the sidecar-less mesh option.

Title: A smart city is a distributed system with traffic lights attached
Description: Microsoft's Mayur Bhandari at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on building smart city platforms: Kafka pipelines, edge processing, AI incident response, privacy.
Body:
When a traffic signal controller lags, the incident report is a traffic jam. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Mayur Bhandari, a software engineer at Microsoft, treated the smart city as an urban operating system: transport, utilities, emergency response and citizen services running on one distributed platform that has to stay up while millions of residents lean on it.

His opening statistic sets the stakes: by 2030 about 60% of the world's population is projected to live in cities. The talk then walks layer by layer through what that platform needs.

## Monoliths don't survive a festival weekend

Mayur's case against monolithic city systems rests on four pillars he wants instead: decentralisation (services keep making decisions when the central hub is offline), elastic scaling for festivals and emergencies, redundancy across regions, and data-driven resource scheduling. A city can't have a single control point, because a single control point is a single point of gridlock.

For transport, that means message-oriented middleware such as Kafka and Pulsar carrying data from traffic sensors, GPS devices, transit apps and citizen incident reports; a service mesh decoupling routing, ticketing and scheduling services; and ML models forecasting congestion so signals adapt before the queue forms.

## Let the platform fix the grid at 3am

The section on AI-driven incident response is the strongest. Traditional IT incident management, he argues, does not scale to a city. The pattern he describes is predictive monitoring that spots anomalies early plus automated remediation: restart failing pods, reroute workloads, provision extra compute. He cites a 42.6% reduction in MTTR from this approach.

His case study is a large metropolitan deployment where an observability platform spotted an anomaly pattern in grid telemetry, isolated the failing systems and reallocated power loads before the outage cascaded. Detection is table stakes; acting before a human wakes up is the goal.

Underneath sits an IoT telemetry pipeline he puts at 5,000+ sensors and terabytes per day across energy, traffic, air quality and water. Edge computing processes data at the gateway so traffic lights and emergency systems don't wait on a round trip to the cloud.

## Privacy is an adoption requirement

Mayur spends real time on governance, which many city-tech talks skip. Data minimisation, secure multi-tenancy and consent frameworks are in his foundation layer, and he reports higher public trust in cities that publish governance dashboards with transparent auditing. His point: residents who don't trust the platform stop using its services, so privacy by design is a delivery concern, not only an ethical one.

He rounds it out with familiar delivery patterns (blue-green, canaries, Kubernetes orchestration) and a sustainability layer that shifts compute towards data centres with renewable energy and reuses telemetry across departments instead of collecting it twice.

## The reference stack

His closing framework is a useful checklist: a foundation layer (distributed service mesh, identity and access management, data governance), a data layer (real-time ingestion, data lakes, ML inference), an application layer of domain microservices, observability, governance, and sustainability on top. The headline outcomes he cites are 1.2 million concurrent operations at 99.7% uptime. Treat the figures as the talk's reported results rather than a benchmark you can reproduce from the slides.

## Who should watch

Engineers working on IoT platforms, public-sector systems, or any domain where "real time" means physical consequences. It is an architecture overview, light on code, heavy on the layers you would need.

- [Rehmat Kharal on taming IoT data streams](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2025_Rehmat_Kharal_streaming_scalability_governance) covers scale and trust in the telemetry layer.

Title: Your security scanner is attack surface too, so write it in Rust
Description: Naresh Yelkoti of U.S. Bank at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust container scanners, artifact signing and policy engines for memory-safe DevSecOps.
Body:
Security tools parse the most hostile input your pipeline sees: container layers, packages and configs pulled from strangers. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Naresh Yelkoti](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Naresh_Yelkoti_memory_security_cloud), a senior information security engineer at U.S. Bank, pointed out that many of those tools are written in C and C++, "which means the tools designed to protect us can introduce new vulnerabilities". His answer is to build the scanners, signers and policy engines in Rust.

Yelkoti has run security pipelines across AWS, Azure and GCP and led migrations from Prisma Cloud to newer platforms, so the talk is grounded in what actually sits in a CI pipeline.

## A scanner is a parser of untrusted input

The core argument: if your container scanner has a buffer overflow, a crafted image can exploit the very tool inspecting it. Rust's ownership, borrowing and lifetime rules remove whole classes of parser and concurrency bugs at compile time, so the tool stops being a new attack vector.

He cites the industry baseline that around 70% of Microsoft's CVEs come from memory safety bugs, and reports from one financial services firm he worked with that its vulnerability backlog dropped by 30% in three months after adding Rust-based scanning.

## What a Rust container scanner looks like

The container section is the most detailed. Traditional scanners extract each image layer, compare installed packages against NVD and vendor advisories, and are often slow and noisy. The Rust design uses three ideas:

- **Zero-copy parsing** of layers straight from disk, without duplicating data in memory.
- **Parallel scanning** with Rayon across images.
- **Async reporting** with Tokio, so pushing results to dashboards never blocks the scan.

In his pipeline, a developer push builds the image, the Rust scanner runs before the image reaches the registry, critical findings block the deploy and go to ServiceNow or Slack, and only clean images are pushed. He also covers secret detection and flagging end-of-life base images.

## Signing, policies and static analysis

Beyond scanning, he walks through three more Rust-built tools. Static analysis on top of the syn and proc-macro2 crates to block insecure patterns such as SQL injection at commit time. Artifact signing and verification with ring and rustls, avoiding OpenSSL pitfalls and time-of-check to time-of-use gaps. And policy engines compiled to WebAssembly for sandboxed execution, with policies hot-swapped without restarts, for example a Kubernetes rule that only signed images may deploy.

His performance claims (three to ten times faster scans than Go or Python tools, 60% less memory, fewer false positives) lean on public reports from Dropbox, Discord and Cloudflare rather than his own benchmarks, and the talk is slide-driven rather than a live demo.

## Start with cargo audit

The integration advice is incremental: pre-commit hooks, GitLab CI jobs, Kubernetes admission controllers and API gateway middleware, no rewrite required. His suggested first step is the boring one, dependency scanning with cargo audit, then grow from there.

## Who should watch

DevSecOps and platform security engineers who maintain scanning and policy tooling, and anyone choosing a language for an internal security tool. If you already ship Rust, the container scanner design is the section to watch.

Title: Rust for insurance claims APIs, from GC pauses to FFI bridges
Description: Nageswara Rao Nelloru of Marquee Technology Solutions at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust claims and fraud APIs, and how to adopt it next to Java systems.
Body:
Claims systems are where garbage collection pauses turn into customer complaints. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Nageswara Rao Nelloru](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Nageswara_Rao_Nelloru_memory_ai_zero), a lead Guidewire developer at Marquee Technology Solutions, made the case for Rust in insurance and financial APIs, and spent the most useful part of the talk on how to introduce it without rewriting the core system.

## The problem: Java latency spikes at claim time

Nelloru's framing comes from insurance. A claim moves from pending approval through submission, issues and clearance, a process he said takes three to ten business days on legacy stacks. Customers now expect near-instant decisions, and the systems behind them must handle tens of millions of daily requests at sub-100 ms response times.

His diagnosis of the incumbents is familiar to anyone who has tuned a JVM: garbage-collected languages show unpredictable latency spikes during collection cycles, and C++ risks memory corruption. Rust removes both, which the abstract sums up as "zero-cost abstractions eliminating GC pauses".

## The numbers he put on the slides

The headline figures come from what he described as aggregated data from several major insurance carriers and financial institutions over three years: claims systems processing about $350 billion annually, 85% faster processing, around 26 million daily requests at roughly 90 ms, uptime moving up to 99.9% and beyond, and 40% lower infrastructure cost from smaller CPU and memory footprints. None of the carriers are named, so take these as reported outcomes rather than benchmarks you can reproduce.

## Fraud checks inside the latency budget

The most concrete case is fraud. A large carrier needed to evaluate about 140 data points per claim across 810,000 daily fraud signals and still respond in under 100 ms. The Rust design runs those checks asynchronously on Tokio, processing multiple fraud signals concurrently under strict memory bounds, with custom memory pools and less copying during deserialization. He reported 99.96% of fraud checks completing under 80 ms and false positives down 31%.

## Adopt at the edges first

The integration section is the part to steal. Nelloru described three patterns:

- **Targeted microservices.** Pick the performance-critical piece (fraud detection, payment processing, real-time checks) and replace only that.
- **A Rust API gateway** in front of existing systems for rate limiting and protocol handling. He said this cut latency by 60% for global payments, and the gateway became the foundation for further adoption.
- **FFI into the Java core.** Expose Rust functions to an existing Java banking system through a foreign function interface. One bank, he said, gained 3.2x throughput this way.

He also points out that the FFI boundary is where `unsafe` code concentrates, so keeping it small is a security decision as well as an architectural one.

## A note on the recording

The auto-generated captions are rough, so lean on the slides for the numbers. The structure of the argument comes through clearly: identify the bottleneck, ship a small bounded service, build team expertise, then expand.

## Who should watch

Engineers in insurance, banking and payments who run JVM-heavy platforms and want a migration story that starts with a gateway or a single service instead of a rewrite. If you need Rust fundamentals, start elsewhere; this is about where Rust fits in a financial estate.

Title: Treat GitHub, GitLab and Gerrit as one platform, not three tools
Description: Vasdev Gullapalli of Qualcomm at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on unified access, policy and event-driven automation across Git systems for 50K+ engineers.
Body:
Source code management is where every developer starts and ends their day, yet many companies still run it as an IT tool. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Vasdev Gullapalli, Senior Staff DevOps Engineer and Manager at Qualcomm, explained how his global team runs GitHub, GitLab and Gerrit for a user base of more than 50,000 engineers (closer to 100,000 accounts once bots and service accounts are counted) as a single platform with unified access, policy and automation.

His thesis, stated bluntly: "SCM is considered as platform. It's not a tool." If you treat it as infrastructure or just another application, he argues, you already have a problem.

## The license lifecycle is developer experience

The first section is about something unglamorous that every large org gets wrong: user management. A developer cannot write a line until they have an SCM license, so activation has to be self-service. Licenses cost money, so deactivation has to be automatic too. And when someone rejoins a project, reactivation has to be just as easy. Cover all three cases, automate them, and onboarding stops depending on the one operations person who knows the process.

The same goes for the next steps of a new developer: which repository to use, read versus push permissions, which CI/CD templates exist, how Git objects are managed. Qualcomm publishes this through public internal repositories with pages and READMEs, so people do not have to ask around.

## Unified access and the minimum security baseline

Across the three systems the goal is one identity model: SCIM provisioning everywhere, SSO so a login in one system carries to the others, and project classification that says how sensitive a codebase is and whether it can be cloned locally. External collaboration, such as working with a partner company, needs explicit controls like GitHub's guest collaborator model so outsiders only see what they should.

Governance is built around a minimum security baseline agreed with the security team. His example policy: no public repositories in any GitHub org, only internal and private ones. Shift-left scanning runs on every push, using built-in options such as CodeQL and GitHub Advanced Security, because a bug found at push time is much cheaper than one found after release. Audit dashboards are centralised, since security, DevOps, developers and product managers all want different views of the same data.

## Automation as event listeners and runbooks

The automation story is the most transferable part. Vasdev's team runs an event-based listener on SCM events, with a runbook per event type:

- A user is created, so the system sends them the onboarding documentation.
- Someone creates a fork in a place it is probably not needed, so they get a proactive note suggesting a better location.
- An IP allowlist on a GitHub repository is changed, removing addresses, so security and the service owners are notified and can ask why.

None of these is exotic, which is the point: small, specific reactions to events, written once, run forever.

## Balance security with developer friction

He is candid that policy can backfire. AI code review is his example: a reviewer bot with strict generic policies floods developers with comments on code they consider fine. The fix is to scope policies at the repository, org or enterprise level and embed configuration per project in CI/CD, with input from developers and leads, rather than one global ruleset.

## The results

Vasdev reports access sprawl down 46%, user onboarding that used to take hours or even days now done in under 30 minutes, and incident response times down 73%, helped by AI chatbots fed with knowledge-base articles. Next on the list: predicting user load and security events from logs with AI tools the team has built.

## Who should watch

Anyone who runs more than one Git platform, or one Git platform for thousands of people. Platform teams fighting license sprawl and access tickets will find specific, copyable patterns here.

Title: When the legacy system has no API, an RPA bot can click for you
Description: Uday Bheemarpu of Clean Earth at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on pairing RPA with Salesforce to automate workflows across systems that lack APIs.
Body:
Every enterprise has at least one system that only speaks through a screen. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Uday Bheemarpu, Information Technology Lead at Clean Earth, explained how robotic process automation fills the gaps that Salesforce's own automation tools cannot reach, and where the combination pays off: order entry into SAP, invoice processing and compliance checks against licensing websites.

His framing is fair to Salesforce. The limits, he says, reflect how enterprises are built: not every system has a modern API, some processes still run on paper or offline, and some need a human to click through an old interface.

## What native tools cover, and where they stop

Uday walks through the Salesforce toolkit first: Flows as a visual workflow builder, Apex for custom logic, REST and SOAP APIs, the Bulk API for large data volumes, and Platform Events for event-driven integration. Powerful, but they depend on what the other side offers.

The gaps cluster in four places: legacy systems with no API or a terminal interface, file-based processes on Excel, CSV and scanned PDFs, external web portals where someone copies data by hand, and cross-system orchestration where each system has different integration capabilities. Middleware can help, but adds cost and complexity of its own.

## RPA works at the UI layer

RPA's trick is that it operates where a human would: in browsers, desktop apps, terminal emulators and even Citrix sessions, only faster and without fatigue. Combined with OCR and natural language processing it can pull data from documents, emails and images. Every bot action is logged, which helps audits and troubleshooting, and bots scale up and down with workload.

## Three scenarios

- **Order processing.** A bot watches Salesforce for new orders, logs into SAP, navigates the screens, types in the order, captures the confirmation number and writes it back to Salesforce. Exceptions go to a human and are reported in Salesforce.
- **Invoice processing.** OCR reads scanned invoices, the bot validates them against purchase orders in Salesforce, enters approved ones into the accounting system, and opens Salesforce cases for discrepancies.
- **Compliance data collection.** On a schedule, bots visit licensing websites, look up the providers listed in Salesforce, capture license status and expiry dates, and update the records.

## Architecture and patterns

The technical design has four pillars: monitoring and governance (dashboards, alerting, SLA management), integration patterns, a security framework (least privilege, credential vaulting, auditability) and a proper development environment with version control and dev, test and prod pipelines.

The integration patterns run both ways. Bot-initiated: bots call Salesforce REST APIs, publish Platform Events, or drive the Salesforce UI when needed. Salesforce-initiated: outbound messages notify an RPA orchestrator, RPA listeners consume Platform Events, or Apex callouts invoke bot endpoints. Which one you pick depends on the system of record, volume, latency needs and operational controls.

## The maintenance tax

His best-practice list is where the practical wisdom sits. Start with process discovery: document the manual steps, find the systems without APIs and calculate ROI to choose use cases. Start small. Design for resilience with error handling, fallbacks for downtime and planned maintenance windows. Keep humans in the loop for exceptions. And the one that bites everyone: when the target website or screen changes, the bot has to be updated too, or its clicks land in the wrong place. He cites typical results of an 80% reduction in processing time, a 95% improvement in error rates and three times the volume handled.

## Who should watch

Salesforce admins and architects with a stubborn legacy system on the other end, and platform engineers deciding whether to build an API wrapper or let a bot click. It is an overview with scenarios rather than a build walkthrough.

Title: Engineering a health platform where latency is a clinical risk
Description: Raphael Shobi A T of ATPCO at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on a microservices health platform for senior travelers, with Kubernetes, chaos tests and compliance.
Body:
When the alert is about a traveler's heart rate, a slow response is a medical problem, not a performance bug. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Raphael Shobi A T, Senior Software Engineer at ATPCO and independent researcher, walked through the engineering behind an AI-powered healthcare platform for senior travelers across 34 countries, and why, as he put it: "Latency is not just a performance metric."

The context is demographic: he cites a projection of 703 million senior citizens travelling internationally by 2030, a group with higher health risks abroad and healthcare systems that rarely talk across borders.

## The numbers the platform runs on

The architecture is microservices on geographically distributed clusters. Raphael reports 12 million API calls a day at 99.97% uptime, more than 50,000 concurrent wearable devices streaming heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation, and alert processing in under 200 milliseconds through an event-driven design, with 47-plus health variables analysed per user. Fault isolation keeps one failing service from turning into a systemic outage.

## Kubernetes that knows what is urgent

Peak travel seasons bring demand surges of up to 10 times normal. The answer is Kubernetes autoscaling driven by live traffic and behavioral patterns, plus predictive scaling from historical usage, followed by validation that the system still meets its SLAs after scaling.

The interesting part is the custom Kubernetes operators that prioritize latency-sensitive work, such as real-time detection, over non-urgent jobs like batch ingestion. In most clusters every pod is equal; here a health alert outranks a backfill by design. A service mesh adds end-to-end encryption between services, health-aware routing, retries, circuit breaking and fallbacks, and telemetry via metrics, tracing and logs, while enforcing HIPAA and GDPR requirements.

## Compliance in the architecture, not the checklist

Data residency was one of the hardest problems. Each jurisdiction has its own rules on where patient data may be stored and processed, so the platform uses region-aware data handling to satisfy HIPAA, GDPR and local residency laws at once, with compliance embedded at both infrastructure and application levels. A distributed pipeline keeps patient records in sync across borders so doctors in different countries see the same up-to-date history.

He also uses a blockchain layer as a tamper-evident ledger of data access across hospitals, insurers and providers, alongside consent management, audit trails and smart contracts for cross-border insurance claims. Whatever you think of blockchain, the requirement it serves (a provable record of who touched which record) is a real one in this domain.

## Breaking it on purpose

Observability covers 150-plus metrics from API latency to device connectivity, and predictive models forecast health anomalies with a reported 87% accuracy. Chaos engineering is treated as a core practice: network partitions between regions to check local operation and resync, deliberately killing database instances to verify failover, load tests at 10 times normal traffic, and wearable disconnection tests to see how the system handles a device returning with a backlog of readings.

## Developer experience as a reliability tool

On the delivery side, GitHub workflows took deployment time from six hours to 12 minutes, developer-friendly APIs and SDKs connect over 1,200 medical facilities, and automated tests simulate real patient scenarios before release. Raphael reports 91% developer satisfaction and treats it as a reliability metric, on the grounds that happy teams keep platforms maintainable. Outcome figures he shares include a 78% reduction in system-related medical delays and 2.3 million medical translations processed.

## Who should watch

Engineers building life-critical or heavily regulated systems, platform teams thinking about workload priority in Kubernetes, and anyone designing chaos experiments beyond killing a random pod. The talk is a high-level architecture tour, and the specific organization behind the platform is not named in it.

Title: Rust for school and plant networks, type-safe configs to zero trust
Description: Prasanth Kosaraju of Dataquest Corp at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust for network provisioning, SDN, monitoring and zero trust in schools and a biotech plant.
Body:
Most Rust networking talks are about packet parsers. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Prasanth Kosaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Prasanth_Kosaraju_memory_safety_systems), a network engineer at Dataquest Corp, came at it from the other side of the rack: what Rust does for the people who provision switches, segment VLANs and run 802.1X across New York City classrooms and a biotech plant.

This is a practitioner's tour rather than a code walkthrough. Rust shows up as provisioning scripts, monitoring services and glue around the Cisco tooling network teams already run.

## Catch the misconfiguration before it reaches a switch

Kosaraju's first argument is about configuration, not speed. Rust's strong static types let you build compile-time validated configuration templates, so a broken VLAN or protocol setting fails the build instead of the network. He contrasts that with finding the error during deployment, mid-outage. His pitch against staying on C or C++ is short: "Rust matches the same speed, but it adds more safety built features."

On the service side he pointed to Tokio, Hyper and Tonic as the crates that make production-grade network services practical, and to Tokio's async runtime for non-blocking resource allocation in SDN and hybrid-cloud setups, with controllers such as ONOS and OpenDaylight on the other end.

## Monitoring that compares the live network to a baseline

The monitoring section is the most concrete. Rust services ingest streaming telemetry over SNMPv3 and NetFlow, compare live configurations against baselines for automated audits, and flag anomalies quickly instead of a day later. His suggested first step for any team is the same: start with monitoring, because visibility pays off before anything else changes.

## Zero trust with the tools you already own

For zero trust he maps the familiar pieces: microsegmentation with TrustSec, identity-based access with 802.1X and certificates (integrating with Cisco ISE), Cisco Umbrella for traffic from outside vendors, TLS and IPsec tunnels, and continuous trust evaluation. The Rust part is the memory-safe code doing authentication and evaluation in between, which is where he argues the common attack vectors used to live.

## Two deployments with numbers

The first case study is a one-to-one device program across about 75 New York City school locations and around 50,000 endpoints, with separate VLANs for admin, students and IoT. Kosaraju reported 99% uptime, a 47% reduction in security incidents and a 78% improvement in provisioning time, and said the Rust-based provisioning scripts ran 40% faster than the traditional setup.

The second is a biotech facility built for cyber resiliency with VRF-based segmentation and redundant paths, which he said saw zero successful intrusions and 99% uptime. Neither case comes with a published write-up, so read them as one engineer's field report.

## Rollouts that respect end-of-life hardware

His implementation advice is pragmatic: inventory end-of-life devices first, wrap legacy systems that lack modern APIs instead of replacing them, prioritise high-impact security components, and migrate in phases rather than all at once.

## Who should watch

Network engineers curious about Rust who live in Cisco ISE, Meraki and VLAN plans rather than in compilers. Rust veterans looking for implementation detail will find more in the packet-processing talks of the same event.

Title: Log anomaly detection needs context, not more thresholds
Description: Konstantin Berezin of Rapyd at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on embedded context agents that enrich logs, score anomalies with ML and alert only on what matters.
Body:
A timeout in your logs means nothing until you know it happened during checkout on Black Friday. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Konstantin Berezin, back-end developer at Rapyd, proposed embedded context agents: small components inside the observability pipeline that enrich every log with business and system context, score it with ML models, and page a human only when an outlier really matters.

## Why the classic approaches drown you

Konstantin lays out the problem in three parts. Volume: microservices across staging, QA and production in several regions produce millions of lines a day, mostly connection-opened and cache-hit chatter. Heterogeneity: one team logs structured JSON, another logs free-form strings. And missing context: the same error can be routine or a crisis depending on what else is happening.

The usual tools each fall short. Threshold rules (more than a hundred errors a minute, ping Slack) are easy and noisy, and they still miss subtle drift. Statistical methods like moving averages and z-scores work for latency and throughput but do not understand what a log line means. Basic ML such as isolation forests and clustering promises more, but breaks on new log types, which is exactly when you need it. The net effect: false positives until engineers stop reading the pages.

## A guard, not a camera

His analogy is a shopping mall. Cameras record everything, but someone has to interpret it: a person walking around a closed mall at night is suspicious, the same person on Black Friday is a customer. In his words, logs without agents are just raw video. The agents are embedded (they live inside your system), contextual (they attach service, deployment, user and region metadata) and autonomous (they alert, correlate and can trigger small fixes).

## The pipeline, end to end

The reference architecture is concrete. Sources are application logs, infrastructure logs from containers and cloud resources, and security events such as access attempts, audit trails and firewall logs. A collector like Fluentd, Logstash or OpenTelemetry normalises them. Kafka sits in the middle as the message bus, for durable high-throughput streaming, replay and backpressure. The agent layer does context enrichment, runs the models and makes a decision about severity and response. Results fan out to Grafana or Kibana, Slack, storage in Postgres, Redis or Elasticsearch, and automated actions such as Kubernetes scaling or blocking an IP.

For the detection core he combines autoencoders, isolation forests, LogBERT for semantic understanding, and DeepLog's LSTM approach to modelling log sequences, plus Microsoft's open-source LogAI library. Agents specialise by domain (network, authentication, performance) and share findings over the bus.

## Three scenarios worth stealing

- A 500 on an order request that matches no known error cluster gets flagged before it disappears into thousands of lines.
- A spike of failed logins from an unusual region, from the same IP range within the same time window, is reframed from technical error to likely attack.
- Every dashboard is green, but slow-query warnings keep rising; individually harmless, the trend triggers an early performance alert before an outage.

## Where LLMs fit

Konstantin is clear-eyed about LLMs. They explain patterns well in human language, but they are not real-time, do not watch streams continuously, get expensive at millions of lines per minute, and raise privacy questions for logs full of sensitive data. His recommended setup is hybrid: ML agents scan and alert in real time, and an LLM helps engineers summarise the incident and suggest root causes afterwards. He also names the open problems: keeping context up to date as services change, explainability of anomaly verdicts, and agents that overlap or conflict.

## Who should watch

Observability and platform engineers designing log pipelines, and teams whose alert channel has become wallpaper. Note the talk starts slightly mid-thought, so give it a minute.
