Title: Scaling a trading platform means optimising for change
Description: Aroma Rodrigues at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on how J.P. Morgan's Athena moved from a monolith to dependency graphs, delta storage and parallel books.
Body:
In most systems data grows; in finance it mutates, constantly and in dependent chains. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Aroma Rodrigues, now a software engineer at Microsoft, told the story of Athena, J.P. Morgan's trading platform, and how it went from barely handling thousands of trades to millions a day. Her main lesson for platform engineers: optimize for change, not just scale.

It is one of the more technical talks of the event and worth the full length, mostly because it explains the finance domain well enough that the architecture decisions make sense.

## Trades, deals and books

Aroma starts with vocabulary. A trade is the atomic market event: trader one buys a hundred units of a corporate bond from trader two. That one trade creates multiple deals, mirror images in each side's book. A book is a ledger of credits and debits grouped by desk and product. Each behaves differently: trades are written once and read often, deals update as markets move, books must be aggregated and reported in real time. Then the trade flows through front office (execution), middle office (validation, enrichment, risk), back office (settlement) and books and P&L, each with different performance, consistency and failure profiles.

Her numbers make the point: front-office bursts of around 10,000 transactions per second in volatile markets, middle-office validation within 30 seconds for regulatory reasons, settlement that may take days.

## The monolith with regulators on top

The starting architecture was single everything: one ingestion instance, one app node, one primary database without replicas or sharding, mixed OLTP and OLAP on the same tables, everything synchronous. Heavy recalculations ran as nightly cron batches of eight to 12 hours, so a failure at 3am meant traders started on stale data. There was no backpressure, a single region (painful for London and Hong Kong traders), and compliance data was just extra rows in the operational database. Storing full daily snapshots of every deal meant terabytes of near-duplicates, and peak-hour lock contention did the rest.

## Recalculate only what changed

The first breakthrough was a dependency graph. Functions are marked with dependency decorators: a position value depends on an instrument and market data, a base-currency value depends on that position and FX rates. When an instrument price moves, the graph finds every calculation downstream of it and updates only those. That single change took end-of-day processing from eight hours to five and made near-real-time P&L feasible.

The second was delta storage: keep the full deal record once, then store only changed fields per day, keep the current head state for processing, and rebuild any point-in-time view by applying deltas. Regulators asking for the full history of one deal across a corporate action that turned it into a different instrument get an answer without full snapshots.

## Books in parallel, compliance apart

Data is geo-distributed, with primary hubs in New York and London, each with three local replicas, synchronous replication within a region and asynchronous between regions. Because trading is mostly regional and tied to legal entities, books can be processed independently; cross-entity trades get a third deal stored in a separate instance so the regional sets stay parallel.

End-of-day became a dependency-aware pipeline: reference data for instruments first, then book processing per book, then P&L once all books finish, with retries per failed book using cached results. Compute building blocks, described as Lambda-like nodes that load a book into their own memory and return results, give horizontal scale without loading the main servers. Operational and compliance data were physically separated, with trades and price changes streamed to immutable audit logs.

Why it matters: a buggy Python analytics script once choked a queue, deals missed their regulatory window, and the result was a hundred-thousand-dollar fine.

## Why Python, and the pitfalls

She also defends Python: duck typing handles bonds, swaps and credit default swaps without rigid schemas, and hot paths drop to C++. Her pitfalls list is honest: optimising the wrong bottleneck before profiling, bolting on data lineage late, and underestimating the operational cost of multi-region systems.

## Who should watch

Engineers on financial, ledger or any heavily audited platform, and anyone whose data model keeps fighting their relational schema. Read it as an architecture story, not a product pitch.

Title: What a 47-step mortgage teaches about agentic platforms
Description: Naganarendar Chitturi of Newrez at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on orchestration, events and audit trails for agentic AI in mortgage processing.
Body:
A typical mortgage, by Naganarendar Chitturi's count, runs through 47 separate steps, each needing judgement and all tangled in dependencies. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, the Senior Solutions Architect at Newrez used that workflow to explain how to build agentic AI platforms that coordinate those steps, and spent as much time on how they break as on how they work. His first lesson: "Orchestration is everything."

## Agents that handle the case nobody wrote a rule for

His definition of agentic AI is practical. A rule-based system that meets an unfamiliar case, say an applicant whose income comes from cryptocurrency mining, stops and waits for a human. An agent recognises it as an income verification problem, looks for guidance and similar past cases, builds a verification path, and records it so the next one is automatic. His other example: an employer switches payroll providers, the new data format breaks the old process, and dozens of applications from that employer pile up for weeks while someone phones vendors. An agent that recognises and shares the new format clears the whole queue.

## Three foundations

He argues you need all three of these or the platform falls apart:

- **Workflow orchestration.** Teams start with a simple queue where agent A hands off to agent B. Then a property in a flood zone during hurricane season needs inspection, flood insurance and evacuation route checks at once, on different timelines, and the queue locks up. His analogy: the gap between a traffic light and air traffic control.
- **Event-driven communication.** A credit agent broadcasts a credit-score-updated event; risk, pricing and compliance agents react in parallel without knowing about each other. When a property valuation service dies at 2am on a Saturday, requests queue and drain when it returns, instead of becoming Monday's crisis.
- **ML pipeline integration.** Real-time inference inside the process, such as fraud models whose confidence drops trigger extra verification.

Event design is the craft. He estimates a mortgage system may carry 4,000 to over 5,000 event types, and each needs just enough context: an income-verification-completed event carries the verified amount, confidence, method and anomalies, but not the raw bank statements. A bonus: the event stream doubles as a flight recorder you can replay.

## Where it breaks

The reality check is the best section. Legacy integration: loan data on a 1980s mainframe with no APIs and a daily batch file, so you end up building a translation agent that speaks mainframe, which may become your most sophisticated component. State management: applications live 60 days or more, rate locks longer, while values, rates and rules shift, which pushes you toward event sourcing so any agent can rebuild state by replay. Variable load: credit analysis takes 30 seconds for a standard W-2 employee and 20 minutes for a self-employed applicant with stock, crypto and foreign assets, so capacity has to adapt automatically.

## Explainable by design

In a regulated industry, saying the AI did it does not work. He describes decision provenance: when a regulator asks about a loan denial from eight months ago, you pull up the agents involved, the data they used, the rules that fired and the exact model versions in seconds. Data minimisation helps too: the credit agent sees aggregated spending patterns, not full statements; the identity agent discards biometrics after use.

Operationally, he suggests monitoring agents like consultants, not servers: track confidence patterns and the decision reversal rate, meaning how often human underwriters overrule an agent. Long-running applications need versioned agent deployments, where in-flight applications keep their agent version, and configuration pulled at runtime. And turn your most experienced underwriters into agent trainers, not competitors.

## Who should watch

Architects designing multi-agent systems for any long-running, regulated workflow, whether loans, claims or patient care. Expect architecture and failure modes, not framework code.

Title: Rust in the packet path, from zero-copy buffers to in-path ML routing
Description: Rahul Tavva of Kairos Technologies at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on zero-copy packet processing, lock-free queues and ML routing decisions in Rust.
Body:
Networks moved from 10 Gbps pipes to 400 Gbps backbones, and the C and C++ code pushing those packets still carries buffer overflows, dangling pointers and race conditions. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, [Rahul Tavva](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2025_Rahul_Tavva_memory_code_zero), a senior network and cloud infrastructure engineer at Kairos Technologies who has migrated more than 2,000 sites to SD-WAN, argued that Rust lets you stop choosing between line-rate performance and memory safety, and showed the patterns that make it work.

It is a compact talk: a problem statement, three techniques, two customer stories and a migration plan. No live code, but the techniques are the kind you can take straight to a design review.

## Every copy of a packet is a tax

His sharpest framing is about copies. "In traditional stack, a single packet might be copied five times." NIC to kernel, kernel to user space, and back again. At 400 Gbps, every extra copy burns CPU cycles you pay for in hardware.

The Rust version maps NIC buffers into user space behind safe abstractions, passes references instead of copying, and lets the borrow checker guarantee there are no dangling pointers or double frees. Tokio handles non-blocking packet I/O. In his tests, moving from copying to this zero-copy approach cut packet processing latency by 40 to 65% and freed CPU cores for other work such as telemetry analysis.

## Three patterns for deterministic throughput

Tavva named three techniques that carry most of the weight:

- **Compact zero-copy serialization** for routing headers and telemetry, so parsing a header does not mean allocating a new struct.
- **Custom allocators** that pre-allocate buffers, because at 400 Gbps a surprise allocation shows up as latency jitter.
- **Lock-free ring buffers** with atomic indices for packet queues.

When hardware access needs `unsafe`, his advice is to isolate it, encapsulate it and audit it. The attack surface shrinks to the few blocks you can actually read in one sitting, which is more than most C codebases can say about their parsers.

## ML in the forwarding path, not beside it

The AI part of the title is about where inference runs. Instead of shipping telemetry to a separate analytics engine and waiting for an answer, the models are trained offline on historical routing data (utilization, jitter, packet drops) and run inside the Rust forwarding path in microseconds. Models can be hot-swapped without stopping traffic. Deterministic performance, with no garbage collector pausing at the wrong moment, is what makes that feasible.

## Two case studies, by industry rather than by name

For a major US exchange, Tavva reported that 94% of the vulnerabilities disappeared, routing decision latency fell from 120 to 32 milliseconds, and the same hardware handled 3.4 times more transactions per second. For a Fortune 500 manufacturer whose production lines stopped during network outages, recovery went from up to 17 minutes to well under a second, uptime reached 99.998%, and security patches went out via hot patching without taking the network down. The customers are not named, so treat these as one practitioner's results rather than benchmarks.

## Rewrite the bottleneck, not the network

The migration plan is the most reusable part. Start with the bottlenecks where safety and performance gains pay back most. Bridge into existing C and C++ through FFI. Run Rust in parallel with the legacy path under production load before trusting it. Use unit, integration and property-based tests before rollout, and move non-critical paths first, core routing last.

## Who should watch

Network engineers and platform teams who own packet-heavy C or C++ code and need an argument, with numbers, for trying Rust on one hot path. If you already write DPDK or eBPF for a living, the patterns will be familiar, and the migration section is still worth the time.

Title: Pick monolith or microservices by team maturity, not hype
Description: Rajani Jayantha of Wayfair at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 gives a decision framework for monolith vs microservices, plus a real routing migration.
Body:
The monolith versus microservices argument usually starts with a conference talk from a company ten times your size. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Rajani Jayantha, Senior Engineer at Wayfair with over 15 years in the industry, offered a decision framework that starts somewhere less glamorous: your team's maturity, your culture and your cloud platform. Her headline advice is that context matters more than trends.

## Both sides, fairly

The talk earns its framework by treating both architectures honestly. Microservices give independent scaling, deployment flexibility, contained failures and freedom to pick a tech stack per service, and she cites studies claiming 30 to 40% cost savings from scaling efficiency and deployment frequency five to ten times higher. The bill: every service call adds network latency, you need service discovery, API versioning, circuit breakers and retries, distributed transactions need eventual consistency and sagas, and the observability burden grows with every service. Without Kubernetes, independent CI/CD pipelines and distributed tracing in place, she argues, the promised benefits never arrive.

The monolith gets a better hearing than it usually does. A single codebase means faster onboarding, simpler debugging and testing, and in-process calls that are far faster than network hops. It shines for MVPs and prototypes, small teams with unclear domain boundaries, predictable workloads, and strong consistency needs like financial transactions. It struggles as it grows: over-provisioning, and development speed that slows year on year in a large codebase.

## The framework: people first

The decision starts with organisational readiness. A monolith fits teams under about 20 developers with basic CI/CD and limited cloud experience; microservices tend to need 50 or more developers with advanced automation and distributed systems skills. Cultural signals matter as much as headcount: is ownership centralised or distributed, is communication synchronous or async, is the organisation conservative or experimental, does it actually learn?

Then come the technical requirements: number of business domains, integration points, consistency needs, realistic growth and traffic projections (she warns against optimistic forecasts built on thin data), and cloud platform capabilities from container orchestration and service meshes to managed databases. If the platform cannot support microservices at scale, the architecture will struggle however nice the diagram looks.

## Architecture as a journey

Rajani's recommended path avoids the big-bang rewrite: start with a modular monolith, use domain-driven design to find service boundaries, extract services gradually with the strangler fig pattern, and build observability, automation and CI/CD alongside. Her rough timelines: 18 to 24 months for a full microservices migration, six to 12 months to optimise a monolith while keeping options open.

## The routing service that earned its split

The real-world example is a monolithic routing application that made scaling hard and turned deployments into a bottleneck, with a team mature enough to take on microservices. They decoupled routing into modular services, built reusable libraries and plugins, recorded decisions in architecture decision records, and added service auto-wiring and shared utilities such as feature toggles, caching and logging. The reported results: deployments three times faster, code-to-production speed up 21 times, uptime up 8.5%, mean time to recovery halved, and a system handling tens of millions of contacts per month.

She closes by noting the choice is no longer binary: serverless, modular monoliths and ML-assisted decomposition all sit between the poles, and hybrids often win. Business value, in her view, decides the architecture, and the most elegant design is worthless if it serves no business goal.

## Who should watch

Tech leads facing a decomposition decision, and anyone who needs a structured way to push back when a planning meeting decides microservices are the answer before asking the question. Teams already deep into service meshes will find the first half familiar; stay for the readiness criteria and the migration numbers.

Title: Catch errors in the middleware, before customers call you
Description: Sreelatha Pasuparthi of Liberty Mutual at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on moving error detection into application middleware with ML-ranked alerts.
Body:
If your first alert is an angry phone call from your biggest client, your monitoring is watching the wrong layer. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Sreelatha Pasuparthi, Principal Software Engineer at Liberty Mutual Insurance, explained how moving error detection into application middleware, and ranking alerts with machine learning, cut detection from hours to minutes. Her abstract puts the result at an 88.5% drop in MTTR, from 162-minute detection delays, across 230K users.

## The Tuesday that started it

The talk opens with an incident story. A flagship e-commerce platform had been failing quietly for over two hours, mis-processing orders and corrupting customer data. Nothing in the extensive monitoring estate noticed; support tickets and a call from the largest enterprise client did. Another catalyst: a database corruption issue that went undetected for nearly three hours.

Meanwhile the alerting that did fire was mostly noise. The average developer got more than 40 alerts a day, and more than three quarters needed no action or duplicated known issues. Engineers became desensitised, on-call turnover grew, and the team had dozens of tools and hundreds of dashboards but still could not tell when things were actually broken for users.

## Detect where the error happens

The central insight is a single sentence worth putting on a sticky note: "Real errors happen in code, not in infrastructure metrics." CPU, memory, network and database graphs are lagging indicators. By placing error capture in the request pipeline, alongside authentication, validation, business logic and persistence middleware, the system records each failure at the moment it occurs, with the user session, the operation, the input and the execution path attached.

The middleware works in phases: immediate capture with minimal processing, enrichment with more context, ML classification, then routing. Each phase is built to fail safely, so if the error reporter itself breaks, the original request carries on. Monitoring that can take production down is not monitoring.

## Not every timeout is an incident

Classification replaces static thresholds. The models look at temporal patterns, correlations between error types, how errors hit different user cohorts, and learn from past incidents and engineer feedback. Priority is dynamic: one user hitting a database timeout is minor, hundreds hitting it at once is an infrastructure problem. The inputs she lists are error frequency and correlation, business context of the affected users, similar past errors and their fixes, and current system state including load and scheduled maintenance.

Routing then respects how people work: developers get Slack, GitHub issues and IDE plugins; operations get runbooks, incident management and PagerDuty escalation; management gets dashboards and summaries. The system learns which channel produces the fastest response for each alert type.

## One root cause, one alert

Cascade handling is the other big win. A connection pool exhaustion produces service timeouts and then frontend exceptions, and traditional monitoring pages for each symptom separately. Because the middleware captures enough context, it can link those downstream alerts to the root cause in real time and keep the incident channel readable. Baselines are dynamic too, learning daily, weekly and seasonal patterns and accounting for deployments and maintenance windows.

## How to roll it out

Her roadmap is pragmatic. Pilot on one well-understood application of moderate complexity, with basic capture and manual routing. Then build reusable middleware components and standards for classification and routing across the portfolio. Only then add ML classification, smart routing and cascade suppression. The success factors she credits are executive support through a period when development velocity dipped, low performance overhead, fail-safe design, and a culture that treats error detection as part of application design.

## Who should watch

Teams drowning in alert noise, SREs whose dashboards are green while customers complain, and platform engineers deciding where instrumentation should live. It describes the architecture rather than a specific vendor tool, so it transfers to whatever stack you run.

Title: Low-code platforms can pull clinical research out of paperwork
Description: Lalitha Potharalanka of the FDA at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on modular low-code platforms that automate clinical trial data capture and compliance.
Body:
In clinical research, the bottleneck is often a spreadsheet, not the science. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Lalitha Potharalanka, Senior Appian Developer at the US Food and Drug Administration, with 18 years in financial and healthcare IT and a background as a QA automation architect, showed how modular low-code platforms take manual data entry and audit scrambles out of clinical trials, and what it takes to get risk-averse research staff to use them.

## Where the hours go

The numbers she opens with make the problem tangible. Research coordinators spend 60% of their time on documentation and manual data entry. A researcher logs into three to five different systems a day just to do core work. And 25% of clinical trials are delayed by administrative bottlenecks rather than scientific ones. The three root causes are paperwork overload, regulatory complexity across ethics boards, agencies and institutional review boards, and fragmented data systems (EHRs, lab systems, trial management tools) that someone has to reconcile by hand.

## Why low-code fits this problem

Her case for low-code rests on three properties. Rapid prototyping, so a team can test and deploy a new workflow in days rather than months, which matters when regulations or trial protocols change. Customisability, because no two trials are alike and each workflow needs tailoring without a rebuild. And accessibility: clinical coordinators and regulatory leads can help design the workflows they live in, instead of filing requirements and waiting.

## A modular platform, five parts

The architecture is a set of independently deployable components. Data capture takes clinical data from electronic forms, APIs or system input and validates it at entry. An integration engine connects EHRs, lab systems and third-party software into one workflow. Workflow automation handles routing, notifications and approvals. Compliance monitoring is built in, with audit trails generated as a side effect of normal work. An analytics dashboard shows performance and bottlenecks. Because each part stands alone, the platform can adapt to new regulatory or clinical needs without a full overhaul.

## From periodic audits to continuous compliance

The strongest idea in the talk is moving compliance from scheduled audits to a continuous property of the system. Validation rules catch inconsistencies as data is entered, automated cross-checks compare data across systems in the background, every interaction lands in an audit trail, and regulatory reports are generated on demand. In her case study, trial setup that used to take weeks dropped to days, and she reports error rates down 87% and compliance preparation time cut by 65%. Her ROI slide adds administrative time down 42%.

## The human half

Lalitha is clear that technology alone does not shift a clinical organisation. Her adoption playbook: involve researchers, coordinators and regulatory staff early so features match real needs; train people and roll out in phases; design interfaces for mixed technical skill; and run small pilots that create internal champions. To overcome resistance she recommends showing regulators and staff how automation strengthens compliance, documenting outcomes rigorously, and securing an executive sponsor.

Looking forward, she points to AI-driven analytics on trial data, blockchain-backed audit records for multi-site trials, global interoperability, and patient-facing platforms with mobile and wearable reporting and trial matching.

## Who should watch

Engineers building systems in heavily regulated domains, teams weighing low-code against custom builds for internal workflows, and anyone who has watched an audit consume a quarter. It is a platform and process talk, light on code and heavy on how regulated organisations actually change.

Title: A Rust emergency dispatch system on Tokio, Kafka and Wasm
Description: Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli of Conduent at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on building life-critical emergency response systems in Rust with Tokio, Kafka and WebAssembly.
Body:
When an earthquake hits, emergency call volume spikes at exactly the moment infrastructure starts failing, and the dispatch system gets no second chance. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli, Senior DevOps Lead and Cloud Lead at Conduent, walked through an emergency dispatch architecture built in Rust and explained why each component is there.

Lakshmi comes to Rust from cloud and DevOps work, and it shows in a good way: the talk spends as much time on Kafka semantics and edge deployment as on the borrow checker, and explains both with patient analogies.

## Survival requirements, not performance requirements

The scenario frames everything: a disaster drives call volumes far above normal, the system must handle very high message rates without dropping one, and uptime targets have to hold while the surrounding infrastructure is collapsing. Lakshmi's point is that these are survival requirements.

Lakshmi traced failures in traditional stacks to two sources: memory-safety bugs in C and C++ code, and garbage-collection pauses in Java at the moment an instant response is needed. Rust addresses both with ownership and borrowing, zero-cost abstractions, compiler-checked concurrency, and deterministic cleanup.

## Invalid states should be unrepresentable

Ownership rules sound simple, the talk notes, but they remove leaks, data races and null references even at high concurrency. The analogy offered is strict airport security: nothing unsafe gets through.

The type-system section is the strongest design idea in the talk. A patient ID is not just an integer; it is a type that can only be constructed validly. Encoding domain rules in types moves error detection from an unpredictable runtime failure to a predictable compile-time check, so the business rules are enforced by the compiler.

## The architecture, component by component

The dispatch system combines four pieces:

- **async/await** for non-blocking I/O. Lakshmi's kitchen analogy: blocking I/O is a chef staring at a pot of pasta until it boils; async is the chef setting a timer and prepping something else.
- **Tokio** as the runtime: task scheduler, I/O event loop, timers.
- **Apache Kafka** as the durable event bus, with a clear explanation of topics, ordered partitions, producers, consumers and brokers, and why replay from an earlier offset and consumer-group failover matter in an emergency system.
- **WebAssembly at the edge** for sandboxed, portable modules with fast cold starts, running close to the incident.

One call flow ties it together: geolocate the caller, pull their information and query historical incidents concurrently, then let an ML model recommend resources and trigger dispatch.

## Edge computing as resilience

The edge section makes the best argument. Processing hazard data locally detects problems faster than a central system, keeps working during network outages, keeps sensitive data local, and reduces bandwidth when the network is saturated. In a disaster, Lakshmi argued, the edge is how the system survives losing the centre. Rust traits let one code path cover environmental sensors, traffic cameras and building structural monitors without runtime penalty.

Fault tolerance closes the design: circuit breakers that isolate failing components, and fallbacks that keep critical operations running in degraded mode.

## What 18 months taught them

Lakshmi reported no memory-related crashes over 18 months of operation, along with easier compliance and lower infrastructure costs. The challenges named are honest: the learning curve, gaps in legacy integrations, and longer compile times, which Lakshmi considers solvable with training and a maturing ecosystem.

## Who should watch

Engineers on public-safety, healthcare or other life-critical systems, and anyone who wants a clear explanation of async Rust and Kafka in one sitting. Rust veterans will find the language material introductory; the architecture is the draw.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Building Resilient Emergency Response Platforms](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Lakshmi_Vara_Prasad_Adusumilli_response_emergency_approach) by Lakshmi Vara Prasad Adusumilli: the same domain from the platform engineering side.
- [Predicting and Mitigating Emergency Situations on the Roads](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Maksim_Kariagin_data_road_emergency) by Maksim Kariagin: a data-driven take on emergencies.
- [Nuclear Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_John_Darrington_nuclear_rust) by John Darrington: Rust in another field where failure is not an option.

Title: Data science stalls on infrastructure, not algorithms
Description: Aishwarya Pai of Deloitte at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on the platform principles and patterns that get ML models from notebooks to production.
Body:
Your model works in the notebook and dies on the way to production, and the culprit is rarely the model. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Aishwarya Pai, Senior Consultant at Deloitte, made the case that the bottleneck in enterprise data science is infrastructure, and that platform engineering is the fix: one standard, self-service foundation so data scientists stop firefighting environments.

The abstract leads with numbers: 58% of ML platforms failing to deliver value, and platform engineering bringing 68% faster model delivery and 37% higher AI success rates. The talk itself is a compact, well-ordered overview rather than a single case study, so treat it as a checklist for an ML platform, not a war story.

## Three failure modes before the first model ships

Aishwarya names the usual suspects. Fragmented tooling, where every team picks its own stack and integration becomes the project. Inconsistent environments, the "works on my machine" problem in ML clothing, where a model behaves differently in production than in development. And deployment bottlenecks, where data scientists build models that engineering teams then struggle to operationalise. She adds resource inefficiency (too much compute idling, or not enough when it matters) and patchwork security that makes compliance a scramble.

## Six principles for the platform

Her answer is a short list of platform principles: abstraction, so data scientists never see the messy infrastructure; self-service, so teams provision environments and deploy models without a ticket; standardisation of patterns and tools; observability across models, data and infrastructure; scalability that follows demand; and security by design rather than as an afterthought.

The foundation underneath is containerisation, which gives consistent runtimes and lets several versions of a model run side by side. On top sit microservices for data integration, training and monitoring, each scaled independently, with orchestration and a service mesh tying them together.

## The patterns that make it boring, in a good way

The section on design patterns is the most useful for engineers. Twelve-factor apps for maintainability. Event-driven architecture, so new data arriving can trigger training automatically. Immutable infrastructure, where every change is a new version and rollbacks are cheap. Circuit breakers and bulkheads to keep one failing workload from taking down the rest. Autoscaling to follow demand and save money.

She describes ML pipelines as the assembly line of data science and lists what a good one needs: orchestration of dependencies and schedules, data lineage and versioning for reproducibility, and fault tolerance so a failed step recovers instead of restarting the world.

## Five audiences, one platform

The part that platform teams often skip: a data science platform serves at least five groups with different needs. Data scientists want fast experiments and easy data access. ML engineers want reliable deployment and monitoring. Platform engineers want visibility into cost, performance and compliance. Security wants control without slowing everyone down. Business stakeholders want results they can measure. Monitoring, she argues, has to cover all four layers: infrastructure, application latency and errors, data freshness and schema quality, and model accuracy and drift.

She closes with expected payoffs (tripled productivity, deployment time cut in half, infrastructure costs down 40%) and a five-step roadmap from assessment through foundation, platform development and operational excellence to continuous evolution. Those are her framing figures, not a single measured case, so read them as targets.

## Who should watch

Platform engineers who have inherited the data science team as customers, and data leads arguing for a shared ML platform instead of one more bespoke pipeline. If you already run a mature MLOps stack, most of this will be familiar; it is an orientation talk, and a tidy one.

Title: Platform thinking is how digital transformation actually ships
Description: Manik and Prachita Kashikar at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 map platform engineering onto a paper-heavy medical invoicing workflow, layer by layer.
Body:
Most digital transformation programmes stall because every team rebuilds the same plumbing. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Manik Kashikar, Principal Consultant at Thoughtworks, and co-presenter Prachita Kashikar argued that platform engineering is the missing operating model, then showed it on a concrete case: medical invoice processing that ran on paper, stamps and manual forwarding.

This is a framing talk with one worked example, not a tooling demo. Its value is the vocabulary: if you have ever had to explain to a business sponsor why building a platform belongs on the transformation roadmap, it gives you the slides in your head.

## A platform is town planning, not a pile of tools

Manik's definition is simple: a platform is a reusable digital foundation that hides complexity, standardises how teams operate and speeds up new work. His analogy: "Think of it like town planning." You lay roads, utilities and rules first, so the houses that follow do not each need their own sewer.

He splits platform strategy into four kinds, each framed "as a service":

- **Engineering platform:** IT as a service for developers. Self-service infrastructure, pipelines and monitoring, so engineers stop doing plumbing.
- **Business capabilities platform:** reusable business services, so new products assemble from parts instead of fresh fragmented builds.
- **Data platform:** data as products, discoverable and governed, so teams subscribe to datasets instead of hunting for them.
- **Customer experience platform:** one profile and consistent personalisation across web, app and partner channels.

The point is that they stack. Delivery infrastructure, API and service boundaries, self-service data, experimentation with feature toggles and telemetry, and customer touch points each become shared capabilities rather than per-team projects.

## Digitisation, digitalisation, transformation

The talk also untangles three words that get used interchangeably. Digitisation converts analogue to digital, like scanning paper. Digitalisation automates the workflows you already have. Digital transformation reimagines how the business creates value with technology at the core. Manik's argument is that a system-centric approach, with siloed apps and brittle integrations, gets you stuck at step two.

## The invoice pipeline, rebuilt as layers

Prachita then takes the healthcare use case. The starting point: a medical invoicing operation handling over a million documents a week, where every invoice needed physical verification of signatures and stamps and manual forwarding to claims teams. The pains are the familiar ones: data entry errors, fraud exposure, no real-time visibility for stakeholders, and a system that only scaled by hiring.

The redesigned flow runs through a web portal: invoices are uploaded in batches, sanity-checked and stored in the cloud, scanned with OCR and NLP to extract fields, and passed through deep learning to pull out signatures and stamps. A government representative still audits those signatures by hand, a deliberate human-in-the-loop step against fraud. Then the insurer approves, rejects or puts the claim on hold, and approvals trigger the payment workflow.

The platform view is the interesting part. The same flow is redrawn as layers: a shared ingestion layer for hospitals, insurers and government bodies; reusable data services (the OCR and NLP engines serve claims, compliance and audit alike); validation as a service, with AI models plus human review; an orchestrated claims processing platform; and an experience layer of chatbots and real-time dashboards. Their summary line is the one to steal for your next architecture review: instead of scaling people linearly, scale capabilities.

## Measuring it in three columns

They close with success metrics split three ways: customer metrics, business value (fraud reduction, compliance by design, lower cost to serve) and operational metrics (uptime, accuracy, fraud detection rate, throughput). Success, in their framing, is when all three move together. The roadmap is phased: value stream mapping and an e-invoicing platform first, then OCR, NLP and fraud detection, then cross-stakeholder automation, dashboards and wider rollout.

## Who should watch

Architects and platform leads who have to sell platform work to business stakeholders, and anyone in regulated, paper-heavy domains like insurance and healthcare. If you want Backstage plugins or Terraform modules, this is the wrong half hour; it stays at the operating-model level.

Title: Self-healing AWS is a four-stage climb, not a switch
Description: Sreeja Reddy Challa at Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025 on building self-healing AWS infrastructure with DevOps Guru, GuardDuty, Lambda and Step Functions.
Body:
Nobody flips a flag and wakes up with autonomous operations. At Conf42 Platform Engineering 2025, Sreeja Reddy Challa, an AWS cloud engineer of seven years speaking as an independent researcher, laid out how platform teams move from reactive firefighting to self-healing AWS infrastructure, and why the human and cultural steps matter as much as the Lambda functions.

Her framing is clear from the start: AI does not replace engineers, it amplifies their judgement by learning from incidents, predicting failures and running the remediations people used to type by hand at 2am.

## Why manual ops stops scaling

The pressure comes from several directions at once: alert and telemetry volume beyond what humans can read, systems that move faster than human reaction time, evolving security threats, compliance overhead, and too few experienced platform engineers to go around. Teams that keep relying on manual processes, she argues, end up paying in operational cost, downtime and agility.

## The AWS building blocks

The architecture is pleasingly concrete. Detection comes from two ML-backed services: Amazon DevOps Guru, which builds baselines from metrics, logs and traces and flags anomalous behaviour, and Amazon GuardDuty, which analyses DNS logs, VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail events for suspicious activity. AWS Config watches resource state against policy and, together with Systems Manager, runs playbooks that correct configuration drift.

Response is event-driven. Findings land in CloudWatch Events, which she calls the central nervous system, routing them to handlers. Lambda functions are the execution engine for individual remediations; Step Functions orchestrate the multi-step ones, with error handling, retries and rollback. Remediation outcomes are fed back so the system learns which fixes work. Severity matters too: critical issues trigger immediate action and escalation, while lower-priority ones queue for automated fixing later.

## Four stages of maturity

The heart of the talk is a maturity model you can hold your own platform against:

1. **Reactive automation.** Scripted remediation for well-understood problems: infrastructure as code, standard dashboards, automated runbooks.
2. **Predictive monitoring.** ML spots behaviour patterns before users feel them, with tools like DevOps Guru and smarter alerting.
3. **Intelligent remediation.** The system diagnoses and fixes most routine problems itself through event-driven, orchestrated workflows that learn from outcomes.
4. **Autonomous operations.** Most operational work runs with minimal oversight; humans handle strategy and the genuinely strange.

Most teams reading this are somewhere between one and two, and that is fine. Her implementation advice is to start in low-risk areas and take one risk at a time.

## Trust is the real migration

Sreeja spends real time on the organisational side, which is the part most self-healing pitches skip. Engineers' roles shift from troubleshooting to designing the systems that troubleshoot. Teams need skills in ML operations, event-driven design and serverless. Trust in automation comes from gradual rollout, monitoring and clear escalation rules, including when a human should step in and when they should not. She also suggests new performance metrics, such as autonomous remediation success rates, and a governance framework for automated decisions. Her timeline estimate is multi-year.

Looking ahead, she points at generative AI drafting remediations for novel failures, explainable AI so teams can see why an action fired, and digital twins of infrastructure for rehearsing cascading failures without touching production.

## Who should watch

AWS platform and SRE teams with a pile of runbooks and an appetite to automate them, and managers who need a maturity model to plan the next two years. It is an architecture and strategy talk with no live demo, so bring your own console.

Title: Rust for edge AI, from no_std operators to Candle and Burn
Description: Anushree Nagvekar of AEye at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust for edge AI, with no_std neural operators, portable SIMD, ARM and RISC-V targets, and the crates to use.
Body:
On an edge device every byte and every CPU cycle counts, and the latency budget for perception is measured in milliseconds the cloud cannot reliably deliver. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Anushree Nagvekar, a software engineering manager at AEye, made the case for Rust as the language of edge AI and showed the implementation patterns that make it work on constrained hardware.

AEye builds lidar for autonomous vehicles, so the examples lean towards perception and safety-critical inference. The second half of the talk, on custom operators and target-specific builds, is where the useful detail lives.

## Why edge AI needs a different language

Anushree's framing: the holy grail for edge AI is latency under 50 ms, which means computing on the device rather than round-tripping to the cloud. On-device means tight memory, small CPUs and real-time deadlines.

Rust's fit, in her telling, is threefold: memory safety without a garbage collector, zero-cost abstractions for clean code with no performance tax, and fine-grained system control. She highlighted safe concurrency across multi-core ARM chips, portable SIMD for vectorized maths without hand-written assembly, and good integration with NPUs and DSPs, even in `no_std` environments.

## Two case studies, two kinds of edge

The first is autonomous vehicles: a tight obstacle-detection budget, high detection success and very high uptime requirements, where Rust's compile-time guarantees remove runtime errors that have long plagued C++ in these systems. The second is industrial IoT security: threat detection on modest hardware with long battery life, where predictable performance is what makes low-power devices viable.

The performance and memory figures she presented are production numbers in her account, without the benchmark detail, so read them as reported results.

## Writing neural operators that fit on a chip

The implementation patterns for custom neural network operators are the part to rewatch:

- **No heap allocations**, which gives `no_std` compatibility for the most constrained embedded targets and keeps latency deterministic.
- **Cache-friendly memory access patterns** to cut memory latency, often the real bottleneck on small devices.
- **Manual loop unrolling** to help the CPU pipeline and make execution times predictable.
- **Direct slice manipulation** written so bounds checks are optimized away in release builds, keeping Rust's safety without paying for checks in the hot loop.

## Compile for the chip you actually have

For ARM and RISC-V processors, Anushree showed using Cargo features and `cfg` attributes to enable instruction sets specific to the target CPU, so the compiler emits architecture-specific binaries that use what the hardware offers. One codebase, several tuned builds. She also mentioned memory-mapped hardware accelerators accessed through safe Rust, giving direct hardware control without dropping into C.

## The ecosystem to start with

Her crate list is short and practical:

- **Candle**, for inference with minimal dependencies.
- **Burn**, a deep learning framework with a strong type system and modular backends, for training.
- **SmartCore**, classic machine learning algorithms, `no_std` compatible.

Her closing advice: add them with Cargo and start experimenting on your own system.

## Who should watch

Embedded and robotics engineers bringing ML onto devices, and Rust developers who want concrete patterns for `no_std` numeric code. ML researchers who live in Python will get a good sense of what deployment on the edge actually demands.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Edge Computing and TinyML for Autonomous IoT](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pradeep_Kumar_Vattumilli_edge_tinyml_ai) by Pradeep Kumar Vattumilli: ML at the smallest scale.

Title: Rust-powered predictive AI for telecom networks and cell towers
Description: Venu Madhav Nadella of Spectrum at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on moving telecom ops from break-fix to prediction with Rust, isolation forests and LSTMs.
Body:
Most telecom outages announce themselves days in advance, in telemetry nobody correlates. That is the premise of Venu Madhav Nadella's talk at Conf42 Rustlang 2025. Venu, Lead Technical Analyst at Spectrum, laid out how a Rust data platform running anomaly detection and failure prediction can move network operations from break-fix to prevention.

The talk mixes architecture, ML and organizational change, with plenty of anecdotes from carriers. It is pitched at the operations leader as much as the engineer.

## Break-fix is the expensive default

Venu's diagnosis of the status quo: fault detection that lets a meaningful share of issues slip through, multi-hour mean time to repair, outages that are mostly unplanned, and engineers switching between many fragmented tools and losing hours each week to manual correlation. Alerts fire after customers complain.

His most telling anecdote is a European carrier that found a large share of its sudden outages had clear precursors, such as memory leaks or temperature spikes, visible in telemetry days ahead. The signal existed; nothing connected the dots.

## Why Rust for telecom AI

Venu's language case is about latency at the wrong moment. A garbage-collection pause in a Java or Python pipeline can be long enough to miss a critical failure signal. Rust's ownership model removes those pauses, the compiler enforces thread safety for highly parallel ingestion, and strong typing catches integration bugs before they ship; he described a compile-time check catching an API mismatch in a billing integration.

He also told the story of a client who asked why not just scale their existing Python service. On the same hardware, he reported, the Rust service handled many times the request rate. Sometimes the tool is the bottleneck, and adding servers just buys a bigger bottleneck.

## Two algorithms do most of the work

The ML section names two workhorses:

- **Isolation forests** for anomaly detection. Instead of profiling normal behaviour, they isolate the odd points directly. Venu's image: rather than describing the haystack, you find what is not hay. His example is spotting the irregular traffic of a DDoS attack quickly.
- **LSTM networks** for failure prediction. They remember patterns over time, so slow degradation, like a cell tower power supply drifting over months, can be flagged weeks before it fails.

The Rust angle is that both run inline with the data stream instead of in nightly batches.

## The platform and the people

The case study is a North American carrier ingesting telemetry from thousands of cell towers, where LSTM predictions flagged failing hardware about two weeks ahead, leading to fewer outages and fewer truck rolls. Venu's figures are the speaker's own from that work.

The architecture: Rust collection adapters normalizing data from many legacy systems into one format, a zero-copy message bus, an explainability layer that turns predictions into plain-English insights, and Rust FFI wrapping old C code (and COBOL billing systems) instead of rewriting them. He added a "why" button on every AI alert showing the top contributing factors, which is how you get engineers to trust the black box.

He was firm that AI does not replace engineers; it changes the job from log-grepping to tuning models. The roadmap has four phases: Rust collectors on one tower type first, isolation forests for quick wins, LSTMs trained on historical failures (starting with non-safety-critical systems), then automation like auto-restarting failed nodes.

## Who should watch

Telecom and network operations engineers, SREs at large infrastructure providers, and anyone building predictive maintenance on high-volume telemetry. The talk is long on outcomes and short on code, so treat it as a blueprint.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [AI-Powered Anomaly Detection for Telecom Service Reliability](https://www.conf42.com/Observability_2025_Ajay_Averineni_service_telecom_reliability) by Ajay Averineni: the observability view of the same problem.
- [Go-Powered Telecom BSS](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Bhaskara_Beeraka_telecom_microservices_scaling) by Bhaskara Beeraka: the business-systems side of a carrier, in Go.

Title: Rust machine vision on the EV line, from battery cells to ADAS
Description: Sankar Subramanian of Lucid Motors at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust-based machine vision for EV manufacturing, covering battery inspection, 3D vision and ADAS calibration.
Body:
On an electric vehicle line, a vision system that crashes is a line that stops, and a missed crack in a battery cell is a thermal event waiting to happen. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Sankar Subramanian, Staff Engineer at Lucid Motors, walked the whole EV manufacturing flow, from cell inspection to ADAS calibration, and showed where Rust-based machine vision fits at each stage.

Sankar brings more than 20 years in control and automation, across semiconductor lasers, fiber optics and EV manufacturing. The result is a talk that is more about the factory than the language, which is exactly why it is interesting.

## Why EVs make inspection harder

EVs pack more components more densely, need micron-level precision, and carry battery safety risks that push manufacturers towards inspecting every part. At line speed, Sankar argued, traditional inspection methods cannot keep up, and the system that replaces them has to be fast and must not fall over in a 24/7 plant where downtime costs add up by the minute.

His Rust case maps to the floor: memory safety to avoid crashes in production, fearless concurrency to process several camera feeds at once without data races, near-C performance to handle high-resolution images at line speed, and FFI to integrate with existing C and C++ vision libraries and ML frameworks.

## The inspection pipeline

The core flow has four stages. Image acquisition captures multiple views of each part at line speed. Pre-processing uses SIMD-optimized Rust for real-time noise reduction and contrast enhancement. AI-based classification runs custom neural networks that catch subtle defects threshold-based systems miss. Automated response rejects the part, flags rework, or adjusts the process based on the defect class.

Sankar reported a clear increase in defect detection rate over conventional machine vision, and stressed that the Rust system avoided the crashes common in C and C++ environments.

## Battery cells and packs get the most attention

The battery section is the most detailed. Electrode alignment for anode and cathode, measured with structured light at sub-millimetre precision. Surface defect detection for microscopic cracks, dents and contamination that could lead to thermal runaway. Electrolyte fill verification with IR imaging. Pack-level thermal monitoring with IR cameras to spot hot spots during formation cycling, with Rust handling the real-time thermal mapping.

At module level he added wire bond assessment, laser weld verification, thermal imaging during module pulsing to find resistance anomalies, and 3D profile mapping after assembly.

## 3D vision, traceability and calibration

Beyond inspection, Sankar covered 3D vision for assembly automation (time-of-flight cameras guiding robots, stereo disparity mapping in optimized Rust, laser triangulation, dense point cloud processing), and integration with the manufacturing execution system: OCR and barcode traceability for every component, assembly sequence verification, and automated documentation for compliance and recall readiness.

At the end of the line, ADAS calibration validates forward cameras, lidar, radar and surround-view cameras within a tight time budget per vehicle, and vision data feeds a factory digital twin for predictive maintenance. The ML side uses transfer learning to cut training data needs, with Rust FFI into TensorFlow and ONNX Runtime and inference deployed on edge devices beside the line.

## Who should watch

Engineers in manufacturing, robotics and industrial automation, and Rust developers curious what a real factory pipeline demands. It is a systems tour rather than a code session; there are no crate-level details, but the domain picture is rich.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Platform Engineering Lessons from Automotive Manufacturing](https://www.conf42.com/Platform_Engineering_2025_Nikunj_Karoliya_complex_automotive_manufacturing) by Nikunj Karoliya: the software platform behind an auto plant.

Title: Rust data pipelines for climate monitoring and public health
Description: Ritesh Kumar Sinha of Kotak Mahindra Bank at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on Rust data engineering with Tokio, Arrow and DataFusion, applied to climate and health data.
Body:
Ritesh Kumar Sinha, AVP at Kotak Mahindra Bank, used his Conf42 Rustlang 2025 talk to argue that Rust's value in data engineering goes beyond speed: predictable pipelines matter most where the data is about satellites watching forests or hospitals tracking an epidemic. The tools are Tokio, Apache Arrow and DataFusion; the examples are climate monitoring and public health.

It is a short talk, well under twenty minutes of material, and best treated as an introduction to the Rust data stack with a clear sense of why it matters.

## The problem: big pipelines, unpredictable runtimes

Ritesh opened with the scale of data the world now produces and the failure modes of the usual tools at that scale: garbage collection making Java pipelines unpredictable, memory leaks risking corruption, Python slowing down. His summary is that petabyte processing needs a rethink for safety and scale, and Rust offers low-level performance with high-level safety.

He added a personal note that will ring true for anyone who has maintained native code: he has seen teams spend weeks on memory issues in C++, which Rust's compiler would have rejected up front.

## The borrow checker as a strict librarian

His explanation of ownership is the friendliest line in the talk: it is like a strict librarian. You can borrow the book, but you cannot keep it forever or lend it out twice. For data pipelines this matters because it makes data flows explicit, so it is always clear which stage owns a buffer, and corruption from two stages writing the same memory simply does not compile.

## The stack, from bytes to SQL

Ritesh walked through three code examples that together sketch a pipeline:

- **Tokio** for async ingestion: read lines without blocking, parse the stream with minimal copying, transform in parallel without locks, then serialize safely to the sink while reusing buffers.
- **Apache Arrow** for zero-copy columnar batches, fast aggregations, and interop with Python for mixed-language teams.
- **DataFusion** for SQL: register a CSV, run an average-temperature query with filters, and get vectorized execution over Arrow data.

He also showed an atomic, lock-free counter for shared metrics, the kind of small detail that keeps a hot loop free of mutex contention.

## Two case studies with a purpose

The first is climate monitoring: terabytes of satellite data arriving at remote sites with limited hardware, processed by efficient Rust pipelines at the edge, for uses like tracking deforestation in near real time. The second is public health: national-scale data for epidemic tracking, where Ritesh stressed memory safety and privacy enforced at compile time and fast queries over very large record sets during a crisis.

The figures he gave for both, along with headline numbers like large throughput gains over JVM tools and big compute savings, are presented without methodology, so take them as the speaker's reported results.

## Fast, safe, and cheaper on the planet

Ritesh closed on an angle few data talks take: efficiency as ethics. Lower compute per record means lower energy use and lower carbon, ownership boundaries help enforce privacy, and efficient processing leaves headroom for bias checks in ML pipelines. His call to action is modest and sensible: try a Rust pipeline in one small part of your next project.

## Who should watch

Data engineers new to Rust who want a quick tour of Tokio, Arrow and DataFusion, and anyone working on environmental or health data who wants the case for predictable pipelines. If you already ship DataFusion in production, this is a refresher.

## Related Conf42 talks

Title: Two edge-cloud orchestration patterns, and why Rust runs the edge
Description: Karthik Mohan Muralidharan of Walmart Global Tech at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on edge inference with cloud remediation and cloud insight with edge reconfiguration.
Body:
A 100 to 200 ms round trip to the cloud sounds fast until a robot needs an answer in under 20. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Karthik Mohan Muralidharan, a Software Engineer at Walmart Global Tech, presented two orchestration patterns for splitting work between edge devices and the cloud, and argued that Rust is the right language for the edge half.

The talk is well structured and pattern-first: a problem statement, two named patterns, the case for Rust, then the implementation challenges with candid answers.

## Cloud-only hits three walls

Karthik's problem statement is clean. Latency: a cloud round trip is too long for real-time control or medical monitoring. Bandwidth: streaming every sensor reading to the cloud around the clock congests networks and inflates bills. Availability: if critical operations depend on the internet connection, the connection is your single point of failure. The conclusion is not edge versus cloud, but both, with clear rules about who does what.

## Pattern one: edge inference, cloud remediation

Flip the traditional flow. Instead of shipping raw data up, run lightweight ML models on the edge devices and make the immediate decision locally. Only results, anomalies and exceptions go to the cloud, which runs heavier analysis and decides on larger remediation, such as dispatching a technician or triggering a workflow.

The benefits follow directly: critical decisions are fast, bandwidth drops, and the system keeps working through network outages. Karthik pointed it at manufacturing and predictive maintenance, and any setting where local responsiveness is the requirement.

## Pattern two: cloud insight, edge reconfiguration

The second pattern runs the other way and is about learning. The cloud aggregates data from the whole fleet, giving a view no single device has. Models find optimization opportunities only visible at that scale, turn them into policies tailored to devices or groups, and push them down so devices update their local behaviour on the fly. His examples range from adjusting a price in a retail store to retiming a traffic light. Centralized intelligence, distributed execution: a feedback loop rather than a pipeline.

## Why Rust at the edge

Karthik's Rust case is specific to devices: memory safety without a garbage collector (no surprise pauses on a constrained device), compiler-enforced freedom from data races for devices juggling many tasks, cross-compilation from small ARM sensors to x86 industrial PCs from one codebase, and zero-cost abstractions. He cited lower memory use than managed-language equivalents, better performance per watt on ARM, and sub-millisecond inference jitter, which is the number real-time systems care about most.

## The hard parts, answered

The implementation section is where the talk earns its keep:

- **Distributed state over flaky links**: a hybrid consistency model, strong for critical data like financial transactions, eventual for analytics, with CRDTs to merge conflicting versions.
- **Security on physically exposed devices**: zero trust (authenticate and authorize every request), capability-based permissions so a device can do only what it must, and ML-based threat detection.
- **Performance**: predictive prefetching caches, content-aware compression instead of generic gzip, and SIMD for hot paths.

His four getting-started rules are worth pinning up: start from the business KPI, design for degraded operation, measure everything from day one, and ship edge workloads in containers.

## Who should watch

Architects of IoT, retail or industrial systems deciding what runs where, and Rust developers moving into embedded or edge work. It is pattern-level rather than code-heavy, so it pairs well with a hands-on edge Rust talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [From Cloud to Edge computing with WebAssembly](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly) by Alex Casalboni: another way to ship code to the edge.

Title: An S3, SQS, Lambda and DynamoDB pipeline with the AWS SDK for Rust
Description: Vamsi Praveen Karanam of Amazon at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 builds a file ingestion pipeline with the AWS SDK for Rust, trade-offs included.
Body:
Vamsi Praveen Karanam, a Software Development Engineer at Amazon, used his Conf42 Rustlang 2025 talk to build one realistic AWS system in Rust step by step: files land in S3, events flow through EventBridge into SQS, Rust workers process them, and results go to DynamoDB. Along the way he showed what the AWS SDK for Rust gives you and, refreshingly, where Rust still costs you.

It is a compact, practical session. If you have been meaning to try Rust on Lambda and want a mental model before reading the docs, it is a good starting point.

## Why Rust on AWS at all

Vamsi's argument is about scale economics. At AWS scale, every millisecond of latency and every MB of memory shows up on the bill. Rust gives predictable C-like performance with compile-time guarantees, and for Lambda and ECS specifically, small binaries mean faster cold starts and lean memory use means smaller invoices.

He compared it fairly against the usual alternatives: Go is strong for Lambda and containers but carries a bigger runtime; Java has the largest ecosystem but pays in cold starts and memory; Node.js develops fast but struggles on CPU-bound work; Python is unbeatable for prototyping and ML libraries but slows down at scale; C++ is fast and error-prone.

## The honest downside slide

This is the part many Rust advocacy talks skip. Vamsi listed the costs: long compile times on large projects, a steep learning curve for ownership and lifetimes, an ecosystem that is maturing but less polished than Java's or Python's, Lambda tooling with fewer templates than Python and Node, and a preference for explicitness over dynamic metaprogramming that makes quick experiments slower. Knowing those up front, he argued, makes the adoption decision realistic rather than religious.

## What the SDK gives you

The AWS SDK for Rust is modular: each service is its own crate, so you pull in S3 or DynamoDB without the rest. Shared configuration through `aws-config` handles credentials and regions. It is built on Tokio and async-first, with retries, pagination and streaming built in, so you write business logic instead of retry loops. Strongly typed request builders mean a malformed request is a compile error, not a 400 in production.

## The pipeline, one hop at a time

The walkthrough maps Rust's strengths to each step:

- **Upload to S3**: typed builders give confidence requests are valid; async lets you upload many files concurrently.
- **EventBridge to SQS**: Rust workers consume and deserialize messages with Serde, scaling across many events without adding threads.
- **Compute on Lambda**: small binaries and faster cold starts, with async letting one function juggle multiple tasks.
- **Persist to DynamoDB**: builders enforce correctness, async queries handle many operations under load.
- **Observability**: the `tracing` crate for structured spans across async workflows, paired with OpenTelemetry and metrics into CloudWatch, plus `anyhow` for error context.
- **Security and deployment**: least-privilege IAM roles, KMS for sensitive data, cross-compiling to musl for small static Lambda binaries, and multi-stage container builds that strip unnecessary dependencies.

## Who should watch

Backend engineers on AWS weighing Rust for Lambda or ECS workloads, and Rust developers who know the language but not the SDK. Teams already running Rust in production on AWS will find it a solid checklist rather than new territory.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Why should you use Rust for Serverless workloads?](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Roman_Boiko_serverless_workloads) by Roman Boiko: the serverless case in more depth.
- [Blazing fast serverless with Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2022_Luca_Bianchi_blazing_fast_serverless) by Luca Bianchi: an earlier take on Rust and Lambda.
- [Patterns for efficient serverless development](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2024_Yan_Cui_patterns_efficient_serverless) by Yan Cui: language-agnostic serverless patterns to pair with the Rust specifics.

Title: Building a data mesh in Rust with Kafka, Arrow and actors
Description: Narendra Reddy Mudiyala of Accenture at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 on the Rust toolkit for data mesh pipelines, from rdkafka and Serde to actors and Wasm.
Body:
Data mesh is an org chart idea: give each domain ownership of its data products. Narendra Reddy Mudiyala's talk at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 is about the plumbing that idea needs, and why he builds it in Rust. Narendra, a senior data engineer at Accenture, walked through the crates, patterns and cloud integration choices behind high-throughput, domain-owned pipelines.

It is a toolkit talk. You leave with a list of specific libraries and patterns rather than a single big claim, which is exactly what you want if you are about to start one of these platforms.

## Why the monolith breaks first

Narendra's starting point is familiar: data volumes grow faster than a central platform team can scale, and the monolithic pipeline becomes the bottleneck every domain queues behind. Data mesh decentralizes ownership to the domain experts who understand the data. That only works if each domain's pipelines are fast and reliable enough to run without a central team babysitting them, and that is the job he gives to Rust.

His reasons are the three you would expect, framed for data work: ownership rules out data races in concurrent processing code, zero-cost abstractions keep high-level transformation code fast, and the type system kills null-pointer and data-mismatch bugs that would otherwise show up as 3am pipeline failures.

## The pipeline toolkit, named

The concrete part is the best part. For processing:

- **Tokio** as the async runtime, so ingestion, transformation and output run concurrently without blocking threads.
- **Serde** for serialization with fewer copies, which matters when serialization is the hidden bottleneck.
- **Apache Arrow** for columnar operations, which Narendra uses for fast analytics on large datasets compared to row-based tooling.

For infrastructure:

- **rdkafka**, the Rust wrapper around the battle-tested librdkafka C library, for high-throughput Kafka consumers.
- **Iterators and zero-allocation patterns** for transformations, so data streams through without piles of temporary objects.
- **Axum with Tower middleware** for the HTTP APIs that expose data products to other domains.

## Benchmark honestly, then choose per component

One section deserves more attention than it usually gets. Narendra described running real-world benchmarks on actual production-shaped workloads, comparing Rust against Python, Java and Scala on latency, throughput, memory, startup time and consistency under load.

His conclusion is not "rewrite everything". Rust often wins for the performance-critical parts, such as real-time event processing and heavy transformations, while another language may be the right call for less time-sensitive components where development speed or ecosystem matter more. Benchmarking, in his phrase, keeps you honest.

## Three patterns for a distributed mesh

The advanced section names three patterns that fit a mesh well:

- **Actor model**: each actor owns its state and communicates by message passing, a natural way to isolate domains, made safe by Rust's concurrency guarantees.
- **Custom derive macros**: enforce validation on incoming data structures across the codebase, so every developer gets it for free rather than remembering to write it.
- **WebAssembly sandboxes**: compile parts of the processing into Wasm modules and run them isolated, useful when data crosses domain or even organizational boundaries.

He closed on data contracts enforced at compile time between microservices, which is the most mesh-specific idea in the talk: if the shape of a data product is a Rust type, a breaking change is a build failure, not a downstream incident.

## Who should watch

Data engineers designing domain-owned pipelines or evaluating Rust for the hot paths of an existing platform. It is a broad survey, so expect a map of tools and patterns rather than deep code.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Data Mesh Unleashed: scalable architectures for AI-driven enterprises](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Arun_Vivek_Supramanian_data_mesh_ai) by Arun Vivek Supramanian: data mesh from the Go side.
- [Scaling Kafka on Kubernetes for 100,000+ messages per second](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Shalini_Katyayani_Koney_kafka_streaming_scalable) by Shalini Katyayani Koney: running the Kafka the consumers read from.
- [Using Rust and WASM](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Andrey_Makarov_wasm_assembly_code_web) by Andrey Makarov: the Wasm half of the sandbox pattern.

Title: How Rust took over the lakehouse, from Arrow to DataFusion
Description: Rahul Joshi of Capital One at Conf42 Rustlang 2025 traces data platforms from Hadoop to lakehouses and shows where Rust components now sit in the stack.
Body:
The JVM carried big data for fifteen years; the newest layer of the lakehouse stack is increasingly written in Rust. At Conf42 Rustlang 2025, Rahul Joshi, Distinguished Data Engineer and Director at Capital One, walked through three eras of enterprise data architecture and showed exactly which pieces of a modern lakehouse Rust now powers.

Rahul brings about 20 years of building data platforms in financial services, and it shows: the talk is a clear history lesson that ends in a practical adoption plan.

## Phase one: Hadoop and the JVM tax

The story starts in the on-premise Hadoop era: HDFS and MapReduce, everything on the JVM. It worked at scale, but Rahul listed the costs plainly. Each task needed its own heap, object headers added bytes to every record, data exchanged between map and reduce tasks had to be serialized and deserialized at every hop, and garbage collection pauses of seconds made run times inconsistent.

His benchmark slide compared word count, the hello world of big data, across Hadoop, Spark and DataFusion, with the Rust engine finishing far ahead. The point is not the toy workload; it is that removing GC and serialization overhead changes the resource profile of the whole job.

## Phase two: warehouses fixed usability and added lock-in

Cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Redshift solved much of Hadoop's usability problem with SQL-friendly analytics. The catch, as Rahul framed it, was proprietary storage formats: you pay compute to load data, compute to query it, and egress to take it out again. Storage and compute were coupled, and ML workloads usually meant copying data somewhere else, creating silos.

## Phase three: the lakehouse, with Rust in the engine room

The lakehouse merges the two with open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) on object storage, ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel, and separate scaling of storage and compute.

This is where the Rust inventory comes in, and it is the slide worth screenshotting:

- **Table formats**: Rust libraries for Delta and Iceberg that let you read and write tables without spinning up Spark.
- **Columnar storage**: Apache Arrow's Rust implementation for zero-copy columnar memory, plus parquet-rs and Lance for storage.
- **Query processing**: Apache DataFusion for SQL and DataFrame APIs with parallel execution and a small footprint.
- **DataFrames**: Polars on top of Arrow.

Rahul quoted recent benchmarks for these: big query-speed gains for DataFusion over Spark on the same hardware, large memory savings for Polars over pandas on a 100 GB dataset, and much faster Parquet loading with arrow-rs than with PyArrow. These come from published and internal tests rather than a live demo, and as always your workload will have opinions.

## Start with the bottleneck, not the rewrite

The practical section is the strongest. Rahul described three integration styles: Rust microservices for the critical processing components, native extensions for Python or JVM code that keep the existing interface, and full replacement of a pipeline for maximum benefit.

His recommendation is the boring correct one. Most organizations start by replacing components already identified as bottlenecks, such as high-throughput ingestion, heavy feature engineering for ML, or interactive SQL that needs sub-second response, and only then consider rewriting more. Measure first, swap the hot path, repeat.

## Who should watch

Data platform engineers and architects deciding where Rust belongs in their stack, and anyone who wants a crisp narrative of how we got from MapReduce to the lakehouse. It is light on code and heavy on architecture.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [LanceDB: an OSS serverless vector database in Rust](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2023_Lei_Xu_lancedb_oss_serverless_vector_db) by Lei Xu: the Lance format Rahul mentions, from the people who build it.
- [Bring your DataOps to the Data Lakehouse](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Jorge_LoaicigaRodriguez_dataops_lakehouse_challenges) by Jorge Loaiciga Rodriguez: running a lakehouse once it exists.
- [Enterprise Data with Lakehouse Architecture at Scale](https://www.conf42.com/Remix_2026_Richa_Solanki_data_lakehouse_enterprise) by Richa Solanki: another enterprise migration story.
