Title: Quantum jobs will make cloud bills even harder to predict
Description: Qumulus developer relations engineer Denish Tomar argues at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 that metered pricing breaks down for quantum workloads.
Body:
Nobody can say exactly what their cloud bill will be next month, and quantum workloads will make that worse. That is the argument Denish Tomar, Developer Relations Engineer at Qumulus, made at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: usage-based pricing already confuses teams running well-understood CPUs and memory, and a quantum job whose runtime, retries and error correction are unknowable in advance turns metering into a guessing game.

This is a vendor talk and it says whose product it shows: the second half presents Qumulus's fixed-resource model as the alternative.

## The $10,000 autoscaling surprise

Tomar opens with a story worth the price of admission. A startup founder's AWS bill came in around $10,000 against a usual $2,000. The cause was one autoscaling mistake: instead of scaling up to five servers it scaled to 50, and instead of running for two hours it ran for three days before anyone noticed. Then came the line items nobody could explain: NAT gateway processing charges, CloudWatch logs, load balancer capacity units, cross-availability-zone transfer, API gateway requests and Lambda cold starts.

His challenge to the audience: open your cloud dashboard and state exactly what you will spend next month. Not approximately. You can't, and that's with technology we have optimised for decades.

## Why quantum makes metering worse

The quantum section explains superposition and entanglement for a general audience (spinning coins, mazes explored in parallel), then gets to the billing point. A quantum algorithm might finish in 30 seconds or 30 hours. It might need one run or 500, because results are probabilistic. It might use cheap basic operations or need error correction that costs a hundred times more. Tomar's example: the same quantum job could cost anywhere from $500 to $5,000, and you wouldn't know which until the bill arrives.

His view is that the big providers are struggling with this too: classical bills meter known quantities, while quantum bills meter unknown time, unknown errors and unknown retries.

## The Qumulus pitch

The alternative he presents is predefined, fixed resources at a fixed price instead of metering each operation, compared to a subscription you use without watching the meter. Qumulus is built on OpenStack, which he argues means no vendor lock-in to anyone's quantum ecosystem. He shares a before-and-after from a startup that moved from AWS: before, a bill that swung widely month to month and a fifth of engineering time spent on cost optimisation; after, a predictable bill and no time spent chasing it. The founder's line, as he tells it, was that the best part was building things instead of optimising for AWS pricing.

His closing line sums it up: "your cloud bill doesn't have to be quantum chaotic".

## How to take it

The diagnosis is the strongest part: unpredictable cost is already an engineering tax, and probabilistic workloads with variable retries make it heavier. Whether fixed-resource pricing is the answer for your team depends on how bursty your workloads are, which the talk doesn't model. The quantum billing figures are projections, not quotes from a provider's price list, so read them as the shape of the problem.

## Who should watch

FinOps practitioners, startup CTOs and platform teams who own the cloud bill, plus anyone planning to experiment with quantum services and wondering how to budget for them. If you already run strict cost controls on AWS, the first half will feel familiar; the quantum billing argument is the new part.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Mastering the chaos: cost-effective cloud monitoring and logging](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_cloud_cost_monitoring) by Pradeep Gaddamidi, on the CloudWatch-style line items from the opening story.
- [Real-time FinOps intelligence for streaming financial events](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2026_Tina_Kanth_finops_streaming_prompts) by Tina Kanth, for watching spend as it happens.
- [Your cloud emits CO2](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Olivier_Bierlaire_your_cloud_emits_co2) by Olivier Bierlaire, another bill your cloud runs up quietly.

Title: Quantum CloudOps means deciding which parts of an app go quantum
Description: Srinivas Sriram Mantrala at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on what DevOps and CloudOps teams must change when quantum joins the cloud.
Body:
The most expensive mistake in a hybrid quantum system will be putting the wrong part of the application on the quantum side. Srinivas Sriram Mantrala made that his closing point at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, in a talk on "Quantum CloudOps": what DevOps and CloudOps teams need to change as quantum processing arrives through cloud providers, which he expects within about five years.

It's a conceptual talk, delivered conversationally, with no demo. Think of it as an operations team's checklist for a technology that isn't on their pager yet.

## Thinking ten moves ahead

Mantrala explains superposition with chess. A strong player can hold maybe ten candidate moves in their head; then for each one, ten replies, and the tree explodes. His pitch for quantum is the ability to process that whole tree of combinations at once and surface the risky branch early. He applies the idea to security, where you want to anticipate the next attack and the one after it, and to operations, finance and medicine, anywhere a wider search beats a sequential one.

## The hybrid infrastructure has three parts

His architecture keeps today's cloud in charge:

- **Quantum processing units**, built on qubits, superposition and entanglement, for the complex algorithms.
- **Classical infrastructure**, the existing cloud that already handles conventional tasks and orchestration.
- **An integration layer** with translators, workload schedulers and real-time processing that distributes work between the two for the best performance.

The integration layer is where operations teams will spend their time, because load balancing now has two very different kinds of backend.

## What DevOps has to learn

The most useful section lists what changes for the people running the platform:

- **CI/CD** pipelines need quantum deployment and testing stages.
- **Observability** (logs, metrics and the analytics on top) has to cover quantum workloads too.
- **Operating models** need updating, and people need training to run quantum-backed applications.
- **Automation** has to extend to quantum resource allocation.
- **APIs** for quantum processing won't look like today's request-response endpoints, and programming models for concurrency may shift with them.

None of this is exotic; it's the same muscle teams built moving from on-prem to cloud. That is the reassuring subtext.

## Where it pays and how to start

Mantrala's list of beneficiaries: security (quantum-resistant encryption to protect sensitive data against future attacks), AI algorithms redesigned for quantum parallelism, pharmaceuticals (running clinical study computations concurrently instead of step by step) and finance (market prediction, portfolio and risk assessment).

Adoption follows the usual path: partner with a cloud provider that offers quantum infrastructure, build proofs of concept, then build the hybrid integration with APIs between quantum and classical services, find the limits, automate workload distribution, measure and improve.

## The design decision that decides the bill

The closing point is the reason to watch. Not everything should run on quantum. Put too much there and you pay for complexity you don't need; put too little and you miss the speed-up where it matters. The new design skill is drawing that line inside each application, per requirement. Every cloud migration has a team that lifted and shifted everything; this is the warning not to do it again.

## Who should watch

DevOps, SRE and platform engineers who want to know what quantum would mean for their pipelines and runbooks, explained without maths. If you want circuit-level detail or architecture diagrams, pair it with a more technical talk.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Principium: the quantum hardware ecosystem](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Archit_Srivastava_principium_hardware_ecosystem) by Archit Srivastava, for what sits behind the cloud API.
- [Quantum computing and AI for network management](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Chaitanya_Kadiyala_Sadha_Chilukoori_quantum_network_management) by Chaitanya Kadiyala and Sadha Chilukoori, an operations use case in more depth.
- [Quantum computing for Rust software development](https://www.conf42.com/Rustlang_2024_Abhinav_Chunchu_quantum_software_development_computing) by Abhinav Chunchu, the developer's view of the same shift.

Title: Quantum-ready architecture is mostly event queues and job routers
Description: JPMorgan Chase's Laxmikanth Mukund Sethu Kumar at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on hybrid patterns that prepare enterprise systems for quantum.
Body:
If your platform already runs on event queues, APIs and Kubernetes jobs, you are closer to quantum-ready than you think. Laxmikanth Mukund Sethu Kumar, Executive Director at JPMorgan Chase, argued exactly that at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025: quantum will coexist with classical computing, not compete with it, and the work enterprise architects can do today is integration, not physics.

The abstract promises a systems view drawn from platforms built for banks, airlines and government, and the talk sticks to it. Quantum mechanics gets one slide; architecture gets the rest.

## What today's DevOps stack is missing

The useful starting point is the gap list. Quantum workloads don't fit existing DevOps stacks yet, and Sethu Kumar names three missing pieces: job orchestration, state isolation for quantum workloads, and latency tolerance. He also asks architects to stop thinking in either/or terms: a qubit's state is probabilistic, and so are its results, so the systems around it should expect distributions, not single answers.

The supply side is already there. AWS Braket, IBM Quantum and Azure Quantum all expose quantum hardware through cloud-native APIs.

## Three tiers and a clean seam

His hybrid architecture is three layers:

- **Application tier**: microservices and APIs, unchanged.
- **Orchestration tier**: quantum job routers and queues.
- **Backend tier**: classical compute, quantum compute, or both.

The rule for the middle layer is the line to remember: decouple the quantum logic from the orchestration logic. Middleware owns session management, job queuing, error retries and result normalisation, so a flaky quantum backend never leaks into your business code.

## Patterns you already know

The design patterns are deliberately familiar:

- **Quantum as a service**, alongside IaaS and SaaS.
- **Quantum triggers from classical event queues** such as Kafka: a classical service publishes, a quantum consumer reacts.
- **Serverless quantum microservices**, for example an AWS Lambda function that kicks off a Braket job.
- **Cloud-native abstractions**: containers for local quantum simulation, Kubernetes job runners for orchestrating quantum flows, and CI/CD pipelines for quantum kernels.

Tools named include the Braket SDK and gRPC bridges. Security is zero trust across both worlds; interoperability depends on vendor-neutral interfaces and standards such as QIR; and observability means quantum job telemetry flowing into Prometheus and OpenTelemetry like everything else. If your quantum job can't be seen on the same dashboard as the rest of the system, it isn't production-ready, whatever the qubit count.

## A five-step roadmap with a safe middle

The roadmap is the most reusable slide: identify quantum-able problems (scheduling, ML model tuning), build a dev sandbox on emulators, integrate with job orchestration and message buses, pilot a hybrid service on a non-critical path, then promote gradually to production workflows. The goal, in his framing, is to experiment without rewriting the stack, using modular adapter layers, simulators and mature hybrid CI/CD.

## Who should watch

Enterprise and platform architects, engineering leads and anyone who has been asked for a quantum strategy and wants one that fits on an architecture diagram. It's short, clear and free of hype. Physicists will find nothing new; integrators will find a checklist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Empowering sector readiness with quantum solutions](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Abdullah_Alsalman_empowering_sector_readiness) by Abdullah Alsalman, readiness from the sector level down.
- [Empowering executives to embrace quantum computing](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Vardaan_Sahgal_empowering_executives) by Vardaan Sahgal, for the conversation with leadership.
- [Quantum computing: building responsive and adaptive systems](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Nitish_Mehrotra_quantum_systems_future) by Nitish Mehrotra, another systems-first view.

Title: Four patterns for putting quantum inside a multi-tenant SaaS
Description: Srikar Kompella of Twilio sketches quantum, edge and multi-tenancy patterns for SaaS at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, from federated learning onward.
Body:
Multi-tenancy started as a way to save money on shared servers; Srikar Kompella thinks its next stage is quantum-aware resource allocation across tenants. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, the Twilio Senior Software Engineer laid out an architecture vision for SaaS built on three pillars (quantum compute, edge processing and advanced multi-tenancy) and four integration patterns that combine them.

It's a forward-looking architecture talk rather than a build log. The value is in the patterns, which are concrete enough to reason about now.

## Three pillars, one platform

Kompella's pillars split the work by what each is good at. Quantum computing, reached on demand through the cloud, takes the optimisation, simulation and pattern-finding problems. Edge processing brings those results close to users so decisions happen in real time and less raw data travels. Multi-tenancy is the delivery framework: fair, cost-effective sharing of scarce quantum processors with strict isolation of each tenant's data in a mixed classical, quantum and edge environment.

The edge piece has one idea worth stealing: train a complex model on the quantum side, then deploy it to local edge runtimes. A factory robot then adjusts on the spot instead of waiting on a central server, and a traffic grid tunes signal timing at each intersection.

## Multi-tenancy grows up in three steps

The talk frames multi-tenancy as an evolution: basic resource sharing with minimal isolation and a focus on cost, then advanced segmentation where tenants share services but keep data and workflows separate, then quantum-aware architectures that allocate resources dynamically across tenant boundaries while still isolating them.

## The four integration patterns

This is the section to watch closely:

1. **Quantum federated learning.** Each tenant (his example: a hospital and a research institute) trains a quantum ML model on its own data inside its own perimeter. Only model updates leave, protected by quantum-resistant cryptography. The platform aggregates them into a better global model and sends it back. Raw data never moves.
2. **Customised quantum edge deployments.** Tenant-specific quantum algorithms go to edge locations based on each tenant's needs, with workloads routed between edge nodes and central quantum machines as demand shifts.
3. **QML-driven resource orchestration.** A quantum ML model forecasts each tenant's resource demand from live metrics, and the platform allocates capacity before the tenant needs it. Think autoscaling that reads ahead.
4. **Secure tenant collaboration.** Quantum-resistant data exchange plus privacy-preserving joint processing, so competitors can pool insights without sharing raw data. His example is rival retailers finding supply-chain inefficiencies that hurt them all, leading to industry consortiums hosted on the platform.

Pattern one is the most grounded: federated learning already exists classically, and the quantum part slots into the model and the crypto rather than the workflow.

## From selling software to selling answers

Kompella's business point is that quantum lets a SaaS company sell results such as optimisation or materials discovery as a service, not just tools. His roadmap is sober: assess the current architecture and find computationally heavy workloads, pick one pattern for a single pilot and measure it, then scale and invest in in-house expertise. He calls it an evolution, not an overnight revolution, which is the right tone.

## Who should watch

SaaS architects and platform engineers who own tenancy, isolation and capacity planning, and who want a vocabulary for where quantum might enter their stack. Skip it if you want benchmarks or code; it's patterns and diagrams.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Optimizing multi-tenant SaaS: scalable architectures for performance, security and cost](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Shinu_Pushpan_saas_multitenancy_security) by Shinu Pushpan, the classical baseline these patterns extend.
- [Quantum-resistant Kubernetes for the post-quantum era](https://www.conf42.com/Kube_Native_2025_Derek_Asir_Muthurajan_Caleb_quantum_security_infrastructure) by Derek Asir Muthurajan Caleb, on the crypto the patterns assume.
- [Product management with multi-tenancy architecture](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Waqas_Khan_multitenancy_optimization_strategy) by Waqas Khan, for the product side of tenancy decisions.

[Watch Srikar Kompella's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Srikar_Kompella_quantum_saas_architecture)

Title: A quantum sidecar for Teamcenter, not a PLM rewrite
Description: Pradeep Karanam at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on sending only the hardest PLM questions from Siemens Teamcenter to cloud quantum hardware.
Body:
Your PLM system already knows every part and option in the product; it just takes forever to answer a big "what if". Pradeep Karanam, Solutions Architect, used his talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 to show a small sidecar that sends only the hardest parts of those questions from Siemens Teamcenter (or any PLM tool) to a cloud quantum computer and writes the answer back. Nothing rewrites Teamcenter's core.

The abstract states the goal plainly: option lists that appear 8x faster and purchase plans that cut shortage risk by one third, without changing anyone's daily workflow.

## The pain is measured in dollars per day

Karanam opens with the business case. He cites a study putting the average cost of a major supply-chain disruption around $22 million, and a stopped production line burning roughly $1.5 million a day. Then the complexity problem: a car like the BMW Mini has trillions of valid option combinations, and the rule engines inside PLM check options close to one by one. His goal is to turn overnight batch jobs into answers you get over a coffee break.

## Four steps over REST

The architecture is the reason to watch. Teamcenter already sends heavy jobs to HPC clusters, so quantum is just another remote backend:

1. Pull the bill of materials or supply data through the Active Workspace REST API.
2. Convert it into the maths a quantum machine understands: a QUBO matrix for optimisation, or a probability model for simulation.
3. Send it to the cloud and wait a few seconds for the best answer.
4. Write the new configuration or risk score back into Teamcenter, where everyone already works.

He calls it a bolt-on microservice, not a rip and replace. For configuration, every rule becomes an energy penalty, and the annealer settles into a valid, low-energy build.

## The hardware list is refreshingly specific

Instead of a generic qubit diagram, the talk names what was reachable through cloud APIs at the time: D-Wave's Advantage2 annealer, Pasqal's neutral-atom machine on Google Cloud, IBM's 127-qubit Eagle, and Fujitsu's Digital Annealer, which he says is already in daily use at a Toyota plant. Gate-model chips, annealers and neutral-atom arrays get one line each on what they are good for. Because today's machines are noisy, the quantum core is always wrapped in classical code.

## Fewer Monte Carlo runs, more design iterations

For supply risk, planners run Monte Carlo simulations when a port closes. Karanam's point is that quantum amplitude estimation reaches the same confidence with about 10,000 scenarios instead of a million, and he cites D-Wave tests where scenario throughput rose sharply. The same pattern applies to engineering: the talk cites faster battery-cooling CFD, fewer crash FEA runs and overnight polymer simulations, all feeding the Teamcenter digital twin.

## Protect while you innovate

Two pieces of advice stand out because they apply even if you never buy quantum time. First, quantum computers threaten today's encryption, and NIST published its first post-quantum standards in 2024, so audit the Teamcenter supplier portal for RSA-2048 and plan the cutover. Second, his risk table: hybrid error-aware code for decoherence, open standards like QIR against vendor lock-in, a "quantum translator" role that speaks both PLM and quantum, and phase-gated ROI checkpoints so projects live or die on real numbers.

The roadmap is staged: a cloud proof of concept on one high-value use case in the first three months, a production microservice benchmarked against CPUs by month twelve, then more sites and post-quantum TLS on the supplier portal by month 24.

## Who should watch

PLM architects, manufacturing IT leads and supply-chain planners who want a quantum pilot small enough to get approved. The talk is short and dense; the four-step REST flow and the risk table are the parts to screenshot.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Quantum and quantum-inspired annealing: the state of play](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Peter_den_Haan_annealing_state_of_play) by Peter den Haan, background on the annealers this design relies on.
- [Standardised collaborative forecasting for stronger supply chains](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Madhusudan_S_Vadigicherla_supply_chain_forecasting) by Madhusudan S Vadigicherla, the classical forecasting side of supply-chain risk.

[Watch Pradeep Karanam's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Pradeep_Karanam_plm_teamcenter)

Title: What SAP AI on BTP actually does, industry by industry
Description: Levi Strauss & Co. SAP project manager Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli tours SAP AI use cases at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025.
Body:
Most ERP users meet SAP's AI as a recommendation in a screen they already use, not as a model they deploy. Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli, SAP Project Manager at Levi Strauss & Co., spent his session at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 mapping which techniques sit behind those features on SAP's Business Technology Platform (BTP), across retail, healthcare, manufacturing, finance, supply chain, energy and agriculture.

Fair warning on scope: this is an SAP AI talk that happened to land at a quantum conference. There are no qubits in it. What it offers instead is a catalogue of classical ML patterns mapped onto the ERP processes they serve, from someone who has spent years leading SAP implementations across manufacturing, pharma, food and beverage and more.

## The stack: BTP underneath, AI core on top

Mandavilli starts with the architecture. BTP provides the integration layer, API management and data orchestration. On top, SAP's AI core offers machine learning services (classification, regression, clustering, anomaly detection), natural language processing (entity extraction, sentiment, document understanding) and computer vision (object detection, defect identification, visual inspection). The pitch is that these plug into existing SAP systems rather than living in a separate data science silo.

## Retail and healthcare: familiar models, specific inputs

For retail, recommendations come from hybrid models that combine collaborative filtering with content-based filtering, using purchase history and browsing patterns. Demand forecasting ensembles LSTM networks with classical ARIMA models and adds external signals like seasonality, market trends and social media sentiment.

Healthcare is the more interesting example. Admission prediction uses regression and classification over historical admissions, seasonal illness patterns, population demographics, facility utilisation and the local event calendar, which is a neat reminder that a marathon in town is a capacity-planning input. NLP mines unstructured clinical notes alongside structured data, with HIPAA compliance kept in the loop.

## Manufacturing gets the numbers

The manufacturing section has the talk's firmest figures, presented as industry results for predictive maintenance: unplanned downtime reduced by up to 50% and maintenance costs down 10 to 40% compared with scheduled maintenance. The loop is IoT sensor data collection, pattern analysis to predict failures, maintenance scheduling before they happen, then continuous learning. For quality, CNN-based visual inspection is cited as catching up to 99% of surface defects against 80 to 90% for traditional machine vision and human inspectors.

## Finance, supply chain, energy, fields

The rest of the tour moves quickly:

- **Finance**: graph neural networks that model relationships between entities to flag fraud, with SHAP and LIME for explainable decisions, and reinforcement learning for forecasting.
- **Supply chain**: multi-objective evolutionary algorithms balancing cost, time and environmental impact, early-warning ensembles, digital twins and automatic rerouting.
- **Energy and utilities**: reinforcement learning for consumption optimisation, hybrid physics-plus-ML renewable forecasting, storage charge cycles and microgrid balancing.
- **Agriculture**: multispectral satellite imagery for moisture stress and pest detection, field sensors, and gradient-boosted trees for yield prediction.

## Who should watch

SAP functional leads, solution architects and project managers who need a vocabulary for which model fits which SAP process, and data scientists joining an SAP shop. If you were hoping for quantum, pick another talk from the same event; if you have an SAP roadmap on your desk, this one is a useful checklist.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [The next generation of SAP Cloud ERP with AI](https://www.conf42.com/Cloud_Native_2025_Sravan_Kumar_Nendrambaka_sap_enterprise_optimization) by Sravan Kumar Nendrambaka, on S/4HANA Cloud editions.
- [AI-driven master data governance for incident management in SAP](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2025_Gobinath_Kasimayan_sap_governance_agility) by Gobinath Kasimayan, because every model above depends on clean master data.
- [Building event-driven AI agents for proactive SAP incident management](https://www.conf42.com/AI_Agents_2026_Pon_Murugesh_Devendren_sap_incidents_events) by Pon Murugesh Devendren, where SAP AI goes agentic.

[Watch Venkata Kalyan Chakravarthy Mandavilli's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Venkata_Kalyan_Chakravarthy_Mandavilli_sap_ai_transformation)

Title: Quantum personalisation in banking starts with a customer data platform
Description: JPMorganChase's Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on the data engineering under quantum-enhanced, real-time financial personalisation.
Body:
Before any qubit touches a bank's recommendation engine, someone has to resolve which of five customer records is the same person. Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu, Vice President and Senior Lead Data Engineer at JPMorganChase, made that the spine of his talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025 on quantum AI-driven personalisation in financial services. The quantum layer sits on top; the customer data platform underneath does most of the work.

## Personalisation as a requirement, not a feature

Boggavarapu's opening argument is commercial: customers expect a bank to anticipate their goals, not just answer their questions. He cites machine learning approaches such as XGBoost and neural networks beating traditional segmentation, and a reference architecture with API-driven microservices serving 15-plus touchpoints in under 200 milliseconds, event processing at more than 50,000 transactions per second and a data lake of five petabytes or more. Those are the targets the rest of the talk designs for.

## The CDP is the central nervous system

The most practical section is the customer data platform. In his telling, a CDP does four jobs:

- **Aggregation**: structured and unstructured data from digital and physical touchpoints, through APIs and ETL.
- **A unified view**: a 360-degree profile built with entity resolution, persistent identifiers and cross-channel attribution.
- **Actionable insight**: recommendations and predictive scoring on top of that profile.
- **Compliance by design**: granular consent management, automated governance workflows and encryption, so GDPR and CCPA are built in, not bolted on.

He calls the CDP the central nervous system for customer data, and every later slide depends on it.

## Where the quantum part comes in

The quantum layer is pitched as pattern recognition across many variables at once. The talk describes a tensor-network architecture analysing hundreds of financial variables simultaneously, quantum annealing for portfolio optimisation and quantum-accelerated gradient descent for faster training. These are presented as capabilities rather than shown in a demo, so this is the part to watch critically.

Generative AI gets equal billing: tailored financial education content, chatbots built on retrieval-augmented generation over a financial knowledge base, and synthetic data generated with differential privacy so models can train without exposing personal data.

## The data engineering problems are the real ones

The section engineers will get the most from is the list of hard problems, all classical:

- **Latency**: memory-mapped databases with non-blocking IO, edge computing and predictive caching.
- **Volume**: auto-scaling microservices on Kubernetes, polyglot storage, stream processing.
- **Security**: post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, zero-knowledge proofs for identity checks and homomorphic encryption.
- **Governance**: graph-based metadata for automated lineage, attribute-based access control and immutable audit trails.

His roadmap is equally grounded: assess the existing data architecture, deploy the CDP and secure API connections, pilot with selected customer segments, then scale across products and channels. If your bank does only the first three steps, you still end up with a better platform, quantum or not.

The talk closes with outcome figures (engagement, conversion and satisfaction gains) presented as results of effective implementations; it doesn't detail the deployments behind them.

## Who should watch

Data engineers and architects at financial institutions planning real-time personalisation, and anyone who wants to see where quantum might plug into an existing data stack. If you came for quantum circuits, this isn't that talk; if you came for how a bank structures customer data, it is.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Innovating FinTech with AI for financial solutions](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Andrei_Alekseev_ai_fintech_financial) by Andrei Alekseev, the classical AI view of the same industry.
- [AI-driven insights for customer retention through personalisation](https://www.conf42.com/Incident_Management_2024_Anandakumar_Kumaravelu_4_ai_retention_personalization) by Anandakumar Kumaravelu, personalisation from the operations side.
- [Journey into quantum: getting started on business benefits](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Daniel_Goldsmith_Pippa_Spencer_Williams_business_benefits) by Daniel Goldsmith and Pippa Spencer Williams, for scoping a first quantum project.

[Watch Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_finance_optimization)

Title: Hybrid quantum-classical edge AI, with the numbers on the slides
Description: Anushree Nagvekar of AEye shows a hybrid quantum-classical split for edge AI at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, with latency, power and capacity figures.
Body:
Give the quantum side the optimisation and leave the IO and control loops to classical hardware. That is the split Anushree Nagvekar, Manager Software Engineering at AEye, argued for at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, in a short, number-dense talk on hybrid quantum-classical processing for edge AI. Her headline claim: neural networks with 3.2x more parameters while staying under 15 milliseconds of latency, against a classical-only ceiling of 1.4x.

## The edge is running out of headroom

The setup is familiar to anyone shipping embedded ML. Nagvekar cites a projection of 75 billion IoT devices by 2027, and data at the edge getting heavier: high-resolution video, medical scans, autonomous vehicle telemetry. Classical edge systems have to trade model complexity against real-time performance, and past a point latency becomes unmanageable. Her framing is that you shouldn't pick a side. The architecture is "not purely classical and not purely quantum", and the division of labour is the interesting part.

## Who does what in the hybrid

The split in the talk is clean enough to sketch on a whiteboard:

- **Quantum**: optimisation-heavy, high-dimensional work such as routing, scheduling and training complex networks.
- **Classical**: deterministic, routine tasks such as IO operations and simple control loops.

The same idea extends to resource allocation. Quantum units optimise across compute, memory, bandwidth and storage, and the talk says they react to changes in under 30 milliseconds, 4.2x faster than classical methods. The pipeline has four steps: detect complex dependencies, explore many configurations in parallel, execute, then predict and adjust as conditions change.

## The numbers, and how to read them

Nagvekar presents a lot of figures: 78% faster optimisation, 67% lower power consumption, latency down to 30 ms from a 120 ms baseline, 41% lower operational cost, and case studies with 82% anomaly detection and 43% fewer false alarms in manufacturing, 91% accuracy in real-time medical imaging with HIPAA compliance maintained, and 37% power savings in smart-infrastructure energy distribution. She says these come from real-world case studies rather than the lab.

The talk doesn't walk through the benchmark setups behind them (hardware, baselines, workloads), so treat them as the claims to go verify, not as a spec sheet. The architecture holds up without them.

On security, the hybrid stack uses lattice-based key exchange, tamper-evident signatures and multivariate polynomial encryption, the post-quantum families that run on ordinary chips, which is the right choice for a device with a battery.

## The roadmap starts on classical hardware

The most useful slide for a team that wants to try this is the rollout plan. Review the current infrastructure and find tasks worth optimising. Then test quantum-inspired algorithms on classical hardware and validate the boost before any real quantum integration. Only then move to hybrid workflows, tune task delegation and data flows, and scale with monitoring feedback loops. It is a gradual, low-risk path, and the classical-first step means you learn something even if the quantum part never pays off.

Future directions in the talk: domain-specific quantum hardware for edge devices, a quantum cloud at the edge, and quantum neural networks.

## Who should watch

Embedded and edge ML engineers who keep bumping into the latency-versus-model-size wall, and architects building industrial, automotive or smart-city systems. It is a quick talk, so it suits a lunch break; budget extra time for checking the numbers.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Using the FLiPN stack for edge AI](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2023_Tim_Spann_David_Kjerrumgaard_flipn_stack_edge_ai_flink_nifi_pulsar) by Tim Spann and David Kjerrumgaard, a classical edge pipeline with Flink, NiFi and Pulsar.
- [QML: the next big thing](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Karthiganesh_Durai_qml_next_big_thing) by Karthiganesh Durai, on the quantum machine learning half of the story.
- [At the edge of robotic applications](https://www.conf42.com/Internet_of_Things_IoT_2024_Chiara_Civardi_Petr_Aubrecht_robotics_applications_edge) by Chiara Civardi and Petr Aubrecht, for what edge constraints look like on robots.

[Watch Anushree Nagvekar's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Anushree_Nagvekar_quantum_edge_ai)

Title: IoT devices outlive RSA, so quantum-safe security starts now
Description: Gayathri Jeganmohan of Microsoft maps quantum computing onto IoT intelligence and security at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, from QKD to quantum signatures.
Body:
A satellite or a medical implant shipped today may still be talking to the network when a quantum computer can read its traffic. That is the sharpest thread in Gayathri Jeganmohan's talk at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, where the Microsoft software engineer split the quantum-meets-IoT story into two halves: what quantum computing can do for IoT intelligence, and what it does to (and for) IoT security.

It's a survey talk, broad rather than deep, and a good map for anyone who owns a fleet of connected devices and keeps hearing the word "quantum" in vendor decks.

## IoT has a data problem before it has a quantum problem

Jeganmohan's starting point is that IoT data is huge, unstructured and noisy: temperature, pressure and a dozen other sensor streams per factory, every second. Her claim is that quantum algorithms can find patterns in that kind of high-dimensional data more efficiently than classical ones, and she walks through where that is being tried:

- **Traffic analytics**: Volkswagen using a quantum algorithm to spot dense traffic areas and optimise urban flow.
- **Anomaly detection**: Cambridge Quantum's tooling for spotting unusual patterns in network traffic.
- **Recommendations**: research at Netflix and Amazon into quantum-inspired collaborative filtering.
- **Fraud**: quantum Monte Carlo methods, with Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan investing.
- **Genomics**: D-Wave working with healthcare startups on DNA analysis workflows.

## Keep the edge small, put the heavy model somewhere else

The machine learning section has the most architectural meat. Edge devices have limited power and energy, so today they lean on the cloud for inference and post-processing. Jeganmohan's picture is a backend where quantum resources handle training (quantum support vector machines and quantum kernel estimation get named) and fast inference, with results offloaded back to the device for real-time decisions. Her target use case is predictive maintenance in factories, plus quantum sensors fusing multiple signals for smart cities, agriculture and autonomous vehicles.

## Four security techniques, one deadline

Security is where the talk gets concrete. RSA and ECC, which today's classical machines can't break, become vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a large enough quantum computer, and IoT was never designed with security in mind to begin with. Jeganmohan lists four responses:

1. **Defence against quantum attacks**: quantum-safe protocols, most urgent for long-lifecycle devices such as vehicles, medical implants and satellites.
2. **Quantum key distribution**: key exchange built on quantum mechanics that detects eavesdropping, with secure links between autonomous vehicles and roadside units as the example.
3. **Quantum random number generation**: truly random keys for secure session start-up on industrial sensors, instead of the pseudo-random output of a `rand` call.
4. **Tamper-proof identity**: quantum signatures, so only authenticated, quantum-signed devices can send actuation signals to critical infrastructure.

One thing worth keeping straight while you watch: post-quantum cryptography runs on ordinary classical chips, while QKD and QRNG need quantum hardware in the loop. For a constrained sensor, that difference decides what you can ship this decade. The talk's first point, protecting long-lived devices against future attacks, is the one you can act on with today's hardware.

## Who should watch

IoT architects, embedded security people and product owners with devices in the field for ten years or more. It is an overview, so expect breadth: if you want protocol detail on QKD, use this as the map and find the specialist talk next.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Quantum-resistant native Go programs](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2021_Mathilde_Raynal_quantumresistant_native_go_programs) by Mathilde Raynal, for what post-quantum code looks like in practice.
- [Transforming IoT data management: scalable architectures and security](https://www.conf42.com/DevOps_2025_Gokul_Balaguruswamy_Naidu_iot_data_security) by Gokul Balaguruswamy Naidu, the classical side of the same data problem.
- [Quantum computing: implications for security](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2022_Robert_Slade_implications_for_security) by Robert Slade, a security veteran's view of the threat.

[Watch Gayathri Jeganmohan's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Gayathri_Jeganmohan_quantum_iot_security)

Title: A plain-language tour of Shor, Grover, QAOA and VQE
Description: Sarah Choudhary walks through the four quantum algorithms worth knowing at Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, plus where pilots run and where the hype is.
Body:
Four algorithms carry most of the weight in quantum computing today, and you can understand all four without a physics degree. At Conf42 Quantum Computing 2025, Sarah Choudhary, a Principal SME architect and data scientist with two decades in data and AI systems, gave a 30-minute tour of Shor, Grover, QAOA and VQE, then spent just as long on what the hardware still can't do. It is an introduction and it says so up front: the promise is clarity for researchers, cloud architects and the merely curious.

## Classical computers aren't wrong, they're the wrong tool sometimes

Choudhary starts with the von Neumann architecture, the 1940s design that took us from floppies to the cloud, and its limit: nature doesn't compute in ones and zeros. Simulating a molecule with classical logic is, in her words, "trying to paint the ocean with a pencil". Later she offers an even better one: modelling quantum systems on a classical machine is like translating poetry with a calculator.

The argument isn't that quantum replaces anything. She is explicit that a quantum computer will not run your spreadsheet faster or replace your phone's processor. It complements classical machines on a specific class of problems that lean on superposition, entanglement and interference. The talk also tells the 2019 Google Sycamore random circuit sampling story honestly, including IBM's rebuttal that a classical supercomputer could have done it in days rather than millennia.

## The four algorithms, one sentence each

The core of the talk is a compact field guide:

- **Shor (1994)** factors large integers exponentially faster than classical methods, which is why RSA has an expiry date and why post-quantum cryptography is now a national security topic.
- **Grover (1996)** searches unsorted data in square-root time. Her haystack example: a million possibilities in about a thousand steps.
- **QAOA** is a hybrid classical-quantum optimiser aimed at routing, load balancing and portfolio problems, where classical solvers settle into a local minimum.
- **VQE** estimates the ground-state energy of molecules, the route to faster drug and materials design.

She ties each to who is testing it: Roche and AstraZeneca on molecular simulation, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase on portfolio optimisation and Monte Carlo, Volkswagen and DHL on traffic and route planning, ExxonMobil and BASF on catalysts.

## Light might beat the fridge

The section most intros skip is photonic quantum computing. Instead of superconducting circuits cooled near absolute zero, photonic machines encode qubits in particles of light, run at room temperature and reuse fibre-optic components that are already mass-produced. Xanadu's Borealis and PsiQuantum get named, along with the honest catch: generating single photons reliably and building logic gates from light is still less mature than superconducting tech.

She then lines up the four hardware families (superconducting at IBM and Google, trapped ions at IonQ and Honeywell, photonics, and the earlier-stage neutral-atom and topological approaches, Microsoft among them) and admits nobody knows which one wins.

## The hype section is the best part

Choudhary is blunt about the NISQ era. Qubits decohere in microseconds, one reliable logical qubit may need hundreds or thousands of physical ones, and for many real-world problems nobody has yet proven a quantum solution beats classical. She also warns that some companies sell quantum solutions that are not quantum at all. Her timeline: hybrid models common in R&D by about 2028, error-corrected systems after that, and quantum as an API call in the cloud after 2032. Treat the dates as a forecast, not a promise.

The closing advice is practical: you can start now with Qiskit, Cirq, Azure Quantum's Q#, Amazon Braket and PennyLane, most of them free to try in the cloud.

## Who should watch

Engineers and architects who need one talk that maps the vocabulary (qubits, interference, NISQ, QAOA) to real problems and real companies. If you already write Qiskit circuits, the history section will be familiar; jump to the hardware comparison and the hype warning.

## Related Conf42 talks

- [Quantum inspired algorithms as a means of getting quantum benefit in the NISQ era](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Abhigyan_Mishra_algorithms_quantum_benefit_nisq_era) by Abhigyan Mishra, for what you can run before the hardware matures.
- [High level programming for quantum circuits](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2024_Vincent_van_Wingerden_programming_quantum_circuits) by Vincent van Wingerden, the next step once the algorithms make sense.
- [Quantum computing: is it real or just hype?](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2023_Michal_Jankowski_real_or_hype) by Michal Jankowski, a second opinion on the hype question.

[Watch Sarah Choudhary's talk](https://www.conf42.com/Quantum_Computing_2025_Sarah_Choudhary_quantum_algorithms_problem)

Title: Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 - when "don't" means nothing to your embeddings
Description: Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 in review, 136 talks on embedding blind spots, LLM evaluation, tiny models, agents, guardrails and ML in finance and health.
Body:
[Conf42 Machine Learning 2025](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) went out on May 8, 2025 with 136 talks, enough to fill a long weekend of viewing. Under the volume sat a sensible mood: less awe at what models can do, more scrutiny of where they quietly fail and what it takes to run them somewhere real. Speakers came from Google DeepMind, Microsoft, Meta, AWS, NVIDIA, Dropbox, Samsung Research, Expedia Group, Palo Alto Networks, Walmart, JPMorgan Chase and many more.

## Your model is more confident than it should be

The talk most likely to change how you build RAG came from [Ritesh Modi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Ritesh_Modi_embedding_models_language) (Microsoft). In *Hallucination by Design* he shows test results where embedding models treat "take medication" and "don't take medication" as the same thing, then walks through the patterns that cause it and how to make GenAI systems more reliable anyway. Negation, it turns out, is a rounding error in vector space.

[Alok Ranjan and Saurabh Suman](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Alok_Ranjan_Saurabh_Suman_modern_approaches_bleu) (Dropbox, San José State University) argued that BLEU and ROUGE can't measure what modern LLMs do, and moved through benchmarks like MMLU and TruthfulQA to real-world and human-in-the-loop evaluation. [Andrei Stroganov and Andrei Visochan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Andrei_Stroganov_Andrei_Visochan_estimation_regression_confidence) (Samsung Research) took the mathematical route: fast, real-time confidence estimation for classification and regression models using C++ compile-time numerical integration. [Gaurav Bansal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Gaurav_Bansal_evaluation_enterprise_language) covered scalable evaluation and QA for enterprise LLMs.

## Small models, tight budgets

Not every model gets an H100. [Max Navrotsky and Oleksandr Gordieiev](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Max_Navrotsky_Oleksandr_Gordieiev_llms_optimization_devices) (VGS, Lutsk National Technical University) shrank GPT-2 for very weak hardware with pruning, quantisation and fine-tuning. [Hitesh Saai Mananchery](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Hitesh_Saai_Mananchery_compression_pixel_video) (Expedia Group) presented R2S, an ML approach to video compression that removes frame redundancy by tracking pixel shifts. At the other end of the scale, [Praneel Madabushini](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Praneel_Madabushini_tesla_openai) (NVIDIA) looked at how Kubernetes handles resource-hungry AI and ML workloads, with lessons drawn from Tesla and OpenAI, and [Bhaskar Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Bhaskar_Goyal_enterprise_cloud_patterns) (Google) covered architectural patterns for cloud-native AI at scale.

## Agents, with and without guardrails

[Naman Goyal](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Naman_Goyal_generation_text_agentic) (Google DeepMind) traced the move from passive text generators to agents that make decisions and act on their environment. [Alex Shershebnev](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Alex_Shershebnev_code_agents_coding) (Zencoder) got practical about AI coding agents and how to build them, and [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_chatbots_bedrock_enterprise) (AWS) showed Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrating enterprise workflows with access to business data and APIs. [Mohamed Najaaf](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Mohamed_Najaaf_guardrails_responsible_bedrock) (AWS) followed with the brakes: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for responsible AI. [Laly Bar-Ilan](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Laly_BarIlan_language_components_understand) (Bit) proposed composable components as the shared language between developers, non-technical teams and AI, so an agent can build features from product intent while humans stay in the loop.

For anyone still fuzzy on the basics, [Veliswa Boya](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Veliswa_Boya_rag_embeddings_vector) (AWS) gave a good first talk on vector embeddings and RAG, and [Sergey Polyashov](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sergey_Polyashov_recommendation_search_scalable) (Microsoft) did the same for search and recommendation systems, trade-offs and pitfalls included.

## ML where mistakes have consequences

Trust and safety got serious treatment. [Georgina Tryfou](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Georgina_Tryfou_moderation_scalable_safety) (Gcore) described an AI system for detecting and moderating harmful content such as CSAM in near real time, with privacy built into the design. [Lianne Potter](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Lianne_Potter_bias_builders_history) (Compromising Positions) went back to the early builders of AI to show how their choices about bias and power still shape what we build. [Arun Vivek Supramanian](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Arun_Vivek_Supramanian_privacy_engineering_ethical) (Amazon) covered privacy, bias and fairness from the data engineering side.

Finance and healthcare filled whole tracks. Highlights include [Venkateswarlu Boggavarapu](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Venkateswarlu_Boggavarapu_fraud_detection_db_graph) (JPMorganChase) on graph databases for fraud detection, [Surendra Lakkaraju](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Surendra_Lakkaraju_ecommerce_fraud) (Amazon) on real-time e-commerce fraud detection, [Sandeep Gourneni](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sandeep_Gourneni_banking_optimization) (Hitachi Digital Services) on LLM-assisted legacy banking code transformation, and [Sachin Telalwar](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Sachin_Telalwar_compliance_healthcare) (Zocdoc) on secure distributed healthcare systems.

## ML out in the world

Some of the most memorable talks left the data centre. [Aroma Rodrigues](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Aroma_Rodrigues_imagination_source_journey) (Microsoft) told the story of an open source journey that began in 2016 with a shoe for visually impaired people, built from an Arduino, an Android phone and an unreasonable amount of optimism. [Dmytro Hlotenko](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Dmytro_Hlotenko_photography_community_serverless) (APA-IT) processed 8,000 event photos in real time on AWS AI and serverless at Community Day DACH 2024, sorting them and delivering them back to the community. [Avraam Tolmidis](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Avraam_Tolmidis_traffic_smart_systems) (Meta) applied multi-agent systems and predictive optimisation to urban traffic, and [Karthikeyan Rajamani](https://www.conf42.com/Machine_Learning_2025_Karthikeyan_Rajamani_iot_accoustic_analysis) (Thomson Reuters) listened to machines, literally, with IoT acoustic analysis for predictive maintenance.

## Sponsors and where to watch

Thanks to [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/) at Gold and [APA Tech](https://apa.at/about/apa-tech/) at Silver. All 136 talks are on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/ml2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDbH1VBaoA60lLAAVqmiLPe). Start with Modi's embedding tests; you will look at your retrieval results differently afterwards.

The series returns with [Conf42 Machine Learning 2026](https://www.conf42.com/ml2026).

Title: Teaching machines to recognize the unseen
Description: Prediction in motion
Body:
# Machine learning is doing… a lot

Machine learning used to be a niche.

Now it’s everywhere. Finance, healthcare, retail, cloud, security, HR, supply chains, marketing, manufacturing, smart cities, and probably something involving your fridge. Subtle.

Conf42 Machine Learning 2025 leans fully into that scale.

This is a big conference. One hundred plus talks across twenty tracks, covering everything from core ML concepts to full-blown AI systems running in production. You’ll find sessions on agents, generative AI, analytics, architecture, cloud, data engineering, security, testing, and the slightly terrifying joy of putting models where real decisions are made.

There’s a strong focus on real-world ML. Fraud detection at scale, healthcare platforms, financial risk modeling, recommendation systems, supply chain forecasting, and enterprise data pipelines all show up. Less “look what the model can do” and more “here’s how we made this work without breaking everything”.

Generative AI and LLMs are everywhere, of course. Evaluation, hallucinations, embeddings, RAG, agents, optimization, and running models on everything from massive clusters to very small devices. Several talks focus on keeping things safe, explainable, and compliant once the hype wears off.

The program also makes room for the human side of ML. Ethics, bias, accessibility, trust, governance, and what happens when AI systems start influencing people, products, and policies at scale. There are talks that zoom out, and others that go deep into very specific problems.

If machine learning is part of your job, your roadmap, or your long-term existential questions, this one’s for you. It’s broad, practical, and very honest about the fact that ML is no longer optional or simple.

Welcome to the mess.

Title: Conf42 SRE 2025: postmortems, pit stops and SLOs over alerts
Description: Conf42 SRE 2025 roundup - postmortem lessons from reality TV and Formula 1, SLOs against alert fatigue, databases without DBAs, and AI in incident response.
Body:
Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) 2025 ran online on April 17, 2025, with 107 talks, one of the largest lineups Conf42 has run. With that many sessions, the tracks covered almost everything that can page you: observability, SLOs, resilience, databases, cloud, fintech, healthcare, and a growing pile of AI. The talks worth starting with, though, were the ones about people: how teams review incidents, decide what deserves an alert, and stay curious about their systems.

Every session is on the [Conf42 SRE 2025 event page](https://www.conf42.com/sre2025) and in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrCu4WV3_Ve7-ChGVhr_-DbU). Below is a guided path through it.

## Incident reviews, from unexpected teachers

[Paige Cruz](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Paige_Cruz_what_real_housewives), Principal Developer Advocate at Chronosphere, gave the most quotable title of the event: what The Real Housewives taught her about postmortem meetings. Bringing "receipts" and holding "the meeting before the meeting" turn out to be useful habits for structured, blame-aware incident reviews. It is funnier than most postmortems and more useful than most postmortem templates.

[Ricardo Castro](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Ricardo_Castro_what_can_we), Principal Engineer and SRE at FanDuel, found his teacher in Formula 1: the race where Red Bull Racing repaired Max Verstappen's car in Hungary and turned a potential disaster into a podium finish. The talk pulls out the incident management lessons that apply when your outage has no pit wall.

[Saurabh Phaltane](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Saurabh_Phaltane_curious_sre_cultivating), a Senior SRE at Google, argued for curiosity as the core SRE skill, balancing breadth and depth and thinking about the system as a whole. [Shaalmali Raychaudhury](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Shaalmali_Raychaudhury_navigating_sre_incident) of PayPal and [Pradeep Gaddamidi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Pradeep_Gaddamidi_deployments_downtime_unexpected) added practitioner stories about incident management and deploy-day fires.

## Alert on what users feel

[Mandi Walls](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mandi_Walls_tackling_alert_fatigue), DevOps Advocate at PagerDuty, took on alert fatigue with SLOs: metrics centred on the user experience give teams a focus, and give them permission to disable alerts that contribute nothing to customer happiness. [Siddharth Joshi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Siddharth_Joshi_reliability_excellence_slo) of Nagarro covered the tooling side of SLO management, and [Gaurav Mittal](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Gaurav_Mittal_slos_failute_prediction) of Nordstrom went beyond SLOs to anomaly detection, finding the signals hidden in your data before they become outages.

[Veliswa Boya](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Veliswa_Boya_application_resilience_whose), Senior Developer Advocate at AWS, asked whose job application resilience is anyway, and how resilience and innovation can coexist through both culture and technical choices. [Sai Sahiti Nemalikanti](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sai_Sahiti_Nemalikanti_designing_failure_using) of AWS followed with patterns for designing for failure.

## Observability you can actually use

[Alok Ranjan](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Alok_Ranjan_fragmented_logs_unified), an Engineering Manager at Dropbox, told the story of unifying fragmented container logs with open-source tools, along with what it taught him about DevOps culture. [Swapnil Kulkarni](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Swapnil_Kulkarni_observe_or_not) of Kloudfuse reframed the debate: whether to observe is not the question; whether observability solves the right use cases is. [Sai KR Pentaparthi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Sai_KR_Pentaparthi_xray_ebpf_o11y) showed eBPF for network-level visibility in cloud-native systems, and [Mohit Menghnani](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Mohit_Menghnani_unlocking_observability_react) of Twilio brought observability to React and Node.js applications.

## Databases without a DBA

[Renato Losio](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Renato_Losio_things_fall_apart), Principal Cloud Architect at Funambol, shared a decade of running managed production databases without DBA expertise, from crashing managed instances to storage costs that grew far faster than planned, plus a warning about trusting benchmarks. [Samuel Baruffi](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Samuel_Baruffi_amazon_aurora_dsql), Principal Global Solutions Architect at AWS, introduced Amazon Aurora DSQL, a serverless distributed SQL database with active-active availability. [Andrei Manakov](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Andrei_Manakov_tradeoffs_distributed_nosql) of ShareChat walked through the real-world CAP trade-offs in distributed NoSQL design.

## Real-time systems with no second chances

Some talks dealt with systems where reliability is not abstract. [Vlad Onetiu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Vlad_Onetiu_serverless_confluent_kafka) of DataIceberg built a real-time earthquake alert system with Lambda functions and Confluent Kafka that checks for event changes every second and sends SMS and email notifications. [Bhushan Gopala Reddy](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Bhushan_Gopala_Reddy_resilient_health_monitoring) of Aruba Networks engineered Bluetooth Low Energy health monitoring for disaster zones. [Srihari Pakalapati](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Srihari_Pakalapati_ransomware_readiness_backup) of Trader Interactive covered ransomware readiness with immutable backups and automated recovery, and [Payal Godhani](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Payal_Godhani_zero_downtime_ml) of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure applied SRE techniques to zero-downtime ML deployments.

## AI on call

AI was everywhere, and the most practical uses were small. [David Asamu](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_David_Asamu_ai_sre_prometheus_nl), who leads the SRE team at Nomba, started from a wish every on-call engineer has had: "What if you could chat with your monitoring metrics?" The talk shows asking Prometheus questions in natural language instead of writing queries mid-incident. [Smita Verma](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Smita_Verma_alerts_action_building) of Adobe built AI-powered autonomous incident response at scale, and [Rahul Amte](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Rahul_Amte_smarter_failure_testing) of Nivid Technologies combined AI with chaos engineering for smarter failure testing. [Peter De Tender](https://www.conf42.com/Site_Reliability_Engineering_SRE_2025_Peter_De_Tender_azure_load_testing) of Microsoft kept it grounded with a hands-on tour of Azure Load Testing.

Beyond these, the lineup ran deep into fintech, healthcare, insurance, and manufacturing reliability, with dozens more case studies on the event page.

## Sponsors and what's next

Thanks to diamond sponsor [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), gold sponsor [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), the [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) newsletter, the [HockeyStick](https://www.hockeystick.show/) podcast, and the media partners on the event page.

The series continued with [Conf42 SRE 2026](https://www.conf42.com/sre2026) and returns as [Conf42 SRE 2027](https://www.conf42.com/sre2027) on March 4, 2027.

Title: When availability becomes a feature
Description: SRE makes it measurable
Body:
# Reliability is everyone’s job (but somehow also yours)

Site Reliability Engineering sounds calm and responsible.

In practice, it’s alerts at odd hours, dashboards you don’t fully trust, postmortems that could have been emails, and a deep, personal relationship with latency. Still, someone has to keep the lights on.

Conf42 SRE 2025 is for the people doing exactly that.

This is a big one. One hundred talks across reliability, observability, incidents, automation, architecture, security, cloud, data, AI, healthcare, fintech, hardware, and just about every place where failure is not an option. If a system needs to stay up, it probably shows up here.

AI plays a starring role. From self-healing infrastructure and anomaly detection to AI-assisted monitoring, chaos engineering, and SRE practices for ML systems, the program digs into how automation is changing reliability work. Sometimes for the better. Sometimes with new things to worry about.

But SRE isn’t just about tools. There are talks on culture, postmortems, ownership, accessibility, inclusion, and the very human side of running complex systems. You’ll hear about quiet engineers, impostor syndrome, and what reliability looks like across different organizations and industries.

The real-world use cases go deep. Healthcare platforms, financial systems, gaming infrastructure, supply chains, cloud migrations, legacy modernization, and systems operating at global scale all make an appearance. From sub-50ms architectures to multi-cloud resilience, this is SRE in production, not theory.

If your job involves preventing outages, responding to incidents, or explaining why five nines is harder than it sounds, this one’s for you. Reliability is a moving target. At least here, you don’t have to chase it alone.

Title: Conf42 Golang 2025: real dependencies in tests, hidden ones in go.mod
Description: Conf42 Golang 2025 roundup: 64 talks on testing Go services, dependency hygiene, Wasm and eBPF, confidential computing and Go in banking and fintech.
Body:
Conf42 Golang 2025 ran on April 3, 2025, with 64 talks, the biggest lineup of any Conf42 Golang so far, under the usual greeting to the gophers from outer space. Two ideas kept coming back: test against real dependencies instead of mocks, and know exactly which dependencies you're carrying. Around them, Go showed up at the edge, in the kernel, inside secure enclaves and in a lot of banks. The full lineup is on the [event page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025) and the recordings are in the [YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIuxSyKxlQrDbxTLhVidTfS-6lJeAH6m-).

## Test against the real thing

Two talks made the same argument from different directions. [Manuel de la Pena](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Manuel_de_la_Pena_testing_go_integration), Staff Software Engineer at Docker and maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, showed a talk-rating service tested against real Postgres, Redis and Redpanda containers, plus an AWS Lambda running inside LocalStack. He then broke the average calculation on purpose and watched the test catch it in seconds. His tour of wait strategies is a good reason never to write `time.Sleep` in a test again.

[Nikolay Kuznetsov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Nikolay_Kuznetsov_testing_go_services) of Zalando gave the companion piece: a practical guide to testing a Go service layer by layer. He leans on the testing trophy over the classic pyramid, since integration tests are now cheap enough to run more of them, and tests the repository layer against a real database rather than a mock. His toolkit covers Testcontainers, mocks generated with mockery, `httptest` for handlers, testify and go-cmp for comparing whole structs, and randomised test data. [Sridhar Dachepelly](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sridhar_Dachepelly_testing_erp_orchestration) of Dell Technologies applied Go to test orchestration in large ERP systems.

## Know what's in your binary

[Andrii Raikov](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Andrii_Raikov_dependencies_code_management), Principal Software Engineer at Delivery Hero, asked the audience to name the indirect dependencies of their current project, then showed why most can't. Importing `fmt` silently pulls in `io`, `os`, `reflect` and more, and a few lines using the AWS SDK make a binary several times bigger. The second half covered patterns he has seen at Delivery Hero: a v2 client library that broke its v1 interfaces and stranded teams on the old version, and a `helpers` package that drifts into circular dependencies. His most practical advice: don't skip the import block in code review.

On the framework side, [Divya Darshana](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Divya_Darshana_http_communication_apis), an open source contributor to GoFr, showed circuit breakers, authentication and health monitoring for inter-service HTTP calls using the GoFr framework. And [Namkat Cedrick](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Namkat_Cedrick_career_experience_journey) of Iknite Studio gave the most personal talk of the day, "How Golang Changed My Life", revisiting old programming fears with a new mindset.

## Go beyond the server

[Alex Casalboni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Alex_Casalboni_cloud_edge_webassembly), Developer Advocate at Edgee, explained why WebAssembly suits edge computing, where logic in the request path has a budget of a few milliseconds. He traced Go's Wasm support from the `wasm` target in Go 1.11 to WASI preview 1 in Go 1.21, pointed to TinyGo for the component model, and showed how Edgee runs analytics SDKs as Wasm components at the edge.

[Pranshu Srivastava](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Pranshu_Srivastava_cilium_ebpf_networking) of Cloudera spoke to people starting with eBPF who don't want to write their user space code in Rust, sharing his experience with Cilium, why he chose it and which mistakes to avoid. [Brian Loomis](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Brian_Loomis_cloud_platforms_resilience), Director of Architecture at Progress, covered a distributed job runner designed to survive an unreliable network. [Utham Kumar](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Utham_Kumar_v2x_communication_vehicles) of Nanyang Technological University took Go into vehicle-to-everything networks for connected cars.

## Security in Go services

[Srinivas Vallabhaneni](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Vallabhaneni_enclaves_security_confidential) of Walmart showed how Go fits confidential computing, keeping sensitive data inside secure enclaves in distributed systems without giving up performance. [Aditi Mallesh](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Aditi_Mallesh_identity_security_microservices) of Microsoft built identity orchestration as high-performance Go microservices across clouds, and [Santosh Bompally](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Santosh_Bompally_security_iac_threat) of Humana combined infrastructure as code with AI-driven threat detection. [Sudeep Shanubhog](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Sudeep_Shanubhog_security_cloud_adaptive) of Tential Solutions covered adaptive, real-time security for Microsoft cloud services written in Go.

## Go where the money moves

Finance had a strong showing. [Srinivas Allam](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Allam_banking_modernization_fintech) of Core ITS described Go modernising a tier-1 bank's legacy IBM iSeries infrastructure with zero-downtime migrations. [Deepu Komati](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Deepu_Komati_fintech_cloud_infrastructure) of PenFed Credit Union built financial decision systems in Go, and [Srinivas Reddy Mosali](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srinivas_Reddy_Mosali_fintech_infrastructure_scaling) of Visa made the case for fintech infrastructure that never blinks. Beyond banking, [Ankita Kamat](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Ankita_Kamat_notification_latency_scaling) of Microsoft used Go's concurrency model for notification systems that handle millions of messages while keeping millisecond latency, [Hardik R Patel](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Hardik_R_Patel_data_pipelines_analytics) of PayPal designed multi-hop data pipelines for real-time analytics, and [Srikar Kompella](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Srikar_Kompella_serverless_migration_aws) of Prime Video used Go for a serverless SaaS migration on AWS.

## Sponsors

Thanks to [SREday](https://www.sreday.com/), our diamond sponsor, and [Rapydo](https://www.rapydo.io/), our gold sponsor. Silver sponsors [Edgee](https://www.edgee.cloud/), [Tential](http://www.tential.com/), [Delivery Hero](https://careers.deliveryhero.com/deliveryhero-jobs) and [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) all joined in, each with a speaker on the lineup. Thanks also to [StarterAI](https://www.starterai.dev/) for the newsletter.

## What's next

All 64 talks are linked from the [Conf42 Golang 2025 page](https://www.conf42.com/golang2025). The gophers return for [Conf42 Golang 2026](https://www.conf42.com/golang2026) on May 21, 2026. Until then, go read your `go.sum`.

Title: Put the database in the test, not in the CI config
Description: Manuel de la Pena of Docker, maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, at Conf42 Golang 2025 on integration tests against Postgres, Redis, Redpanda and LocalStack.
Body:
If reproducing one failing integration test means starting the whole application, the test setup is in the wrong place. At Conf42 Golang 2025, [Manuel de la Pena](https://www.conf42.com/Golang_2025_Manuel_de_la_Pena_testing_go_integration), Staff Software Engineer at Docker and maintainer of Testcontainers for Go, showed how to move databases, brokers and even AWS Lambda out of the CI configuration and into the Go test that needs them.

The talk is mostly live code: one small service, four real dependencies, four test files, and timings on screen. It shows Docker's open source library, and it is about as practical as Go testing talks get.

## The CI server is a bad place for dependencies

Manuel starts with the setup many teams still run. A CI server, Jenkins or GitLab runners or GitHub Actions, is configured by you or a platform team to start every database, queue and cloud emulator your tests need. Those dependencies must match production versions and configuration, and the workers must be big enough to run all of them next to the tests.

Every dependency upgrade becomes a CI change, often in a system developers don't own. Each new service adds load to shared runners. And when a test fails, there's no easy way to run just that test on your laptop.

## Containers as test fixtures

Testcontainers for Go gives your test code programmatic access to the Docker engine: create, start, stop and terminate containers right where they're used. Testing the persistence layer means starting one Postgres container in that test, not the whole stack.

Each container's well-known port (5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL) is mapped to a random host port, so many containers can run in parallel. Manuel lists three benefits: consistency, because dependencies run in containers instead of on your host; test data isolation, because each container has its own data; and build speed. Onboarding shrinks to installing Docker and running the tests, which the project calls the clone and run experience.

## One service, four dependencies

The demo app rates conference talks in real time. It stores ratings in PostgreSQL through `pgx`, caches in Redis, streams events through Redpanda with the `franz-go` Kafka client, and calls an AWS Lambda to compute statistics.

Each repository takes a connection string, which is what makes it testable. The Postgres test uses the Postgres module with an init SQL script, database name and credentials, waits until a log line appears twice, and hands the connection string to the repository. On the Postgres 15 Alpine image it passes in about 10 seconds. Redis needs no customisation and passes in about seven. Redpanda, with topic auto-creation on, takes 14 seconds on the first run because it pulls the image, and five on the next.

The Lambda test is the clever one. A Makefile builds and zips the function. The test starts LocalStack, copies the zip into the container, and runs the create-function command inside it once the container is up. It then reads the function URL and swaps in the randomly mapped port. Then Manuel breaks the average calculation on purpose, reruns, and the test catches it in seconds: total count correct, average wrong. A Lambda tested end to end on a laptop, with no AWS account involved.

## The parts of the API worth knowing

The second half tours the building blocks behind the modules:

- **ContainerRequest** defines image, exposed ports, network and readiness conditions.
- **Lifecycle hooks** run your code before and after create, start, readiness, stop and terminate.
- **Files** are copied in after the container is created but before it starts, so a database can boot with a known state.
- **Ryuk**, the extra container you may have spotted in `docker ps`, cleans up containers, networks, volumes and images when tests finish.
- **Wait strategies** replace `time.Sleep`: wait for an exec result, an exit, a file, a health check, a listening port, an HTTP response with a given status or header, a log line or regex, a SQL query, or all of them together.

Testcontainers can also build an image from a Dockerfile and run it, which is handy when the dependency is your own service.

## Who should watch

Go developers whose integration tests either live only in CI or don't exist, and platform teams tired of maintaining test databases on shared runners. If you already use Testcontainers, the LocalStack Lambda pattern and the wait strategies list are the parts to steal.
